The Bucks were 26-28 and chasing a playoff berth with Brandon Jennings and Monta Ellis. Redick offered shooting and another experienced guard. Harris was only 20 and had not secured a consistent Milwaukee role. Orlando was rebuilding after the Dwight Howard era and could prioritize developmental upside over immediate wins. The transaction therefore exchanged a proven short-term specialist for a young forward whose scoring and positional size had not yet been fully tested. Orlando later traded him to Detroit for a poor return, but that separate decision does not erase the value acquired in 2013. The Magic turned an expiring veteran into a young starter with substantial market value and multiple productive seasons, supporting an A-plus for this specific trade. Redick’s Milwaukee peak was a useful floor-spacing guard role, though his shooting percentages dipped and the crowded Jennings-Ellis backcourt limited the fit. Short control can be justified for a contender, but the Bucks’ ceiling was a low seed and their first-round matchup was overwhelming. Orlando did not reach the postseason during Harris’s tenure, a limitation that should be acknowledged, but team context was rebuilding rather than contention. sections.body: Milwaukee’s best counterfactual is that Harris remained blocked and never developed without a larger role. The Bucks may also have believed Redick’s shooting would stabilize a volatile backcourt. Those are reasonable ideas, but the price and objective were mismatched. A team chasing the eighth seed should be especially cautious about surrendering a controlled 20-year-old. Harris went on to play for several teams and earn major contracts, but the Magic deserve credit only for the seasons and value they controlled. Redick continued an excellent career after Milwaukee, yet those later seasons belonged elsewhere. The transaction’s legacy is the contrast between patient development and a hurried playoff push. sections.heading: Portland Identified the Ready-Made Guard Its Rebuild Needed
sections.body: Portland’s draft-night move was a bet on immediate translation rather than distant upside. Roy arrived from Washington as a polished ballhandler, midrange scorer and decision-maker who could organize an offense from either guard spot. The Trail Blazers had begun rebuilding around young talent and needed a dependable perimeter leader more than another developmental project. He won Rookie of the Year, quickly became the face of the franchise and helped Portland return to the playoffs after several difficult seasons. That immediate alignment between player readiness and organizational need gave Portland value before the full star trajectory was known. Minnesota received a useful prospect, but the Timberwolves moved away from the player whose temperament and skill set most directly solved Portland’s problems. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Minnesota Preferred Foye’s Athletic Scoring Profile
sections.body: Minnesota’s side was built around Randy Foye, selected one spot after Roy. Foye was a powerful combo guard with scoring bursts, three-point range and the athletic profile to play beside Kevin Garnett. The Timberwolves believed his upside and age fit their roster, and the swap also included cash. Foye became a starter and produced his best Minnesota season in 2008-09, showing that the organization did not receive an empty return. The issue was not that Foye could not play; it was that Roy developed into a substantially better creator and late-game option almost immediately. The Timberwolves’ evaluation produced a rotation guard, while Portland’s produced a franchise centerpiece. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Roy Became an All-Star Before Injuries Changed the Story
sections.body: Roy’s first three healthy seasons established the top end of the trade. He became a three-time All-Star, made two All-NBA teams and led a young Portland group to fifty-four wins in 2008-09. His pacing, footwork and shot creation gave the Trail Blazers a stable offensive identity, especially in close games. Knee degeneration then reduced his availability and forced an early retirement, preventing the transaction from delivering a decade of star play. The injury belongs in the grade because realized durability matters, but it cannot erase the elite seasons Portland did receive. Minnesota never obtained a comparable peak from Foye, even though Roy’s career ended far earlier than expected. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Foye Produced but Never Matched Roy’s Peak
sections.body: Foye’s Minnesota tenure was respectable and should be graded accordingly. He averaged double figures, handled significant minutes and improved as a shooter, but he did not become the primary creator the Timberwolves needed as Garnett’s era ended. His role shifted between point guard and shooting guard without producing a lasting positional answer. After three seasons, Minnesota packaged Foye and Mike Miller to Washington for the No. 5 pick in the 2009 draft. That trade preserved some residual value and prevents a failing grade, because Foye helped create the asset that became Ricky Rubio. Even with that continuation, Minnesota’s direct return did not approach Roy’s All-NBA impact or Portland’s rapid competitive revival. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: The Later Rubio Pick Softened Minnesota’s Loss
sections.body: The Rubio conversion is the strongest argument for narrowing Portland’s margin. Minnesota did not simply lose Foye for nothing. By moving him with Miller, the Timberwolves acquired the fifth pick and selected Rubio, who later became a long-term starter, gifted passer and important franchise figure. That downstream result gives the original Foye asset a meaningful second life beyond his own Minnesota production. Still, the chain required additional value in Miller, years of waiting and another major decision before Rubio reached the court. Portland’s Roy value was direct and immediate, while Minnesota’s best outcome depended on a later package rather than Foye alone. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Portland Still Won Despite the Shortened Career
sections.body: Portland’s A-plus reflects how much value Roy generated before his knees failed. The Trail Blazers acquired a star without surrendering an established player or additional first-round capital, and Roy helped change the franchise’s credibility, record and culture. His 2011 playoff comeback against Dallas became a final reminder of the player Portland had briefly possessed. The shortened career limits the lifetime totals but not the quality of the acquisition. Minnesota earns B-minus because Foye contributed and later helped produce Rubio, not because the initial player comparison was close. The verdict remains Trail Blazers Win because Portland captured the rare star outcome at essentially the same draft slot. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win. Portland exchanged Randy Foye’s rights and cash for Brandon Roy, who became Rookie of the Year, a three-time All-Star and the leader of a fifty-four-win team before knee injuries shortened his career. Minnesota received useful play from Foye and later included him in the deal that produced Ricky Rubio, which earns B-minus. Portland’s star peak still merits A-plus.

featuredDeepDive.heading: Brandon Roy’s Short Prime Still Created Lasting Franchise Value
featuredDeepDive.intro: The trade is a useful test of how injuries should affect retrospective grading. Roy did not provide the decade Portland expected, yet his healthy seasons delivered a level of play, leadership and organizational renewal that Minnesota never received from Foye. sections.heading: Roy Changed Portland’s Timeline Immediately
sections.body: Portland had endured a prolonged transition and needed a player capable of making the young roster coherent. Roy became that player almost at once. He controlled tempo, accepted difficult possessions and gave teammates a reliable organizer in the final minutes. His presence allowed LaMarcus Aldridge and the rest of the developing core to grow within a competitive structure. The Trail Blazers improved from twenty-one wins before his arrival to forty-one in his second season and then fifty-four in his third. That acceleration is transaction value, not merely an appealing narrative, because it changed playoff expectations and validated the rebuild. Minnesota’s Foye years did not produce a similar organizational shift. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: His Late-Game Skill Was More Valuable Than Raw Athleticism
sections.body: Foye’s athleticism and scoring potential were understandable attractions, but Roy’s game proved more scalable. Roy did not depend on overwhelming speed. He used balance, change of pace, strength and advanced reads to create efficient shots for himself and others. Those tools translated against playoff defenses and in late-clock situations. Foye could score in stretches, yet his tweener role made it harder to build an offense around him. Portland’s evaluation succeeded because it prioritized functional basketball skill over the more obvious physical profile. The gap between a useful combo guard and a dependable primary initiator became the central difference between the returns. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: The 2008-09 Season Captured the Trade’s Ceiling
sections.body: The 2008-09 Trail Blazers won fifty-four games with Roy as an All-NBA centerpiece. He averaged more than twenty points, handled the hardest perimeter assignments on offense and guided one of the league’s youngest successful teams. Portland lost in the first round, but the season established a plausible championship trajectory built around Roy and Aldridge. That competitive peak matters because stars are acquired to create windows, even when those windows later close unexpectedly. Minnesota’s return never generated a comparable season with Foye as a central figure. The trade therefore produced a clear top-end winner before injuries complicated the long-term trade details. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Knee Risk Limits the Grade Less Than It Limits the Career
sections.body: Roy’s knees were not a minor footnote; they ended the expected value stream. Portland eventually used the amnesty provision on his contract, and his attempted comeback elsewhere could not restore the player he had been. A purely career-total comparison would therefore reduce the grade sharply. Trade grading should also recognize that Portland received multiple elite seasons on a rookie-scale contract before the decline. The injury was devastating but did not make the original acquisition ineffective. That balance is why Portland earns A-plus rather than a hypothetical perfect score unconstrained by durability. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Asset Chain Deserves Real Credit
sections.body: Minnesota’s B-minus recognizes that Foye retained enough value to help acquire Rubio. Rubio’s arrival gave the Timberwolves years of playmaking, defense and connection with the fan base. The chain demonstrates why outgoing assets should be followed beyond their first stop when the later conversion is direct and documented. At the same time, Mike Miller was part of the package, so Rubio cannot be credited entirely to Foye. The Timberwolves salvaged a meaningful outcome but did not recreate the star Portland obtained. The downstream success narrows the grade gap without changing the verdict. The grade follows the value that actually reached the court, the length of team control, the competitive setting and the usefulness of any later asset conversion. That approach does not require the losing side to have acted foolishly in real time, but it does require the final return to justify the opportunity cost.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Roy’s career ended too soon, but Portland still received the best player, the highest peak and the strongest immediate organizational impact. Minnesota deserves credit for Foye’s useful seasons and the later Rubio conversion. Those benefits make the loss respectable rather than catastrophic, while Portland remains the clear winner.

sections.heading: Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On the eve of the 2009 draft, Minnesota sent Randy Foye and Mike Miller to Washington for the No. 5 pick, Etan Thomas, Darius Songaila and Oleksiy Pecherov. The Timberwolves used the selection on Ricky Rubio. Washington was trying to add shooting and backcourt scoring around a veteran core expected to return to the playoffs. Minnesota was beginning another reset and valued the lottery pick more than two established players who did not fit its timetable. The deal therefore exchanged immediate rotation certainty for premium draft upside, with the additional Washington veterans serving as salary and roster pieces rather than the main value. The No. 5 pick was the transaction’s center of gravity from the moment it was agreed. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The teams were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information. In Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller, the named assets and the role each club could actually offer explain why the deal was available.

sections.heading: Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Minnesota’s winning case is Rubio’s sustained value. Although he remained in Spain for two more seasons, he arrived in 2011 as a creative passer and disruptive defender who immediately changed the team’s style. The Wolves were competitive when he was healthy during his rookie year before an ACL tear ended the season. Over his Minnesota tenure he organized offense, generated steals, improved transition play and became one of the franchise’s most recognizable players. He never developed into an efficient high-volume scorer, so the return did not reach superstar territory. It still produced far more useful control than Washington received. A long-term starting point guard from the fifth pick is a strong outcome, especially when the outgoing players left Washington after one season. The winning grade is not based on reputation alone. It follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Those elements align on the winning side of Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller.

sections.heading: Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Washington’s logic was understandable but the execution failed. Foye had averaged 16.3 points in his third season and offered another ball handler. Miller was an elite shooter and versatile rebounder who appeared ideal beside Arenas, Jamison and Butler. The Wizards believed a healthy veteran core could rebound from a 19-win season. Instead, Arenas’s suspension and the collapse of the roster ended the plan. Miller played well when available but appeared in only 54 games, and Foye did not become a long-term answer. Both departed in 2010. The Wizards neither reached the playoffs nor retained a durable asset from the package. An F reflects the short control, failed competitive objective and loss of a top-five pick. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. A useful veteran season, cap relief or a credible roster fit can have value even when the other team receives the larger prize. The grade should preserve that distinction instead of collapsing every loss into an F.

sections.heading: Ricky Rubio pick / Randy Foye and Mike Miller: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The deal must be judged without importing every later 2009 draft mistake into this one. sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Peak Impact
sections.body: Butler’s Philadelphia peak came in the 2019 postseason, when he repeatedly handled closing possessions, pressured the rim and guarded across the perimeter. Covington’s Minnesota peak was as an elite team defender and high-volume three-point shooter, while Saric supplied secondary scoring and spacing. Those are valuable complementary roles, but Butler’s ability to create offense under playoff pressure belonged to a different tier. The Sixers paid for that tier and received it, even if only briefly. Minnesota’s package was better suited to depth and flexibility than to replacing Butler’s star impact, which explains both the B- grade and the directional verdict. sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Control and Durability
sections.body: Minnesota controlled Covington and Saric on contracts that allowed later trades, while Philadelphia controlled Butler only through the season before free agency. That control advantage is the strongest argument for the Wolves. The Sixers partially protected themselves by completing the Miami sign-and-trade, but the return did not match Butler’s value. Even so, short control can justify a high grade when it creates a genuine title chance, and Philadelphia came within one possession of advancing past the eventual champion. The Wolves’ longer control created multiple asset paths, but the organization’s later choices did not convert them into a star-level return. sections.body: Philadelphia’s postseason result separates the trade. Butler helped beat Brooklyn, then pushed Toronto through seven games while serving as a primary creator and defender. The final loss does not eliminate the fact that the Sixers became a credible championship threat. Minnesota’s incoming players did not produce a comparable playoff run for the Wolves, though Covington’s later trade chain eventually contributed to a stronger roster. sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Minnesota could have accepted a different offer earlier or kept Butler until the deadline, but both paths carried the risk of worsening chemistry and leverage. Philadelphia could have retained Covington and Saric, preserving depth around Embiid and Simmons, yet the roster would still have lacked Butler’s late-game creation. The Sixers’ decision was defensible because title opportunities are scarce and the East was open after major roster changes. The Wolves’ decision was defensible because the relationship had become untenable. The counterfactual does not produce an obvious hidden winner; it shows why Philadelphia’s higher peak and Minnesota’s respectable floor can coexist in the final grades. sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: The trade is remembered as the beginning of Butler’s brief Philadelphia chapter and the end of a volatile Minnesota experiment. For the Sixers, it remains a symbol of how close the roster came to a deeper run and how difficult it was to retain the star combination afterward. For the Wolves, Covington and Saric became bridges to later roster moves rather than long-term cornerstones. The transaction did not permanently solve either franchise’s problems, but it clearly transferred the best immediate player and playoff outcome to Philadelphia. A- and B- capture a winner without turning the losing side’s damage control into a failure. Legacy summarizes the transaction’s place in franchise history, but the final grade remains tied to direct production, downstream conversion and the competitive identity created by the return.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid a Historic Price for a Defensive Identity
sections.body: The Timberwolves sent Patrick Beverley, Malik Beasley, Jarred Vanderbilt, Leandro Bolmaro, Walker Kessler's draft rights, four first-round picks and a 2026 swap right to Utah for Rudy Gobert. The scale created an immediate burden: the deal could not be justified by ordinary playoff qualification. Minnesota was betting that elite rim protection would organize the entire roster, reduce the defensive burden on Karl-Anthony Towns and accelerate Anthony Edwards into real contention. The first season looked awkward, but the later results showed the wager was about structure rather than a one-year statistical upgrade.

sections.heading: Utah Secured Both Immediate Players and a Long Asset Timeline
sections.body: The Jazz did not need every incoming veteran to remain in Utah for the return to work. Beverley, Beasley and Vanderbilt could be rerouted; Kessler became an immediate rotation center; the 2023 pick became Keyonte George; the 2025 selection became Will Riley; and the 2027 and 2029 picks remain future opportunities. The 2026 swap also gave Utah optionality. This is why the trade cannot be graded only by comparing Gobert with Kessler. Utah purchased years of decision-making power and the ability to continue converting pieces across multiple transactions.

sections.heading: The 2024 Defense Validated Minnesota’s Basketball Theory
sections.body: In Gobert's second Minnesota season, the Timberwolves produced the league's top defense, won 56 games and reached the Western Conference finals. Gobert won his fourth Defensive Player of the Year award, becoming the first Timberwolf to receive it. His screening, rebounding and paint control also supported the offense even when his own scoring volume was modest. The playoff victory over defending champion Denver supplied the strongest evidence that Minnesota had not merely assembled a strong regular-season defense. The roster could translate its size and coverage flexibility against the league's best opponent.

sections.heading: Consecutive Conference Finals Changed the Trade From Disaster to Contender Bet
sections.body: Minnesota returned to the Western Conference finals in 2025, making the Gobert-era Wolves the first version of the franchise to reach that stage in consecutive seasons. Gobert delivered a 27-point, 24-rebound closeout against the Lakers and continued to anchor the interior through another deep run. The Wolves did not win the championship, but repeated final-four appearances matter in a league where Minnesota had reached that round only once before the trade. The realized return has therefore exceeded the early ridicule and reached genuine contender territory.

sections.heading: The Future Picks Prevent a Final Minnesota Victory
sections.body: Utah still controls premium future outcomes, particularly the 2027 and protected 2029 first-round selections. Minnesota's roster will age, contracts will change and later picks could land higher than the early conveyances. The Jazz also received enough pieces to build additional transaction chains. That unresolved upside is not theoretical filler; it is part of the original price. A trade that has already transformed Minnesota can still become more favorable to Utah if those picks produce stars or high-value moves. The verdict must preserve that open horizon.

sections.heading: Matching A-Minus Grades Best Capture the Two Different Wins
sections.body: Minnesota should rise from B+ to A- because Gobert delivered a Defensive Player of the Year season and anchored consecutive conference-final teams. Utah should also rise to A- because it converted one veteran star into Kessler, George, Riley, movable veterans, a swap and two still-unresolved firsts. Neither side has completed the full value cycle, and neither outcome deserves to be described as a failure. Even Trade with matching A- grades recognizes that Minnesota purchased contention while Utah purchased a premium rebuilding portfolio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: This remains an Even Trade, upgraded to A- for both Minnesota and Utah. The Wolves paid extraordinary capital, but Gobert became the defensive anchor of a 56-win team, won the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year award and helped produce consecutive Western Conference finals. Utah acquired Kessler, George, Riley, multiple movable veterans, a swap and future 2027 and 2029 firsts. Minnesota has already received contender-level impact; Utah still owns meaningful unresolved upside. Both organizations achieved the strategic result they sought.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Rudy Gobert Trade Became Two Successful Projects Instead of One Obvious Winner
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Gobert deal was treated as a referendum almost immediately, first because the price reset the star-trade market and then because Minnesota's opening season looked clumsy. A longer view reveals two distinct value systems. Minnesota used Gobert to construct a defense capable of supporting Edwards through deep playoff runs. Utah used the return to create a long sequence of players, picks and future choices. The trade can be expensive for the Wolves and excellent for the Jazz without being a loss for either side.

sections.heading: The First Season Exposed the Integration Cost
sections.body: Gobert joined a roster built around Towns at center, Edwards as an emerging high-usage guard and limited perimeter shooting. Injuries and unfamiliar coverage responsibilities made the first season uneven. Minnesota won 42 games and exited in the first round, which made the price look detached from the immediate result. That criticism was fair at the time. The important distinction is that integration cost is not the same as permanent failure. The Wolves later adjusted the defensive scheme, expanded Jaden McDaniels' role and built lineups that used size as an advantage rather than a spacing problem.

sections.heading: Gobert’s Value Appeared in the Entire Defensive Ecosystem
sections.body: Elite rim protection affects more than blocked shots. Perimeter defenders can pressure the ball more aggressively when they trust the back line. Weak-side helpers can stay closer to shooters. Defensive rebounds end possessions and create transition opportunities for Edwards. Gobert's screening also creates offensive advantages that do not appear as assists. Minnesota's top-ranked defense in 2023-24 reflected a system organized around those effects. The DPOY award acknowledged the individual center, but the more important trade return was the environment his presence allowed the roster to build.

sections.heading: The Denver Series Supplied the Proof Against the Hardest Matchup
sections.body: Nikola Jokic is the center most often cited as evidence that traditional rim protectors cannot survive the postseason. Minnesota defeated Denver in seven games in 2024 by using Gobert, Towns, Naz Reid and versatile wings across changing assignments. Gobert was not flawless and did not guard every possession one-on-one. His size, rebounding and help positioning still formed part of the collective answer. The series mattered because it demonstrated that the Wolves' expensive defensive structure could survive a sophisticated champion rather than merely overwhelm weaker regular-season offenses.

sections.heading: Utah’s Return Must Be Evaluated as a Portfolio
sections.body: Kessler's shot blocking and rebounding made him the most visible early asset, but the Jazz return was intentionally broader. George became a lead-guard development project from the 2023 pick, Riley arrived from the 2025 selection and the veteran pieces created additional flexibility. The 2027 and 2029 picks may become the most valuable assets of all, depending on Minnesota's future. Portfolio trades are designed so that no single miss destroys the return. Utah acquired enough independent chances that the overall package can remain strong even if several pieces plateau.

sections.heading: The Deal Raised Minnesota’s Ceiling at the Cost of Future Control
sections.body: The Wolves traded optionality for competitive certainty. They surrendered the ability to draft or trade several future firsts, but they gained an elite defensive center whose skills translated immediately once the roster stabilized. Consecutive conference finals are a rare outcome and should be valued accordingly. The remaining question is whether the team can sustain contention as Gobert ages and the future picks convey. That tension is why A- is more appropriate than A+: the achieved ceiling is real, while the long-term bill has not finished arriving.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: An A-/A- Even Trade is the most defensible current grading scale. Minnesota transformed from an uncertain playoff team into a repeat conference finalist with Gobert as the defensive anchor, validating the basketball thesis behind the risk. Utah obtained a deep portfolio whose most consequential future selections may not yet have conveyed. The deal no longer resembles the automatic Minnesota disaster described after year one, but the Wolves also have not erased the extraordinary opportunity cost. Both sides created major value in different forms.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: At the 2005 trade deadline, Golden State acquired Baron Davis from the New Orleans Hornets for Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash. Davis was a two-time All-Star with a substantial contract, a history of back trouble and a deteriorating relationship with the organization. New Orleans was enduring a disastrous season and chose financial and cultural separation over waiting for a healthier market. Golden State, outside the playoff picture and desperate for a franchise guard, absorbed the risk without surrendering a first-round pick or a premium young player. The transaction was direct: star upside went to the Warriors, while the Hornets received two veterans and relief from a difficult long-term commitment. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The teams were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information. In Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash, the named assets and the role each club could actually offer explain why the deal was available.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Golden State’s case begins with the rarity of acquiring a true lead creator for a modest package. Davis gave the Warriors power at the point of attack, deep shooting range, transition playmaking and the confidence to control late possessions. The immediate team did not become a contender, but the roster gradually aligned around his strengths. Under Don Nelson in 2006-07, Davis led a fast, switchable group that won 16 of its final 21 regular-season games, reached 42-40 and ended a 13-year playoff drought. The first-round upset of 67-win Dallas made the trade part of franchise identity. Golden State did not acquire years of quiet competence; it acquired the player who made “We Believe” possible. The winning grade is not based on reputation alone. It follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Those elements align on the winning side of Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: New Orleans’ side is easier to understand than to praise. Claxton was a useful reserve guard and had championship experience, but he did not become a long-term starter for the Hornets. Dale Davis was near the end of his career and did not provide sustained value. The cash and salary relief mattered to a franchise navigating injuries, losses and uncertainty, yet those benefits did not produce a visible asset chain comparable to Davis’s impact in Golden State. The Hornets were not trading a healthy star in a stable environment, so the grade should acknowledge constrained leverage. A D rather than an F reflects the real medical and contractual risk. The return nevertheless lacked picks, youth or durable production, leaving the basketball outcome clearly one-sided. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. A useful veteran season, cap relief or a credible roster fit can have value even when the other team receives the larger prize. The grade should preserve that distinction instead of collapsing every loss into an F.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Timing shaped the market. Davis had played only 18 games for New Orleans that season and was owed major money. The Hornets were 11-46 near the deadline, temporarily playing amid a period of franchise instability and preparing for a broader reset. Golden State could afford to gamble because its alternative was continued irrelevance. The Warriors already had athletic wings and needed a guard capable of creating advantages without a set play. Davis’s physical style and pull-up shooting fit that need. The same contract that reduced his price for New Orleans became acceptable to Golden State because star talent rarely became available to the franchise in free agency. The trade was a classic risk transfer: one team prioritized certainty and flexibility, the other prioritized ceiling. Leverage was never equal. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough, not whether it predicted every future event.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: There was no complicated pick tree to rescue the losing side. The value remained concentrated in the named players. Claxton left after a limited Hornets tenure, and Dale Davis did not become a building block. Golden State received Davis through the 2007-08 season, enough time for the playoff breakthrough and another 48-win campaign. The Warriors later lost him in free agency after he opted out, so the deal did not deliver a decade of control. That shorter horizon prevents the trade from matching the franchise’s greatest dynasty-building moves, but it does not diminish the acquisition price. The Warriors paid a package with little enduring value and received multiple seasons of star-level creation plus a historic postseason run. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. This trade’s trade details are strongest when the analysis follows what each piece actually became, how long the club retained it and whether it helped the next transaction.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: The proper verdict is Warriors Win, not the generic “Partner Win.” Golden State earns an A-plus because the acquisition cost was modest, the player reached a star level and the team achieved a culturally defining upset. New Orleans remains at D because its leverage was compromised but its return still failed to create a meaningful future asset. The Hornets can argue that moving the contract was necessary; they cannot show that Claxton, Dale Davis or the cash replaced Davis’s value. The revised counterpart grade now matches Golden State’s A-plus rather than understating the winning side. This is a clear win with context, not a claim that New Orleans had unlimited alternatives. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose. The final labels should name the franchises, align the counterpart grade with the actual opponent and reserve A-plus for truly exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Golden State wins because Baron Davis produced the “We Believe” breakthrough and a historic playoff upset at the cost of two veterans and cash. New Orleans faced real health and contract constraints, but its return created almost no lasting basketball value.

featuredDeepDive.heading: How Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash Changed Two Franchise Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: The transaction is best understood by following the actual assets, the roles available on each roster and the years of control that followed. This deep dive tests Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash across peak value, durability, postseason use, realistic alternatives and historical legacy.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Peak Impact
sections.body: Davis’s 2007 postseason is the peak that decides the page. Against Dallas he repeatedly broke the first line of defense, punished switches and controlled tempo. Golden State’s small lineups worked because Davis could rebound, initiate and create shots from well beyond the arc. His emotional authority also mattered for a franchise that had not played a postseason game since 1994. Claxton’s best Hornets contribution was competent guard play; Dale Davis’s prime had occurred elsewhere. At their peaks after the trade, the returns were not close. Davis was the central player in one of the largest first-round upsets in league history, while New Orleans’ incoming pieces never became central to a winning era. Peak seasons matter because stars alter matchups, roster construction and postseason ceilings in ways that ordinary cumulative minutes do not. The comparison here turns on the highest-impact basketball each side received while the player remained under team control.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Control and Durability
sections.body: Golden State received roughly three and a half seasons rather than full career control, and Davis’s availability remained uneven. That is the principal limitation on the A-plus. Yet the Warriors captured the most valuable portion of the contract: the 2007 breakthrough and a 48-win 2007-08 season. New Orleans received shorter and less productive control over its incoming players. The comparison is therefore not simply a star versus role players; it is useful star seasons versus transitory veteran value. The Warriors accepted health risk and were rewarded. The Hornets reduced financial risk but did not convert the relief into a direct asset chain that changes the grade. Durability is more than games played. It includes contractual control, repeated role stability and the ability to build subsequent rosters around the return. A shorter brilliant window can beat longer average service, but the length and reliability of that window still affect the grade.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Postseason Translation
sections.body: The postseason translation is unusually vivid. Golden State entered the 2007 playoffs as the eighth seed and faced a Dallas team that had won 67 games and reached the previous Finals. Davis’s combination of scoring, passing, rebounding and pressure defense powered a six-game upset. The Warriors then lost to Utah in the second round, so the run did not end in a championship. Its significance was still enormous: it ended a generation of frustration and gave the franchise a modern identity before the Stephen Curry era. New Orleans received no comparable playoff benefit from the incoming package. The gap between a historic series victory and minimal postseason return supports the wide grade margin. Playoff results are evidence rather than the only test. Deep runs reveal whether a skill set survives scouting, pressure and slower possessions. They should be attributed only to the team that received the player in this trade, without borrowing championships earned after later moves.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: A fair counterfactual asks whether New Orleans could realistically have waited for a better offer. Davis’s health, salary and dissatisfaction all depressed the market, and the team had reasons to seek a clean break. Waiting might have produced another injury or a more public conflict. Golden State’s gamble also could have failed if the back problems persisted. Those risks explain why the price was low. They do not change what happened: Davis recovered enough to become a star again, while the Hornets’ return evaporated. The Warriors deserve credit for taking a risk that other teams declined, and New Orleans deserves only limited protection from the result because it did not secure draft upside as insurance. Counterfactuals are most useful when they describe realistic alternatives available at the time. They are least useful when they simply name a future superstar selected later or assume the losing team could have demanded an offer that the market never produced.

sections.heading: Baron Davis / Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: The trade’s legacy is the image of Davis leading the “We Believe” crowd and attacking the Mavericks with no fear. It was not the beginning of the later championship dynasty, but it reintroduced the Warriors to national relevance and demonstrated the force of an engaged Bay Area fan base. For the Hornets/Pelicans lineage, the deal is remembered as a star exit during a turbulent period rather than a foundational reset. The grades capture that difference. Golden State’s A-plus rewards ceiling, price and cultural impact. New Orleans’ D recognizes difficult circumstances without pretending that short-term veterans and cash were adequate basketball compensation. Legacy compresses years into a familiar story, but the grade should remain tied to transactions. The final accounting weighs direct production, downstream conversion, contract value and the competitive identity created by the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Golden State wins because Baron Davis produced the “We Believe” breakthrough and a historic playoff upset at the cost of two veterans and cash. New Orleans faced real health and contract constraints, but its return created almost no lasting basketball value.

sections.heading: New Orleans Needed a Defensive Center Beside Chris Paul
sections.body: The Hornets had found their franchise point guard in Chris Paul and needed a center whose game could amplify his speed, passing and defensive pressure. Tyson Chandler had disappointed relative to his draft position in Chicago, but he was still only 23 and possessed the length, mobility and rebounding ability New Orleans lacked. The Hornets sent veteran P.J. Brown and young guard J.R. Smith, accepting Smith’s scoring upside in exchange for a cleaner roster fit. Chandler did not require post touches or isolation plays. He could sprint into screens, dive to the rim, control the glass and protect the paint. Those skills created a natural partnership with Paul and gave New Orleans a defensive identity capable of supporting a rising offense.

sections.heading: The Paul-Chandler Partnership Became an Elite Competitive Engine
sections.body: Chandler’s best New Orleans season came in 2007-08, when the Hornets won 56 games, captured the Southwest Division and reached the conference semifinals. His screen setting and vertical spacing turned Paul’s pick-and-roll into one of the league’s most difficult actions to defend. On the other end, Chandler rebounded, challenged shots and gave the perimeter defenders confidence to apply pressure. His box-score scoring remained modest, but his efficiency and structural impact were substantial. New Orleans did not need him to become a traditional star. It needed him to make Paul’s strengths more dangerous and cover weaknesses elsewhere. The trade accomplished that objective at a high level and helped produce the strongest season in the franchise’s early New Orleans era.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a Veteran but Quickly Discarded the Upside Piece
sections.body: Brown provided one season of dependable frontcourt minutes and veteran leadership for a Bulls team that reached the second round. That contribution prevents Chicago’s return from being completely empty. The larger problem was J.R. Smith. Chicago acquired a 20-year-old scorer with significant athletic and shooting potential, then traded him to Denver days later for Howard Eisley and two second-round picks. Smith developed into a long-term NBA scorer and Sixth Man of the Year elsewhere, but the Bulls captured almost none of that value. The original Chandler trade therefore cannot be defended by pointing to Smith’s later career. Chicago’s realized return was largely one Brown season and modest secondary assets, far below Chandler’s impact in New Orleans.

sections.heading: Chandler’s Later Career Confirms the Talent Evaluation Without Belonging Entirely to New Orleans
sections.body: Chandler later became a Defensive Player of the Year and championship center in Dallas, evidence that New Orleans correctly identified a young player whose best basketball remained ahead. Those later achievements do not count fully as Hornets value because the franchise traded him in 2009. They still inform the process evaluation: the acquisition was not a fluke based on a brief hot stretch. Chandler’s tools and role were sustainable at the highest level. New Orleans received several prime development years and a major competitive peak before making a separate decision to move him. The A-plus grade rests on what he delivered with Paul, while his later success reinforces how sharply the Hornets understood his fit and age curve.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Decision Reflected a Change in Direction After Ben Wallace Arrived
sections.body: The Bulls had signed Ben Wallace and no longer saw Chandler as the center of their frontcourt plan. Moving his contract for Brown created a veteran rotation and financial clarity. That context makes the trade understandable, particularly after Chandler’s inconsistent offense and injury concerns in Chicago. It does not make the outcome favorable. Wallace’s Bulls tenure declined quickly, Chandler improved in New Orleans and Smith’s upside was discarded almost immediately. Chicago solved a short-term roster overlap by surrendering two younger players whose later value exceeded the return. A C-minus captures Brown’s useful season and the logic of the moment while recognizing that the organization lost both the best direct player and the best secondary upside.

sections.heading: The Existing Pelicans Verdict Is Right but the Grades Should Widen
sections.body: The prior record already said Pelicans Win, with New Orleans A and Chicago D-plus. The explicit verdict should remain, but the grades should become New Orleans A-plus and Chicago C-minus. Chandler’s fit with Paul, role on a 56-win division champion and prime-age value justify the top mark. Chicago’s Brown season was useful enough to avoid a D, even though the Smith reroute and Chandler’s growth made the outcome clearly poor. The revised grading scale better separates process from result. Chicago had a plausible reason to change centers; New Orleans made the superior talent and fit judgment and received the far more consequential competitive return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans A-plus, Chicago C-minus. Chandler became the defensive, rebounding and pick-and-roll partner who helped Chris Paul lead a 56-win division champion. Brown gave Chicago a useful veteran season, but the Bulls quickly rerouted Smith and retained little of his later upside. Chicago’s short-term logic prevents an F; New Orleans’ identification of a young center perfectly matched to its franchise guard earns the A-plus.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Tyson Chandler Unlocked Chris Paul’s First Great Contender
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2006 trade worked because New Orleans evaluated interaction rather than isolated production. Chandler had not become a major scorer in Chicago, and Paul did not need another player who required the ball. He needed a center who could turn a screen into a scoring threat, finish above the rim, rebound missed shots and defend behind aggressive perimeter pressure. Chandler’s movement and length transformed Paul’s passing windows and gave the Hornets a dependable defensive backbone. Chicago was reshaping its frontcourt around Ben Wallace and chose the certainty of Brown, but it failed to retain Smith’s upside. The exchange shows how a player labeled disappointing in one system can become essential when his skills are paired with the correct creator and role.

sections.heading: Vertical Spacing Made Paul’s Passing Even More Dangerous
sections.body: Chandler’s rim runs forced the weak-side defense to choose between tagging the center and staying attached to shooters. Paul could manipulate that choice with pace, hesitation and precise lob placement. Even when Chandler did not receive the pass, his dive created space for David West’s midrange game and perimeter shooters. This form of spacing does not appear in three-point totals, but it changes defensive geometry just as clearly. Chandler’s willingness to screen, sprint and finish without demanding post touches made him ideal for a young point guard who controlled every possession. The Hornets acquired a center whose offensive value came from magnifying Paul rather than competing with him.

sections.heading: Rebounding Allowed New Orleans to Play More Aggressively
sections.body: Chandler’s work on the glass ended possessions and created transition opportunities for Paul. Perimeter defenders could pressure the ball knowing the center had the length and mobility to cover behind them. On offense, his rebounds generated extra chances without disrupting the team’s shot distribution. Those possessions mattered for a roster that relied heavily on Paul and West to create efficient offense. Chandler also handled many of the physical center matchups that would otherwise wear down the frontcourt. His rebounding was therefore both statistical production and lineup infrastructure. New Orleans became harder to score against and faster after misses because the acquired center controlled the first step of both transitions.

sections.heading: Brown’s Season Had Value but No Long-Term Multiplier
sections.body: Brown started, defended and supplied veteran professionalism for a young Bulls team. Chicago won 49 games and reached the second round, so his contribution should not be dismissed. The limitation is that the value ended quickly. He did not become part of the next core, create premium trade capital or produce a competitive leap unique to his presence. Chandler, by contrast, became more valuable because his partnership with Paul improved both players and shaped the entire system. Trade returns are strongest when they multiply existing talent. Brown filled a role; Chandler changed what the Hornets could become. That difference separates C-minus from A-plus even before considering Smith’s lost upside.

sections.heading: The Smith Reroute Removed Chicago’s Best Chance to Balance the Deal
sections.body: Smith was inconsistent and immature, but he was also a young guard with rare athleticism and deep shooting range. Had Chicago developed or later traded him for meaningful value, the original package would look more defensible. Instead, the Bulls moved him almost immediately for a modest return. Denver received years of scoring and eventually a major role-player asset, while Chicago’s connection to that value disappeared. This is an important grading principle: a team receives credit for what it realizes from an asset, not for what the asset later becomes after being surrendered again. Smith’s career demonstrates that Chicago possessed upside briefly, but the Bulls’ own follow-up decision prevented that upside from improving their side of the trade.

sections.heading: New Orleans Won Through Fit Before Chandler Reached His Full Peak
sections.body: Chandler’s later championship and Defensive Player of the Year season came elsewhere, but New Orleans did not need those achievements to justify the trade. The Hornets received the best seasons of the early Paul era, including a division title and a near conference-final run. Chandler’s athletic prime began to emerge in the exact window when Paul became an MVP candidate. That timing produced high value even though the franchise later moved him. The A-plus grade recognizes a near-perfect acquisition relative to cost and roster need. New Orleans traded one veteran and one talented but unsettled guard for a center who became indispensable to its best team of the period.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. Chandler’s defense, rebounding and vertical partnership with Paul gave New Orleans a structural advantage that reached its peak in a 56-win season. Chicago received a useful year from Brown but failed to capture Smith’s later upside and watched Chandler become the superior long-term center. The trade was not merely a talent swap; it was a lesson in matching a young player’s specific strengths to the franchise star who could maximize them.

sections.heading: New Orleans Traded Ayón for Anderson
sections.body: On July 11, 2012 New Orleans acquired Ryan Anderson from Orlando in a sign-and-trade and sent Gustavo Ayón to the Magic. The club later known as the Pelicans received a forward who could score from the perimeter and change the spacing around its young frontcourt. Orlando took a reserve big man who offered a different role and contractual profile. The exchange did not include an additional premium first-round pick in the recorded player routing, so the value comparison depends on the actual performances of Anderson and Ayón.

sections.heading: Anderson Brought Four Seasons of Shooting
sections.body: Anderson became a high-volume three-point option and significant scorer for New Orleans over four seasons. His role as a stretch forward gave the team offensive spacing alongside its other bigs, a more durable contribution than a brief reserve spell. Ayón's tenure with Orlando was much shorter, limiting the Magic's direct realized return. The value distinction is especially visible because the two incoming players performed different jobs; the grade measures their contributions for the acquiring teams rather than assuming their careers were interchangeable.

sections.heading: Why the Return Favored New Orleans
sections.body: A sign-and-trade helped New Orleans acquire Anderson in a negotiated move rather than simply losing the opportunity to add him. Orlando obtained Ayón, but his immediate Magic contribution did not develop into a matching rotation role across the same four-year horizon. Anderson's shooting and scoring were tangible results inside New Orleans' own roster. The historical evaluation is stronger when it follows those distinct team tenures, not when it uses vague language about later franchise decisions that had no direct link to the original player swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. New Orleans earns A- for four years of Ryan Anderson's scoring and floor spacing. Orlando receives D because Gustavo Ayón supplied only a limited short-term return. The outcome is a player-for-player advantage driven by Anderson's actual New Orleans tenure rather than an unrelated future pick or speculative downstream transaction.

featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Regrading Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon
featuredDeepDive.intro: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon is best understood by separating the original transaction logic from the value that became visible afterward. On July 11, 2012, Orlando sent restricted free agent Ryan Anderson to New Orleans in a sign-and-trade for second-year big man Gustavo Ayon. Anderson had just won Most Improved Player and was one of the league's most prolific stretch forwards. New Orleans was willing to pay him and used Ayon, an inexpensive rotation center, as the outgoing basketball asset. The deeper review follows direct production, role, control, playoff translation and the traceable asset chain, while avoiding hypothetical draft choices and unrelated later moves. The result is Pelicans Win, with the grades calibrated to the amount of basketball value each franchise actually captured.

sections.heading: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon: Peak Value Versus Total Value
sections.body: Anderson gave New Orleans exactly the offensive identity the transaction targeted. He created spacing well beyond the arc, scored efficiently without needing the ball on every possession and provided frontcourt rebounding. Across four seasons he remained a significant rotation piece despite injury interruptions, including a 2015-16 season in which he again approached his peak scoring level. For the price of Ayon, that is substantial realized value. Peak impact and total accumulated value answer different questions. A short All-Star-level stretch can be worth more than several replacement-level seasons, while a dependable starter retained for years can outweigh a brief statistical spike. The regrade balances both dimensions so that neither longevity nor peak production becomes the only test.

sections.heading: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon: Control, Contract and Availability
sections.body: Orlando was entering a major transition around the Dwight Howard breakup and chose not to match the financial commitment required to keep Anderson. New Orleans was rebuilding around younger talent and had room to invest in a modern shooting big. That contract context explains why the acquisition price was small, but it does not erase the difference in what each team ultimately received. Control matters only when the player or pick remains useful. Years on a contract are not inherently valuable if injuries or poor fit prevent the asset from helping the team, while a short contract can still be excellent when it directly advances a contender's objective. The same logic applies to draft rights: the value is the control itself and what the team actually did with it, not the best player who could have been chosen in hindsight.

sections.heading: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon: Team Fit and Competitive Translation
sections.body: The trade's basketball meaning becomes clearer when the roster around it is considered. The deal anticipated the premium the league would soon place on frontcourt shooting. New Orleans acquired a proven specialist at that skill for a low-cost center and received multiple useful seasons. Orlando's decision may have fit a broader rebuild, but the specific trade return was too short-lived to balance the trade details. Role fit can magnify or suppress a player's raw production, especially for shooters, centers and secondary creators whose value depends on lineup context. Postseason use is credited when the acquired player actually held a meaningful role, but team wins are not assigned to one transaction unless the connection is direct.

sections.heading: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon: The Best Realistic Counterfactual
sections.body: The fairest alternative is not a fantasy offer assembled with perfect hindsight. The question is whether the team could reasonably have kept the outgoing asset, accepted a different documented type of return, preserved a pick or avoided paying to solve a self-created problem. For this trade, the realistic comparison begins with the leverage described at the time: On July 11, 2012, Orlando sent restricted free agent Ryan Anderson to New Orleans in a sign-and-trade for second-year big man Gustavo Ayon. Anderson had just won Most Improved Player and was one of the league's most prolific stretch forwards. New Orleans was willing to pay him and used Ayon, an inexpensive rotation center, as the outgoing basketball asset. That standard makes the verdict stricter than a trade-day reaction but more disciplined than simply ranking the careers of every name connected to the transaction.

sections.heading: Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon: How the Trade Should Be Remembered
sections.body: The deal anticipated the premium the league would soon place on frontcourt shooting. New Orleans acquired a proven specialist at that skill for a low-cost center and received multiple useful seasons. Orlando's decision may have fit a broader rebuild, but the specific trade return was too short-lived to balance the trade details. Historical memory tends to collapse transactions into one famous player, one playoff moment or one draft pick. A better summary preserves the mechanics, the team timelines and the value actually harvested from each incoming asset. That is why the final label remains Pelicans Win: it captures the relative result while the letter grades show how good or bad each side's own outcome was.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. New Orleans clearly won the Ryan Anderson sign-and-trade. Anderson became a high-volume floor-spacing forward and important scorer for four seasons, while Gustavo Ayon lasted only part of one season in Orlando before being waived. The result is based on the direct exchange, the years of useful control, and only those downstream assets that remain clearly connected to the original transaction.

sections.heading: Jrue Holiday / Nerlens Noel and first-round pick: The Deal's Actual Shape
sections.body: The first task is to separate the transaction mechanics from the later reputation of the names involved. On July 12, 2013, New Orleans acquired Jrue Holiday and the rights to Pierre Jackson from Philadelphia for the rights to Nerlens Noel and a top-five-protected 2014 first-round pick, later the No. 10 selection. The Pelicans had just renamed the franchise and wanted to accelerate around Anthony Davis with an established young guard. Philadelphia had hired Sam Hinkie and was beginning a long rebuild, making draft position and team control more valuable than an immediate All-Star. The teams were operating on deliberately different clocks. Holiday's early Pelicans seasons were interrupted by leg injuries, but the patience eventually paid off. He became one of the league's best defensive guards, supplied secondary playmaking and helped New Orleans sweep Portland in the 2018 first round. His value extended beyond box-score scoring because he could defend the opponent's best perimeter creator. Philadelphia received two credible rebuilding assets. Noel became a productive defensive center, while the 2014 pick became Elfrid Payton and was traded on draft night for Dario Šarić's rights and additional draft value. The Sixers did not turn the package into a star, but it fed the broader accumulation strategy.

sections.heading: Jrue Holiday / Nerlens Noel and first-round pick: The Acquiring Team's Case
sections.body: The stronger side of the deal comes into focus when role, age and organizational need are considered together. On July 12, 2013, New Orleans acquired Jrue Holiday and the rights to Pierre Jackson from Philadelphia for the rights to Nerlens Noel and a top-five-protected 2014 first-round pick, later the No. 10 selection. Holiday's early Pelicans seasons were interrupted by leg injuries, but the patience eventually paid off. He became one of the league's best defensive guards, supplied secondary playmaking and helped New Orleans sweep Portland in the 2018 first round. His value extended beyond box-score scoring because he could defend the opponent's best perimeter creator. New Orleans paid for certainty because Davis was already good enough to justify support. Philadelphia accepted delayed value because short-term wins were not the priority. Holiday's injuries initially made the Pelicans' decision look aggressive, yet his age and later recovery allowed the team to realize the long control it had purchased. The most important later development came in 2020, when New Orleans traded Holiday to Milwaukee for Eric Bledsoe, George Hill and a large package of first-round picks and swaps. That return extended the value of the 2013 acquisition well beyond Holiday's seven seasons with the Pelicans.

sections.heading: Jrue Holiday / Nerlens Noel and first-round pick: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: A sound review also measures what the other team received without reducing the package to a punch line. On July 12, 2013, New Orleans acquired Jrue Holiday and the rights to Pierre Jackson from Philadelphia for the rights to Nerlens Noel and a top-five-protected 2014 first-round pick, later the No. 10 selection. Philadelphia received two credible rebuilding assets. Noel became a productive defensive center, while the 2014 pick became Elfrid Payton and was traded on draft night for Dario Šarić's rights and additional draft value. The Sixers did not turn the package into a star, but it fed the broader accumulation strategy. The Pelicans had just renamed the franchise and wanted to accelerate around Anthony Davis with an established young guard. Philadelphia had hired Sam Hinkie and was beginning a long rebuild, making draft position and team control more valuable than an immediate All-Star. The teams were operating on deliberately different clocks. The Sixers' process was coherent: trade a valuable veteran before his next contract for multiple young assets. The Pelicans' process was also coherent: exchange uncertain picks for a proven 23-year-old at a premium position. The final grade turns on execution after the deal, where Holiday's development and resale value surpassed Philadelphia's conversions.

sections.heading: New Orleans Paid a Defensible Price for a Rare Star Pairing
sections.body: The Pelicans acquired DeMarcus Cousins and Omri Casspi for Buddy Hield, Tyreke Evans, Langston Galloway, a top-three-protected 2017 first-round pick and a second-round pick. For a team already built around Anthony Davis, the price was aggressive without resembling the enormous multi-pick packages later required for stars. Cousins was in his prime, under contract through the following season and capable of scoring, rebounding and creating offense from the center position. New Orleans was justified in believing that the opportunity was too unusual to ignore.

sections.heading: Cousins and Davis Needed Time but Eventually Became Overwhelming Together
sections.body: The immediate post-trade results were uneven as two high-usage big men and a reconfigured supporting cast learned new roles. By the following season, the experiment had become far more convincing. Cousins was producing roughly 25 points, 13 rebounds and five assists per game, while Davis retained his own superstar output. Their passing and shooting allowed New Orleans to play through either big, punish switches and overwhelm conventional frontcourts. The pairing was no longer merely theoretical when the season changed in January 2018.

sections.heading: The Achilles Rupture Ended the Evaluation Before the Playoffs Could Test It
sections.body: Cousins ruptured his left Achilles late in a win over Houston, ending his season after the Pelicans had built a winning record with him in the lineup. New Orleans later swept Portland and reached the second round without him, which proved that Davis, Jrue Holiday and the remaining roster had real quality. It did not show that Cousins was unnecessary. The injury removed the chance to see the intended frontcourt in a postseason series and transformed an expiring star acquisition into a short, incomplete window.

sections.heading: Sacramento’s Return Was More Durable Than New Orleans’
sections.body: Buddy Hield became the central realized asset for the Kings, developing into one of the league’s most prolific volume three-point shooters and remaining productive long after Cousins left New Orleans. Sacramento also received the first-round pick that became the rights to Zach Collins, then redirected that selection into the rights to Justin Jackson and Harry Giles, plus the second-round pick used on Frank Mason. The draft outcomes were mixed, but the combination of Hield and multiple shots at young talent gave Sacramento years of usable value.

sections.heading: The Kings Won in Hindsight Without Maximizing a Franchise Star
sections.body: A winning verdict for Sacramento should not be confused with praise for every element of the process. Cousins was an All-NBA talent, and the Kings completed the deal during All-Star weekend after years of organizational instability had weakened their leverage. Hield became a good player rather than a replacement superstar, and the draft capital did not produce a new franchise centerpiece. Sacramento’s advantage comes from durability and availability: its return remained on the floor while New Orleans received only 65 regular-season games from Cousins.

sections.heading: New Orleans Deserves a Better Grade Than the Injury-Driven Result Suggests
sections.body: A D+ treats the Pelicans as though they emptied the franchise for an obviously reckless gamble. The actual package and the level Cousins reached beside Davis support a more measured B-. The process created a legitimate high-end outcome, and the partnership was working before a catastrophic injury that could not reasonably have been forecast. Sacramento still earns a B and the slight edge because Hield and the draft assets produced the longer return. The gap should remain narrow enough to distinguish bad luck from bad evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento receives the slight win with a B, while New Orleans moves to B-. The Kings obtained years of production from Buddy Hield and additional draft opportunities, whereas the Pelicans received only 65 regular-season games from Cousins before his Achilles rupture and subsequent departure. New Orleans nevertheless paid a defensible price for a prime All-NBA center, and the Cousins-Davis pairing had developed into a genuine threat before the injury. The realized value favors Sacramento, but the quality of the original gamble makes this a narrow edge rather than a condemnation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The DeMarcus Cousins Trade Was a Good Gamble With an Unfinished Test
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Cousins transaction resists a simple lesson because the process and result point in different directions. New Orleans acquired a prime star without surrendering the kind of unrestricted draft package that later defined blockbuster trades. Sacramento recovered a productive young shooter and multiple draft assets after its relationship with Cousins had deteriorated. Then a torn Achilles removed the central player before the postseason could judge the experiment. A useful verdict must acknowledge both the Pelicans’ rational ambition and the Kings’ more durable return.

sections.heading: All-Star Weekend Timing Reflected Sacramento’s Weakening Leverage
sections.body: The trade became public around the 2017 All-Star Game, producing shock because Cousins had represented Sacramento as the franchise’s centerpiece only hours earlier. The Kings had spent years cycling through coaches, roster ideas and public tension with their star. That environment mattered to the price. New Orleans could offer a recent lottery pick in Hield, expiring or movable veterans and protected draft capital without including every premium asset it controlled. Sacramento accepted a reset package because the organization no longer believed a stable Cousins era was available.

sections.heading: The Two-Big Offense Was More Modern Than the Label Suggested
sections.body: Pairing two centers appeared contrary to the league’s move toward smaller lineups, but Davis and Cousins were not traditional stationary bigs. Both could handle the ball, pass and score away from the rim. Cousins’ three-point range pulled opposing centers from the paint, while Davis could attack slower defenders in space or dominate as a screener. The Pelicans could invert actions, run offense through the elbows and force opponents to choose which All-Star received the favorable matchup. The concept was ambitious, but it was not strategically obsolete.

sections.heading: January 2018 Was the Point at Which the Bet Looked Vindicated
sections.body: By the time Cousins was injured, New Orleans had moved beyond the awkward first months of integration. The team was winning, Cousins had recorded major triple-double performances, and the Davis-Cousins combination was creating matchup problems no other roster could replicate. The injury occurred late in a statement victory over Houston, making the abrupt change especially severe. Instead of entering the postseason with two elite bigs, the Pelicans had to rebuild their identity around Davis, Holiday, Nikola Mirotic and faster lineups in a matter of weeks.

sections.heading: Hield Supplied the Kings With a Long-Term NBA Asset
sections.body: Hield never became the singular replacement for Cousins, but he did become a high-volume shooter who could start, score and later function as a valuable trade piece. That matters because star-trade returns often fail when none of the young players become dependable rotation pieces. Sacramento also had opportunities with the associated draft picks, even though the Collins selection was converted into Jackson and Giles and neither became a cornerstone. The Kings’ return was imperfect, yet it created more seasons of usable value than New Orleans ultimately retained.

sections.heading: A Counterfactual Championship Claim Would Go Too Far
sections.body: It is tempting to imagine that a healthy Cousins would have transformed the 2018 Pelicans into a championship threat after they swept Portland. That conclusion cannot be proven. Golden State remained a historically strong opponent, and integrating Cousins into the playoff rotation would have created its own defensive challenges. The more supportable claim is narrower: New Orleans never received the postseason evaluation it purchased. Cousins’ regular-season performance showed that the pairing could work, while the Achilles injury prevented the franchise from learning how far it could travel.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Kings hold a slight edge because Hield and the draft assets outlasted the Pelicans’ brief Cousins era. Sacramento’s B recognizes a meaningful return without pretending it fully replaced an All-NBA franchise player. New Orleans earns B- because the acquisition price was reasonable, Cousins played at a star level beside Davis and the failure was driven primarily by a catastrophic injury rather than an incoherent plan. The trade did not become the Pelicans’ breakthrough, but it was a serious basketball idea whose final examination never occurred.
