sections.heading: Toronto Accepted One-Year Risk for a Championship Ceiling
sections.body: The Raptors had won 59 games in 2017-18 but had again been eliminated by Cleveland, leaving the organization with evidence that its established core had reached a postseason ceiling. Trading DeMar DeRozan, Jakob Poeltl and a protected first for Kawhi Leonard and Danny Green was emotionally difficult and contractually risky. Leonard had played only nine games the previous season and could become a free agent after one year. Toronto proceeded because a healthy Leonard offered a level of two-way shot creation unavailable elsewhere. The deal was not a long-term security play. It was a deliberate decision to exchange continuity for a credible championship path. Green’s shooting and defense also mattered, giving the Raptors two starters whose skills fit immediately beside Kyle Lowry, Pascal Siakam and Marc Gasol.

sections.heading: Leonard Supplied the Postseason Offense Toronto Had Been Missing
sections.body: Leonard’s value became clearest when playoff possessions slowed down. He could create a shot against set defenses, draw multiple defenders and guard elite wings without being hidden. Toronto survived a seven-game series against Philadelphia, including Leonard’s Game 7 winner, then recovered from a 2-0 deficit against Milwaukee before defeating Golden State in the Finals. His scoring carried the Raptors through difficult stretches while the roster’s depth and defense completed the run. Green contributed spacing, perimeter defense and lineup stability throughout the regular season. Toronto did not merely win because the conference changed around it. The acquired star repeatedly solved the exact playoff problem that had ended prior seasons. One championship and a Finals MVP make the Raptors’ A-plus grade secure even though Leonard left after one year.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received Real Value Under Severe Leverage Constraints
sections.body: The Spurs were negotiating after the relationship with Leonard had deteriorated and his trade request became public. That weakened their leverage and reduced the number of destinations willing to offer premium assets without a long-term commitment. San Antonio still obtained DeRozan, a four-time All-Star entering his prime; Poeltl, a young starting-caliber center; and a protected first that became Keldon Johnson. DeRozan produced three efficient seasons, expanded as a playmaker and helped maintain respectability. Poeltl became a valuable defender and was later traded back to Toronto for another first-round pick. Johnson developed into a substantial scorer and long-term rotation piece. This package did not match Leonard’s championship peak, but it was much stronger than a typical distressed-star return. A B better reflects the volume and durability of value than the prior B-minus.

sections.heading: The Championship Makes “Slight Edge” Too Cautious
sections.body: The old verdict called the trade a slight partner edge, language that understates the central result. Toronto won the championship in Leonard’s only season and received Finals MVP-level performance from him. San Antonio’s package was respectable, but no combination of regular-season production and secondary asset value equaled the title. The correct verdict is Raptors Win. That wording does not require treating the Spurs as reckless or empty-handed. Their B recognizes the difficult circumstances and the multiple useful assets that followed. Toronto’s A-plus recognizes a rare case in which a one-year rental delivered the best possible outcome. A championship cannot be reduced to a modest edge when the acquired star was the defining player of the run and the outgoing package never produced comparable team success.

sections.heading: Poeltl and Johnson Prevent the Spurs Side From Becoming a Failure
sections.body: Poeltl’s development is important to the final grading scale. He became an excellent screen setter, rebounder and interior defender, then generated another first-round pick when San Antonio later traded him. Johnson, selected with Toronto’s first, grew into a high-volume scorer and durable piece of the Spurs’ transition into a younger roster. DeRozan’s tenure also had value beyond raw wins; he handled difficult offensive possessions and developed playmaking that helped younger teammates. None of those outcomes created a contender, and San Antonio eventually moved into a rebuild. Still, the return spread value across multiple seasons and assets. A B says the Spurs managed a damaged situation competently. It avoids the opposite mistake of allowing Toronto’s championship to erase every useful result on the other side.

sections.heading: Both Organizations Achieved Their Immediate Objectives, but Only One Won the Title
sections.body: Toronto wanted a player capable of changing its postseason identity and received exactly that. San Antonio wanted to avoid a pure prospect package, remain competitive and preserve future value despite limited leverage. DeRozan, Poeltl and Johnson accomplished much of that narrower objective. The difference is the ambition and payoff of the two plans. The Raptors risked a beloved franchise star and future uncertainty to chase a championship, then won it. The Spurs stabilized a rupture but could not replace an MVP-caliber wing. The grades should therefore be Toronto A-plus and San Antonio B, with an explicit Raptors win. This formulation respects the quality of San Antonio’s recovery while assigning decisive weight to the highest achievement in professional basketball.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — Toronto A-plus, San Antonio B. Leonard and Green gave Toronto the two-way playoff ceiling required to win the 2019 championship, and Leonard earned Finals MVP in his only Raptors season. San Antonio recovered DeRozan, Poeltl and the pick used on Keldon Johnson, then extracted additional value from Poeltl later. That is a good distressed-asset return, not an equal outcome. The championship makes the verdict decisive rather than slight.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Toronto’s One-Year Kawhi Gamble Redefined the Value of a Rental
featuredDeepDive.intro: Most teams hesitate to surrender a franchise icon and future assets for a star who may leave within a year. Toronto’s 2018 decision demonstrated that contract length cannot be evaluated separately from competitive timing. The Raptors possessed depth, a strong regular-season infrastructure and a roster that had already revealed its limitations. Leonard did not need to promise a decade in Toronto for the trade to succeed. He needed to be healthy enough and dominant enough during the exact season when the rest of the roster was ready. San Antonio, meanwhile, needed to recover value after losing leverage in a broken relationship. The trade therefore became two separate tests: whether Toronto could maximize a short championship window and whether the Spurs could turn a forced move into a useful multi-asset return.

sections.heading: Masai Ujiri Chose Ceiling Over Sentiment
sections.body: DeRozan had embraced Toronto and helped transform the Raptors into a perennial playoff team. Moving him risked damaging trust and alienating a fan base that identified closely with his loyalty. Basketball logic nevertheless pointed toward a change. The existing core had produced excellent regular seasons without proving it could generate enough half-court offense against the strongest playoff defenses. Leonard offered a different category of solution: a large wing who could defend the opponent’s best scorer and create efficient offense late in the clock. Ujiri accepted the reputational and emotional cost because the roster’s supporting pieces were ready for a player of that caliber. The move was ruthless, but it was not random. It aligned the team’s strongest competitive season with the rare availability of a genuine postseason superstar.

sections.heading: Load Management Was Part of the Trade’s Success, Not a Side Note
sections.body: Toronto did not treat Leonard’s health as an ordinary regular-season matter. The club managed his workload, rested him frequently and relied on its depth to preserve a high seed. That approach reduced regular-season volume but increased the probability that he would be available for the playoff burden the trade was designed to address. The Raptors could make that choice because Lowry, Siakam, Serge Ibaka, Fred VanVleet and the rest of the rotation were capable of winning without Leonard every night. The strategy reveals how organizational context affects trade value. A team without depth might have needed Leonard to carry the regular season and arrived at the playoffs depleted. Toronto built a plan around the asset’s medical uncertainty, then received his best basketball when the games became most important.

sections.heading: Danny Green Made the Package More Complete
sections.body: Green is sometimes treated as salary attached to Leonard, but his inclusion improved the trade’s immediate fit. He shot at a high level during the regular season, defended opposing guards and wings, and allowed Toronto to maintain size without sacrificing spacing. His presence reduced the need to acquire another playoff-caliber starter after the trade. The Raptors effectively received both a superstar and a role player with championship experience, each suited to the team’s defensive identity. San Antonio’s outgoing package therefore contained more present value than Leonard alone. Green’s impact did not decide the grade, but it helped Toronto preserve depth and lineup flexibility across an exhausting postseason. In a one-year championship wager, avoiding a second transaction to fill the starting lineup was a meaningful advantage.

sections.heading: San Antonio Built a Chain Rather Than Finding a Replacement
sections.body: No realistic return was likely to replace Leonard directly. The Spurs instead created a chain of value. DeRozan absorbed primary offensive responsibility and improved as a facilitator. Poeltl developed into a strong defensive center and later brought back another first-round pick. The original protected first became Johnson, who provided scoring and remained part of the younger roster. That chain explains the B grade. San Antonio did not win the trade, but it avoided the barren outcome that often follows a public star request. The package also gave the organization time to move from the veteran era toward a rebuild without immediately collapsing. A reader can acknowledge each branch of that value while still recognizing that the Raptors’ championship outcome sits on an entirely different level.

sections.heading: A Championship Can Justify a Rental Even When the Star Leaves
sections.body: Leonard’s departure for the Clippers did not retroactively weaken Toronto’s trade. The Raptors acquired him for a defined competitive purpose and completed that purpose. They did not surrender a future superstar who later dominated elsewhere for them; they surrendered good players and a late first for the only championship in franchise history. The title changed the organization’s standing, validated years of roster building and created permanent value for the fan base and franchise. This is why Toronto’s grade remains A-plus despite receiving only one season. Duration matters when outcomes are similar. It matters less when a short tenure delivers the singular achievement that longer tenures often fail to produce. The deal established a standard for aggressive contenders: a rental can be worth a premium when the roster is genuinely ready to win immediately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win. Toronto transformed a high-performing but limited playoff core into a champion by acquiring the exact superstar skill set it lacked and managing Leonard’s season around the postseason. San Antonio salvaged a credible multi-asset package from a damaged relationship, making a B appropriate. The difference is not subtle. Leonard was the defining player of a championship run, Green strengthened the lineup, and the Raptors achieved the maximum return possible from a one-year gamble.

sections.heading: Rashard Lewis sign-and-trade / trade exception: The Deal's Actual Shape
sections.body: The first task is to separate the transaction mechanics from the later reputation of the names involved. On July 11, 2007, Seattle sent Rashard Lewis to Orlando in a sign-and-trade that returned a heavily protected second-round pick and a trade exception worth roughly $9.25 million. Lewis had opted out and selected Orlando, leaving Seattle with little conventional leverage. The Magic wanted a large shooting forward beside Dwight Howard, while new Seattle general manager Sam Presti was dismantling an aging roster and collecting flexible assets. The sign-and-trade solved contract mechanics for Orlando and created optionality for Seattle. Orlando's basketball return was immediate. Lewis stretched defenses far beyond the power-forward position, made the 2009 All-Star team and helped the Magic reach the NBA Finals. His shooting opened the lane for Howard and made the Hedo Türkoğlu-led offense unusually difficult to match with traditional frontcourts. Seattle's paper return initially looked small, but the exception was the valuable piece. Nine days later, the club used it to absorb Kurt Thomas's salary from Phoenix and received two first-round picks. The 2008 pick became Serge Ibaka, a foundational defender on Oklahoma City's first contender and a later source of additional trade value.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady sign-and-trade / future first-round pick: The Deal's Actual Shape
sections.body: The first task is to separate the transaction mechanics from the later reputation of the names involved. On August 3, 2000, Toronto completed a sign-and-trade that sent 21-year-old Tracy McGrady to Orlando for a future first-round draft pick. McGrady had shown flashes beside cousin Vince Carter but wanted a larger role and a return to Florida. Orlando entered the summer with major cap space and paired his arrival with the pursuit of Grant Hill. Toronto faced the weak negotiating position that often accompanies an unrestricted player's chosen destination. Orlando received the version of McGrady Toronto had only begun to see. He won Most Improved Player in 2000-01, became a perennial All-Star and All-NBA selection, and led the league in scoring twice. His 32.1 points per game in 2002-03 represented one of the greatest wing-scoring seasons of the era. Toronto at least extracted an asset from a departure it could not simply veto. That matters when judging front-office process. The problem is what the asset became: a delayed first-round slot that did not return a productive NBA player to the Raptors' side of the trade details. It was compensation in form, not in meaningful realized impact.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Got Two Seasons of Useful Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Schultz immediately joined the Lakers' rotation. He played all 66 regular-season games in 1951-52, averaging 4.1 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.5 assists, then appeared in 12 playoff games during a championship run. He returned for 40 more regular-season games in 1952-53 as Minneapolis won another title. Schultz was not a star, but 106 regular-season appearances plus postseason minutes gave the Lakers a real basketball return from a cash purchase.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Monetized Rights but Left No Traceable Basketball Return
sections.body: Fort Wayne moved a player who was not part of its active 1951-52 rotation, so selling the rights was defensible roster management. The problem for the retrospective grade is that the cash amount is unknown and no player, pick or later transaction can be tied to it. That makes the Pistons' return impossible to credit beyond the financial payment itself, while the Lakers' side produced documented on-court value across two championship seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B+, Fort Wayne C. The Lakers received 106 regular-season games and postseason depth from Schultz, including contributions to consecutive championship teams. Fort Wayne converted inactive rights into cash, but the amount and any basketball use of that money are undocumented. The win is clear without overstating Schultz's role.

sections.heading: A Five-Asset Exchange With a Later Player Attached
sections.body: On October 26, 1956, Minneapolis sent Slater Martin, the draft rights to Jerry Bird and a player to be named later to New York for Walter Dukes and the draft rights to Burdette Haldorson. Later records identify the player to be named later as Phil Jordon. The Knicks' historical record and Basketball-Reference ledgers agree on the core exchange. Bird was a 1956 first-round pick serving in the military, while Haldorson never appeared in an NBA game.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Turned Walter Dukes Into Larry Foust
sections.body: Dukes started at center for the Lakers in 1956-57, playing 71 games and averaging 10.1 points and 11.2 rebounds. Minneapolis then traded him to Detroit for Larry Foust. Foust became an All-Star in each of his first two Lakers seasons and played 191 regular-season games for the franchise. Haldorson's rights added no NBA production, but the Dukes-to-Foust chain gave Minneapolis several seasons of high-level center play.

sections.heading: New York Converted a Short Slater Martin Stay Into Willie Naulls
sections.body: Martin played only 13 games for the Knicks before New York traded him to St. Louis for Willie Naulls. That conversion became the strongest asset in the deal. Naulls developed into a long-term Knicks scorer and made multiple All-Star teams, including three straight from 1960 through 1962. Bird later appeared in 11 games for New York, while Jordon contributed limited minutes. Both teams managed their incoming assets well, but the Martin-to-Naulls branch produced the larger and longer peak.

sections.heading: The Knicks' Value Came Through a Second Move
sections.body: Slater Martin lasted only 13 games with New York, so the Knicks' eventual advantage wasn't built on a lengthy Martin tenure. The club subsequently traded him for Willie Naulls, who developed into a productive Knicks scorer and four-time All-Star. That follow-on move belongs in the transaction chain, but it doesn't mean Naulls joined New York in the original October 1956 exchange. Minneapolis also extracted substantial value by receiving Walter Dukes. He averaged 11.2 rebounds across 71 Lakers games in 1956-57 before the franchise moved him for Larry Foust, who later made two All-Star appearances as a Laker. The older player-to-be-named-later accounting for Phil Jordon also needs to stay distinct from the immediately named draft rights. The A-to-A- margin rests on those documented paths, not on counting the initial trade as a direct Naulls-for-Foust swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Minneapolis A-. This was a productive trade for both sides. The Lakers got a strong season from Dukes and then two All-Star seasons from Foust. The Knicks turned Martin into Naulls, whose multi-year All-Star run gave New York the slightly better long-term result. The edge is real, but it is much closer than a one-sided verdict would suggest.

sections.heading: Jack George for Guy Sparrow Was a Straight Player Swap
sections.body: Philadelphia sent Jack George to New York for Guy Sparrow on January 27, 1959. Team and league transaction ledgers agree on the one-for-one exchange, with no draft pick, cash term or later condition attached. Both were veteran players by the time of the trade, so the result turns on how much useful NBA value each club received after the swap rather than on a hidden asset chain.

sections.heading: George Gave New York 110 Games of Rotation Value
sections.body: George played 25 games for the Knicks in 1958-59, 69 the next season and 16 more in 1960-61. Across 110 New York appearances he averaged 8.2 points, 3.0 assists and 2.8 rebounds. His All-Star peak had already occurred in Philadelphia, so the Knicks did not acquire a star version of George, but they did receive more than a season and a half of useful veteran backcourt play.

sections.heading: Sparrow Never Established the Same Role in Philadelphia
sections.body: Sparrow appeared in 23 games for the Warriors after the trade and 11 more in 1959-60. His 34-game Philadelphia stay produced 3.4 points and 2.4 rebounds per game in a limited role, and 1959-60 became his final NBA season. The contrast is straightforward: New York extracted far more remaining service from George than Philadelphia did from Sparrow.

sections.heading: The Two Clubs Got Different Amounts of a Veteran's Final Seasons
sections.body: The difference is visible even when the players' earlier reputations are excluded. George appeared in 25 games after joining New York during 1958-59, then 69 the following season before adding another 16 in 1960-61. Those appearances provided continuity in the Knicks' backcourt for parts of three campaigns. Philadelphia, by contrast, received only 23 Sparrow games in the first partial season and 11 in the next, after which his NBA career ended. That's not a hypothetical comparison of their draft pedigree or peak talent; the two clubs actually received radically different remaining terms of service. It also explains why New York's B+ isn't a claim that George arrived as an All-Star. The value was a reliable veteran rotation contribution from a straight one-for-one exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B+, Philadelphia C-. George was no longer at his All-Star peak, but 110 games of regular rotation work clearly exceeded Sparrow's 34-game, low-minute Warriors tenure. This was a useful veteran win for New York, not a franchise-changing steal.

sections.heading: The Clippers Sold Jared Jordan's Rights for Cash
sections.body: Los Angeles drafted Jared Jordan 45th overall in 2007, then sent his draft rights to New York for cash on September 30. The cash amount was not disclosed. This was a small rights transaction, not a trade that needs a long asset-chain explanation: the Clippers chose to monetize a second-round prospect, while the Knicks paid for a chance to evaluate him in camp.

sections.heading: New York's Flier Ended Before the Regular Season
sections.body: The Knicks signed Jordan to a non-guaranteed contract after acquiring his rights, but waived him on October 25. He never appeared in a regular-season NBA game for New York and continued his career outside the NBA after camp. That leaves the Knicks with no realized NBA production from the asset they bought, while the Clippers at least retained the cash they received.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Stays Small
sections.body: The result favors Los Angeles, but the scale matters. No public source establishes the amount of cash, and New York was taking a low-cost chance on a recent second-round pick rather than sacrificing a rotation player or premium draft asset. A modest win for the Clippers fits the evidence better than the previous record, which incorrectly treated Jordan's rights as if they produced meaningful Knicks value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B-, New York C. The Clippers converted rights they were willing to move into cash. The Knicks' prospect flier produced no regular-season NBA value and ended with Jordan being waived before opening night. Because the cash amount is unknown and the stakes were small, the verdict is a narrow Clippers win rather than a major steal.

sections.heading: Washington Consolidated Four Seconds Into a First
sections.body: Philadelphia sent Reggie Jackson and its 2026 first-round asset — the least favorable of the Clippers, Thunder and the protected Rockets pick — to Washington for Jared Butler and four future second-round picks. Washington waived Jackson immediately, so the deal was never about adding the veteran guard. The Wizards were paying multiple smaller assets to move up the draft-capital ladder from seconds to a first.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Still Got Real Value From Jared Butler
sections.body: The Sixers did not leave the trade empty-handed. Butler played 28 games for Philadelphia after the deal, started 17 and averaged 11.5 points with 4.9 assists in 24.4 minutes per game. Philadelphia also kept the four second-round assets. That production makes the return more useful than a simple “four seconds for a first” summary suggests, even though the first-rounder remained the strongest single asset in the exchange.

sections.heading: The First Became No. 30 and Stayed Useful as Trade Currency
sections.body: The 2026 first ultimately landed at No. 30, where Koa Peat was selected. Washington had already included that Oklahoma City-derived first in the larger February 2026 package that brought Anthony Davis to the Wizards. The pick was only one component of that later deal and should not be credited with the entire Davis return, but its inclusion shows why Washington valued consolidating into a first-round asset in the first place.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win — Washington A-, Philadelphia C. Washington turned Butler and four seconds into a first-round asset that ultimately became pick No. 30 and later functioned as part of a major trade package. Philadelphia got a productive post-deadline stretch from Butler and retained four future seconds, so the return was not empty. The first-round premium, however, gives Washington the stronger package and supports the existing verdict.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: San Francisco traded Tom Gola to New York on December 5, 1962 for Willie Naulls and Kenny Sears. Basketball-Reference's Warriors and Knicks transaction pages, the league ledger and all three player histories agree on the date and package. The transaction moved one versatile veteran to New York in exchange for two established forwards whose best Knicks seasons were already behind them. That makes the deal more nuanced than a simple one-for-two headcount comparison.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: Gola immediately became a major Knicks rotation player. He played 52 games after the trade in 1962-63, averaging 12.0 points, 7.1 rebounds and 4.3 assists in 35.5 minutes per game. He followed with 74 games in 1963-64, 77 in 1964-65 and 74 in 1965-66. Across the four post-trade seasons, New York received 277 regular-season games. His scoring declined as he aged, but he continued to rebound, facilitate and fill multiple perimeter and frontcourt roles. The volume and continuity are the core of New York's realized advantage.

sections.heading: San Francisco Return
sections.body: Naulls gave the Warriors 47 games for the remainder of 1962-63, averaging 11.0 points and 6.7 rebounds in 26.1 minutes per game. Sears played 54 games that season at 6.1 points and 2.6 rebounds, then returned for 51 games in 1963-64 at 3.3 points and 1.8 rebounds. San Francisco therefore received 152 combined regular-season games from the two players. Naulls was then sold to Boston in September 1963, producing an additional financial return, while Sears' NBA career ended after the 1963-64 season.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The Warriors did not come away empty. Naulls remained a useful scorer and rebounder for half a season, Sears supplied depth for a season and a half, and Naulls retained enough rights value to be sold. But the package was short-lived. Gola stayed with New York for four seasons and played nearly twice as many regular-season games by himself as Naulls and Sears combined for San Francisco. He also handled a much larger role immediately after the trade, including more than 35 minutes per game in the first partial season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, A/B. New York receives an A for acquiring four seasons and 277 games of useful two-way play from Gola. San Francisco receives a B because Naulls and Sears produced real short-term value and Naulls generated a later cash sale, but the combined player return lasted only 152 games. Confidence is high because the transaction structure, all three player identities and the season-by-season production are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought an Immediate Floor General
sections.body: The expansion Bulls acquired Guy Rodgers from San Francisco for Jim King, Jeff Mullins and cash. Rodgers was exactly the kind of veteran organizer a new team could use: he played 81 games in 1966-67, averaged 18.0 points and 11.2 assists, and gave Chicago a functioning offense from day one. His Bulls tenure, however, was almost entirely contained in that first season; he played only four more games for Chicago.

sections.heading: Mullins Turned the Warriors Return into a Long-Term Win
sections.body: King was useful in his own right, giving San Francisco 167 games across parts of four seasons. Mullins was the asset that changed the scale of the deal. He remained with the Warriors for ten seasons, became a high-volume scorer and posted three straight 20-point seasons from 1968-69 through 1970-71. The verified package also included cash, and the team and league ledgers do not support the stray draft-pick entry that had appeared in the older record.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Still Earns a Strong Grade
sections.body: Rodgers was not a bad acquisition simply because Mullins became the best long-term player. Chicago was building an expansion roster and received an elite passer who could handle a heavy workload immediately. That made the trade productive for the Bulls in the short term. The Warriors still gained far more cumulative value because Mullins stayed for a decade and King added several seasons of useful play beside him.

sections.heading: The Contemporary Ledgers Rule Out a Phantom Draft Pick
sections.body: The Warriors, Bulls and league transaction records identify Rodgers going to Chicago in exchange for Jim King, Jeff Mullins and cash. They do not support the extra unidentified draft pick that appeared in an older summary, nor do they require treating King or Mullins as unspecified players to be named later. That matters because the Warriors' case is already strong based on actual players: Mullins supplied a decade of Golden State service and King added 167 regular-season appearances. On the Chicago side, Rodgers' value is grounded in his 81 games, 18.0 points and league-leading 11.2 assists per game during the inaugural 1966-67 season. The completed comparison needs no fictional future asset. Correct transaction scope is particularly important when grading early expansion-era deals, where player movement and protective agreements can otherwise become mixed together.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A+, Chicago B+. Rodgers gave the Bulls an excellent first season and justified the short-term logic of the move. San Francisco received the deeper return: King supplied multi-season value, Mullins became a decade-long core scorer, and cash came with them. The gap is substantial, but Chicago's side was useful rather than disastrous.

sections.heading: A Three-Team Deal With Six Verified Player Assets
sections.body: The December 16, 1963 trade sent Bob Boozer from Cincinnati and Johnny Egan from Detroit to New York. Detroit received Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy from the Knicks, while Cincinnati received Larry Staverman from Detroit. One piece arrived later: on May 1, 1964, New York transferred Hub Reed's rights to Detroit to complete the Egan obligation. The league and all three team transaction ledgers support those player movements; they do not support the cash entry that had survived in the older canonical record.

sections.heading: Boozer and Egan Gave New York the Best Immediate Return
sections.body: Boozer played 49 games for the Knicks after the trade in 1963-64 and all 80 games the next season. Across those 129 games, he averaged roughly 15.4 points and 7.9 rebounds. Egan added 42 games at 14.1 points and 5.8 assists immediately after the trade, 74 more games in 1964-65 and seven at the start of 1965-66. New York therefore received two real rotation pieces at once, and both produced more direct value than the outgoing package.

sections.heading: Detroit Got Useful Depth; Cincinnati Lost the Value Race
sections.body: Detroit did not leave empty-handed. Butcher played 138 games for the Pistons over parts of three seasons, Duffy contributed a shorter stint, and Reed's rights arrived as the deferred completion. Cincinnati's return was much lighter: Staverman played 34 games for the Royals in 1963-64 and averaged 4.0 points and 2.8 rebounds. The gap between Boozer plus Egan and the other returns makes New York the clear winner without pretending Detroit received nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Detroit B-, Cincinnati C-. The Knicks acquired the two strongest immediate players and received 252 combined regular-season games from Boozer and Egan. Detroit earned a useful multi-season guard in Butcher and later received Reed's rights, which keeps its grade respectable. Cincinnati turned Boozer into a much smaller Staverman return and finishes third in the deal.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On May 11, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves traded Bailey Howell to the Philadelphia 76ers for Bob Kauffman and a 1971 second-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference's league transaction ledger identifies the future pick as No. 30 in 1971, when Buffalo selected Spencer Haywood. The historical franchise is Buffalo even though the canonical TradeVerdicts team key follows the modern Clippers lineage.

sections.heading: Buffalo Return
sections.body:
Kauffman became an immediate centerpiece for the new franchise. In Buffalo's inaugural 1970-71 season he played 78 games, averaged 20.4 points, 10.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists, and made the All-Star team. He followed with 18.9 points and 10.2 rebounds in 1971-72 and 17.5 points with 11.1 rebounds in 1972-73. Kauffman was an All-Star in all three seasons. By 1973-74 his role had fallen to 17.6 minutes per game, but he still appeared in 74 games as the Braves reached the playoffs for the first time.

Across four Buffalo seasons, Kauffman provided 306 regular-season games and three All-Star selections. Buffalo eventually lost him to New Orleans in the 1974 expansion draft, so there was no later trade return to add. The direct value was already substantial: the Braves obtained a frontcourt anchor at age 24 and received his best NBA seasons.
The 1971 pick requires more careful treatment. Buffalo used the acquired second-rounder on Haywood at No. 30. By then Haywood had already signed with Seattle and had played for the SuperSonics after winning the legal fight that challenged the NBA's four-years-out-of-high-school rule. Buffalo drafted him hoping to secure his rights, but Haywood remained with Seattle and never played for the Braves. The pick therefore counts as a verified draft outcome, not as realized Buffalo player production.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body:
Howell was a Hall of Fame forward near the end of his career, not an empty salary slot. At age 34 he played all 82 games for Philadelphia in 1970-71, averaging 10.7 points and 5.4 rebounds in 19.4 minutes. He also appeared in all seven of the 76ers' playoff games. That is useful one-season value, especially from a veteran who had been an important part of Boston's 1968 and 1969 championship teams.

The limitation is duration. Howell's Philadelphia season was his final NBA campaign. The 76ers received a capable rotation forward for one year, while Buffalo received four years of Kauffman with three All-Star appearances. Even after assigning zero on-court value to the Haywood pick, the player-for-player outcome strongly favors Buffalo.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
The clearest comparison is Kauffman's prime against Howell's final season. Kauffman became the leading veteran presence on an expansion roster and produced three consecutive All-Star seasons before helping the franchise reach its first postseason in year four. Howell remained productive in Philadelphia, but his 82 regular-season games and seven playoff appearances were the end of his career.

The Haywood draft outcome adds historical interest without inflating Buffalo's grade. Buffalo did use the acquired pick on a future Hall of Famer, but the selection never became a Braves player because Haywood's Seattle rights survived the dispute. Treating his Seattle career as Buffalo value would be wrong.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves Win, A-/B-. Buffalo receives an A- for acquiring Kauffman's four-year run and three All-Star seasons, with no extra basketball credit assigned for Haywood beyond documenting the draft outcome. Philadelphia receives a B- because Howell gave the club a full, productive final season and playoff minutes, but the return was far shorter and less valuable than Kauffman's Buffalo tenure. Confidence is high because the transaction, draft outcome and player production are well documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's San Francisco and Portland transaction logs describe Jim Barnett going to the Warriors for three draft choices: Portland's 1971 second-round pick at No. 25, used on Charlie Yelverton; a 1971 third-round pick at No. 42, used on Bill Smith; and a 1972 second-round pick at No. 26, used on Dave Twardzik. Those logs date the transaction March 23, 1971. Pro Sports Transactions ties the same three selections to Barnett but dates the exchange March 27. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Golden State Return
sections.body: Barnett was a real return, not a throwaway veteran. In 1971-72 he played 80 games for Golden State, averaging 12.4 points, 3.1 rebounds and 3.9 assists in 27.5 minutes. He remained with the Warriors for three full seasons, playing 82 games in 1972-73 and 77 in 1973-74 while staying around 12 points per game. His first Golden State postseason was especially useful: the veteran guard gave the club experienced scoring and playmaking as it reached the 1972 playoffs. That durability keeps the Warriors' grade respectable even though Portland eventually realized more value from the pick package.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Yelverton supplied the quickest return from the package. As a rookie in 1971-72 he played 69 games for Portland, averaging 7.9 points, 2.9 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 17.8 minutes, but that was his only NBA season. Smith, the No. 42 pick, played 22 games for Portland as a rookie at 8.3 points and 6.1 rebounds in 20.4 minutes, then appeared in only eight more NBA games the next season. Twardzik took longer to reach Portland because he spent four seasons in the ABA after being drafted. Once he arrived, however, he became the package's defining piece. He joined the Trail Blazers in 1976-77 and was part of the championship rotation, averaging 10.9 points and 2.8 assists in 25.3 minutes across 14 playoff games.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The delayed Twardzik payoff is what moves the transaction beyond an even exchange. Golden State received three productive Barnett seasons, so the Warriors did not lose the trade because their acquisition failed. Portland instead won because the three-pick package produced multiple NBA contributors and one player who later became part of the franchise's first championship team. Yelverton and Smith offered early but limited value; Twardzik supplied the long-tail upside and meaningful postseason production. The comparison is retrospective, but it does not pretend Portland could have known in 1971 that a 1972 second-round pick would leave for the ABA and then return in time to help a title team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, A-/B-. Portland receives an A- because all three picks became NBA players and Twardzik eventually provided championship-level rotation value, giving the package both breadth and a high-value long-term outcome. Golden State receives a B- because Barnett was a productive three-year contributor rather than a miss, including an 80-game first season and continued double-digit scoring. Confidence is high on the asset chain and player outcomes, with the March 23 versus March 27 source-date discrepancy noted in the record. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records the September 19, 1972 exchange as New York sending Milt Williams to Golden State for an undisclosed draft pick or future draft consideration in the 1973 draft. RealGM independently records Williams moving from the Knicks to the Warriors that day. Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages are less complete for this specific exchange, so the specialist transaction database and RealGM supply the strongest direct evidence for the trade mechanics. The exact draft round, pick number and eventual selected player remain unresolved, which prevents this archive from assigning New York a specific draft outcome.

sections.heading: Golden State's Intended Return
sections.body: Williams had a small NBA résumé before the deal. He appeared in five games for New York in 1970-71 and ten for Atlanta in 1971-72 after the Hawks claimed him from the Knicks on waivers. New York later reacquired his rights before sending him to Golden State. The Warriors were therefore acquiring a veteran fringe point guard rather than a proven rotation player. That can still have practical roster value in training camp, but hindsight grading depends on what actually reached the regular-season court.

sections.heading: Zero Warriors Games
sections.body: Golden State received no regular-season production from Williams. RealGM and Pro Sports Transactions both record the Warriors waiving him on October 9, 1972, less than three weeks after the trade and before the regular season began. Basketball-Reference lists Williams as playing in another professional league during 1972-73, and he does not appear on Golden State's 47-35 roster. The Warriors reached the Western Conference Finals without him. For this transaction, Golden State's realized return is therefore zero NBA games, minutes, points or assists.

sections.heading: Williams' Later Career
sections.body: Williams did return to the NBA, but not through Golden State. Seattle signed him in October 1973, and he played 53 games for the SuperSonics in 1973-74, averaging 3.1 points and 1.9 assists in 9.5 minutes. He later appeared briefly in the ABA. Those later games confirm that Williams still had professional ability, but they cannot be credited to the Warriors because Golden State had already waived him and received no compensation when he left. Hindsight grading must follow the asset chain actually retained by each team.

sections.heading: New York's Unresolved Consideration
sections.body: The Knicks' return is harder to value. Pro Sports Transactions labels it an undisclosed draft pick or future draft consideration in the 1973 draft, but the reviewed sources do not resolve the round, selection number or player produced by that consideration. The archive therefore does not attach one of New York's 1973 picks to this deal without evidence. That uncertainty caps the Knicks' grade: they clearly received a contractual asset, but the realized basketball payoff cannot be measured with the same precision as a known draft selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge, D/C. Golden State receives a D because Williams never played a regular-season game for the Warriors and was waived before opening night. New York receives a C because the Knicks obtained future draft consideration, but the exact 1973 asset and downstream player remain unidentified. The gap stays modest because an unresolved future consideration cannot be treated as a successful draft return merely because Golden State received zero games. Confidence is medium-high on the player movement and waiver, but only medium on New York's complete return because the pick identity is still unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Pick Swap Is Straightforward
sections.body: Buffalo and Phoenix transaction ledgers, the NBA league record and Pro Sports Transactions all agree on the May 29, 1975 exchange. Buffalo sent the No. 16 pick in the 1975 draft to Phoenix for one of the Suns' 1976 first-round selections. Phoenix immediately used No. 16 on Ricky Sobers. One year later Buffalo used the acquired Phoenix pick at No. 6 on Adrian Dantley. The Suns' historical media guide independently describes the same swap from Phoenix's side, making the transaction mechanics unusually well documented for a draft-pick-only trade from this era.

sections.heading: Dantley Gave Buffalo Elite Rookie Value
sections.body: Buffalo's pick outcome was excellent. Dantley played 77 games in 1976-77, started 76 of them and averaged 20.3 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 52 percent from the field. He won NBA Rookie of the Year. A single season at that level is far more valuable than the legacy A-minus grade suggested, especially because the Braves acquired him without surrendering an existing rotation player. His Buffalo tenure was short, but it was high-end production from the moment he arrived.

sections.heading: Buffalo Converted Dantley Into Another High-Level Player
sections.body: On September 1, 1977, Buffalo traded Dantley and Mike Bantom to Indiana for Billy Knight. Knight then played 53 games for the Braves in 1977-78 and averaged more than 20 points per game before the franchise's move to San Diego. Knight was later included in the large August 1978 Boston trade. Because Bantom was part of the Dantley-for-Knight package, the full value of Knight cannot be credited solely to the 1975 Phoenix pick. Still, the move proves Dantley retained major trade value after his Rookie of the Year season.

sections.heading: Sobers Was a Real Two-Year Suns Contributor
sections.body: Phoenix also received more than a placeholder. Sobers played 78 games as a rookie in 1975-76, averaging 9.2 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists. He appeared in 19 playoff games during the Suns' run to the 1976 NBA Finals and averaged 13.0 points in the postseason. Sobers improved in 1976-77, playing 79 games and averaging 13.6 points and 3.0 assists. That gives Phoenix 157 regular-season games plus a meaningful playoff run before the club converted him into another asset.

sections.heading: The Sobers-to-Buse Chain Was Exceptionally Productive
sections.body: Phoenix traded Sobers to Indiana on September 6, 1977 for Don Buse. Buse then started all 82 games for the Suns in both 1977-78 and 1978-79 and played 81 more in 1979-80. He earned All-Defensive First Team honors in each of those three Phoenix seasons. That is 245 regular-season games of elite defensive guard play created directly from Sobers. Unlike Buffalo's Dantley-to-Knight transaction, Phoenix did not have to add another player to acquire Buse, so the downstream attribution is much cleaner.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Gets the Narrow Edge
sections.body: Buffalo won the star-quality portion of the pick swap. Dantley was immediately the best individual player produced by the transaction and his Rookie of the Year season was outstanding. Phoenix, however, created a longer uninterrupted chain: two Sobers seasons, a Finals run and then three full Buse seasons with first-team All-Defense recognition. Buffalo's later Knight value is meaningful but partly depends on adding Bantom, which makes it less attributable to Dantley alone. The difference is enough to move the historical verdict away from the legacy claim of a clear Buffalo win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ because Sobers contributed 157 games and a Finals run, then was traded one-for-one for Buse, who added 245 games and three straight All-Defensive First Team seasons. Buffalo receives an A because the acquired pick became Dantley, the 1977 Rookie of the Year, and Dantley retained enough trade value to help acquire Knight. Both franchises extracted major value. The Suns' advantage comes from the longer, cleaner downstream asset chain rather than from Dantley being a poor outcome. Confidence is high on the pick identities, player outcomes and downstream Sobers-to-Buse transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: October 24 Is the Canonical Completed Transaction Date
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Knicks, Seattle SuperSonics and NBA transaction ledgers all record the Spencer Haywood trade on October 24, 1975. Eddie Donovan's Knicks executive history uses the same date and package. A contemporary Black World report says the trade was announced Thursday afternoon, which was October 23, explaining the date on the duplicate Seattle import superseded in this review. For the canonical archive, October 24 is the stronger completed-transaction date because the team, league and executive records all align there.

sections.heading: The Package Included Gene Short and a Conditional 1979 First
sections.body: New York sent Gene Short, the No. 9 pick in the 1975 draft, plus a future first-round pick. Later transaction references describe the pick as conditional on Short failing to remain with Seattle for a specified period. He appeared in only seven SuperSonics games and was waived on November 24. The Knicks signed him as a free agent two days later. The condition therefore triggered, and Seattle ultimately held New York's 1979 first-round selection, which landed at No. 6.

sections.heading: Contemporary Reporting Supports a Large Cash Component
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's standard transaction ledger does not list cash, so this review does not treat the dollar figure as league-ledger data. A Black World report published October 30, 1975 says the Knicks sent rookie Eugene Short and cash estimated at $1.5 million for Haywood. Later historical accounts repeat a $1.5 million figure. Because the amount was reported contemporaneously rather than reconstructed decades later, the archive preserves it as reported cash with an explicit source caveat rather than deleting it or presenting it as an undisputed official amount.

sections.heading: Haywood Gave New York Four Seasons of High-Level Production
sections.body: Haywood immediately became a full-time Knicks starter. In 1975-76 he played 78 games and averaged 19.9 points and 11.3 rebounds in 37.1 minutes. He remained productive through parts of four seasons in New York, totaling 210 regular-season appearances and averaging roughly 17 points and nine rebounds for the club. The Knicks reached the playoffs once during that span, so the acquisition did not create a sustained contender, but the on-court return was far beyond a short rental or declining-name acquisition.

sections.heading: Seattle's Pick Became James Bailey at No. 6
sections.body: The conditional first conveyed in 1979 and Seattle selected Rutgers forward James Bailey sixth overall. Bailey played 67 games as a rookie, then made a major jump in 1980-81 by appearing in all 82 games and averaging 14.0 points, 7.4 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in 31.0 minutes. Across his Seattle tenure he played 159 regular-season games before moving on. That production gives the future pick substantial realized value even though Bailey never reached Haywood's star level.

sections.heading: Gene Short Added Almost No Seattle Value
sections.body: Short's part of the return was brief. He averaged 1.9 points in seven Seattle games before the club waived him one month after the trade. New York then brought him back as a free agent, and he played 27 additional games for the Knicks before his NBA career ended. His limited Seattle stay is still important because it activated the conditional-pick mechanism, but his own playing contribution should not be mistaken for a meaningful part of Seattle's realized return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B+/B+. New York receives a B+ because Haywood supplied 210 games of strong frontcourt production and was immediately a near-20-point, double-digit-rebound starter. Seattle also receives a B+ because the SuperSonics obtained a reported major cash payment and a conditional first that became James Bailey, who produced a strong 1980-81 season and 159 Seattle games. Short himself added little, and neither side turned the transaction into sustained championship-level value during the relevant window. Confidence is high on the player movement, October 24 effective date, conditional pick outcome and player production; the cash amount remains explicitly reported rather than official-ledger confirmed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sources.title: Haywood Coming To The Rescue, October 30 1975

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Verify Malone for the 1978 First-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: the Braves sent their 1978 first-round pick to Portland for Moses Malone. The pick later landed at No. 3 and became Rick Robey. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bob MacKinnon's Buffalo record preserve the same structure. Those primary ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions reports an additional $232,000 payment from Buffalo, so this review records that amount as secondary-source evidence without treating it as part of the primary-ledger consensus.

sections.heading: Buffalo Held Malone for Only Six Days
sections.body: Malone's direct Buffalo production was almost nonexistent. Basketball-Reference credits him with two Braves games and six total minutes before the next transaction. That small sample should not be mistaken for the value Buffalo actually captured, because the Braves did not waive him or lose him for nothing. On October 24, they traded Malone to Houston for a 1977 first-round pick and a 1978 first-round pick. The proper hindsight chain therefore follows those two assets rather than grading Buffalo only on Malone's two appearances.

sections.heading: The First Houston Pick Became George Johnson
sections.body: Buffalo moved the 1977 first-rounder to Golden State in January 1977 for George Johnson. Johnson immediately became a starting center for the Braves, appearing in 39 games with 39 starts and averaging 10.3 rebounds while providing rim protection. Golden State ultimately used the pick on Wesley Cox. For Buffalo, Johnson is the realized return attributable to that branch of the Malone resale rather than Cox's later career.

sections.heading: The Second Houston Pick Stayed Alive in the Tiny Archibald Package
sections.body: The 1978 first-rounder acquired from Houston was the pick that later became No. 4 Micheal Ray Richardson. Buffalo did not simply use that selection. In September 1977 the Braves sent George Johnson, that 1978 first and their 1979 first-round pick to the Nets for Tiny Archibald. Because the Archibald trade contained three outgoing assets, this review does not credit the entire Archibald return to the Houston pick alone. It does show that the second first-rounder retained substantial trade utility long after Buffalo's six-day ownership of Malone ended.

sections.heading: Portland Turned the No. 3 Pick Into the No. 1 Pick
sections.body: Portland's incoming 1978 first-rounder became even more valuable before draft night. On June 8, 1978, the Trail Blazers sent Johnny Davis and the No. 3 pick that became Rick Robey to Indiana for the No. 1 pick. Portland used that selection on Mychal Thompson. The original Buffalo pick was therefore not merely a theoretical top-three asset; it was a central component in Portland's move to the first overall selection.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson Supplied Seven Seasons of Portland Value
sections.body: Thompson played 551 regular-season games for Portland from 1978-79 through 1985-86, totaling 18,913 minutes, 9,215 points and 4,878 rebounds. He missed 1979-80 with a leg injury but otherwise became a long-term starting-caliber frontcourt piece. Portland later included Thompson with Larry Krystkowiak in the 1986 trade for Steve Johnson. Johnny Davis was also required in the 1978 pick swap, so this review does not pretend the entire Thompson career came from the Malone trade alone. Still, the No. 3 pick was indispensable to reaching No. 1 and generated the strongest durable player outcome in this asset tree.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge, A+/A. Portland receives an A+ because the first-round pick obtained for Malone became the key draft asset in the move from No. 3 to No. 1, producing 551 Mychal Thompson games and seven seasons of frontcourt value. Buffalo receives an A because acquiring Malone for one future first and reported cash created an immediate asset arbitrage: six days later the Braves turned him into two first-rounders, one of which became George Johnson and the other remained part of the later Tiny Archibald package. Buffalo's handling of Malone after October 18 belongs to the downstream chain rather than erasing the quality of the acquisition. Confidence is high on the pick-for-Malone structure and all traced basketball assets; the reported $232,000 cash remains secondary-source-only.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Confirm a Two-Player Package for Garrett and Two Firsts
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers all record the January 13, 1977 exchange the same way. Cleveland sent Rowland Garrett plus its 1977 and 1978 first-round picks to Milwaukee for Gary Brokaw and Elmore Smith. The first-round picks later became No. 11 Ernie Grunfeld in 1977 and No. 12 George Johnson in 1978.

sections.heading: Smith Gave Cleveland Three Seasons of Real Frontcourt Value
sections.body: Smith was the strongest direct asset Cleveland received. He played 36 games for the Cavaliers after the trade in 1976-77, averaging 8.7 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. He followed with 81 games in 1977-78 at 12.5 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.2 blocks, then appeared in 24 more games in 1978-79. Across his Cleveland tenure he played 141 regular-season games and averaged 10.5 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks.

sections.heading: Brokaw Was a Shorter-Term Secondary Return
sections.body: Brokaw played 39 games for Cleveland after the deal, averaging 7.2 points and 3.0 assists. The Cavaliers traded him to Buffalo for future considerations in October 1977. Because the primary ledgers do not identify a concrete later player or pick emerging from those future considerations, this review credits Cleveland for Brokaw's 39 games and acknowledges the subsequent transaction without inventing a downstream asset.

sections.heading: Garrett Was the Smallest Milwaukee Piece
sections.body: Garrett played 33 games for the Bucks after the trade, averaging 4.7 points and 2.2 rebounds. The 1976-77 season was his final NBA season. His direct value therefore does little to separate the packages, which puts most of Milwaukee's case on the two first-round picks.

sections.heading: Grunfeld Became a Useful Two-Year Buck
sections.body: Milwaukee used the No. 11 pick in 1977 on Ernie Grunfeld. He played 73 games as a rookie and all 82 in 1978-79, improving from 6.9 to 10.3 points per game. After 155 Milwaukee games, the Bucks traded Grunfeld and a 1980 second-round pick to Kansas City for Richard Washington in October 1979. This review credits Grunfeld's direct Milwaukee service and notes that he retained transaction value, without assigning the entire later Washington return to him because Milwaukee also sent a pick.

sections.heading: Johnson Added Another First-Round Rotation Piece
sections.body: The 1978 first-rounder became George Johnson at No. 12. Johnson played 67 games for Milwaukee as a rookie, averaging 6.2 points and 5.4 rebounds. The Bucks sold his player rights to Denver in October 1979. That gives Milwaukee another season of direct production plus a later transactional return, although the financial amount is not specified in the primary source used here.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee receives a B+ because two first-round picks became legitimate NBA rotation players who combined for 222 Bucks games, with Grunfeld also retaining later trade value. Cleveland receives a B- because Smith was a productive three-year center and Brokaw added a short guard stint, so the Cavaliers did receive meaningful basketball value. The difference comes from Milwaukee turning both premium picks into useful players while Garrett's limited tenure did not undermine the package. Confidence is high on the trade structure, draft outcomes and direct player production.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on a Three-Asset Lakers Return
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles, Kansas City and league transaction ledgers all record the June 1, 1977 exchange the same way. The Lakers sent Lucius Allen to the Kings for Ollie Johnson, Kansas City's 1978 first-round pick and Kansas City's 1978 second-round pick. The draft slots later became No. 5 Purvis Short and No. 26 Ron Carter, but the first-round branch requires an important correction: Los Angeles did not draft Short.

sections.heading: The No. 5 Pick Became Part of the Jamaal Wilkes Compensation Package
sections.body:
On July 11, 1977, the Lakers signed Jamaal Wilkes as a veteran free agent from Golden State. Los Angeles sent cash and the 1978 first-round pick acquired in this trade to the Warriors as compensation. Golden State later used that pick on Short. This review therefore does not credit Short's Warriors career to the Lakers. It credits the pick as one component of the compensation package that brought Wilkes to Los Angeles.

That downstream use was enormously valuable. Wilkes immediately played 51 games for the Lakers in 1977-78 and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. He then played all 82 games in 1978-79, 1979-80 and 1981-82, with 81 games in 1980-81. In the 1980 championship run he averaged 21.3 points in the six-game NBA Finals against Philadelphia. Two years later he averaged 19.7 points in another six-game Finals win over Philadelphia. Because cash was also part of the free-agent compensation, this review treats Wilkes as a major shared downstream return rather than assigning every ounce of his Lakers value to the pick alone.

sections.heading: Johnson Turned Into Two Full Seasons of Lou Hudson
sections.body: Ollie Johnson never played a regular-season game for Los Angeles after the trade. On September 30, 1977, the Lakers sent him to Atlanta for Lou Hudson. Hudson then appeared in all 82 games in 1977-78, averaging 13.7 points, and played 78 more games in 1978-79 at 9.8 points. Across two Lakers seasons he totaled 160 regular-season games and 1,891 points. The Johnson branch therefore produced a meaningful veteran return even though Johnson himself never suited up for the Lakers.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Produced a Lakers Reserve
sections.body: Los Angeles kept the 1978 second-round pick and selected Ron Carter at No. 26. Carter played 46 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1978-79 and appeared twice in the playoffs. His role was modest, but the pick produced actual roster value rather than expiring unused.

sections.heading: Allen Gave Kansas City One Strong Season and a Short Second Year
sections.body: Allen started the trade's other side with a useful 1977-78 season. He played 77 games for Kansas City, averaging 11.9 points and 4.7 assists in 27.9 minutes. He returned for 31 games in 1978-79 at 5.1 points and 1.4 assists, then his NBA career ended. Basketball-Reference lists no later Allen transaction producing another Kansas City player or draft asset, so this review stops the branch there.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A+/B-. Los Angeles receives an A+ because all three incoming branches created realized value: the first-round pick helped secure Wilkes, Johnson became two productive Hudson seasons, and the second-rounder became Carter. Kansas City receives a B- because Allen supplied 108 games and a useful first season, but there was no comparable downstream asset after his short tenure. The gap is large without pretending the Lakers directly drafted Short or that the Wilkes compensation consisted of the pick alone. Confidence is high.

sources.title: Ollie Johnson Career and Transaction History

sections.heading: The June 7 Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Buffalo, Milwaukee and the league transaction ledgers agree on the core exchange. The Braves sent the 1977 first-round pick that became No. 3 Marques Johnson to Milwaukee. The Bucks sent Swen Nater plus the first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong to Buffalo. The trade happened three days before the draft, so the pick identities were not yet actual drafted players when the teams exchanged them.

sections.heading: Buffalo's No. 13 Pick Became a Different Asset Before the Draft
sections.body:
The stale version of this record credits Buffalo with Tate Armstrong as though the Braves drafted and kept him. They did not. On June 10, Buffalo traded the No. 13 pick to Chicago for a second-round pick. Chicago then drafted Armstrong at No. 13, while Buffalo used the incoming second-rounder at No. 24 on Larry Johnson. Armstrong's own transaction history confirms the full chain from Buffalo to Milwaukee, back to Buffalo, then to Chicago.

Johnson provided almost no NBA return. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger lists him as Buffalo's No. 24 selection, and his player page records only four regular-season games, 38 minutes and six points before his NBA career ended in 1977-78. This review therefore credits Buffalo with the actual Johnson outcome rather than Armstrong's Chicago career.

sections.heading: Nater Was a Major Franchise Return
sections.body:
Nater supplied far more value. He played 78 games for Buffalo in 1977-78 and averaged 15.5 points and 13.2 rebounds in 35.6 minutes per game. After the franchise moved to San Diego, he stayed for six more seasons and appeared in 348 Clippers games. Across the Buffalo and San Diego portions of the same franchise, that is 426 regular-season games.

His rebounding remained a defining part of his value. He averaged 8.9 rebounds in 1978-79, then continued as a major frontcourt piece through the early 1980s. Basketball-Reference's franchise split lists 348 San Diego appearances alone, on top of the 78 Buffalo games from his first season after the trade.

sections.heading: Nater Also Retained Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: On October 10, 1983, San Diego traded Nater and the rights to Byron Scott to the Lakers for Norm Nixon, Eddie Jordan and two future second-round picks. The Clippers then used those two picks in another trade for Ricky Pierce one week later. Nater clearly remained part of a valuable package, but this review does not assign the whole Nixon or Pierce return to him because Byron Scott and other assets were also involved.

sections.heading: Marques Johnson Became Milwaukee's Franchise Star
sections.body: Milwaukee used the No. 3 pick on Marques Johnson. He played 80 games as a rookie, then 77, 77, 76, 60, 80 and 74 over the next six seasons. That is 524 regular-season games in seven Bucks seasons. Johnson made four All-Star teams during that run and earned All-NBA First Team in 1979-80 plus All-NBA Second Team in 1980-81 and 1981-82. He also became the central scorer on the teams that restored Milwaukee to sustained playoff contention after the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar era.

sections.heading: Johnson's Value Extended Into a Major 1984 Trade
sections.body: Milwaukee did not lose Johnson for nothing. On September 29, 1984, the Bucks traded Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash to the Clippers for Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce. Johnson was one piece of a multi-asset outgoing package, so this review does not credit the entire incoming trio to him. His inclusion nevertheless demonstrates that the No. 3 pick still carried major transaction value seven years after the original Buffalo deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, A+/A-. Milwaukee receives an A+ because the No. 3 pick became a seven-year franchise star with four All-Star selections, three All-NBA honors and substantial later trade value. Buffalo receives an A- because Nater gave the franchise 426 games across Buffalo and San Diego, including elite first-season rebounding, and remained part of a major 1983 trade package. The recast No. 13 pick produced only four NBA games from Larry Johnson, which limits that branch. Buffalo received a very good return; Milwaukee simply converted the premium draft slot into the best player and the stronger peak outcome. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Exchange Is Straightforward
sections.body: Indiana, Buffalo and the league transaction ledgers all record the same September 1, 1977 deal: the Pacers sent Billy Knight to the Braves for Adrian Dantley and Mike Bantom. There is no draft-pick or cash ambiguity in the cited ledgers, so this review starts from a stable three-player transaction.

sections.heading: Buffalo Got an Immediate All-Star Season From Knight
sections.body:
Knight was already one of Indiana's best scorers before the trade, and he remained highly productive in Buffalo. He played 53 regular-season games for the Braves in 1977-78, averaging 22.9 points, 7.2 rebounds and 3.0 assists in 40.7 minutes. He also made the 1978 All-Star team.

That is a strong direct return. Buffalo did not merely acquire a famous name; it received one of the league's most productive forwards for most of a season.

Knight also retained transaction value when the franchise moved to San Diego. On August 4, 1978, the Clippers sent Knight, Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes and two second-round picks to Boston for Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams. Because Knight was only one of five outgoing assets, this review does not assign that entire Boston package to him.

sections.heading: Bantom Became Indiana's Durable Return
sections.body:
The most important Pacers asset was Bantom. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, starting 78 and averaging 15.3 points, 7.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He followed with 81 games in 1978-79 at 17.0 points and 9.3 rebounds, then played 77 games in 1979-80 at 14.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 4.3 assists.

Across those three Indiana seasons, Bantom appeared in 240 regular-season games. That kind of multi-year availability and production gives the Pacers a much longer realized return than Buffalo received from Knight before the franchise's next major reshuffle.

sections.heading: Dantley Added Elite Short-Term Production and a Downstream Trade Branch
sections.body:
Dantley's Pacers stay was brief but spectacular. He played 23 games, started all 23 and averaged 26.5 points, 9.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 41.2 minutes.

On December 13, 1977, Indiana traded Dantley and Dave Robisch to the Lakers for James Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash. Edwards became a productive young center for Indiana and Tatum played a regular role that season. This review does not credit the entire return to Dantley because Robisch was also outgoing, but Dantley was clearly one of the central pieces used to create that second asset cycle.

sections.heading: The Teams Both Got Real Value, but Indiana Got More of It
sections.body: Buffalo's side should not be downgraded simply because Knight stayed only one season. His 53 games were high-level, All-Star-caliber production. The problem is that Indiana received both a productive three-year starter in Bantom and a 23-game scoring burst from Dantley before recycling Dantley into another useful package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Edge, A/B+. Indiana receives an A because Bantom produced 240 games over three seasons and Dantley added elite short-term production plus meaningful downstream trade value. Buffalo receives a B+ because Knight was excellent, made the All-Star team and remained part of a later blockbuster package, but his direct Braves tenure lasted only 53 games. The trade was productive for both teams; Indiana's advantage comes from depth and duration rather than Buffalo receiving a weak player. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Package Is Clear, Including Cash
sections.body:
Indiana, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all describe the December 13, 1977 deal the same way: the Pacers sent Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch to the Lakers for James Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash.

The cash amount is not disclosed in the cited transaction records. This review therefore keeps cash as a verified asset without inventing a dollar figure. The key correction is evaluative rather than structural: this trade should be judged by what each franchise actually received and later converted, not by Dantley's Hall of Fame career after he left Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Edwards Became Indiana's Long-Term Centerpiece
sections.body:
Edwards played 58 games for Indiana after the trade in 1977-78, averaging 15.4 points and 7.5 rebounds. He then played 82 games in 1978-79 at 16.7 points and 8.5 rebounds, 82 more in 1979-80 at 15.7 points and 7.0 rebounds, and 81 in 1980-81 at 15.6 points and 7.0 rebounds.

That is 303 regular-season Pacers games across four seasons, with Edwards functioning as a high-minute starting center for nearly the entire run. It is the most durable direct team-specific return in the transaction.

When Edwards signed with Cleveland as a veteran free agent in May 1981, Indiana received 1981 and 1982 second-round picks as compensation. The picks became Ray Blume and Guy Morgan. Their later value was limited, but the compensation extended the Edwards asset branch beyond his four productive seasons.

sections.heading: Tatum Added a Productive Half-Season and a First-Round Pick
sections.body:
Tatum played 57 games for Indiana in 1977-78, starting 40 and averaging 14.4 points, 4.0 assists and 3.6 rebounds. His Pacers tenure lasted only that season, but Indiana did not simply lose him for nothing.

On July 19, 1978, the Pacers traded Tatum to Boston for a 1980 first-round pick, later used on Carl Nicks. Tatum's 57 productive games plus a first-round downstream asset make him more than a minor secondary piece in the original return.

sections.heading: Dantley Was Excellent for Los Angeles, but Only for Two Seasons
sections.body:
Dantley played 56 Lakers games after the trade in 1977-78 and averaged 19.4 points and 7.2 rebounds. He returned for 60 games in 1978-79 at 17.3 points and 5.7 rebounds.

That gives Los Angeles 116 regular-season Dantley games. He was still an emerging high-efficiency scorer, but the Lakers did not receive the Utah version of Dantley that later became a perennial All-Star and elite scorer. This review does not transfer those Utah seasons backward into the Lakers' realized return.

Los Angeles did preserve asset value. On September 13, 1979, the Lakers traded Dantley to Utah for Spencer Haywood. That downstream return belongs to the Lakers branch and keeps the Dantley acquisition from being evaluated as only a two-season rental.

sections.heading: Robisch Supplied Depth and Later Helped Bring Back Chones
sections.body:
Robisch played 55 Lakers games in 1977-78 and 80 in 1978-79, for 135 regular-season games. His scoring was modest at 4.7 and 4.8 points per game, but he supplied frontcourt depth and availability.

In October 1979 the Lakers traded Robisch with a 1980 third-round pick to Cleveland for Jim Chones. Because another draft asset was included, this review does not credit all of Chones's value to Robisch alone. Still, the branch shows Robisch retained useful transaction value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Edge, A/A-. Indiana receives an A because Edwards alone produced 303 high-minute games over four seasons, Tatum added 57 productive games and a future first-round pick, and the package included verified cash. Los Angeles receives an A- because Dantley was an excellent scorer for 116 games, Robisch added 135 games, and both players generated useful downstream trades. Dantley's later Hall of Fame career strengthens his overall biography, but most of that value occurred after the Lakers traded him away. On team-specific realized value, Indiana produced the longer and deeper return. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The source-backed Package Is a 1981 First for a 1978 First
sections.body:
Golden State, Portland and the league transaction ledgers all agree on the June 7, 1978 transaction. The Warriors sent a 1981 first-round pick to the Trail Blazers and received Portland's 1978 first-round pick.

The legacy archive entry described Golden State's outgoing asset as a 1979-or-1981 first. This review normalizes that language to the source-supported 1981 first because all three authoritative transaction ledgers use that year.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the No. 22 Pick on Raymond Townsend
sections.body:
Portland's 1978 first landed at No. 22, where Golden State selected Raymond Townsend. He played 65 games as a rookie, averaging 4.7 points in 11.9 minutes, then appeared in 75 games in 1979-80.

Across two Warriors seasons, Townsend played 140 regular-season games and scored 710 points. He was a real NBA contributor, but he never became a high-impact starter or long-term core player for Golden State.

That direct return gives the Warriors more value than a failed draft pick, but it remains limited for a first-round asset.

sections.heading: Portland Held the Future Pick for Less Than Two Years
sections.body:
The Blazers did not wait until 1981 to use the pick. On February 8, 1980, Portland traded the future Golden State first to New Jersey together with Maurice Lucas and a 1980 first-round pick for Calvin Natt.

That later transaction is the key downstream branch. The Golden State pick was one of three assets Portland used to acquire a productive young forward. It therefore had substantial market value even before the draft.

sections.heading: Calvin Natt Became an Immediate Portland Contributor
sections.body:
Natt joined Portland during his rookie season and averaged 20.4 points in 25 games after the trade. He then played 74 games in 1980-81 at 13.4 points and 75 games in 1981-82 while averaging 18.4 points per 36 minutes.

This review does not assign all of Natt's Portland production to the 1981 first because Maurice Lucas and another first-round pick were also part of the package. The correct conclusion is narrower: the Golden State pick remained valuable enough to serve as one of the central pieces in a major trade for a productive forward.
