sections.heading: Houston Bought Motiejunas Upside but Paid With More Than One Asset
sections.body: Houston’s draft-night deal with Minnesota brought back Jonny Flynn, the rights to Donatas Motiejunas and a conditional 2012 second-round pick. The outgoing package was Brad Miller, the rights to Nikola Mirotic, the rights to Chandler Parsons, a future first-round pick and cash. The Rockets did immediately reacquire Parsons from Minnesota in a separate cash transaction, so his later Houston career should not be counted as Minnesota’s long-term gain from this exchange. Even after removing that shortcut, the original package was broad enough that Houston needed more than one useful player to justify the price.

sections.heading: Motiejunas Became the Best Direct Houston Return
sections.body: Motiejunas developed into a real rotation big for Houston. Basketball-Reference credits him with 44 games as a rookie, 62 in 2013-14 and 71 in 2014-15, when he started 62 games and averaged 12.0 points. Flynn did not provide a comparable return: he appeared in only 11 games for the Rockets before Houston moved him to Portland in the Marcus Camby trade. The 2012 second-round pick from Minnesota went to Portland in that same deal and became the No. 40 selection used on Will Barton. Houston therefore extracted value, but most of it came from Motiejunas.

sections.heading: Minnesota Converted the Draft Assets Again
sections.body: Minnesota’s side was not primarily about Brad Miller’s playing time. Miller appeared in only 15 games for the Timberwolves. The more important pieces were the draft assets: Minnesota moved Mirotic’s rights to Chicago on the same night, sold Parsons’ rights back to Houston for cash and retained the future first that eventually became the No. 26 pick in 2013. Minnesota later packaged that pick, used on Andre Roberson, with Malcolm Lee in a trade with Golden State. Those moves did not create a single star for the Wolves, but they gave the franchise more usable asset branches than the Miller contract alone suggests.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Stay Modest
sections.body: This was not a disaster for Houston. Motiejunas became a legitimate contributor, and the front office later recycled Flynn and the second-round pick into the Camby transaction. Minnesota also failed to turn every incoming piece into lasting on-court production. The difference is that Houston surrendered multiple draft assets plus Miller and cash to acquire a package whose direct NBA return centered heavily on Motiejunas. Minnesota preserved more optionality and later trade value across several branches, which supports a Wolves edge without treating Parsons’ Houston career or Roberson’s Oklahoma City career as Minnesota production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Houston C, Minnesota B+. Donatas Motiejunas became a useful Rocket and gives Houston a credible return, but Jonny Flynn lasted only 11 games in Houston and the acquired second-round pick was later sent to Portland. Minnesota received Brad Miller plus several draft assets, immediately converted Mirotic and Parsons into other value, and retained the future first that became the No. 26 pick in 2013 before trading that asset again. The gap is not enormous because Minnesota did not turn the package into a franchise cornerstone, but the broader asset return and Houston’s limited payoff outside Motiejunas make the listed B+ and C grades defensible.

sections.heading: Houston Bought Back the Rights It Had Just Sent to Minnesota
sections.body: The Chandler Parsons transaction is unusual because it was part of a frantic draft-night asset chain. Houston selected Parsons at No. 38, then his rights moved to Minnesota inside the larger Jonny Flynn-Donatas Motiejunas deal before the Rockets reacquired Parsons in a separate transaction. The canonical record lists Houston sending $1.5 million and a conditional 2012 second-round pick that did not convey. That left the Rockets with the player rights while Minnesota’s realized basketball return from this specific follow-up deal was effectively the cash payment.

sections.heading: Parsons Became an Immediate Starter and a Three-Year Core Wing
sections.body: Parsons signed with Houston in December 2011 and quickly turned a second-round rights purchase into real rotation value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 63 games and 57 starts as a rookie, followed by 76 starts in 2012-13 and 74 more in 2013-14. His scoring climbed from 9.5 points per game as a rookie to 15.5 and then 16.6 in the next two seasons. Houston therefore received three years of starting production from an asset obtained for cash and a condition that never triggered.

sections.heading: Minnesota Monetized the Pick but Did Not Retain a Basketball Asset
sections.body: Minnesota’s side is easier to trace. Transaction ledgers record the $1.5 million cash payment and the conditional 2012 second-rounder, with the pick marked as not exercised. Cash has value, especially on a night when the Timberwolves were repeatedly moving draft rights, but it did not create a player or future selection for the franchise from this particular exchange. The contrast is sharper because Parsons was not a speculative rights stash; he joined Houston that same year and became a starter almost immediately.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grades Stay Conservative Despite a Clear Result
sections.body: Houston’s canonical B and Minnesota’s D+ are milder than the outcome gap might suggest, and the editorial should preserve those grades rather than rewrite the record with hindsight. The Rockets paid real cash for a second-round player who had not yet appeared in the NBA, so the acquisition still carried normal draft uncertainty. Once the result is known, however, the verdict is straightforward: Houston obtained multiple seasons of starter-level production, while Minnesota’s conditional pick never conveyed. The Rockets won the transaction without needing any downstream asset theory to make the case.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston B, Minnesota D+. Houston reacquired the draft rights to Chandler Parsons for $1.5 million and a conditional second-round pick that did not convey. Parsons then started 207 regular-season games across three seasons for the Rockets, including full-time starting roles in 2012-13 and 2013-14. Minnesota realized the cash but no lasting basketball asset from the conditional pick. The canonical grades are intentionally conservative, but the completed outcome favors Houston because a low-cost draft-rights purchase became a productive starting wing.

sections.heading: New Orleans Turned Its Only Draft Pick Into Cash
sections.body: New Orleans used the No. 45 pick in the 2011 draft on Josh Harrellson and then sent his rights to New York for cash. Contemporary reporting framed the move as a deliberate decision by the Hornets after the players they preferred were no longer available. General manager Dell Demps said the club chose the cash and intended to pursue other ways to improve the roster. That makes the trade easier to understand on draft night even though the basketball return was intentionally limited.

sections.heading: The Knicks Got a Real Rookie Rotation Player
sections.body: Harrellson gave New York useful value almost immediately. Basketball-Reference credits him with 37 games, four starts and 540 minutes during the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season. He averaged 4.4 points and 3.9 rebounds in 14.6 minutes per game, then appeared in four playoff games. Those numbers are modest, but they are meaningful for a second-round rights purchase made entirely with cash rather than another player or future draft asset.

sections.heading: His Knicks Tenure Lasted One Season, but the Rights Still Produced Value
sections.body: Harrellson did not become a long-term Knicks piece. New York included him with Toney Douglas, Jerome Jordan and future second-round picks in the July 2012 sign-and-trade that brought Marcus Camby from Houston. Harrellson was therefore part of the Knicks for only one season, and his individual value inside the later package cannot be isolated from the other assets. The direct 2011-12 rotation minutes remain the safest evidence for grading this transaction.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Stay Modest
sections.body: New Orleans received cash and avoided attaching any additional basketball asset, so a C+ is more appropriate than treating the sale as a major loss. The exact cash amount is not needed to judge the basic outcome because the Hornets knowingly exchanged a mid-second-round opportunity for financial flexibility. New York’s B reflects the fact that Harrellson became a useful rookie reserve without turning into a lasting starter or major trade chip. The Knicks still earned the better return because they converted cash into actual NBA minutes and playoff availability.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New Orleans C+, New York B. The Hornets sold the No. 45 pick after deciding the remaining draft board did not justify keeping the selection, so their side was a conscious cash-for-rights decision rather than an accidental loss of an asset. New York turned that purchase into 37 regular-season games, four starts and a small playoff role from Josh Harrellson before moving him in the Marcus Camby package the following summer. The payoff was modest, but it was tangible enough to give the Knicks the better result.

sections.heading: Miami Paid a Multi-Asset Price to Get Norris Cole
sections.body: Miami moved aggressively for the No. 28 pick after the 2011 draft. The Heat sent Minnesota the rights to Bojan Bogdanovic, a future second-round pick and cash for the rights to Norris Cole. That price was more than a simple pick swap, but it targeted an immediate backcourt need for a team already built around championship contention. Cole joined the rotation right away rather than functioning as a future stash or developmental project.

sections.heading: Cole Became a Reliable Piece of Two Championship Teams
sections.body: The basketball return for Miami is easy to document. Cole played all 65 regular-season games as a rookie, then appeared in 80 games in 2012-13 and all 82 in 2013-14. He averaged 19.4 minutes per game in his first season and remained a regular reserve through three straight Finals runs. Basketball-Reference lists him as a two-time NBA champion, so the Heat converted the deal directly into usable rotation minutes during the franchise’s most successful stretch.

sections.heading: Minnesota Converted Bogdanovic Again and Kept the Extra Pick
sections.body: Minnesota did not hold Bogdanovic’s rights for long. The Timberwolves moved those rights to New Jersey on the same draft night for cash and a 2013 second-round pick, while also keeping the future second-rounder received from Miami. That means the Wolves turned the Cole transaction into several separate assets rather than one player. The 2014 Miami second-rounder eventually became the No. 44 pick used on Markel Brown, giving the package another realized draft outcome.

sections.heading: The Outcome Is Closer Than the Player Names Suggest
sections.body: Bojan Bogdanovic eventually became the best NBA player associated with the exchange, but Minnesota did not keep his rights long enough to receive that production. Miami, meanwhile, got immediate value from Cole and used him throughout two title runs. The canonical B+ for Miami therefore fits the direct result. Minnesota’s A- reflects the larger package and the extra asset conversion, but the verdict should stay narrow because the Wolves’ benefit came through draft capital and cash rather than years of Bogdanovic production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge — Miami B+, Minnesota A-. Miami gave up the rights to Bojan Bogdanovic, a future second-round pick and cash to secure Norris Cole, then received three-plus seasons of regular rotation play and two championship rings with Cole on the roster. Minnesota immediately converted Bogdanovic’s rights into another second-round pick and cash while retaining Miami’s future second-rounder. The Wolves assembled the broader asset return, but Cole’s real contribution to a title contender keeps the gap small rather than turning this into a one-sided hindsight result.

sections.heading: Minnesota Traded a Future Pick for Draft Rights
sections.body: Four days after the 2011 draft, Minnesota sent Portland a future second-round pick for the rights to Tanguy Ngombo, the No. 57 selection. Portland had acquired Ngombo’s rights from Dallas during its draft-night three-team transaction, then moved them to the Timberwolves. The deal was a straightforward bet on an international prospect: Minnesota surrendered a distant pick whose exact draft position was still unknown in exchange for a player it could hold outside the NBA roster.

sections.heading: Ngombo Never Produced NBA Value for the Timberwolves
sections.body: The rights never turned into NBA minutes for Minnesota. RealGM’s draft history lists Ngombo with zero NBA seasons, and his professional career continued overseas rather than with the Timberwolves. That leaves Minnesota’s side with no realized NBA production from the acquired asset. The original idea still had some logic because the cost was deferred, but the completed outcome gives the franchise nothing tangible to offset the future pick it surrendered.

sections.heading: The Pick Eventually Became No. 37 in the 2015 Draft
sections.body: Basketball-Reference traces the outgoing pick to the 2015 second round, where it became the No. 37 selection used on Richaun Holmes. The important point for this transaction is the pick value itself, not every later move involving Holmes. Portland had converted draft rights that did not generate NBA value for Minnesota into a future second-round asset that ultimately landed near the top of the round. That is a materially better realized return than a dormant rights holding.

sections.heading: Portland’s Advantage Is Clear Even Without Overcrediting Holmes
sections.body: The canonical A for Portland and D+ for Minnesota reflect a wide outcome gap, but the analysis should stop at assets directly tied to this deal. Portland did not necessarily keep or develop every ounce of value associated with Holmes, and hindsight should not pretend the Blazers were guaranteed to make the same selection. Even with that restraint, the transaction worked in Portland’s favor: it exchanged Ngombo’s rights for a future pick that conveyed at No. 37, while Minnesota received no NBA production from Ngombo.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Minnesota D+, Portland A. Minnesota gave up a future second-round pick for the rights to Tanguy Ngombo, but those rights never produced NBA minutes for the Timberwolves. The pick conveyed in 2015 at No. 37, creating real draft value for Portland’s side of the transaction. The grade gap does not depend on assigning the Blazers every later accomplishment of Richaun Holmes; the direct comparison is enough. Portland received a valuable early-second-round asset, while Minnesota’s acquired rights generated no NBA return.

sections.heading: The Three-Team Structure Was Built Around Tyson Chandler
sections.body: The December 2011 transaction was essentially a sign-and-trade pathway for Tyson Chandler to New York, with Washington helping complete the asset routing. The Knicks received Chandler plus the draft rights to Ahmad Nivins and Giorgos Printezis. Dallas received Andy Rautins, a protected 2012 second-round pick from Washington that did not convey, and a large trade exception. Washington received Ronny Turiaf, cash, New York’s 2013 second-round pick and Dallas’ 2012 second-round pick while sending out only the protected pick.

sections.heading: Chandler Immediately Justified New York’s Side
sections.body: Chandler’s first Knicks season produced the clearest result in the deal. The NBA named him the 2011-12 Defensive Player of the Year, making him the first Knick to win the award. New York’s defense improved with Chandler anchoring the middle, and he remained a central starter through the 54-win 2012-13 season. The rights pieces were secondary; the Knicks acquired the one asset in the transaction that became an immediate high-impact NBA player.

sections.heading: Dallas Gained Flexibility but Lost the Best Basketball Asset
sections.body: Dallas’ return was built more around financial flexibility than player value. Rautins did not become a Mavericks contributor, and the protected Washington second-rounder did not convey. The trade exception was real value and was used immediately as part of the mechanism that allowed Dallas to acquire Lamar Odom, but the Mavericks still had to send a future first-round pick in that separate deal. That makes it inappropriate to credit the Chandler trade with Odom as if he were a direct return.

sections.heading: Washington Quietly Collected a Useful Package
sections.body: Washington’s B is supported by the amount of value it collected for participating in the structure. The Wizards added Turiaf, cash and two second-round picks while the protected pick they sent Dallas never conveyed. One of the incoming selections became the No. 46 pick in 2012 and the other became No. 54 in 2013. The package did not approach Chandler’s impact, but Washington turned its role as facilitator into multiple concrete assets without giving up a comparable player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — Dallas D+, New York A, Washington B. New York acquired Tyson Chandler and immediately received Defensive Player of the Year production from the centerpiece of the trade. Dallas created financial flexibility, but its direct player and protected-pick return produced little lasting basketball value compared with the championship center it sent away. Washington did well as the third team, collecting Turiaf, cash and two second-round picks. The strongest realized value still belongs to the Knicks because Chandler was both the most important asset on trade day and the best direct NBA outcome afterward.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought High on the Reigning Sixth Man of the Year
sections.body: Dallas acquired Lamar Odom from the Lakers on December 11, 2011, one day after creating the large trade exception in the Tyson Chandler sign-and-trade. Odom had just won the 2010-11 Sixth Man of the Year award and had been a major part of two Los Angeles championship teams, so the idea was easy to understand for the defending champions. The Mavericks sent a protected first-round pick while also receiving a 2012 second-round pick and future second-round considerations. On trade day, it looked like Dallas had turned cap flexibility into a proven veteran without breaking up its remaining core.

sections.heading: Odom's Dallas Season Collapsed Almost Immediately
sections.body: The basketball return never came close to the expectation. Odom played 50 games for Dallas, started four and averaged 6.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists while shooting 35.2 percent from the field. Basketball-Reference shows a sharp fall from his final Lakers season, when he averaged 14.4 points and 8.7 rebounds. The Mavericks and Odom separated before the postseason, leaving Dallas with no playoff contribution from the centerpiece of the trade and only a short, ineffective regular-season stint.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Preserved Asset Value and Gained a Large Exception
sections.body: The Lakers' return was not a star replacement, but it was more durable. ESPN reported that Los Angeles received an $8.9 million trade exception and a protected first-round pick, while the canonical ledger also tracks the 2013 second-round swap option as not exercised. The first eventually conveyed in 2014 and became the No. 21 pick associated with Mitch McGary. Los Angeles did not need that pick to produce a franchise player for the exchange to grade well; it converted an unhappy veteran into real draft capital and financial flexibility while Dallas absorbed the downside.

sections.heading: The Outcome Was Lopsided Even Without Overstating the Pick
sections.body: The fairest reading does not pretend Los Angeles replaced Odom's prior championship production through one draft pick. What matters is that Dallas paid first-round value for a player who delivered 50 poor regular-season games and did not appear in the playoffs, while the Lakers exited with an exception and a protected first that ultimately conveyed. The unused second-round swap and the No. 55 pick Dallas received add context but do not change the result. The canonical F for Dallas and B+ for Los Angeles fit the completed asset record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Dallas F, LA Lakers B+. Dallas acquired Lamar Odom expecting championship-level versatility from the reigning Sixth Man of the Year, but his Mavericks season produced 6.6 points per game across 50 appearances and ended before the playoffs. The additional second-round assets did little to offset that failure. Los Angeles received an $8.9 million trade exception and a protected first-round pick that later conveyed in 2014. The Lakers did not recreate Odom's peak with those assets, but they preserved useful value while Dallas spent a first-round asset on a one-season experiment that never worked.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned One Fringe Wing Into Multiple Chances
sections.body: Minnesota sent Lazar Hayward to Oklahoma City on December 13, 2011 and received Robert Vaden plus two second-round assets. The immediate player swap was modest: neither Hayward nor Vaden projected as a core piece. The draft compensation changed the equation. One pick became the No. 58 selection in 2012, which the Timberwolves used on Robbie Hummel, while the conditional follow-up became the No. 59 asset in 2013 associated with Bojan Dubljevic. Minnesota effectively traded one end-of-rotation player for several low-cost chances to find usable value.

sections.heading: Hummel Supplied the Only Durable NBA Return From the Deal
sections.body: The most useful outcome was Robbie Hummel. Basketball-Reference credits him with 98 games and nine starts for Minnesota across the 2013-14 and 2014-15 seasons after spending his first post-draft year in Spain. He averaged 3.9 points and 2.7 rebounds in a reserve role. Those numbers are modest, but they still represent tangible multi-season NBA production from a late second-round pick. Robert Vaden did not become an NBA contributor, while Dubljevic never played in the league.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Got a Short Hayward Stint
sections.body: Oklahoma City acquired Hayward as a depth option for a contender. He appeared in 26 regular-season games for the Thunder in 2011-12 and averaged fewer than six minutes per game, then played five postseason games during the run to the NBA Finals. The role had some immediate utility, especially compared with Vaden's lack of NBA minutes, but it was brief. Hayward was waived before the following season, so Oklahoma City did not receive a lasting rotation piece for the two draft assets it sent out.

sections.heading: The Wolves Edge Comes From Modest Value, Not a Hidden Jackpot
sections.body: This transaction should not be inflated into a major win. Minnesota's best return was a useful reserve who played 98 games, while Oklahoma City received a fringe contributor for part of one season and a Finals run. Still, the Timberwolves created more realized value from the package and retained additional draft optionality. The canonical B+ for Minnesota and C+ for Oklahoma City are appropriately measured: neither side changed its franchise trajectory, but Minnesota converted a replaceable player into the better aggregate return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B+, Oklahoma City C+. Minnesota sent Lazar Hayward to the Thunder and received Robert Vaden plus second-round assets that produced Robbie Hummel and the rights associated with Bojan Dubljevic. Hummel later played 98 NBA games for the Timberwolves, giving Minnesota the transaction's most durable realized contribution. Hayward appeared in 26 regular-season games and five playoff games for Oklahoma City before his tenure ended. The gap is modest, but Minnesota extracted more useful value from a low-level exchange and deserves the higher grade.

sections.heading: New Orleans Solved a Point-Guard Need With Greivis Vasquez
sections.body: The Christmas Eve 2011 swap was a straight player-for-player deal: New Orleans sent Quincy Pondexter to Memphis and received Greivis Vasquez. The Hornets were short on experienced point guards after the Chris Paul trade, and the move gave them an immediate ball-handler without spending another draft asset. Vasquez played all 66 games in the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season, started 26, then moved into the full-time starting job the next year. The transaction matched a clear roster need and quickly produced a larger role than New Orleans had been getting from Pondexter.

sections.heading: Vasquez Became a Full-Time Starter and a Major Creator
sections.body: Vasquez's second New Orleans season created the gap in the deal. The Pelicans' franchise media guide credits him with 78 starts in 2012-13, 13.9 points per game and 704 assists. Across his two seasons with the franchise, he logged 144 games, 104 starts and 1,063 assists. He was not a franchise centerpiece, but New Orleans turned a reserve wing into a starting point guard who handled a large share of the offense and then retained trade value when the roster changed again in 2013.

sections.heading: Memphis Still Got Real Rotation Value From Pondexter
sections.body: This was not a one-sided failure for Memphis. The Grizzlies' media guide credits Pondexter with 168 regular-season games over parts of four seasons, including 59 appearances in 2012-13 while shooting 39.5 percent from three. He fit the defensive, low-usage wing role Memphis needed around its core and was part of multiple playoff teams. Injuries later interrupted his run, but the Grizzlies received useful rotation minutes rather than an empty return. That is why the canonical B- is much more appropriate than treating the deal as a major loss.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Role, Production and Preserved Value
sections.body: Both players helped their new teams, but Vasquez had the stronger realized outcome. New Orleans received a starter and lead passer for two seasons, then included him in the 2013 multi-team transaction that brought Tyreke Evans to the franchise. Pondexter was a useful wing in Memphis, yet he never held an equivalent offensive role and his availability became uneven. The canonical grades capture that distinction without exaggerating it: New Orleans won the exchange, while Memphis still received a credible contributor who fit its contending roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — Memphis B-, New Orleans A-. Greivis Vasquez became a full-time starter in New Orleans, produced 704 assists in 2012-13 and later retained value in the Tyreke Evans transaction. Quincy Pondexter gave Memphis legitimate wing depth, including a strong three-point season in 2012-13, so the Grizzlies did not come away empty. The difference is that Vasquez carried a much larger role and delivered more immediate creation before becoming another usable transaction asset. New Orleans earned the better result, but both teams received meaningful NBA value.

sections.heading: Cleveland Sold a Short-Term Guard for Draft Capital
sections.body: Cleveland moved Ramon Sessions and Christian Eyenga to the Lakers at the 2012 trade deadline and took back Luke Walton, Jason Kapono, cash, a lottery-protected 2012 first-round pick and the right to swap a 2013 first. The veterans were not the point of the transaction. Cleveland was rebuilding, Sessions could opt out after the season, and the Cavaliers used the deal to convert a useful guard into additional draft control. The structure matched the franchise's timeline far better than simply keeping Sessions through a losing season.

sections.heading: The 2012 First Helped Cleveland Move Up for Tyler Zeller
sections.body: The Lakers' 2012 first conveyed at No. 24, where Cleveland selected Jared Cunningham. One day later, the Cavaliers packaged Cunningham with Jae Crowder and Bernard James in a draft-night deal with Dallas for Kelenna Azubuike and the rights to Tyler Zeller, the No. 17 pick. Zeller became a regular Cleveland starter over the next two seasons. The incoming first therefore created more value than Cunningham's own NBA career suggests because Cleveland immediately used it as part of a move up the board.

sections.heading: The 2013 Swap Produced Another First-Round Upgrade
sections.body: Cleveland also exercised the 2013 swap right. Basketball-Reference records the Cavaliers moving from the least favorable first they controlled to the Lakers' No. 19 slot, which became Sergey Karasev, while Los Angeles ended up with the No. 30 asset associated with Nemanja Nedovic. Karasev was not a major NBA success, but the mechanism still delivered exactly what a rebuilding team wanted: another opportunity to improve draft position. Walton contributed veteran minutes, while Kapono was waived almost immediately, so the draft pieces carried the long-term case.

sections.heading: Sessions Helped the Lakers, but Only for One Postseason Run
sections.body: Los Angeles did get useful short-term production. Sessions played 23 regular-season games for the Lakers, started 19 and averaged 12.7 points with 6.2 assists, then started all 12 playoff games as the team reached the second round. That immediate help keeps the Lakers' side from grading as a disaster. The problem is duration: Sessions left after the season, Eyenga barely played, and Los Angeles surrendered both a first-round pick and a valuable swap right for a point guard rental. Cleveland retained the stronger aggregate value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, LA Lakers C+. The Lakers got a productive 23-game run from Ramon Sessions and used him as a playoff starter, so the deal addressed an immediate need. Cleveland, however, turned a player with an uncertain future into a 2012 first-round pick, a 2013 first-round swap, cash and salary ballast. The 2012 pick became part of the Tyler Zeller draft-night package, and Cleveland exercised the 2013 swap for the No. 19 slot. Los Angeles bought short-term help; Cleveland acquired multiple pieces of rebuild capital and won the transaction on lasting value.

sections.heading: San Antonio Paid a First to Reshape a Contender
sections.body: San Antonio used the 2012 trade deadline to turn Richard Jefferson, the injured T.J. Ford and a protected first-round pick into Stephen Jackson. The Spurs were already contending and valued Jackson's familiarity with Gregg Popovich's system, while moving Jefferson also changed the financial shape of the roster. Golden State took on the longer contract and received the draft asset as the price. The exchange was therefore built around two different timelines: San Antonio wanted immediate playoff help, while the Warriors were willing to absorb salary for a future first.

sections.heading: Jackson Gave the Spurs the Immediate Wing Help They Wanted
sections.body: Jackson joined a 50-win team and played 21 regular-season games for San Antonio, averaging 8.9 points, 3.9 rebounds and 2.0 assists in a reserve role. He then appeared in 14 playoff games as the Spurs swept their first two series and reached the Western Conference Finals. The stay did not become a long second Spurs chapter, and the team waived him late the following season, but the 2012 return was useful at exactly the point San Antonio had targeted. That short-term contribution is a major reason the canonical grade remains an A.

sections.heading: Golden State's First Became Festus Ezeli
sections.body: The draft pick gave Golden State its lasting return. The Warriors used the No. 30 selection in 2012 on Festus Ezeli, who went on to play 170 regular-season games for the franchise and appeared in 55 playoff games. Ezeli was part of the 2015 championship roster and supplied frontcourt minutes during the early rise of the Stephen Curry-era contender. T.J. Ford was waived almost immediately and never played for Golden State, while Jefferson filled a smaller veteran role across parts of two seasons before moving on.

sections.heading: Both Teams Created Value, Which Makes the Margin Small
sections.body: This is one of the cases where hindsight can support strong grades on both sides. San Antonio sacrificed a first but received an immediate playoff rotation player and moved off Jefferson's contract while pursuing another title run. Golden State accepted the salary burden and turned the attached pick into a center who later contributed to a championship team. The Spurs' benefit arrived sooner and directly served a contender, while the Warriors' best value took time to develop. That balance fits the canonical slight San Antonio edge rather than a sweeping win for either franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge — Golden State A-, San Antonio A. Stephen Jackson gave the Spurs immediate rotation and playoff value during a 2012 run to the Western Conference Finals, which fit San Antonio's win-now purpose. Golden State still did very well by receiving the first-round pick that became Festus Ezeli, a future championship rotation center, while Richard Jefferson supplied additional veteran minutes. The trade produced useful value on both timelines. San Antonio gets the narrow edge for converting its outgoing package into immediate contender help, but Golden State's long-term return keeps the grades close.

sections.heading: Minnesota Bought a Known Fit Before the Draft
sections.body: Minnesota sent the No. 18 pick in the 2012 draft to Houston for Chase Budinger and the draft rights to Lior Eliyahu. Budinger was not a mystery to the Timberwolves. He had played for Rick Adelman in Houston, shot 40.2 percent from three in 2011-12 and was entering his age-24 season. The Wolves were trying to add shooting and athleticism around Kevin Love and Ricky Rubio, so the logic was immediate rather than developmental. Houston took the opposite approach by turning a useful veteran wing into a first-round swing.

sections.heading: Budinger Helped, but Injuries Limited the Original Plan
sections.body: Budinger's Minnesota tenure never became the breakout the Wolves hoped for, largely because injuries interrupted his first two seasons. Basketball-Reference credits him with 23 games in 2012-13 and 41 in 2013-14 before he reached 67 appearances in 2014-15. Across those three seasons he played 131 games for Minnesota, usually as a reserve floor-spacer. The production was useful rather than transformative, but it gave the Wolves multiple seasons of NBA minutes from the primary player they acquired.

sections.heading: The Eliyahu Rights Eventually Produced Another NBA Return
sections.body: The unusual part of Minnesota's package lasted far longer than Budinger. Lior Eliyahu never played in the NBA, but the Wolves retained his draft rights for seven years. In July 2019, Minnesota traded those rights to Golden State and received Shabazz Napier and Treveon Graham. That later transaction does not retroactively turn Eliyahu into a star asset, but it does mean the rights were not dead inventory. They ultimately generated two more NBA players, giving the original 2012 return a small additional layer of realized value.

sections.heading: Houston Has a Strong Counterargument in Terrence Jones
sections.body: Houston used the No. 18 pick on Terrence Jones, and his best stretch was better than Budinger's Minnesota peak. Jones started 71 games in 2013-14 while averaging 12.1 points and 6.9 rebounds, then remained a productive frontcourt piece when healthy over the next two seasons. His Rockets tenure was also shortened by injuries and ended after 2015-16 without another major asset coming back. The canonical grading gives Minnesota only a slight edge, which fits a deal where both teams received legitimate value and neither side found a lasting cornerstone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge — Houston C, Minnesota C+. Houston turned the No. 18 pick into Terrence Jones, who produced the highest individual season in the transaction and started 71 games in 2013-14. Minnesota received three seasons of Chase Budinger and preserved value in Lior Eliyahu's rights long enough to use them in the 2019 acquisition of Shabazz Napier and Treveon Graham. The result is close and debatable, but the canonical grades favor Minnesota's broader realized package by a narrow margin rather than treating Houston's productive draft pick as a miss.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Moved Down Two Spots and Added a Starting Center
sections.body: Milwaukee sent the No. 12 pick in the 2012 draft plus Jon Brockman, Shaun Livingston and Jon Leuer to Houston for Samuel Dalembert, cash, the No. 14 pick and a future second-rounder. The Bucks only moved down two places in the first round, which limited the draft cost while adding a veteran center and another future asset. Houston was making a different calculation: the Rockets wanted to move up for Jeremy Lamb and were willing to attach Dalembert plus secondary consideration to get there.

sections.heading: John Henson Gave Milwaukee Years of Frontcourt Value
sections.body: Milwaukee used the No. 14 pick on John Henson, and that became the most durable direct return in the transaction. Henson played regularly for the Bucks from 2012 through 2018, developing from a reserve into a 69-game starter in 2017-18 while providing rebounding and rim protection. His first six full seasons alone produced hundreds of appearances for Milwaukee. The additional second-round pick later became the No. 54 selection associated with Nemanja Dangubic, while Dalembert supplied 47 games and 23 starts in 2012-13.

sections.heading: Houston's Real Value Was Jeremy Lamb's Place in the Harden Package
sections.body: Jeremy Lamb never played a regular-season game for Houston, but that does not mean the No. 12 pick produced nothing. Four months after the draft, the Rockets included Lamb with Kevin Martin, two first-round picks and a second-round pick in the deal for James Harden, Cole Aldrich, Daequan Cook and Lazar Hayward. Lamb therefore carried real transaction value into one of the franchise's defining moves. The important limit is attribution: Houston did not acquire Harden for Lamb alone, so the entire Harden outcome cannot be assigned to this one draft-night trade.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Broader Direct Return Supports the Canonical Edge
sections.body: The Rockets created strategic value by moving up for an asset later used in the Harden trade, which is why a B is defensible. Milwaukee still came away with the stronger direct package. Henson became a long-term rotation big, Dalembert gave the Bucks a season of center minutes, the future second survived as another draft asset, and Milwaukee received cash while only sliding from No. 12 to No. 14. Brockman, Livingston and Leuer did not become comparable Houston contributors. The canonical A- for Milwaukee reflects the depth and duration of the realized return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Houston B, Milwaukee A-. Houston moved up from No. 14 to No. 12 for Jeremy Lamb, and Lamb soon became one component of the package that brought James Harden to the Rockets. That gives Houston genuine downstream value, but it should not be treated as if Lamb alone acquired Harden. Milwaukee received the No. 14 pick used on John Henson, Samuel Dalembert, a future second-round pick and cash. Henson became a long-term Bucks rotation big, while Dalembert contributed for a season. Milwaukee's deeper direct return earns the higher canonical grade.

sections.heading: Miami Traded the No. 27 Pick for a Longer Asset Chain
sections.body: Miami selected Arnett Moultrie at No. 27 in the 2012 draft and immediately sent his rights to Philadelphia. In return, the Heat received the rights to Justin Hamilton plus a protected future first-round obligation. The protection was important: if Philadelphia stayed inside the protected range through 2015, the obligation would convert into second-round picks instead. That is ultimately what happened. The trade therefore became less about one first-rounder for another and more about whether Philadelphia could extract enough from Moultrie to justify giving Miami multiple chances at later value.

sections.heading: Moultrie Never Developed Into the Rotation Piece Philadelphia Expected
sections.body: Moultrie played 59 NBA games, all for Philadelphia, and averaged 3.6 points and 3.1 rebounds. He appeared in 47 games as a rookie but only 12 the following season, and his NBA career ended after two years. That is a thin return for a team that moved up to secure a first-round prospect. Philadelphia did get real minutes from him, so this was not a zero-value outcome, but the production never approached the level needed to erase the future draft cost.

sections.heading: Hamilton Gave Miami Some NBA Minutes and the Pick Obligation Kept Paying
sections.body: Hamilton eventually reached Miami and appeared in 31 games across two seasons for the franchise, including 24 games and five starts in 2014-15. His role was modest, but it still gave the Heat direct NBA value from the player-rights portion of the package. More importantly, Philadelphia's protected first never conveyed as a first-rounder. The obligation converted into two second-round selections, tied in the canonical ledger to the 2015 No. 33 pick that became Jordan Mickey and the 2016 No. 31 pick that became Deyonta Davis.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Comes From Optionality and Realized Depth
sections.body: Miami did not uncover a star here, and the later second-round names should not be treated as if the Heat personally developed every downstream outcome. The advantage is simpler. Miami moved one late first-round prospect who produced 59 low-minute NBA games and received a player who later contributed in Miami plus a protected asset that survived long enough to become two additional selections. Philadelphia paid the larger opportunity cost for the weaker completed return. The canonical A- for Miami and D+ for Philadelphia reflect that imbalance without turning a secondary draft-night trade into something larger than it was.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami A-, Philadelphia D+. The 76ers acquired Arnett Moultrie, who played 59 NBA games and averaged 3.6 points before his league career ended. Miami received Justin Hamilton, who later appeared in 31 games for the Heat, plus a protected future first-round obligation that eventually converted into two second-round picks. The Heat did not land a franchise-changing player, but they turned one late first-round draft right into more playable depth and substantially more asset optionality. Philadelphia paid first-round value for a player whose impact never justified the cost.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid Two Seconds to Create Immediate Cap Room
sections.body: This July 13, 2012 NBA roster transaction was primarily a salary-clearing move for Minnesota. The Timberwolves sent veteran center Brad Miller's contract and two future second-round selections to the franchise then known as the New Orleans Hornets, receiving only a heavily protected 2017 second-rounder in return. Minnesota's own announcement said the move helped create room for an offer sheet to restricted free agent Nicolas Batum. That context explains why the Wolves accepted a weak asset return: the primary benefit was financial flexibility in July 2012, not the expectation that the incoming selection would become a player.

sections.heading: The Incoming Minnesota Pick Never Conveyed
sections.body: The protection ultimately erased Minnesota's only incoming draft asset. Basketball-Reference records the 2017 second-round selection as conditional and not conveyed. That left the Wolves with no player or realized selection from this transaction itself. Miller was near the end of his career and did not provide long-term value to the other side, but Minnesota also surrendered the 2013 second-rounder later associated with Lorenzo Brown and a 2016 second-rounder later associated with Rade Zagorac. Even without assigning those players directly to New Orleans, the selections retained transaction value.

sections.heading: New Orleans Reused the Package Two Weeks Later
sections.body: The Hornets did not simply sit on the outgoing pieces. On July 27, New Orleans rerouted Miller's contract and the 2016 second-round selection to Phoenix while sending the 2013 second-round selection back to Minnesota inside the three-team Robin Lopez-Hakim Warrick transaction. The franchise transaction history confirms that sequence. This is the strongest reason the counterparty grades well: the July 13 package became usable roster-building currency almost immediately, while the protected selection sent to Minnesota never produced anything. The value was transactional rather than a direct on-court contribution from Miller.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grade Reflects the Cost of a Cap-Space Bet
sections.body: Minnesota's C+ is not an indictment of clearing Miller's contract by itself. The front office was trying to open room for Batum, and salary flexibility can justify attaching draft capital. The hindsight problem is that the only incoming selection disappeared under its protection while the two outgoing seconds remained useful enough to be moved again. The canonical B+ for the Hornets franchise and C+ for Minnesota appropriately captures that imbalance. It was a modest NBA transaction, but New Orleans preserved more practical value from assets Minnesota treated as the cost of creating space.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win — Minnesota C+, Charlotte B+. The canonical franchise label is Charlotte, although the team was the New Orleans Hornets when the NBA transaction occurred. Minnesota sent Miller's contract plus 2013 and 2016 second-round selections to clear cap space and received a protected 2017 second-rounder that never conveyed. New Orleans then reused the acquired pieces in the July 27 Robin Lopez-Hakim Warrick transaction. Minnesota had a defensible short-term cap objective, but the completed asset record favors the Hornets franchise because its package retained immediate roster-building utility while the Wolves' only incoming draft asset produced no realized value.

sections.heading: New York Turned a Broad Asset Package Into a Starting Point Guard
sections.body: The July 2012 sign-and-trade brought Raymond Felton back to New York along with Kurt Thomas. Portland received Jared Jeffries, Dan Gadzuric, the draft rights to Kostas Papanikolaou and Giorgos Printezis, a protected future second-round pick and cash. The outgoing package looked large on paper, but much of it consisted of rights, reserve contracts and future optionality. New York's goal was immediate: install a proven point guard for a veteran roster trying to win in 2012-13.

sections.heading: Felton Supplied Real Rotation Value on a 54-Win Team
sections.body: Felton started all 68 games he played in 2012-13 and averaged 13.9 points and 5.5 assists. He also started all 12 postseason games, averaging 14.1 points and 4.7 assists as New York reached the second round. That is the clearest realized value in the transaction. Thomas was a smaller piece, but Felton gave the Knicks two seasons of starting point-guard minutes before he was moved again in the 2014 Tyson Chandler deal.

sections.heading: Portland Collected Optionality Rather Than Immediate Production
sections.body: The Trail Blazers did not get comparable on-court value from the veterans. Jeffries was a limited reserve, while Gadzuric did not make the regular-season roster. Portland's better outcomes came from the non-roster assets. Papanikolaou remained a meaningful international prospect and his rights were later moved to Houston, while the package also included Printezis' rights, a future second-round selection and cash. That gave Portland several ways to recycle value, even though none matched Felton's direct contribution to New York.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Rewards Proven Impact Without Ignoring Portland's Asset Work
sections.body: New York's B+ and Portland's C+ fit the completed record. The Knicks surrendered more pieces, but the best player value in the transaction was Felton's role on the 2012-13 Atlantic Division winner and playoff team. Portland deserves credit for turning a departing Felton into multiple assets instead of losing him for nothing, which keeps the result from being a lopsided verdict. The difference is that New York received the most useful NBA production tied directly to this transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B+, Portland C+. Raymond Felton became New York's starting point guard immediately, started 68 games during a 54-win regular season and remained in that role throughout the 2013 playoff run. Portland received several contracts, draft rights, a future second-round pick and cash, and Papanikolaou's rights retained later transaction value. The Trail Blazers did reasonable asset work for a player who was leaving, but New York secured the strongest realized return: a two-year starter who helped a veteran contender win its division and reach the second round.

Kostas Papanikolaou Named Rising Star Of Euroleague

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Several Assets for One Reserve
sections.body: Cleveland sent Jon Leuer to Memphis on January 22, 2013 and received Marreese Speights, Wayne Ellington, Josh Selby and a protected future first-round pick. The Cavaliers' own release emphasized both the added frontcourt and backcourt depth and the value of another future first. That made the transaction unusually favorable on asset count before hindsight even entered the picture. Memphis had a different objective: shedding salary responsibility as it worked below the luxury-tax line, so the Grizzlies accepted a lighter basketball return in exchange for financial relief.

sections.heading: Speights and Ellington Gave Cleveland Immediate NBA Minutes
sections.body: The veteran portion of Cleveland's return was useful right away. Speights appeared in 39 games for the Cavaliers after the trade and averaged 10.2 points and 5.1 rebounds in 18.4 minutes. Ellington also joined the rotation, while Selby was a smaller developmental piece. None became a long-term Cleveland cornerstone, but the deal still produced substantially more near-term playing value than the Cavaliers surrendered. Leuer played only 19 regular-season games for Memphis in 2012-13 before developing into a steadier reserve over the next two seasons.

sections.heading: The Memphis First Became the Most Important Piece
sections.body: The protected first-round pick extended the value well beyond 2013. Cleveland held the Memphis obligation until January 2015, then packaged it with another first-round pick to acquire Timofey Mozgov and a second-round selection from Denver. Cleveland's own coverage later described the broader sequence as turning Dion Waiters and the Memphis pick into J.R. Smith, Iman Shumpert and Mozgov. The Memphis pick eventually conveyed in 2017 at No. 20, but Cleveland had already converted its rights into a starting-caliber center for a team pursuing the championship.

sections.heading: Memphis Had a Financial Logic, but the Basketball Return Lagged
sections.body: Memphis did not make this move because Leuer was expected to equal the entire outgoing package. The Grizzlies were managing salary and soon made the larger Rudy Gay transaction as well. Leuer became a useful reserve, appearing in 49 games in 2013-14 and 63 in 2014-15, so Memphis did receive real NBA value. The problem is the opportunity cost. Cleveland received two productive rotation players plus the first-round asset later used in the Mozgov deal. That realized return supports the canonical A- for Cleveland and C+ for Memphis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, Memphis C+. Cleveland exchanged Jon Leuer and salary flexibility for Marreese Speights, Wayne Ellington, Josh Selby and a protected Memphis first-round pick. Speights gave the Cavaliers 39 productive games immediately, Ellington added rotation depth, and the future first later became part of the package that brought Timofey Mozgov to a contender. Memphis did get useful reserve seasons from Leuer and achieved its short-term financial objective, but the Grizzlies surrendered too much playable and transferable value for the completed basketball return to keep pace.

sections.heading: Miami Paid a Small Price to Open a Roster Spot
sections.body: Miami's deadline-day objective was roster flexibility. The Heat sent Dexter Pittman, a 2013 second-round pick and cash to Memphis for the draft rights to Ricky Sanchez. Pat Riley said directly that Miami needed flexibility and therefore had to move someone. Pittman had appeared in only four Heat games that season and was spending time with the Sioux Falls Skyforce, so this was not a rotation-breaking departure for the defending champions. The price was the draft pick and cash attached to clear the roster position.

sections.heading: Pittman Barely Contributed in Memphis
sections.body: The player portion of Memphis' return was short-lived. Pittman appeared in seven games for the Grizzlies, totaling 20 minutes, and was waived on April 14. That means the transaction was not a win because Memphis uncovered a useful center. The more durable value sat in the second-round pick. Miami received Sanchez's rights, but Sanchez never became an NBA contributor for the Heat, leaving the exchange with little direct basketball return on Miami's side.

sections.heading: The No. 60 Pick Created a Later Asset Chain
sections.body: Memphis used the 2013 second-rounder on Janis Timma with the No. 60 pick. Timma never played for the Grizzlies, but his rights retained value. In June 2015, Memphis sent those rights to Orlando for Luke Ridnour, then moved Ridnour to Charlotte for Matt Barnes. That downstream conversion is the strongest part of the Grizzlies' case. It does not turn a minor 2013 transaction into a blockbuster, but it shows that the draft asset Miami surrendered remained usable long after Pittman was gone.

sections.heading: The Grades Reflect Useful Optionality, Not Star Production
sections.body: The canonical B- for Memphis and C+ for Miami appropriately keep the result modest. Miami achieved the roster flexibility it wanted during a championship season, so the move was defensible in context. Memphis, however, received cash, a player it could evaluate and a second-round asset that later helped produce additional transaction value. Sanchez's rights did not create a comparable NBA outcome for Miami. The completed record therefore gives the Grizzlies a slight edge without overstating what was ultimately a small deadline trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge — Memphis B-, Miami C+. Dexter Pittman played only seven games for Memphis before being waived, so he was not the deciding factor. The better return came from the 2013 second-round pick, which became Janis Timma at No. 60 and later helped Memphis acquire Luke Ridnour before Ridnour was moved for Matt Barnes. Miami's goal was roster flexibility, and Ricky Sanchez's rights cost the Heat little immediate production, but those rights never generated comparable NBA value. Memphis extracted more usable optionality from a small transaction.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Paid a Late Second for Defensive Wing Insurance
sections.body: Oklahoma City acquired Ronnie Brewer at the 2013 deadline for its 2014 second-round pick and cash. The Thunder's own release framed Brewer as a defensive-minded, high-character veteran with playoff experience who could deepen the wing rotation. The cost was modest for a 60-win contender: one future second that ultimately landed at No. 59. New York, meanwhile, had seen Brewer fall out of its rotation after he opened the season as a starter, so converting a minimum-salary reserve into a pick and cash made sense.

sections.heading: Brewer's Actual Thunder Role Was Very Small
sections.body: The basketball return did not become a major piece of Oklahoma City's season. Brewer played 14 regular-season games for the Thunder, logged 142 total minutes and averaged 1.5 points. In the playoffs he appeared in only one game for 8:24 and did not play again during the run. That keeps the deal firmly in depth-move territory. Oklahoma City did not uncover a postseason stopper, but it acquired a veteran defender for a low draft price without disturbing the core of a team trying to contend immediately.

sections.heading: New York Turned the Pick Into Part of the Bargnani Package
sections.body: The second-rounder retained value after the deadline. It became the 2014 No. 59 selection, Xavier Thames, but New York did not use it itself. In July 2013 the Knicks sent that pick to Toronto with Steve Novak, Marcus Camby, Quentin Richardson, a 2016 first-round pick and a 2017 second-round pick for Andrea Bargnani. The later Bargnani transaction should not be charged entirely to this Brewer deal, yet it shows that the asset New York received was transferable rather than empty consideration.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grades Reward Cost Control More Than Production
sections.body: The B+ for Oklahoma City and B- for New York describe a narrow, situational edge rather than a large talent win. Brewer supplied only limited minutes, so the Thunder's case rests on acquiring experienced defensive depth at a late-second-round cost during a contention season. New York deserves credit for getting a real pick and cash for a player no longer central to its rotation. The difference is modest because neither side produced major standalone value, and the pick's later use occurred inside a separate, much larger transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Oklahoma City B+, New York B-. The Thunder paid a future second-round pick and cash for Ronnie Brewer, adding a veteran defender at a low acquisition cost, although Brewer ultimately played only 14 regular-season games and one playoff game for Oklahoma City. New York converted a diminished rotation player into a real asset: the 2014 No. 59 pick later used in the Andrea Bargnani package. The canonical edge stays with Oklahoma City because the price was small and the roster fit was defensible, but the completed return was close enough that this belongs among the narrower wins.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned the No. 9 Pick Into Two First-Round Prospects
sections.body: On draft night in 2013, Minnesota selected Trey Burke at No. 9 and immediately sent his rights to Utah for the rights to Shabazz Muhammad at No. 14 and Gorgui Dieng at No. 21. Utah's own release confirms the one-for-two structure. The move fit both teams' priorities at the time: the Jazz wanted a point guard badly enough to move up five spots, while the Timberwolves chose volume and positional variety. In hindsight, the extra first-round swing became the decisive feature because Dieng developed into the most durable player in the package.

sections.heading: Dieng Became the Trade's Most Valuable Long-Term Piece
sections.body: Gorgui Dieng spent seven seasons with Minnesota and appeared in 498 games for the franchise. He started all 82 games in 2016-17, averaged 7.9 points and 6.2 rebounds across his Timberwolves tenure, and provided years of dependable frontcourt minutes. Muhammad's contribution was shorter, but he still supplied useful bench scoring, including 13.5 points per game in 2014-15 and 10.5 in 2015-16. Minnesota did not hit twice at a star level, yet the combined return created far more sustained roster value than a typical draft-night split.

sections.heading: Burke Had a Real Utah Run, but It Never Matched the Price
sections.body: Trey Burke was not a bust in the sense of providing nothing. He played 210 games for Utah over three seasons, started 111 of them, averaged 12.1 points and 4.2 assists for the Jazz, and made the 2014 All-Rookie team. The problem is what Utah paid to secure that role. Burke's shooting efficiency was uneven, his starting role disappeared by year three, and the Jazz moved on after the 2015-16 season. That makes the direct comparison difficult for Utah: one useful but limited guard did not equal Minnesota's longer runway from Dieng plus Muhammad's secondary scoring.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is Driven by Depth, Durability and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Minnesota's A- does not require treating Muhammad as a major success or pretending Burke lacked NBA value. The winning case rests on turning one lottery selection into two rotation players and getting nearly 500 franchise games from Dieng alone. Utah's F reflects the opportunity cost of consolidating two first-round picks for a guard who never became a long-term starter there. This is exactly the kind of draft-night transaction where the number of bites matters only because one of them turned into sustained production. The Wolves extracted more years, more lineup utility and more total value from the same draft range.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota A-, Utah F. Utah acquired the rights to Trey Burke, who played 210 games for the Jazz and had a respectable three-year run, but the cost was the rights to Shabazz Muhammad and Gorgui Dieng. Muhammad delivered several seasons of bench scoring, while Dieng became the trade's anchor by playing 498 games for Minnesota and developing into a dependable long-term frontcourt piece. Burke's Utah tenure was useful rather than transformative, and the Jazz surrendered two first-round opportunities to get him. The canonical grades appropriately reward Minnesota for converting one selection into the deeper, longer-lasting package.

sections.heading: New York Paid a Premium for Two Injury-Hit Seasons of Bargnani
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Andrea Bargnani from Toronto on July 10, 2013 and sent Steve Novak, Marcus Camby, Quentin Richardson, two second-round selections and a future first-round mechanism the other way. New York was trying to add frontcourt scoring and floor spacing to a 54-win team, but the return never justified that price. Bargnani appeared in only 71 games across two seasons with the Knicks, starting 61, and averaged 13.9 points and 4.9 rebounds. His availability and overall impact were too limited for a deal carrying first-round capital.

sections.heading: Toronto's Best Asset Became the No. 9 Pick in 2016
sections.body: The veterans were not the lasting value for Toronto. Camby and Richardson did not become meaningful Raptors contributors, while Novak lasted one season before Toronto moved him to Utah with the 2017 second-round pick. The 2014 second-rounder also carried limited direct value. The centerpiece was the 2016 first-round obligation. Because of the pick-swap structure involving Denver and New York, Toronto ultimately received the No. 9 selection and used it on Jakob Poeltl. That alone gave the Raptors a young, controllable player from a contract Toronto had wanted to move.

sections.heading: Poeltl Extended the Asset Chain Into a Championship Trade
sections.body: Poeltl played two seasons in Toronto before becoming part of a much larger move. In July 2018, the Raptors sent DeMar DeRozan, Poeltl and a protected first-round pick to San Antonio for Kawhi Leonard and Danny Green. Leonard then led Toronto to the 2019 championship. The title should not be credited entirely to the 2013 Bargnani transaction, because DeRozan and the later first were major parts of the Leonard package. Still, Poeltl was a real, traceable asset produced by the first-round pick New York surrendered, and he retained enough value to enter that blockbuster five years later.

sections.heading: The A+ and F Grades Reflect Both Production and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Toronto's A+ is not based on pretending every outgoing piece became a star. It reflects escaping Bargnani's contract, obtaining multiple movable assets and eventually converting the first-round component into Poeltl. New York's F follows from the opposite side: the Knicks gave up a future lottery-level asset plus additional pieces for 71 games of uneven, injury-interrupted production. Even if New York would not have drafted Poeltl itself, surrendering that selection eliminated the opportunity. The completed record makes this one of the clearest asset-value losses of the era.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — New York F, Toronto A+. Bargnani gave the Knicks 71 games across two seasons, but New York surrendered three veteran contracts, two second-round selections and the first-round mechanism that became the No. 9 pick in 2016. Toronto used that pick on Jakob Poeltl, who later became part of the 2018 package for Kawhi Leonard and Danny Green. The Leonard trade required far more than Poeltl, so the championship cannot be assigned to this transaction alone. The direct comparison is still decisive: Toronto converted a declining contract into useful optionality and a lottery pick, while New York received too little production for the draft capital it spent.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned a Rotation Forward Into Future Draft Leverage
sections.body: Milwaukee moved Luc Mbah a Moute to Sacramento in July 2013 rather than carry a veteran forward into a retooling season. The Bucks received a conditional 2016 second-round asset tied to Sacramento and New Orleans plus a future 2019 second-round swap mechanism. On trade day, that was not an obvious star return. It was a package built around future draft flexibility for a player whose defensive value was clearer than his scoring ceiling. The later outcome is what pushes Milwaukee's grade so high.

sections.heading: The 2016 Pick Became Malcolm Brogdon
sections.body: The most important piece of the deal was the 2016 second-round selection that ultimately landed at No. 36. Milwaukee used it on Malcolm Brogdon. He immediately became a rotation player and won 2016-17 Rookie of the Year, then developed into a starting-caliber guard before later leaving the Bucks in a sign-and-trade. The original Mbah a Moute deal did not guarantee that result, but Brogdon is directly traceable to the acquired draft asset. That realized player value is the core reason Milwaukee's canonical grade reaches A+.

sections.heading: Sacramento Still Extracted Useful Value From Mbah a Moute
sections.body: Sacramento's side was not empty. Mbah a Moute gave the Kings a proven defensive wing and appeared in nine games before the franchise moved him to Minnesota in November 2013 for Derrick Williams. That quick resale matters because Sacramento did not simply lose the asset after a short stay; it converted him into another former No. 2 overall pick who remained on the roster beyond that season. The canonical B grade reflects a defensible acquisition and a second transaction that preserved some value even though the original return did not approach Milwaukee's eventual payoff.

sections.heading: The Pick-Swap Tail Adds More Depth to Milwaukee's Side
sections.body: The 2019 second-round swap component also stayed alive long after Mbah a Moute left Sacramento. The canonical asset ledger ties Milwaukee's side of that mechanism to the No. 42 selection associated with Admiral Schofield and Sacramento's side to the No. 60 selection associated with Vanja Marinkovic. Those names are secondary to Brogdon, but they show why the Bucks did more than exchange a veteran for one lottery ticket. Milwaukee acquired a layered draft package whose most valuable piece became a major rotation player while Sacramento's strongest benefit came from shorter-term roster utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A+, Sacramento B. Sacramento acquired Luc Mbah a Moute and later flipped him for Derrick Williams, so the Kings produced real value from the player they received. Milwaukee still wins the hindsight comparison because the 2016 second-round asset became Malcolm Brogdon, a Rookie of the Year winner and high-level contributor, while the 2019 swap mechanism added another usable draft component. The gap is not based on Sacramento receiving nothing. It comes from Milwaukee turning one veteran forward into a draft package that produced the best player outcome connected to the transaction.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought a Veteran Bench Piece for a Finals Push
sections.body: Indiana acquired Luis Scola in July 2013 with a very specific competitive window in mind. The Pacers had just reached the Eastern Conference finals and wanted a proven reserve big behind David West and Roy Hibbert. Scola fit that role immediately. He played all 82 games in 2013-14, gave Indiana reliable second-unit scoring and rebounding, and stayed for a second season. The problem in hindsight is not that Scola failed. It is that the price included two useful young players and a future first-round pick.

sections.heading: Gerald Green and Miles Plumlee Helped Phoenix Right Away
sections.body: Phoenix did not have to wait for the draft asset to see a return. Gerald Green became one of the breakout scorers on the 48-win 2013-14 Suns, while Miles Plumlee moved from a limited Indiana role into a full-time starting opportunity. Neither player became a franchise cornerstone, but both provided immediate rotation value on a team that dramatically outperformed expectations. That matters when comparing the packages: Phoenix received present-tense production at the same time Indiana was using Scola for its own contender, so the Suns were not trading current value solely for future upside.

sections.heading: The First-Rounder Extended Phoenix's Asset Advantage
sections.body: The protected first-round pick conveyed in 2014 at No. 27 and became Bogdan Bogdanovic. Phoenix did not get Bogdanovic's eventual NBA production directly because his draft rights were later moved, but the selection remained a meaningful asset in the Suns' portfolio. It was ultimately part of the 2016 draft transaction that brought Marquese Chriss to Phoenix. That downstream path should not be scored as if Bogdanovic starred for the Suns, yet it reinforces the central point: Phoenix received a first-round asset on top of Green and Plumlee for a veteran Indiana used for two seasons.

sections.heading: Indiana's Context Softens the Loss Without Erasing It
sections.body: The Pacers were a legitimate title contender, so spending future value for a dependable veteran was rational. Scola appeared in 174 regular-season games for Indiana across two seasons and also played in two postseason runs. That makes a C+ more appropriate than treating the deal as a total failure. Phoenix still earned the higher grade because its package was broader and more durable. Green and Plumlee contributed immediately, and the first-rounder preserved value beyond the initial season. The canonical A for Phoenix and C+ for Indiana capture both the contender logic and the stronger completed return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Indiana C+, Phoenix A. Luis Scola gave the Pacers the veteran reserve they wanted for a team chasing the Finals, and his two seasons in Indiana were genuinely useful. Phoenix nevertheless received the deeper package: Gerald Green and Miles Plumlee became meaningful contributors right away, while the protected first-round pick conveyed at No. 27 and remained an asset beyond the trade. Indiana's decision made sense for its competitive window, but the Suns extracted more total value from both the immediate roster pieces and the future draft component.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought a Veteran Backup for a Playoff Run
sections.body: Golden State entered the 2014 deadline as a 50-win-caliber playoff team that needed steadier reserve point-guard minutes behind Stephen Curry. The Warriors sent Kent Bazemore and MarShon Brooks to the Lakers for Steve Blake, choosing immediate lineup reliability over two younger guards who had not established regular roles. Blake did exactly that job. He appeared in 28 regular-season games for Golden State, averaged 21.7 minutes and 3.6 assists, and gave the second unit a veteran ball-handler during the stretch run. That is modest value, but it directly served the team's competitive window.

sections.heading: Bazemore Found a Much Larger Role in Los Angeles
sections.body: The Lakers' best return was Kent Bazemore. After averaging only 6.1 minutes in 44 games for Golden State that season, he jumped into a 28-minute role in Los Angeles. Bazemore appeared in 23 games, started 15 and averaged 13.1 points before a foot injury ended his season. The production was real even though the stint was brief. Los Angeles gave a buried young wing enough opportunity to show he belonged in an NBA rotation, which is why the Lakers' side cannot be treated as empty despite the lower canonical grade.

sections.heading: Brooks Added Depth, but Neither Lakers Piece Stayed
sections.body: MarShon Brooks also received more opportunity after the deal, appearing in 18 games for Los Angeles after playing only seven times for Golden State. He scored efficiently in a small role but did not become part of the Lakers' longer-term roster. Bazemore also left in free agency that summer. That short duration limits the hindsight payoff from the two-player package. The Lakers unlocked more immediate production from Bazemore than Golden State had, but they did not convert either incoming player into a durable asset that survived beyond the 2013-14 season.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is Small Because Both Teams Got What They Needed
sections.body: This was never a franchise-altering deadline move. Golden State wanted a dependable reserve guard for a playoff push and got 28 games of usable Blake minutes before he left in free agency. Los Angeles wanted younger players and found a short-term contributor in Bazemore, but the roster value disappeared after the season. The canonical B- for Golden State and C for the Lakers reflect a narrow Warriors edge rather than a landslide. Blake's role matched the contender's objective more directly, while Los Angeles generated a useful audition without retaining the best piece of its return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B-, Los Angeles C. Steve Blake gave a 51-win Warriors team the veteran backup point guard it wanted for the stretch run, appearing in 28 games and stabilizing reserve minutes behind Stephen Curry. Kent Bazemore was the most productive individual after the trade, averaging 13.1 points in 23 games for Los Angeles, while MarShon Brooks added depth. The difference is durability and fit: Golden State received the role it was specifically buying for a playoff team, while both Lakers acquisitions were gone after the season. It is a modest Warriors win, not a one-sided deal.

sections.heading: Miami Used the Deal to Open a Roster Spot
sections.body: Miami's deadline move with Sacramento was more administrative than talent-driven. The Heat sent Roger Mason Jr. and cash to the Kings for a heavily protected 2015 second-round pick. Contemporary reporting made the purpose clear: Miami wanted an open roster spot for the buyout and free-agent market while defending its Eastern Conference title. Mason had appeared in 25 games and averaged 3.0 points for the Heat. Moving him gave the front office flexibility without sacrificing a core rotation player, so the immediate value was the roster spot rather than the incoming pick.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Never Became an Asset
sections.body: The draft return looked better on paper than it did in practice. Basketball-Reference records the 2015 second-round pick as conditional and not conveyed, matching the narrow protection range in the canonical ledger. Miami therefore did not turn the deal into a future player or selection. That limits how high the Heat can be graded. The franchise accomplished its short-term roster-management goal, but the nominal draft asset never produced basketball value. This was not a hidden pick win; it was a flexibility transaction whose upside effectively ended once the selection failed to convey.

sections.heading: Sacramento Was Taking Cash, Not Building Around Mason
sections.body: Sacramento's side was similarly modest. The Kings received Mason and cash, but reporting at the deadline indicated that Mason was expected to be waived rather than incorporated into the rotation. The transaction history confirms the exchange but provides no durable player return to offset the outgoing conditional pick. The cash consideration still had real economic value, which keeps Sacramento from an automatic failing grade. In basketball terms, though, the Kings did not add a player who became part of their future, and the protected pick they sent was structured so narrowly that it never cost them a realized selection.

sections.heading: The Slight Heat Edge Comes From Achieving the Actual Objective
sections.body: The canonical C+ for Miami and C for Sacramento fit the small scale of the deal. Neither side created a valuable long-term asset, and the 2015 pick disappeared under its protections. Miami earns the slight edge because the transaction did exactly what a contender wanted at the deadline: remove a fringe veteran from the roster and create an opening for another addition. Sacramento received cash and avoided losing a real draft choice, so its outcome was not damaging. The difference is simply that Miami extracted a usable roster-management benefit while Sacramento's basketball return was essentially temporary.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge — Miami C+, Sacramento C. Miami sent Roger Mason Jr. and cash to Sacramento for a heavily protected 2015 second-round pick that never conveyed. The Heat did not gain draft value, but they did create the open roster spot they wanted for the post-deadline market without moving a core contributor. Sacramento received cash and was expected to waive Mason, while the conditional pick ultimately cost the Kings nothing. With almost no durable basketball value on either side, Miami's successful roster-flexibility objective is enough for only a narrow edge rather than a meaningful trade win.
