sections.heading: Houston Paid a First-Round Pick to Clear Lin's Contract
sections.body: Houston's July 2014 deal was driven by cap space, not by a belief that Sergei Lishchuk's draft rights were equal to Jeremy Lin. The Rockets sent Lin, a protected 2015 first-round pick and a conditional 2015 second-rounder to Los Angeles while taking back no NBA salary. The immediate objective was to create room for a major free-agent move, with Chris Bosh the primary target at the time. Bosh stayed in Miami, so the most ambitious version of Houston's plan never materialized. That leaves the draft cost exposed in hindsight.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Got a Full Season of Useful Guard Play
sections.body: Lin was not merely salary ballast for the Lakers. He appeared in 74 games, started 30 and averaged 11.2 points and 4.6 assists in 25.8 minutes during the 2014-15 season. Los Angeles was rebuilding and won only 21 games, but Lin supplied legitimate NBA minutes while preserving future flexibility because his contract expired after the season. The Lakers' own announcement emphasized both the player and the draft assets. Even before the first-round pick was used, the transaction produced a serviceable rotation guard at no long-term salary commitment.

sections.heading: The First-Rounder Became Larry Nance Jr.
sections.body: The protected first conveyed immediately in 2015 at No. 27, where Los Angeles selected Larry Nance Jr. Nance developed into a long-term NBA rotation forward and center, giving the Lakers several seasons of athletic frontcourt play before he was later moved in another transaction. The conditional second-round pick did not convey, so it adds no realized value. Even with that miss, the combination of one Lin season and a genuine first-round contributor is far stronger than the dormant Lishchuk rights Houston received in return.

sections.heading: The Cap-Space Logic Explains Houston's Decision, Not the Final Grade
sections.body: The Rockets had a coherent reason to move Lin. His expiring contract stood between Houston and the flexibility needed to chase another star, and the Lakers could absorb it without sending salary back. Historical grading still has to count what the teams actually surrendered and received. Houston gave up the useful guard plus the pick that became Nance and ended with draft rights that never produced an NBA contribution. The canonical D for Houston and A for Los Angeles reflect the completed asset imbalance while acknowledging that the Rockets were buying cap room rather than evaluating the players as equals.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Houston D, Los Angeles A. The Lakers absorbed Jeremy Lin's expiring contract, received 74 games of useful guard play and also acquired the protected first-round pick that conveyed at No. 27 and became Larry Nance Jr. The conditional second-rounder never conveyed, but Los Angeles still produced two meaningful basketball assets from the package. Houston received the rights to Sergei Lishchuk while clearing space for a free-agent pursuit that did not land Chris Bosh. The cap strategy was understandable; the realized return was not close to the value the Lakers extracted.

sections.heading: Chicago Attached Two Seconds to Clear Randolph's Salary
sections.body: Chicago's July 2014 transaction was a cap-space move tied to a much larger offseason plan. The Bulls sent Anthony Randolph, two future second-round picks and cash to Orlando for the draft rights to Milovan Rakovic. Contemporary reporting said Chicago was clearing roughly the final $1.8 million on Randolph's contract as it created room for Pau Gasol and Nikola Mirotic. Rakovic's rights were therefore a return mechanism, not the basketball target. The Bulls were paying draft capital so Orlando would absorb a contract they did not intend to keep.

sections.heading: Orlando Waived Randolph but Kept the Draft Assets
sections.body: Anthony Randolph provided essentially no basketball value to the Magic because Orlando waived him the next day. The durable return came from the two second-rounders and cash. The 2015 selection conveyed at No. 51, where Orlando drafted Tyler Harvey. Harvey never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so that branch did not create on-court value. Even so, the Magic had turned dormant Rakovic rights into two usable draft chances plus cash, which gave the franchise more optionality than the player portion alone suggests.

sections.heading: The 2016 Pick Became Another Tradeable Asset
sections.body: The second pick conveyed in 2016 at No. 47 and became Jake Layman. Orlando did not keep Layman; on draft night, the Magic moved his rights to Portland for a future second-round pick and cash. That later second was eventually used in another transaction, so the value chain continued beyond the original Bulls deal. Layman's eventual six-year NBA career belongs to Portland and Minnesota, not Orlando, but the Magic still deserve credit for converting the incoming selection into another asset package rather than letting the pick disappear.

sections.heading: Chicago's Cap Objective Keeps the Deal From Looking Worse
sections.body: The Bulls did accomplish the operational goal behind the trade. Moving Randolph helped open the room needed for a summer in which Chicago added Gasol and Mirotic, and Randolph was not part of the planned rotation. That context supports the canonical C+ rather than treating every outgoing pick as a pure loss. Orlando still gets the higher B because it received cash and two selections for rights to a player who never reached the NBA. Neither pick became a direct Magic contributor, but one was recycled into additional value while Chicago's incoming asset itself produced nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Chicago C+, Orlando B. The Bulls used Anthony Randolph, two second-round picks and cash to clear salary for a broader 2014 offseason plan, receiving only the rights to Milovan Rakovic. Orlando waived Randolph immediately, but the two picks still conveyed: No. 51 in 2015 became Tyler Harvey, and No. 47 in 2016 became Jake Layman before the Magic flipped Layman's rights for another future second and cash. Chicago's cap-space objective was legitimate, but Orlando extracted the stronger realized asset package from a transaction built around absorbing salary.

sections.heading: New York Turned Two Fringe Guards Into a Rotation Forward
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Quincy Acy and Travis Outlaw from Sacramento in August 2014 while sending Wayne Ellington, Jeremy Tyler and the unencumbered rights to their 2016 second-round pick. The immediate basketball value came from Acy. He played 68 games for New York, started 22 and supplied rebounding, physicality and frontcourt depth during a season when the roster was being reworked around Carmelo Anthony. Outlaw never became part of the regular rotation, but Acy gave the Knicks a usable player from a package built around two guards who were not in their long-term plans.

sections.heading: Sacramento Waived Both Incoming Players Before the Season
sections.body: The Kings did not receive lasting player value from the deal. Wayne Ellington was waived in early September, and Jeremy Tyler followed only days later. That made the draft consideration the core of Sacramento's return. The removal of protection on New York's 2016 second-round pick mattered because it turned a conditional asset into an unencumbered selection. Sacramento later routed that pick to Houston in the Jason Terry trade, so the Kings did preserve and reuse its value rather than simply letting it expire.

sections.heading: The Pick Eventually Became Chinanu Onuaku
sections.body: The unprotected 2016 second-rounder eventually landed at No. 37 and was used on Chinanu Onuaku. Sacramento did not make that selection because the pick had already been sent to Houston, but the chain is directly traceable to the asset acquired from New York. That gives the Kings more credit than the waived Ellington and Tyler alone would justify. It still does not outweigh Acy's actual Knicks contribution, especially because Sacramento's benefit from the pick came through a later trade rather than from a player it developed itself.

sections.heading: Acy's One-Year Role Creates the Narrow Knicks Advantage
sections.body: This was a modest transaction, not a franchise pivot. Acy became a real rotation player for New York for one season, while the Kings received an upgraded draft asset that they quickly used as trade currency. The canonical B- for the Knicks and C for Sacramento reflect that balance. New York got the more immediate and visible basketball return. Sacramento avoided a total loss because the unprotected second retained utility even after Ellington and Tyler were waived. The difference is enough for a Knicks win, but not enough to treat the deal as a major heist.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B-, Sacramento C. Quincy Acy gave New York 68 games and 22 starts, providing a useful frontcourt role after the Knicks moved Wayne Ellington and Jeremy Tyler. Sacramento waived both incoming players before the season, but the Kings did gain the unencumbered rights to New York's 2016 second-round pick and later used that asset in another trade. The pick eventually became No. 37 Chinanu Onuaku in Houston's hands. Sacramento preserved some value, yet Acy's direct contribution gives the Knicks the stronger realized return.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Used the Deal to Open a Roster Spot
sections.body: Oklahoma City moved Hasheem Thabeet and cash to Philadelphia in August 2014 for a protected 2015 second-round pick and a trade exception. By then, Steven Adams had taken over the backup-center role and Thabeet's place in the rotation had narrowed. The Thunder's practical gain was flexibility: they cleared a roster spot and created an exception they had a year to use. This was never a player-for-player talent exchange. Oklahoma City was paying cash to move a reserve whose role had diminished while preserving a small chance at a future pick.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Never Conveyed
sections.body: The draft component ultimately produced no player for Oklahoma City. Basketball-Reference records the 2015 second-round pick as conditional and not conveyed, matching the highly restrictive protection in the canonical asset ledger. That strips away the most obvious path to long-term upside on the Thunder side. The trade exception still had transactional utility, but it is harder to value than a player or a draft selection because its worth depended on a later move. In realized terms, Oklahoma City gained flexibility rather than a durable basketball asset.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took the Cash and Quickly Moved On From Thabeet
sections.body: Philadelphia's return was also modest. The 76ers acquired Thabeet and cash, then waived the center before the regular season. He never appeared in a game for Philadelphia, so the B+ grade cannot be read as credit for on-court production. The stronger part of the 76ers' outcome was economic: they used available flexibility to absorb a contract, collected cash and ultimately did not surrender the protected second-round pick. The transaction fit the asset-accumulation approach Philadelphia was using during that rebuilding period.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Reflects Cost Avoided More Than Talent Acquired
sections.body: Neither franchise found a rotation player through this trade. Oklahoma City achieved a legitimate roster-management goal, which keeps its canonical C+ from looking harsh, but the protected pick never arrived and the return ended with an exception. Philadelphia's B+ is similarly contextual rather than star-driven. The 76ers accepted a player they did not keep, received cash and retained the draft selection because the conditions were never met. That leaves Philadelphia with the better completed value despite the deal's very small basketball footprint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Oklahoma City C+, Philadelphia B+. The Thunder cleared Hasheem Thabeet from a crowded center rotation and received a trade exception, but the protected 2015 second-round pick never conveyed. Philadelphia waived Thabeet before the season, so there was no player payoff, yet the 76ers collected cash and ultimately gave up no realized draft asset. Oklahoma City's flexibility had real value, but Philadelphia extracted the better completed return at minimal basketball cost. This is a narrow mechanism win rather than a consequential talent trade.

sections.heading: New York Paid Two Future Pick Assets for a Player It Immediately Waived
sections.body: The Knicks sent Travis Outlaw, their 2019 second-round pick and a 2018 second-round swap arrangement to Philadelphia for Arnett Moultrie. The transaction was completed on the final day of preseason roster cuts, and New York waived Moultrie the same day. Philadelphia also waived Outlaw immediately, so neither veteran created on-court value for his new team. That leaves the draft assets as the meaningful substance of the deal, and the Knicks surrendered far more future value than they received for a player who never appeared in a regular-season game for them.

sections.heading: The 2018 Swap Moved Philadelphia Up to No. 39
sections.body: The 2018 second-round mechanism eventually moved Philadelphia ahead of New York in the draft order. The Sixers ended up with the No. 39 selection, used on Isaac Bonga, while the lower side of the swap was tied to No. 43. Philadelphia did not keep Bonga; it traded his draft rights to the Lakers for another 2019 second-round pick and cash. That is still directly traceable value from the Knicks trade because the original swap created the No. 39 asset Philadelphia was able to monetize four years later.

sections.heading: New York's 2019 Second Became the First Pick of Round Two
sections.body: The larger cost was New York's unprotected 2019 second-rounder. The pick ultimately landed at No. 31 and became Nicolas Claxton, although Philadelphia had already sent it to Brooklyn in the 2017 Jahlil Okafor and Nik Stauskas trade for Trevor Booker. Philadelphia therefore did not receive Claxton's NBA career, but the pick still functioned as a premium trade asset before draft night. For the Knicks, giving up a selection that became the first pick of the second round for Moultrie looks especially poor because Moultrie's New York tenure ended before it began.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Won Through Asset Conversion, Not Outlaw
sections.body: The canonical grades correctly separate the transaction from the players' names. Outlaw and Moultrie were both waived, so the deal's hindsight value comes almost entirely from what happened to the picks. Philadelphia turned the 2018 position into Bonga's draft rights and another trade package, while the 2019 New York second became useful currency in the Booker transaction. The Knicks received no Moultrie minutes and only the weaker side of the 2018 swap. That is enough to support an A for Philadelphia and an F for New York.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — New York F, Philadelphia A. Arnett Moultrie never played for the Knicks after they acquired and waived him on the same day, while Travis Outlaw was also waived by Philadelphia. The difference is the draft capital New York attached. Philadelphia moved up to No. 39 in the 2018 second round, later turning Isaac Bonga's rights into another pick and cash, and it also received New York's 2019 second-rounder, which eventually landed at No. 31. The Sixers converted those assets into real transaction value; the Knicks received almost nothing in return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Rebuilt Its Wing Rotation in One Move
sections.body: Cleveland entered January 2015 with a talented roster that still had obvious fit problems around LeBron James, Kyrie Irving and Kevin Love. The three-team deal sent Dion Waiters to Oklahoma City and brought J.R. Smith and Iman Shumpert from New York to the Cavaliers, along with Oklahoma City's protected first-round pick. Smith immediately supplied high-volume perimeter shooting, while Shumpert gave Cleveland a bigger defensive guard and wing option. Both became regular postseason pieces as the Cavaliers reached the Finals in 2015 and then won the 2016 championship.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Became Trade Currency for Mozgov
sections.body: The protected Oklahoma City first was not simply a distant bonus. Two days after this trade, Cleveland sent that pick and another first-rounder to Denver for Timofey Mozgov. The Oklahoma City selection eventually conveyed in 2016 and became No. 26, Furkan Korkmaz, after moving through later transactions. Cleveland never drafted Korkmaz, so his career should not be credited to the Cavaliers. The value Cleveland actually realized was the ability to use the incoming first as part of the price for Mozgov, another starter-level piece in the club's immediate title push.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Got a Useful Scorer but Not the Best Outcome
sections.body: The Thunder acquired Waiters and gave up the protected first that went to Cleveland. Waiters became a genuine rotation player in Oklahoma City, appearing in 78 games in 2015-16 and averaging double figures while helping the Thunder reach the Western Conference finals. That supports the canonical C rather than treating Oklahoma City's side as empty. The issue is comparative value: one useful guard season and a half did not match the combination of Smith, Shumpert and the first-round asset Cleveland immediately repurposed for another win-now acquisition.

sections.heading: New York's Salary Reset Came at a Severe Basketball Cost
sections.body: New York's motivation was financial. Moving Smith and Shumpert helped clear future salary and opened room in a season that had already collapsed, but the basketball return was thin: Lou Amundson, Alex Kirk and a 2019 second-round pick from Cleveland, with partner-only routing handled separately in the canonical ledger. Amundson gave the Knicks some frontcourt minutes, Kirk was waived, and the later second eventually became the No. 33 selection associated with Carsen Edwards after further transactions. Against the championship-level value Cleveland extracted from Smith and Shumpert, the Knicks' realized return supports the canonical F.

sections.heading: The Championship Context Makes Cleveland's A Easy to Defend
sections.body: Smith and Shumpert were not temporary rentals that disappeared before the Cavaliers' window opened. Smith remained a major floor-spacing guard through four straight Finals trips and started throughout the 2016 championship postseason. Shumpert stayed through the 2018 season and supplied defense across multiple playoff runs. Add the first-round pick that helped acquire Mozgov, and Cleveland turned one difficult backcourt fit in Waiters plus ancillary assets into three pieces that directly supported a title contender. That combination of role fit, postseason longevity and asset conversion is why the Cavaliers clearly won the completed trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A, New York F, Oklahoma City C. Cleveland turned Dion Waiters and ancillary outgoing assets into J.R. Smith, Iman Shumpert and a protected first-round pick, then used that pick as part of the Timofey Mozgov trade. Smith and Shumpert became multi-year playoff contributors and both were part of the 2016 championship team. Oklahoma City received useful production from Waiters, so its return was defensible. New York gained salary relief but little comparable basketball value. The completed results give Cleveland the strongest package by a wide margin.

sections.heading: Cleveland Paid a Premium for the Center It Needed
sections.body: Two days after remaking its wing rotation, Cleveland sent two protected first-round picks to Denver for Timofey Mozgov and a 2015 second-round pick. The price was substantial, but the timing explains it. The Cavaliers were 19-17 on the day of the trade and needed a true rim-protecting center to stabilize a roster built to contend immediately around LeBron James, Kyrie Irving and Kevin Love. Mozgov stepped directly into the starting lineup, giving Cleveland size, rebounding and interior defense for the second half of the season.

sections.heading: Mozgov Became a Major Part of the 2015 Finals Run
sections.body: Mozgov started 45 of his 46 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade and remained the starting center throughout the 2015 postseason. He averaged double figures in the playoffs and played one of the best games of his career in the NBA Finals, scoring 28 points in Game 4 against Golden State. His role shrank during the 2016 championship run, but he still gave Cleveland immediate value at exactly the position it had targeted. The Cavaliers were buying fit and timing, not long-term upside.

sections.heading: Denver Turned One Veteran Into Two First-Round Assets
sections.body: Denver's side was equally defensible. The Nuggets moved a 28-year-old center and a late second-round pick for two protected first-rounders, one originally from Oklahoma City and one tied to Memphis. Those selections ultimately became No. 26 in 2016 and No. 20 in 2017 after later routing, associated with Furkan Korkmaz and Harry Giles III. Denver did not simply receive two names on draft night; it acquired two flexible first-round assets for a player who no longer fit the franchise's timeline.

sections.heading: The Second-Rounder Added Little to Cleveland's Return
sections.body: The 2015 second-round pick sent with Mozgov became No. 53 and was used on Sir'Dominic Pointer. He never appeared in an NBA game for Cleveland, so that piece does not materially change the trade's hindsight balance. The deal still comes down to Mozgov's immediate contribution versus the opportunity cost of two first-round selections. Cleveland got the center it wanted for a Finals run and eventual championship window. Denver got the kind of draft capital a resetting team should demand for a useful veteran.

sections.heading: Different Timelines Produced the Same Grade
sections.body: Cleveland and Denver were solving different problems. The Cavaliers had no reason to prioritize distant draft flexibility over a starting center who could help immediately, while the Nuggets had every reason to convert Mozgov into future assets. Cleveland extracted real postseason value and reached the Finals that spring. Denver extracted two first-round picks from a player it could replace during a rebuild. Neither side captured enough extra value to separate from the other, which is why the canonical B grades and even verdict hold up.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Cleveland B, Denver B. The Cavaliers paid two protected first-round picks for Timofey Mozgov and a late second-rounder, then used Mozgov as their starting center during the 2015 Finals run and into the 2016 championship season. Denver received two first-round assets that ultimately conveyed at No. 26 in 2016 and No. 20 in 2017 after later routing. Cleveland paid a high price but got immediate contender value; Denver converted a veteran center into strong future capital. Both teams achieved the objective that fit their timeline.

sources.title: Nuggets Acquire Two First-Round Picks from Cavaliers

sections.heading: New Orleans Bought Flexibility More Than a Player
sections.body: At the 2015 trade deadline, New Orleans sent Oklahoma City a protected 2016 second-round pick for Ish Smith, the draft rights to Latavious Williams, a protected 2015 second-round pick and cash. The Pelicans waived Smith immediately, so this was never really an attempt to add him to the rotation. The transaction was a small asset-and-cash move completed on the same day New Orleans also acquired Norris Cole, Justin Hamilton and Shawne Williams in a separate deal.

sections.heading: Neither Conditional Pick Ever Conveyed
sections.body: The draft terms ended up cancelling much of the theoretical upside on both sides. The 2015 second-rounder sent to New Orleans was heavily protected and never conveyed. Oklahoma City's incoming 2016 second was also conditional and never conveyed. That means neither franchise ultimately turned the pick exchange into a drafted player. In hindsight, the trade is easier to judge through the cash, the rights to Williams and the roster mechanics than through the nominal draft capital.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Kept the Tangible Value
sections.body: Hoops Rumors reported that New Orleans received about $801,000 in cash along with Smith, Williams' rights and the conditional pick. Smith was waived, Williams never became an NBA contributor for the Pelicans and the 2015 pick disappeared under its protection. Even so, New Orleans gave up no realized draft asset because its 2016 second did not convey. The cash therefore became the clearest piece of completed value in the transaction, which is enough to push the Pelicans ahead on a very small deal.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Created a Trade Exception but Little Lasting Return
sections.body: RealGM records Oklahoma City receiving the conditional 2016 second and a trade exception. The exception had roster-management utility, but the pick never produced a player and the deal did not leave a lasting basketball asset. The Thunder were clearing pieces around a much larger deadline overhaul that brought in Enes Kanter, D.J. Augustin, Kyle Singler and Steve Novak. This side transaction served that broader flexibility, but on its own the realized return was thin compared with the cash New Orleans banked.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B, Oklahoma City C-. Both conditional second-round picks failed to convey, Ish Smith was waived immediately by New Orleans and Latavious Williams never became a Pelicans rotation piece. The difference is that New Orleans still collected roughly $801,000 in cash while surrendering no realized draft asset. Oklahoma City gained a trade exception and theoretical pick value, but the pick never materialized. The edge is modest, yet the Pelicans finished with the more tangible completed return.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Paid Two Real Assets for One Short-Lived Season
sections.body: On draft night in 2015, Milwaukee acquired Greivis Vasquez from Toronto for the draft rights to Norman Powell and a protected future first-round pick. The Bucks were coming off a 41-win playoff season and wanted another ball-handler for a young roster, so the idea was understandable. The cost was the problem. Vasquez played only 23 games for Milwaukee before an ankle injury ended his season, averaged 5.7 points and 4.0 assists, and left in free agency the following summer.

sections.heading: Powell Became a Long-Term Rotation Player for Toronto
sections.body: Powell was the 46th pick, but Toronto quickly found more value than his draft slot suggested. By April of his rookie season he had earned Eastern Conference Rookie of the Month, and he became a recurring part of the Raptors' postseason rotation. Powell stayed through the 2020-21 season and was part of the 2019 championship team. He was not a star from day one, but Toronto received years of useful wing production from a player Milwaukee had just selected and immediately traded.

sections.heading: The Future First Became O.G. Anunoby
sections.body: The second half of Toronto's return became even more valuable. The protected Clippers-origin first-round pick conveyed in 2017 at No. 23, where the Raptors selected O.G. Anunoby. Anunoby developed into a high-level two-way starter and later became a major trade asset in his own right. Milwaukee did not merely sacrifice an uncertain future pick; the selection actually conveyed and became one of Toronto's core defenders. Pairing that outcome with Powell turns the deal from a routine draft-night swap into a major hindsight loss for the Bucks.

sections.heading: Toronto Converted One Veteran Into Years of Wing Value
sections.body: Vasquez had helped Toronto before the trade, but the Raptors sold at the right time. They replaced a veteran reserve guard with two younger assets that both became legitimate NBA contributors. Powell gave Toronto depth across multiple playoff runs, while Anunoby grew into a starting forward with elite defensive value. The Raptors also avoided paying for Vasquez's next contract and moved forward with Kyle Lowry, Cory Joseph and younger guards. The trade aligned roster timing, development and asset value unusually well.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is One of the Clearest in This Queue
sections.body: Injuries alone do not make a trade bad, but Milwaukee's downside was already visible in the acquisition price. A one-year reserve guard cost the rights to a second-round wing plus a protected first. The later outcomes amplified that risk dramatically: Vasquez lasted 23 games, Powell became a long-term rotation player and the first became Anunoby. Toronto's canonical A+ and Milwaukee's F therefore do not depend on inventing downstream value. Both major incoming assets can be traced directly to the transaction and both produced substantial value for the Raptors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — Milwaukee F, Toronto A+. Milwaukee received only 23 games from Greivis Vasquez after sending Toronto the rights to Norman Powell and a protected future first-round pick. Powell became a multi-year rotation wing and a member of Toronto's 2019 championship team. The first-rounder conveyed at No. 23 in 2017 and became O.G. Anunoby, who developed into a premier two-way starter. The Bucks' original need for another ball-handler was reasonable, but the price produced almost no durable return while Toronto converted both incoming assets into major value.

sections.heading: New York Turned Two Future Seconds Into a Productive Young Center
sections.body: New York acquired the draft rights to Willy Hernangomez, the No. 35 pick in 2015, from Philadelphia for two future second-round picks and cash. Hernangomez stayed in Spain for another season before joining the Knicks in 2016-17, and his rookie year immediately gave the transaction real basketball value. He played 72 games, averaged 8.2 points and 7.0 rebounds and earned NBA All-Rookie First Team honors. For two future seconds, the Knicks obtained a young center who became a useful rotation piece rather than a draft-and-stash that never arrived.

sections.heading: Hernangomez's Rookie Season Was the High Point of the Knicks Return
sections.body: The value did not keep climbing forever. Hernangomez's role shrank in his second New York season, and the Knicks traded him to Charlotte in February 2018 after 98 total games and 22 starts with the franchise. That limits how high the New York side should be graded. Still, the original deal produced two NBA seasons, a strong rookie campaign and a player with enough value to be moved again. The Knicks did not find a long-term starter, but they received more than a speculative second-round gamble.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Banked Two Future Picks and Cash
sections.body: Philadelphia's return was built for a much longer timeline. The two New York second-rounders eventually landed in the 2020 and 2021 draft asset chains, with the canonical ledger associating them with No. 36 Tyler Bey and No. 50 Filip Petrusev. The 76ers did not need Hernangomez in 2015 and instead converted his rights into extra future draft inventory plus cash. Those assets retained transaction value for years, even though neither eventual selection developed into a player whose NBA production clearly eclipsed what Hernangomez gave New York.

sections.heading: Both Sides Extracted Reasonable Value From a Modest Deal
sections.body: The hindsight result is unusually balanced for a second-round rights trade. New York got the best immediate player outcome: Hernangomez became an All-Rookie First Team center and a real rotation contributor. Philadelphia got multiple future shots and cash for a player it had just selected in the second round. The later pick outcomes did not turn the Sixers' side into a major win, while Hernangomez's short New York tenure keeps the Knicks from separating either. The canonical B+ grades on both sides fit a deal where each team achieved a sensible objective.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New York B+, Philadelphia B+. The Knicks acquired Willy Hernangomez for two future second-round picks and cash, then received a 72-game All-Rookie First Team season and 98 total games from him before moving him in 2018. Philadelphia chose future flexibility instead, collecting two second-round assets that eventually entered the 2020 and 2021 draft chains. Hernangomez produced the strongest direct NBA value, but his New York stay was brief enough that the Sixers' multi-pick return still holds up. Neither side created a decisive advantage.

sections.heading: New York Bought Three Useful Seasons for a Modest Asset Cost
sections.body: New York acquired Kyle O'Quinn from Orlando in a July 2015 sign-and-trade, sending cash and giving the Magic the right to swap 2019 second-round picks. The move brought the Queens native home without costing the Knicks a first-round pick or a young rotation player. O'Quinn then appeared in 221 regular-season games over three seasons for New York. He was mostly a reserve, but he gave the frontcourt rebounding, passing and interior defense at a price that never blocked the club from making larger roster moves.

sections.heading: O'Quinn Became More Valuable as His Knicks Tenure Went On
sections.body: O'Quinn's best New York season came in 2017-18, when he played 77 games and averaged 7.1 points, 6.1 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 18.0 minutes while shooting 58.3 percent. His per-minute production was strong throughout the three-year run, and he finished that final season with a 20.0 PER and 4.8 win shares. He declined his player option in 2018 and left as an unrestricted free agent, so the Knicks did not recover another trade asset at the end. Even so, three seasons of legitimate rotation-center play represented a strong return for the original cost.

sections.heading: Orlando Did Extract Real Value From the 2019 Swap
sections.body: The Magic's return should not be treated as cash alone. Orlando acquired the right to exchange 2019 second-round positions with New York, and the swap ultimately moved the Magic side into the No. 33 slot instead of No. 47. That No. 33 asset was later routed in the February 2019 Markelle Fultz trade, so it retained transaction value beyond the original O'Quinn deal. The No. 47 slot also moved through later Knicks and Kings transactions before Ignas Brazdeikis was selected there. Those downstream moves make player-to-player hindsight messy, but they confirm that Orlando's second-round mechanism had useful value.

sections.heading: The Knicks Still Won the Original Exchange
sections.body: Orlando's compensation was defensible for a player it was prepared to move, yet New York received the most direct basketball value. O'Quinn became a dependable three-year rotation piece and produced his best NBA season as a Knick. The Magic improved a future second-round position and received cash, but the original transaction did not deliver a comparable on-court contributor to Orlando. New York therefore earns the stronger grade even after giving the swap mechanism credit. The canonical A for the Knicks and C+ for the Magic fit the gap between proven rotation production and a useful but secondary draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Orlando C+. The Knicks acquired Kyle O'Quinn for cash and Orlando's right to swap 2019 second-round picks, then received 221 games and three useful rotation seasons from him. Orlando did gain real value when the swap moved its side into the No. 33 slot, an asset later used in the Markelle Fultz trade, but that return never matched O'Quinn's direct contribution in New York. For a modest acquisition cost, the Knicks landed a productive reserve center who improved during his tenure and gave the club dependable frontcourt minutes.

sections.heading: Indiana Chased a Better Fit for Its Faster Offense
sections.body: Indiana swapped Damjan Rudez for Chase Budinger as Larry Bird was reworking the roster around a smaller, quicker style. Budinger offered more off-the-dribble athleticism than Rudez and entered camp healthy enough for Paul George to praise what he had shown in offseason workouts. The idea was reasonable: add a veteran wing who could shoot, run and attack closeouts without surrendering a draft asset. The problem was that the role never developed into much. Budinger appeared in 49 games for the Pacers, started twice and averaged 4.4 points in 14.9 minutes.

sections.heading: Budinger Did Not Last the Full Season in Indiana
sections.body: The Pacers never received the bounce-back season they were hoping for. Budinger shot 41.8 percent from the field and only 29.0 percent from three in Indiana, production that made him expendable as the rotation tightened. The club waived him on March 5, 2016, and Phoenix signed him for the stretch run. Indiana therefore turned one year of Rudez's inexpensive contract into roughly two-thirds of a season of reserve wing minutes. That is useful enough to avoid a failing grade, but not enough to call the gamble a success.

sections.heading: Minnesota's Biggest Win Was Financial
sections.body: Rudez was not a major on-court upgrade. He played 33 games for Minnesota, averaged 2.3 points in 8.4 minutes and shot 34.0 percent from three before leaving after the season. The value came from the contract exchange. Budinger had exercised a $5 million option for 2015-16, while Rudez was making a little more than $1 million with another low-cost team option. Minnesota reduced its salary commitment by several million dollars while taking back a shooter who could fill a limited bench role. For a young roster centered on Karl-Anthony Towns and Andrew Wiggins, that flexibility was more useful than keeping an expensive reserve wing.

sections.heading: Neither Player Changed a Franchise, but Minnesota Improved Its Position
sections.body: This was a modest trade, and the grades should stay proportional to the stakes. Indiana's basketball logic was understandable, yet Budinger's 49-game stay ended in a waiver and produced no lasting return. Minnesota received little production from Rudez, but it accomplished the cleaner organizational objective by moving Budinger's larger expiring salary for a far cheaper contract without attaching a pick. That cost reduction is the clearest durable benefit created by the deal. It supports the canonical B for Minnesota and C+ for Indiana even though neither incoming player became an important long-term piece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B, Indiana C+. The Pacers acquired Chase Budinger to add a more athletic wing to a faster offense, but he averaged 4.4 points in 49 games and was waived before the season ended. Minnesota received only 33 low-minute games from Damjan Rudez, yet the Timberwolves also moved Budinger's roughly $5 million expiring salary for Rudez's much smaller contract. The on-court exchange was minor on both sides; Minnesota's financial flexibility creates the difference in the final grades.

sections.heading: Portland Bought a Young Wing for Almost Nothing
sections.body: Portland acquired Maurice Harkless from Orlando in July 2015 for a conditional 2020 second-round pick. Harkless was only 22 and had just fallen out of the Magic rotation, so the Trail Blazers were buying upside at a very small acquisition cost. The bet worked immediately. Harkless appeared in 78 games in his first Portland season, moved into the starting lineup late in the year and then started all 11 playoff games as the Blazers reached the second round.

sections.heading: Harkless Became a Four-Year Rotation Staple
sections.body: The first season was not a one-year spike. Harkless spent four seasons in Portland, appearing in 274 regular-season games and starting 173 of them. His best shooting year came in 2017-18, when he hit 41.5 percent from three, and he remained a useful defender and transition finisher even when his offensive role changed. He also played 33 playoff games for the franchise, starting 32, including 16 starts during Portland's run to the 2019 Western Conference Finals.

sections.heading: Orlando's Conditional Pick Produced No Drafted Player
sections.body: Orlando later sent the Portland 2020 second-round right to Cleveland in the January 2016 Joe Harris transaction. That pick was protected from Nos. 31 through 55. Portland ultimately used its own No. 46 selection in 2020, so the protected obligation did not transfer to Orlando or Cleveland. Portland, meanwhile, received years of real rotation value from Harkless.

sections.heading: This Low-Cost Bet Paid Off for Portland
sections.body: The Trail Blazers were rebuilding their supporting cast around Damian Lillard after losing several veterans in the 2015 offseason. Harkless fit that timeline, improved enough to earn another contract and became a dependable starter on playoff teams. Orlando had understandable reasons to clear a crowded wing rotation after Harkless' poor 2014-15 season, but the return never developed into comparable value. The canonical A for Portland and C+ for Orlando fit the difference between a four-year contributor and a conditional pick that never conveyed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A, Orlando C+. Portland acquired Maurice Harkless for a conditional 2020 second-round pick and received 274 regular-season games, 173 starts and four playoff runs from him. Orlando later rerouted the conditional pick, and the protected Portland obligation ultimately did not convey because the Trail Blazers' 2020 second-rounder landed at No. 46. Harkless became a useful long-term wing on teams that repeatedly reached the postseason.

sections.heading: Orlando Took a Nearly Free Look at a Former First-Round Guard
sections.body: Orlando acquired Shabazz Napier and cash from Miami in July 2015 for a conditional 2016 second-round pick. The pick was protected through No. 55, so the Magic were risking only the final five selections of the round. Miami's motivation was financial: the Heat were trimming salary and luxury-tax exposure after Napier's rookie season. For Orlando, the deal was a low-cost depth move behind Elfrid Payton and Victor Oladipo.

sections.heading: Napier Gave the Magic One Season of Reserve Minutes
sections.body: Napier did not become a long-term answer, but Orlando still received usable NBA value. He appeared in 55 games in 2015-16 and averaged 3.7 points and 1.8 assists in 10.9 minutes per game. He never started and shot 33.8 percent from the field, so the acquisition did not develop into a major rotation win. Even so, the Magic got a full season of backup-guard availability while also receiving cash in the original trade.

sections.heading: Miami's Draft Return Never Conveyed
sections.body: The conditional pick was protected Nos. 31 through 55 in the 2016 draft and otherwise extinguished. Orlando's own second-round position landed well inside that protected range, so Miami never received a player from the pick. That leaves the Heat's return as salary and tax relief rather than basketball value. The financial logic was real, but the trade ledger still ends with Orlando receiving Napier and cash while Miami received no converted draft asset.

sections.heading: Orlando Eventually Recovered a Little More Value
sections.body: The Magic moved on after one season, trading Napier to Portland for cash in July 2016. That exit did not create a major downstream asset, but it reinforces how little Orlando had committed to the experiment. Miami cleared a player it no longer prioritized, while Orlando obtained 55 games and later recovered cash without surrendering a draft pick that actually conveyed. The canonical B+ for Orlando and C+ for Miami fit a modest trade where one side extracted tangible use from almost no acquisition cost.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B+, Miami C+. Orlando acquired Shabazz Napier and cash for a top-55-protected 2016 second-round pick that never conveyed. Napier played 55 games for the Magic before Orlando later traded him to Portland for cash. Miami achieved its salary and luxury-tax objective, so the move was not pointless, but the Heat received no realized draft value. Orlando's low-risk acquisition produced the stronger completed return.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned Wallace Into Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Golden State acquired Jason Thompson from Philadelphia on July 31, 2015, only four days after the Warriors had received Gerald Wallace in the David Lee trade. Thompson was coming off a season in which he played 81 games and started 63 for Sacramento, so the defending champions were exchanging an aging wing who was unlikely to play for a veteran big who could compete for reserve minutes. Warriors general manager Bob Myers specifically framed Thompson as a depth addition, one of the strengths of the 2015 title roster.

sections.heading: The Basketball Return Was Useful but Brief
sections.body: Thompson never became a major part of Golden State's rotation. He appeared in 28 games, started once and averaged 2.1 points and 1.9 rebounds in 6.4 minutes. By February 2016, the Warriors waived him to open a roster spot for Anderson Varejao. That limits how much credit Golden State deserves for the player return, but Thompson still gave the club more on-court use than Wallace gave Philadelphia and helped cover the frontcourt during the first half of a 73-win season.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Main Return Was Financial and Conditional
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Wallace, cash and the right to swap a 2016 first-round position with Golden State under the deal's conditions. Wallace never appeared in a game for the 76ers; Philadelphia waived him before training camp and remained responsible for his guaranteed salary. The first-round swap also was not exercised. The Sixers therefore did not create a lasting player or draft return from the transaction, although taking on Wallace's contract fit a rebuilding roster that had ample cap room and valued additional cash and optionality.

sections.heading: A Small Warriors Edge Fits the Outcome
sections.body: Neither side landed a long-term contributor, so this trade belongs in the modest-win category. Golden State reduced its luxury-tax burden, replaced a player it did not plan to use with a veteran frontcourt option and received 28 games before changing course. Philadelphia absorbed Wallace, waived him without a game played and never used the swap right. The canonical B for the Warriors and C+ for the 76ers capture the narrow gap: Golden State extracted some roster value, while Philadelphia's conditional upside never turned into an asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B, Philadelphia C+. The Warriors exchanged Gerald Wallace for Jason Thompson, lowered their luxury-tax burden and received 28 games of reserve frontcourt depth. Thompson was waived in February to make room for Anderson Varejao, so the upside was limited. Philadelphia waived Wallace before he played a game for the franchise, and the 2016 first-round swap right was never exercised. Golden State's return was modest, but it produced the more useful completed outcome.

sections.heading: Memphis Upgraded Its Backup Guard Spot
sections.body: Memphis acquired Mario Chalmers and James Ennis from Miami on November 10, 2015, for Beno Udrih and Jarnell Stokes. The Grizzlies were 3-5 and looking for more punch behind Mike Conley, while Chalmers had become expendable after Miami committed to Goran Dragic. Chalmers quickly justified the basketball side of the deal. In 55 games with Memphis he averaged 10.8 points, 3.8 assists and 1.5 steals in 22.8 minutes, and the Grizzlies went 5-2 in his seven starts.

sections.heading: Chalmers Helped Until a Major Injury Ended the Run
sections.body: The value was real even though it did not last through the postseason. Chalmers tore his right Achilles in March 2016 and Memphis waived him after the injury. Before that, he had become a useful secondary creator and defensive guard on a roster that was being hit hard by injuries. The Grizzlies later brought him back for the 2017-18 season, which adds a little more organizational value beyond the original 55-game stint, even though the first tenure ended abruptly.

sections.heading: Ennis Was a Small Asset With a Later Memphis Payoff
sections.body: Ennis played only 10 games for Memphis during the 2015-16 season and spent substantial time in the D-League before the Grizzlies waived him in March. His inclusion still was not meaningless. He finished that season with New Orleans, played well in a nine-game audition and then returned to Memphis on a multi-year contract in July 2016. That second Grizzlies stint came through free agency rather than direct contractual control from this trade, so it should not be over-credited, but the organization had already evaluated him up close because of this deal.

sections.heading: Miami's Best Return Was Financial Flexibility
sections.body: Miami's logic was primarily financial. ESPN reported that the swap was expected to save roughly $6 million in luxury-tax payments, while the Heat also had a crowded backcourt. Udrih gave Miami 36 games and five starts before a right-foot injury ended his season, and Stokes spent much of his time in the D-League before Miami moved him to New Orleans in February 2016. The Heat accomplished an important payroll objective and received usable depth, but Memphis got the best on-court contributor in Chalmers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis B+, Miami B-. Chalmers gave Memphis 55 useful games at 10.8 points and 3.8 assists per game before his Achilles injury, while Ennis provided a secondary development flier. Miami cut salary and reduced its repeater-tax exposure, which was a legitimate organizational goal, but Udrih's contribution lasted 36 games and Stokes produced little NBA value before being moved. The Heat got the financial relief they wanted; the Grizzlies received the stronger basketball return.

sections.heading: The Clippers Paid for a Short-Term Wing Upgrade
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Jeff Green from Memphis at the 2016 deadline for Lance Stephenson and a protected future first-round pick. The idea was easy to understand: the Clippers were trying to strengthen a contender around Chris Paul, Blake Griffin and DeAndre Jordan, and Green gave them a bigger scoring wing who could play either forward spot. He appeared in 27 regular-season games for Los Angeles, started 10 and averaged 10.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 26.3 minutes.

sections.heading: Green's Stay Ended After One Playoff Run
sections.body: Green also played all six games of the Clippers' first-round loss to Portland, but the rental ended there. He entered free agency and signed with Orlando in July 2016. Los Angeles therefore spent a future first-round asset for 33 total games, including the playoffs, without retaining Green beyond that season. The short-term logic was defensible for a team chasing a deep playoff run, but the result did not deliver enough postseason value to offset the draft cost.

sections.heading: Memphis Got Production and Preserved Future Value
sections.body: Stephenson was more productive in Memphis than he had been with the Clippers, averaging 14.2 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 26 games. The more important return was the protected Clippers first. Memphis later sent that future pick to Boston on draft night in 2016 for the rights to Deyonta Davis and Rade Zagorac. The pick eventually conveyed in 2019 at No. 20, where Matisse Thybulle was selected. Memphis did not draft Thybulle, but the eventual slot confirms the real value of the future first it had acquired.

sections.heading: The Draft Asset Creates the Hindsight Gap
sections.body: Neither Davis nor Zagorac became a major long-term piece for Memphis, so the Grizzlies' return was not a franchise-changing haul. Still, they received useful immediate scoring from Stephenson and turned an expiring Green into a first-round asset that could be redeployed. Los Angeles got only a partial season from Green before he left in free agency. The canonical A- for Memphis and C for the Clippers reflects the cost of surrendering a real first-rounder for a rental who did not alter the team's playoff outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A-, LA Clippers C. Green gave Los Angeles 27 regular-season games and six playoff appearances before leaving in free agency. Memphis received 26 productive games from Stephenson plus a protected first-round pick, then converted that pick into Deyonta Davis and Rade Zagorac. The pick later conveyed at No. 20 in the 2019 draft, where Matisse Thybulle was selected. The Clippers made a reasonable contender's bet, but the completed value of a short rental did not justify the first-round cost.

sections.heading: Miami Used the Deadline Deal to Cut Its Tax Bill
sections.body: Miami sent Jarnell Stokes and roughly $700,000 in cash to New Orleans on February 18, 2016, for a top-55-protected 2018 second-round pick. Stokes had appeared in only seven games for the Heat, and the transaction was primarily a salary-and-tax move rather than a basketball upgrade. Contemporary reporting estimated that moving his remaining salary reduced Miami's projected luxury-tax obligation by a little more than $2 million and opened another roster spot.

sections.heading: New Orleans Monetized Its Available Roster Flexibility
sections.body: The Pelicans did not need Stokes to make the deal worthwhile. They absorbed his minimum contract, received the cash payment and waived him the next day. In practical terms, New Orleans used available roster and salary flexibility to collect cash while giving up a second-round pick that was protected so heavily that it initially had limited expected value. Stokes never played a game for the Pelicans, so the player himself added no on-court return.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Useful Trade Currency for Miami
sections.body: Miami did not keep the 2018 second-rounder until draft night. In July 2016, the Heat sent that same New Orleans pick plus cash back to the Pelicans for Luke Babbitt. Babbitt then appeared in 68 games for Miami during the 2016-17 season and started 15. The pick eventually became No. 51 in the 2018 draft, where Tony Carr was selected, but by then it had moved through later transactions. For this deal, Miami's clearest realized value was the ability to turn the acquired pick into a rotation shooter.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Won the Small Transaction on Cost
sections.body: This was a minor deadline move, but the completed accounting favors New Orleans. The Pelicans collected cash, carried Stokes for one day and ultimately reacquired their own protected pick in the later Babbitt trade. Miami achieved an important tax objective and eventually used the pick as trade currency, so the Heat did receive practical value. The canonical A- for New Orleans and C+ for Miami reflects the Pelicans' low-cost use of cap space versus the price Miami paid to shed salary.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans A-, Miami C+. New Orleans absorbed Stokes, received about $700,000 and waived him the next day, turning spare flexibility into cash without sacrificing a lasting player. Miami cut more than $2 million from its projected luxury-tax bill and later used the protected 2018 second-round pick in the Luke Babbitt trade, so the Heat still accomplished real financial and roster goals. The Pelicans, however, extracted value for taking on a contract they did not intend to keep.

sections.heading: Miami Paid a Pick to Finish Its Tax Escape
sections.body: Miami traded Brian Roberts and its unprotected 2021 second-round pick to Portland on February 18, 2016, for cash considerations. Roberts had been a member of the Heat for only two days after arriving in the three-team Courtney Lee deal. The move was the final piece of Miami's deadline effort to get below the luxury-tax line. Contemporary reporting estimated that the transaction saved the Heat about $7.6 million in combined salary and tax payments and also kept the franchise out of the repeater tax.

sections.heading: Portland Got a Backup Guard for the Stretch Run
sections.body: The Trail Blazers used their cap position to take on Roberts while adding future draft capital. Roberts appeared in 21 regular-season games for Portland, averaging 2.9 points in 6.5 minutes, and he also saw limited playoff action during a run to the Western Conference semifinals. He was a short-term reserve rather than a rotation-changing addition, then returned to Charlotte in free agency that summer.

sections.heading: The 2021 Second Became Real Trade Currency
sections.body: The second-round pick had more lasting usefulness than Roberts. Portland later included Miami's 2021 second, another future second and cash in the 2018 draft-night trade for the rights to Gary Trent Jr. The Miami pick eventually traveled from Sacramento to Atlanta and became No. 48 in 2021, where the Hawks selected Sharife Cooper. Portland did not make that selection itself, but it had already extracted value from the asset by using it in the Trent transaction.

sections.heading: Different Objectives Produced Comparable Value
sections.body: Portland received a temporary backup guard and a future pick without giving up a basketball asset, while Miami received only cash on the transaction ledger. The Heat's payoff was financial: getting under the tax line protected millions of dollars and preserved flexibility for the rest of the season. Portland's payoff was asset accumulation, with the pick later helping another trade. The canonical C+ grades and Even Trade verdict fit because each side accomplished its immediate objective without creating a decisive standalone return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Miami C+, Portland C+. Miami moved Roberts after only two days and used the deal to finish its escape from the luxury tax, a transaction reported to save roughly $7.6 million in salary and tax costs. Portland got 21 regular-season games from Roberts and an unprotected 2021 second-round pick, then later used that pick as part of the package for Gary Trent Jr. The Heat gained major financial relief; the Trail Blazers gained modest player value and a useful asset. Neither side produced enough direct value to separate from the other.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought a Useful Second-Round Prospect
sections.body: Milwaukee selected Patrick McCaw with the No. 38 pick in the 2016 NBA Draft, then sold his draft rights to Golden State for $2.4 million in cash. For the Warriors, the transaction was a low-risk way to add a long, defensive-minded wing to a championship roster without surrendering another player or future pick. McCaw made the team immediately and earned a real rookie role rather than spending the season as a developmental stash.

sections.heading: McCaw Contributed on Back-to-Back Champions
sections.body: As a rookie, McCaw appeared in 71 regular-season games, started 20 and averaged 4.0 points in 15.1 minutes. He also played in 15 postseason games, including three starts, during Golden State's 2017 title run. McCaw returned for 57 games and 10 starts in 2017-18, again averaging 4.0 points, before injuries reduced his playoff role. Across two Warriors seasons, he logged 128 regular-season games and 30 starts while being part of two championship teams.

sections.heading: The Warriors Did Not Keep Him Long Term
sections.body: The return was useful but finite. McCaw became a restricted free agent after his second season and did not accept Golden State's qualifying offer. After a prolonged standoff, he signed Cleveland's offer sheet in December 2018; the Warriors declined to match. Cleveland waived him days later, and McCaw eventually joined Toronto and won another championship. Golden State therefore received two inexpensive rotation seasons for its cash payment but no downstream asset when the relationship ended.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Chose Cash Over a Basketball Asset
sections.body: Milwaukee's side is straightforward: the Bucks turned the No. 38 selection into $2.4 million rather than keeping McCaw or another player at that spot. Cash has organizational value, and second-round outcomes are uncertain, so the decision was not catastrophic. Hindsight still favors Golden State because McCaw became a rotation contributor on two title teams at a minimal acquisition cost. The canonical B+ for the Warriors and C+ for Milwaukee reflects useful championship depth against a return that never produced on-court value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B+, Milwaukee C+. Golden State paid $2.4 million for the rights to Patrick McCaw and received 128 regular-season games, 30 starts and postseason minutes across two championship seasons. McCaw's Warriors tenure ended after a restricted-free-agency standoff, so the deal did not create a lasting asset beyond those two years. Milwaukee received cash rather than basketball value from the No. 38 pick. For a contender buying a second-round prospect with money alone, Golden State extracted the stronger completed return.

sections.heading: Miami Turned a Protected Pick Into Shooting
sections.body: Miami acquired Luke Babbitt from New Orleans on July 10, 2016, sending back the Pelicans' own 2018 second-round pick plus cash. The Heat had acquired that pick only months earlier in the Jarnell Stokes salary trade. Babbitt filled a clear roster need as a floor-spacing forward: he entered the deal as a career 40.3 percent three-point shooter and had hit 40.3 percent from deep for New Orleans in 2015-16.

sections.heading: Babbitt Gave the Heat One Useful Season
sections.body: Babbitt became a regular starter for Miami. He played 68 games, started 55 and averaged 4.8 points in 15.7 minutes while making 41.4 percent of his three-point attempts. That was useful low-cost spacing for a team that recovered from an 11-30 start to finish 41-41, although the Heat still missed the playoffs. Babbitt left for Atlanta in free agency after the season, so Miami's direct return was one year of rotation shooting rather than a lasting asset.

sections.heading: New Orleans Recovered Its Own Second-Rounder
sections.body: The Pelicans received cash and regained the 2018 second-round pick they had sent to Miami in the Stokes trade. That pick later became No. 51 in the 2018 draft, where New Orleans selected Penn State guard Tony Carr. Carr never produced NBA regular-season value for the Pelicans, which caps the upside of the return, but the transaction restored draft optionality and cash for a player who was entering the final year of his contract.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is Intentionally Small
sections.body: Miami got the better immediate basketball production because Babbitt played a real role and shot efficiently from three. New Orleans, however, turned an expiring reserve into cash plus a future pick that eventually conveyed, preserving value after Babbitt was no longer central to its plans. The canonical B for the Pelicans and B- for Miami therefore describes a narrow hindsight edge rather than a decisive win: one side recovered an asset, while the other received a useful but temporary contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pelicans Edge — New Orleans B, Miami B-. Babbitt gave the Heat 68 games, 55 starts and 41.4 percent three-point shooting during the 2016-17 season, but he left after one year and Miami missed the playoffs. New Orleans received cash and recovered its own 2018 second-round pick, which eventually became No. 51 and Tony Carr. Carr did not become an NBA contributor, keeping this close, but the Pelicans preserved a draft asset while moving an expiring player. The completed value supports only a slight edge.

sections.heading: The Clippers Traded a Former First-Rounder for a Future Pick
sections.body: Los Angeles sent C.J. Wilcox and cash to Orlando on July 15, 2016, for Devyn Marble and a 2020 second-round pick. Wilcox had been the No. 28 pick in 2014 but had appeared in only 44 games over two Clippers seasons. Los Angeles waived Marble the same day, making the future second the real target. The trade also created a $1.2 million trade exception for the Clippers.

sections.heading: Orlando Got Almost No NBA Production From Wilcox
sections.body: The Magic were taking a low-cost look at a shooter who had made 39.1 percent of his threes for the Clippers in 2015-16 and had produced in the D-League. It did not turn into a rotation piece. Wilcox appeared in 22 games for Orlando, averaged 1.0 point in 4.9 minutes and shot 20.0 percent from three. Orlando declined his 2017-18 option and waived him in April 2017, ending the experiment after one season.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Became Useful Trade Currency
sections.body: The pick was more valuable than its eventual No. 32 slot suggests because Los Angeles used it before the 2020 draft. In 2018, the Clippers sent the rights to Miles Bridges plus two future second-round picks to Charlotte for the rights to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. The 2020 second acquired from Orlando was one of those two picks. It later became Vernon Carey Jr. for Charlotte, but the Clippers had already converted its value into part of the package that moved them from No. 12 to No. 11.

sections.heading: A Minor Deal Produced a Real Downstream Asset
sections.body: Marble never played for Los Angeles, and Wilcox provided only 22 games for Orlando, so the player swap itself was negligible. The difference is the pick. Los Angeles turned a player outside its rotation into a future second that later helped facilitate the Gilgeous-Alexander draft-night move. Orlando received cash and a prospect audition, but neither created durable basketball value. The canonical B for the Clippers and C+ for the Magic appropriately keeps the win modest while recognizing the pick's later utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — LA Clippers B, Orlando C+. The Clippers waived Devyn Marble immediately, but the 2020 second-round pick they received became useful currency in the 2018 trade that brought Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's draft rights to Los Angeles. Orlando got only 22 games from C.J. Wilcox before waiving him, plus cash considerations. The pick ultimately became No. 32 and Vernon Carey Jr. after reaching Charlotte, but its direct value to the Clippers had already been realized in the Gilgeous-Alexander move.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Found a Real Long-Term Starter
sections.body: Oklahoma City acquired Jerami Grant from Philadelphia on November 1, 2016, for Ersan Ilyasova and a protected future first-round pick. Grant was 22 and already had 144 NBA games behind him, but his offensive role was still developing. With the Thunder he grew from a reserve into a full-time starter. By 2018-19 he played 80 games, started 77 and averaged 13.6 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.3 blocks while shooting 39.2 percent from three.

sections.heading: Grant Also Returned Another First-Round Pick
sections.body: The Thunder did not lose Grant for nothing. In July 2019 they traded him to Denver for a top-10-protected 2020 first-round pick after his career-best season. That pick ultimately landed at No. 25, where Immanuel Quickley was selected before the rights moved through another draft-night transaction. For Oklahoma City, the Grant acquisition therefore produced nearly three seasons of useful forward play and a first-round asset on the way out, supporting a strong B+ even in a losing trade.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Immediate Production and the Better Pick Outcome
sections.body: Ilyasova gave Philadelphia 53 games and 40 starts in 2016-17, averaging 14.8 points before the 76ers moved him to Atlanta at the deadline for Tiago Splitter and additional second-round considerations. The larger payoff took four years. Oklahoma City's protected first conveyed in 2020 at No. 21, and Philadelphia selected Tyrese Maxey. Maxey developed into an All-Star guard, turning what began as a patient draft asset into the most valuable individual outcome tied to the original deal.

sections.heading: Both Teams Executed Well, but Maxey Breaks the Tie
sections.body: This is not a case where Oklahoma City made a bad decision. Grant developed exactly the way the Thunder hoped, helped playoff teams and later brought back another first. Philadelphia simply converted its side into more total value: useful Ilyasova production, a later trade return from Ilyasova and, most importantly, the pick that became Maxey. The canonical A for Philadelphia and B+ for Oklahoma City capture that distinction. The 76ers win the hindsight comparison without turning the Thunder's process into a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Oklahoma City B+. Jerami Grant became a starting-caliber two-way forward for the Thunder and later returned a 2020 first-round pick in the Denver trade. Philadelphia received 53 games from Ersan Ilyasova, later moved him again for additional value, and held the protected Oklahoma City first until it conveyed at No. 21 in 2020. That selection became Tyrese Maxey, whose All-Star development creates the decisive hindsight edge. Oklahoma City still earned a strong return; Philadelphia simply produced the best asset.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Dillon Brooks With a Future Second
sections.body: Houston selected Dillon Brooks with the No. 45 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, then traded his draft rights to Memphis for a future second-round pick. The Grizzlies were buying a four-year Oregon wing who had just been named Pac-12 Player of the Year, and the price was modest. Brooks immediately made the roster and started 74 games as a rookie, turning a draft-night rights purchase into an everyday player instead of a developmental lottery ticket.

sections.heading: Brooks Became a Six-Season Memphis Starter
sections.body: Brooks stayed with the Grizzlies through the 2022-23 season and became one of their most-used perimeter defenders. He appeared in 345 regular-season games for Memphis across six seasons, started the large majority of them and averaged double figures in scoring in five straight seasons after his rookie year. His final Memphis season ended with All-Defensive Second Team honors. The relationship eventually ran its course, but the original trade had already produced years of starting minutes and playoff defense.

sections.heading: Houston's Pick Became De'Anthony Melton
sections.body: The future second conveyed in 2018 at No. 46, where Houston selected De'Anthony Melton. Melton became a productive NBA guard, but none of that production came for the Rockets. Before his rookie season, Houston packaged Melton with Ryan Anderson in a trade to Phoenix for Marquese Chriss and Brandon Knight. The pick therefore had legitimate transaction value, yet the Rockets never received the long-term on-court benefit that Melton later provided elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Gap Comes From Retained Player Value
sections.body: Both sides turned a second-round asset into something useful, but Memphis captured far more of the basketball value. Brooks became a six-year rotation fixture and defensive starter for a playoff team. Houston used Melton before he played a regular-season game for the franchise, and the return from the Phoenix deal did not approach Brooks' Memphis tenure. The canonical A for the Grizzlies and D for the Rockets reflects the durability gap rather than the simple fact that both original assets became NBA players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A, Houston D. Memphis acquired Dillon Brooks' draft rights for a future second and received six seasons, 345 regular-season games and an All-Defensive Second Team selection from him. Houston's pick became De'Anthony Melton at No. 46 in 2018, but the Rockets traded Melton to Phoenix before he played a regular-season game for them. Houston did recover trade value through that package, yet Memphis received the far stronger direct basketball return from the original exchange.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned No. 28 Into Two Prospects
sections.body: Utah acquired the draft rights to Tony Bradley, the No. 28 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, from the Lakers for the rights to Josh Hart at No. 30 and Thomas Bryant at No. 42. Los Angeles effectively moved back two spots while adding an extra second-round prospect. Hart became an immediate rotation guard and wing, while Bryant gave the Lakers another inexpensive developmental big without requiring a future pick or veteran player.

sections.heading: Hart Produced and Then Helped Bring Anthony Davis
sections.body: Hart played 130 regular-season games over two Lakers seasons before his value became part of a much larger transaction. In July 2019, Los Angeles sent Hart, Brandon Ingram, Lonzo Ball, the draft rights to De'Andre Hunter and additional draft capital to New Orleans for Anthony Davis. Hart was not the centerpiece of that package, but the Lakers converted the No. 30 rights acquired here into two years of useful minutes and a real component of the trade for a franchise-changing star.

sections.heading: Bryant Added Upside Even Though Los Angeles Let Him Go
sections.body: Bryant played only 15 NBA games for the Lakers as a rookie and was waived in June 2018, so Los Angeles did not capture his later breakout with Washington. His inclusion still strengthened the original draft-night return because he became a productive NBA center after leaving. The Lakers cannot be credited with Washington's production, but landing both Hart and Bryant for Bradley's rights shows how much prospect value they created by moving down only two spots.

sections.heading: Utah Received a Reserve Center and Little Else
sections.body: Bradley spent three seasons with the Jazz and appeared in 70 games, starting three, while averaging 4.4 points and 4.2 rebounds in 10.4 minutes. Utah traded him to Detroit in 2020 with the rights to Saben Lee for cash considerations. Bradley was a usable reserve, but his Jazz tenure never approached Hart's direct Lakers value, much less Hart's inclusion in the Davis package. The canonical A- for Los Angeles and F for Utah reflects an unusually wide gap for a small draft-night move.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — LA Lakers A-, Utah F. Los Angeles moved from No. 28 to No. 30, added the No. 42 rights and came away with Josh Hart and Thomas Bryant. Hart gave the Lakers 130 regular-season games before becoming part of the 2019 Anthony Davis trade. Bryant later proved he belonged in an NBA rotation, even though most of that value came after Los Angeles waived him. Utah received 70 games from Tony Bradley and eventually moved him for cash. The realized-value gap clearly favors the Lakers.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Ivan Rabb at No. 35
sections.body: Memphis acquired the draft rights to Ivan Rabb, the No. 35 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, from Orlando for a future second-round pick. Rabb was a 20-year-old California forward who had averaged 14.0 points and 10.5 rebounds as a college sophomore. The Grizzlies were buying a young frontcourt prospect at a familiar second-round price, and he did reach the NBA rotation during both seasons he spent with the franchise.

sections.heading: Rabb's Memphis Run Never Grew Past Reserve Value
sections.body: Rabb played 85 regular-season games for Memphis across 2017-18 and 2018-19, starting 18. He averaged 5.7 points and 4.3 rebounds in 14.6 minutes while shooting 55.5 percent from the field. Those numbers gave the Grizzlies some real return from the No. 35 rights, but he never established himself as a long-term starter and his NBA career ended after those two Memphis seasons. The acquisition produced usable depth rather than a durable core piece.

sections.heading: Orlando's Pick Became Talen Horton-Tucker
sections.body: The future second conveyed in 2019 at No. 46, where Orlando selected Talen Horton-Tucker. The Magic did not keep him. On draft night they traded his rights to the Lakers for a 2020 second-round pick and cash considerations, reported at $2.2 million. Horton-Tucker later became a rotation player in Los Angeles, but Orlando's realized value from the original Memphis asset was the cash plus another future second, not Horton-Tucker's later NBA production.

sections.heading: The Magic Preserved More Asset Value
sections.body: Memphis received two seasons of reserve minutes from Rabb, while Orlando turned the outgoing No. 35 rights into a future second and then converted that pick again for cash plus another second. Neither path produced a franchise-changing player for the team that held the asset, which keeps the trade in modest territory. The canonical B for Orlando and C for Memphis reflects the Magic's better asset preservation against Rabb's limited two-year NBA run rather than crediting Orlando with Horton-Tucker's Lakers career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Memphis C. Ivan Rabb gave Memphis 85 games, 18 starts and two seasons of reserve frontcourt production after the Grizzlies acquired his No. 35 draft rights. Orlando's future second became the No. 46 pick in 2019 and Talen Horton-Tucker, whose rights the Magic immediately moved to the Lakers for a 2020 second-round pick and cash. Orlando did not capture Horton-Tucker's later player value, but it preserved and re-used the draft asset more effectively than Memphis converted Rabb into lasting value.
