sections.heading: Indiana Swapped a Former 1st-Rounder for a Young Guard
sections.body: Indiana sent T.J. Leaf and a 2027 second-round pick to Oklahoma City for Jalen Lecque on November 25, 2020. Leaf had been the No. 18 pick in the 2017 draft but had fallen out of the Pacers' rotation by the end of his third season. Lecque was only 20 and had arrived in Oklahoma City days earlier through the Chris Paul trade with Phoenix. The Pacers were effectively exchanging a player they had already moved past for a younger developmental guard, but attaching a future second made the bet more expensive than a straight prospect swap.

sections.heading: Lecque Barely Reached the Pacers' Rotation
sections.body: Lecque appeared in four regular-season games for Indiana in 2020-21, totaling 12 minutes, five points, five rebounds and two assists. The Pacers assigned him to the Fort Wayne Mad Ants in January, recalled him in March and waived him on March 25. His NBA career ended after nine total games across Phoenix and Indiana. That leaves very little realized return for a team that surrendered both Leaf and a future pick. The idea of buying a younger upside guard was reasonable; the actual result was four brief appearances and no lasting roster value.

sections.heading: Leaf Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Oklahoma City
sections.body: The Thunder did not extract on-court value from Leaf either. Oklahoma City acquired him as a 23-year-old former 1st-round pick and described him as a frontcourt player who might benefit from a new opportunity, but the experiment lasted only through training camp and preseason. The Thunder waived Leaf on December 18, 2020, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the franchise. That keeps this from being a player-development win for Oklahoma City and is why the canonical grade stops at B instead of climbing higher.

sections.heading: The 2027 Second Is the Durable Piece
sections.body: The trade still leans toward Oklahoma City because the Thunder retained Indiana's 2027 second-round pick after Leaf was waived. As of October 2026, that selection has not yet been made, so the asset should be treated as unresolved rather than credited with a future player or draft slot. Its value is simply that Oklahoma City turned Lecque, who produced almost nothing for Indiana, into an additional draft asset that survived beyond both players' time with their new teams. The Pacers' side ended in March 2021; the Thunder's side still contains a live piece entering the 2027 draft cycle.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Indiana C+, Oklahoma City B. Indiana received only four games and 12 minutes from Jalen Lecque before waiving him in March 2021. Oklahoma City got no regular-season minutes from T.J. Leaf and waived him in December 2020, so the player-for-player portion produced little for either side. The difference is Indiana's 2027 second-round pick, which remains an unresolved but still-live asset as of October 2026. That future selection gives the Thunder more durable value from a transaction in which neither incoming player became part of the receiving team's long-term rotation.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Paid to Fix the Horford Fit
sections.body: Philadelphia sent Al Horford, the rights to Theo Maledon and Vasilije Micić, a protected future 1st-round pick and cash to Oklahoma City for Danny Green, Terrance Ferguson and Vincent Poirier. The transaction was primarily a roster correction for the 76ers after Horford's lone Philadelphia season produced an awkward frontcourt fit. Green immediately gave the club a lower-usage wing who could defend and space the floor, while Ferguson and Poirier were secondary pieces. The Sixers improved their lineup balance, but doing so required surrendering a substantial package rather than simply swapping comparable veterans.

sections.heading: Green Delivered Exactly What Philadelphia Needed
sections.body: Danny Green started all 69 regular-season games he played for Philadelphia in 2020-21, averaging 9.5 points and shooting 40.5 percent from three. The 76ers finished with the Eastern Conference's best regular-season record, and Green's shooting fit far more naturally around Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons than Horford had the year before. That immediate basketball payoff keeps Philadelphia's side from being treated as a failure even with the B- grade. Ferguson and Poirier added little, but Green was a real starter on a team that won the conference's No. 1 seed.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Rebuilt Horford's Value and Kept the Extras
sections.body: Horford played 28 games for Oklahoma City, averaging 14.2 points, 6.7 rebounds and 3.4 assists while shooting 36.8 percent from three. The Thunder later moved him to Boston with Moses Brown and a 2023 second-round pick for Kemba Walker, the No. 16 pick in the 2021 draft and a 2025 second-rounder. That later trade should not be credited entirely to Horford because Oklahoma City sent additional assets with him, but it does show that absorbing his contract did not leave the franchise stuck with dead salary. Maledon also played 65 games as a rookie, giving the Thunder another immediate return from the original package.

sections.heading: The Protected 1st Became a Real Lottery-Adjacent Asset
sections.body: The future 1st carried protections for several years before finally conveying in 2026. Oklahoma City held the No. 17 selection tied to that asset and used it on Ebuka Okorie before his rights were routed onward in draft-night trades. The important point for this transaction is the conversion from a protected future claim into the No. 17 pick, not Okorie's later destination or career. Combined with Horford's restored market value, Maledon's rookie contribution, Micić's rights and the cash component, that realized draft asset gives Oklahoma City more total return than Philadelphia received from its fit-improving package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Oklahoma City A-, Philadelphia B-. Philadelphia solved a real lineup problem and received 69 starts plus 40.5 percent three-point shooting from Danny Green on the East's No. 1 seed, so the deal accomplished its immediate purpose. Oklahoma City, however, took on Al Horford, received useful rookie minutes from Theo Maledon, retained the rights to Vasilije Micić, added cash and ultimately saw the protected 1st convey as the No. 17 pick in 2026. Horford also regained enough value to be moved again in a separate multi-asset trade. The Sixers improved their fit, but the Thunder accumulated the stronger long-term package.

sections.heading: New York Bought a Playoff Guard for a Modest Price
sections.body: The Knicks reacquired Derrick Rose from Detroit on February 8, 2021 for Dennis Smith Jr. and Charlotte's 2021 second-round pick, while Detroit's canonical package also includes the resulting traded player exception. Rose already knew Tom Thibodeau's system and arrived on a team trying to turn an unexpectedly strong start into a playoff berth. New York did not have to sacrifice a core rotation player or a 1st-round pick, which kept the downside limited even before Rose's second Knicks tenure proved successful.

sections.heading: Rose Became One of the Knicks' Best Offensive Options
sections.body: Rose played 35 regular-season games for New York after the trade, averaging 14.9 points and 4.2 assists while shooting 48.7 percent from the field and 41.1 percent from three. The Knicks finished 41-31 and earned the East's No. 4 seed, their first playoff appearance since 2013. His value became even clearer against Atlanta: Rose averaged 19.4 points, 5.0 assists and 4.0 rebounds across five first-round games. New York lost the series, but the player acquired for a reserve guard and a second-rounder became its leading playoff scorer.

sections.heading: Detroit Got a Look at Smith and Converted the Pick
sections.body: Detroit's return was not empty. Dennis Smith Jr. played 20 games for the Pistons, starting nine and averaging 7.3 points, 3.7 assists and 2.7 rebounds in 19.6 minutes. The second-round pick became No. 42 in the 2021 draft, where Detroit selected Michigan forward Isaiah Livers. Livers later supplied rotation minutes for the Pistons, giving the draft asset more staying power than Smith's short stint. The trade exception added another piece of roster flexibility, so Detroit did recover multiple forms of value while moving a veteran from a rebuilding team.

sections.heading: The Timing Made the Gap Larger
sections.body: Detroit was rebuilding and Rose was 32, so moving him for a younger guard and a draft pick was a defensible direction. The hindsight gap comes from what New York extracted immediately at a very low acquisition cost. Rose helped a 41-win team secure home court in the first round, then carried a larger offensive burden once the postseason began. Smith's Detroit run lasted only 20 games, while Livers was a useful second-round outcome rather than a franchise-changing return. The Pistons gained assets; the Knicks acquired the most influential player in the transaction at exactly the point their season needed him.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — Detroit C+, New York A. Detroit had a rational reason to move Derrick Rose and received a real return in Dennis Smith Jr., the No. 42 pick that became Isaiah Livers and a trade exception. New York still won the deal decisively because Rose became a high-impact rotation guard on a 41-31 team, helped the Knicks secure the East's No. 4 seed and averaged 19.4 points in their first playoff series since 2013. The acquisition price was modest, the immediate fit was excellent and the postseason value was far greater than the assets New York surrendered.

sections.heading: Miami Turned an Inactive Contract Into a Starting Wing
sections.body: Miami acquired Trevor Ariza from Oklahoma City on March 17, 2021 for Meyers Leonard and a 2027 second-round pick, while the Thunder also generated a traded player exception. Ariza had not appeared in an NBA game since March 2020 and never suited up for Oklahoma City, so Miami was buying a veteran fit rather than current-season production. The Heat needed another switchable forward after reaching the 2020 Finals, and Leonard was no longer part of their playing rotation. The cost was meaningful because of the future second, but it did not remove a contributor from Miami's active postseason group.

sections.heading: Ariza Became an Immediate Rotation Piece
sections.body: Ariza played 30 regular-season games for the Heat, starting 27 and averaging 9.4 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 28.0 minutes. He also averaged 1.0 steal and shot 35.0 percent from three. Miami reached the playoffs and used him in all four games of its first-round series against Milwaukee. The postseason ended in a sweep, so Ariza did not reproduce the kind of long run the franchise had enjoyed a year earlier, but the trade still converted an unavailable player and a future second into a veteran who immediately handled starter-level minutes down the stretch.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Was Really Buying the Future Pick
sections.body: Meyers Leonard never played for the Thunder. Oklahoma City announced the trade with the 2027 second-round pick and a trade exception as the durable pieces, then waived Leonard on March 25, eight days after acquiring him. That timeline makes the asset logic unusually clear: the Thunder were not evaluating Leonard as a basketball addition. They used salary mechanics to move Ariza, who had not played for them, and added another future selection to a rebuilding stockpile. As of October 2026, the 2027 pick has not been made, so it should remain unresolved rather than credited with a player or draft slot that does not yet exist.

sections.heading: The Grades Reflect Different Kinds of Value
sections.body: Miami's B+ comes from realized on-court value. Ariza became a starter, absorbed real minutes and filled a positional need for a playoff team. Oklahoma City's B- recognizes that the Thunder gave up no 2020-21 production because Ariza never appeared for them and still came away with a future second plus a trade exception. The gap stays modest because Miami's playoff run lasted only four games and the Thunder's most important return remains unresolved. The Heat won the near-term basketball exchange, while Oklahoma City executed a defensible asset-collection move that may still gain value when the 2027 selection finally conveys.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami B+, Oklahoma City B-. Miami turned Meyers Leonard, who was no longer contributing on the court, plus a 2027 second-round pick into 30 regular-season games and 27 starts from Trevor Ariza. Ariza gave the Heat 28.0 minutes per game, defensive versatility and another veteran forward for their playoff rotation. Oklahoma City still achieved its rebuilding objective: Leonard never played for the Thunder and was waived eight days later, while the franchise retained the future second and generated a trade exception. The unresolved pick keeps the Thunder's side from grading poorly, but Miami received the stronger realized return.

sections.heading: Miami Chased Oladipo's Upside at the Deadline
sections.body: Miami acquired Victor Oladipo from Houston on March 25, 2021 for Kelly Olynyk, Avery Bradley and a 2022 1st-round pick-swap mechanism. The Heat were coming off a Finals run but had slipped offensively, so adding a two-time All-Star without surrendering a premium unprotected pick was an understandable gamble. Oladipo had already moved from Indiana to Houston in the James Harden transaction and was headed toward free agency. Miami was betting that a change of team could unlock enough two-way guard play for another postseason run before it had to make a long-term contract decision.

sections.heading: Oladipo's First Miami Run Lasted Four Games
sections.body: The upside case collapsed almost immediately. Oladipo appeared in four games for the Heat before injuring his right knee on April 8 against the Lakers. Miami later announced that he would undergo season-ending surgery on his right quadriceps tendon, eliminating him from the 2021 playoffs. The Heat eventually brought him back after rehabilitation, so the relationship did not end with those four games, but the return attributable to this deadline trade was still badly interrupted at the moment Miami needed it most. That limited realized impact is the central reason the canonical Miami grade lands at C.

sections.heading: Olynyk Produced Immediately in Houston
sections.body: Kelly Olynyk gave the Rockets a much more tangible short-term return. He played 27 games for Houston, starting 24 and averaging 19.0 points, 8.4 rebounds and 4.1 assists in 31.1 minutes. He shot 54.5 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Those numbers came for a 17-win team and did not alter Houston's rebuilding trajectory, but they still represent substantial realized production from an expiring veteran acquired for a player the Rockets had decided to move. Avery Bradley added another veteran contract and rotation option, while Olynyk became the clear basketball centerpiece of Houston's package.

sections.heading: The Swap Never Added Extra Value
sections.body: Houston also received a conditional 2022 1st-round swap mechanism tied to Miami, Brooklyn and Houston pick positions, but the canonical ledger records that option as not exercised. That means the draft component should not be inflated in hindsight: Houston's win rests primarily on Olynyk's production and the fact that Oladipo's first Miami stint was derailed almost immediately. The Rockets did not uncover a foundational asset, and Olynyk left after the season, which keeps the grade at B+ rather than turning the trade into a major franchise victory. It was a good salvage job from a deteriorating Oladipo situation, not a transformational return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston B+, Miami C. Houston moved Victor Oladipo before free agency and received 27 productive games from Kelly Olynyk, who averaged 19.0 points, 8.4 rebounds and 4.1 assists while shooting 54.5 percent from the field. Avery Bradley added another roster piece, while the 2022 swap mechanism ultimately was not exercised. Miami's gamble produced only four games before Oladipo injured his right knee and later underwent season-ending quadriceps surgery. The Heat's upside logic was understandable, but the realized value from the transaction favored Houston by a clear margin.

sections.heading: Indiana Used the No. 31 Rights as Immediate Trade Currency
sections.body: Indiana sent the draft rights to Sandro Mamukelashvili and Georgios Kalaitzakis plus two future second-round picks to Milwaukee for the rights to Isaiah Todd, the No. 31 selection in the 2021 draft. Todd never became a Pacers player. Indiana moved his rights days later with Aaron Holiday and cash in the multi-team transaction that brought Isaiah Jackson to the Pacers. Because Holiday was also part of that separate package, Jackson's full value cannot be assigned to this deal, but Todd's rights clearly served as useful same-night trade currency rather than becoming a dead asset.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got the Best Direct NBA Contributor
sections.body: Mamukelashvili gave the Bucks tangible NBA value from the original package. Milwaukee kept him on a two-way contract across two seasons, and he appeared in 65 games before the club waived him in March 2023. He averaged 3.2 points and 2.1 rebounds in 9.6 minutes with the Bucks while also producing at a much higher level for the Wisconsin Herd. Georgios Kalaitzakis had a smaller role, appearing in nine regular-season games for Milwaukee as a rookie. Neither became a core player, but Mamukelashvili supplied more direct NBA service than Indiana received from Todd himself.

sections.heading: The Two Seconds Added More Asset Value
sections.body: Milwaukee also received two future second-round picks, which widened the return beyond the two draft-rights prospects. The 2024 obligation eventually resolved to the No. 46 slot, where Cam Christie was selected after the pick had moved through later transactions. The 2026 obligation also continued through subsequent routing and ultimately resolved to the No. 32 slot, where Richie Saunders was selected. Those downstream selections should not be credited to Milwaukee as if the Bucks drafted and developed both players, but the realized pick positions show that Indiana surrendered real second-round capital in addition to the two 2021 prospects.

sections.heading: Indiana's Logic Was Defensible but Expensive
sections.body: The Pacers were trying to move up from Nos. 54 and 60 to No. 31, then use that higher selection inside a separate deal for Isaiah Jackson. That sequencing makes more sense than evaluating the transaction as Indiana simply choosing Todd over Mamukelashvili. Even so, the price included two future seconds and a prospect in Mamukelashvili who produced 65 NBA games for Milwaukee. Indiana did obtain a more flexible draft asset and quickly converted it, but the Bucks accumulated more direct and traceable value from the exchange itself. That distinction supports a Milwaukee win without treating the Pacers' side as irrational.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Indiana C+, Milwaukee A-. Indiana acquired the No. 31 draft rights to Isaiah Todd and immediately used those rights with Aaron Holiday and cash in the separate multi-team deal that brought Isaiah Jackson to the Pacers, so the asset had real utility. Milwaukee still received the stronger package from this transaction: Sandro Mamukelashvili played 65 games for the Bucks, Georgios Kalaitzakis reached the NBA, and the two future seconds eventually resolved to valuable second-round slots. The Pacers' sequencing had a purpose, but Milwaukee extracted more direct value from the assets Indiana surrendered.

sections.heading: Portland Bought the No. 43 Pick for Cash and a Future Second
sections.body: Portland acquired the draft rights to Greg Brown III, the No. 43 pick in the 2021 NBA Draft, from New Orleans for cash and Portland's own 2026 second-round pick. The Trail Blazers were buying a developmental forward with obvious athletic upside at a modest acquisition cost. Brown had averaged 9.3 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.0 block in 26 games as a freshman at Texas, and Portland's official release described him as a high-ceiling prospect. For a team trying to add inexpensive youth around an expensive veteran core, the logic was straightforward.

sections.heading: Brown Reached the Rotation but Never Locked Down a Long-Term Role
sections.body: Greg Brown III played 64 regular-season games for Portland across two seasons. As a rookie he appeared in 48 games, made six starts and averaged 4.7 points and 2.8 rebounds in 13.3 minutes. His second season shrank to 16 appearances and 5.8 minutes per game before Portland moved on. Brown later appeared in six games for Dallas, but his Portland tenure never grew into the kind of durable rotation role that would make surrendering a future second look cheap in hindsight. The Blazers did get real NBA minutes from the pick, just not a lasting contributor.

sections.heading: The 2026 Pick Eventually Became a Real Second-Round Asset
sections.body: The draft component is no longer hypothetical. Basketball-Reference's Portland and New Orleans transaction histories now identify the 2026 second as the pick that later became Ja'Kobi Gillespie, selected No. 42 in the 2026 NBA Draft. Gillespie was drafted by San Antonio, so New Orleans did not simply keep the selection and use it itself; later routing affected the final destination. Still, the original Pelicans return contained a second-round asset that ultimately landed in the upper half of Round 2, plus cash. That realized pick position gives the New Orleans side more substance than a future-pick placeholder suggested at the time.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Took the Better Long-Horizon Side of a Small Deal
sections.body: This was a minor draft-night transaction, so the grade gap should stay proportional. Portland received 64 games from Brown and gave a young forward a real audition. New Orleans, however, sold the No. 43 rights for cash and a future second that eventually resolved at No. 42. The Pelicans effectively moved down one slot in draft value across five years while also receiving cash, although later transactions mean they cannot be credited with Gillespie's NBA career. The result is not a major win, but the asset math aged better for New Orleans than Portland's short-lived player return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B, Portland C. Portland acquired Greg Brown III at No. 43 and received 64 regular-season games from him over two seasons, including 48 appearances as a rookie. The gamble produced some NBA value but not a lasting rotation player. New Orleans received cash and Portland's 2026 second-round pick, which later resolved to the No. 42 selection used on Ja'Kobi Gillespie. Later routing prevents the Pelicans from being credited with Gillespie himself, but the original asset still matured into a useful second-round slot. For a small draft-night deal, that is enough to preserve the canonical New Orleans edge.

sections.heading: New York Turned One Early Second Into Two Prospects
sections.body: New York sent the draft rights to Jeremiah Robinson-Earl, the No. 32 pick in 2021, to Oklahoma City for the rights to Rokas Jokubaitis at No. 34 and Miles McBride at No. 36. The structure was simple but aggressive: the Knicks moved down twice inside the second round and came away with two players instead of one. Jokubaitis offered a longer-term overseas development path, while McBride arrived as a defense-first guard after averaging 15.9 points, 4.8 assists and 1.9 steals at West Virginia.

sections.heading: McBride Became the Best Player in the Deal
sections.body: Miles McBride turned the trade from a clever draft-night maneuver into a clear New York win. Through the 2025-26 season he had appeared in 277 regular-season games for the Knicks, starting 43, while developing from a deep reserve into a trusted two-way rotation guard. He averaged 12.0 points in 41 games during 2025-26 and shot 41.3 percent from three. McBride was also part of New York's 2026 championship team. A No. 36 pick becoming a multi-year contributor on a title roster is substantial realized value.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Still Got Legitimate NBA Production
sections.body: Jeremiah Robinson-Earl was not a miss for the Thunder. He played 49 games and started 36 as a rookie, then added 43 games and 20 starts in 2022-23. Across those two Oklahoma City seasons he provided frontcourt minutes, rebounding and floor spacing on a young roster before the Thunder eventually moved him. That return is enough to keep the Oklahoma City side at a respectable B rather than treating the transaction as one-sided. The problem is that Robinson-Earl's value never reached the level McBride ultimately produced for New York.

sections.heading: Jokubaitis Was Extra Optionality, Not the Reason for the Grade Gap
sections.body: Rokas Jokubaitis added another development asset to New York's side, but the hindsight case does not need to exaggerate his contribution. The Knicks controlled his NBA draft rights while he continued his career in Europe, giving the franchise an additional option after already securing McBride. The decisive difference is the conversion of No. 36 into a long-term rotation guard and champion. Oklahoma City received useful minutes from Robinson-Earl, but New York extracted a stronger player outcome while also retaining the second prospect's rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Oklahoma City B. Oklahoma City received real value from Jeremiah Robinson-Earl, who played 92 regular-season games for the Thunder across two seasons and started 56 of them. New York still finished with the superior return. Miles McBride grew from the No. 36 pick into a 277-game Knicks contributor through 2025-26, became a reliable two-way rotation guard and was part of the franchise's 2026 championship team. Rokas Jokubaitis added another asset on top of that. The Thunder's side was productive, but McBride created the durable separation reflected in the canonical grades.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought the Veteran Organizer It Needed
sections.body: Cleveland acquired Ricky Rubio from Minnesota for Taurean Prince, a 2022 second-round pick and cash considerations. The Cavaliers were adding a veteran playmaker to a young backcourt led by Darius Garland, and Rubio immediately fit that job. He was not acquired to carry the offense; he was there to steady second units, create shots for teammates and give a rising roster another trusted ball-handler. The price was meaningful but manageable: a useful veteran wing, a second and cash rather than a premium first-round asset.

sections.heading: Rubio Was Excellent Until the ACL Tear
sections.body: Rubio played only 34 games before tearing the ACL in his left knee on December 28, 2021, but his impact during that stretch was unusually strong. He averaged 13.1 points, 6.6 assists, 4.1 rebounds and 1.44 steals in 28.5 minutes, and Cleveland credited his leadership as part of a 22-win improvement from the prior season. His peak was a 37-point, 10-assist night at Madison Square Garden in which he hit eight three-pointers off the bench. The injury shortened the return, yet the pre-injury production and fit were real.

sections.heading: Minnesota Got Two Useful Prince Seasons
sections.body: Taurean Prince gave Minnesota more longevity than Rubio's first Cleveland stint. Prince played 69 games in 2021-22 and another 54 in 2022-23, supplying wing size and shooting on two playoff teams. In his first Timberwolves season he shot 37.6 percent from three and averaged 7.3 points in 17.1 minutes. That is legitimate rotation value, and it is why Minnesota's canonical B should not be treated like a failed return. The Wolves also received the 2022 second that became the No. 40 selection, Bryce McGowens, plus cash considerations.

sections.heading: Rubio's Value Extended Beyond the 34 Games
sections.body: The strongest Cleveland argument is not simply that Rubio had better box-score production. After his injury, the Cavaliers used his expiring contract in the February 2022 trade that brought Caris LeVert from Indiana, then re-signed Rubio in free agency that summer. The original acquisition therefore helped Cleveland twice: first as a high-level veteran guard during the team's breakout start, then as salary and trade structure in the LeVert deal. Minnesota received useful Prince minutes and a second-round asset, but Cleveland extracted more leverage from Rubio's contract and on-court fit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, Minnesota B. Ricky Rubio gave Cleveland 34 high-impact games at 13.1 points and 6.6 assists per night before a season-ending ACL tear, then his contract became part of the trade that brought Caris LeVert to the Cavaliers. Minnesota still received a good return: Taurean Prince played 123 regular-season games over two seasons, helped two playoff teams and supplied needed wing shooting, while the included 2022 second became the No. 40 pick. The Timberwolves realized useful value, but Rubio's immediate effect and Cleveland's later use of his contract created the stronger overall result.

sections.heading: The Clippers Bought a Late-Second Upside Bet
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired the draft rights to Brandon Boston Jr., the No. 51 pick in the 2021 draft, from New Orleans on August 7, 2021. The Clippers' announcement described the return as cash considerations, while Basketball-Reference's transaction ledger also tracks a protected 2022 Sacramento second-round pick that would go to the Pelicans only if it landed from No. 55 through No. 60. It did not convey. That left Los Angeles with a young wing prospect for cash and a conditional asset that never became an NBA pick for New Orleans.

sections.heading: Boston Gave Los Angeles Three Seasons of Real NBA Minutes
sections.body: Boston never became a core player, but the Clippers did receive usable value from the rights they purchased. He appeared in 105 regular-season games over three seasons for Los Angeles and logged 1,353 minutes. As a rookie he played 51 games and averaged 6.7 points in 14.9 minutes, giving an injury-hit Clippers roster another developmental scorer. His role shrank over the next two years and he left after the 2023-24 season, so this was not a hidden star outcome. It was still a successful conversion of a very small outgoing package into three years of roster depth.

sections.heading: New Orleans' Draft Return Never Materialized
sections.body: The Pelicans had acquired Boston's rights from Memphis as part of the larger August 7 transaction that also brought Jonas Valanciunas and Trey Murphy III to New Orleans. Moving the No. 51 rights immediately for cash and a protected future second was defensible asset recycling at the time. The problem in hindsight is simple: the protected 2022 second did not convey. New Orleans therefore did not receive a future player or draft selection from the Clippers side of this exchange, while Boston became an actual three-season contributor in Los Angeles. That creates a modest but clear Clippers edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B-, New Orleans C-. Brandon Boston Jr. produced 105 regular-season games and 1,353 minutes for the Clippers after arriving as the No. 51 pick, including a 51-game rookie season at 6.7 points per game. New Orleans received cash and a protected 2022 second-round pick that did not convey. The Pelicans' decision to monetize a late second-round prospect was understandable, but Los Angeles turned the transaction into three seasons of real NBA depth without surrendering a pick that ultimately transferred.

sections.heading: New York Took a Cheap Swing on Cam Reddish
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Cam Reddish, Solomon Hill and Brooklyn's 2025 second-round pick from Atlanta for Kevin Knox II and Charlotte's protected first-round obligation. The first was protected through 2025 and would become Charlotte's 2026 and 2027 second-round picks if it never conveyed. That structure made the trade a calculated upside play for New York: Reddish was a 22-year-old former top-10 pick, Knox was already outside the Knicks' rotation, and New York also received a second-round asset back in the deal.

sections.heading: Reddish Never Became a Core Knick
sections.body: The upside bet did not turn into a long-term answer. Reddish played 15 games for New York after the trade in 2021-22 and 20 more in 2022-23, totaling 35 regular-season appearances, eight starts and 653 minutes. His role fluctuated under Tom Thibodeau and he eventually fell out of the rotation. Solomon Hill did not add on-court value for New York and was waived six days after the trade. The player return therefore fell well short of the star-level outcome the Knicks hoped Reddish might reach.

sections.heading: The Knicks Still Recycled Both Meaningful Assets
sections.body: New York did recover value from the pieces it acquired. Reddish was included in the February 2023 package that brought Josh Hart from Portland, though the Knicks also surrendered a protected first-round pick and other assets in that deal, so Reddish should not be credited as the sole price for Hart. The 2025 Brooklyn second later became the No. 36 pick and was included in the 2024 Mikal Bridges trade with the Nets. Neither downstream move makes the Reddish trade a home run, but both show that New York retained useful asset value after the original experiment stalled.

sections.heading: Atlanta Never Got the First-Round Pick It Wanted
sections.body: Atlanta's side aged less favorably than the original B+ grade suggested. Knox played 17 games and 111 minutes for the Hawks, averaging 2.7 points, before leaving after the season. More importantly, Charlotte's protected first never conveyed. The obligation instead converted into Charlotte's 2026 second-round pick, which became No. 45, plus a 2027 second-round pick that is still future as of this review. Those seconds preserve some value for Atlanta, but they are a clear step down from the first-round asset that drove the trade logic in January 2022.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B-, Atlanta C+. Cam Reddish never became a lasting rotation piece in New York, but the Knicks paid a modest price, received the 2025 Brooklyn second in the same trade and later reused both Reddish and that pick in larger deals. Atlanta got only 17 low-minute games from Kevin Knox II, and the protected Charlotte first never conveyed, leaving the Hawks with the 2026 No. 45 second-round pick and a future 2027 second. The remaining 2027 asset could improve Atlanta's final return, but through the current checkpoint New York produced the stronger realized package.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Immediate Help for a Surprise Contender
sections.body: The Cavaliers made this deal while sitting 33-21 and trying to turn an unexpected leap into a playoff run. Ricky Rubio was already out for the season with a torn ACL, so Cleveland sent his contract, a lottery-protected first, Houston's 2022 second and Utah's 2027 second to Indiana for Caris LeVert and Miami's 2022 second. The price was not light, but the logic was straightforward: Cleveland needed another ball-handler and scorer beside Darius Garland, and LeVert was a proven rotation player who could help immediately.

sections.heading: LeVert Gave Cleveland Three Years of Real Rotation Value
sections.body: LeVert was not a rental. He played 199 regular-season games for Cleveland across parts of four seasons, averaging between 10.2 and 14.0 points per game in each of those Cavaliers stints. He started 53 of those games, handled secondary creation and stayed in the rotation through multiple playoff seasons. In February 2025, Cleveland also included LeVert with Georges Niang, three second-round picks and two swaps in the deal for De'Andre Hunter. LeVert therefore retained downstream trade value, although he cannot be credited as the sole cost of acquiring Hunter.

sections.heading: Indiana Turned the Draft Compensation Into Two Rotation Players
sections.body: The Pacers did not need Ricky Rubio to play a minute for the return to work. Houston's 2022 second became the No. 31 pick, which Indiana used on Andrew Nembhard. By 2025-26, Nembhard was averaging 16.9 points and 7.7 assists, and he had already appeared in 265 regular-season games for the Pacers. Cleveland's protected first stayed in the lottery in 2022, then conveyed at No. 26 in 2023, where Indiana selected Ben Sheppard. Sheppard had reached 185 career games by the end of 2025-26 and was averaging 7.1 points that season.

sections.heading: The Extra Assets Kept the Scale Tilted Toward Indiana
sections.body: Cleveland's incoming 2022 second became Luke Travers at No. 56. Travers eventually reached the NBA, but through 2025-26 he had appeared in only 24 games for the Cavaliers. Indiana, meanwhile, still had the 2027 Utah second-round pick from the original transaction as an unresolved future component in the canonical ledger. That makes the contrast clear: Cleveland received a useful veteran and a fringe second-rounder, while Indiana turned two of its picks into Nembhard and Sheppard and still had another second-round asset left to settle.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Cleveland C+, Indiana B+. Cleveland got meaningful value from Caris LeVert, who played 199 regular-season games for the Cavaliers and later became one piece of the De'Andre Hunter trade. That keeps this from being a bad deal for Cleveland. Indiana still came away with the stronger package. Andrew Nembhard became a high-minute starting guard, Ben Sheppard developed into another rotation wing, and the 2027 second-round pick remained an additional asset through this checkpoint. Rubio never played for Indiana, but the draft return was productive enough that the Pacers did not need him to.

sections.heading: Denver Paid a Future First to Move Into the 2022 Draft
sections.body: Denver sent JaMychal Green and a protected 2027 first-round pick to Oklahoma City for the draft rights to Peyton Watson, the No. 30 pick, plus two future second-rounders. The deal fit the Nuggets' timeline. Green was a veteran reserve on a roster trying to create more room for younger, cheaper players, while Watson gave Denver a long-term defensive prospect without waiting for another draft cycle. Oklahoma City took the opposite side of the bet, converting a late first and two seconds into another future first for its asset stockpile.

sections.heading: Peyton Watson Became the Piece Denver Was Hoping For
sections.body: Watson needed time, but the development curve eventually justified Denver's patience. He played only 23 regular-season games as a rookie, then 80 in 2023-24 and 68 in 2024-25. By 2025-26 he had moved into a much larger role, starting 40 of 54 games while averaging 14.6 points, 4.9 rebounds and 1.1 blocks. That is real starter-level production from the No. 30 pick, and it is the strongest realized value on either side of the original transaction through this checkpoint.

sections.heading: The Two Seconds Also Stayed Useful
sections.body: Denver did not simply receive Watson. The 2024 second was later sent to Portland for the draft rights to Ismael Kamagate. The 2023 second became the No. 40 pick, Maxwell Lewis, and Denver used that pick in a larger 2023 draft-night transaction that also involved a separately acquired 2024 first. That move helped the Nuggets get the Nos. 29 and 32 selections used on Julian Strawther and Jalen Pickett. The No. 40 pick should not be credited for that entire return, but it remained a usable trade asset rather than disappearing.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City's Case Still Depends on the Future First
sections.body: JaMychal Green never became on-court value for the Thunder; Oklahoma City waived him in July 2022. The lasting return is Denver's protected first, which is scheduled to convey no earlier than 2027 and is protected in the top five through 2029 before a fallback second-round outcome. Because that pick is still unresolved, Oklahoma City's side cannot be fully graded as a finished result. The Thunder could still narrow or erase Denver's current edge depending on where that selection eventually lands.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, Oklahoma City B+. Peyton Watson developed from a late first-round project into a 2025-26 starter averaging 14.6 points, and Denver also extracted additional utility from the two second-rounders. Oklahoma City got no games from JaMychal Green, but the protected 2027 first is still a meaningful unresolved asset. The grades therefore describe the trade through the current checkpoint, not a forever verdict: Denver has already realized high-end value, while Oklahoma City's best piece has not conveyed yet.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned the No. 48 Pick Into a Future Second and Cash
sections.body: The Timberwolves drafted Kendall Brown at No. 48 in 2022, then immediately sent his rights to Indiana. Minnesota received a 2026 second-round pick plus cash considerations. It was a small draft-night transaction, but the structure favored patience: the Wolves moved a late second-round prospect for another second four years later and added cash without taking back a player or contract.

sections.heading: Brown Barely Became NBA Value for Indiana
sections.body: Brown reached the league with the Pacers, but his NBA role never developed beyond the edge of the rotation. He appeared in 21 regular-season games across 2022-23 and 2023-24, started none of them and averaged 1.4 points per game. Indiana did get an NBA player from the No. 48 rights, which keeps the return from being empty, but the production was too limited to give the Pacers a strong realized case.

sections.heading: The Future Pick Finally Resolved at No. 59
sections.body: The 2026 second-rounder was the least favorable of the Heat, Pacers and Spurs selections. By the 2026 draft, Minnesota held the No. 59 pick and used it on Purdue forward Trey Kaufman-Renn. That result closes an important open item in the original trade record. Kaufman-Renn had not yet established an NBA career at this checkpoint, so the pick should be credited as a realized draft asset, not treated as proven player production.

sections.heading: This Was a Modest Win, Not a Franchise-Changing One
sections.body: Minnesota's edge comes from what did not happen as much as what did. Brown never became a meaningful Pacers rotation player, while the Wolves preserved the pick value until 2026, added cash and ultimately made another selection. The return is still a late second-round outcome, and the cash amount was not disclosed. That keeps the grading restrained even though Minnesota finished with the better side of the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Indiana C, Minnesota B. Indiana acquired Kendall Brown's rights and received only 21 regular-season games from him. Minnesota received cash plus the 2026 second-round pick that ultimately became No. 59 Trey Kaufman-Renn. Kaufman-Renn's NBA value is still unresolved, so this is not a major hindsight victory. It is a straightforward asset-management win: the Wolves moved a late pick, preserved another future pick and reached the next draft decision with more usable value than Indiana realized from Brown.

sections.heading: Houston Traded Down Three Spots and Added Two Seconds
sections.body: Minnesota wanted Wendell Moore Jr. badly enough to move from No. 29 to No. 26 on draft night in 2022. Houston sent Moore's rights to the Timberwolves and received the rights to TyTy Washington Jr. plus Minnesota's 2025 and 2027 second-round picks. The player swap itself was only three draft slots, so the two extra seconds were the real reason the Rockets had a path to win the deal even if Washington never became a long-term rotation guard.

sections.heading: Neither Drafted Player Became a Core Piece
sections.body: Washington played 31 games for Houston as a rookie, starting twice and averaging 4.7 points in 14.0 minutes. He was gone after one season. Moore lasted two seasons with Minnesota but appeared in only 54 regular-season games and averaged 1.1 points. The Timberwolves later included him with the No. 37 pick in a 2024 trade with Detroit. Because Moore was bundled with another draft asset, the later return cannot fairly be credited to Moore alone.

sections.heading: Houston Kept Using the Extra Picks as Trade Currency
sections.body: The 2025 Minnesota second did not stay with Houston through the draft. The Rockets sent Washington and two second-rounders to Atlanta as part of the five-team Dillon Brooks transaction in July 2023. That Minnesota pick ultimately landed at No. 51 in 2025, when Mohamed Diawara was selected after additional trades. Houston's 2027 Minnesota second also moved again: it was one of the two seconds sent to Oklahoma City with Kevin Porter Jr. in October 2023. These picks had downstream utility, but neither should be treated as if it alone bought Brooks or resolved the Porter transaction.

sections.heading: The Extra Asset Depth Decides a Low-End Deal
sections.body: There is no star outcome on either side. Washington did not stick in Houston, and Moore did not become a meaningful Minnesota rotation player. The difference is that Houston also received two future seconds and was able to use both in later transactions. Minnesota received the player it targeted but little NBA production from him. That is enough for a clear Houston edge, although the Rockets' return still belongs in the lower half of the grading scale because none of the incoming pieces became a major on-court contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston C, Minnesota D. TyTy Washington Jr. gave Houston only 31 games, so the player portion of the return was limited. Wendell Moore Jr. was even less useful to Minnesota, producing 54 games at 1.1 points per game before being moved in a package with another pick. Houston also received Minnesota's 2025 and 2027 seconds and later used both as trade assets. The Rockets did not uncover a cornerstone, but they got more usable value from moving down three spots than Minnesota realized from moving up.

sections.heading: Memphis Consolidated Two First-Round Slots Into LaRavia and a Future Second
sections.body: The draft-night structure was unusual. Minnesota sent the rights to No. 19 pick Jake LaRavia plus a future second-rounder to Memphis and received the rights to No. 22 Walker Kessler and No. 29 TyTy Washington Jr. Memphis was effectively willing to give up two later first-round slots to secure LaRavia, but the future second kept the deal from becoming a one-player bet. That second ultimately landed at No. 45 in 2023, where the Grizzlies selected GG Jackson II.

sections.heading: LaRavia Became Useful Rotation Value Before Memphis Moved Him
sections.body: LaRavia never became a star in Memphis, but he did become an NBA rotation forward. He played 35 games as a rookie, 35 more in 2023-24 and 47 for the Grizzlies in 2024-25 before being traded to Sacramento at the deadline. His final Memphis stretch was his most efficient, with 7.3 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists per game in 20.9 minutes. Memphis later included him in a three-team transaction, so the downstream return cannot be assigned to LaRavia alone, but the original pick produced 117 regular-season games for the franchise.

sections.heading: The Future Second Became the Best Direct Asset in the Deal
sections.body: The 2023 second-round pick became No. 45 GG Jackson II, and that is what pushes the hindsight result toward Memphis. Jackson made the 2023-24 All-Rookie Second Team after averaging 14.6 points in 48 games as a 19-year-old. After an injury-limited 2024-25, he returned to play 55 games with 28 starts in 2025-26 and averaged 12.5 points. Through that season he had already played 132 regular-season games for Memphis. Turning a future second into a young rotation scorer with an All-Rookie season gave the Grizzlies more direct value than the trade looked capable of producing on draft night.

sections.heading: Minnesota Used Both Incoming Rights as Trade Currency
sections.body: The Timberwolves did not keep either player they acquired. Walker Kessler was included less than two weeks later in the much larger Rudy Gobert trade with Utah, while TyTy Washington Jr. was rerouted to Houston with two future seconds for Wendell Moore Jr. Kessler clearly carried real transaction value because he was part of the Gobert package, but that deal also contained four veteran players, four first-round picks and a pick swap. Minnesota therefore deserves credit for preserving value, not the full value of Gobert. Washington's next move produced much less, leaving Memphis with the stronger direct player return from this specific exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis B+, Minnesota B. Memphis received 117 regular-season games from Jake LaRavia and used the future second-round pick on GG Jackson II, an All-Rookie selection who had already reached 132 games for the Grizzlies through 2025-26. Minnesota kept value alive by using Walker Kessler in the Rudy Gobert package and TyTy Washington Jr. in the Wendell Moore Jr. deal, but neither player ever suited up for the Timberwolves. Memphis produced more direct, attributable value from both incoming assets, while Minnesota's return depended on larger follow-up transactions.

sections.heading: Detroit Turned the Headline First-Round Pick Into Jalen Duren Almost Immediately
sections.body: The most valuable piece Detroit received never reached the 2025 draft in Pistons hands. The Milwaukee 2025 first-round pick was moved the next day in the draft-night transaction that brought Detroit the rights to No. 13 pick Jalen Duren while the Pistons absorbed Kemba Walker. Detroit's own reporting explicitly tied that first-rounder from the Jerami Grant deal to the move for Duren. The underlying pick eventually became No. 19 Nolan Traore elsewhere, but Detroit's realized return from the asset was Duren, not the player selected three years later.

sections.heading: Duren Became the Result That Changed the Hindsight Grade
sections.body: Duren turned a future pick into a foundational center. He played 276 regular-season games for Detroit across his first four seasons and earned both an All-Star selection and All-NBA Third Team honors in 2025-26. That outcome carries more weight than the original pick number because Detroit converted the asset while it controlled it. The trade did not single-handedly acquire Duren — taking on Walker's contract was also part of the transaction — but the Milwaukee first was the draft capital Detroit supplied. That direct link gives the Pistons a premium realized return from the Grant package.

sections.heading: The Rest of Detroit's Package Kept Producing Trade Currency
sections.body: The smaller pieces did not sit untouched. Detroit later sent Gabriele Procida's rights with Kevin Knox II and a 2024 second-round pick to Utah for Simone Fontecchio; Fontecchio then played 91 regular-season games for the Pistons. Detroit's 2025 second-round pick was later included with Marvin Bagley III, Isaiah Livers and another second in the Washington deal for Danilo Gallinari and Mike Muscala. The 2026 New Orleans-Portland second-round component also fed into the broader 2026 pick obligation Detroit sent Boston when it moved from No. 31 to No. 25 for Marcus Sasser. That obligation ultimately produced No. 38 Braden Smith after later transactions. Those chains should be credited only proportionally because each follow-up deal included additional assets.

sections.heading: Portland Still Received Four Productive Seasons From Grant
sections.body: Portland did not lose this trade because Grant failed. He played 221 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers from 2022-23 through 2025-26, averaging at least 14.4 points in every season and topping 20 points per game in each of his first two Portland years. The Blazers then used Grant with Kris Murray in the June 2026 trade for Ja Morant. Morant cannot be assigned entirely to Grant because Murray was part of the outgoing package, but Grant clearly retained transaction value after four seasons of useful production. That keeps Portland's grade strong even though Detroit's Duren outcome ultimately carries more historical weight.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A, Portland B+. Portland received 221 regular-season games of productive Jerami Grant basketball and later used him as one of the pieces in the Ja Morant trade. Detroit, however, immediately converted the Milwaukee first-rounder from this deal into the draft capital used to acquire Jalen Duren, who reached 276 games, an All-Star selection and All-NBA Third Team honors through 2025-26. The remaining Detroit assets also stayed active in later transactions. Portland got a good player and years of production; Detroit extracted the higher-end franchise return.

sections.heading: An Eight-Player Trade Was Really a Roster and Cap Transaction
sections.body: Houston and Oklahoma City exchanged eight veterans at the end of training camp, but the names made the deal look larger than its basketball impact. The Rockets sent David Nwaba, Sterling Brown, Trey Burke and Marquese Chriss to the Thunder for Derrick Favors, Maurice Harkless, Ty Jerome, Théo Maledon, a conditional 2026 second-round pick and cash. Oklahoma City also generated two trade exceptions. ESPN reported that the deal moved the Thunder roughly $10 million below the luxury-tax line, making financial flexibility the central Oklahoma City return.

sections.heading: Neither Team Kept the Incoming Players
sections.body: The player swap produced no regular-season games for either acquiring team. Oklahoma City waived Sterling Brown on October 1 and released Trey Burke, Marquese Chriss and David Nwaba on October 17. Houston followed the same pattern on its side: Ty Jerome was waived October 1, Maurice Harkless and Théo Maledon on October 11, and Derrick Favors on October 17. That makes the trade exceptions, cap savings, cash and future pick more important to the evaluation than the eight-player headline.

sections.heading: Houston's Future Second Became No. 47 in 2026
sections.body: The draft asset eventually resolved. The pick was the second-most favorable — equivalently, the second-least favorable — among Oklahoma City, Dallas and Philadelphia's 2026 second-rounders, and it became Philadelphia's selection at No. 47. Tyler Nickel was selected in that slot. Houston did not keep the pick through draft night; it sent the asset to Phoenix as one piece of the seven-team Kevin Durant transaction in July 2025. The pick therefore produced real trade currency for the Rockets even though Nickel never became a Houston player.

sections.heading: The Later Durant Deal Adds Context, Not the Whole Value
sections.body: Houston's 2026 second was only one component of the much larger package that brought Kevin Durant to the Rockets, so Durant cannot be credited to this 2022 transaction by himself. The same caution applies after Phoenix received the pick: the Suns later used No. 47 Tyler Nickel with additional future seconds in the four-team draft-night trade that landed Koa Peat. What can be credited directly is simpler. Houston received cash plus a second-round asset that stayed useful for nearly three years, while Oklahoma City received cap relief and trade exceptions but no lasting player or draft asset from the incoming quartet.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston B+, Oklahoma City B-. Both teams achieved their immediate roster-management goals, and Oklahoma City's cap savings plus two trade exceptions were legitimate value. Houston, however, also received cash and the 2026 second-round pick that became Philadelphia's No. 47 selection, Tyler Nickel, before using that pick as one piece of the Kevin Durant package. With every incoming player on both sides waived before the regular season, that durable draft asset gives Houston the stronger attributable return.

sections.heading: Miami Used the Deal to Open a Roster and Tax Path
sections.body: Miami sent Dewayne Dedmon and its own 2028 second-round pick to San Antonio for cash considerations two days before the 2023 trade deadline. The basketball return was intentionally small. NBA.com reported that moving Dedmon created room under the luxury-tax line and opened flexibility for additional roster moves, while Basketball-Reference records that Miami also received a trade exception. The Heat were paying a future second to remove a veteran center who had fallen out of the rotation and to improve their short-term roster and cap position.

sections.heading: San Antonio Kept the Pick and Quickly Moved On From Dedmon
sections.body: The Spurs did not acquire Dedmon for an on-court role. San Antonio waived him on February 9, two days after the trade, and he later signed with Philadelphia. That leaves Miami's 2028 second-round pick as the durable basketball asset on the Spurs side. Because the selection is still years away, its eventual player value cannot be graded yet. The correct hindsight treatment is to credit San Antonio for acquiring a real future asset while keeping the grade restrained until the pick conveys and becomes a known selection.

sections.heading: The Heat Got the Financial Result They Wanted
sections.body: Miami's side was not designed to win a player-for-player comparison. Dedmon had appeared in 30 games for the Heat that season, averaging 5.7 points and 3.6 rebounds in 11.7 minutes, but he had played sparingly after a January suspension and was no longer central to the rotation. By moving his contract, Miami gained cash, a trade exception and more room below the tax line. Those are legitimate results for a deadline salary move, even though none of them equal the long-term upside of retaining a future second-round pick.

sections.heading: The Unresolved 2028 Pick Keeps the Verdict Narrow
sections.body: This trade should not be graded as if San Antonio already turned the 2028 second into a productive player. The pick remains unresolved, and Dedmon never appeared in a game for the Spurs after the transaction. Miami, meanwhile, accomplished the immediate cap and roster objective that motivated the move. The remaining difference is asset durability: San Antonio still owns the future draft value, while Miami's return was consumed as financial flexibility. That supports a modest Spurs edge rather than a decisive win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge — Miami C+, San Antonio B-. Miami achieved the immediate purpose of the transaction by moving Dewayne Dedmon, receiving cash and a trade exception, and creating additional tax and roster flexibility. San Antonio waived Dedmon two days later, so its lasting return is the Heat's 2028 second-round pick. Because that pick is still unresolved, the advantage stays narrow, but the Spurs retain the stronger durable asset.

sections.heading: Miami Paid Future Draft Value for Immediate Flexibility
sections.body: Miami sent Victor Oladipo and its own 2029 and 2030 second-round picks to Oklahoma City in a July 2023 salary move. NBA.com reported that the deal created a $9.45 million trade exception for the Heat and added financial flexibility while the club was already above the tax line. That immediate cap benefit was the point of the transaction. Miami was not trying to replace Oladipo with another rotation player; it was converting an injured contract and two future seconds into room to maneuver.

sections.heading: Oladipo Never Became an Oklahoma City Rotation Piece
sections.body: The player portion of Oklahoma City's return did not produce games for the Thunder. When the trade was completed, Oladipo was recovering from a torn left patellar tendon suffered during the 2023 playoffs, and NBA.com reported there was no timetable for his return. Basketball-Reference later records Oklahoma City sending Oladipo and Jeremiah Robinson-Earl to Houston in October 2023. Because Robinson-Earl was part of that later package too, the Houston return should not be credited to Oladipo alone.

sections.heading: The Two Miami Seconds Are Still the Durable Core of the Return
sections.body: Basketball-Reference identifies both incoming draft assets as Miami's own second-round picks in 2029 and 2030. As of this review, neither selection has been made, so the trade cannot be graded as though Oklahoma City already turned either pick into a productive NBA player. The Thunder still deserve credit for holding two real future assets, but the unresolved status keeps the hindsight verdict restrained.

sections.heading: The Hindsight Edge Belongs to Oklahoma City, but It Is Narrow
sections.body: Miami received the financial result it wanted: the Heat moved an injured salary, created a $9.45 million trade exception and gained flexibility during an offseason in which tax positioning mattered. Oklahoma City accepted the contract and retained two future Miami seconds, giving the Thunder more durable basketball value than a temporary exception. With both picks unresolved and Oladipo never playing for Oklahoma City, the evidence supports a modest Thunder advantage rather than a decisive win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge — Miami C+, Oklahoma City B-. Miami accomplished the immediate salary-management goal by moving Victor Oladipo and creating a $9.45 million trade exception. Oklahoma City never got on-court production from Oladipo, but it retained Miami's own 2029 and 2030 second-round picks. Because both selections remain unresolved, the Thunder's edge is real but limited.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought a Real Rotation Forward for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: Indiana acquired Obi Toppin from New York for two future second-round picks in July 2023. The Pacers' own release confirms the basic price, while Basketball-Reference identifies the outgoing selections as 2028 and 2029 seconds. The 2028 asset is the less favorable of Indiana and Phoenix, and the 2029 asset is the less favorable of Indiana and Washington. Both remain unresolved, so neither should be graded as if New York already converted it into a player.

sections.heading: Toppin Quickly Became Part of Indiana's Core Rotation
sections.body: The realized return is already substantial on Indiana's side. After his first Pacers season, the team re-signed Toppin in July 2024 and basketball president Kevin Pritchard called him an integral part of the run to the Eastern Conference Finals. By April 2026, Indiana's own player review described Toppin as entering the third year of that four-year contract. Even after a foot injury limited him to 24 games in 2025-26, he averaged 11.6 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists while shooting 50.3 percent from the field.

sections.heading: New York Still Owns Draft Value, but the Return Has Not Matured
sections.body: The Knicks did not get nothing. Two future seconds preserve optionality, and the unusual pick conditions mean the exact draft slots will not be known until those years arrive. That is why a harsh failing grade would overstate the hindsight case. But as of this review, New York's side remains future value only while Indiana has already received multiple seasons of useful NBA production and was sufficiently satisfied to give Toppin a new four-year deal.

sections.heading: The Pacers Hold the Clear Hindsight Advantage
sections.body: This is the kind of trade where realized production can be weighed without pretending the future picks are worthless. Indiana paid a modest draft price, found a role that fit Toppin and retained him beyond the original contract. New York still has two unresolved assets that could improve its side later, but there is no current evidence that either has matched the value Indiana already received. The proper verdict is a Pacers win with the Knicks kept above a failing range until the picks resolve.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A-, New York C+. Indiana turned two future second-round picks into Obi Toppin, received immediate rotation value and then re-signed him to a four-year contract after an Eastern Conference Finals run. New York still holds the unresolved 2028 and 2029 second-round assets, so its return retains real future value. The Pacers nevertheless own the clear realized advantage today.

sections.heading: Dallas Turned a Future Swap Into Immediate First-Round Currency
sections.body: Dallas sent Oklahoma City the right to swap 2028 first-round picks and received a 2024 first-round pick. NBA.com's trade tracker confirms the two-way asset exchange, while the Mavericks' own transaction history shows that Dallas immediately used the incoming 2024 first in its separate Daniel Gafford trade with Washington. The value of the February 8 deal therefore was not the drafted player attached to the pick months later; it was the first-round currency Dallas needed to complete a win-now frontcourt move.

sections.heading: The Pick Became No. 26, but Dillon Jones Was Not Dallas' Realized Return
sections.body: The 2024 selection ultimately became the No. 26 pick, used on Dillon Jones. Washington later sent that pick to New York, and the Knicks then traded Jones' draft rights to Oklahoma City for five future second-round picks. That later path matters because it prevents double-counting. Oklahoma City did eventually acquire Jones, but only through a separate June transaction with an additional five-second-round-pick cost. Dallas' realized value from this February trade is better traced to the asset it forwarded for Gafford.

sections.heading: Gafford Gave Dallas Immediate Playoff Value
sections.body: NBA.com reported that the Mavericks sent Richaun Holmes and the 2024 first obtained via Oklahoma City to Washington for Daniel Gafford. The league's 2024 Dallas draft profile later described the Gafford and P.J. Washington deadline moves as choices that prioritized the present and boosted the team's trajectory. Dallas reached the 2024 NBA Finals with Gafford in the rotation, giving the acquired first-round asset a clear and immediate competitive use rather than leaving it as abstract draft capital.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Still Owns Meaningful 2028 Upside
sections.body: The Thunder side cannot be graded as a failed return because the 2028 swap remains unresolved. Oklahoma City converted a late 2024 first into a future right that could still move the Thunder upward in the 2028 first round depending on the two teams' records. The current hindsight edge belongs to Dallas because its asset was already converted into productive playoff help, but the unfinished swap keeps the gap narrower than a one-sided result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas A-, Oklahoma City B-. Dallas converted a 2028 swap concession into a 2024 first-round asset and immediately used that pick to help acquire Daniel Gafford, who became part of a Finals roster. Oklahoma City still owns the unresolved 2028 swap and later reacquired Dillon Jones only through a separate five-second-round-pick trade. The Mavericks have the stronger realized return today, while the Thunder retain meaningful future upside.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned a Departing Reserve Into Draft Currency
sections.body: Golden State sent Cory Joseph, cash and a top-55-protected 2025 Charlotte second-round pick to Indiana for a 2024 second-round pick. NBA.com reported that Indiana waived Joseph immediately after the trade, while Basketball-Reference records that the protected 2025 Charlotte pick did not convey. The Warriors therefore moved a reserve guard they were prepared to part with, plus cash and a pick that ultimately disappeared, and secured a live 2024 draft asset in return.

sections.heading: The Incoming Pick Reached No. 52 and Fed a Complicated Draft-Night Route
sections.body: The acquired second became the No. 52 selection in the 2024 draft. NBA.com's draft results list Quinten Post at No. 52 and show the rights moving from Golden State to Oklahoma City, then Portland, then back to Golden State. The offseason trade tracker adds the surrounding context: the Warriors also acquired Lindy Waters III in that June routing. Post should not be treated as a simple one-step February return, but the pick Golden State acquired from Indiana was real draft-night currency at the center of the later sequence.

sections.heading: Post Eventually Produced Two Warriors Seasons
sections.body: The downstream player value became tangible. NBA.com reported in July 2026 that Post's two-season Warriors run ended only after Golden State declined to match Memphis' three-year, $30 million offer sheet. In his final Warriors season, he averaged 7.7 points and 4.0 rebounds across 67 games. That production cannot all be credited mechanically to the February trade because additional draft-night moves were involved, but it reinforces that Golden State's acquired No. 52 asset had meaningful realized value.

sections.heading: Indiana's Return Produced Little Basketball Value
sections.body: Indiana's side is easier to resolve. Joseph never played a game for the Pacers after the transaction because the team waived him the same day. The protected Charlotte second did not convey, leaving cash considerations as the durable piece of the return. Golden State also created a trade exception according to Basketball-Reference. The Warriors' side therefore produced the stronger combination of asset value, roster flexibility and downstream use, while Indiana's return generated little on-court or draft value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A-, Indiana C. Golden State moved Cory Joseph, cash and a protected second that never conveyed for the 2024 second-round pick that became No. 52. The later draft-night routing was more complicated than a direct pick-to-player conversion, but that asset helped Golden State finish the sequence with Quinten Post and Lindy Waters III. Indiana waived Joseph immediately and received no drafted player from the protected 2025 pick.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Bought Back the Right to Rebuild on Its Own Schedule
sections.body: Brooklyn's most important return was control of its own 2025 and 2026 first-round picks. The Nets' official release says the 2025 pick came back with Houston's prior swap right negated, while the 2026 first also returned outright. Those assets became the No. 8 pick in 2025 and the No. 6 pick in 2026. Brooklyn used them on Egor Demin and Mikel Brown Jr., giving the franchise two lottery selections it otherwise would not have controlled. The strategic value was just as important as the names: Brooklyn could lose games without sending the upside of its own draft position to Houston.

sections.heading: Houston's 2025 Swap Became a Real Top-10 Asset
sections.body: Houston did not simply trade away Brooklyn's picks and wait for distant compensation. The Rockets received the right to swap either their own or Oklahoma City's 2025 first for Phoenix's 2025 first, and that path produced the No. 10 selection. NBA.com's 2025 draft material shows Khaman Maluach at No. 10, with the pick ultimately routed to Phoenix. The league's offseason trade tracker then places Maluach in the seven-team Kevin Durant deal. Houston cannot be credited with Durant as a one-asset return from this trade, but the No. 10 pick clearly became a meaningful component of a later star acquisition.

sections.heading: The 2027 and 2029 Pieces Keep Houston's Side Open-Ended
sections.body: The Rockets also received Phoenix's 2027 first-round pick and the rights to the two most favorable 2029 firsts among Dallas, Houston and Phoenix. Those assets are still unresolved as of this review. That limits any attempt to declare a permanent winner. Houston has already converted the 2025 swap into useful trade currency and still owns major future optionality, while Brooklyn has already turned both returned picks into lottery selections. The remaining 2027 and 2029 outcomes can still move the historical grade in either direction.

sections.heading: The Best Current Read Is a High-End Even Trade
sections.body: This deal looks better for both teams now than it did on transaction day. Brooklyn recovered the exact draft control a rebuilding team needed and received two top-eight selections in consecutive drafts. Houston replaced those rights with Phoenix-linked and multi-team future capital, then realized a top-10 pick from the 2025 swap and used that selection inside a much larger Durant package. Because the 2027 and 2029 firsts are not settled, assigning a decisive winner would overstate what is known. The current record supports equal high grades without pretending the future assets are already resolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Brooklyn A-, Houston A-. Brooklyn regained its own 2025 and 2026 first-round control, which became No. 8 Egor Demin and No. 6 Mikel Brown Jr. Houston's 2025 Phoenix swap became the No. 10 pick and later served as one component of the Kevin Durant trade, while the Rockets still hold the unresolved 2027 Phoenix first and two 2029 first-round rights. Both sides have already created substantial traceable value, and too much future value remains open to justify a permanent winner.

sections.heading: The Direct Exchange Was Waters for the No. 52 Draft Rights
sections.body: Golden State sent the rights to No. 52 pick Quinten Post to Oklahoma City for Lindy Waters III. NBA.com's draft-night report and the Thunder's official release agree on that first step. That distinction matters because the direct two-team record should not pretend Golden State received Post in the same exchange. The Warriors acquired Waters here; Oklahoma City acquired Post's rights. Everything that happened to those rights afterward belongs to a traceable draft-night chain, not the initial asset ledger.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Turned Post's Rights Into Ajay Mitchell
sections.body: The Thunder immediately used Post's rights and cash to acquire the rights to No. 40 pick Oso Ighodaro from Portland, then moved Ighodaro to New York in the path that brought back No. 38 pick Ajay Mitchell. Oklahoma City's own release documents those steps, while NBA.com summarized the broader routing as a sequence that let the Thunder get Mitchell. By April 2026, NBA.com described Mitchell as an important part of Oklahoma City's rotation, giving the downstream value real basketball weight rather than leaving it as a draft-night abstraction.

sections.heading: Golden State Reacquired Post in a Separate Portland Transaction
sections.body: Golden State also came out of the broader draft-night sequence with Post, but only after the rights passed through Oklahoma City and Portland. NBA.com's 2024 draft results list No. 52 as moving Warriors-to-Thunder-to-Blazers-to-Warriors, and Basketball-Reference records Golden State later sending cash to Portland for Post. That separate reacquisition should not be rewritten into the original two-team package. It still matters to the hindsight story because Post became a rotation big for two Warriors seasons, averaging 7.7 points and 4.0 rebounds across 67 games in his final Golden State season before Memphis signed him in 2026.

sections.heading: Both Front Offices Extracted More Than the Original Ledger Suggests
sections.body: The original C-level grades undersell what the linked transactions produced. Golden State obtained Waters and, with an additional cash transaction, recovered the same No. 52 player it had drafted. Oklahoma City used the incoming rights as a bridge to Mitchell, who developed into a meaningful rotation player. Waters later left Golden State in the February 2025 multi-team Jimmy Butler transaction, but that later deal should not be credited as if Waters alone bought Butler. The strongest current read is a win-win draft-night sequence with the direct trade itself serving as the first link.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Golden State A-, Oklahoma City A-. The Warriors directly acquired Lindy Waters III for Quinten Post's draft rights, then separately reacquired Post from Portland for cash. Oklahoma City used Post's rights plus cash in the chain that ultimately produced Ajay Mitchell. Post became a useful two-season Warriors rotation big, and Mitchell developed into an important Thunder rotation player. Both sides created strong traceable value, but the later routing must stay separate from the original asset ledger.
