sections.heading: Milwaukee Sold Kevin O’Shea Midseason
sections.body: Milwaukee sold Kevin O'Shea's player rights to Baltimore on February 3, 1952. O'Shea had already appeared in 43 games for the Hawks and averaged 25.0 minutes, 6.0 points, 2.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Baltimore was therefore paying for an established rotation guard, not taking a speculative flyer.

sections.heading: Baltimore Expanded O’Shea’s Role Right Away
sections.body: O'Shea played 22 games for the Bullets to finish 1951-52 and averaged 29.5 minutes, 8.7 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.2 assists. He came back for 46 more games in 1952-53, giving Baltimore 68 regular-season appearances from the purchase across two seasons.

sections.heading: The Hawks Took Cash After Already Using Him
sections.body: Milwaukee had received 43 games from O'Shea after acquiring him earlier in the season, then chose to monetize the remaining rights. The cash amount is not preserved, and the surviving record does not identify a later player, pick or transaction created from those proceeds. That leaves the Hawks with real but unmeasurable value.

sections.heading: Two Seasons of Service Give Baltimore the Edge
sections.body: Baltimore received the better documented basketball outcome because O'Shea immediately handled more minutes and stayed into the next season. The result was useful rather than franchise-changing, which keeps the Bullets in the B range instead of higher. Milwaukee's unknown cash return belongs in the middle, not at zero.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Baltimore Bullets Win — Milwaukee Hawks C, Baltimore Bullets B. Milwaukee sold Kevin O'Shea's player rights to Baltimore for cash on February 3, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Baltimore, league and player transaction records agree on the date and sale structure. O'Shea immediately took on a larger role in Baltimore, averaging 8.7 points and 29.5 minutes across 22 games after the move, then returned for 46 more games in 1952-53. Milwaukee's cash amount is not preserved, so Baltimore owns the stronger measurable basketball return without the evidence supporting an extreme grade gap.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Traded Dike Eddleman for Art Burris and Cash
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Dike Eddleman to Fort Wayne on February 11, 1952 for Art Burris and cash. The source review also fixes the old TradeVerdicts identity error that called the outgoing Hawk Thomas Eddleman. The verified player was Dike Eddleman, who had already appeared in 50 Milwaukee games that season.

sections.heading: Eddleman Gave Fort Wayne 85 Games
sections.body: Eddleman played 16 games for the Pistons to finish 1951-52, then returned for 69 more in 1952-53. Across those 85 appearances he became a real rotation forward rather than a short rental, adding 615 points and 236 rebounds in the second season alone.

sections.heading: Burris Lasted Only 12 Games in Milwaukee
sections.body: Burris appeared in 12 games for the Hawks after the trade, averaging 22.4 minutes, 5.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.3 assists. Those were the final NBA games of his career. Milwaukee also received cash, but the amount is not available in the reviewed public record.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Won the Measurable Part of the Swap
sections.body: The Pistons obtained substantially more on-court value: 85 post-trade games from Eddleman compared with 12 from Burris. Cash keeps Milwaukee's return from being treated as empty, but nothing in the surviving record closes that basketball gap. A moderate Fort Wayne win fits the evidence better than an extreme grade spread.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Milwaukee Hawks C, Fort Wayne Pistons B. Milwaukee traded Dike Eddleman to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Art Burris and cash on February 11, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Fort Wayne transaction logs agree on the exchange and correct the legacy Atlanta-side intake, which called Eddleman 'Thomas.' Eddleman played 16 games for Fort Wayne to finish 1951-52 and then 69 more games for the Pistons in 1952-53. Burris played 12 games for Milwaukee after the trade and never appeared in another NBA season. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record, so Fort Wayne owns the stronger measurable basketball return without making Milwaukee's consideration equivalent to zero.

sections.heading: Rochester Bought Cal Christensen Before the Season
sections.body: Milwaukee sold Cal Christensen's player rights to Rochester on August 8, 1952. Christensen had already logged 24 games for the Hawks the previous season, so Rochester was acquiring a 25-year-old forward with NBA experience. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed transaction records.

sections.heading: Christensen Stayed for Three Royals Seasons
sections.body: Christensen played 59 games in 1952-53, then 70 in 1953-54 and 71 in 1954-55. His three Rochester seasons totaled 200 regular-season games and 3,635 minutes. That is strong roster utility for a cash purchase even though he was never a star.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Return Was Financial, Not Roster-Based
sections.body: The Hawks received cash and no identified player or pick. The absence of a dollar figure means the economic logic cannot be reconstructed precisely, and the payment should not be dismissed as worthless. What can be measured is that Milwaukee gave up a player who remained in another team's rotation for the rest of his NBA career.

sections.heading: Rochester’s Longevity Wins the Comparison
sections.body: Three seasons and 200 games give Rochester the clear measurable advantage. Christensen's biggest workload came in 1953-54, when he logged 1,654 minutes, and he remained useful through 1954-55. Milwaukee's unknown cash return keeps the grade gap moderate, but the Royals received far more verifiable basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Milwaukee Hawks C, Rochester Royals B. Milwaukee sold Cal Christensen's player rights to the Rochester Royals on August 8, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Rochester and league transaction logs agree on the date and sale structure. Christensen then spent three seasons with Rochester, appearing in 200 regular-season games and 3,635 minutes for the Royals. He played 59 games in his first Rochester season, then 70 and 71 over the next two years. Milwaukee received cash, but the reviewed public transaction records do not preserve the amount, leaving Rochester with the stronger measurable basketball return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Swapped Mel Payton for Don Lofgran
sections.body: Philadelphia traded Mel Payton to Indianapolis for Don Lofgran on September 11, 1952. This was a straight one-for-one exchange between two active forwards, not a cash or rights transaction. Payton had played 45 games for the Warriors as a rookie, while Lofgran already had parts of two seasons with the Olympians.

sections.heading: Lofgran Absorbed Heavy Minutes for a Bad Warriors Team
sections.body: Lofgran played 64 games in 1952-53 and logged 1,788 minutes, averaging 27.9 minutes, 7.4 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.7 assists. Philadelphia received more total minutes and small counting-stat edges, but Basketball-Reference credited him with only 0.1 win shares on a 12-win team.

sections.heading: Payton Produced a Similar One-Year Indianapolis Return
sections.body: Payton appeared in 66 games for Indianapolis, averaging 7.1 points and 4.7 rebounds in 1,424 minutes. He posted 2.1 win shares and also played in both games of the Olympians' 1953 playoff series against Minneapolis. Like Lofgran, he did not stay with his new club beyond the season.

sections.heading: The Near-Mirror Returns Point to an Even Trade
sections.body: Philadelphia received more minutes and slight raw-stat advantages; Indianapolis received two more games, the better win-share total and a brief playoff contribution. Neither player became a lasting asset and no extra consideration changed hands. The old lopsided grading does not fit two returns this close.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Philadelphia Warriors C+, Indianapolis Olympians C+. Philadelphia traded Mel Payton to the Indianapolis Olympians for Don Lofgran on September 11, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Indianapolis and league transaction logs agree on the one-for-one exchange. The players produced remarkably similar counting-stat returns in 1952-53: Lofgran appeared in 64 games for the Warriors, while Payton played 66 for Indianapolis. Lofgran logged more minutes and slightly more points and rebounds, but Payton posted the stronger Basketball-Reference win-share total and also appeared in Indianapolis' two playoff games. Neither side received durable multi-season value, making the old lopsided grading difficult to support.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Veteran Kleggie Hermsen
sections.body: Boston sold Clarence "Kleggie" Hermsen's player rights to Indianapolis on November 17, 1952. The transaction was previously mislabeled as a 1952 draft-rights move, but Hermsen was a 29-year-old veteran who had already played four games for the Celtics that season. The corrected framing makes this a simple veteran cash sale.

sections.heading: Indianapolis Received Only Six Games
sections.body: Hermsen appeared in six games for the Olympians and logged 40 total minutes. He scored 10 points, grabbed 12 rebounds and recorded four assists, with Basketball-Reference crediting him with minus-0.3 win shares. He never appeared in another NBA season.

sections.heading: The Celtics Converted a Marginal Roster Piece Into Cash
sections.body: Boston's cash return is undisclosed, which limits the upside that can responsibly be assigned to the Celtics. The opportunity cost is much easier to see: Hermsen had played only 22 minutes for Boston before the sale and produced just 40 more minutes afterward. Boston moved a player with almost no remaining NBA value.

sections.heading: A Small Boston Win Fits the Evidence
sections.body: Indianapolis bought the final six games of Hermsen's career and received almost no positive statistical return. Any legitimate payment compares favorably with that result, but the unknown amount keeps Boston's grade modest. The trade favors the Celtics without becoming a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston Celtics C, Indianapolis Olympians D+. Boston sold Kleggie Hermsen's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians on November 17, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Boston, Indianapolis and league transaction logs agree on the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts record correctly linked Clarence Hermsen to the transaction but mislabeled the asset as 1952 draft rights; Hermsen was a veteran who had already played four games for Boston that season. Indianapolis received only six games and 40 minutes from him before his NBA career ended. Boston's cash amount is not preserved, but the Celtics received the stronger measurable return from a player who produced very little after the sale.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Traded the No. 1 Pick for Don Sunderlage
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Mark Workman to Philadelphia for Don Sunderlage on November 19, 1952. The verified transaction logs show a straight player-for-player trade, correcting the old record that added cash. Sunderlage was Philadelphia's 1951 first-round pick and remained in military service when Milwaukee acquired his rights; he was not a 1952 draft-rights asset.

sections.heading: Sunderlage’s Delayed Debut Produced an All-Star Season
sections.body: Sunderlage did not play for Milwaukee until 1953-54, but the wait produced the best season either player delivered after the deal. He appeared in 68 games, averaged 32.8 minutes and 11.2 points, and was selected to the NBA All-Star Game.

sections.heading: Workman Gave Philadelphia One Modest Season
sections.body: Workman, the first overall pick in the 1952 draft, played 60 games for the Warriors and averaged 5.3 points and 3.1 rebounds in 1,001 minutes. He did not return to Philadelphia the next season, appeared in 14 games for Baltimore in 1953-54 and then left the NBA.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Clearly Won the One-for-One Exchange
sections.body: Sunderlage's delayed arrival produced a substantially better peak than Workman's Philadelphia season. Once the unsupported cash component is removed, the comparison is direct: Milwaukee traded five early games of Workman for an eventual All-Star season, while Philadelphia received one modest year from the No. 1 pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee Hawks B+, Philadelphia Warriors D+. Milwaukee traded Mark Workman to the Philadelphia Warriors for Don Sunderlage on November 19, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all describe a straight one-for-one exchange; the legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly added cash and labeled Sunderlage as 1952 draft rights. Sunderlage was Philadelphia's 1951 first-round pick and was still in military service at the time. When he returned in 1953-54, he played 68 games for Milwaukee, averaged 11.2 points and made the All-Star team. Workman, the 1952 No. 1 overall pick, played 60 games for Philadelphia and averaged 5.3 points. The verified outcome strongly favors Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Milwaukee and Baltimore Exchanged Active Veterans
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Eddie Miller to Baltimore for George Ratkovicz on November 24, 1952. Each player had already appeared in 10 games for his original club that season, so the swap moved two active rotation veterans rather than prospects or rights. Both entered substantial roles immediately.

sections.heading: Ratkovicz Gave Milwaukee 139 Games
sections.body: Ratkovicz played 61 games for the Hawks after the trade, then 69 in 1953-54 and nine more in 1954-55. His Milwaukee total reached 139 regular-season games, and he logged more than 2,000 minutes in each of his first two full Hawks stretches.

sections.heading: Miller Became a Double-Figure Baltimore Scorer
sections.body: Miller played 60 games for Baltimore after the move and averaged 11.6 points and 10.2 rebounds. He returned for all 72 games in 1953-54, averaging 10.0 points and 7.5 rebounds. Across 132 Bullets games he averaged 10.7 points and 8.7 rebounds.

sections.heading: Different Strengths Produce a Legitimate Draw
sections.body: Baltimore can claim the stronger scoring and rebounding peak, while Milwaukee received seven more games and parts of three seasons from Ratkovicz. Both teams upgraded the usefulness of the player they acquired, and neither side created a notable downstream asset chain. The returns are close enough to support equal grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Milwaukee Hawks B, Baltimore Bullets B. Milwaukee traded Eddie Miller to the Baltimore Bullets for George Ratkovicz on November 24, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Baltimore and league transaction logs agree on the straight one-for-one exchange. Both clubs received real multi-season rotation value. Ratkovicz played 139 games for Milwaukee over parts of three seasons after the trade, including 61 games and 2,038 minutes in 1952-53. Miller played 132 games for Baltimore across two seasons, averaging 10.7 points and 8.7 rebounds for the Bullets. The returns are close enough that the source-backed record supports a balanced result rather than forcing a winner.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold an Active Rookie, Not Draft Rights
sections.body: Syracuse sold Jim Brasco's player rights to Milwaukee on November 25, 1952. The old TradeVerdicts record treated Brasco as an unexercised 1952 draft-rights asset, but he had already played 10 games for the Nationals after Syracuse selected him in the second round. Milwaukee was buying an active rookie guard.

sections.heading: Brasco Played Ten More NBA Games
sections.body: Brasco appeared in 10 games for Milwaukee, averaging 13.7 minutes, 4.4 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.9 assists. His shooting percentage improved from .229 with Syracuse to .304 with the Hawks, but the sample stayed small and he never appeared in another NBA season.

sections.heading: Syracuse Received an Undisclosed Cash Payment
sections.body: The Nationals' return was cash. The amount is not preserved, so there is no responsible way to assign a precise financial value or claim that the payment created a later roster asset. Syracuse did, however, monetize a player who had only 10 NBA games left after the transaction.

sections.heading: Low Impact on Both Sides Keeps This Even
sections.body: Milwaukee obtained short-term reserve depth and nothing beyond the season. Syracuse received money for a player whose NBA career was almost over. With neither side generating durable basketball value and the cash amount unknown, a balanced C-level result fits better than a forced winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Milwaukee Hawks C, Syracuse Nationals C. Syracuse sold Jim Brasco's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on November 25, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Milwaukee and league transaction logs all describe a sale, not a 1952 draft-rights transfer. Brasco had already appeared in 10 games for Syracuse after being selected by the Nationals in the second round of the 1952 draft. He then played 10 games for Milwaukee before his NBA career ended. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record, so neither side produced enough measurable value to justify a strong directional verdict.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Bought Frank Kudelka for Cash
sections.body: Baltimore sold Frank Kudelka's player rights to Philadelphia on December 1, 1952. Kudelka was an established veteran who had already played 16 games for the Bullets that season, so the Warriors were purchasing immediate backcourt depth rather than a developmental asset. The cash amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: Kudelka’s Warriors Stint Lasted Twenty Games
sections.body: Kudelka appeared in 20 games for Philadelphia, averaging 17.0 minutes, 4.2 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The Warriors waived him on January 20, 1953, less than two months after the sale, and he never played another NBA game.

sections.heading: Baltimore Sold the Final Stretch of His Career
sections.body: Baltimore's side is difficult to quantify because the payment is undisclosed, but the player cost is clear. The Bullets gave up only the final 20 games of Kudelka's NBA career, and Philadelphia did not turn him into another roster asset or trade return.

sections.heading: Neither Side Created a Lasting Advantage
sections.body: Philadelphia received a small amount of useful reserve production and then moved on. Baltimore received cash for a veteran with almost no remaining NBA longevity. The old wide grade gap overstates what happened; the verifiable outcomes are modest enough to support an even C/C result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Philadelphia Warriors C, Baltimore Bullets C. Baltimore sold Frank Kudelka's player rights to the Philadelphia Warriors on December 1, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Kudelka had played 16 games for Baltimore that season before the move, then appeared in 20 games for Philadelphia, averaging 17.0 minutes, 4.2 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The Warriors waived him on January 20, 1953, and he never played another NBA game. Because Baltimore's cash return is undisclosed and Philadelphia received only a short final stint, the source-backed record supports a balanced low-impact result.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Bill Calhoun from Syracuse
sections.body: Syracuse sold Bill Calhoun's player rights to Milwaukee on December 2, 1952. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Syracuse, Milwaukee and league-wide 1952-53 transaction pages. Calhoun was a veteran guard-forward, not a developmental rights asset. He had already played four professional seasons before 1952-53 and had appeared in 13 games for Syracuse after arriving from Baltimore in an October trade. Milwaukee bought a player who could take on a substantial role immediately.

sections.heading: Calhoun Became a Three-Year Hawks Regular
sections.body: Calhoun became one of Milwaukee's busiest players after the transaction. He appeared in 49 games for the Hawks in 1952-53, logging 1,909 minutes while averaging 39.0 minutes, 10.3 points, 5.1 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He returned for all 72 games in 1953-54 and another 69 in 1954-55. Across three Milwaukee seasons, Basketball-Reference credits him with 190 games, 6,388 minutes, 1,555 points, 814 rebounds and 565 assists. The Hawks therefore acquired far more than a short rental; Calhoun became a multi-year rotation regular.

sections.heading: Syracuse Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Syracuse received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That consideration was real and should not be treated as zero, yet the surviving record provides no player, draft pick or later transaction directly traceable to the proceeds. The Nationals had used Calhoun for only 13 games after acquiring him from Baltimore, then chose to monetize his rights. From a roster standpoint, they surrendered the remaining three NBA seasons of a player who still had substantial minutes ahead of him.

sections.heading: One Hundred Ninety Games Give Milwaukee the Win
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return. Calhoun played 190 games for the Hawks and remained a high-minute contributor through 1954-55, while Syracuse's side of the exchange is limited to an undisclosed cash payment. The unknown payment argues against an extreme grade gap, but the volume and duration of Calhoun's Milwaukee tenure make a directional verdict appropriate. The prior even-grade treatment understates how much basketball value Milwaukee realized after the sale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee B+, Syracuse C-. Syracuse sold Bill Calhoun's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on December 2, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Calhoun had played 13 games for Syracuse after arriving from Baltimore earlier that season, then became a major Milwaukee rotation player. He appeared in 49 games for the Hawks in 1952-53, 72 in 1953-54 and 69 in 1954-55, totaling 190 Milwaukee games and 6,388 minutes across three seasons. The cash amount Syracuse received is not preserved, so Milwaukee owns the clearly stronger measurable basketball return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Ed Mikan to Indianapolis
sections.body: Philadelphia sold Ed Mikan's player rights to Indianapolis on December 11, 1952. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on both team pages and in the league-wide 1952-53 ledger. Mikan was a veteran center who had already played 19 games for Philadelphia that season after serving as a regular rotation player for the Warriors in 1951-52. Indianapolis purchased immediate frontcourt depth rather than a prospect or draft asset. The surviving transaction logs identify the deal as a sale but do not preserve the cash amount Philadelphia received.

sections.heading: Mikan Gave the Olympians 43 Reserve Games
sections.body: Mikan appeared in 43 games for the Olympians after the sale, totaling 569 minutes. He averaged 13.2 minutes, 3.0 points and 2.7 rebounds while shooting .247 from the field. The role was real but limited, and the transaction did not create any durable value beyond that season. Indianapolis ceased operations after 1952-53, and Mikan did not play another NBA game. The club therefore received a short reserve-center stint rather than a multi-year contributor or an asset that could be moved later.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took Cash for a Short-Term Player
sections.body: Philadelphia received cash. Because the amount is unknown, the Warriors' side cannot be valued precisely, but it should not be treated as zero. The measurable opportunity cost was modest: after the sale, Mikan supplied 43 low-minute games before his NBA career ended. Philadelphia did not give away a player who later developed into a major contributor elsewhere, and no additional consideration accompanied the sale. That makes the cash return more defensible than the legacy F grade suggested.

sections.heading: Limited Value on Both Sides Leaves This Even
sections.body: Neither side created much lasting value. Indianapolis got 43 games of reserve frontcourt play, while Philadelphia received an undisclosed payment for a player with less than one NBA season remaining. The Olympians gained more measurable on-court production, but the scale of that production was too small to justify a decisive winner, especially with the cash amount unknown. A balanced grade better reflects the limited stakes and the verified outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Philadelphia C, Indianapolis C. Philadelphia sold Ed Mikan's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians on December 11, 1952. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Indianapolis and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Mikan had played 19 games for Philadelphia that season before the move, then appeared in 43 games for Indianapolis, averaging 13.2 minutes, 3.0 points and 2.7 rebounds. The Olympians folded after the season, so the transaction produced no lasting player or asset chain. Because Philadelphia's cash return is undisclosed and Indianapolis received only a short reserve stint, the source-backed record supports a balanced low-impact result.

sections.heading: Milwaukee and Baltimore Made a Five-Player Swap
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Don Boven, Pete Darcey and George McLeod to Baltimore on January 2, 1953 for Stan Miasek and Dave Minor. Basketball-Reference's 1952-53 league transaction ledger gives that exact five-player structure. The source-backed review also fixes a serious identity defect in the legacy TradeVerdicts record: the third outgoing Hawk was George McLeod, a 1952 Milwaukee draft pick, not George McCloud. The bad spelling had incorrectly attached the 1953 transaction to the much later NBA player George McCloud. That false edge is removed and reassigned to a new canonical George McLeod identity.

sections.heading: Miasek and Minor Gave Milwaukee 80 Games
sections.body: Miasek and Minor both became meaningful rotation players for the Hawks during the remainder of the season. Miasek appeared in 40 Milwaukee games, averaging 11.0 points and 7.7 rebounds. Minor also played 40 games, averaging 32.7 minutes, 8.0 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists. Together they supplied 80 post-trade appearances and filled substantial roles for a Milwaukee team trying to stabilize its lineup. Neither player remained in the NBA beyond 1952-53, so the value was concentrated in that season, but it was real and immediate.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received Less Direct Production
sections.body: Baltimore's three-player package produced much less direct on-court value. Boven played 23 games for the Bullets, averaging 14.3 minutes and 4.6 points, before Baltimore moved him again on February 16. McLeod made his NBA debut after the trade and appeared in 10 games, totaling 85 minutes and 12 points; those were the only NBA games of his career. Darcey had already appeared in 12 games for Milwaukee, but Basketball-Reference credits him with no Baltimore appearances after the transaction and no later NBA season.

sections.heading: Immediate Rotation Value Favors the Hawks
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger realized package. The Hawks got 80 combined games from two veterans who both handled regular rotation roles, while Baltimore received 33 combined appearances from Boven and McLeod plus a non-playing Darcey. Boven's subsequent trade value keeps Baltimore's side from being a complete miss, yet it does not offset the larger body of useful production Milwaukee received immediately. The source-backed evidence supports a moderate Hawks advantage rather than the legacy even-grade treatment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee B, Baltimore C. Milwaukee traded Don Boven, Pete Darcey and George McLeod to the Baltimore Bullets for Stan Miasek and Dave Minor on January 2, 1953. Basketball-Reference's league transaction log confirms that exact five-player exchange and corrects the legacy TradeVerdicts spelling 'George McCloud' to George McLeod. Miasek and Minor each played 40 games for Milwaukee after the trade, giving the Hawks 80 combined appearances and substantial rotation minutes. Baltimore received 23 games from Boven, 10 from McLeod and no NBA appearances from Darcey after the deal, although Boven retained trade value and moved again in February.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne and Baltimore Swapped Four Players
sections.body: Fort Wayne sent Jack Kerris and Ralph O'Brien to Baltimore on February 16, 1953 for Fred Scolari and Don Boven. Basketball-Reference lists the same four-player trade on the Fort Wayne and Baltimore transaction pages and in the league-wide 1952-53 ledger. That source agreement exposes the key legacy defect: no cash is listed as part of the deal. The unsupported cash asset is removed from the canonical record so the exchange is evaluated strictly as Kerris and O'Brien for Scolari and Boven.

sections.heading: Scolari Extended the Pistons Return into 1953-54
sections.body: Scolari supplied the most durable post-trade value. He played 16 games for Fort Wayne to finish 1952-53, logging 505 minutes, then returned for 64 games and 1,589 minutes in 1953-54. Boven added 17 regular-season games after the trade, with 377 minutes, 104 points and 58 rebounds, and he appeared in eight playoff games during Fort Wayne's postseason run. Together, Scolari and Boven gave the Pistons 33 regular-season appearances immediately after the exchange, while Scolari's next full season extended the return to 97 combined regular-season games.

sections.heading: Baltimore Got 31 Games from Kerris and O’Brien
sections.body: Kerris played 17 games for Baltimore after the trade, logging 442 minutes with 95 points, 88 rebounds and 48 assists. O'Brien appeared in 14 games and 182 minutes, scoring 72 points with 20 rebounds and 17 assists. Both players finished their NBA careers with Baltimore at the end of the season. The Bullets therefore received 31 combined regular-season games and no later NBA value from the package. Removing the unsupported cash component also leaves no additional consideration to narrow the difference.

sections.heading: Scolari’s Second Season Gives Fort Wayne the Edge
sections.body: Fort Wayne received the stronger realized return. The immediate 1952-53 playing-time difference was not enormous, but Scolari's 64-game 1953-54 season gave the Pistons a second year of rotation value that Baltimore did not receive from Kerris or O'Brien. Boven also contributed during the 1953 playoffs. Baltimore's package was useful for the final weeks of the season, but both incoming players exited the NBA afterward. The source-backed evidence supports a moderate Pistons advantage rather than the legacy even-trade grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne B, Baltimore C. Fort Wayne traded Jack Kerris and Ralph O'Brien to the Baltimore Bullets for Fred Scolari and Don Boven on February 16, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Baltimore and league transaction logs all show a straight four-player exchange; the legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly added cash to Baltimore's return. Scolari played 16 games for Fort Wayne to finish 1952-53 and another 64 in 1953-54, while Boven added 17 regular-season games and eight playoff appearances. Baltimore received 17 games from Kerris and 14 from O'Brien, with neither player appearing in another NBA season. The verified outcome favors Fort Wayne.

sections.heading: The July 1 Jack Nichols Sale Is Unsupported
sections.body: The surviving Milwaukee, Boston and league transaction pages do not support a July 1, 1953 cash sale of Jack Nichols to Boston. The legacy listing therefore cannot be treated as a separate completed NBA trade.

sections.heading: The Verified Nichols Trade Happened on November 29
sections.body: The verified Nichols transaction occurred on November 29, 1953, when Boston sent John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh to Milwaukee for Nichols. TradeVerdicts already preserves that six-player exchange as its own canonical record.

sections.heading: Keeping Both Rows Would Double-Count One Move
sections.body: Treating the July entry as valid would create a false extra movement for Nichols and contaminate team and player relationship histories. The conflict is not a grading question; it is a provenance problem that requires one verified trade and one superseded legacy route.

sections.heading: Preserve the Legacy Route but Supersede the Trade
sections.body: TradeVerdicts keeps this route privately so the original source conflict remains auditable, but excludes it from public/indexable treatment and hindsight grading. No winner or team grades are assigned because the July transaction itself is not established.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. This July 1, 1953 Jack Nichols-for-cash listing is retained only as legacy source provenance. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Boston and league transaction logs do not record that sale. They instead show Milwaukee trading Nichols to Boston on November 29, 1953 for John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh, a transaction already represented by a separate canonical TradeVerdicts record. Nichols also played 15 Milwaukee games in 1953-54 before the November move, making the July transfer incompatible with his documented season. The July record is therefore a duplicate/malformed record, not a separate completed trade. No team grade is assigned because the route is retained only for provenance.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sold Mel Hutchins to Fort Wayne
sections.body: Milwaukee sold Mel Hutchins' player rights to Fort Wayne on August 23, 1953. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on both team pages and in the 1953-54 league ledger. The source wording and Hutchins' career history require a structural repair to the legacy asset. He was not a 1953 draft-rights player: Milwaukee had drafted him second overall in 1951, and he had already completed two NBA seasons for the Hawks, including an All-Star season in 1952-53. Fort Wayne therefore purchased the rights to an established 24-year-old frontcourt player.

sections.heading: Hutchins Became a Four-Year Pistons Cornerstone
sections.body: Hutchins became a core Piston for four seasons. He played 72 games in 1953-54, 72 in 1954-55, 66 in 1955-56 and 72 in 1956-57. Across that Fort Wayne run he logged 282 games and 10,681 minutes, with 3,287 points, 2,427 rebounds and 847 assists. He made the All-Star team in 1954, 1956 and 1957, while Basketball-Reference also shows him fourth in MVP voting in 1955-56 and eighth in 1956-57. Fort Wayne reached the NBA Finals in both 1955 and 1956 with Hutchins playing a major role.

sections.heading: The Hawks Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Milwaukee received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That is legitimate consideration and should not be treated as zero, yet there is no documented player, pick or later asset chain attached to the proceeds. In basketball terms, the Hawks sold a player who had just averaged 11.7 points and 11.2 rebounds while making the All-Star team, and Hutchins then remained a high-minute starter for four more seasons. The scale of that lost production is unusually large for a cash sale.

sections.heading: Three All-Star Seasons Make This a Pistons Win
sections.body: Fort Wayne received a major competitive return. Hutchins gave the Pistons four full seasons, three All-Star selections with the franchise, substantial MVP-vote recognition and frontcourt production during consecutive Finals runs. Milwaukee's unknown cash return adds uncertainty, but the documented basketball value is too large to support a balanced grade. This is a clear Pistons win even while avoiding assumptions about the undisclosed payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Milwaukee D, Fort Wayne A. Milwaukee sold Mel Hutchins' player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons on August 23, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: Hutchins was already a two-year NBA veteran and a 1953 All-Star. He then played all four of the next seasons for Fort Wayne, totaling 282 games, 10,681 minutes, 3,287 points and 2,427 rebounds. Hutchins made three All-Star teams as a Piston and helped Fort Wayne reach consecutive NBA Finals in 1955 and 1956.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Don Barksdale from Baltimore
sections.body: Baltimore sent Don Barksdale to Boston on August 27, 1953 for Jim Doherty, Herm Hedderick, Mo Mahoney, Vernon Stokes and cash. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Boston and league-wide transaction logs all list that date and package, so the legacy August 28 route is corrected by one day. The source-backed review also normalizes two player names from the old intake: Francis Mahoney is the player known in the NBA record as Mo Mahoney, and Herman Hedderick is Herm Hedderick.

sections.heading: Barksdale Gave the Celtics 135 Games
sections.body: Barksdale gave the Celtics two full seasons of useful frontcourt play. He appeared in 63 games in 1953-54, averaging 21.6 minutes, 7.3 points and 5.5 rebounds, then played all 72 games in 1954-55 while averaging 10.5 points and 7.6 rebounds. Across the two seasons he totaled 135 regular-season appearances and averaged 9.0 points and 6.6 rebounds for Boston. The production was below his Baltimore All-Star peak, but the Celtics received a legitimate multi-year rotation starter from a package built mostly around fringe or future players.

sections.heading: Baltimore’s Four Players Produced Almost Nothing
sections.body: The Bullets received very little measurable NBA production from the four players. Mahoney appeared in two Baltimore games and did not score. Hedderick remained in military service throughout 1953-54 and later played only five NBA games, all for New York in 1954-55. Basketball-Reference lists Doherty and Stokes as drafted players but credits neither with an NBA appearance. Baltimore also received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record. That financial consideration deserves credit, but it cannot erase the large difference in realized playing value.

sections.heading: Two Productive Seasons Give Boston the Win
sections.body: Boston acquired the only durable NBA contributor in the transaction. Barksdale supplied 135 games over two seasons, while Baltimore's four-player return produced only Mahoney's two Bullets appearances and no later Baltimore value from the other three players. The undisclosed cash payment prevents an extreme bottom grade for the Bullets, but the documented basketball outcome remains heavily tilted toward Boston.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-, Baltimore D+. Baltimore traded Don Barksdale to the Boston Celtics on August 27, 1953 for Jim Doherty, Herm Hedderick, Mo Mahoney, Vernon Stokes and cash. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Boston and league transaction logs all agree on the August 27 date, correcting the legacy August 28 route. Barksdale then played 135 regular-season games across two Boston seasons, averaging 9.0 points and 6.6 rebounds for the Celtics. Baltimore received only two NBA games from Mahoney; Hedderick was still in military service and later played five games for New York, while Doherty and Stokes never appeared in an NBA game.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Lew Hitch from Minneapolis
sections.body: Minneapolis sold Lew Hitch's player rights to Milwaukee on October 27, 1953. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Lakers, Hawks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Hitch as 1953 draft rights, but that is not historically possible: the Lakers drafted him in 1951, and he had already played 131 regular-season games across two Minneapolis seasons before this transaction. The canonical asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player sale.

sections.heading: Hitch Played All 72 Games for the Hawks
sections.body: Whatever the later rights bookkeeping, Milwaukee received substantial immediate basketball value. Basketball-Reference credits Hitch with all 72 Hawks games in 1953-54, including 2,452 minutes. He averaged 34.1 minutes, 8.0 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists, giving a 21-win Milwaukee team one of its heaviest workloads. Hitch's 3.3 win shares were also the strongest single-season total of his career to that point.

sections.heading: The Lakers Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Minneapolis received cash, but the reviewed public transaction pages do not preserve the amount. The Lakers had already captured two championship seasons from Hitch before selling his rights, so this was not a case of giving away an untested player. The cash return has real but unquantifiable value. The record also becomes complicated because Basketball-Reference separately lists Milwaukee trading Hitch back to Minneapolis for Bobby Watson on December 21 even though its player statistics credit Hitch's entire 1953-54 season to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: A Full High-Minute Season Gives Milwaukee the Edge
sections.body: The October transaction itself favors Milwaukee because the Hawks obtained a full 72-game season and a large frontcourt workload from Hitch, while the Lakers' cash return cannot be measured. The later December transaction entry is preserved as a separate source-backed record and should not be used to erase the value Milwaukee clearly received during 1953-54. The uncertainty is enough to keep the grade gap moderate rather than extreme.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee B, Minneapolis C. Minneapolis sold Lew Hitch's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on October 27, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: Hitch was a veteran who had already played two NBA seasons and won two championships with the Lakers. Basketball-Reference credits Hitch with all 72 Milwaukee games in 1953-54, when he averaged 34.1 minutes, 8.0 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists.

sections.heading: Baltimore Bought Rookie Jim Fritsche from Minneapolis
sections.body: Minneapolis traded Jim Fritsche to Baltimore for cash on November 11, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bullets and league-wide transaction pages all record the same deal. Fritsche had been the ninth overall pick in the 1953 draft, but the defending-champion Lakers used him for only two games and eight total minutes before moving him. Baltimore was buying a young frontcourt player with first-round pedigree, while Minneapolis chose immediate financial consideration instead of carrying him as a developmental piece.

sections.heading: Fritsche Became a Full-Season Bullets Reserve
sections.body: Fritsche became a regular part of the Bullets' rotation almost immediately. He appeared in 66 Baltimore games during 1953-54, totaling 1,213 minutes, 280 points, 217 rebounds and 73 assists. His per-game line of 18.4 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.3 rebounds was modest, but it was meaningful availability for a club that needed bodies and developmental minutes. Baltimore also retained enough asset value to move Fritsche again on October 26, 1954, when the Bullets traded him to Fort Wayne for Ken Murray.

sections.heading: The Lakers Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Lakers received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction records. That prevents a precise financial comparison. Minneapolis had already made the decision quickly: Fritsche played only two games and eight minutes for the Lakers before the trade. Because the club was defending a championship and had a veteran-heavy frontcourt, converting a little-used rookie into cash was understandable. Still, the surviving record does not show another player, pick or identifiable downstream asset tied to the payment.

sections.heading: Baltimore Got More Measurable Roster Value
sections.body: Baltimore received the stronger measurable basketball return. Fritsche supplied 66 games and more than 1,200 minutes in the season immediately after the trade, then retained enough value to be exchanged again the next fall. The Lakers' side was real but economically opaque. Fritsche never became a major NBA player, so the gap should remain moderate rather than dramatic, but the Bullets clearly extracted more documented roster value from the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Minneapolis C, Baltimore B-. Minneapolis traded rookie forward Jim Fritsche to the Baltimore Bullets for cash on November 11, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, Baltimore and league transaction logs agree on the exchange. Fritsche, the ninth overall pick in the 1953 draft, had appeared in only two Lakers games before the move. He then played 66 games for Baltimore that season, averaging 18.4 minutes, 4.2 points, 3.3 rebounds and 1.1 assists.

sections.heading: Syracuse Swapped Noble Jorgensen for Bob Lavoy
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Bob Lavoy to Syracuse on November 23, 1953 for Noble Jorgensen. Basketball-Reference lists the same transaction on the Hawks, Nationals and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, leaving no meaningful package ambiguity. Lavoy was a 27-year-old power forward who had played three full seasons for Indianapolis before the Olympians folded and had appeared in eight games for Milwaukee that fall. Jorgensen was an older center whose best Syracuse years were already behind him.

sections.heading: Lavoy Helped a Finals Team for 60 Games
sections.body: Lavoy immediately became a useful frontcourt reserve for a contender. He played 60 games for Syracuse during the remainder of 1953-54, logging 1,152 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 323 points, 287 rebounds and 68 assists in those games, along with 3.0 win shares. The Nationals finished 42-30, advanced through the Eastern playoffs and took Minneapolis to seven games in the NBA Finals. Lavoy was not a star, but Syracuse acquired a veteran who filled regular minutes during a Finals season.

sections.heading: Jorgensen Never Played for Milwaukee
sections.body: Jorgensen did not produce a comparable post-trade return. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA career ending with the 1952-53 Syracuse season, when he appeared in 70 games. He has no 1953-54 Milwaukee line and no later NBA season. That means the Hawks exchanged eight early-season games of Lavoy for player rights that generated no documented NBA appearances. Jorgensen had been a useful center earlier in his career, but the timing of this transaction left Milwaukee with no measurable on-court value.

sections.heading: Useful Rotation Minutes Make Syracuse the Winner
sections.body: Syracuse clearly received the stronger realized return. Lavoy supplied 60 regular-season games and more than 1,100 minutes to a team that reached the NBA Finals, while Jorgensen never appeared for Milwaukee. The gap is meaningful but should not be inflated into a franchise-altering outcome because Lavoy was a rotation player and his NBA career ended after the season. A solid but not extreme Syracuse advantage best matches the surviving record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Milwaukee C-, Syracuse B. Milwaukee traded Bob Lavoy to the Syracuse Nationals for Noble Jorgensen on November 23, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Syracuse and league transaction logs agree on the straight player-for-player swap. Lavoy had played only eight games for Milwaukee after the Indianapolis Olympians folded, then appeared in 60 games for Syracuse, logging 1,152 minutes with 323 points and 287 rebounds for a club that reached the 1954 NBA Finals. Jorgensen never appeared in another NBA game after the trade; Basketball-Reference lists his final NBA season as 1952-53. The verified realized value therefore favors Syracuse.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned Max Zaslofsky into a Longer Asset Chain
sections.body: Baltimore sent Max Zaslofsky to Milwaukee on November 25, 1953 for Bob Houbregs. Basketball-Reference records the same player-for-player exchange on both team transaction pages and in the league-wide 1953-54 ledger. Zaslofsky was a proven veteran scorer who had already made an All-Star team and led the BAA in scoring earlier in his career. Houbregs was the third overall pick in the 1953 draft and only 21 years old, so Baltimore was trading established production for a younger frontcourt piece.

sections.heading: Houbregs Gave Baltimore Real Rookie Minutes
sections.body: Houbregs immediately handled a major role for the Bullets. He appeared in 59 Baltimore games during 1953-54, logging 1,804 minutes with 544 points, 329 rebounds and 114 assists. He averaged more than 30 minutes per game after the trade and remained with Baltimore for 10 games in 1954-55 before the franchise folded. His later NBA career continued elsewhere, but Baltimore's direct return was still substantial: the Bullets received most of a season of starter-level minutes from a rookie with meaningful upside.

sections.heading: Zaslofsky Became Chuck Share One Month Later
sections.body: Zaslofsky's direct Milwaukee stint was short but productive. He appeared in nine games, averaging 33.2 minutes and 15.1 points. More importantly, the Hawks retained his asset value. On December 21 they traded Zaslofsky to Fort Wayne for Chuck Share. Share then played 47 Milwaukee games that season and 69 in 1954-55 before remaining with the franchise after its move to St. Louis. He became the club's regular center for years and was part of the 1958 NBA championship team.

sections.heading: The Share Conversion Pushes Milwaukee Ahead
sections.body: Baltimore received useful immediate value from Houbregs, so this was not a one-sided failure. The Bullets got 59 games and heavy minutes from a young frontcourt player. Milwaukee, however, turned Zaslofsky into both short-term scoring and the trade asset that produced Share, whose multi-year run became part of the Hawks' rise into a championship contender. The downstream chain creates a clear Milwaukee advantage while still recognizing that Baltimore's return was real.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee A-, Baltimore B-. Baltimore traded veteran guard Max Zaslofsky to the Milwaukee Hawks for rookie big man Bob Houbregs on November 25, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the straight swap. Houbregs became a major Baltimore rotation player immediately, appearing in 59 games and logging 1,804 minutes with 544 points and 329 rebounds in 1953-54. Zaslofsky played only nine Milwaukee games, but on December 21 the Hawks flipped him to Fort Wayne for Chuck Share, who became Milwaukee/St. Louis' starting center and remained with the franchise through its 1958 championship season.

sections.heading: Boston Sent Five Players for Jack Nichols
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Jack Nichols to Boston on November 29, 1953 for John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh. Basketball-Reference records that exact package on the Hawks, Celtics and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, and the Red Auerbach and Ben Kerner executive ledgers independently preserve the same exchange. The structure looks large because Boston sent five names, but the source-backed review has to distinguish roster rights from actual NBA production. Nichols was the only player in the package who produced measurable post-trade NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Nichols Still Supplied 16 Celtics Games
sections.body: Nichols appeared in six Celtics games in 1953-54, seven in 1954-55 and three in 1955-56. Across those three partial seasons he totaled 16 games, 542 minutes, 214 points, 147 rebounds and 64 assists. The role was small, but it was real. Boston received a veteran forward who could fill rotation minutes over several seasons without surrendering a player who later emerged as a meaningful NBA contributor. Nichols' best Boston stretch came immediately after the deal, when he averaged 35.2 minutes and 16.7 points across six games in 1953-54.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Five Names Produced No NBA Return
sections.body: Azary, Eydt, Lillis, Maze and Unruh generated no documented NBA regular-season appearances after the trade. Basketball-Reference preserves their draft or player identities, but none became an NBA rotation piece for Milwaukee. That makes the five-player return look much larger on paper than it was in realized basketball value. The Hawks effectively exchanged a veteran who still had some usable NBA minutes for a group of rights and fringe assets that did not translate into league production.

sections.heading: The Small Realized Edge Goes to Boston
sections.body: Boston received the stronger realized return because Nichols was the only asset in the transaction to play another NBA game. At the same time, 16 games across three seasons is too little to treat this as a major win. The Celtics gained useful depth at very low realized opportunity cost, while Milwaukee's five-player package never produced a corresponding NBA contribution. The source-backed result should therefore favor Boston without exaggerating the importance of the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Milwaukee D+, Boston B-. Milwaukee traded Jack Nichols to the Boston Celtics for John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh on November 29, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Boston and league transaction logs all verify the six-player package. Nichols then appeared in 16 regular-season games for Boston across three seasons, totaling 542 minutes, 214 points and 147 rebounds. The five players sent to Milwaukee never produced an NBA regular-season appearance after the trade. Boston therefore received the only measurable on-court value, although Nichols' limited role keeps the hindsight advantage modest rather than dramatic.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Swapped Zaslofsky for Chuck Share
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Max Zaslofsky to Fort Wayne on December 21, 1953 for Chuck Share. Basketball-Reference lists the same exchange on the Hawks, Pistons and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The move came less than a month after Milwaukee acquired Zaslofsky from Baltimore, so the Hawks effectively converted a veteran scoring guard into a younger center with size and upside. Share had been the first overall pick in the 1950 draft and was still only 26, while Zaslofsky was an established scorer entering the later stage of his career.

sections.heading: Share Became a Long-Term Hawks Center
sections.body: Share's role expanded immediately after the trade. He played 47 games for Milwaukee in 1953-54, logging 1,421 minutes with 528 points and 493 rebounds. His averages jumped to 30.2 minutes, 11.2 points and 10.5 rebounds per game, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 4.6 win shares for the Hawks portion of the season. He stayed with the franchise through the move to St. Louis, became a regular center for several years and remained on the roster during the 1958 championship season.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Still Got Useful Veteran Scoring
sections.body: Zaslofsky was not a throwaway return. He appeared in 45 Pistons games in 1953-54, averaging 25.9 minutes and 11.0 points while contributing 495 total points. He then played 70 games for Fort Wayne in 1954-55 at 11.2 points per game and remained on the roster into 1955-56. For a team trying to contend immediately, adding an experienced scorer had clear utility. The Pistons received more short-term perimeter production than Share had been giving them before the deal, and the exchange helped both teams address different roster needs.

sections.heading: Longevity Gives Milwaukee the Better Outcome
sections.body: Both sides received real value, but Milwaukee's return aged better. Zaslofsky provided two useful Fort Wayne seasons, while Share became a multi-year starting-caliber center, followed the franchise to St. Louis and remained part of the roster through the 1958 title run. The gap is therefore about longevity and franchise fit rather than one team receiving nothing. Fort Wayne's return deserves a strong grade, but Share's sustained role gives the Hawks the superior realized outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee A, Fort Wayne B+. Milwaukee traded Max Zaslofsky to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Chuck Share on December 21, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs agree on the straight swap. Share immediately became Milwaukee's starting-caliber center, playing 47 games after the trade and averaging 30.2 minutes, 11.2 points and 10.5 rebounds. He remained with the Hawks through the franchise's move to St. Louis and was still on the roster during the 1958 NBA championship season.
