sections.heading: Milwaukee and Minneapolis Swapped Hitch and Watson
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Lew Hitch to Minneapolis for Bobby Watson on December 21, 1953. Basketball-Reference lists the same transaction on the Hawks, Lakers and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, and the Ben Kerner and Max Winter executive ledgers preserve the exchange as well. The transaction itself is therefore well supported. The difficult part is the roster chronology that follows. Hitch's 1953-54 line is entirely credited to Milwaukee, and Watson did not appear in an NBA game until the following season.

sections.heading: Hitch Ultimately Gave the Lakers More Service
sections.body: Hitch became the more valuable NBA player. Basketball-Reference credits him with 57 Milwaukee games and 17 Minneapolis games in 1954-55, then 69 more Minneapolis games in 1955-56. Across those two Lakers stints after the recorded trade, he supplied regular frontcourt minutes, rebounding and interior depth. His 1954-55 Minneapolis segment produced 17 games, 323 minutes, 98 points and 93 rebounds, and the next season he appeared in 69 games.

sections.heading: Watson Produced Only 13 Milwaukee Games
sections.body: Watson's NBA career was brief. He debuted in 1954-55 and played 63 total games that season, 50 with Minneapolis and 13 with Milwaukee. His Milwaukee segment averaged 12.0 minutes, 2.2 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.3 assists. He did not play another NBA season. That is a real contribution, but it is a small one, and the same season split that places Watson in both Minneapolis and Milwaukee underscores why the 1953 transaction ledger cannot be read as a complete movement timeline.

sections.heading: The Chronology Is Messy but Minneapolis Still Leads
sections.body: The player-value comparison favors Minneapolis because Hitch had the longer and more productive NBA career after this period, including 86 regular-season games for the Lakers across 1954-55 and 1955-56. Watson's only NBA season produced 13 Milwaukee games. The uncertainty lies in transaction timing, not in which player generated more eventual NBA value. That warrants a Lakers edge, but the grade gap stays moderate because the public records do not fully reconcile when each player's rights and roster status changed hands.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Milwaukee C+, Minneapolis B. Milwaukee traded Lew Hitch to the Minneapolis Lakers for Bobby Watson on December 21, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Minneapolis and league transaction logs agree on the exchange, but the surviving season tables create a chronology problem: Hitch is credited with all 72 of his 1953-54 games for Milwaukee, while Watson did not make his NBA debut until 1954-55. That next season, Hitch played 57 Milwaukee games and 17 for Minneapolis, while Watson played 50 Minneapolis games and 13 for Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Sold Fred Schaus to New York
sections.body: Fort Wayne sold Fred Schaus' player rights to New York on December 29, 1953. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Pistons, Knicks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset called this draft rights, but that classification is historically wrong. Schaus was already a veteran NBA forward in his fifth season and had played 23 Fort Wayne games in 1953-54 before the transaction. The asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player sale rather than a draft-rights transfer.

sections.heading: Schaus Became a 44-Game Knicks Rotation Piece
sections.body: Schaus moved directly into a meaningful Knicks role. Basketball-Reference credits him with 44 New York games after the sale, totaling 1,243 minutes, 387 points, 217 rebounds and 88 assists. He averaged 28.3 minutes, 8.8 points, 4.9 rebounds and 2.0 assists in the Knicks segment of the season. New York finished 44-28 and reached the Eastern Division round-robin, so the acquisition supplied useful veteran minutes for a contender rather than merely preserving a future right.

sections.heading: The Pistons Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Fort Wayne received cash, and the reviewed public transaction pages do not preserve the amount. That prevents a precise financial valuation. The Pistons had already received 23 Schaus appearances that season before selling his rights, and the move cleared a veteran from the roster while returning money. The surviving record does not identify another player, draft selection or downstream basketball asset tied to the payment, so the Pistons' side has to be graded conservatively rather than treated as equivalent to New York's documented rotation production.

sections.heading: New York Bought the Better Measurable Return
sections.body: The Knicks received the stronger measurable return. Schaus played 44 games and more than 1,200 minutes for New York immediately after the sale, while Fort Wayne's cash return is legitimate but unquantified. This was not a franchise-changing acquisition because Schaus' NBA career ended after 1953-54, but it was clearly more than a speculative rights purchase. The proper hindsight gap is moderate: New York bought one useful stretch of veteran production, while Fort Wayne accepted an undisclosed financial return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — Fort Wayne C, New York B. Fort Wayne sold Fred Schaus' player rights to the New York Knicks for cash on December 29, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, New York and league transaction logs agree on the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Schaus as draft rights, but he was an active veteran in his fifth NBA season and had already played 23 games for the Pistons that year. After the sale he played 44 games for New York, logging 1,243 minutes with 387 points, 217 rebounds and 88 assists.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Veteran Guard Bob Harrison
sections.body: Minneapolis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to Milwaukee on February 2, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same sale on the Lakers, Hawks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. Harrison was not an untested prospect: he had already played four full seasons plus 40 games of 1953-54 for Minneapolis, won three NBA championships with the Lakers and remained an active rotation guard. The transaction is therefore best understood as the sale of a veteran player's rights for cash, with the amount not preserved in the reviewed public record.

sections.heading: Harrison Played 96 Hawks Games
sections.body: Harrison immediately became one of Milwaukee's heaviest-minute guards. He played 24 Hawks games to finish 1953-54, averaging 34.3 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists. He then appeared in all 72 Milwaukee games in 1954-55, averaging 31.9 minutes, 10.1 points, 3.1 rebounds and 3.5 assists. That is substantial realized value from a February cash purchase: the Hawks added an experienced guard who could handle starter-level minutes across the remainder of one season and the entirety of the next.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Took Cash from a Deep Championship Roster
sections.body: The Lakers received cash, but the reviewed transaction pages do not disclose the amount. Minneapolis had already extracted considerable value from Harrison before the sale, including three championship seasons and more than four years of regular rotation work. The timing also came during another championship season, so the Lakers were moving an established veteran from a deep roster rather than giving away an unknown asset. Still, the cash cannot be translated into an identifiable player, pick or downstream basketball return in the surviving transaction record.

sections.heading: Starter-Level Minutes Give Milwaukee the Win
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return because Harrison supplied 96 regular-season games across the remainder of 1953-54 and all of 1954-55, including starter-level minutes and double-digit scoring in the latter season. Minneapolis' financial return was real but opaque. The Lakers' prior success with Harrison reduces the sting of the sale, but prior championships are not part of the post-trade return. The result therefore favors Milwaukee without treating the move as a franchise-changing transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee A-, Minneapolis C. Minneapolis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks for cash on February 2, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Harrison was already a five-year NBA veteran and three-time champion, so the deal was a veteran player-rights transfer rather than a speculative acquisition. He played 24 Milwaukee games to finish 1953-54, averaging 34.3 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists, then appeared in all 72 Hawks games the next season at 10.1 points per game.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought Leo Barnhorst from Baltimore
sections.body: Fort Wayne acquired Leo Barnhorst from Baltimore for cash on February 12, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same transaction on the Pistons, Bullets and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. Barnhorst had been a productive Indianapolis Olympians forward and a two-time All-Star, but by February 1954 he was 29 and in the final season of his NBA career. Baltimore had already used him in 55 games that season before converting the veteran into cash.

sections.heading: Barnhorst Was a Short Late-Career Rental
sections.body: Barnhorst appeared in 17 regular-season games for the Pistons after the trade. Basketball-Reference credits him with 185 minutes, 29 points, 37 rebounds and 12 assists in that segment. His per-game line fell to 10.9 minutes, 1.7 points, 2.2 rebounds and 0.7 assists, a sharp reduction from the 34.2 minutes and 7.9 points he had averaged in Baltimore. He also appeared in four playoff games, but the regular-season acquisition did not develop into a longer-term roster piece because 1953-54 was his final NBA season.

sections.heading: The Bullets Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Baltimore received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction pages. The Bullets had already received most of Barnhorst's final-season value before the sale: 55 games, 1,879 minutes and 432 points. Moving him for cash late in the season therefore looks less like surrendering a long-term asset and more like monetizing the end of a veteran's NBA career. Without the cash amount, however, the exact financial benefit cannot be measured against Fort Wayne's brief on-court return.

sections.heading: Limited Value on Both Sides Leaves It Even
sections.body: The transaction produced limited post-deal basketball value on both sides. Fort Wayne received 17 games and 185 regular-season minutes from Barnhorst, while Baltimore received an undisclosed cash payment. That is not enough evidence for a decisive winner. Barnhorst's prior All-Star seasons make the name more recognizable than the actual 1954 return, and the source-backed grade should reflect what happened after the transaction rather than his earlier reputation. A balanced C-level result best matches the surviving evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Fort Wayne C, Baltimore C. Fort Wayne acquired Leo Barnhorst from the Baltimore Bullets for cash on February 12, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Baltimore and league transaction logs agree on the deal. Barnhorst was a two-time All-Star but near the end of his NBA career. He played 17 regular-season games for the Pistons after the trade, totaling 185 minutes, 29 points, 37 rebounds and 12 assists, and he did not play another NBA season. Because Baltimore's cash return is undisclosed and Fort Wayne received only a short, low-minute stint, the surviving record does not support a large hindsight edge for either side.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Chuck Cooper from Boston
sections.body: Boston sold Chuck Cooper's player rights to Milwaukee on May 28, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same sale on the Celtics, Hawks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, and Red Auerbach's executive ledger independently preserves it. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Cooper as 1954 draft rights, but that cannot be correct: Boston had drafted him 13th overall in 1950, and he had already played four NBA seasons for the Celtics. The asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player sale.

sections.heading: Cooper Gave the Hawks 105 Games
sections.body: Cooper became a regular Hawks forward immediately. In 1954-55 he appeared in 70 games, totaling 1,749 minutes, 576 points, 383 rebounds and 151 assists. His per-game line was 25.0 minutes, 8.2 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.2 assists, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 2.4 win shares. He stayed with the franchise after its move to St. Louis and played 35 more Hawks games in 1955-56 before finishing that season with Fort Wayne. Milwaukee therefore received more than one year of real rotation production from the transaction.

sections.heading: Boston Took Cash After Four Cooper Seasons
sections.body: Boston received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction logs. The Celtics had already received four full seasons from Cooper before the sale, including 272 regular-season games. Moving a veteran for financial consideration after that much use is understandable, especially for a club continuing to reshape its roster under Auerbach. Still, the surviving record does not tie the payment to a player, draft pick or downstream basketball asset that can be valued against Cooper's documented Milwaukee production.

sections.heading: Sustained Rotation Value Favors Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return. Cooper played 105 regular-season games for the Hawks across Milwaukee and St. Louis after the sale, with 70 of those coming in a full 1954-55 campaign. Boston's cash return was legitimate but unquantified. Cooper was not a franchise-changing acquisition at that stage of his career, so the grade gap should remain moderate, but the Hawks clearly received sustained rotation value rather than a speculative right.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee B+, Boston C. Boston sold Chuck Cooper's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks for cash on May 28, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Boston, Milwaukee, league and Red Auerbach transaction logs all agree on the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts record mislabeled the asset as 1954 draft rights, but Cooper had been Boston's 13th overall pick in 1950 and had already completed four NBA seasons. He then played 70 Milwaukee games in 1954-55, averaging 25.0 minutes, 8.2 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.2 assists, and remained with the franchise for 35 games after its move to St. Louis in 1955-56.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Swapped Don Sunderlage for Pep Saul
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Don Sunderlage to Minneapolis for Pep Saul on September 18, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same exchange on both teams' 1954-55 transaction pages. The players entered from very different points. Sunderlage was 24 and coming off an All-Star rookie season for Milwaukee in which he averaged 11.2 points across 68 games. Saul was 30, a veteran guard and three-time champion with Minneapolis whose role had gradually declined. The swap therefore traded youth and recent peak production for a more experienced but lower-usage guard.

sections.heading: Saul Played 65 Games for the Hawks
sections.body: Saul played 65 games for the Hawks in 1954-55, logging 1,139 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 287 points, 134 rebounds and 104 assists, or 17.5 minutes, 4.4 points, 2.1 rebounds and 1.6 assists per game. Those are modest numbers, but he stayed available for nearly the entire season and gave Milwaukee far more total minutes than the outgoing player produced for Minneapolis. The 1954-55 campaign was Saul's final NBA season, so his value was concentrated entirely in that one-year return.

sections.heading: Sunderlage’s Lakers Role Shrunk Sharply
sections.body: Sunderlage's Lakers stint was much smaller than his All-Star year in Milwaukee. He appeared in 45 games but averaged only 9.0 minutes, 2.5 points, 1.2 rebounds and 0.8 assists. His season totals were 404 minutes, 114 points, 56 rebounds and 37 assists. He did not play another NBA season. Minneapolis therefore acquired the younger player with the stronger recent résumé, but the realized result never matched that upside. His role collapsed, and the trade did not produce a long-term Lakers contributor.

sections.heading: One Final Season Favors Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger post-trade return because Saul supplied almost three times as many minutes and materially more total production in the only season either player had left in the NBA. That does not make the swap a major win: Saul was a low-usage veteran on a 26-win team, and Sunderlage's Lakers tenure still produced 45 games. But hindsight should follow realized value rather than the players' pre-trade reputations. On that basis, the Hawks got the more useful final-season guard.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Milwaukee B-, Minneapolis C. Milwaukee traded Don Sunderlage to the Minneapolis Lakers for Pep Saul on September 18, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Minneapolis transaction logs agree on the straight veteran-guard swap. Saul played 65 games for Milwaukee in 1954-55, totaling 1,139 minutes with 287 points, 134 rebounds and 104 assists. Sunderlage played 45 games for Minneapolis, totaling 404 minutes with 114 points, 56 rebounds and 37 assists, and neither player appeared in another NBA season. Because Milwaukee received substantially more minutes and total production from the only post-trade season either player played, the measurable hindsight edge goes to the Hawks.

sections.heading: Boston Swapped Bob Harris for Fred Scolari
sections.body: Fort Wayne traded Fred Scolari to Boston on October 16, 1954 for Bob Harris. Basketball-Reference records the same exchange on the Celtics, Pistons and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages, and both Red Auerbach and Fred Zollner's executive ledgers preserve it. The source-backed review also fixes an identity problem in the legacy Boston intake. 'rights to Bob Harris (Anderson)' is not a separate player shell or a draft-rights asset; it is Robert Anderson Harris, the veteran forward Boston had acquired from Fort Wayne in December 1950.

sections.heading: Scolari Supplied 59 Celtics Games
sections.body: Scolari played 59 games for Boston in 1954-55, the final season of his career. His role was smaller than it had been during his All-Star years, but he still supplied 619 minutes, 191 points, 77 rebounds and 93 assists. He averaged 10.5 minutes, 3.2 points and 1.6 assists for a 36-36 Celtics team that reached the Eastern Division Finals. Boston did not acquire a long-term piece, but it received a usable veteran reserve for nearly the full season and the only measurable post-trade NBA production in the deal.

sections.heading: Harris Never Played for Fort Wayne Again
sections.body: Harris had already completed his final NBA season before the trade. Basketball-Reference lists his career ending in 1953-54 after four Boston seasons, and he never appeared in a Fort Wayne game following the October 1954 transaction. The Pistons were reacquiring a player they had originally drafted third overall in 1949 and traded to Boston in 1950, but the return did not translate into additional NBA minutes. The legacy wording 'rights to Bob Harris' is therefore better understood as veteran player rights, not a new prospect or draft asset.

sections.heading: A Full Reserve Season Gives Boston the Edge
sections.body: Boston received the stronger realized return. Scolari's 59 games and 619 minutes were modest, but they still represent a full season of reserve utility. Fort Wayne received no post-trade NBA appearances from Harris. Because Scolari was at the end of his own career and played a limited role, the result should not be treated as a major organizational win. A moderate Celtics advantage best matches the documented outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B, Fort Wayne C-. Fort Wayne traded Fred Scolari to the Boston Celtics for Bob Harris on October 16, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Boston, Fort Wayne, league and executive transaction logs all agree on the straight player-for-player swap. The legacy TradeVerdicts text 'rights to Bob Harris (Anderson)' refers to veteran forward Robert Anderson Harris, who had played four seasons for Boston and whose NBA career ended in 1953-54; he never appeared for Fort Wayne after the trade. Scolari played 59 Boston games in 1954-55, totaling 619 minutes, 191 points, 77 rebounds and 93 assists. Boston therefore received the only measurable post-trade NBA value.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Swapped Ken Murray for Jim Fritsche
sections.body: Baltimore sent Jim Fritsche to Fort Wayne on October 26, 1954 for Ken Murray. Basketball-Reference records the same trade on the Bullets, Pistons and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages, and Fred Zollner's executive ledger independently preserves the exchange. Fritsche was a second-year forward who had played 66 Baltimore games the previous season after arriving from Minneapolis. Murray was a veteran guard who had already spent parts of two seasons with Fort Wayne around two years of U.S. Army service. The swap therefore exchanged a younger reserve forward for a more experienced guard.

sections.heading: Fritsche Supplied 16 Games to a Finals Team
sections.body: Fritsche appeared in 16 Pistons games during 1954-55, logging 151 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 45 points, 32 rebounds and four assists, or 9.4 minutes, 2.8 points and 2.0 rebounds per game. Those were the final games of his NBA career. The contribution was small, but it gave a deep Fort Wayne team another reserve frontcourt option during a season in which the Pistons finished first in the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals.

sections.heading: Baltimore Got Six Games Before the Franchise Folded
sections.body: Murray played only six games for Baltimore before the franchise disbanded on November 27. He logged 134 minutes with 56 points, 11 rebounds and 26 assists in those games. After the Bullets folded, Philadelphia selected him in the dispersal draft, and he played 60 Warriors games during the remainder of the season. That later Philadelphia production should not be credited to Baltimore as trade return; it followed the dissolution of the franchise rather than a subsequent Bullets transaction.

sections.heading: A Small Edge Belongs to Fort Wayne
sections.body: Fort Wayne received the slightly stronger direct return, but the difference is small. Fritsche produced 16 games and 151 minutes for the Pistons, while Murray supplied six games and 134 minutes before Baltimore ceased operations. Neither side retained a durable asset from the exchange. Murray's later 60-game Philadelphia season demonstrates that he still had NBA value, but Baltimore did not realize that value after the franchise folded. A narrow Pistons edge fits the documented outcome without overstating a minor transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne C+, Baltimore C. Baltimore traded Jim Fritsche to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Ken Murray on October 26, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Fort Wayne, league and executive transaction logs agree on the straight player-for-player swap. Fritsche appeared in 16 games for Fort Wayne, totaling 151 minutes, 45 points and 32 rebounds before his NBA career ended. Murray played six games for Baltimore before the Bullets disbanded on November 27, then was selected by Philadelphia in the dispersal draft and played 60 Warriors games.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold Jackie Moore to Milwaukee
sections.body: Syracuse sold Jackie Moore's player rights to Milwaukee on November 1, 1954. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Nationals, Hawks and league-wide transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated Moore as a 1954 draft-rights player, but RealGM's transaction history shows that Moore went undrafted and signed with Syracuse as a free agent. He had already made his NBA debut for the Nationals on October 31. The canonical asset is therefore veteran/current player rights rather than draft rights.

sections.heading: Moore Lasted One Hawks Game
sections.body: Moore appeared in only one game for the Hawks, logging 13 minutes with two points, four rebounds and one assist. Milwaukee eventually placed him on waivers on February 14, 1955. Philadelphia signed him the following day, and his career continued there for three seasons. The later Warriors run included 131 games and a place on the 1956 championship roster, but that value did not accrue to Milwaukee because the Hawks had already relinquished him. The direct Hawks return from the November sale was therefore almost entirely limited to one brief appearance.

sections.heading: The Nationals Converted a Marginal Roster Spot into Cash
sections.body: Syracuse received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record. The Nationals had used Moore for one five-minute appearance before selling his rights, so they converted a player who was not part of their established rotation into immediate consideration. Syracuse then went on to win the 1955 NBA championship without Moore. The unknown amount prevents a precise financial grade, but the transaction cost the Nationals almost no realized on-court value while producing a tangible payment.

sections.heading: Syracuse Captured the Better Immediate Return
sections.body: Syracuse received the stronger direct return. Milwaukee bought a young player's rights, used him once, and waived him roughly three and a half months later. Moore later demonstrated that he could be a useful NBA reserve in Philadelphia, but the Hawks did not capture that value. The Nationals' cash return is unquantified, so the gap should remain moderate, but the one-game Milwaukee outcome is too small to support an even grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — St. Louis D+, Syracuse C+. Syracuse sold Jackie Moore's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on November 1, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale, while RealGM confirms Moore went undrafted in 1954 and had signed with Syracuse as a free agent. That makes the legacy TradeVerdicts 1954 draft-rights classification incorrect. Moore played one game for Milwaukee, totaling 13 minutes, before the Hawks waived him in February. Philadelphia signed him the next day, and he went on to play 131 Warriors games across three seasons.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Veteran Forward Alex Hannum
sections.body: Rochester sold Alex Hannum's player rights to Milwaukee on December 10, 1954. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Royals, Hawks and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated Hannum as 1954 draft rights, but that is impossible. He had entered the NBA in 1949 and played six seasons before the transaction, including all 72 games for Rochester in 1953-54. Milwaukee therefore bought the rights to an established veteran forward rather than a developmental prospect.

sections.heading: Hannum Gave the Hawks 124 Games
sections.body: Hannum stepped directly into the Hawks' rotation. He appeared in 53 Milwaukee games during 1954-55, logging 1,088 minutes and averaging 20.5 minutes, 5.9 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists. He returned for 71 games after the franchise moved to St. Louis in 1955-56, adding 1,480 minutes. That gives the Hawks franchise 124 games across the two seasons immediately following the sale. Hannum's later return to St.

sections.heading: Rochester Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Rochester received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. The Royals had received three productive seasons from Hannum before selling his rights, including a full 72-game campaign in 1953-54. Converting a 31-year-old veteran into cash was therefore a defensible roster decision. Still, the surviving record contains no player, pick or later asset chain tied to the payment, while Milwaukee received two seasons of documented rotation production.

sections.heading: Two Seasons of Rotation Value Favor Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return. Hannum supplied 124 games across the next two seasons and remained a regular frontcourt option, while Rochester's cash consideration cannot be quantified. The legacy A-/D+ treatment overstates the separation because Hannum was a useful veteran rather than a star and the cash amount is unknown. A clear but moderate Hawks advantage better reflects what the transaction itself produced.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B+, Rochester C. Rochester sold Alex Hannum's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on December 10, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Rochester, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: Hannum was a six-year NBA veteran who had played all 72 games for Rochester the previous season. He appeared in 53 games for Milwaukee in 1954-55 and 71 for the St. Louis Hawks in 1955-56, giving the franchise 124 games before his next roster move. Rochester received undisclosed cash, so Milwaukee owns the stronger measurable basketball return without justifying the legacy A-/D+ gap.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Zeke Zawoluk to Rochester
sections.body: Philadelphia sold Zeke Zawoluk's player rights to Rochester on May 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Warriors, Royals and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. Zawoluk had just finished his third NBA season and was still only 24, so Rochester was not purchasing the rights to a long-retired veteran. He had appeared in 67 Philadelphia games in 1954-55 after playing 71 the year before, giving the Royals a reasonable basis to expect usable frontcourt depth. Philadelphia chose cash instead of carrying his rights into another season.

sections.heading: The Royals Received No NBA Games
sections.body: The expected on-court return never arrived. Basketball-Reference lists Zawoluk's NBA career ending with the 1954-55 Philadelphia season. He has no 1955-56 Rochester line and no later NBA appearance. That makes the transaction easy to separate from deals where a buyer received even a short reserve stint: the Royals acquired rights that produced zero documented NBA games. Zawoluk's earlier career had been respectable, but none of that prior production belongs to Rochester's side of this exchange.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Turned the Rights into Cash
sections.body: The Warriors received cash. The amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs, so the precise financial return cannot be measured. Still, Philadelphia converted an outgoing player right into consideration and then watched the player leave the NBA without producing another game. That is the strongest possible evidence that the sale did not cost the Warriors future on-court value. The legacy F grade therefore reverses the actual realized outcome.

sections.heading: Zero Rochester Production Gives Philadelphia the Win
sections.body: Philadelphia received the superior realized return. Rochester paid for player rights that never generated an NBA appearance, while the Warriors received cash for a player whose career ended before the next season. The unknown payment argues against assigning an extreme top grade to Philadelphia because the size of the financial benefit remains unavailable. Even so, the direction of the result is clear: Rochester realized no basketball value from the asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Philadelphia B, Rochester C-. Philadelphia sold Zeke Zawoluk's player rights to the Rochester Royals on May 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Rochester and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Zawoluk had just completed his third NBA season, appearing in 67 games for the Warriors at 16.7 minutes, 6.4 points and 3.8 rebounds per game. He never appeared in another NBA game after the transaction, so Rochester received no realized on-court value from the rights it purchased. Philadelphia's cash return is undisclosed, but converting a player whose NBA career had ended into consideration gives the Warriors the stronger hindsight outcome.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Swapped Monk Meineke for Odie Spears
sections.body: Fort Wayne sent Monk Meineke to Rochester on September 30, 1955 for Odie Spears. Basketball-Reference records the same swap on both team transaction pages and in the league-wide 1955-56 ledger. Meineke had spent his first three NBA seasons with Fort Wayne and had been the league's first Rookie of the Year in 1952-53. Spears was a veteran forward with seven prior BAA/NBA seasons and had just completed four straight years with Rochester. The deal therefore exchanged two established rotation players rather than prospects or rights.

sections.heading: Spears Helped a Finals Team for a Full Season
sections.body: Spears gave the Pistons one full, useful season. He appeared in all 72 regular-season games in 1955-56, averaging 19.1 minutes, 6.8 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists. Fort Wayne won the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals, so Spears' availability came during a contending season. His Pistons tenure ended the next fall, however. Basketball-Reference's 1956-57 transaction log shows St. Louis claiming him on waivers from Fort Wayne on November 15, 1956. The return was therefore meaningful but short.

sections.heading: Meineke Gave the Royals Franchise 136 Games
sections.body: Meineke appeared in 69 games for Rochester in 1955-56, averaging 18.1 minutes, 7.1 points, 4.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists. He did not play in 1956-57, then returned when the Royals franchise moved to Cincinnati and played 67 games in 1957-58. Across those two post-trade franchise seasons, he logged 136 games. The second stint was lighter at 11.8 minutes per game, but it still extended Rochester/Cincinnati's return beyond the single season Fort Wayne received from Spears.

sections.heading: The Extra Season Tilts the Deal to Rochester
sections.body: Both teams got legitimate rotation value, which makes the legacy lopsided grading too harsh. Spears contributed all season to a Finals team, while Meineke supplied a similar first-year workload and later returned for another 67 games with the same franchise lineage. That extra season gives Rochester the more durable realized return, but the difference is not large enough for a decisive grade gap. A narrow Royals advantage best matches the documented outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Fort Wayne B-, Rochester B. Fort Wayne traded Monk Meineke to the Rochester Royals for Odie Spears on September 30, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Rochester and league transaction logs agree on the straight player-for-player swap. Spears played all 72 games for the Pistons in 1955-56, averaging 19.1 minutes, 6.8 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists before Fort Wayne waived him the following November. Meineke played 69 games for Rochester at 18.1 minutes, 7.1 points and 4.6 rebounds, then returned to the same franchise after its move to Cincinnati for 67 more games in 1957-58.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Arnie Risen from Rochester
sections.body: Rochester sold Arnie Risen's player rights to Boston on October 26, 1955. Basketball-Reference records Boston acquiring Risen's rights and Rochester selling them on the same date, while the legacy Boston source preserves cash as the consideration. Risen was no ordinary late-career reserve at the time of the deal. He was a four-time All-Star with Rochester, had been a major part of the Royals' 1951 championship team and remained a productive veteran center. Boston was buying experience and interior depth just before the franchise's championship window opened.

sections.heading: Risen Became Three Years of Celtics Center Depth
sections.body: Risen contributed immediately. He played 68 games in 1955-56, averaging 8.1 points and 8.1 rebounds while logging 1,597 minutes. He returned for 43 games in 1956-57 and 63 in 1957-58, giving Boston 174 regular-season appearances across three seasons. His role became smaller as Bill Russell took over the center position, but Risen remained useful veteran depth and appeared in 10 playoff games during Boston's 1957 championship run. He added another 10 playoff appearances in 1958.

sections.heading: Rochester Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Rochester received cash, but the reviewed records do not preserve the amount. That consideration was real and may have reflected the Royals' decision to move on from a 31-year-old veteran after seven seasons with the franchise. The basketball opportunity cost, however, is visible. Risen still had three NBA seasons left, remained productive enough to play 174 Boston games and became part of a championship roster. The Royals did not receive a player, pick or identifiable downstream basketball asset in the documented exchange.

sections.heading: A Championship Contributor Makes Boston the Winner
sections.body: Boston received the stronger realized return. Risen was no longer at his Rochester peak, but three seasons of center depth, 174 regular-season games and a role on the 1957 championship team easily outweigh an undisclosed cash return in the measurable basketball record. The unknown payment keeps Rochester from receiving the lowest possible grade, and the trade should not be confused with Boston's later acquisition of Russell as the primary cause of the dynasty. Still, the Celtics clearly extracted substantial value from a player Rochester sold.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-, Rochester C. Rochester sold Arnie Risen's player rights to the Boston Celtics on October 26, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Rochester, Boston and league transaction logs agree on the transfer, while the legacy Boston intake identifies cash as the consideration. Risen then played three seasons for Boston, appearing in 174 regular-season games and 23 playoff games. He averaged 8.1 points and 8.1 rebounds in 68 games during 1955-56, then remained an important veteran center on Boston's first championship team in 1956-57.

sections.heading: St. Louis Bought Bob Schafer from Philadelphia
sections.body: Philadelphia sold Bob Schafer's player rights to St. Louis on December 3, 1955. Basketball-Reference lists the same sale on the Warriors, Hawks and league-wide 1955-56 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset labels the move as 1955 draft rights, but Schafer had already made his NBA debut and played 12 games for Philadelphia before the sale. He was therefore a current player whose rights were being transferred, not an unsigned draft-rights prospect. The canonical asset is corrected accordingly.

sections.heading: Schafer Supplied 42 Games and Playoff Depth
sections.body: Schafer became a regular reserve for the Hawks for the remainder of the season. He appeared in 42 games, totaling 496 minutes, 193 points, 58 rebounds and 44 assists. His per-game line of 11.8 minutes, 4.6 points, 1.4 rebounds and 1.0 assist was modest, but the Hawks also used him in four playoff games during a run that reached the Western Division Finals. The return ended after that season. Schafer later played 11 games for Syracuse in 1956-57, the final NBA appearances of his career.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Warriors received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs. Philadelphia had used Schafer sparingly for 12 games and then converted his remaining rights into consideration. The opportunity cost was 42 St. Louis regular-season games and a small playoff role, not a long-term starter or a player who later generated another major asset. That makes Philadelphia's side more defensible than the legacy F grade suggested.

sections.heading: A Short Useful Hawks Stint Creates a Narrow Edge
sections.body: St. Louis received more measurable basketball value because Schafer supplied 42 games and playoff depth, but the scale and duration were limited. Philadelphia received legitimate but undisclosed cash for a player it had barely used and who had only one additional NBA season after leaving the Hawks. The appropriate source-backed result is a narrow Hawks advantage, not a major long-term win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B-, Philadelphia C+. Philadelphia sold Bob Schafer's player rights to the St. Louis Hawks on December 3, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, St. Louis and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: Schafer had already played 12 NBA games for Philadelphia before the transaction. He then appeared in 42 regular-season games for St. Louis, averaging 11.8 minutes, 4.6 points, 1.4 rebounds and 1.0 assist, plus four playoff games. Schafer left the Hawks after the season and finished his NBA career with 11 Syracuse games in 1956-57. St.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Sold Rookie Johnny Horan to Minneapolis
sections.body: Fort Wayne sold Johnny Horan's player rights to Minneapolis on December 16, 1955. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Pistons, Lakers and league-wide 1955-56 transaction pages. Horan had been Fort Wayne's first-round pick in the 1955 NBA Draft and had already appeared in seven regular-season games for the Pistons, so the legacy draft-rights classification is no longer appropriate at the transaction date. This was a sale of an active rookie's player rights, not the transfer of an unsigned draft claim.

sections.heading: Horan Played Only 12 Lakers Games
sections.body: Horan's Lakers stint was brief. He appeared in 12 games after the sale, totaling 50 minutes, 12 points, six rebounds and one assist. His averages were 4.2 minutes and 1.0 point per game, and Basketball-Reference lists 1955-56 as his only NBA season. Minneapolis therefore received a player who could fill a small amount of reserve time but no multi-season contribution, no later trade asset and no durable rotation role. The acquisition was real, but the realized basketball value was limited.

sections.heading: The Pistons Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Pistons received cash. The public transaction pages do not preserve the amount, which prevents a precise financial comparison. Fort Wayne had already tested Horan in seven games and moved his rights before his rookie season ended. Because Horan played only 12 more NBA games after the sale, the Pistons did not surrender meaningful long-term production. Converting a marginal rookie role into cash was therefore a defensible outcome even without knowing the exact payment.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Escaped with the Better Return
sections.body: The source-backed result favors Fort Wayne modestly. Minneapolis obtained only 50 minutes of low-impact play before Horan's NBA career ended, while the Pistons at least received financial consideration. The unknown cash amount keeps the result from becoming a large grade gap, and Horan's 12 appearances mean the Lakers did receive something of value. Still, the legacy Lakers-win framing overstates what Minneapolis actually realized.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne B-, Minneapolis C-. Fort Wayne sold Johnny Horan's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers on December 16, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Minneapolis and league transaction logs all verify the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly treated Horan as an unresolved draft-rights asset, but he had already been Fort Wayne's first-round pick in the 1955 draft and had appeared in seven Pistons games before the transaction. After the sale, Horan played 12 games for Minneapolis, totaling 50 minutes, 12 points and six rebounds, and those were the final NBA games of his career.

sections.heading: St. Louis and Rochester Exchanged Four Players
sections.body: The legacy Atlanta record describes a January 8, 1956 trade in which St. Louis sent Dick Ricketts and Chris Harris to Rochester for Jack Coleman and Jack McMahon. RealGM's league transaction history supports the four-player structure but splits the postings: Harris is listed as acquired by Rochester on January 8, while Ricketts, Coleman and McMahon are listed on January 9. Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages omit the swap entirely, even though its season splits confirm that all four players changed clubs.

sections.heading: Coleman and McMahon Became Long-Term Hawks
sections.body: Coleman and McMahon became durable Hawks pieces. Coleman played 41 St. Louis games after the trade in 1955-56 and then 72 games in each of the next two seasons. Across his three Hawks seasons he appeared in 185 regular-season games and remained with the franchise through the 1958 championship. McMahon supplied even more longevity: 36 games after the trade, then 72 games in each of the next three seasons before a final 25-game St. Louis season in 1959-60.

sections.heading: Ricketts Still Gave the Royals Three Useful Seasons
sections.body: Ricketts was a meaningful return rather than a throw-in. The 1955 first overall pick played 39 Rochester games after the deal, then 72 in 1956-57 and another 72 after the franchise moved to Cincinnati in 1957-58. His Royals-family total reached 183 games, with 9.5 points and 6.2 rebounds per game across that run. Harris added 26 games in 1955-56 but did not play another NBA season. Rochester therefore received one legitimate multi-year frontcourt contributor plus a short-term reserve.

sections.heading: Two Durable Pieces Put St. Louis Ahead
sections.body: Both clubs extracted real value, which makes the old D+ treatment for Rochester too harsh. The difference is package depth and longevity. Ricketts gave the Royals three useful seasons, but St. Louis received two multi-year contributors whose combined Hawks tenure exceeded 450 regular-season games and included the franchise's 1958 championship season. Coleman remained a productive frontcourt piece, while McMahon became a long-term guard and playmaker. That cumulative return gives the Hawks the stronger outcome without turning the deal into a failure for Rochester.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis A, Rochester B. The St. Louis Hawks and Rochester Royals completed a four-player exchange in early January 1956, with St. Louis receiving Jack Coleman and Jack McMahon while Rochester received Dick Ricketts and Chris Harris. RealGM splits the transaction postings across January 8 and January 9, while the legacy Atlanta source record uses January 8; Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages omit the swap even though its season statistics confirm all four players changed teams. Coleman and McMahon became multi-year Hawks contributors and remained with the franchise through the 1958 championship season.
