sections.heading: Syracuse Bought Bob Harrison from St. Louis
sections.body: St. Louis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to Syracuse on December 2, 1956. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Hawks, Nationals and league-wide 1956-57 transaction pages. Harrison had been an established NBA guard for years and made the 1956 All-Star team with St. Louis, but his role collapsed early in 1956-57: he appeared in only 10 Hawks games and averaged 4.8 minutes before the sale. Syracuse was therefore buying a veteran whose current fit had deteriorated, while St. Louis chose cash rather than continuing to carry him.

sections.heading: Harrison Immediately Reclaimed a Major Role
sections.body: Harrison immediately recovered a substantial role. He appeared in 56 Syracuse games over the rest of 1956-57, averaging 31.5 minutes, 9.9 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.7 assists. The next season he played all 72 games for the Nationals, adding 25.0 minutes, 7.2 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.3 assists per game. Across those two Syracuse seasons he supplied 128 regular-season appearances and became a steady backcourt contributor on teams that reached the playoffs both years. That is far more than a short emergency stint.

sections.heading: The Hawks Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Hawks received cash, but the reviewed public transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That makes the financial return impossible to measure precisely. St. Louis did have a rational basketball reason to move Harrison because his role had nearly disappeared before the sale, and the Hawks were building around a different core. The later outcome shows that Harrison still had useful NBA basketball left, however, so the unknown cash has to be weighed against two full Syracuse seasons of proven production.

sections.heading: Two Strong Nationals Seasons Decide the Trade
sections.body: Syracuse received the stronger measurable return. Harrison gave the Nationals 128 games over two seasons and immediately regained starter-level minutes after barely playing in St. Louis. The Hawks' cash return should not be treated as zero, and the undisclosed amount prevents an extreme grade gap. Still, the realized basketball value is clear enough to move this well beyond the legacy even-trade framing. Syracuse bought a veteran at a moment when his prior team had little use for him and extracted two productive seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — St. Louis C, Syracuse B+. St. Louis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to the Syracuse Nationals on December 2, 1956. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Syracuse and league transaction logs all verify the sale. Harrison had appeared in only 10 Hawks games that season before the move, but he immediately became a major Syracuse guard, playing 56 games at 31.5 minutes and 9.9 points per game in 1956-57. He then played all 72 games for the Nationals in 1957-58, averaging 25.0 minutes and 7.2 points. The undisclosed cash return gives St.

sections.heading: The December 10 Martin-Naulls Record Is Misdated
sections.body: The surviving St. Louis, New York and league transaction records do not support a separate Slater Martin-for-Willie Naulls trade on December 10, 1956. The same player package is documented on December 12, so this earlier legacy row cannot stand as an independent transaction.

sections.heading: The Verified Trade Happened on December 12
sections.body: TradeVerdicts already stores the verified December 12 exchange as the canonical Martin-Naulls trade. That record matches the team transaction pages and executive ledger, while the December 10 date survives only through the older source lineage.

sections.heading: Both Players Belong to the Canonical December 12 Deal
sections.body: Martin became an immediate St. Louis All-Star and helped the Hawks reach the NBA Finals, while Naulls developed into a four-time All-Star in New York. Those outcomes belong to the verified December 12 transaction and should not be counted twice.

sections.heading: Keep the Legacy Route but Supersede the Duplicate
sections.body: The route stays in the private archive for provenance, but it is excluded from public/indexable treatment and hindsight grading. No winner or team grades are assigned because the duplicate date itself is not a completed trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. This December 10, 1956 Slater Martin-for-Willie Naulls listing is retained only as legacy source provenance. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis Hawks and New York Knicks transaction logs both place the exchange on December 12, 1956, as does the franchise executive record. TradeVerdicts already contains that verified December 12 transaction as a separate canonical record. The two rows describe the same players moving between the same teams, so keeping both would double-count one NBA trade. The December 10 record is therefore superseded, while the December 12 record remains the canonical transaction for full source-backed analysis. No team grade is assigned because this route is retained only as legacy provenance.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Togo Palazzi to Syracuse
sections.body: Boston sold Togo Palazzi's player rights to Syracuse on December 29, 1956. Basketball-Reference lists that date on the Celtics, Nationals and league-wide 1956-57 transaction pages. The legacy Boston source record had carried November 29, and that stale date survived in the stored date reference even after the canonical tradeDate was corrected to December 29. This pass aligns the route metadata with the verified transaction date while preserving the original source provenance. Boston was converting a reserve forward into cash; Syracuse was buying a 24-year-old who had already shown he could score in limited minutes.

sections.heading: Palazzi Became a Three-Year Nationals Rotation Piece
sections.body: Palazzi's role grew immediately after the sale. He played 42 Syracuse games in 1956-57, averaging 18.6 minutes, 10.7 points and 4.5 rebounds. He then appeared in 67 games in 1957-58 and 71 in 1958-59, remaining a regular part of the Nationals' rotation. Across those first three Syracuse seasons he gave the club 180 regular-season appearances. His scoring settled into the eight-to-nine-point range after the initial burst, but the durability and repeated rotation use make the acquisition much more valuable than a short-term roster patch.

sections.heading: Boston Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Celtics received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public ledgers. That consideration has real value and should not be treated as zero. Boston also had a crowded roster and was in the opening year of its championship dynasty, so moving a reserve whose role had shrunk was understandable. Palazzi had played 21 Boston games that season before the sale and averaged only 11.1 minutes. The transaction did not derail Boston's title path, but hindsight still shows that the player rights carried several seasons of useful NBA production.

sections.heading: One Hundred Eighty Syracuse Games Decide the Deal
sections.body: Syracuse received the stronger measurable basketball return. Palazzi supplied 180 games over three seasons after the transaction and remained a regular contributor, while Boston's cash return cannot be quantified. The gap is meaningful but not franchise-changing because Palazzi was a rotation forward rather than a star and Boston was already positioned to contend without him. A clear Nationals edge with a solid but not extreme grade best matches the documented outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Boston C, Syracuse B+. Boston sold Togo Palazzi's player rights to the Syracuse Nationals for cash on December 29, 1956. Basketball-Reference's Boston, Syracuse and league transaction logs agree on the date, correcting the stale November 29 date inherited from the original source record. Palazzi immediately became a useful Syracuse rotation forward, playing 42 games at 18.6 minutes and 10.7 points per game in 1956-57. He then remained with the Nationals for 67 games in 1957-58 and 71 in 1958-59.

sections.heading: Rochester Sold Lew Hitch to Philadelphia
sections.body: Rochester sold Lew Hitch's player rights to Philadelphia on January 4, 1957. Basketball-Reference lists the same date on the Royals, Warriors and league-wide transaction pages, and the Les Harrison executive ledger independently records the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts route was dated January 5, so this pass corrects the date and route metadata while preserving the original source lineage. Hitch had joined Rochester as a free agent in July 1956 and played 30 games before the move. Philadelphia was purchasing an experienced reserve big man for the second half of the season.

sections.heading: Hitch Gave the Warriors 38 Reserve Games
sections.body: Hitch played 38 games for the Warriors after the sale, averaging 15.2 minutes, 3.7 points and 3.5 rebounds. He was not a high-impact acquisition, but Philadelphia received regular reserve minutes through the rest of a 37-win season and playoff appearance. Those 38 games were the final appearances of Hitch's NBA career, so there was no downstream multi-year value. The return was nevertheless tangible and considerably more useful than a dormant player right.

sections.heading: The Royals Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Royals received cash, but the public ledgers do not preserve the amount. Rochester had already gotten 30 games from Hitch that season and was able to monetize his remaining rights before his career ended. That makes the sale defensible and prevents a low grade. At the same time, because the cash amount is unknown, there is no basis for claiming that it clearly exceeded the value of the 38 reserve games Philadelphia received.

sections.heading: A Modest Basketball Return Gives Philadelphia the Edge
sections.body: The deal is close, with a modest Philadelphia edge. The Warriors received half a season of useful depth, while Rochester received real but unquantified financial consideration. Hitch's short remaining career limits the upside on Philadelphia's side, and the Royals did not give away a future starter or long-term asset. The old C-/F split substantially overstated the gap. A mild Warriors advantage better matches the documented outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge — Philadelphia B-, Rochester C+. Rochester sold Lew Hitch's player rights to the Philadelphia Warriors on January 4, 1957, not January 5 as the legacy route recorded. Basketball-Reference's Rochester, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all agree on the January 4 date. Hitch had played 30 Royals games that season at 18.5 minutes, 4.8 points and 4.0 rebounds per game before the sale, then appeared in 38 games for Philadelphia at 15.2 minutes, 3.7 points and 3.5 rebounds. Those were the final 38 games of his NBA career.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne and New York Made a Five-Asset Swap
sections.body: Fort Wayne sent Mel Hutchins and its 1957 first-round pick to New York on April 3, 1957 for Harry Gallatin, Nat Clifton and Dick Atha. Basketball-Reference records the same five-asset exchange on the Pistons, Knicks and league-wide transaction pages. The draft pick later became Charlie Tyra at No. 2 overall. One structural problem in the legacy record is clear: Atha was not a draft-rights asset. He had already appeared in 25 games for New York in 1955-56, so the transaction moved his player rights as an established NBA player.

sections.heading: Gallatin and Clifton Delivered Immediate Detroit Production
sections.body: Gallatin gave the Pistons the strongest immediate return. In 1957-58, the franchise's first season in Detroit, he played all 72 games and averaged 27.6 minutes, 14.9 points and 10.4 rebounds. Clifton added 68 games, 1,435 minutes, 525 points and 403 rebounds in his final NBA season. Atha returned from his lost 1956-57 season to appear in 18 Detroit games. The group was old, but it supplied 158 regular-season appearances in 1957-58 and gave the newly relocated club substantial veteran frontcourt production.

sections.heading: Tyra Became the Knicks’ Long-Term Asset
sections.body: Hutchins had been a four-time All-Star with the Pistons, but his Knicks stint was short. He appeared in only 18 games in 1957-58 before his NBA career ended. Tyra became the enduring asset. He played 270 regular-season games for New York across four seasons, including 68 games as a rookie while averaging 17.4 minutes, 7.4 points and 7.1 rebounds. He never became an All-Star, but his multi-year rotation value gave the Knicks a younger and longer-lived return than the veteran package sent to Detroit.

sections.heading: New York’s Longevity Creates a Slight Edge
sections.body: Both teams received useful value. Detroit got the stronger single-season veteran impact, led by Gallatin's double-double production and Clifton's regular minutes. New York received much less from Hutchins than his reputation suggested, but Tyra supplied four seasons and 270 games. The longevity advantage is enough to nudge the deal toward the Knicks, though the gap is small because Detroit's 1957-58 return was meaningful and immediate. The source-backed result should therefore be a modest New York edge rather than the extreme grades carried by the legacy perspectives.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — Detroit B, New York B+. Fort Wayne traded Mel Hutchins and its 1957 first-round pick, which New York used at No. 2 on Charlie Tyra, to the Knicks on April 3, 1957 for Harry Gallatin, Nat Clifton and Dick Atha. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, New York and league transaction logs agree on the package. The legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly classified Atha as draft rights even though he had already played 25 NBA games for New York in 1955-56. Gallatin and Clifton gave the Pistons strong veteran production in 1957-58, while Atha added 18 games.

sections.heading: Rochester and Minneapolis Swapped Major Packages
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Rochester and Minneapolis transaction logs agree on the full April 17, 1957 package. The Royals sent Bob Burrow, Ed Fleming, Hot Rod Hundley, Monk Meineke and Art Spoelstra to the Lakers for Clyde Lovellette and Jim Paxson. Hundley had just been selected No. 1 overall by Rochester, so the asset was not a vague future right: it was the rights to the top pick in the same day's draft. The historical team names matter here. Rochester moved to Cincinnati for the 1957-58 season, while the Lakers were still in Minneapolis.

sections.heading: Lovellette Gave Rochester the Best Immediate Season
sections.body: Lovellette immediately delivered star production. In 1957-58 he played 71 games for Cincinnati and averaged 23.4 points and 12.1 rebounds, finishing 12th in MVP voting. Paxson also gave the Royals 67 games at 9.8 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The direct return therefore included an elite center season plus a full year of rotation wing play. The Lovellette asset also retained major transaction value. In September 1958 Cincinnati traded him to St. Louis for Gerry Calvert, Wayne Embry, Darrell Floyd, Jim Palmer and Ken Sidle.

sections.heading: Hundley Became the Lakers’ Longest-Lived Return
sections.body: Hundley became the durable centerpiece of the Lakers package. He played all six seasons of his NBA career for the franchise, 431 regular-season games in total, and made the All-Star team in 1960 and 1961. His best season was 1959-60, when he averaged 12.8 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.6 assists. He remained a rotation guard after the franchise moved to Los Angeles and participated in multiple deep playoff runs. Fleming also supplied real value: 170 Minneapolis games over three seasons, including 72 games at 8.8 points and 6.8 rebounds in 1957-58.

sections.heading: Both Franchises Extracted A-Level Value
sections.body: The legacy slight Rochester edge underweights Hundley and Fleming, while a Lakers win would underweight how strong Lovellette was immediately and how much transaction value he retained. Rochester received the best single season in the deal and then turned that star into a package that included Embry. Minneapolis received the longest direct player value through Hundley's six seasons and two All-Star selections, plus meaningful Fleming and Spoelstra contributions. Both sides extracted high-level value from different time horizons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Rochester A, Minneapolis A. On April 17, 1957, Rochester sent Bob Burrow, Ed Fleming, Monk Meineke, Art Spoelstra and the draft rights to No. 1 pick Hot Rod Hundley to Minneapolis for Clyde Lovellette and Jim Paxson Sr. Rochester got one elite Lovellette season at 23.4 points and 12.1 rebounds plus a useful Paxson year, then converted Lovellette into a package led by future five-time All-Star Wayne Embry. Minneapolis received six full Hundley seasons, including two All-Star selections, plus three useful Fleming seasons and other depth. Both franchises created substantial value, making an even result more defensible than the legacy slight Rochester edge.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Dick McGuire for a First-Round Pick
sections.body: Detroit acquired Dick McGuire from New York for a 1958 first-round pick that became Mike Farmer. The package itself is well established, but the exact date is not. Basketball-Reference and RealGM place the trade on April 3, 1957, alongside the separate Hutchins/Tyra-for-Gallatin/Clifton/Atha transaction. Later Pistons media guides also use April 3. By contrast, a September 24, 1957 Associated Press report says Detroit had just obtained McGuire, and Pistons guides published closer to the period describe the acquisition as a September 1957 move. Pro Sports Transactions lists September 23.

sections.heading: McGuire Gave Detroit Three Productive Seasons
sections.body: McGuire gave Detroit three productive final NBA seasons. He appeared in 69 games in 1957-58, 71 in 1958-59 and 68 in 1959-60, totaling 208 regular-season games and 5,840 minutes. He averaged 6.6 assists in his first Detroit season and 6.2 in the next, made the Western Conference All-Star team in both 1958 and 1959, and finished eleventh in MVP voting in 1958-59. He later became the Pistons' player-coach, so the acquisition also carried organizational value beyond the box score, although the trade grade here is based primarily on realized playing contribution.

sections.heading: New York Turned the Pick into Mike Farmer
sections.body: The Knicks used the acquired first-round pick on Mike Farmer. Farmer played all 72 games as a rookie in 1958-59 and 67 more in 1959-60, then appeared in two New York games in 1960-61 before moving to Cincinnati. Across his first two Knicks seasons he logged 3,081 minutes, but his advanced production was modest: Basketball-Reference credits 0.1 win shares in 1958-59 and minus-0.1 in 1959-60. Farmer later remained an NBA player for several more seasons, but most of that later value came with Cincinnati and St. Louis rather than New York.

sections.heading: Two All-Star Seasons Give Detroit the Win
sections.body: Detroit received the stronger realized return. McGuire provided 208 games, two All-Star selections and high-level playmaking over three seasons, while Farmer gave New York two full seasons of rotation minutes without approaching McGuire's impact. The Knicks did receive a young first-round player who stayed in the league, so this is not a failed asset conversion. The date conflict lowers confidence in the transaction chronology, not in the asset package or player outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A-, New York B-. Detroit acquired Dick McGuire from the New York Knicks for its 1958 first-round pick, later used at No. 3 on Mike Farmer. The transaction date is unusually conflicted across historical sources: contemporary September 24, 1957 reporting says Detroit had just obtained McGuire, early Pistons media guides place the move in September, while Basketball-Reference, RealGM and later Pistons guides index it to April 3. TradeVerdicts preserves the September 23 route date but flags the discrepancy rather than pretending the archive is unanimous. McGuire then played 208 games over three Detroit seasons and made the 1958 and 1959 All-Star teams.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Larry Costello to Syracuse
sections.body: Philadelphia sold Larry Costello's player rights to Syracuse on October 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse transaction page, the league-wide 1957-58 ledger and Warriors executive Eddie Gottlieb's transaction record all preserve the move. The Warriors received cash. A later biographical account places the price at $5,000, but the primary transaction ledgers reviewed here do not preserve the amount, so TradeVerdicts treats the financial return as real but unquantified. Costello was 26 and had just returned from military service for a full Warriors season, making this a sale of an established NBA guard rather than a speculative right.

sections.heading: Costello Became a Long-Term Nationals All-Star
sections.body: Costello became one of the Nationals' defining guards almost immediately. He played all 72 games in 1957-58, logged 2,746 minutes and averaged 14.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.4 assists while making the All-Star team. In 1958-59 he raised his scoring to a career-high 15.8 points per game, averaged 5.4 assists and finished seventh in MVP voting. Costello made five consecutive All-Star teams with Syracuse from 1958 through 1962, earned All-NBA recognition in 1960-61, and remained with the franchise after its move to Philadelphia.

sections.heading: The Warriors Received Only Cash
sections.body: The Warriors received cash and no player or draft asset. The exact amount is not preserved in the Basketball-Reference transaction logs, which limits the precision of the financial comparison. What can be measured is the opportunity cost. Costello had already shown he could handle a full NBA role, and Syracuse received years of starting-caliber point-guard play, repeated All-Star production and eventual championship-era continuity from the purchase. Even a meaningful cash payment would have needed extraordinary non-roster value to match what the Nationals and later 76ers received on the court.

sections.heading: The Gap in Basketball Value Is Massive
sections.body: This is one of the clearest early-NBA cash-sale outcomes in the archive. Syracuse acquired a six-time All-Star who became a long-term franchise floor general, while Philadelphia received only financial consideration. The Warriors did not surrender an unknown prospect; Costello had already returned from military service and played a full season in Philadelphia. The gap in realized basketball value is therefore large even without assigning a precise dollar value to the cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia D, Syracuse A+. Philadelphia sold Larry Costello's player rights to the Syracuse Nationals on October 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, league and Eddie Gottlieb executive transaction ledgers agree on the sale. Costello immediately became an All-Star point guard for Syracuse, playing all 72 games in 1957-58 and averaging 14.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.4 assists. He then made five consecutive All-Star teams with Syracuse from 1958 through 1962, later earned another All-Star selection after the franchise became the Philadelphia 76ers, and finished his playing career on the 1967 championship team. The Warriors received cash, but the long-term basketball value overwhelmingly favored Syracuse.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Veteran Tom Marshall from Cincinnati
sections.body: Detroit acquired Tom Marshall's player rights from Cincinnati on December 10, 1957 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Pistons transaction page records Detroit acquiring Marshall's rights, and Pro Sports Transactions preserves the cash going to the Royals. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset was labeled draft rights, but Marshall had already played three NBA seasons for Rochester/Cincinnati and was 27 years old. The canonical asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player transaction rather than a draft-rights move.

sections.heading: Marshall Lasted Only Nine Pistons Games
sections.body: Marshall's Detroit stint was extremely short. Basketball-Reference credits him with nine Pistons games, 66 total minutes, 21 points and eight rebounds. He averaged 7.3 minutes and 2.3 points per game. Detroit waived him on February 18, 1958, only a little more than two months after acquiring his rights. That makes the purchase a low-impact roster trial rather than a transaction that created durable rotation value.

sections.heading: The Royals Took Cash and Reclaimed Marshall
sections.body: The Royals received cash, although the amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction sources. More importantly in hindsight, Cincinnati reclaimed Marshall on waivers on February 20, two days after Detroit let him go. Marshall then played 29 additional Cincinnati games in 1957-58. The cash return is therefore paired with the practical fact that the Royals regained the same veteran after Detroit received only nine games from him.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Won the Asset Cycle
sections.body: Cincinnati realized the stronger outcome. Detroit paid cash for a player who lasted nine games, while the Royals received financial consideration and then recovered Marshall during the same season. The exact cash amount is unknown, so the grade should not imply a large financial windfall, but the asset path is unusually unfavorable to Detroit. The source-backed record also makes clear that this was a veteran-rights purchase rather than the draft-rights transaction carried by the legacy shell.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Detroit C-, Rochester B+. Detroit acquired Tom Marshall's player rights from the Cincinnati Royals for cash on December 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction log and Pro Sports Transactions agree on the move, while Marshall's career record shows the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: he was a veteran in his fourth NBA season. Marshall played only nine games for Detroit, averaging 7.3 minutes and 2.3 points, before the Pistons waived him on February 18, 1958. Two days later Cincinnati claimed him back, and he finished the season with 29 additional Royals games.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Joe Holup from Syracuse
sections.body: Syracuse sold Joe Holup's player rights to Detroit on December 28, 1957 for cash. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Nationals, Pistons and league-wide 1957-58 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Holup as draft rights, but that does not fit the chronology. Syracuse had selected him fifth overall in the 1956 draft, and he had already completed a 71-game rookie season plus 16 games in 1957-58 before the sale. The canonical asset is therefore repaired to a veteran direct-player rights transaction.

sections.heading: Holup Supplied 105 Pistons Games
sections.body: Holup became a useful rotation forward after arriving. He played 37 Detroit games over the remainder of 1957-58, logging 607 minutes, then appeared in all 68 games in 1958-59 and logged 1,502 minutes. Across the two Pistons seasons he supplied 105 regular-season appearances. His scoring was modest and his efficiency was limited, but Detroit received dependable availability and more than two thousand minutes from a player purchased in-season. Basketball-Reference also credits him with playoff appearances for Detroit in both seasons.

sections.heading: The Nationals Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Nationals received cash, but the reviewed transaction ledgers do not preserve the amount. Syracuse had already received a full rookie season and the first 16 games of Holup's second year before selling his rights, so the move was not a giveaway of an unknown prospect. Still, the player remained in the NBA for the rest of 1957-58 and all of 1958-59, which means the Nationals surrendered more than a fringe right with no future use.

sections.heading: Two Useful Seasons Give Detroit the Edge
sections.body: Detroit received the stronger measurable basketball return. Holup was not an All-Star or a high-impact starter, but 105 regular-season games and more than two thousand minutes across two seasons represent meaningful rotation value. Syracuse's financial return was legitimate but unquantified. That combination supports a moderate Pistons advantage rather than the legacy near-even treatment or an exaggerated high grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B, Syracuse C. Detroit acquired Joe Holup's player rights from the Syracuse Nationals for cash on December 28, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Syracuse and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: Holup was a second-year NBA forward who had already played 87 regular-season games for Syracuse. After the sale, he played 37 games for Detroit to finish 1957-58 and all 68 games in 1958-59, giving the Pistons 105 regular-season appearances across two seasons. Syracuse received cash, but the amount is undisclosed.

sections.heading: St. Louis Swapped Dave Plunkett for Walt Davis
sections.body: St. Louis sent Dave Plunkett to Philadelphia on January 19, 1958 for Walt Davis. Basketball-Reference records the same exchange on the Hawks, Warriors and league-wide transaction pages, and both franchise executive ledgers preserve it as well. The old Atlanta-source record used 'Buddy Davis,' but Basketball-Reference identifies Buddy as a nickname for Walter Francis Davis. That alias has already been merged into the canonical Walt Davis player shell, and this pass aligns the trade asset itself with that verified identity.

sections.heading: Davis Contributed During a Championship Season
sections.body: Davis gave the Hawks useful depth immediately. He played 26 regular-season games after the trade, totaling 287 minutes, 127 points and 86 rebounds. That works out to 11.0 minutes, 4.9 points and 3.3 rebounds per game. More importantly, he remained on the roster for the postseason and appeared in nine playoff games while St. Louis won the 1958 NBA championship. His playoff role was small, but the Hawks received a real rotation piece during the most successful season in franchise history.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received No Post-Trade NBA Games from Plunkett
sections.body: Plunkett had been St. Louis' sixth-round pick in the 1956 draft and had already made his NBA debut before the exchange. Basketball-Reference lists his career length as one rookie season and does not show a 1957-58 Philadelphia line or any later NBA season. The Warriors therefore acquired player rights that produced no documented post-trade NBA contribution. That makes this materially different from a low-minute swap where both teams at least received some floor time.

sections.heading: The Only Realized Value Went to the Hawks
sections.body: St. Louis received the only realized post-trade NBA value and did so during a championship run. Davis was not a major part of the Hawks' core, so the deal should not be inflated into a franchise-changing transaction. Still, 26 regular-season games plus nine playoff appearances are clearly preferable to an incoming player who never appeared for Philadelphia. The source-backed evidence supports a solid Hawks win rather than the legacy even-trade framing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B+, Philadelphia D+. St. Louis traded Dave Plunkett to the Philadelphia Warriors for Walt Davis on January 19, 1958. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all verify the exchange. The legacy TradeVerdicts record called the incoming Hawk 'Buddy Davis'; Basketball-Reference identifies Buddy as the nickname of Walter Francis 'Walt' Davis, so the canonical asset is normalized to Walt Davis. Davis appeared in 26 regular-season games for St. Louis after the trade and nine playoff games during the Hawks' 1958 championship run. Plunkett's Basketball-Reference career ends before a Philadelphia season appears, leaving St. Louis with the only documented post-trade NBA value.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Swapped Art Spoelstra for Bo Erias and Cash
sections.body: Minneapolis sent Art Spoelstra to New York on February 5, 1958 for Bo Erias and cash. Basketball-Reference records the same package on both team transaction pages, in the league-wide ledger and in the executive transaction records for John Kundla and Fred Podesta. Spoelstra was a fourth-year NBA center who had played 50 games for the Lakers that season before the deal. Erias had not yet appeared in an NBA game, so Minneapolis was exchanging a known reserve for an untested 25-year-old forward plus financial consideration.

sections.heading: Erias Immediately Became the Larger Rotation Piece
sections.body: Erias debuted for the Lakers on February 9 and immediately became a real rotation piece. He appeared in 18 games over the rest of 1957-58, totaling 401 minutes, 148 points, 83 rebounds and 26 assists. His averages of 22.3 minutes, 8.2 points and 4.6 rebounds were all meaningful for a late-season acquisition. Erias did not play another NBA season, so the return was short-lived, but Minneapolis still received the better individual post-trade production and cash on top of it.

sections.heading: New York Got 17 Games from Spoelstra
sections.body: Spoelstra played 17 games for the Knicks, averaging 12.2 minutes, 3.9 points, 3.0 rebounds and 0.4 assists. Basketball-Reference lists those 17 New York games as the final NBA appearances of his four-year career. He therefore gave the Knicks some frontcourt depth, but his role was smaller than Erias' role in Minneapolis and there was no later season or downstream trade value to extend the return.

sections.heading: The Better Short-Term Return Went to Minneapolis
sections.body: Both players gave their new teams only the remainder of the 1957-58 season, which keeps this from becoming a major hindsight judgment. The difference is that Erias played more minutes, scored more, rebounded more and came with cash. Spoelstra's New York stint was shorter and represented the end of his NBA career. The source-backed evidence therefore reverses the legacy slight-Knicks framing and supports a clear but modest Lakers advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B, New York C. Minneapolis traded Art Spoelstra to the New York Knicks for Bo Erias and cash on February 5, 1958. Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, New York and league transaction logs all verify the package. Erias made his NBA debut four days later and played 18 games for the Lakers, averaging 22.3 minutes, 8.2 points, 4.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists. Spoelstra appeared in 17 games for New York at 12.2 minutes, 3.9 points and 3.0 rebounds per game, and those were the final NBA games of his career. With the better on-court return plus cash, Minneapolis received the stronger realized value.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Acquired Frank Selvy for Two Player Rights
sections.body: Minneapolis acquired Frank Selvy from St. Louis on February 16, 1958 for the rights to Dick Boushka and Terry Rand. The transaction is unusually important to describe with source discipline. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis and league logs, John Kundla's executive ledger, Ben Kerner's executive ledger and the Lakers' own all-time transaction history all describe a trade. Pro Sports Transactions instead labels Selvy's movement a loan for the remainder of 1957-58. A later legacy Hawks record also places Selvy back under St. Louis control before a reported October 1958 move to New York.

sections.heading: Selvy Delivered Real Late-Season Minutes
sections.body: Whatever the rights mechanism, Selvy unquestionably played for the Lakers after February 16. Basketball-Reference credits him with 12 Minneapolis games in 1957-58, totaling 231 minutes, 76 points, 35 rebounds and 19 assists. He averaged 19.3 minutes and 6.3 points in that stint after playing only 7.5 minutes per game in 26 St. Louis appearances earlier in the season. Minneapolis therefore received real late-season rotation value from a player who had barely been used by the eventual champion Hawks.

sections.heading: St. Louis Received Rights That Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: Boushka and Rand were legitimate Lakers draft-rights assets, not fabricated names. Minneapolis had selected Boushka in the third round of the 1955 draft and Rand in the second round of the 1956 draft. Neither player, however, produced an NBA appearance after the rights transfer. Basketball-Reference identifies Boushka as an Olympic gold medalist and later AAU player without an NBA game, while Rand also chose the industrial/AAU route and never appeared in the league. St. Louis therefore received two recognizable prospects but no realized NBA minutes from either right.

sections.heading: The Uncertain Rights Mechanism Still Favors the Lakers
sections.body: The immediate basketball outcome favors Minneapolis because Selvy supplied 12 games and more than 200 minutes while the two rights sent to St. Louis produced no NBA appearances. The uncertain loan-versus-trade mechanics keep the conclusion from being overstated: if Selvy's rights reverted to the Hawks after the season, St. Louis retained future contractual value that a simple permanent-trade label would miss. That uncertainty affects the size of the advantage, not the documented 1957-58 production gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B, St. Louis D+. On February 16, 1958, Minneapolis acquired Frank Selvy from St. Louis for the rights to Dick Boushka and Terry Rand. Basketball-Reference, the Lakers' official transaction history and both franchise executive ledgers describe an outright trade, while Pro Sports Transactions preserves the older wording that Selvy was loaned to Minneapolis for the rest of 1957-58. That distinction is noted rather than forced: Selvy played 12 Lakers games after the move, totaling 231 minutes and 76 points, while neither Boushka nor Rand ever appeared in an NBA game. The immediate realized value therefore favors Minneapolis, even with uncertainty about whether Selvy's rights reverted to St.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sent Five Rights for Clyde Lovellette
sections.body: St. Louis agreed on August 5, 1958 to send the rights to Wayne Embry, Jim Palmer, Darrell Floyd, Ken Sidle and Gerry Calvert to Cincinnati for Clyde Lovellette. Basketball-Reference's league transaction page and Ben Kerner executive ledger use the August 5 date, while the St. Louis and Cincinnati team transaction pages record September 16, the date Lovellette was formally delivered as the player to be named later.

sections.heading: Lovellette Gave the Hawks Four High-End Seasons
sections.body: Lovellette immediately became a major frontcourt scorer for the Hawks. He played 70 games in 1958-59, 68 in 1959-60, 67 in 1960-61 and 40 in 1961-62. Across four St. Louis seasons he appeared in 245 games, averaged 19.3 points and 9.6 rebounds, made the All-Star team in 1960 and 1961, and received MVP votes in 1960-61. He also remained a substantial playoff contributor during a period when St. Louis returned to the NBA Finals in 1960 and 1961. For a contender built around Bob Pettit, acquiring an established All-NBA-level center produced immediate win-now value.

sections.heading: Wayne Embry Became Cincinnati’s Long-Term Centerpiece
sections.body: The Royals received the longer-lived package. Embry became their starting center almost immediately and stayed for eight seasons, playing 603 regular-season games from 1958-59 through 1965-66. He made five straight All-Star teams from 1961 through 1965 and became one of the franchise's foundational frontcourt players. Palmer also supplied 87 Cincinnati games across two seasons, including 67 games as a rookie at 10.3 points and 7.0 rebounds per game.

sections.heading: Both Sides Won but the Royals Got More Longevity
sections.body: Both clubs realized substantial value, which makes this one of the stronger two-sided trades in the early archive. St. Louis received the better immediate player and four seasons of high-end production during a championship-contending window. Cincinnati received far more longevity through Embry, plus useful early production from Palmer. Lovellette's peak Hawks impact keeps the difference narrow, but Embry's eight-year tenure and five All-Star selections give the Royals the slightly stronger total return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Edge — St. Louis A-, Cincinnati A. St. Louis traded the draft rights to Wayne Embry, Jim Palmer, Darrell Floyd, Ken Sidle and Gerry Calvert to the Cincinnati Royals on August 5, 1958 for Clyde Lovellette, who was delivered as the player to be named later in September. Basketball-Reference's league and Ben Kerner executive ledgers place the agreement on August 5, while the St. Louis and Cincinnati team pages record the completed Lovellette transfer on September 16. Lovellette gave the Hawks four strong seasons, 245 games and two All-Star selections.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sent Frank Selvy to New York for a Second-Rounder
sections.body: St. Louis traded Frank Selvy to New York on October 22, 1958 for a 1959 second-round draft choice. The Knicks' historical media guide explicitly records Selvy arriving from St. Louis for that pick on October 22, and Pro Sports Transactions plus RealGM independently preserve the same move. Basketball-Reference's 1958-59 team and league transaction pages do not list it, so the transaction is kept with a source-gap note rather than pretending every archive agrees. The pick was subsequently used by St. Louis at No. 14 overall on Alan Seiden.

sections.heading: Selvy Became a Full-Season Knicks Rotation Guard
sections.body: Selvy immediately became a useful rotation guard for the Knicks. He appeared in 68 games during 1958-59, averaging 21.3 minutes, 9.8 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting .385 from the field. New York went 40-32 and reached the Eastern Division playoffs, so the acquired player contributed meaningful regular-season offense to a winning team. Selvy did not become a long-term Knick; he was waived in October 1959 and later resumed his career elsewhere. Even so, one full productive season is substantial realized value for a second-round pick.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Alan Seiden and Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: The Hawks used the acquired 1959 second-round pick on Alan Seiden at No. 14 overall. Seiden was a decorated St. John's guard and a consensus All-American, but Basketball-Reference does not record an NBA regular-season career for him. That means the draft asset generated no measurable NBA production for St. Louis. The selection itself was legitimate value at the time, but hindsight has to distinguish draft pedigree from realized professional return.

sections.heading: New York Realized the Clear Advantage
sections.body: New York received the clear realized advantage. Selvy supplied 68 games and almost 10 points per game in the season immediately after the trade, while the pick St. Louis received became a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The archival omission on Basketball-Reference lowers confidence in the transaction mechanics slightly, but the Knicks media guide and independent transaction databases align on the date and consideration. The result therefore supports a decisive Knicks edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — St. Louis D, New York B+. St. Louis traded Frank Selvy to the New York Knicks on October 22, 1958 for a 1959 second-round draft pick that became Alan Seiden at No. 14 overall. The transaction is preserved in the Knicks' historical media guide, Pro Sports Transactions and RealGM's Selvy timeline even though Basketball-Reference's 1958-59 team and league transaction pages omit it. Selvy then played 68 games for New York in 1958-59, averaging 21.3 minutes and 9.8 points per game. St. Louis used the acquired pick on Seiden, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career for him. The verified realized value therefore favors New York.

sections.heading: St. Louis Swapped Park and Stephens for Si Green
sections.body: St. Louis sent Med Park and Jack Stephens to Cincinnati for Si Green in January 1959. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Royals, league and executive transaction ledgers all place the deal on January 14 and list only those three players. RealGM uses January 10, which explains the legacy TradeVerdicts date, but the stronger four-ledger agreement supports moving the canonical date to January 14 while retaining the disagreement in audit metadata. The source-backed review also removes an unsupported cash asset and corrects the legacy 'Ned Park' spelling to Med Park, whose full name was Medford R. Park.

sections.heading: Green Gave the Hawks 186 Games
sections.body: Green gave the Hawks the larger body of post-trade value. He played 26 St. Louis games to finish 1958-59, then 70 in 1959-60, 76 in 1960-61 and 14 more in 1961-62 before being traded to Chicago. Across those segments he appeared in 186 regular-season games for St. Louis and developed from a reserve into a substantial backcourt contributor. His 1960-61 season was the strongest full Hawks year of the run: 25.9 minutes, 9.2 points, 5.0 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game.

sections.heading: Park Was Productive for Cincinnati
sections.body: Park was a useful return rather than a throw-in. He played 33 Cincinnati games after the trade in 1958-59, averaging 27.2 minutes, 9.7 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.4 assists, then appeared in 74 games in 1959-60 at 25.0 minutes, 8.7 points, 4.1 rebounds and 2.9 assists. That produced 107 Royals games over two seasons. Stephens, however, did not add any post-trade NBA value. Basketball-Reference lists his entire NBA career as the 72 games he played for St. Louis in 1955-56, so Cincinnati's realized package is essentially Park's two seasons.

sections.heading: The Extra Longevity Tilts It to St. Louis
sections.body: Both teams received useful NBA production, but St. Louis got more longevity and a player who remained relevant to later roster construction. Green supplied 186 Hawks games over parts of four seasons, compared with Park's 107 Cincinnati games over two seasons and no post-trade NBA appearances from Stephens. Cincinnati's return was respectable enough to avoid a wide grade gap, especially because Park immediately handled substantial minutes. The verified outcome supports a moderate Hawks edge rather than the legacy Royals-favored verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Edge — St. Louis B+, Cincinnati B-. St. Louis traded Med Park and Jack Stephens to the Cincinnati Royals for Si Green in January 1959. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Cincinnati, league and executive transaction ledgers all date the exchange to January 14, while RealGM uses January 10; the canonical record follows the four matching Basketball-Reference ledgers and preserves the date conflict in audit notes. The same verified sources show no cash component, and they correct the legacy 'Ned Park' transcription to Med Park. Green then played 186 regular-season games for St. Louis through November 1961, while Park gave Cincinnati 107 games across two seasons and Stephens never returned to the NBA.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Acquired Hub Reed for a Later Rights Asset
sections.body: Cincinnati acquired Hub Reed from St. Louis on November 4, 1959 for a player to be named later. A contemporary November 5 newspaper item reports the Reed acquisition on those terms, and Cincinnati's 1961 media guide says Reed joined the Royals on November 4. On December 22, contemporary wire coverage reported that St. Louis received the rights to Bob Boozer, Cincinnati's No. 1 overall pick from the 1959 draft, to complete the earlier Reed transaction. RealGM also records the Hawks' acquisition of Boozer's rights on December 22.

sections.heading: Reed Supplied Four Royals Seasons
sections.body: Reed became a durable Royals rotation big. Basketball-Reference credits him with 69 Cincinnati games in 1959-60, 75 in 1960-61, 80 in 1961-62 and 80 in 1962-63, or 304 regular-season games across four seasons. His Cincinnati aggregate was 6.6 points and 6.0 rebounds per game, with his largest role coming immediately after the trade when he averaged 9.7 points and 8.9 rebounds in 69 games. That is substantial realized value for a player acquired as part of a midseason roster adjustment.

sections.heading: St. Louis Never Received Bob Boozer NBA Games
sections.body: Boozer was an extremely valuable prospect, but the Hawks did not turn the acquired rights into any Bob Boozer NBA games. He spent 1959-60 outside the NBA, and RealGM records Cincinnati reacquiring his draft rights from St. Louis on April 15, 1960. Boozer then signed with Cincinnati before the 1960-61 season and ultimately played 269 regular-season games for the Royals through the first 32 games of 1963-64. Because the April rights return is a separate transaction, this record does not credit Boozer's later Cincinnati production as an additional direct asset from the November trade.

sections.heading: The Direct Value Strongly Favors Cincinnati
sections.body: The direct realized value strongly favors Cincinnati. Reed produced four seasons and 304 games for the Royals, including a substantial 1959-60 role immediately after his arrival. St. Louis temporarily controlled the rights to a future productive NBA player but never received a Boozer appearance, and those rights returned to Cincinnati before Boozer entered the league. The exact mechanics of the later rights return are inconsistently represented across modern transaction databases, so it would overstate the evidence to treat Boozer's full Cincinnati career as part of this one trade or to assign a zero-value label to the rights themselves.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Cincinnati A-, St. Louis C+. Cincinnati acquired Hub Reed from St. Louis on November 4, 1959 for a player to be named later, which contemporary reporting and later transaction records identify as the rights to No. 1 overall pick Bob Boozer on December 22. A 1961 Cincinnati media guide and a November 5, 1959 newspaper report confirm Reed joined the Royals at that time, while December reporting confirms Boozer's rights completed the exchange. Reed played 304 regular-season games for Cincinnati across four seasons. Boozer never played for St. Louis; RealGM records his rights returning to Cincinnati on April 15, 1960 before his NBA debut.

sections.heading: Detroit Sold Barney Cable to Syracuse
sections.body: Detroit sold Barney Cable's player rights to Syracuse on November 10, 1959. The Pistons, Nationals and league transaction pages all use the same date, and the Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone executive ledgers independently record the sale. That evidence supports the legacy cash-for-player structure and removes the ambiguity created by the old thin summary. The cash amount is not preserved in the public ledgers, so the retrospective grade has to treat Detroit's return as real but unquantified financial value rather than inventing a dollar figure.

sections.heading: Cable Became a Two-Season Nationals Rotation Piece
sections.body: Cable gave the Nationals substantially more than a short trial. Syracuse's 1962 media guide credits him with 125 regular-season games across two seasons. Basketball-Reference shows that he played 75 games in 1960-61 and logged 1,642 minutes, making him a regular frontcourt rotation piece rather than an end-of-bench acquisition. He also appeared in all three games of Syracuse's 1960 division semifinal against Philadelphia. The Nationals therefore converted cash into two seasons of meaningful depth during a period in which they remained a playoff team.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Detroit received cash and moved on from a player who had appeared in only 31 games as a rookie in 1958-59. From the Pistons' perspective, monetizing the rights to a reserve forward was a defensible roster decision. The problem for a hindsight comparison is that the cash amount is unknown, while Cable's post-trade basketball value is directly visible. Without a documented premium or another asset attached to the sale, there is no basis for treating Detroit's return as equal to 125 games of rotation production.

sections.heading: One Hundred Twenty-Five Games Give Syracuse the Win
sections.body: Syracuse wins the realized-value comparison because Cable stayed for two seasons and played a genuine role. Detroit did receive immediate guaranteed consideration, so this is not a lopsided failure for the Pistons. Cable was never a star and Syracuse eventually lost him to Chicago in the 1961 expansion draft without a trade return. Still, the Nationals got much more basketball utility than the legacy write-up suggested, and the known on-court value outweighs an undisclosed cash payment in the absence of evidence that the payment was unusually large.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Detroit C+, Syracuse B+. Detroit sold the player rights to Barney Cable to the Syracuse Nationals on November 10, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Syracuse, league, Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure. Cable then became a real rotation piece for Syracuse: the Nationals' 1962 media guide credits him with 125 regular-season games across two seasons, and Basketball-Reference lists 75 games and 1,642 minutes in 1960-61 alone. Detroit received guaranteed financial consideration, but the public records do not preserve the amount.

sections.heading: New York Sold Ron Sobie to Minneapolis
sections.body: New York sold Ron Sobie's player rights to Minneapolis on December 1, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Lakers and league transaction pages all record the same date and structure. Fred Podesta's New York executive ledger and Bob Short's Minneapolis ledger independently match the transaction, while RealGM lists the player as Ron Sobiezczyk. Those records support normalizing the malformed legacy 'Ron Sobie)' label to Ron Sobie while retaining the longer surname variants as aliases rather than treating them as different players.

sections.heading: Sobie Played One Lakers Game
sections.body: The Lakers received almost no on-court return. Sobie appeared in one game for Minneapolis during the 1959-60 season, played 13 minutes, made one field goal and finished with two points, two rebounds and two assists. That became the final game of his four-year NBA career. Minneapolis did reach the Western Division Finals that season, but Sobie did not become a meaningful part of the rotation or playoff run. The transaction therefore produced essentially one brief regular-season appearance for the acquiring club.

sections.heading: The Knicks Received Guaranteed Cash
sections.body: The Knicks received cash, and the surviving public transaction ledgers do not preserve the amount. That limits how aggressively the financial return can be graded, but the basic outcome is still favorable. New York moved the rights to a player who had already appeared in 191 games for the franchise and was nearing the end of his NBA career, then received guaranteed consideration rather than carrying an asset that generated almost no future league production. No later player or draft obligation was attached to the sale in the verified ledgers.

sections.heading: New York Clearly Won the Realized-Value Comparison
sections.body: This is a straightforward realized-value edge for New York. Minneapolis paid cash for rights that yielded one 13-minute appearance and no later NBA value. New York's return cannot be measured precisely because the cash amount is unknown, so the Knicks should not receive an elite grade for the transaction. Even a modest payment, however, compares favorably with the tiny basketball return the Lakers received. The deal is best understood as a successful rights sale for New York and a low-cost acquisition that simply did not work for Minneapolis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — Minneapolis C-, New York B. New York sold Ron Sobie's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers on December 1, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's league, Knicks, Lakers, Fred Podesta and Bob Short transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure, while RealGM records the same acquisition under Sobie's longer surname form. The Lakers received almost no realized basketball value: Sobie appeared in one Minneapolis game, played 13 minutes and scored two points, and he never played in the NBA again. New York's cash return is not publicly quantified, but the Knicks converted rights to a player at the end of his NBA career into guaranteed consideration.

sections.heading: New York Bought Jim Palmer from Cincinnati
sections.body: New York acquired Jim Palmer from Cincinnati on December 4, 1959, with the archival source record preserving cash as the outgoing Knicks asset. RealGM's league transaction page, Knicks transaction history and Palmer player profile all independently place the move on December 4. The accessible public records do not preserve the cash amount, so the source-backed review keeps the verified player movement and legacy cash structure while treating the financial side conservatively rather than inventing a price.

sections.heading: Palmer Gave the Knicks 109 Games
sections.body: Palmer immediately joined the Knicks' center rotation. He appeared in 54 games after the trade in 1959-60, averaging 20.0 minutes, 8.0 points and 5.1 rebounds. He returned for 55 games in 1960-61 and averaged 5.3 points and 3.3 rebounds in 12.5 minutes. Across the two New York seasons he played 109 regular-season games, averaged 6.6 points and 4.2 rebounds and supplied 1,770 total minutes. That is useful realized value for a cash acquisition, even though Palmer was a supporting big rather than a long-term starter.

sections.heading: The Royals Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Royals received cash, but the public transaction records located for this review do not identify the amount. Palmer had already played 87 Cincinnati games over parts of two seasons, including 20 games in 1959-60 before the trade, so Cincinnati was moving an established rotation center rather than unused rights. The unknown payment prevents a precise financial comparison. It also means the Royals should receive some credit for monetizing a player they chose to move instead of being treated as if they received nothing.

sections.heading: Two Useful Seasons Create a Knicks Edge
sections.body: New York's side is easier to measure: 109 games and two seasons of frontcourt depth. Cincinnati's return is real but unquantified. Because Palmer remained in the NBA only through the end of 1960-61, the Knicks did not acquire a long-duration asset, yet they still received substantially more on-court value than a token roster move would suggest. The evidence supports a moderate Knicks edge, not an overwhelming one, because the missing cash figure could materially affect how favorable the deal looked to Cincinnati at the time.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Edge — New York B+, Cincinnati B-. New York acquired Jim Palmer from the Cincinnati Royals for cash on December 4, 1959. RealGM's league, Knicks and Palmer transaction records all preserve the same date and team movement. Basketball-Reference documents Palmer's post-trade New York production. Palmer played 54 games for the Knicks in 1959-60 and 55 more in 1960-61, giving New York 109 games over two seasons at 6.6 points and 4.2 rebounds per game. Cincinnati's cash amount is not preserved in the accessible public ledgers, so the Royals' return cannot be valued precisely.

sections.heading: New York and Minneapolis Exchanged Players Picks and Cash
sections.body: New York and Minneapolis completed a five-asset transaction on January 24, 1960. The Knicks sent Ray Felix and their 1960 fourth-round pick, later used on Ben Warley, while the Lakers sent Dick Garmaker and their 1960 second-round pick, later used on Dave Budd. Pro Sports Transactions also records $25,000 moving from New York to Minneapolis, a term not shown on the Basketball-Reference team or league transaction pages.

sections.heading: Garmaker and Budd Combined for 450 Knicks Games
sections.body: Garmaker gave New York immediate scoring and playmaking. He played 26 games after the trade in 1959-60 and 71 more in 1960-61, totaling 97 Knicks games, 1,441 points and nearly 3,000 minutes. His 1960-61 season was especially useful: 15.6 points, 3.9 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game. The second-round pick became Dave Budd, who then spent his entire five-year NBA career with New York. Budd played 353 games for the Knicks, averaged 7.1 points and 4.6 rebounds, and supplied a steady frontcourt rotation role through 1964-65.

sections.heading: Felix Still Gave the Lakers 189 Games
sections.body: Felix became a useful but declining center for Minneapolis and then Los Angeles. He played 31 games after the trade in 1959-60, 78 games in 1960-61 and 80 more in 1961-62, totaling 189 regular-season appearances for the Lakers after the exchange. His post-trade Lakers scoring was modest, but he still provided rebounding and veteran center minutes during the franchise's move to Los Angeles and remained on the roster through the 1962 Finals season. The fourth-round pick became Ben Warley.

sections.heading: New York Built the Stronger Multi-Year Return
sections.body: The trade looks very different once the draft outcomes and post-trade careers are followed through. Minneapolis received 189 games from Felix, no NBA games from Warley and the documented cash payment. New York received 97 games from Garmaker plus 353 from Budd, including several seasons of useful rotation production. The Knicks therefore turned an aging center, a lower pick and cash into two players who collectively delivered 450 games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — Minneapolis B, New York A-. On January 24, 1960, New York sent Ray Felix, the 1960 fourth-round pick that became Ben Warley and $25,000 to Minneapolis for Dick Garmaker and the 1960 second-round pick that became Dave Budd. Basketball-Reference's league, Knicks, Lakers and executive ledgers all confirm the player-and-pick exchange, while Pro Sports Transactions preserves the $25,000 cash term. Garmaker then gave New York 97 games across the rest of 1959-60 and 1960-61, and Budd played all 353 games of his five-year NBA career for the Knicks. Felix produced 189 regular-season games for the Lakers through 1961-62, while Warley never appeared for the franchise after being drafted.

sections.heading: The Archive Preserves a Separate Gambee-for-Cash Entry
sections.body: The Atlanta-source ledger preserves a January 31, 1960 entry in which St. Louis sent Dave Gambee to Cincinnati for cash. That entry overlaps the better-corroborated same-day Piontek exchange, which also lists Gambee moving to the Royals with Hub Reed. The public Basketball-Reference executive ledger and RealGM transaction history support Gambee’s movement to Cincinnati, but they describe it as part of the Piontek trade rather than as a clearly independent sale.

sections.heading: Gambee Played Nineteen Games for Cincinnati
sections.body: Whatever the bookkeeping structure, Gambee’s Cincinnati stint is measurable. He appeared in 19 games for the Royals after the move, averaging 11.1 minutes, 5.0 points and 3.9 rebounds. It was a short stay, but it gave Cincinnati actual rotation production before his rights returned to St. Louis in April. The Hawks’ side of this particular archival entry is only an undisclosed cash payment.

sections.heading: The Cash Amount Is Not Publicly Preserved
sections.body: The surviving public ledgers do not identify the payment, and the same-day overlap prevents treating the cash record as unquestionably separate from the Piontek package. St. Louis therefore receives credit for converting a lightly used forward into financial consideration, but the return cannot be valued precisely. No player, pick or other downstream basketball asset is attached to the Hawks in this record.

sections.heading: A Modest Royals Edge Fits the Verifiable Outcome
sections.body: Cincinnati obtained 19 games from Gambee, while St. Louis received unquantified cash. That is enough for a narrow realized-value advantage to the Royals, not a sweeping judgment. The archival collision is material and should remain visible: this page evaluates the canonical cash entry as stored while acknowledging that stronger independent sources fold Gambee into the simultaneous Piontek-and-Reed exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge — St. Louis C+, Cincinnati B-. Atlanta acquired cash from Royals (per NBAGuide) in exchange for Dave Gambee.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sent Gambee and Reed for Dave Piontek
sections.body: Basketball-Reference’s executive ledgers and historical date index agree that Cincinnati sent Dave Piontek to St. Louis on January 31, 1960 for Dave Gambee and Hub Reed. The exchange moved one established forward to a contender and gave the Royals two younger frontcourt players. Unlike the overlapping cash entry in the legacy archive, this three-player structure is consistently preserved by independent transaction sources.

sections.heading: Piontek Helped Immediately but Faded Quickly
sections.body: Piontek played 25 games for St. Louis after the trade, averaging 28.9 minutes, 7.8 points and 4.8 rebounds. He also appeared during the Hawks’ run to the 1960 NBA Finals. His role shrank the next season to 29 games and 8.8 minutes per night, leaving St. Louis with 54 regular-season games over two years before Chicago selected him in the 1961 expansion draft.

sections.heading: Reed Became the Larger Cincinnati Return
sections.body: Reed supplied the most durable value in the deal. He played 69 games for Cincinnati after the trade in 1959-60 and averaged 9.7 points and 8.9 rebounds, then remained with the Royals for three more seasons. Gambee added 19 games before his rights moved back to St. Louis and ultimately on to Syracuse. Cincinnati therefore received both the best single-season production and the longest tenure.

sections.heading: The Two-Player Package Clearly Outlasted Piontek
sections.body: St. Louis received useful short-term minutes from Piontek during a Finals season, so the trade was not empty for the Hawks. Cincinnati nevertheless obtained far more cumulative production through Reed alone, with Gambee adding a smaller contribution. The verified careers support a clear Royals win while still recognizing why a contender could value Piontek’s immediate veteran role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — St. Louis C, Cincinnati B+. Atlanta acquired Dave Piontek from Royals in exchange for Dave Gambee; Hubert Reed.

sections.heading: St. Louis Built a Four-Asset Package for Larry Foust
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, St. Louis and league transaction ledgers all date the Larry Foust deal to February 1, 1960, one day later than the legacy Atlanta-source record. The verified core package sent Foust to St. Louis for Chuck Share and the draft rights to Nick Mantis and Willie Merriweather. Pro Sports Transactions and the APBR Lakers chronology also preserve a $10,000 cash payment from St. Louis to Minneapolis. Because the stronger cluster of team, league and chronology sources uses February 1, the source-backed review corrects the canonical date while retaining the cash term supported outside Basketball-Reference.

sections.heading: Foust Strengthened Two Finals Teams
sections.body: Foust gave the Hawks a useful veteran center for the rest of his NBA career. He played 25 games after the trade in 1959-60, then 68 games in 1960-61 and 57 more in 1961-62. Across those 150 St. Louis regular-season games he scored 1,359 points and grabbed 899 rebounds. His role was no longer the All-Star-level centerpiece it had been earlier in the decade, but he remained a dependable interior contributor on teams that reached the 1960 and 1961 NBA Finals. The immediate return was especially efficient: Foust averaged 10.2 points and 7.3 rebounds in 22.6 minutes during his 25-game finish to the 1959-60 season.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Received Almost No Lasting Production
sections.body: The Lakers received several assets on paper, but very little of the basketball value lasted. Share appeared in only three regular-season games for Minneapolis before his NBA career ended. Mantis played 10 games for the Lakers in 1959-60, totaling 71 minutes and 21 points, then spent the next two seasons outside the NBA before later resurfacing elsewhere. Merriweather never played in an NBA game. The $10,000 cash payment gave Minneapolis guaranteed financial consideration, and that prevents the return from being graded as a complete zero. Still, the three basketball assets produced only 13 Lakers regular-season appearances combined.

sections.heading: The Contender Converted Spare Parts into a Starting Center
sections.body: This is one of the clearer veteran-for-depth exchanges in the early archive. St. Louis gave up an aging reserve center, two draft-rights assets with limited or no NBA impact, and cash, then received 150 games from Foust plus meaningful frontcourt minutes on two Finals teams. Minneapolis gained flexibility and some money, but the actual player return barely materialized. Share was at the end of his career, Mantis never became part of the rotation, and Merriweather never reached the league. The difference is not superstar upside; it is simply that one side received three seasons of usable NBA production while the other received almost none.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis A-, Minneapolis C. St. Louis acquired Larry Foust from the Minneapolis Lakers in a transaction Basketball-Reference dates to February 1, 1960. The Hawks sent Chuck Share plus the draft rights to Nick Mantis and Willie Merriweather, while Pro Sports Transactions and a contemporary Lakers chronology also preserve a $10,000 cash payment to Minneapolis. Foust then played 150 regular-season games for St. Louis over the remainder of his career, contributing to consecutive NBA Finals runs in 1960 and 1961. Share appeared in only three regular-season games for Minneapolis, Mantis played 10, and Merriweather never appeared in the NBA. The surviving evidence therefore supports a clear Hawks win and also corrects the legacy January 31 date to February 1.
