sections.heading: St. Louis Reacquired Gambee’s Player Rights
sections.body: The canonical archive records St. Louis reacquiring Dave Gambee’s rights from Cincinnati in mid-April 1960 for cash. Public transaction histories corroborate the return of Gambee’s rights, although they differ by one day and do not consistently preserve the consideration: RealGM dates the acquisition to April 14, while Ben Kerner’s Basketball-Reference ledger lists April 15. The cash term therefore rests on the legacy team ledger and should be treated conservatively.

sections.heading: The Hawks Never Received Another Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Gambee had already played 19 Cincinnati games after the January trade, but he did not appear in another regular-season game for St. Louis after his rights came back. In September the Hawks sold those rights to Syracuse. The reacquisition thus functioned as an offseason asset transaction rather than a roster move that directly helped the Hawks on the court.

sections.heading: The Rights Still Retained Transfer Value
sections.body: St. Louis did preserve a marketable asset. Five months later Syracuse bought Gambee’s rights, and he immediately became a substantial Nationals contributor. The public record does not reveal either cash amount, so it is impossible to prove a financial profit on the two sales. Still, recovering control of a player whose rights could be moved again gave the Hawks more than a dead roster claim.

sections.heading: A Slight Hawks Edge Is the Appropriate Ceiling
sections.body: Cincinnati received cash of unknown size; St. Louis received rights that later generated another cash sale but no intervening Hawks games. That supports only a slight St. Louis edge. The uncertain payment and one-day date discrepancy rule out a stronger grade, while the later Syracuse transaction supplies the clearest evidence that Gambee’s rights retained real value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — St. Louis C+, Cincinnati C. Atlanta acquired rights to Dave Gambee from Royals in exchange for cash.

sections.heading: The Archive Links Gambee’s Return to Bob Boozer’s Rights
sections.body: This canonical entry treats St. Louis’s reacquisition of Dave Gambee as the return for Cincinnati receiving Bob Boozer’s draft rights. Independent histories preserve both movements but split the timing: RealGM lists Gambee returning on April 14 and Cincinnati acquiring Boozer’s rights on April 15. That makes the linked exchange plausible while requiring a clear date note instead of pretending every ledger records one perfectly matched transaction.

sections.heading: Gambee Never Played Again for St. Louis
sections.body: The Hawks did not turn the reacquired rights into additional games from Gambee. They sold his rights to Syracuse in September 1960, where he became a long-term rotation forward. St. Louis therefore realized only the unquantified proceeds of that later sale from the player side of this entry, not the seven productive seasons Gambee subsequently gave the Nationals and 76ers.

sections.heading: Boozer Became a Major Cincinnati Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Boozer debuted for Cincinnati in 1960-61 and played 269 regular-season games for the Royals across parts of four seasons. He averaged 13.7 points and 10.2 rebounds in his second year and 14.3 points with 11.1 rebounds in his third. The former No. 1 pick later became an All-Star and an NBA champion, but Cincinnati’s grade rests on the substantial production it directly received before trading him in 1963.

sections.heading: The Rights Gap Makes This a Decisive Royals Win
sections.body: Cincinnati obtained several seasons of starting-level frontcourt production from Boozer. St. Louis recovered Gambee’s rights but received no additional Hawks games from him and soon converted the asset to undisclosed cash. Even allowing for the date ambiguity and the value of that later sale, the directly realized basketball return is overwhelmingly on Cincinnati’s side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — St. Louis D, Cincinnati A. Atlanta acquired Dave Gambee from Royals (AP) in exchange for rights to Bob Boozer.

sections.heading: St. Louis Exchanged Bob Ferry for Ed Conlin
sections.body: St. Louis traded Bob Ferry to Detroit for Ed Conlin on April 16, 1960. The Hawks, Pistons and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on the date and straightforward player-for-player structure. Ferry had just completed his rookie season after St. Louis selected him in the first round of the 1959 draft. Conlin was an established veteran who had arrived in Detroit in the George Yardley trade a year earlier. There is no additional cash or draft component attached to this April transaction in the verified ledgers, so the source-backed review keeps the package simple and judges the result from the players' actual post-trade paths.

sections.heading: Ferry Became a Four-Year Detroit Rotation Center
sections.body: Ferry became a durable rotation center for four full Pistons seasons. He played 79 games in 1960-61, 80 in 1961-62, 79 in 1962-63 and 74 in 1963-64, totaling 312 regular-season appearances. Across those seasons he scored 3,851 points and collected 1,968 rebounds. His strongest scoring season was 1961-62, when he averaged 13.9 points and 6.3 rebounds, and he remained an important frontcourt piece through 1963-64. Detroit later included Ferry in the June 1964 multi-player trade with Baltimore that brought Terry Dischinger, Don Kojis and Rod Thorn to the Pistons, giving his tenure identifiable downstream value beyond the four seasons he played directly.

sections.heading: Conlin Never Played a Regular-Season Game for the Hawks
sections.body: Conlin never played a regular-season game for the Hawks. St. Louis acquired him in April after the 1959-60 season and then traded him on October 17, 1960 with cash to the Philadelphia Warriors for Ernie Beck and Woody Sauldsberry before the next regular season began. That downstream conversion means the Hawks did not simply lose the asset for nothing, and both Beck and Sauldsberry subsequently appeared for St. Louis. Still, Conlin himself provided no on-court return to the Hawks, while the later package came only after St. Louis added cash and moved him again. The direct April exchange therefore produced almost no immediate basketball value for the Hawks.

sections.heading: Detroit Won the Direct Value Comparison
sections.body: Detroit clearly received the more durable asset. Ferry gave the Pistons 312 games, four seasons of frontcourt minutes and later became part of another substantial trade package. St. Louis used Conlin as an offseason bridge asset and converted him before he ever appeared for the club. The Hawks' later Beck-Sauldsberry return deserves recognition, but it should not erase the difference between four years of direct production and a player who never suited up for the acquiring team. Ferry was not an All-Star, yet his reliability, scoring and rebounding make the original one-for-one trade decisively favorable to Detroit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — St. Louis C+, Detroit A-. St. Louis traded Bob Ferry to the Detroit Pistons for Ed Conlin on April 16, 1960. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Pistons and league transaction ledgers all preserve the same date and one-for-one package. Ferry became a four-season Detroit rotation center, playing 312 regular-season games from 1960-61 through 1963-64 and totaling 3,851 points and 1,968 rebounds before he was included in the 1964 Bailey Howell trade with Baltimore. Conlin never appeared in a regular-season game for St. Louis; the Hawks moved him with cash to Philadelphia before the next season began. Although that later move returned Ernie Beck and Woody Sauldsberry, Detroit received the far stronger direct and durable value from the original exchange.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sold Dave Gambee’s Rights to Syracuse
sections.body: St. Louis sold Dave Gambee's player rights to Syracuse for cash on September 22, 1960. The St. Louis, Syracuse and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all use that date, while the Ben Kerner and Danny Biasone executive ledgers independently preserve the move from each front office. Gambee had originally been a first-round St. Louis pick in 1958, spent only a brief early stint with the Hawks, moved through Cincinnati and returned to St. Louis as a rights asset before this sale. The public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, so the Hawks' financial return cannot be measured precisely.

sections.heading: Gambee Became a Seven-Season Franchise Fixture
sections.body: Gambee immediately became a substantial rotation forward for the Nationals. He played 79 games in 1960-61 and all 80 in 1961-62, when he averaged 16.7 points and 7.9 rebounds. He remained with the franchise through its move from Syracuse to Philadelphia, playing 60 games in 1962-63, 41 in 1963-64, 80 in 1964-65, 72 in 1965-66 and 63 in 1966-67. That is 475 regular-season games across seven seasons for the same franchise. His role diminished over time, but he remained a useful frontcourt option long enough to be part of the 1966-67 Philadelphia championship roster.

sections.heading: The Hawks Received Only Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Hawks received cash and no later player, pick or conditional asset appears on their side of the verified transaction. That makes the exact return impossible to quantify, and an undisclosed sale price should not be treated as worthless. Still, St. Louis gave up the rights to a 23-year-old forward who immediately became a starter-level scorer for Syracuse. The Hawks were already a strong contender and reached the 1961 NBA Finals without Gambee, so the move did not derail their short-term team success. Retrospectively, however, the cash payment had to be weighed against seven seasons and 475 games of useful production that materialized for the buyer.

sections.heading: Syracuse Bought the Durable Basketball Asset
sections.body: Syracuse received the more durable basketball asset by a wide margin. Gambee gave the franchise two high-volume early seasons, remained productive through the transition to Philadelphia and lasted through the 1967 championship year. St. Louis received a one-time payment whose amount is unavailable. The Hawks' competitive context and the unknown price keep this from being treated as a catastrophic decision, but the realized basketball gap is clear. A cash-only acquisition that produces 475 games and seven seasons of roster continuity is far more valuable in hindsight than a sale with no identifiable downstream basketball asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — St. Louis C+, Syracuse A-. St. Louis sold Dave Gambee's player rights to the Syracuse Nationals on September 22, 1960 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Nationals, league and executive ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure. Gambee became a seven-season Syracuse/Philadelphia fixture, playing 475 regular-season games for the franchise from 1960-61 through 1966-67. He averaged 16.7 points and 7.9 rebounds in 1961-62 and later remained on the roster through Philadelphia's 1967 championship season. The public ledgers do not preserve the cash amount St. Louis received. The realized value therefore favors the Nationals/76ers clearly: they purchased a long-term rotation forward while the Hawks received a one-time, unquantified payment.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sent Ed Conlin and Cash to Philadelphia
sections.body: St. Louis sent Ed Conlin and cash to Philadelphia for Woody Sauldsberry and Ernie Beck on October 17, 1960. The Hawks, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all preserve the same package. Conlin had never played a regular-season game for St. Louis after arriving from Detroit in April, so the Hawks were converting an offseason asset plus cash into two established Warriors. Philadelphia, meanwhile, consolidated two veterans into one younger wing and financial consideration. The surviving public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, which limits how precisely the Warriors' return can be valued.

sections.heading: Sauldsberry Supplied the Best Hawks Return
sections.body: Sauldsberry became the main basketball return for the Hawks. He played 69 games in 1960-61, averaging 7.5 points and 7.1 rebounds in 21.6 minutes, then appeared in 14 more St. Louis games in 1961-62 before being traded to the Chicago Packers. Across 83 Hawks games he averaged roughly 7.4 points and 6.8 rebounds. St. Louis later included Sauldsberry with Joe Graboski and Si Green in the November 1961 trade that brought Barney Cable and Archie Dees back, so he retained some transactional value beyond his direct minutes. Beck's Hawks stay was much shorter: seven games at 2.7 points before St. Louis sold his rights to Syracuse on November 28, 1960, recovering another cash return.

sections.heading: Conlin Gave the Warriors Two Rotation Seasons
sections.body: Conlin gave the Warriors more games than either incoming Hawk did individually. He played 77 games in 1960-61 and 70 more in 1961-62, totaling 147 regular-season appearances for Philadelphia. His role was modest but steady: 7.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 1.6 assists per game in the first season, followed by 4.6 points and 2.2 rebounds in 1961-62. Across the two seasons he averaged about 5.8 points and 2.8 rebounds. Philadelphia also received cash in the original transaction, but the amount is not preserved in the public ledgers located for this review. Conlin left the NBA after the 1961-62 season, so the Warriors did not turn the deal into a long-duration asset.

sections.heading: The Secondary Value Nudges the Deal toward St. Louis
sections.body: The exchange is closer than the old archive grades suggested. Philadelphia received 147 games from Conlin plus cash, while St. Louis received 90 combined games from Sauldsberry and Beck before both were moved again. The difference is that Sauldsberry supplied stronger rebounding and comparable scoring on a per-game basis, then remained part of a later Hawks trade package, while Beck was sold for additional cash after his brief stay. Those secondary conversions give St. Louis a slight realized-value advantage, but Philadelphia's two full seasons of Conlin make a low grade inappropriate. This was a useful asset reshuffle for both clubs rather than a one-sided result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B+, Philadelphia B-. St. Louis traded Ed Conlin and cash to the Philadelphia Warriors for Woody Sauldsberry and Ernie Beck on October 17, 1960. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Warriors and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and four-part package. Sauldsberry played 83 regular-season games for St. Louis over parts of two seasons, averaging 7.4 points and 6.8 rebounds, while Beck appeared in seven Hawks games before his rights were sold to Syracuse. Conlin became a two-season Philadelphia rotation wing, playing 147 games at 5.8 points and 2.8 rebounds per game. The Hawks received the slightly stronger overall return because Sauldsberry provided comparable short-term value and later remained usable in another trade, while Beck also generated a cash recovery.

sections.heading: New York Sold Mike Farmer’s Rights to Cincinnati
sections.body: New York sold Mike Farmer's player rights to Cincinnati for cash on November 14, 1960. The Knicks, Royals and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on the date and identify the move as a sale rather than a player swap. Farmer had been the third pick in the 1958 draft and had spent parts of three seasons with New York before the move. The public transaction record does not preserve the amount of cash Cincinnati paid, so New York's financial return cannot be graded with precision. What can be measured is what Farmer produced immediately after the Royals acquired him and what value Cincinnati still retained when it moved his rights again the following summer.

sections.heading: Farmer Immediately Joined the Royals Rotation
sections.body: Farmer became a real rotation player for the Royals immediately. He appeared in 57 games in 1960-61 and averaged 22.7 minutes, 7.5 points and 6.6 rebounds per game. That was far more than a token end-of-roster role and gave Cincinnati useful frontcourt depth during Oscar Robertson's rookie season. The Royals then sold Farmer's rights to St. Louis in August 1961. Farmer spent the next season in the ABL before returning to the NBA with the Hawks, where he played 80 games in 1962-63, 76 in 1963-64, 60 in 1964-65 and nine in 1965-66. Cincinnati therefore received one productive season and still retained a transferable asset afterward.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Preserved a Transferable Asset
sections.body: The Knicks received cash and no later player, pick or conditional asset appears on their side of the verified transaction. Because the amount is undisclosed, the sale cannot be treated as if New York received nothing. Farmer also was not a star in New York and had averaged modest scoring numbers during his first three seasons, so moving him for financial consideration was understandable on the transaction date. Retrospectively, however, the Knicks surrendered a 24-year-old former lottery-level pick who immediately became a regular contributor for another team and later extended his NBA career for several additional seasons. The one-time payment produced no identifiable basketball asset for New York.

sections.heading: One Season Plus a Later Sale Beat Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: Cincinnati received the stronger realized return. The Royals bought a player who gave them 57 games and nearly 23 minutes per night, then preserved enough value to sell his rights again the next summer. New York's return was limited to an undisclosed cash payment. That does not make the move catastrophic, because Farmer's ceiling was that of a useful rotation forward rather than a franchise player, but the Royals extracted both present and future value from the same asset. In a minor rights sale, that is enough to create a clear separation between the two sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — New York C+, Cincinnati A-. New York sold Mike Farmer's player rights to the Cincinnati Royals on November 14, 1960 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Royals and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure. Farmer immediately played 57 games for Cincinnati in 1960-61, averaging 7.5 points and 6.6 rebounds in 22.7 minutes per game. Cincinnati then sold his rights to St. Louis in August 1961, and Farmer later produced four more NBA seasons for the Hawks. The public ledgers do not preserve New York's cash amount. In realized basketball value, Cincinnati clearly came out ahead because it bought a useful rotation forward, received a full season of production and still retained a saleable rights asset afterward.

sections.heading: St. Louis Bought Phil Rollins from Cincinnati
sections.body: Cincinnati sold Phil Rollins to St. Louis for cash on November 28, 1960. The league and team transaction ledgers preserve the player movement as a sale, and the canonical record contains no player or draft asset going back to the Royals. The payment amount is not public, so Cincinnati’s return has to be described as guaranteed but unquantified financial consideration.

sections.heading: Rollins Played Only Seven Games for the Hawks
sections.body: Rollins’s St. Louis tenure was brief. He appeared in seven games, averaged 10.1 minutes, 2.6 points and 1.6 assists, and then moved to New York during the same season. Those minutes gave the Hawks a real reserve guard, but not the sustained production implied by a decisive win grade. His 40 later Knicks games belong to New York, not to the value St. Louis directly received.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Monetized a Shrinking Role
sections.body: Rollins had played 72 games for Cincinnati in 1959-60 but only 14 for the Royals in 1960-61 before the sale, with his minutes falling to 6.1 per game. Selling him therefore converted a reduced rotation role into cash. Because the amount is unknown, the Royals cannot be credited with a measurable basketball asset, yet the timing was sensible and the outgoing player’s Hawks impact was small.

sections.heading: The Results Support Only a Narrow Hawks Advantage
sections.body: St. Louis received seven games from Rollins; Cincinnati received undisclosed cash. The Hawks can take a slight edge because they bought a player who immediately appeared for them, but the limited stint does not support a wide grade separation. The verdict remains Hawks-favorable to match the canonical record, while the evidence calls for a restrained assessment of what either side actually gained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis C+, Cincinnati D+. Atlanta acquired Phil Rollins from Royals in exchange for cash.

sections.heading: St. Louis Sold Beck Six Weeks After Acquiring Him
sections.body: The Hawks sold Ernie Beck's player rights to Syracuse for cash on November 28, 1960. The league and both team transaction ledgers agree on the date and sale structure. Beck had reached St. Louis only six weeks earlier in the Ed Conlin trade, appeared in seven Hawks games, and was moved again before the season was half over.

sections.heading: Syracuse Received Only Three Games
sections.body: Beck's Nationals tenure was almost over as soon as it began. He played three regular-season games for Syracuse, averaging 6.7 minutes, 2.3 points and 3.7 rebounds. Those were the final NBA appearances of a career that began with Philadelphia in 1953, so Syracuse did not acquire continuing rotation value.

sections.heading: The Cash Return Cannot Be Priced
sections.body: Public transaction records do not preserve the amount Syracuse paid. That prevents a precise financial valuation and keeps the Hawks' grade modest. The basketball comparison is still clear: St. Louis recovered some consideration for rights that produced only three more NBA games.

sections.heading: Avoiding Dead Value Gives the Hawks the Edge
sections.body: This was a minor disposal rather than a franchise-shaping move. St. Louis had already received seven games from Beck and then monetized the remaining rights; Syracuse paid for three short appearances. The unknown price rules out a strong verdict, but the realized outcome supports a narrow Hawks advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Edge — St. Louis B-, Syracuse C+. St. Louis recovered undisclosed cash for Ernie Beck, whose Nationals tenure lasted only three games.

sections.heading: Detroit Sold a Recent Draft Pick to Los Angeles
sections.body: Detroit sold Ron Johnson's player rights to the Lakers for cash on December 15, 1960. The Pistons, Lakers and league ledgers all use December 15, correcting the December 16 date carried by the older archive record. Johnson had been the 12th overall selection in the 1960 draft but played only six games for Detroit.

sections.heading: Johnson Barely Entered the Lakers Rotation
sections.body: Los Angeles used Johnson in eight regular-season games. He averaged 5.4 minutes, 0.8 points and 1.9 rebounds, then never appeared in another NBA season. The purchase therefore produced neither immediate rotation help nor a developmental payoff.

sections.heading: An Undisclosed Price Limits the Claim
sections.body: The public ledgers identify a cash sale but do not reveal the amount. Detroit cannot receive credit for a known basketball asset or a measurable windfall. It can receive limited credit for recovering financial consideration after determining quickly that its second-round pick was not part of the club's plans.

sections.heading: Eight Games Are Not Enough to Justify the Purchase
sections.body: The Lakers took a reasonable low-cost chance on a recent draft choice, but the outcome was eight low-minute appearances. Detroit's return is unpriced, so this is not a decisive win. In realized terms, however, converting the rights into cash was slightly better than the value Los Angeles obtained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Edge — Detroit B-, Los Angeles C+. The Lakers received only eight games from Ron Johnson while Detroit recovered undisclosed cash.

sections.heading: The Knicks Bought Rollins from St. Louis
sections.body: St. Louis sold Phil Rollins' player rights to New York for cash on December 17, 1960. The league and both team ledgers preserve the same date and direction. Rollins had played seven games for the Hawks earlier in the season before becoming a midyear Knicks addition.

sections.heading: Rollins Supplied a Useful Half Season
sections.body: Rollins appeared in 40 regular-season games for New York, averaging 16.5 minutes, 5.8 points and 2.5 assists. Those were the final NBA games of his career, so the Knicks did not buy long-term upside, but they did receive a credible reserve role for the remainder of the season.

sections.heading: St. Louis Received an Unpriced Payment
sections.body: No public ledger preserves the amount New York paid. That makes it impossible to compare the payment directly with the value of 40 games, and it keeps the Hawks from receiving anything more specific than credit for monetizing a player they no longer intended to use.

sections.heading: New York Won a Modest Rotation Deal
sections.body: Forty games of usable guard play are enough to give the Knicks the better realized result. The short tenure and unknown price keep the margin modest. This was a successful depth purchase for New York, not a major loss for St. Louis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Edge — St. Louis C+, New York B. Phil Rollins gave the Knicks 40 useful games before his NBA career ended.

sections.heading: New York Purchased an Immediate Starting Center
sections.body: Cincinnati sold Phil Jordon to New York for cash on January 18, 1961. The Royals, Knicks and league ledgers agree on the transaction. Jordon immediately took a large role for a New York team that needed interior production, rather than arriving as a speculative end-of-roster purchase.

sections.heading: Jordon Delivered 107 Knicks Games
sections.body: Jordon averaged 13.1 points and 8.1 rebounds in 31 games after the sale, then played 76 more games in 1961-62 at 11.9 points and 6.3 rebounds. Across a season and a half, New York received 107 regular-season games before moving him in September 1962.

sections.heading: Cincinnati's Cash Return Is Unknown
sections.body: The surviving public records do not identify the amount paid. The Royals may have had sound financial or roster reasons for selling, but there is no player or pick return to compare with Jordon's production. The absence of a price warrants restraint on Cincinnati's grade, not neutrality about the on-court outcome.

sections.heading: The Knicks Bought Real Production
sections.body: New York converted cash into a starting-caliber center who contributed immediately and remained useful for another full season. That is substantially more value than most cash purchases in this portion of the archive. Even without the sale price, the verified playing return makes the Knicks the clear winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-, Cincinnati C+. Phil Jordon gave New York 107 games and starting-level center production for an undisclosed cash price.

sections.heading: Chicago Flipped McNeill on Expansion Day
sections.body: The expansion Chicago Packers acquired Bob McNeill and Charlie Tyra from New York for Dave Budd on May 16, 1961, then sold McNeill's rights to Philadelphia for cash that same day. The linked transactions explain why McNeill never appeared for Chicago despite passing through the Packers' ledger.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Twenty-One Games
sections.body: McNeill played 21 games for the Warriors in 1961-62, averaging 10.1 minutes, 4.1 points and 2.3 assists. Philadelphia then sold his rights to the Lakers in December. The Warriors obtained a brief reserve contribution and another cash return, but neither payment is publicly quantified.

sections.heading: Both Cash Figures Matter
sections.body: Chicago's sale price and Philadelphia's later resale price are absent from the public transaction ledgers. Without them, the Packers' immediate return cannot be compared responsibly with the Warriors' 21 games and later recovery. Treating the short playing stint alone as decisive would ignore the principal asset on both sides.

sections.heading: The Record Supports Facts, Not a Winner
sections.body: The transaction chain is clear even though its economics are not. Chicago monetized a player acquired moments earlier; Philadelphia received limited bench service and then resold the rights. The evidence is sufficient to describe the outcome, but not to assign defensible team grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence — Bob McNeill played 21 games for Philadelphia, but the original sale price and the Warriors' later cash recovery are unknown.

sections.heading: The Surviving Ledgers Conflict on Direction
sections.body: RealGM, Pro Sports Transactions and the 1962 Knicks media guide support Cincinnati selling Sam Stith's rights to New York on May 16, 1961. Basketball-Reference also preserves a contradictory same-day entry showing New York selling the rights back to Cincinnati. The reciprocal listings prevent treating either cash record as uncomplicated on its own.

sections.heading: Stith Ultimately Played for New York
sections.body: The playing outcome is less ambiguous. Stith signed with the Knicks and appeared in 32 games during 1961-62, averaging 13.8 minutes, 4.4 points and 1.9 assists. It was his only NBA season, so New York received a short reserve contribution rather than a durable asset.

sections.heading: The Price and Exact Structure Are Missing
sections.body: No public source in the record identifies the cash amount, and the two-direction ledger conflict leaves open whether there were separate same-day rights actions or duplicated bookkeeping. Those uncertainties are material because the transaction was a cash-for-rights move with modest on-court value.

sections.heading: Do Not Force a Grade Through a Source Conflict
sections.body: New York clearly received the only verified NBA service, but 32 reserve games do not justify ignoring the unresolved cash and direction questions. The accurate editorial outcome is to document the conflict and withhold team grades until stronger evidence resolves the transaction structure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence — Sam Stith played 32 games for New York, but reciprocal ledger entries and an unknown cash amount prevent a defensible winner.

sections.heading: New York Reversed an Expansion-Draft Loss
sections.body: The Knicks reacquired Dave Budd from the expansion Chicago Packers on May 16, 1961 after losing him in the April expansion draft. New York sent the rights to Charlie Tyra and Bob McNeill, while Chicago immediately sold McNeill's rights to Philadelphia for cash.

sections.heading: Budd Returned for Four Productive Seasons
sections.body: Budd played 292 regular-season games for New York from 1961-62 through 1964-65. His best post-trade season came in 1962-63, when he averaged 9.5 points and 5.1 rebounds. The Knicks recovered a familiar forward and received several years of dependable service.

sections.heading: Tyra Was Chicago's Direct Basketball Return
sections.body: Tyra played 78 games for the Packers in 1961-62, averaging 6.7 points and 7.8 rebounds. McNeill never played for Chicago because his rights were sold the same day. That cash payment adds value for the Packers, but the amount is not publicly preserved.

sections.heading: Budd's Longevity Separates the Outcomes
sections.body: Chicago received a full season from Tyra and an unpriced payment for McNeill, so the expansion club did not come away empty. Budd nevertheless gave New York almost four times as many games and multiple useful seasons. The direct playing value makes the Knicks the clear winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-, Chicago B-. Dave Budd delivered 292 post-trade games, outlasting Charlie Tyra's one Packers season and McNeill's undisclosed cash return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Hatton to the Expansion Packers
sections.body: The Warriors sold Vern Hatton's player rights to Chicago for cash on May 31, 1961. League and team transaction records support the sale, and the Packers' inaugural media guide places Hatton on the expansion roster. The public record does not preserve the purchase price.

sections.heading: Hatton Played Fifteen Games in Chicago
sections.body: Hatton appeared in 15 games for the Packers, averaging 26.4 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists. Chicago then sold his rights back to Philadelphia on November 29. The Warriors moved those rights to St. Louis one day later, and Hatton finished his NBA career with 25 Hawks games.

sections.heading: The Rights Generated Three Unpriced Sales
sections.body: The May purchase, November buyback and next-day St. Louis sale all lack public cash figures. That omission matters more than usual because the asset changed hands repeatedly for money. Fifteen games measure Chicago's basketball return, but they do not reveal the net financial result for either franchise.

sections.heading: A Transaction Chain Is Not a Grade
sections.body: The sequence can be documented without pretending the economics are known. Chicago received a brief but meaningful rotation stint; Philadelphia sold, reacquired and resold the same rights. With every price missing, any winner or letter grade would be invented.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence — Vern Hatton played 15 games for Chicago, but three linked cash transactions remain unpriced.

sections.heading: St. Louis Exchanged Walker for a Fourth-Round Pick
sections.body: The Hawks traded Horace Walker's rights to the expansion Chicago Packers on June 24, 1961 for a 1962 fourth-round draft pick. The league ledger, St. Louis team ledger and Marty Blake executive record agree on the structure and identify Chico Vaughn as the player later selected with the pick.

sections.heading: Walker Started Immediately for Chicago
sections.body: Walker played 65 games in the Packers' first season, averaging 20.5 minutes, 6.7 points and 7.2 rebounds. It was his only NBA season. Chicago therefore received a useful inaugural-year frontcourt contributor, but no value beyond that one campaign.

sections.heading: Vaughn Became a Multi-Year Hawks Guard
sections.body: Vaughn joined St. Louis in 1962-63 and played 77 games as a rookie, averaging 10.1 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.3 assists. He remained with the Hawks for five NBA seasons before continuing his career in the ABA, giving St. Louis substantially more tenure than Walker gave Chicago.

sections.heading: Both Sides Benefited, but the Pick Lasted Longer
sections.body: The Packers obtained a real contributor for an expansion roster, so this was not a failed acquisition. St. Louis converted rights to a player who never suited up for the Hawks into a guard who contributed across several seasons. Vaughn's longer service creates a modest Hawks advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — St. Louis B-, Chicago C+. Horace Walker helped the expansion Packers for one season, while the fourth-round pick became multi-year Hawks guard Chico Vaughn.

sections.heading: The Royals Sold Farmer's Rights to St. Louis
sections.body: Cincinnati sold Mike Farmer's player rights to the Hawks for cash in August 1961. The exact day is not preserved in Basketball-Reference, which lists the move as August with an unknown date, so the archive's August 1 route should be treated as approximate rather than exact.

sections.heading: Farmer Spent the Next Season in the ABL
sections.body: Farmer did not join St. Louis immediately. He played in the American Basketball League during 1961-62, meaning the rights purchase produced no NBA service in its first season. The delay is important context, but it did not erase the Hawks' control of his NBA rights.

sections.heading: St. Louis Eventually Received Three Full Seasons
sections.body: Farmer returned to the NBA with the Hawks in 1962-63 and played all 80 games, averaging 7.4 points and 4.6 rebounds. He followed with 76 games in 1963-64 and 60 more in 1964-65. The delayed acquisition ultimately produced 216 regular-season games for St. Louis.

sections.heading: The Long Tenure Supports the Hawks' Grade
sections.body: Cincinnati's cash amount is unknown, so the Royals' return cannot be priced. St. Louis nevertheless turned that payment into three seasons of rotation service after waiting through Farmer's ABL year. The result favors the Hawks modestly while preserving the date and price limitations.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — St. Louis C, Cincinnati C. Farmer eventually supplied 216 Hawks games, but the sale price and exact August 1961 date remain unknown.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: St. Louis traded Frank Radovich, Bob McDonald and cash to Philadelphia for Joe Graboski on August 19, 1961. The Hawks, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all preserve the same date and package. Graboski was a veteran forward-center with more than a decade of professional experience, while Radovich was a 1961 second-round pick and McDonald a sixth-round pick whose NBA value had not yet materialized. St. Louis was therefore paying two younger assets plus cash for an established player.

sections.heading: St. Louis Return
sections.body: Graboski's direct Hawks tenure was extremely short. He appeared in only three regular-season games for St. Louis in 1961-62, averaging 2.7 points and 3.0 rebounds in 9.3 minutes per game. His value did not end there, however. On November 21, the Hawks included Graboski with Si Green and Woody Sauldsberry in the trade that brought Barney Cable and Archie Dees from the expansion Chicago Packers. Because that later transaction involved five players, it is not possible to isolate an exact dollar-like share of the return attributable to Graboski.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Radovich gave the Warriors 37 regular-season games in 1961-62, averaging 2.4 points and 1.4 rebounds in only 4.7 minutes per game. He also appeared briefly in the playoffs, but his NBA career ended after that season. McDonald never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. That leaves Philadelphia with a small amount of low-minute player production plus the unknown cash payment. The cash matters because it was guaranteed value at the time, but the two basketball assets did not develop into rotation pieces with meaningful longevity.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Neither side produced a major long-term winner from the exchange. Philadelphia received more direct games because Radovich stayed on the roster for 37 appearances, yet those minutes were minimal and McDonald never reached the league. St. Louis received only three Graboski games, but the Hawks were able to reuse him in another multi-player trade within three months. That downstream utility gives the Hawks a modest realized-value advantage, although the unreported cash amount and inability to isolate Graboski's exact share of the later Cable-Dees package keep the gap narrow.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Edge, B-/C+. St. Louis receives a B- for acquiring the only established veteran in the deal and preserving some downstream trade value despite receiving just three direct games. Philadelphia receives a C+ because Radovich supplied 37 low-minute appearances, McDonald never played in the NBA, and the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes, with the principal uncertainty limited to the financial term and the exact value Graboski contributed to the later Chicago trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Finalized Five-Player Exchange
sections.body: On November 21, 1961, St. Louis sent Si Green, Joe Graboski and Woody Sauldsberry to the expansion Chicago Packers for Barney Cable and Archie Dees. The source record also preserves an earlier proposed package involving Ralph Davis, Fred LaCour and a player to be named later that the NBA Board of Governors disallowed. The canonical trade therefore uses only the five-player package that actually went through.

sections.heading: Chicago Received Two Immediate Rotation Players
sections.body: The Packers got substantial immediate use from the deal. Si Green played 57 games for Chicago that season and averaged 13.8 points, 6.1 rebounds and 4.9 assists. Woody Sauldsberry played 49 games at 11.7 points and 9.5 rebounds per game. Graboski added 12 games before Chicago later sold his rights to Syracuse. The expansion club therefore turned two outgoing players into multiple rotation contributors.

sections.heading: St. Louis Got Cable but Little from Dees
sections.body: Barney Cable became the useful part of the Hawks return, playing 52 games for St. Louis in 1961-62 and another 42 the next season before moving back to the Chicago franchise. Archie Dees appeared in only eight Hawks games after the trade. Cable had value, but the overall St. Louis return was much thinner than the volume of immediate production Chicago received from Green and Sauldsberry.

sections.heading: The Realized Basketball Value Favors Chicago
sections.body: This trade is unusually clear for an early-1960s multi-player exchange because the acquired players produced meaningful NBA minutes immediately. Chicago received two major rotation pieces for its inaugural season, while St. Louis received one useful forward and a very short Dees stint. The Board-disallowed version should not be mixed into the valuation. On the completed transaction alone, Chicago realized the stronger basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win — St. Louis D, Chicago A. The finalized five-player trade gave the Packers major immediate production from Si Green and Woody Sauldsberry, while St. Louis received a useful Barney Cable stint but little from Archie Dees.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Chicago sold Vern Hatton's player rights back to Philadelphia for cash on November 29, 1961. The transaction is the middle leg of an unusually compressed rights chain. Philadelphia had sold Hatton to the expansion Packers on May 31. Hatton then played 15 games for Chicago before the Packers returned his rights to the Warriors. One day later, Philadelphia sold the same rights to St. Louis.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: The Packers' side is straightforward in structure but difficult to value precisely. Chicago received cash after getting 15 regular-season games from Hatton earlier in the season. During those games he averaged 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 26.4 minutes per game, so the original May purchase did produce usable rotation minutes before the rights were sold back.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: The Warriors reacquired Hatton's rights but did not use him in another regular-season game. On November 30, just one day after getting the rights back, Philadelphia sold them to St. Louis. Hatton then appeared in 25 games for the Hawks, averaging 3.7 points and 1.8 rebounds in 9.2 minutes per game before his NBA career ended. Philadelphia therefore treated the reacquired rights as a short-lived transaction asset rather than a roster addition. The November 30 St. Louis sale also involved cash, but that amount is likewise unavailable.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: This record is a good example of why an unknown cash transaction should not be graded solely from player appearances. Chicago got a known 15-game contribution before selling the rights, while Philadelphia received no new on-court value from the November 29 acquisition. But Philadelphia may have made money by reselling the rights the following day, and Chicago may have received meaningful cash when it exited. Because both sides' actual transaction value is concentrated in undisclosed financial terms, the player record does not settle the comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The November 29 Chicago-to-Philadelphia rights sale is verified, Hatton's 15 Packers games are verified, and Philadelphia's November 30 resale to St. Louis is verified. The relevant cash amounts are not. Those missing financial terms are material enough that no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the chronology and player identity but intentionally limited on comparative value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sources.title: Chicago Packers/Washington franchise transaction history - RealGM

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: St. Louis acquired Vern Hatton's player rights from Philadelphia for cash on November 30, 1961. The date is important because Philadelphia had reacquired those same rights from Chicago only one day earlier. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, Hawks and league transaction ledgers preserve the sequence, making the chronology unusually clear even though the economics are not. The Warriors effectively used Hatton's rights as a one-day transaction asset, while St. Louis paid to add a veteran guard who had already appeared for the expansion Packers earlier in the season. The cash amount St.

sections.heading: St. Louis Return
sections.body: Hatton appeared in 25 regular-season games for the Hawks during 1961-62. He averaged 3.7 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 9.2 minutes per game. That is a measurable return, but it is a modest one. Hatton did not become a regular starter, did not remain with St. Louis beyond the season and never appeared in another NBA campaign. The Hawks therefore bought a short reserve stint rather than a durable roster piece.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: The Warriors received cash one day after buying Hatton's rights back from Chicago. Philadelphia never used him in another regular-season game. In practical terms, the Warriors' return was purely financial: whatever difference existed between the November 29 buyback price and November 30 resale price. Neither amount is preserved in the public team or league ledgers. That missing information is the central issue for retrospective grading. Philadelphia may have profited on the flip, broken even or accepted a loss to move the rights quickly. The basketball record alone cannot answer that question.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: St. Louis has the only direct on-court value because Hatton actually played 25 games for the Hawks. But those games were limited in both minutes and production, and they are not large enough to overwhelm an unknown cash term. Philadelphia's side is entirely financial, and the Warriors' one-day turnaround makes the missing prices even more important than in a simple one-way sale. Assigning letter grades would imply a value comparison that the evidence cannot establish. The defensible conclusion is to document the player outcome while keeping the transaction ungraded.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The November 30 Philadelphia-to-St. Louis rights sale is verified, Hatton's 25 Hawks games are verified, and the one-day turnaround from Philadelphia's November 29 reacquisition is verified. The relevant cash amounts are not. Because the player return was brief and the financial terms are material, no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the chronology and player identity but intentionally limited on comparative value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Philadelphia sold Bob McNeill's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers for cash in December 1961. Basketball-Reference's league ledger and both team transaction pages agree on the direction and player, but they do not preserve an exact day; each lists the transaction only as occurring sometime in December. The canonical archive keeps December 1 as a sorting placeholder, but the source-backed record should treat the day as approximate rather than exact.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: McNeill did reach the court for the Lakers. He appeared in 29 regular-season games during 1961-62, averaging 1.8 points, 1.4 assists and 0.8 rebounds in 7.9 minutes per game. He also appeared in five playoff games as Los Angeles advanced to the NBA Finals. That is real value, but it is limited reserve production rather than a rotation-changing acquisition. McNeill never played another NBA season after 1961-62. The Lakers therefore purchased a short-term depth guard whose contribution was measurable but modest.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: The Warriors received cash, but the amount is not identified in the public transaction ledgers located for this review. Philadelphia had already used McNeill in 21 regular-season games earlier in 1961-62, where he averaged 4.1 points and 2.3 assists in 10.1 minutes per game. By selling his rights in December, the Warriors converted a reserve player they were no longer using into a financial return. Without the sale price, however, there is no responsible way to compare that cash with the 29 games Los Angeles later received.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: This is not a case where player production is large enough to overwhelm an unknown cash term. Los Angeles received 29 low-minute regular-season games and five playoff appearances. Philadelphia received an unpriced cash payment after already getting 21 games from McNeill before the sale. The exact date is also only month-level in the surviving ledgers. Those limitations do not undermine the transaction's existence, but they do prevent a precise retrospective value judgment. A forced Lakers win would overstate 29 reserve appearances, while a forced Philadelphia win would assume too much about an unknown payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The December 1961 Philadelphia-to-Los Angeles rights sale is verified, McNeill's 29 Lakers regular-season games and five playoff appearances are verified, and the player identity is secure. The exact day and cash amount are not. Because the on-court return was modest and the financial term is material, no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the transaction direction and player outcome, with limited confidence only on the exact day and relative financial value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: St. Louis Return
sections.body: McMillon immediately gave the Hawks meaningful frontcourt production. He played 48 regular-season games for St. Louis in 1961-62, averaging 11.8 points and 6.3 rebounds in 21.6 minutes per game while shooting .470 from the field. Those are substantial numbers for a midseason cash acquisition, especially compared with the 5.1 points and 4.6 rebounds he had averaged in 14 Detroit games earlier that season. The Hawks did not merely receive a short bench cameo; they obtained a productive rotation forward for the remainder of the year.

sections.heading: Downstream Value
sections.body: McMillon's value also survived beyond those 48 games. On June 14, 1962, St. Louis traded him and Al Ferrari to the Chicago Packers for Bill Bridges and Ralph Davis. That later deal was a multi-player package, so McMillon's exact share of the return cannot be isolated. Even so, his inclusion demonstrates that the Hawks retained a tradable asset after already receiving meaningful on-court production. This is stronger realized value than a cash-only acquisition that disappears at season's end.

sections.heading: Detroit Return
sections.body: The Pistons received cash and no basketball asset. Detroit had used McMillon for three-plus seasons, including 78 games in 1960-61, so moving him during a reduced 1961-62 role was understandable. The unknown cash amount is an important caveat because it may have been meaningful in the early-1960s team economy. However, unlike some rights sales where the acquired player barely appeared, McMillon produced nearly 50 useful games and then remained part of another NBA trade package. That realized value is large enough to support a modest St. Louis edge even without knowing the exact payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, B+/C+. St. Louis receives a B+ for acquiring 48 games of productive frontcourt play and preserving downstream trade value into the June 1962 Bridges-Davis deal. Detroit receives a C+ because the Pistons converted a player whose role had diminished into cash, but the amount is unknown and no future basketball asset is documented. Confidence is high on the corrected December 1 date, the player identity and the realized production; confidence is lower only on the financial term and McMillon's precise share of the later multi-player trade.

The unknown cash amount is a meaningful caveat because it may have reflected a reasonable price for a player outside Boston's regular rotation.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison

New York received more than 200 games across three seasons, including a 1961-62 stretch in which Butler played starter-level minutes and scored nearly 15 points per game. Boston's return may have been financially sensible at the time, but the surviving record gives no evidence that the cash later became a comparable basketball asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict

sections.heading: St. Louis Traded Two Veterans for Davis and Bridges

sections.heading: Bill Bridges Became the Centerpiece of the Hawks Return
sections.body: Bridges developed into a durable Hawks forward. After 27 games as an NBA rookie in 1962-63, he played 80, 79, 78, 79 and 82 games over the next five St. Louis seasons and earned All-Star recognition in 1966-67 and 1967-68. The rights acquired in this trade therefore became a multi-year starter-level asset rather than a speculative hold.

sections.heading: Chicago Received Limited Long-Term Production
sections.body: Al Ferrari appeared in 18 games for the Chicago Zephyrs in 1962-63 and played only a small role. Shellie McMillon, who had just produced 48 useful games for St. Louis in 1961-62, did not play another NBA season after the trade. Chicago acquired two known players, but the package did not generate anything close to the multi-season value St. Louis received from Bridges.

sections.heading: The Rights Asset Decided the Hindsight Result
sections.body: Ralph Davis was part of the St. Louis return, but Bridges is enough to separate the deal. The Hawks converted a pair of outgoing veterans into a future two-time All-Star who became a major frontcourt piece for years. Chicago received only brief Ferrari production and no post-trade NBA season from McMillon. That difference supports the strong St. Louis grade already attached to the canonical record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis A-, Chicago C. Bill Bridges became a long-term Hawks starter and two-time All-Star, while the outgoing Ferrari-McMillon package produced only limited post-trade NBA value for the Chicago franchise.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Wayne Embry from Cincinnati
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Wayne Embry from the Royals on September 15, 1966. Cincinnati received a 1967 draft pick that became No. 28 selection Sam Smith plus cash.

sections.heading: The Celtics Chose Immediate Frontcourt Help
sections.body: Boston’s side centered on an established veteran rather than waiting on a later draft asset. The B+ grade reflects the useful present-day value Embry supplied to a team still operating in a championship window.

sections.heading: The Royals Received a Pick and Cash
sections.body: Cincinnati gained both the No. 28 selection and financial consideration. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources, and the pick did not create enough realized value to close the gap with Boston’s veteran return.

sections.heading: The Completed Outcome Favors Boston
sections.body: TradeVerdicts assigns Boston a B+ and Cincinnati a D. The Celtics received the more useful basketball asset, while the Royals’ pick-and-cash package did not develop into comparable on-court value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Cincinnati D. Boston acquired Wayne Embry from Royals in exchange for 1967 pick (No. 28, Sam Smith); cash.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Sent LeRoy Ellis to Baltimore for Jim Barnes
sections.body: The Lakers traded LeRoy Ellis to the Bullets for Jim Barnes on September 22, 1966. The deal was a direct frontcourt swap, and both players contributed after changing teams.

sections.heading: Ellis Became a Four-Year Baltimore Regular
sections.body: Ellis played 311 regular-season games for the Bullets. He averaged 14.9 points and 12.0 rebounds in 1966-67, then followed with 12.4 points and 11.1 rebounds the next season.

sections.heading: Barnes Supplied Shorter Lakers Depth
sections.body: Barnes appeared in 122 games for Los Angeles across parts of two seasons, mostly in a reserve role. That was useful value, but the tenure and production were clearly smaller than Baltimore’s return from Ellis.

sections.heading: Baltimore Wins Without Erasing the Lakers’ Return
sections.body: The A for Baltimore and B for Los Angeles capture a clear difference rather than a total mismatch. The Bullets received the stronger multi-season starter while the Lakers still got meaningful frontcourt minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Los Angeles B, Baltimore A. Los Angeles traded LeRoy Ellis to Baltimore for Jim Barnes on September 22, 1966. Ellis became the stronger immediate asset, playing 311 regular-season games for the Bullets over four seasons.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Johnny Austin’s Rights to Baltimore
sections.body: The Celtics sold Johnny Austin’s player rights to the Bullets for cash on October 11, 1966. Team transaction records and Austin’s player history support the rights-sale structure.

sections.heading: Austin’s Baltimore Stay Was Extremely Brief
sections.body: Austin appeared in only four games for the Bullets. The documented player record shows 5.8 points per game on 22.7 percent shooting, leaving Baltimore with very little realized basketball value from the purchase.

sections.heading: Boston Converted the Rights into Cash
sections.body: The Celtics received financial consideration instead of retaining a player who did not become a meaningful NBA contributor for Baltimore. The amount is undisclosed, so the exact value of Boston’s side cannot be calculated.

sections.heading: A Modest Celtics Edge Fits the Evidence
sections.body: Boston’s B versus Baltimore’s C reflects the better realized outcome without overstating an unknown cash sale. The Bullets received only four games, while Boston at least monetized the asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B, Baltimore C. Boston sold Johnny Austin's player rights to Baltimore for cash.

sections.heading: New York Purchased Neil Johnson’s Rights
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Neil Johnson’s player rights from Baltimore for cash on October 31, 1966. The transaction gave New York a reserve big man while the Bullets took an undisclosed financial return.

sections.heading: Johnson Played 94 Games for the Knicks
sections.body: Johnson appeared in 51 games at 3.4 points and 3.3 rebounds during 1966-67, then played 43 more the following season. That produced two seasons of measurable depth from the purchased rights.

sections.heading: Expansion Ended New York’s Control
sections.body: Phoenix selected Johnson from the Knicks in the 1968 expansion draft. New York therefore did not preserve a later trade asset, limiting the long-term upside of the original purchase.

sections.heading: The Knicks Hold a Small Realized Advantage
sections.body: The B- versus C+ split recognizes 94 games of direct basketball value while respecting the unknown cash payment Baltimore received. It is a modest Knicks win, not a major historical swing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — New York B-, Baltimore C+. New York acquired Neil Johnson's player rights from Baltimore for cash on October 31, 1966. Johnson gave the Knicks 94 regular-season games across two seasons, including 51 games at 3.4 points and 3.3 rebounds in 1966-67 and 43 more the next year.

sections.heading: Chicago Swapped Len Chappell for George Wilson
sections.body: The Bulls traded Len Chappell to Cincinnati for George Wilson on November 25, 1966. Both incoming players appeared in the NBA after the deal, making this a comparison of short-term rotation returns.

sections.heading: Wilson Played 43 Games Before the Expansion Draft
sections.body: Wilson averaged 4.6 points and 3.8 rebounds in 10.4 minutes across 43 Bulls games. Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft, ending Chicago’s control after less than a season.

sections.heading: Chappell Lasted Longer with Cincinnati
sections.body: Chappell gave the Royals 54 games that season and 10 more in 1967-68. The extra games create a modest realized advantage, although Cincinnati also moved on without preserving a major downstream asset.

sections.heading: The Royals Edge Is Narrow
sections.body: Cincinnati’s B- against Chicago’s C+ reflects the slightly larger direct return. Neither side secured a long-term piece, so the grades stay close rather than turning a brief player swap into a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Royals Edge — Chicago C+, Cincinnati B-. Chicago traded Len Chappell to Cincinnati for George Wilson on November 25, 1966. Wilson played 43 games for the Bulls after the trade, averaging 4.6 points and 3.8 rebounds in 10.4 minutes, before Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft.

sections.heading: Three Teams Reworked Their Frontcourts in January 1967
sections.body: The January 16 deal sent Mel Counts from Baltimore to Los Angeles, Ray Scott from Detroit to Baltimore, and Rudy LaRusso plus a compensatory 1967 first-round pick from the Lakers to Detroit after LaRusso refused to report.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received the Best Direct Player Return
sections.body: Scott played 263 games for the Bullets through 1969-70. He averaged 19.0 points and 13.2 rebounds immediately after the trade, then 16.4 points and 13.7 rebounds the following season.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Also Landed Sustained Production
sections.body: Counts played 271 Lakers games through 1969-70, giving Los Angeles a strong multi-year return. That explains the Lakers’ A- despite Baltimore holding the highest grade in the transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Package Did Not Convert as Well
sections.body: Detroit received 57 games from No. 4 pick Sonny Dove and later sold LaRusso’s rights to San Francisco. The A for Baltimore, A- for Los Angeles and C+ for Detroit reflect the much stronger realized production on the other two sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Baltimore A, Los Angeles A-, Detroit C+. The January 16, 1967 three-team trade sent Mel Counts from Baltimore to Los Angeles, Ray Scott from Detroit to Baltimore, and Rudy LaRusso plus a compensatory 1967 first-round pick from the Lakers to Detroit after LaRusso refused to report. Baltimore realized the strongest direct return: Scott played 263 Bullets games through 1969-70, including 19.0 points and 13.2 rebounds immediately after the trade and 16.4 points with 13.7 rebounds the next season.

sections.heading: Indiana Sold Goose Ligon’s Rights to Kentucky
sections.body: The Pacers sold Goose Ligon’s player rights to the Kentucky Colonels for cash on July 22, 1967. The Pacers and Colonels transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure, and Kentucky signed Ligon the next day.

sections.heading: Ligon Became an Early ABA Standout
sections.body: Ligon played 78 games at 16.2 points and 11.9 rebounds in 1967-68, then appeared in 75 games the next season and earned an ABA All-Star selection. He played all 84 games in 1969-70.

sections.heading: Indiana’s Financial Return Is Unknown
sections.body: The Pacers received cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the public transaction record. Without that figure, the Indiana side can only be measured as a sale that surrendered three seasons of high-level production.

sections.heading: Kentucky Created the Clearer Value
sections.body: The Colonels’ A against Indiana’s C reflects three full seasons from a major early-ABA contributor. The unknown sale price prevents a harsher Pacers grade, but the basketball return decisively favors Kentucky.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Colonels Win — Indiana C, Kentucky A. Indiana sold Goose Ligon's rights to the Kentucky Colonels for cash on July 22, 1967. The Pacers and Colonels transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure, and Kentucky signed Ligon the next day.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Steve Chubin to Anaheim for Cash
sections.body: The Denver Rockets sold Steve Chubin to the Anaheim Amigos on October 12, 1967, one day before the inaugural ABA season began. Denver received cash while Anaheim acquired a guard who immediately became one of its primary offensive players.

sections.heading: Chubin Produced an Excellent First ABA Season
sections.body: Chubin played 77 games for the Amigos and averaged 18.2 points, 5.6 rebounds and 4.7 assists in 31.7 minutes per game. For a franchise that existed in Anaheim for only one season, that was a major realized return from a simple cash purchase.

sections.heading: Denver’s Return Cannot Be Precisely Valued
sections.body: The Rockets received undisclosed cash and no on-court asset from the transaction itself. The missing amount keeps Denver’s C from being treated as a total loss even though there is no comparable basketball production to measure.

sections.heading: Anaheim Clearly Won on Realized Value
sections.body: The Amigos’ A against Denver’s C reflects the quality and volume of Chubin’s season. Anaheim acquired a leading contributor immediately, while Denver’s financial return remains unknown.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Amigos Win — Denver C, Anaheim A. Denver sold Steve Chubin to the Anaheim Amigos for cash on October 12, 1967, one day before the inaugural ABA season began. Anaheim immediately turned the purchase into one of the strongest player returns in its one-season franchise history.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Bobby Lloyd for a Future Pick
sections.body: The New Jersey Americans acquired Bobby Lloyd from the Pittsburgh Pipers for a future draft choice on October 15, 1967 and signed him the same day. The surviving transaction ledgers do not identify the year or round of Pittsburgh’s pick.

sections.heading: Lloyd Gave the Americans Two Seasons
sections.body: Lloyd played 58 games as a rookie, averaging 8.1 points in 17.2 minutes, then returned for 67 games with the renamed New York Americans at 9.9 points per game. That produced 125 franchise appearances from the acquired player.

sections.heading: Pittsburgh’s Draft Return Is Unresolved
sections.body: The Pipers received a future draft choice, but its year, round and realized outcome are not identified in the available ledgers. That uncertainty prevents the Pittsburgh side from being graded as if the pick had no value.

sections.heading: The Documented Return Favors the Nets Franchise
sections.body: New Jersey’s B+ against Pittsburgh’s C reflects the 125 known games Lloyd supplied. The result is a clear edge rather than an overwhelming win because the final value of the future pick cannot be reconstructed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New Jersey B+, Pittsburgh C. New Jersey acquired Bobby Lloyd from the Pittsburgh Pipers for a future draft choice on October 15, 1967 and signed him the same day. Lloyd gave the Americans 58 games as a rookie, averaging 8.1 points in 17.2 minutes, then returned for 67 games with the renamed New York Americans in 1968-69 at 9.9 points per game.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Gary Keller to Minnesota
sections.body: The Rockets sold Gary Keller to the Minnesota Muskies for cash on October 16, 1967. Minnesota acquired a frontcourt player who immediately entered the rotation during the ABA’s inaugural season.

sections.heading: Keller Stayed with the Franchise Through Its Move
sections.body: Keller played 69 games for Minnesota at 7.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.6 minutes, then followed the franchise to Miami and added 53 games in 1968-69. The purchase therefore produced 122 regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Denver Received Only an Undisclosed Financial Return
sections.body: The Rockets received cash but no traceable on-court asset from the sale itself. Because the amount is unknown, Denver’s side cannot be compared dollar-for-dollar with the production Minnesota and Miami received.

sections.heading: The Muskies-Floridians Franchise Earns the Edge
sections.body: The B+ versus C split recognizes two seasons of useful depth from Keller. Denver did monetize the asset, but the measurable basketball return clearly belongs to Minnesota and its successor franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Muskies Win — Denver C, Minnesota/Miami B+. Denver sold Gary Keller to the Minnesota Muskies for cash on October 16, 1967. Minnesota turned the purchase into 69 regular-season games in the ABA's inaugural season, with Keller averaging 7.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.6 minutes per game.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent Guy Rodgers to Cincinnati for a Package
sections.body: The Bulls traded Guy Rodgers to the Royals on October 20, 1967 for Flynn Robinson, second-round picks in 1968 and 1969, and cash. Chicago received multiple chances to create value while Cincinnati consolidated the exchange into the veteran guard.

sections.heading: Robinson Became the Immediate Bulls Return
sections.body: Robinson played 91 games for Chicago, averaging 16.0 points in 73 games in 1967-68 and 19.1 points in 18 more before a 1968 trade to Milwaukee. He supplied meaningful production before becoming another movable asset.

sections.heading: One Draft Pick Also Turned into Johnny Baum
sections.body: The 1969 second-round pick became Johnny Baum, who added 65 Bulls games. The 1968 selection became Ron Dunlap and produced no NBA games, so the draft portion of the package was mixed rather than uniformly successful.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Depth Beats Cincinnati’s Short Rodgers Tenure
sections.body: Rodgers played 75 games for Cincinnati before Milwaukee selected him in the 1968 expansion draft. Chicago’s A- versus Cincinnati’s B- reflects the deeper package and additional realized assets the Bulls preserved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-, Cincinnati B-. Chicago traded Guy Rodgers to Cincinnati on October 20, 1967 for Flynn Robinson, second-round picks in 1968 and 1969, and cash. Robinson gave the Bulls 91 regular-season games, averaging 16.0 points in 73 games in 1967-68 and 19.1 points in 18 more before a 1968 trade to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: The Verified Heyman-Leibowitz Trade Occurred on December 2
sections.body: New Jersey traded Art Heyman to Pittsburgh for Barry Leibowitz on December 2, 1967, correcting the legacy November 29 date and spelling. Both players became immediate contributors after the exchange.

sections.heading: Heyman Helped Power the ABA Champion Pipers
sections.body: Heyman played 54 regular-season games for Pittsburgh at 20.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 4.4 assists, then added 15 playoff games at 18.9 points. That made him a major part of the Pipers’ championship season.

sections.heading: New Jersey Preserved Value Beyond Leibowitz
sections.body: Leibowitz played 24 games for the Americans at 11.4 points before being traded to Oakland for Levern Tart. Tart then gave the franchise 31 games at 19.0 points and another 35 games the next season.

sections.heading: Pittsburgh Wins, but New Jersey’s Chain Was Strong
sections.body: The A- versus B+ grades capture a narrow but meaningful difference. Heyman delivered championship-level immediate value, while New Jersey still converted its return into another productive scorer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pipers Win — New Jersey B+, Pittsburgh A-. New Jersey traded Art Heyman to Pittsburgh for Barry Leibowitz on December 2, 1967, correcting the legacy November 29 date and spelling. Heyman became a major contributor to the ABA champion Pipers, playing 54 regular-season games at 20.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 4.4 assists plus 15 playoff games at 18.9 points.
