sections.heading: New York Bought Dennis Grey from Los Angeles
sections.body: The New York Nets acquired Dennis Grey from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on September 19, 1969. Grey had averaged 9.1 points and 5.5 rebounds in 58 games for Los Angeles as a rookie.

sections.heading: Grey’s Nets Stint Was Extremely Brief
sections.body: He appeared in only four games for New York, totaling 74 minutes, 18 points and 25 rebounds. The Nets therefore received only a small amount of realized basketball value from the purchase.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Stars’ financial return is not identified in the available transaction record. Without the amount, it cannot be compared precisely against four games of Grey production.

sections.heading: The Evidence Does Not Support a Clear Winner
sections.body: Both sides received something, but neither return can be shown to be meaningfully stronger. Equal C grades and an Even Trade verdict fit a transaction with limited measurable value on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New York Nets C, Los Angeles Stars C. New York acquired Dennis Grey from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on September 19, 1969. Grey had averaged 9.1 points and 5.5 rebounds in 58 games for Los Angeles as a rookie, but his Nets stint was brief: four games, 74 minutes, 18 points and 25 rebounds in 1969-70.

sections.heading: Atlanta Took a Low-Cost Shot on Gene Tormohlen
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Gene Tormohlen from Phoenix for a 1970 third-round pick that became Vann Williford at No. 48. The structure was simple: the Hawks traded a future selection for a veteran attempting to return after a year away.

sections.heading: Tormohlen’s Comeback Barely Reached the Court
sections.body: Tormohlen played only two games and 11 total minutes for Atlanta before his NBA career ended. The Hawks therefore received almost no measurable on-court return from the acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix’s Pick Also Produced No NBA Value
sections.body: The Suns used the selection on Williford, but he never appeared in the NBA. He later played 38 ABA games for Carolina, which does not count as realized Phoenix value from the draft pick.

sections.heading: Neither Side Converted the Asset into Meaningful Value
sections.body: With Atlanta receiving two brief appearances and Phoenix receiving a drafted player who never played for the Suns, the completed NBA return is minimal on both sides. Equal C grades fit the lack of durable value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Atlanta C, Phoenix C. Atlanta acquired Gene Tormohlen from Phoenix on September 20, 1969 for a 1970 third-round pick that became Vann Williford at No. 48.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired Fred Hetzel for Craig Raymond and a Pick
sections.body: Philadelphia obtained Fred Hetzel from Cincinnati in early October 1969 for Craig Raymond and a future second-round selection. The strongest team and league ledgers point to October 4, one day later than the legacy TradeVerdicts date.

sections.heading: Hetzel Gave Philadelphia a Full Season of Rotation Value
sections.body: Hetzel played 63 games for the 76ers, averaging 6.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 12.0 minutes per game. Portland selected him in the 1970 expansion draft, so Philadelphia’s return was useful but limited to one season.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Got No Games from Raymond
sections.body: The Royals waived Raymond within a week of the trade. The future second-round pick is confirmed by a Cincinnati media guide, but the exact year and eventual player remain unresolved in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: The Measurable Return Favors Philadelphia
sections.body: Philadelphia received known NBA production while Cincinnati’s known player return disappeared almost immediately and the pick cannot yet be traced confidently. A B- for the 76ers and C for Cincinnati reflects that evidence gap without overstating the win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Cincinnati C, Philadelphia B-. Philadelphia acquired Fred Hetzel from Cincinnati in early October 1969 for Craig Raymond and a future second-round pick. The strongest team and league ledgers date the trade October 4, while the legacy TradeVerdicts record and Pro Sports Transactions use October 3.

sections.heading: Indiana Took Three Players from Carolina
sections.body: The Pacers acquired Art Becker, Spider Bennett and Tony Jackson from the Carolina Cougars for George Peeples and Ron Perry. The five-player exchange gave both ABA teams multiple paths to realize value.

sections.heading: Becker Was Indiana’s Only Meaningful Direct Return
sections.body: Becker played all 82 games for the 1970 ABA champions and 51 more the following season before Indiana moved him to Denver. Bennett and Jackson never played a game for the Pacers after the trade.

sections.heading: Carolina Received the Stronger Long-Term Package
sections.body: Peeples played 165 games over two Cougars seasons and averaged 11.7 points with 9.4 rebounds in 1970-71. Perry lasted 19 games but was flipped for Larry Miller, creating an additional productive asset chain.

sections.heading: The Cougars Built More Durable Value
sections.body: Indiana got a championship-season contributor in Becker, but Carolina extracted more games, more production and a downstream return from its package. The A- versus B+ split gives the Cougars a narrow but real edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cougars Win — Indiana B+, Carolina A-. Indiana acquired Art Becker, Spider Bennett and Tony Jackson from the Carolina Cougars on October 9, 1969 for George Peeples and Ron Perry. Becker became the only meaningful direct Pacers return, playing all 82 games for the 1970 ABA champions and 51 more the next season before Indiana moved him to Denver.

sections.heading: Detroit Sent Dave Gambee to San Francisco for a Future Pick
sections.body: San Francisco acquired veteran forward Dave Gambee from Detroit on October 10, 1969 for a future draft choice. Team, league and Warriors media-guide records all confirm the player-for-pick structure.

sections.heading: Gambee Supplied One Known Warriors Season
sections.body: Gambee played 73 games for San Francisco in 1969-70, totaling 951 minutes while averaging 7.2 points and 3.3 rebounds. That gives the Warriors side a clear measurable return.

sections.heading: The Detroit Pick Cannot Be Identified Reliably
sections.body: The reviewed public sources do not establish the year, selection number or eventual player tied to Detroit’s future draft choice. Without that identity, the Pistons side cannot be evaluated on equal terms.

sections.heading: The Responsible Outcome Is No Grade
sections.body: A known one-season player return is not enough to declare a winner when the opposing draft asset remains unresolved. The record stays at Insufficient Evidence until the pick can be tied to a verified downstream outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence San Francisco acquired veteran forward Dave Gambee from Detroit on October 10, 1969 for a future draft pick. Detroit, San Francisco and NBA transaction ledgers all confirm the player-for-pick structure, and the Warriors' official media guide independently records Gambee's acquisition for a draft choice.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On March 24, 1970, the ABA New York Nets acquired the contractual rights to Jim McMillian from the Los Angeles Stars. New York sent Los Angeles a future draft pick. Pro Sports Transactions records the player-rights-for-pick structure but leaves the future pick's year and round unidentified. Its ABA draft ledger also shows that the Stars had selected McMillian in the second round, 15th overall, of the 1970 ABA draft.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body:
McMillian was a valuable basketball player, but that is different from the value of the ABA rights New York acquired. He did not play for the Nets. The NBA's Los Angeles Lakers selected him 13th overall in the 1970 NBA draft, and he began his NBA career that fall. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA debut as October 16, 1970 and credits him with 631 regular-season games over nine seasons.

His NBA production underscores what the Nets hoped to acquire. McMillian played 81 games as a Lakers rookie in 1970-71, averaging 8.4 points and 4.1 rebounds. A year later he played 80 games and averaged 18.8 points and 6.5 rebounds for the 1971-72 Lakers. He became an important scorer on a championship team and later continued his career with Buffalo, New York and Portland.

For this ABA transaction, however, none of that production became a Nets return. New York held rights to a good player who chose the NBA path. TradeVerdicts therefore separates McMillian's career value from the realized value of the rights asset: the player succeeded, but the Nets did not receive his games.

sections.heading: Stars Return
sections.body:
Los Angeles received a future draft pick. The surviving transaction entry does not specify the draft year, round, selection number or player outcome. That gap matters. It would be misleading to assign the Stars a particular player or to credit them with later production that cannot be traced to this pick.

Even with the outcome unresolved, the Stars did convert an ABA rights asset they did not ultimately use into another piece of draft capital. That is a more tangible transaction result than New York's rights, which never became an ABA appearance. The value cannot be graded aggressively because the pick may have produced little or nothing; the historical record simply does not establish the final result.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The transaction is unusual because the best player involved had a productive career outside the league in which the trade occurred. McMillian's Lakers career shows that Los Angeles had drafted a legitimate prospect, but the Nets' acquired rights never converted into on-court ABA value. The Stars at least received a future pick, although the unidentified outcome prevents a complete realized-value comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Stars Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ for converting McMillian's unused ABA rights into future draft capital. New York receives a C because the rights did not produce a Nets appearance, even though the player himself became a strong NBA contributor. Confidence is medium on the verdict: the March 24 transaction and McMillian's career path are well supported, but the future pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed records. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On April 15, 1970, the San Diego Rockets sold the player rights to Don Kojis to the Seattle SuperSonics. Basketball-Reference lists the move from both team perspectives and in the league transaction log. RealGM also records Seattle acquiring Kojis from San Diego on that date. The reviewed sources establish the transfer, but none publishes the sale price. TradeVerdicts therefore keeps the Rockets' return as cash with the amount unknown.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body:
Kojis was already an established NBA forward. He had made the All-Star team in 1967-68 and 1968-69 with San Diego, then averaged 15.3 points and 6.9 rebounds in 56 games during 1969-70. Seattle was not buying a speculative prospect. It was acquiring the rights to a veteran who had recently been one of San Diego's leading scorers.

The move produced immediate usable value. Kojis played 79 games for Seattle in 1970-71, averaging 14.6 points, 5.5 rebounds and 27.1 minutes. He remained in the rotation the next season, appearing in 73 games and averaging 11.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 25.4 minutes. Across the two seasons, that is 152 regular-season appearances and nearly 4,000 minutes from the purchased rights.

Seattle later moved Kojis in August 1972 as part of a separate transaction with Kansas City-Omaha. This verdict does not assign the entire value of that later package back to the 1970 sale because Kojis was bundled with another player. The direct return is already enough to judge the original purchase: Seattle received two seasons of dependable rotation production.

sections.heading: San Diego Return
sections.body:
San Diego received cash. That asset should not be treated as worthless, especially in an era when player sales were a normal roster-management tool. The problem is documentation, not the existence of value. Without a verified sale price, there is no responsible way to compare the financial return with a player contract, draft choice or later on-court production.

That uncertainty is why the Rockets are not given a failing grade. They monetized the rights to a 31-year-old veteran after a season in which he played 56 games. But the surviving basketball record shows exactly what Seattle received, while the cash side cannot be quantified from the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Seattle's advantage is the clearest part of the record. The SuperSonics turned the purchased rights into 152 games, 1,989 points and 770 rebounds over two seasons. Kojis was not a franchise-changing acquisition, but he was a regular contributor on teams that improved from 38 wins in 1970-71 to 47 wins in 1971-72.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win. Seattle Win, B/C. Seattle receives a B for obtaining two productive veteran seasons for an undisclosed cash price. San Diego receives a C because the club did receive a real asset, but the amount is unknown and there is no documented basketball return to compare with Kojis' Seattle production. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction and player value, but only medium on the overall economic comparison because the sale price remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On April 23, 1970, the Chicago Bulls traded Clem Haskins to the Phoenix Suns for center Jim Fox and a 1971 second-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the date and package. The pick became Villanova forward Howard Porter at No. 32 overall. The source-backed review also resolves the legacy 'Jim Fox / Sonny Fox' identity to NBA center Jim Fox, whose Basketball-Reference identifier is foxji01.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body:
Haskins was the best immediate player in the transaction. He had just completed an 82-game Chicago season with 1,668 points and 624 assists. In Phoenix he played 82 games in 1970-71 and averaged 17.8 points, 4.7 assists and 4.0 rebounds. He followed with 79 games at 15.7 points in 1971-72, then remained with the Suns for 77 games in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74. That is 319 regular-season games across four Phoenix seasons.

Haskins' role declined after his first two Suns seasons, but Phoenix still received sustained guard production rather than a short rental. Across his four years with the club he logged 8,620 minutes. That direct longevity is the strongest part of the Suns' case and makes the legacy Bulls-win language too simplistic if the evaluation stops at the first transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body:
Fox gave Chicago a useful first season. He played all 82 games in 1970-71, averaging 9.7 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 19.9 minutes. He appeared in 10 more Bulls games the following season before Chicago moved him on November 9, 1971. Porter, selected with the acquired second-round pick, played 67 games as a rookie and 43 more in 1972-73. His Chicago role was modest, at 6.0 points per game in his first season and 5.1 in his second, but the pick still produced 110 NBA appearances for the Bulls.

Fox's later trade is what changes the hindsight comparison. Chicago sent Fox and a 1972 second-round pick to Cincinnati for Norm Van Lier and a 1972 third-round pick. Van Lier then played 535 regular-season games across seven Bulls seasons. During that Chicago tenure he made three All-Star teams, earned an All-NBA Second Team selection in 1973-74 and repeatedly appeared on the All-Defensive teams. The 1970 trade did not acquire Van Lier directly, and Chicago had to add another pick in 1971, so the full value of Van Lier cannot be credited to Phoenix's original assets. Fox nevertheless remained a meaningful component of the deal that brought him back.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
If the trade is judged only by direct post-trade games, Phoenix has the stronger side: Haskins delivered 319 Suns games, while Fox and Porter combined for 202 Bulls games. Chicago's package becomes more valuable when the later disposition of Fox is traced. He was not simply lost; he helped form the package for Van Lier, who became a long-term Chicago point guard and one of the league's leading defensive guards of the era. Porter also supplied two seasons from a second-round selection.

The later Van Lier exchange prevents a simple direct-production verdict. Chicago had to attach an additional second-round pick, and it also received a third-round pick, so Van Lier's entire seven-year Bulls career is not attributable to Fox alone. Even with that discount, Fox's retained trade value plus Porter's 110 games pushes Chicago's long-term realized package ahead of Phoenix's very good Haskins return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A-/B+. Chicago receives an A- for one useful Fox season, 110 games from the acquired draft pick and the important downstream role Fox played in the trade that brought Norm Van Lier back to Chicago. Phoenix receives a B+ for four productive Haskins seasons and 319 regular-season games, including two years of high-level scoring and playmaking. The gap is narrower than the legacy verdict suggested because Haskins clearly outperformed Fox and Porter on direct value. Confidence is high on the transaction, identities and player production, and medium-high on the final comparative grade because downstream value requires an attribution discount. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: The Los Angeles Lakers sent Mel Counts to the Phoenix Suns for Gail Goodrich in May 1970. The package itself is unanimous across the reviewed sources, but the exact date is not. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Suns and league transaction ledgers all list May 20, and RealGM also uses May 20. Pro Sports Transactions lists May 21, which matches the existing TradeVerdicts route date. This review preserves the May 21 canonical route and records the one-day source conflict rather than silently changing a live identifier.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body:
Goodrich returned to the franchise that had drafted him in 1965 after Phoenix had selected him in the 1968 expansion draft. His first season back was already productive: 79 games, 17.5 points and 4.8 assists per game in 1970-71. One year later he became the leading scorer on one of the most famous teams in league history. Goodrich averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games for the 1971-72 Lakers, narrowly leading Jerry West in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, produced a 33-game winning streak and captured the NBA championship.

The return lasted far beyond that title season. Goodrich made four consecutive All-Star teams from 1972 through 1975 and led the Lakers in scoring for four straight seasons from 1971-72 through 1974-75. He averaged 23.9 points in 1972-73, 25.3 in 1973-74 and 22.6 in 1974-75, then added 19.5 points and 5.6 assists in his final Lakers season in 1975-76. The franchise later retired his No. 25, and Goodrich was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.
Phoenix Return

Counts gave Phoenix legitimate frontcourt depth rather than disappearing after the trade. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 6.3 rebounds and 20.9 minutes. In 1971-72 he appeared in 76 more games, although his role fell to 11.9 minutes and 5.2 points per game. Across the two Suns seasons, Counts supplied 156 regular-season appearances and more than 2,500 minutes.

That production keeps Phoenix from receiving a failing grade. Counts was a veteran seven-footer who could score and rebound in a reserve role, and he remained available nearly every night. But Phoenix had just received two strong Goodrich seasons before making the deal, including a 20.0-point, 7.5-assist campaign in 1969-70. Trading that 27-year-old guard for a useful but lower-impact veteran center created a large long-term opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
The direct realized return is decisive. Counts gave Phoenix two useful seasons; Goodrich gave Los Angeles six, four All-Star selections and the highest scoring average on the 1972 champions. In the 1972 postseason he averaged 23.8 points across all 15 games as the Lakers won the title. The Lakers then continued to receive high-volume scoring from him through the middle of the decade.

This is also a case where no elaborate downstream chain is needed to establish the result. The acquired player himself produced the value. Phoenix's return was real, but the difference in role, longevity and championship contribution is too large to call the trade close.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A+/C+. Los Angeles receives an A+ for reacquiring a Hall of Fame guard who became a four-time All-Star during his second Lakers tenure, led the 1972 champions in regular-season scoring and remained a major offensive piece for six seasons. Phoenix receives a C+ for 156 games of useful center depth from Counts, with the grade recognizing that he was productive even though the Suns surrendered the much more valuable player. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes and medium-high overall because the historical transaction ledgers disagree by one day on the date. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On June 17, 1970, the Atlanta Hawks traded Gary Gregor to the expansion Portland Trail Blazers for Jerry Chambers. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, Atlanta transaction log, Portland executive register and team-to-team trade ledger agree on the date and one-for-one package. Portland had selected Chambers from Phoenix in the expansion draft only weeks earlier, so the deal immediately converted one expansion selection into a younger frontcourt piece with recent Atlanta experience.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body:
Gregor became a regular part of Portland's first two rosters. In 1970-71 he appeared in 44 games and averaged 13.1 points and 10.4 rebounds per 36 minutes. His larger contribution came in 1971-72, when he played all 82 games and averaged 11.1 points, 7.2 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 28.9 minutes. Across the two Portland seasons, Basketball-Reference's trade ledger credits him with 126 games, 10.6 points, 7.3 rebounds, 2.1 assists and 2.5 win shares.

Portland also retained a small amount of value after Gregor left. Philadelphia signed him as a veteran free agent on September 11, 1972 and sent Portland a 1974 second-round pick as compensation. The Trail Blazers used that selection at No. 36 on Rubin Collins, who never appeared in an NBA game. The compensation therefore matters as a verified asset outcome, but it does not add realized player production to the original trade.
Atlanta Return

Chambers gave Atlanta one useful season. He played 65 games in 1970-71, averaging 8.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 18.0 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits 1.5 win shares from that season, and he also appeared in four playoff games. The role was smaller than Gregor's eventual Portland role, but Chambers was not a zero-value acquisition.

Atlanta moved Chambers again on July 26, 1971, packaging him with Walt Hazzard to Buffalo for Herm Gilliam and Don May. That later transaction preserves some downstream value, but Chambers cannot responsibly be credited with the entire Gilliam-May return because Hazzard was bundled with him. The same attribution rule used elsewhere in the archive prevents a secondary package from being counted as if Atlanta had obtained both players solely for Chambers.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
The direct comparison favors Portland. Gregor played 126 games for the Trail Blazers to Chambers' 65 for Atlanta, and the trade-partner ledger gives Portland 2.5 future win shares against Atlanta's 1.5. Gregor also carried enough value after his Portland tenure to trigger a second-round compensation pick when Philadelphia signed him. Collins never reached the NBA, so that pick does not transform the deal, but it still extends Portland's asset chain beyond Gregor's two seasons.

Atlanta received a useful reserve season and later included Chambers in another trade, which keeps the Hawks' return respectable. Portland simply received more playing time, more aggregate production and one additional verified asset. The gap is real without being large enough to treat Atlanta's side as a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, B/C+. Portland receives a B for two productive Gregor seasons, 126 games and the later veteran-free-agent compensation pick. Atlanta receives a C+ for 65 useful Chambers games and some downstream package value before his departure. Confidence is high because the transaction date, player production and subsequent transactions are consistently documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On June 18, 1970, the Denver Rockets traded Larry Jones, Greg Wittman and a 1971 second-round draft choice to the Miami Floridians for Larry Cannon, Don Sidle and Miami's 1971 first-round choice. Basketball-Reference's ABA transaction ledger, Denver transaction log and Floridians transaction log all describe the same six-asset exchange. Pro Sports Transactions resolves the incoming first-round pick as No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft, used on Ken Durrett, while Denver's outgoing second-round pick remains listed without a verified player outcome.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body:
Cannon produced the best single season on Denver's side. In 1970-71 he played 80 games, averaged 26.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 5.2 assists, posted 7.2 win shares and made the All-ABA Second Team. That is substantial immediate value from a player who had averaged 11.8 points as a Miami rookie. Cannon did not extend the return into a second Denver regular season, however; he signed with Memphis in October 1971.

Sidle also helped right away. He played 54 Denver games in 1970-71 and averaged 16.1 points and 9.0 rebounds with 4.2 win shares. Denver traded Sidle with Wayne Chapman to Indiana on February 1, 1971 for John Barnhill and Art Becker. That downstream exchange preserved asset value, but Sidle cannot be credited with the entire Barnhill-Becker return because Chapman was part of the package.

The first-round pick became Ken Durrett at No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft. Denver moved Durrett's rights to Virginia on January 22, 1971 for another 1971 first-round choice and a player to be named later or cash. Pro Sports Transactions identifies that replacement first-rounder as No. 5 Cliff Meely. Meely played in the NBA rather than for Denver in the ABA, so the original Miami pick did not generate realized Denver player production through that branch.
Floridians Return

Jones was the most durable and productive long-term player in the deal. He played all 84 games for the Floridians in 1970-71, averaging 24.3 points, 5.4 rebounds and 4.6 assists in 43.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star Game, finished seventh in MVP voting and produced 8.8 win shares. Jones followed with 66 games in 1971-72 at 17.6 points, 4.7 rebounds and 3.2 assists, adding 8.1 win shares. Across two Florida seasons, that is 150 games, 21.4 points, 5.1 rebounds, 4.0 assists and 16.9 win shares per Basketball-Reference.

Wittman contributed only five Floridians games before Miami traded him and a draft choice to Texas for Charlie Beasley on October 26, 1970. His direct production was minimal, and the unidentified Denver second-round pick cannot be assigned an invented player outcome. Florida therefore wins this comparison because of Jones rather than because every piece of its package paid off.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
Denver got real value. Cannon's 1970-71 season was excellent and Sidle supplied another productive frontcourt season before being moved. Combined, those two players gave Denver 134 regular-season games and 11.4 win shares in 1970-71. The problem is duration. Cannon left after one Denver season, Sidle was traded during that same campaign, and the first-round-pick branch did not lead to a player who appeared for Denver.

Jones alone gave Florida 150 games and 16.9 win shares over two seasons, while also delivering an All-Star season and a top-seven MVP finish in the first year. That longer direct return outweighs Denver's two-player burst even before Wittman's small contribution is considered. The original record's slight-Denver-edge framing was therefore too favorable to the Rockets once the realized player outcomes are measured.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Floridians Win, A-/B+. Florida receives an A- because Jones supplied two strong seasons, 150 games and 16.9 win shares, including an All-Star year immediately after the trade. Denver receives a B+ for Cannon's All-ABA season, Sidle's useful 54-game run and a first-round asset that retained transaction value even though its eventual rights chain did not produce Denver games. Confidence is high on the trade package, direct production and first-round pick identity; the outgoing Denver second-round pick remains an unresolved historical outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On June 20, 1970, the defending champion New York Knicks sent Nate Bowman and Mike Silliman to the expansion Buffalo Braves. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, Knicks transaction page and executive records describe Buffalo's return as cash. Contemporary and franchise media guides complicate the paperwork: Buffalo's 1971 guide says Silliman was acquired for future considerations, while a later Clippers franchise guide says Bowman and Silliman came for future considerations or a future draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions preserves still more alternate wording. Those entries describe competing versions of the same return, not four separate assets, so this review consolidates them into one disputed non-player consideration rather than counting each alternative.

sections.heading: Buffalo Return
sections.body:
Bowman gave the new franchise 44 games in 1970-71. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 3.1 points, 3.9 rebounds and 0.9 assists while producing 0.0 win shares in Basketball-Reference's accounting. The role was larger than his final Knicks season only at the margins: Buffalo needed frontcourt bodies, but Bob Kauffman, John Hummer and Cornell Warner handled far more of the meaningful center and forward workload. Bowman left Buffalo as a free agent after the season and played 18 ABA games for Pittsburgh in 1971-72, so the Braves did not receive a downstream trade asset.

Silliman was a different kind of gamble. New York had drafted the West Point forward in 1966, but military service delayed his NBA debut until Buffalo acquired his rights. The Braves' 1971 media guide highlighted his Army career and 1968 Olympic gold-medal captaincy, while also noting a toe operation before his rookie season. He ultimately played 36 games, averaging 10.2 minutes, 2.5 points, 1.7 rebounds and 0.6 assists with 0.3 win shares. He became a free agent after that single NBA season.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: The Knicks' exact compensation cannot be reproduced with enough certainty to pretend the historical record is cleaner than it is. Basketball-Reference and executive logs say cash. Buffalo's contemporary media guide uses future considerations for Silliman, and the later Clippers franchise guide describes the combined acquisition as future considerations or a future draft choice. No verified player outcome or durable downstream asset was identified from that consideration in this research pass. The archive therefore records a single disputed non-player return and does not convert alternate source wording into multiple assets.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
Buffalo received 80 combined regular-season games and 849 minutes from Bowman and Silliman, but only 0.3 combined win shares. Both were gone after the Braves' inaugural season. New York, meanwhile, moved fringe depth after a championship season and received some form of non-player consideration without giving up a player who became a long-term Buffalo building block.

That makes the original slight-Knicks verdict too confident, but it also does not justify swinging the result toward Buffalo. The Braves got usable roster bodies for year one; the Knicks shed two low-impact assets for compensation whose precise form remains disputed. Neither side created durable realized value from the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C+/C+. Buffalo receives a C+ for 80 combined games from Bowman and Silliman, but neither player became a lasting piece and their combined impact was minimal. New York receives a C+ for turning fringe depth into a non-player consideration without losing meaningful long-term production. Confidence is medium because the June 20 date and player movement are well documented while the exact return conflicts across historical sources. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Denver and Kentucky completed a two-stage ABA transaction. On July 14, 1970, the Rockets sent the rights to Walt Piatkowski to the Colonels for future considerations. Denver's team transaction ledger, Kentucky's ledger and the ABA league log all record the same deal. Kentucky's ledger then identifies the future consideration on October 2: Wayne Chapman was sent to Denver. Pro Sports Transactions independently preserves the same July exchange and October completion, so the asset routing and timing are well supported.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body:
Chapman gave Denver actual rotation value. In 47 games for the 1970-71 Rockets, he averaged 22.3 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Basketball-Reference records 1,049 minutes and 468 points for his Denver stint. The efficiency was limited, but this was not a token appearance or an unrealized right; Chapman played a regular role for more than half a season. Denver's own 1971 media guide described him as a defensive and outside-shooting depth piece acquired from Kentucky before the season.

Chapman also retained some downstream transaction utility. On February 1, 1971, Denver packaged him with Don Sidle and sent both to Indiana for John Barnhill and Art Becker. Because that was a two-for-two trade, the later return cannot be credited to Chapman alone, but his inclusion confirms that Denver still held a movable player asset after receiving the future consideration. That secondary value is useful context without inflating his direct production.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body:
Kentucky received Piatkowski's rights after he had played two seasons for Denver. The timing proved unfavorable. Basketball-Reference records that Piatkowski did not play in 1970-71 because he retired and worked as a teacher. He never appeared for the Colonels. He briefly returned to the ABA in 1971-72, but those six games came with the Floridians, not Kentucky, and therefore did not create realized value for the Colonels from this transaction.

That distinction is important for a rights trade. Piatkowski had been an actual ABA contributor before July 1970, so Kentucky was not acquiring a meaningless name. In hindsight, though, the rights never became a Kentucky roster contribution, while the player sent later as the consideration became an immediate Denver rotation piece.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The gap is real but not enormous. Chapman scored 468 points in 47 Denver games and remained tradeable into February, which gives the Rockets a concrete return. His poor shooting efficiency and short stay prevent the acquisition from becoming a major win. Kentucky, meanwhile, received no games from Piatkowski and no documented downstream asset from his rights. The Colonels' side therefore falls below an even grade despite Piatkowski's prior ABA track record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver Nuggets Win, C+/D. Denver receives a C+ for more than half a season of useful rotation minutes from Chapman plus limited residual trade value. Kentucky receives a D because Piatkowski retired for the entire 1970-71 season, never played for the Colonels and later resurfaced only briefly with another ABA club. Confidence is high on the July trade, the October delivery of Chapman and both players' subsequent records. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix's official media guide and the Lakers' transaction history record the deal directly: on May 20, 1970, the Suns acquired Mel Counts from Los Angeles for Gail Goodrich. Goodrich had been Phoenix's leading backcourt star after the 1968 expansion draft, averaging 23.8 points as an All-Star in the franchise's first season and 20.0 points with 7.5 assists in 1969-70. The trade sent him back to the franchise that had originally drafted him in 1965.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: Goodrich became a championship-level lead scorer. The Lakers' official alumni profile credits him with six more Los Angeles seasons after the trade, four consecutive team scoring titles from 1971 through 1975, All-Star selections in 1972, 1973, 1974 and 1975, and All-NBA First Team in 1974. He played 466 regular-season games in that second Lakers stint. His peak came during the 1971-72 championship season, when he averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games and led the club in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, set the 33-game winning-streak record and captured the title. He stayed above 19 points per game in every season of the stint and later had No. 25 retired by the Lakers. That is elite sustained value from a one-for-one acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Counts gave the Suns two useful seasons rather than disappearing immediately. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points and 6.3 rebounds in 20.9 minutes, then appeared in 76 games in 1971-72 at 5.2 points and 3.4 rebounds in a reduced role. Phoenix therefore received 156 regular-season games from Counts. In October 1972, the Suns preserved a little more value by sending Counts to Philadelphia for a 1973 second-round pick and cash; that pick became No. 33 Gary Melchionni. The downstream pick was modest, but it means the Phoenix side included both two seasons of frontcourt depth and a small exit return.

finalVerdict.heading: Hindsight Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Lakers win overwhelmingly. Goodrich supplied six seasons, four post-trade All-Star selections, an All-NBA First Team season and championship-leading scoring. That supports an A+ grade. Phoenix cannot be graded as if Counts produced nothing: 156 games, a double-digit scoring first season and a later second-round return are legitimate assets. A C+ captures useful but ordinary value that was nowhere near Goodrich's Hall of Fame-level Lakers run. Final verdict: Los Angeles Lakers Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: The legacy Seattle record says the SuperSonics sent Dorie Murrey to the Baltimore Bullets on July 1, 1970 for a 1971 second-round pick. That sequence conflicts with the stronger transaction record. Seattle's 1969-70 ledger records Murrey leaving the franchise in the May 11 expansion draft, and Portland's media guide identifies Murrey as one of the Trail Blazers' expansion selections. Once Portland selected him, Seattle no longer held the player rights described by this July listing.

sections.heading: Documented Transaction
sections.body: The supported trade occurred after the 1970-71 season had begun. Basketball-Reference's Portland, Baltimore and league transaction ledgers all record Portland sending Murrey to Baltimore on October 22, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft pick. Harry Glickman's Portland executive log and Jerry Sachs' Baltimore executive log agree on the same structure. Portland's own media guide also records Murrey as acquired from Seattle in the expansion draft and later traded to Baltimore.

sections.heading: Pick Outcome
sections.body: The 1971 second-rounder became the No. 27 pick, Rick Fisher. Basketball-Reference's 1971 draft register shows Fisher selected by Portland at that slot. He did not appear in an NBA regular-season game, so the pick produced no NBA playing value. Murrey played only two games for Portland before the October trade and then continued his NBA career with Baltimore. Those outcomes belong to the October 22 Portland-Baltimore transaction, not to the malformed July Seattle record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. The July 1 Seattle-Baltimore entry is a legacy timing/team attribution error that duplicates the later Portland-Baltimore Murrey trade after Seattle had already lost Murrey in the expansion draft. TradeVerdicts preserves the legacy archive entry privately for provenance but excludes it from canonical hindsight grading and future public/indexable consideration. The October 22 Portland-Baltimore record remains the canonical transaction.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: New York acquired Billy Paultz's ABA rights from the Virginia Squires in August 1970 for a draft choice and cash. The surviving records disagree by one day: Pro Sports Transactions dates the exchange August 10, while Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs list August 11. The canonical TradeVerdicts record remains dated August 10 because that is the established source route, but the discrepancy is documented rather than silently resolved. All of the sources agree on the substance of the deal: Paultz went to New York, with a draft choice and cash going to Virginia.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: Paultz became immediate frontcourt value. As a rookie in 1970-71 he played 83 games and averaged 14.7 points and 11.3 rebounds while shooting 52.4 percent. He stayed with the Nets for five seasons, appearing in 404 games and averaging 15.6 points and 11.2 rebounds for the franchise. He was an ABA All-Star in 1973 and 1975 as a Net, helped New York reach the 1972 ABA Finals and was a major part of the 1974 ABA championship team. The Nets' own historical feature ranks his rebounding among the best in franchise history.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia received cash plus an unspecified draft choice. Basketball-Reference does not identify the round, year or player outcome, and Pro Sports Transactions likewise leaves the pick details unresolved. That missing information prevents an aggressive low grade for the Squires: an unidentified pick or cash amount could have produced value that the current record cannot trace. The grade therefore reflects documented realized value rather than assuming the return was worthless.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The identifiable return is overwhelmingly on New York's side. Paultz supplied five seasons of starting-caliber center play, two All-Star selections with the Nets and a championship contribution. He also remained an asset at the end of the run, when New York traded him to San Antonio in September 1975. Virginia's side is much harder to reconstruct because neither the cash amount nor the draft-choice outcome is identified in the available ledgers. That uncertainty narrows how harshly the Squires can be judged, but it does not erase the scale of the value New York actually received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ for converting a modestly documented package into five productive seasons from Paultz, including championship and All-Star value. Virginia receives a C because the consideration is confirmed but incompletely traceable; the surviving sources do not support pretending the draft pick or cash had zero value. Confidence is medium because the transaction itself and Paultz's career are well documented while the exact date differs by one day across major ledgers and the Squires' pick outcome remains unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: New York acquired Rick Barry from the Virginia Squires on September 2, 1970 for a 1971 first-round ABA draft choice and cash. Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs agree on the date and basic structure. Pro Sports Transactions identifies the pick as the No. 5 selection and reports the cash at roughly $200,000 to $250,000. Its draft-trade ledger links that selection to Cliff Meely. The cash figure is therefore treated as reported rather than exact.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: Barry delivered star production immediately. He averaged 29.4 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.0 assists in 59 regular-season games in 1970-71, made the ABA All-Star team and finished fifth in MVP voting. In 1971-72 he played 80 games and averaged 31.5 points, 7.5 rebounds and 4.1 assists while making another All-Star team. Brooklyn's own historical coverage still lists 31.5 points per game as the highest single-season scoring average in franchise history. The Nets reached their first ABA Finals in 1972, with Barry as their primary scorer.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia's return was not empty. The Squires received a premium 1971 first-round pick plus a large cash payment for the era. The pick did not simply disappear from the asset chain: transaction ledgers show Virginia later sent a 1971 first-round choice to Denver in the January 22, 1971 Ken Durrett deal, while the draft-trade ledger traces the Nets-originated No. 5 selection to Cliff Meely. That routing means the original pick had real transaction utility even though Meely did not play for Virginia. The Squires also went 55-29 in 1970-71 after moving Barry, so the franchise remained competitive in the short term.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The decisive advantage is the level of production New York actually received. Barry supplied two elite scoring seasons, two All-Star selections and a trip to the ABA Finals. The acquisition lasted only two seasons before his contractual situation returned him to Golden State, which keeps this from being an automatic top-tier grade. Virginia, meanwhile, converted a player who did not want to remain with the relocated franchise into premium draft capital and substantial cash. The Squires deserve more credit than a simple star-for-pick summary suggests, but the identifiable on-court return still falls short of Barry's New York impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York earns a B+ because Barry delivered exactly the type of elite production a team hopes to buy with a first-round pick and cash, culminating in the franchise's first ABA Finals appearance. Virginia receives a C because the Squires obtained a valuable first-round asset and meaningful cash, then remained a 55-win team, but the surviving asset chain does not show a direct return comparable to Barry's two seasons in New York. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Barry's performance and the pick identity; the only material uncertainty is whether the reported cash was $200,000 or $250,000.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On September 10, 1970, the San Diego Rockets traded Art Williams to Boston for the Celtics' 1971 fifth-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Celtics, Rockets and league transaction pages, while the executive histories for Red Auerbach and Pete Newell independently preserve the deal. The pick became the No. 78 selection in the 1971 draft, which the Rockets used on Jacksonville forward Greg Nelson.

sections.heading: Celtics Return
sections.body: Williams was not acquired to become a star, but Boston received far more than a one-season rental. He played 74 games in 1970-71, then 81 in each of the next two seasons and 67 in 1973-74. Across four Celtics seasons he appeared in 303 regular-season games and Basketball-Reference credits him with 11.1 win shares. His best Boston season by raw production was 1971-72, when he averaged 5.1 points, 4.0 assists and 3.2 rebounds in 16.4 minutes per game. He remained part of the roster when the 1973-74 Celtics went 56-26 and won the NBA championship.

sections.heading: Rockets Return
sections.body: San Diego converted Williams into a late draft asset rather than losing him for nothing. The pick landed at No. 78 overall in the fifth round, and the Rockets selected Greg Nelson out of Jacksonville. Nelson never appeared in an NBA game, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value. That outcome matters because the comparison is not between Williams and an abstract future pick anymore; the asset can be traced to a specific selection and player. The low round softens the opportunity cost, but the Rockets still moved a useful veteran and received no NBA production from the draft outcome.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The scale of the deal is modest, yet the result is unusually straightforward. Boston surrendered a fifth-round pick that became a non-NBA player and received four seasons from a dependable reserve guard. Williams was never one of the Celtics' primary scorers, but his 303 games, positive win-share total and role through the 1974 title season represent substantial realized value for the price. San Diego's pick outcome never reached the league. That makes the trade a strong example of a contender extracting practical roster value from a low-cost future asset rather than a franchise-altering blockbuster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, B+/D+. Boston earns a B+ because a fifth-round pick became four years of useful guard depth, including a place on the 1974 championship roster. The Rockets receive a D+ because the No. 78 pick was correctly preserved and used, but Greg Nelson never played an NBA game and the asset produced no realized league value. Confidence is high: the transaction date, compensation, draft outcome and Williams' Boston production all agree across Basketball-Reference's team, league, executive, player and draft records.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Milwaukee and Seattle completed the deal on September 17, 1970. Basketball-Reference's team transaction logs record Lucius Allen and Bob Boozer going to the Bucks for Zaid Abdul-Aziz and cash. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part exchange and reports the cash at $100,000. The amount is therefore treated as reported rather than exact, but the player movement itself is well established.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Return
sections.body: The Bucks received both short-term and longer-term value. Boozer played 80 regular-season games in 1970-71, averaging 9.1 points and 5.4 rebounds, then appeared in all 14 playoff games as Milwaukee won the NBA championship. Allen played 61 games that season and stayed with the Bucks deep into 1974-75. His role expanded quickly: 13.5 points and 4.2 assists per game in 1971-72, 15.5 and 5.3 in 1972-73, then 17.6 and 5.2 in 1973-74. Basketball-Reference credits Allen with 8.2 win shares in that 1973-74 season, when Milwaukee returned to the NBA Finals.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body: Seattle's side deserves more credit than a one-sided title-team story would suggest. Abdul-Aziz immediately gave the SuperSonics frontcourt production, averaging 10.9 points and 7.7 rebounds in 61 games in 1970-71. He improved in 1971-72 to 13.8 points and 11.3 rebounds in 58 games before Seattle later moved him to Houston in 1972. The reported $100,000 also had real value, even though a cash payment cannot be translated cleanly into on-court production. Seattle therefore received a useful starting-caliber big man plus money rather than an empty return.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The separation comes from Milwaukee combining two forms of value. Boozer supplied immediate rotation minutes on a championship team, while Allen developed into one of the Bucks' primary guards and remained productive across several seasons. Seattle received two useful years from Abdul-Aziz and cash, so the transaction did not cripple the franchise or leave it without a basketball return. But Milwaukee's package contributed to the 1971 title immediately and kept producing through another Finals run in 1974. That combination of championship utility and multi-year guard production outweighs Seattle's return without making the deal a historical fleecing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee earns a B+ for getting a title-season contributor in Boozer and several productive seasons from Allen at the cost of Abdul-Aziz and reported cash. Seattle receives a B- because Abdul-Aziz was a legitimate rebounder and scorer for two seasons and the cash payment added value, even though the SuperSonics did not receive the same championship or long-term impact. Confidence is high on the player movement and career outcomes; the only meaningful qualifier is that the $100,000 figure is reported rather than independently documented as a precise cash ledger.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Utah transaction logs agree that the Rockets sent Jeff Congdon to the Stars on September 19, 1970 for a draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions narrows that compensation to a second-round pick, but leaves the year and eventual selection unresolved. That distinction matters: the existence and round of the pick are supported, while assigning a specific drafted player would require a link the surviving ledgers do not establish.

sections.heading: Utah Return
sections.body: Congdon became a useful guard for a strong Stars team. Basketball-Reference credits him with 38 Utah games in 1970-71, averaging 7.7 points, 4.1 assists and 2.3 rebounds in 25.9 minutes. Utah finished 57-27 and went on to win the ABA championship. Congdon did not stay through the playoff run, however. The Stars traded him to the New York Nets on January 7, 1971 for another draft choice and a player to be named later, so Utah's direct return from this September deal lasted only part of the regular season.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Denver's return cannot be evaluated responsibly from the current record. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger shows multiple second-round picks changing hands and explicitly marks some chains as unknown. It does not connect the Congdon consideration to a named Denver selection. The Rockets' own second-round slot in the 1971 ABA draft produced Marv Roberts, but the available sources do not establish that the Utah pick acquired here became that selection. Treating Roberts, Roger Brown, Garry Nelson or another player as the outcome would turn an unresolved chain into a fabricated conclusion.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Utah clearly received some immediate basketball value: Congdon played regular rotation minutes for 38 games on the eventual ABA champions. Denver clearly received a second-round asset. What is missing is the step needed for a fair hindsight comparison—what Denver ultimately did with that specific pick. Congdon's later move to New York also limits how much long-term value can be assigned to Utah. With one side traceable for only part of a season and the other side's draft outcome unidentified, a winner or letter-grade comparison would imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The transaction itself is verified, the second-round nature of Denver's compensation is supported, and Congdon's Utah production is measurable. The draft year and ultimate player outcome remain unresolved in the available ledgers, however, so Denver's realized return cannot be priced. This record stays intentionally ungraded until a primary or reliable transaction source closes that asset chain. Confidence is high that the trade occurred as described, but low for any value verdict because the decisive draft outcome is still unknown.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Boston, Baltimore and league transaction logs all record the October 2, 1970 move as a sale of Jim Barnes's player rights from the Celtics to the Bullets. Pro Sports Transactions describes the same exchange as Barnes to Baltimore for cash. The sources agree on the structure, but none of the reliable ledgers used here identifies the cash amount. That missing figure limits how aggressively Boston's side can be graded, even though the transaction itself is well established.

sections.heading: Baltimore Return
sections.body: Barnes did not become a lasting part of Baltimore's rotation. Basketball-Reference credits him with 11 games for the 1970-71 Bullets, averaging 9.1 minutes, 3.4 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.7 assists. The club waived him on November 13, only six weeks after acquiring his rights. Those 11 appearances were the final NBA games of Barnes's career. Because the Bullets moved on so quickly, the realized basketball return was limited even before considering what they paid.

sections.heading: Boston Return
sections.body: Boston's return was cash, and the amount remains unknown in the transaction sources. That prevents assigning the Celtics a high grade based on a financial figure that cannot be verified. The practical result is still favorable: Boston received consideration for a player who produced only a short reserve stint in Baltimore and did not play another NBA season. For a minor roster transaction, converting an expendable player asset into cash is a positive outcome even if the exact dollar value is lost to the historical record.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison is modest rather than dramatic. Baltimore received 11 games of low-minute frontcourt depth and then waived Barnes. Boston received an unquantified cash payment and gave up no future NBA production beyond that brief stretch. That makes the Celtics' side more efficient in hindsight, but the unknown cash amount keeps the gap from being treated like a major win. The transaction is best understood as a low-impact sale in which Boston extracted some value from a player the Bullets did not retain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, C+/D+. Boston earns a C+ because the team turned Barnes's rights into cash without surrendering meaningful future NBA value. Baltimore receives a D+ because Barnes lasted 11 games before being waived. Confidence is medium-high: the sale, Barnes's Baltimore statistics and the waiver date are all independently documented, while the exact cash amount remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's league and Portland transaction logs describe the October 7, 1970 move as Portland selling Pat Riley's player rights to Los Angeles. The Lakers team transaction page records the acquisition of his rights without naming a return, and Portland's own media guide also says the expansion club sold Riley to the Lakers. A modern Lakers media guide instead labels the move a waiver claim. Because the surviving sources disagree on the transaction mechanism while multiple ledgers support a sale, this record preserves the cash asset already attached to the canonical trade but treats the exact amount as unresolved.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: Riley became a real rotation piece rather than a name attached to a transaction ledger. Basketball-Reference credits him with 296 regular-season games for the Lakers, totaling 2,316 points across six listed seasons. His most important team result came in 1971-72. Riley played 67 regular-season games for the 69-win Lakers and appeared in all 15 playoff games, averaging 16.3 minutes and 5.2 points during the championship run. That contribution was not star-level, but it is meaningful realized value for an acquisition made just before the 1970-71 season. His later coaching career is historically famous but is not part of this trade grade.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Portland had selected Riley from the San Diego Rockets in the 1970 expansion draft, then moved his rights to Los Angeles before playing its first regular-season game. The reliable sale descriptions do not identify the amount Portland received. That makes the Trail Blazers' side difficult to value precisely and argues against an especially harsh grade. What can be measured is the opportunity cost: Riley gave Los Angeles several years of reserve production and a role on a championship team, while Portland's return is not traceable to a durable basketball asset in the sources used for this audit.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison favors Los Angeles without turning the transaction into a franchise-altering steal. Riley was a reserve, not a centerpiece, and the unknown cash amount means Portland may have received reasonable short-term value for a player it did not intend to keep. Still, Los Angeles obtained nearly 300 regular-season games and postseason minutes from Riley, including a championship run, in exchange for consideration whose exact value has not survived in the transaction record. That is enough realized surplus to support the existing Lakers-win framing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B/C-. Los Angeles earns a B for turning a modest acquisition into a multi-year rotation player who contributed throughout the 1972 title season. Portland receives a C- because the club monetized an expansion-draft asset but gave up the only clearly measurable long-term basketball value in the exchange. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the transaction sources conflict between sale and waiver language and the cash amount is not documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Kentucky and league transaction logs agree that the Pacers acquired Warren Jabali on October 13, 1970 for a 1971 first-round draft choice and cash. Indiana's modern media guide uses the same description. That establishes the core exchange cleanly. The more difficult piece is the draft outcome. Pro Sports Transactions traces the pick as probably the No. 7 selection used on Willie Sojourner and shows that selection reaching Virginia through Kentucky, but its own wording is explicitly probabilistic. WrestleVerdicts therefore preserves the existing Sojourner relationship as a probable historical outcome rather than upgrading it to a fully verified pick chain.

sections.heading: Indiana Return
sections.body: Jabali supplied real short-term value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 62 regular-season games for Indiana in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists in 25.6 minutes. He also appeared in all 11 of the Pacers' playoff games, averaging 7.8 points and 3.6 rebounds. Indiana reached the ABA Western Division finals before losing to Utah, so Jabali's season included meaningful postseason minutes rather than empty production on a noncompetitive roster. His Pacers tenure was still brief: on September 24, 1971, Indiana sent him to the Floridians for a draft choice and cash.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body: Kentucky's return was less visible on the court but not empty. The Colonels received cash plus Indiana's 1971 first-rounder. The surviving draft-trade ledger identifies that selection as probably No. 7, Willie Sojourner, and records the pick moving to Virginia through Kentucky. That path fits a broader chain in which Kentucky had acquired Jabali from the Washington Capitols in July 1970 for a 1971 first-round pick and cash. Because the exact contractual linkage between those obligations is not fully documented in the sources used here, this audit does not claim Kentucky directly drafted Sojourner or that the Indiana pick definitively satisfied the earlier Washington obligation. The safe conclusion is that Kentucky recovered a first-round asset and cash when it moved Jabali.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Indiana received the clearest immediate basketball return: a rotation guard who played 62 games and contributed in the postseason. Kentucky received financial consideration and a premium draft asset, but the pick's final identity is only probable in the available transaction database and did not become a Kentucky player. That makes a winner declaration too aggressive. Indiana's one-season use of Jabali was valuable, yet the Pacers paid a first-rounder plus cash and did not retain him beyond the following September. Kentucky, meanwhile, converted a player it had held for only a few months into another first-round asset and cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Indiana earns a B- for receiving a useful starter-level guard for a playoff team and later retaining some value by trading him again. Kentucky also earns a B- because a first-round pick plus cash was a meaningful return for a player whose stay in Indiana lasted one season. Confidence is medium because the main transaction is well documented but the pick's eventual No. 7 Willie Sojourner identity remains labeled probable rather than certain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Nets, Colonels and ABA transaction logs all agree on the core transaction: New York sent Walt Simon to Kentucky on October 14, 1970 for a draft choice. The surviving ledgers do not identify the year, round or eventual player tied to that pick. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger documents several traded selections but does not connect this Simon transaction to a specific New York choice. That missing link is important because it prevents treating the Nets' return as worthless simply because its outcome is not currently traceable.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body: Simon gave the Colonels immediate and durable rotation value. In 1970-71 he played all 84 regular-season games, averaged 7.7 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists, and stayed in the rotation as Kentucky advanced through two playoff rounds before losing the ABA Finals to Utah. His value did not end with that first season. Basketball-Reference's franchise totals credit Simon with 314 games across four Kentucky seasons, 2,780 points, 1,152 rebounds and 746 assists. That works out to 8.9 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists per game over the full stint. He was not a franchise centerpiece, but four years of useful wing minutes is a strong realized return for an otherwise unspecified future pick.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: The Nets received a future draft choice, but the current source trail does not identify its year, round or drafted player. The 1971 ABA draft ledger is especially useful because it explicitly traces a number of traded picks involving New York and Kentucky, including other deals from the same period, yet it does not establish a Simon-to-Nets pick chain. That makes this a source gap rather than proof that the selection failed. New York therefore keeps a neutral grade instead of being penalized as though the asset vanished without value.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison is asymmetric. Kentucky's side can be measured: Simon played 314 games for the Colonels and remained part of competitive teams that reached the 1971 ABA Finals and posted a 68-16 regular-season record in 1971-72. New York's side cannot be measured beyond knowing that a draft choice changed hands. Because the pick outcome is unresolved, the proper conclusion is not that Kentucky won by a landslide. It is that the Colonels banked several seasons of documented production while the Nets' return remains unverified. That supports a clear but restrained Kentucky advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Colonels Win, B/C. Kentucky receives a B for turning a future pick into four seasons of Walt Simon, including 314 games of dependable rotation production. New York receives a C because the compensation itself is verified but its eventual player outcome is not. Confidence is medium: the transaction and Simon's Kentucky career are well documented, while the exact draft asset remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cincinnati, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all record the same October 16, 1970 deal: the Royals received Darrall Imhoff and a future draft choice while the 76ers received Connie Dierking and Fred Foster. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part structure and, importantly, also leaves the draft choice unidentified. That means the player side of the trade is traceable, but the exact year, round and ultimate outcome of Cincinnati's pick are not. The verdict therefore has to leave room for value that the surviving source chain cannot price.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Return
sections.body: Imhoff was acquired to help a team that wanted more rebounding and an outlet for Bob Cousy's faster offense. Cincinnati's 1971 media guide described the trade in those terms after the club had been outrebounded through much of the preseason. On the floor, Imhoff played 34 games in 1970-71, averaging 8.1 points and 6.9 rebounds in 24.3 minutes. His Cincinnati run was interrupted and did not develop into a long stay: he appeared in only nine more Royals games in 1971-72 before finishing that season with Portland. The future draft choice could alter the long-term accounting, but no reliable ledger used here identifies what it became.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Philadelphia received two veterans with different value curves. Dierking played 53 games in 1970-71, averaging 5.8 points and 4.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes, then retired. Foster provided the more durable return. He played 66 games for the 76ers in 1970-71 and another 74 in 1971-72, when his role expanded to 23.0 minutes per game and 11.9 points. That second season is the clearest realized advantage in the deal: Philadelphia got a useful rotation scorer after Foster had been Cincinnati's third-leading scorer the year before the trade.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The documented player value favors Philadelphia. Dierking and Foster combined for 119 games in the remainder of 1970-71, and Foster stayed productive for another full season. Imhoff supplied useful rebounding in Cincinnati but played only 43 games for the Royals across two seasons. The unresolved draft choice prevents a harsher grade for Cincinnati because an unidentified pick cannot responsibly be assigned zero value. Still, on what can actually be traced, Philadelphia received more usable NBA minutes and the best post-trade season from any player in the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B-/C+. Philadelphia receives a B- for getting two rotation players, highlighted by Foster's 11.9-point 1971-72 season. Cincinnati receives a C+ because Imhoff contributed when available and the future draft choice may have carried additional value that cannot currently be identified. Confidence is medium: the transaction and player outcomes are well documented, but the draft asset remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Chicago and Portland's transaction logs agree that the Bulls sent Shaler Halimon to the Trail Blazers on October 20, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft choice. Basketball-Reference and Pro Sports Transactions both trace that pick to No. 20 overall, where Chicago selected Weber State center Willie Sojourner. This is a resolved draft chain: the pick year, round, slot and player outcome are all known.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Halimon became a regular immediately for the first-year Trail Blazers. He appeared in 79 Portland games, averaging 20.6 minutes, 8.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists. For an expansion roster, that is meaningful one-season utility rather than a cameo. Portland did not retain the value beyond that year, however. The club placed Halimon on waivers in July 1971 and Atlanta claimed him, so the transaction produced one full season but no later trade return for the Blazers.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Chicago's pick became Sojourner, a productive Weber State rebounder selected 20th overall in the 1971 NBA Draft. The pick was real and reasonably valuable, but it never turned into Bulls production. Basketball-Reference lists no NBA games for Sojourner; he instead began his professional career in the ABA with the Virginia Squires and ultimately played 309 ABA games. His talent therefore was not the issue. The hindsight problem for Chicago is that the draft asset did not create NBA minutes, points or a later NBA transaction return for the Bulls.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Portland received exactly one useful season. Halimon was neither a star nor a long-term building block, and the Blazers waived him before year two. Chicago received an exact second-round outcome with legitimate professional ability, but none of that ability was realized for the Bulls because Sojourner played in the ABA. Under a team-realized-value standard, 79 NBA games and a regular rotation role beat a draft selection that never suited up for the acquiring franchise. The margin is clear, though the short duration of Halimon's stay keeps Portland's grade modest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, B-/D+. Portland receives a B- for getting 79 games of useful rotation play from Halimon during its expansion season. Chicago receives a D+ because the No. 20 pick was successfully traced and used on a capable player, but Sojourner never produced NBA value for the Bulls. Confidence is high because the trade, exact draft outcome and post-trade playing records are all well documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
