sections.heading: The Recorded Agreement
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Carolina and ABA transaction ledgers all record a September 20, 1972 exchange in which the Rockets sent cash to the Cougars for Wayne Hightower. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same direction, and Alex Hannum's executive record also lists Denver trading cash for Hightower. Taken alone, those ledgers make the move look like a completed cash purchase. The source-backed review found an important second layer, however: later biographical reporting says the arrangement was voided before Hightower joined Denver for the regular season. The archive therefore keeps the dated transaction record but no longer grades it as a completed trade.

sections.heading: Why the Deal Was Voided
sections.body: Hightower was coming off an abbreviated 1971-72 season with Carolina, where he played only 13 games after a blood-clot issue had disrupted the previous year. Biographical sourcing reports that Carolina agreed to sell him to Denver, but Hightower arrived late to the Rockets' preseason training camp. Hannum then voided the transaction. The same account says Hightower's contract was returned to Carolina and Denver refused to send the agreed cash. That detail changes the evaluation completely: neither the player asset nor the financial consideration became a realized post-transaction return.

sections.heading: Denver Roster Evidence
sections.body: Denver's 1972-73 roster supports the voided-deal account. A historical Rockets roster archive lists Hightower only under the preseason section rather than among regular-season players. Basketball-Reference's team page likewise shows no Hightower appearance for the 47-37 Rockets. Denver's regular-season frontcourt included Julius Keye, Dave Robisch, Byron Beck, Marv Roberts and others, but Hightower logged zero games, minutes, points or rebounds. The absence is not a small sample produced by injury after the trade; it is consistent with the contract never becoming part of Denver's regular-season roster.

sections.heading: Carolina's Position
sections.body: Carolina's transaction page records the sale, but the later voiding means the Cougars did not ultimately receive the agreed cash according to the biographical account. Hightower also did not return to the 1972-73 Carolina roster. The historical record therefore describes a failed transfer rather than a conventional one-sided deal. Carolina had attempted to monetize the contract and Denver had attempted to acquire veteran frontcourt depth, yet the agreement unraveled before either side realized the intended asset. No reviewed source identifies a later compensation mechanism that replaced the voided arrangement.

sections.heading: How the Archive Treats It
sections.body: The canonical record remains useful because multiple transaction ledgers preserve September 20 as an agreement date. Removing it entirely would hide a real historical event in the transaction record. Treating it as an ordinary completed trade would be worse, because that would falsely imply Denver paid cash and acquired Hightower for basketball purposes. The correct source-backed treatment is to preserve the record, flag the deal as voided before completion, mark Hightower as a zero-game Denver preseason presence, and mark the cash as agreed but unpaid. No downstream value should be assigned to either asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: No Completed Trade. Denver receives no grade because Hightower's contract was returned and he played zero regular-season games for the Rockets. Carolina receives no grade because the agreed cash was not ultimately sent according to the voided-deal reporting. Confidence is medium-high: the September 20 agreement is strongly corroborated by transaction ledgers, and the zero-game roster outcome is clear, while the voiding mechanics rely on later biographical reporting rather than a surviving team transaction note. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Portland and league transaction pages agree that the 76ers traded Dave Wohl to the Trail Blazers for Dale Schlueter on October 2, 1972. The swap was a direct player-for-player move with no pick or cash component in the reviewed ledgers. Both players were established role players: Schlueter was a veteran center who had averaged 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds for Portland the previous season, while Wohl was a second-year point guard coming off 79 games for Philadelphia as a rookie. That makes the trade straightforward to evaluate through the production each team actually retained.

sections.heading: Schlueter in Philadelphia
sections.body: Schlueter became one of the more durable players on a historically bad 76ers team. He appeared in 78 games during 1972-73, started ten, and averaged 5.4 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes. He totaled 1,136 minutes and 354 rebounds. Philadelphia went 9-73, so his individual contribution did not translate into team success, but the trade still produced a full season of reliable center minutes. For a one-for-one exchange, that volume alone already exceeded what Portland received from Wohl.

sections.heading: Wohl's Short Portland Stay
sections.body: Wohl played only 22 games for the Trail Blazers. He averaged 5.4 points and 3.1 assists in 17.9 minutes and logged 393 total minutes. Portland then waived him on December 6, 1972, barely two months after the trade. Buffalo claimed him immediately. Wohl went on to play 56 games for the Braves during the same season and remained an NBA guard for several more years, but Portland received no compensation for that later career because its relationship with him ended on waivers. The Blazers' realized return is therefore limited to those 22 appearances.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Converts Schlueter Again
sections.body: Philadelphia extracted a second return from Schlueter instead of simply letting him leave. On February 1, 1973, the 76ers traded him to Atlanta for Don May. May played 26 games for Philadelphia over the remainder of 1972-73 and averaged 11.9 points and 5.5 rebounds in 23.2 minutes. He returned for 56 games in 1973-74, giving the 76ers 82 regular-season appearances across two seasons after the Schlueter conversion. That downstream value extends the original Wohl trade well beyond Schlueter's own Philadelphia games.

sections.heading: How Much the Team Context Counts
sections.body: Neither side turned this trade into a competitive breakthrough. Philadelphia's 1972-73 season remains the worst full-season record in franchise history, and Portland also missed the playoffs. The grade therefore should not treat Schlueter's 78 games or May's later production as star-level value. Still, hindsight grading is about realized asset value, not team reputation alone. Philadelphia received a playable center, then used that center to acquire another rotation player. Portland received a guard it waived after 22 games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B+/D+. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Schlueter supplied 78 games and the club then converted him into Don May, who added 82 more Philadelphia appearances across two seasons. Portland receives a D+ because Wohl gave the Blazers only 22 games before being waived for no return. The gap is clear even though neither incoming player became a star and Philadelphia's team results were poor. Confidence is high on the transaction, game totals and Schlueter-to-May downstream chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Date Correction and Trade Structure
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, New York and league transaction ledgers all place the Eddie Mast trade on October 9, 1972. Richie Guerin's Atlanta executive record and Red Holzman's New York record use the same date. The legacy archive carried October 7 from an older legacy source, so this review corrects the canonical trade date to October 9 while retaining the old date as a superseded source value. The basketball structure is straightforward: Atlanta received Mast, and New York received Atlanta's 1973 second-round pick, later used at No. 28 on Pat McFarland.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Return
sections.body: Mast had barely played for the Knicks, appearing in only 12 regular-season games across 1970-71 and 1971-72. Atlanta gave him a larger role after the trade. In 1972-73 he appeared in 42 games, logged 447 minutes, scored 119 points and collected 136 rebounds. That works out to 2.8 points and 3.2 rebounds in 10.6 minutes per game. The Hawks went 46-36 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals, so Mast's contribution was limited to reserve frontcourt depth rather than a major rotation role. Still, 42 actual NBA appearances represent a measurable return from the transaction.

sections.heading: New York's Draft Asset
sections.body: The Knicks held the second-round pick through the 1973 draft and used it on McFarland with the 28th overall selection. That identifies the pick outcome precisely, but it does not create NBA production for New York. McFarland never appeared in an NBA game. Basketball-Reference lists his professional career entirely in the ABA: 67 games for the Denver Rockets in 1973-74, 70 for the Denver Nuggets in 1974-75 and 11 for the San Diego Sails in 1975-76. Those games cannot be credited to the Knicks because New York never received NBA service or a later trade return from the drafted player.

sections.heading: Why the Pick Still Has Some Value
sections.body: A second-round selection is not worthless simply because the selected player never appeared for the drafting team. New York acquired a real draft asset and exercised it on a player who proved capable of playing 148 professional ABA games. The hindsight grade therefore should not treat the Knicks' side as if it received literally nothing on transaction day. But realized-value grading follows what the franchise ultimately obtained from the asset. In New York's case, no NBA games, minutes, points, trade return or compensatory pick are documented from McFarland.

sections.heading: Mast's Limited Ceiling
sections.body: Atlanta's advantage also needs to stay modest. Mast did not become a long-term Hawk. His 42-game 1972-73 season was his only year in Atlanta and his final NBA season. He played only 447 minutes, and no later transaction converted him into another player or pick. The Hawks therefore received useful roster depth rather than a lasting asset chain. That makes this a small win, not a franchise-changing trade. The comparison comes down to 42 documented NBA games on one side versus a second-round pick that produced zero Knicks appearances on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge, B-/D+. Atlanta receives a B- because Mast supplied 42 regular-season games and useful reserve minutes on a 46-win playoff team. New York receives a D+ because the pick became McFarland, who never played in the NBA or generated a documented Knicks trade return, though the club did acquire and exercise a legitimate second-round asset. Confidence is high on the corrected October 9 date, the pick outcome and the player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction pages agree that the Kings acquired Toby Kimball from the Bucks on October 9, 1972 for a 1973 fourth-round pick that later became No. 59 Clyde Turner. Pro Sports Transactions adds a second Milwaukee asset: cash. A 1973 Kansas City-Omaha media guide independently describes Kimball as acquired from Milwaukee for a draft choice and cash, which supports keeping both pieces in the canonical ledger. The payment amount is not reported, so Milwaukee's financial return is verified but unpriced.

sections.heading: Kansas City-Omaha's Return
sections.body: Kimball was a 30-year-old veteran frontcourt reserve when the Kings acquired him. He played 67 games in 1972-73, averaging 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 643 minutes, 236 points and 191 rebounds. Those numbers are modest, but they are genuine NBA production from a fourth-round pick-and-cash package. On a 36-46 team, Kimball functioned as a low-minute reserve behind the club's heavier frontcourt options rather than as a core starter.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Draft Return
sections.body: The draft component did not become NBA production for the Bucks. Milwaukee used the acquired selection on Minnesota forward Clyde Turner with the 59th pick in the 1973 draft. The Bucks' draft history shows no NBA games or statistical line for Turner. That leaves the cash payment as Milwaukee's only realized return that can be credited with certainty. Because the amount is unknown, it cannot be converted into a basketball-equivalent value or treated as a major offset to Kimball's 67 games.

sections.heading: Kimball's Next Move
sections.body: Kansas City-Omaha did not keep Kimball beyond one season. On September 28, 1973, the Kings sold his player rights to Philadelphia. Basketball-Reference records the sale, and Kimball then played 75 games for the 76ers in 1973-74. Those Philadelphia games do not count as Kansas City-Omaha production, but the sale shows the Kings retained some residual contractual value after receiving a season of direct play. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed transaction pages, so the downstream cash cannot be quantified.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: This is a small transaction rather than a franchise-changing one. Kansas City-Omaha received one year of usable reserve minutes and later sold the player's rights. Milwaukee received a fourth-round selection that produced no NBA games plus an unpriced cash component. The cash keeps the Bucks from receiving a failing grade, but the basketball ledger favors the Kings because Kimball actually appeared in 67 games and the club still had an asset to sell when his season ended.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- for 67 games of reserve frontcourt production and a later rights sale. Milwaukee receives a C+ because the Bucks obtained cash and the No. 59 pick, but Clyde Turner never played in the NBA and the payment cannot be valued precisely. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and Kimball production, with moderate uncertainty around the unreported cash amounts. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Direct Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all place the exchange on October 10, 1972: the Bucks sent a 1973 second-round pick to the 76ers for Gary Gregor. Wayne Embry's executive ledger records the same deal. The pick later became No. 33, used by Phoenix on Gary Melchionni. Pro Sports Transactions also records cash moving from Milwaukee, and a historical Bucks media guide independently includes cash, though that guide labels the draft choice as a 1974 second-rounder. Because the team, league and same-day Phoenix chain consistently identify the asset as a 1973 second-round pick, the archive keeps 1973 as the canonical year and preserves the cash as a verified but unpriced secondary component.

sections.heading: Gregor's Milwaukee Stay
sections.body: Milwaukee received almost no lasting NBA value from Gregor. He appeared in nine games for the Bucks, totaling 88 minutes, 27 points, 32 rebounds and nine assists. His averages were 3.0 points and 3.6 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. Pro Sports Transactions records Milwaukee waiving him on November 15, barely five weeks after the trade. Gregor then joined the New York Nets of the ABA in December and played 40 games there during 1972-73. Those ABA games demonstrate that he still had professional value, but they cannot be credited to Milwaukee after the Bucks released him.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Same-Day Pick Conversion
sections.body: Philadelphia did not keep the pick until draft night. On the same date, the 76ers traded a 1973 second-round selection to Phoenix for veteran center Mel Counts. The Philadelphia and Phoenix transaction ledgers both identify that selection as the pick later used on Gary Melchionni, linking Milwaukee's outgoing draft asset to the Suns transaction. Pro Sports Transactions describes the activity as a three-club transaction, while Basketball-Reference presents the Milwaukee-Philadelphia and Philadelphia-Phoenix exchanges as separate trades. For this archive, Milwaukee's canonical record remains bilateral, with Phoenix treated only as downstream pick lineage rather than a direct Bucks counterparty.

sections.heading: Counts and the Next Trade
sections.body: Counts played only seven games for Philadelphia, logging 47 minutes and scoring ten points. His direct production was therefore even smaller than Gregor's Milwaukee stint. The difference is that Philadelphia retained transactional value. On November 2, the 76ers packaged Counts with Bill Bridges and sent them to the Los Angeles Lakers for Leroy Ellis and John Trapp. Because Bridges was a substantial part of that later package, the original Milwaukee pick cannot be credited with all of Ellis and Trapp's value. It can, however, be credited with helping Philadelphia obtain Counts, who remained a named asset in a subsequent trade less than a month later.

sections.heading: Why Melchionni Is Not a Philadelphia Return
sections.body: The legacy asset label says the pick became Gary Melchionni, which is useful for draft-lineage identification but can be misleading if read as Philadelphia player production. Phoenix held the selection at draft time and chose Melchionni 33rd overall in 1973. He never played for Philadelphia as a result of this transaction. The source-backed record therefore keeps his name attached to the pick only as the final selection identity and marks the real Philadelphia return as the pick's same-day conversion into Counts. That distinction prevents downstream draft identity from being double-counted as 76ers on-court value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B/D+. Philadelphia receives a B because the second-round pick and cash gave the club immediate trade flexibility: the pick was rerouted for Counts, and Counts remained part of another trade three weeks later. The grade stops well short of elite because Counts contributed only seven Philadelphia games and cannot be assigned the full value of the later Bridges package. Milwaukee receives a D+ because Gregor played just nine games and 88 minutes before being waived. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and same-day Phoenix routing, with moderate uncertainty on the cash detail because the supporting records disagree on the pick year even while agreeing that cash was included. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Pacers and ABA transaction ledgers agree that Indiana sent cash to the Virginia Squires for Don Buse in August 1972. The important source conflict is the day: the canonical import carries August 10, while Basketball-Reference lists the trade under August ? and then records Indiana signing Buse on August 15. The archive therefore keeps the established canonical date but does not present that day as independently verified. No reviewed source supplies the cash amount, so Virginia's consideration remains real but unpriced.

sections.heading: Immediate Pacers Return
sections.body: Buse joined Indiana immediately and played 77 games as a rookie in 1972-73, averaging 5.4 points, 2.9 assists and 1.4 steals in 19.3 minutes. The Pacers went 51-33 and won the ABA championship, and Buse appeared in 14 playoff games during that title run. He was not yet the team's central star, but the rights purchase already produced a useful rotation guard on a champion in its first season. That alone gives Indiana a concrete return that cannot be matched to any identified basketball asset on Virginia's side.

sections.heading: Development Into a Star
sections.body: The long-term payoff made the transaction exceptional. Buse grew from reserve guard into one of the ABA's best defenders and playmakers. By 1974-75 he was an All-Defensive First Team selection. In 1975-76 he started all 84 games, averaged 12.5 points, 8.2 assists and 4.1 steals, earned All-Star and All-ABA recognition, and again made the All-Defensive First Team. His 689 assists led the ABA. Indiana had acquired the rights to that production for an undisclosed cash payment four years earlier.

sections.heading: NBA Merger Value
sections.body: The value survived the ABA-NBA merger. In 1976-77 Buse started 76 of 81 games for the NBA Pacers, averaged 8.0 points, 8.5 assists and 3.5 steals, made the NBA All-Star team and the All-Defensive First Team, and led the entire NBA in both assists and steals. Basketball-Reference credits him with 685 assists and 281 steals that season. That combination matters for hindsight grading because the transaction did not merely buy a short ABA stint; it secured a guard who remained elite after the league context changed.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia received cash, but the amount is unknown and no reviewed source ties it to a later player, pick or traceable basketball return. That does not make the consideration literally worthless, and the archive does not invent a dollar value or assume the Squires spent it poorly. It does mean the measurable comparison is dramatically one-sided. Indiana received five seasons of Buse before trading him to Phoenix in 1977, including an ABA championship season, multiple All-Defensive selections and league-leading playmaking and steals production. Virginia's side has no comparable documented basketball asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, A/F. Indiana receives an A because a cash purchase of player rights produced a championship contributor who developed into an ABA All-Star, All-ABA guard, repeated All-Defensive selection and then an NBA All-Star who led the league in assists and steals. Virginia receives an F because its return is only an unpriced cash payment with no identified downstream basketball asset in the reviewed record. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction structure and career outcome, with the exact August day preserved as a source-date caveat. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Seattle and league transaction pages agree on the October 20, 1972 structure: the Bulls sent Kenny McIntosh to the SuperSonics for Gar Heard and Seattle's 1973 third-round pick. Chicago used that selection at No. 39 on Arkansas guard Martin Terry. The trade therefore gave Chicago one immediate rotation player plus a draft asset, while Seattle received a young forward who had played only 46 games for the Bulls. The reviewed sources do not add cash or another hidden component, so the canonical ledger remains a straightforward player-for-player-and-pick transaction.

sections.heading: Heard's Chicago Season
sections.body: Heard became useful immediately. After appearing in only three games for Seattle at the start of 1972-73, he played 78 for Chicago. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,535 minutes, 807 points and 447 rebounds, or 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds in 19.7 minutes per game. Chicago went 51-31 and reached the Western Conference semifinals. Heard was not a featured star, but his scoring rate and rebounding gave the Bulls much more immediate production than the player they surrendered produced for Seattle that season. He also appeared in two playoff games before the Bulls' postseason ended.

sections.heading: The Martin Terry Pick
sections.body: The draft asset added little realized value. Chicago selected Martin Terry with the 39th pick in the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Terry as a Chicago draft choice but shows no NBA statistical line. The pick therefore produced zero NBA games for the Bulls. That prevents the extra selection from turning the trade into a major draft win, yet it still matters that Chicago received an additional asset on top of a productive player. The source-backed ledger marks Terry as a verified zero-game draft outcome rather than treating the third-round pick as unresolved.

sections.heading: McIntosh in Seattle
sections.body: Seattle received more longevity from McIntosh than the original shorthand suggests. He played 56 games for the SuperSonics in 1972-73, averaging 4.5 points and 4.0 rebounds in 19.7 minutes. He then appeared in 69 games in 1973-74 and increased his role to 29.8 minutes, 7.4 points and 5.2 rebounds per game. McIntosh played six more Seattle games in 1974-75. In all, the SuperSonics received 131 regular-season appearances, 3,262 minutes, 783 points and 598 rebounds. He was a legitimate rotation player, which keeps Seattle's grade respectable despite Heard's stronger per-game impact.

sections.heading: Heard's Downstream Value
sections.body: Chicago did not simply lose Heard for nothing after one season. On September 10, 1973, the Bulls traded Heard and 1973 first-round pick Kevin Kunnert to Buffalo for John Hummer plus second-round picks in 1974 and 1975. That package later produced Leon Benbow with the 1974 pick, while Hummer played 18 Chicago games before being traded to Seattle for another 1975 second-round pick. Heard cannot be credited with the entire Buffalo return because Kunnert was a meaningful co-asset, so the archive treats the downstream value as supporting evidence rather than assigning all later players and picks to this 1972 trade.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The direct comparison is closer than the old A-/C shorthand implied. Heard gave Chicago 78 games at 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds, while McIntosh gave Seattle 131 games and stayed in a larger role for most of 1973-74. Chicago's advantage comes from receiving the more productive player immediately, adding a draft pick at no extra player cost, and retaining enough value in Heard to use him in another multi-asset trade the next year. Seattle's side was useful but did not produce a comparable downstream transaction in the reviewed record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A-/B. Chicago receives an A- because Heard supplied a strong 78-game season, the Bulls also received the No. 39 pick, and Heard remained a tradable asset in the 1973 Buffalo deal. Seattle receives a B because McIntosh played 131 games across parts of three seasons and provided legitimate rotation minutes, even though his scoring efficiency and overall impact were lower. Martin Terry's zero-game outcome limits Chicago's draft bonus, and the Kunnert component prevents over-crediting Heard for the later Buffalo package. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player production, draft identity and immediate downstream transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland, league and executive transaction logs agree that the Cavaliers traded Charlie Davis to the Trail Blazers on October 24, 1972 for Portland's 1974 third-round pick. Cleveland later used that selection at No. 38 on Clarence "Foots" Walker. Portland's official historical media guide adds cash to the Blazers' outgoing package, matching the cash asset preserved in the legacy archive entry. Because the amount is not reported, the archive credits Cleveland with receiving cash but does not assign it a numerical basketball value. The draft pick remains the transaction's decisive asset.

sections.heading: Portland's Charlie Davis Return
sections.body: Davis immediately joined the Portland rotation. He played 69 games for the Trail Blazers in 1972-73, logging 1,333 minutes while averaging 8.9 points, 1.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with 612 points that season. His role collapsed the next year: Davis appeared in only eight games in 1973-74, totaling 90 minutes and 31 points. Portland's media guide records the club waiving him on October 30, 1973. In all, the Blazers received 77 regular-season games, 1,423 minutes and 643 points before the player asset left without a trade return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Waits for the Pick
sections.body: Cleveland had to wait until the 1974 draft to realize its main return. The Cavaliers selected Walker 38th overall out of West Georgia. He immediately made the NBA roster and played 72 games as a rookie in 1974-75. Walker averaged only 4.2 points and 2.7 assists in 14.9 minutes, but the early role demonstrated that the third-round pick had already become a usable rotation guard rather than a speculative asset that never reached the league. He then appeared in 81 games during Cleveland's 1975-76 breakthrough season.

sections.heading: Six Seasons of Cavaliers Value
sections.body: Walker remained with Cleveland through 1979-80. His Cavaliers game totals were 72, 81, 62, 81, 55 and 76, or 427 regular-season appearances across six seasons. His role grew over time. He averaged 5.6 assists in 1977-78, 5.8 in 1978-79 and 8.0 in 1979-80, when he also scored 9.4 points per game in 31.9 minutes. He was never an All-Star, but a third-round pick producing six seasons and eventually handling full-time point-guard duties represents unusually strong realized value for the draft slot.

sections.heading: Different Types of Return
sections.body: Portland's side should not be dismissed. Davis gave the Blazers one full season of legitimate scoring and another short stint before his release. A 77-game return is meaningful for a player acquired with a third-round pick and cash. The difference is duration. Cleveland transformed that same pick into 427 games, multiple seasons of rotation minutes and several years of starting-level point-guard responsibility. The unpriced cash only adds to Cleveland's side rather than being needed to create the advantage.

sections.heading: Downstream Context
sections.body: Walker's Cleveland value continued until September 24, 1980, when the Cavaliers traded him to New Jersey. His later Nets production is not part of this direct return, but the fact that Cleveland still had a movable player asset after six seasons reinforces the durability of the original pick. Davis, by contrast, was waived by Portland after eight games in his second Blazers season. The transaction therefore produced both more direct games and a longer asset life for Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, A/B-. Cleveland receives an A because Portland's third-round pick became Foots Walker, who supplied 427 regular-season games over six seasons and developed into the club's primary point guard by the end of the decade; the unpriced cash is additional value. Portland receives a B- because Davis contributed 77 games and one useful scoring season, but he was waived before the end of 1973 and produced no retained downstream asset. Confidence is high on the pick identity, player production and transaction date; the only material uncertainty is the cash amount, which the official Portland media guide confirms without pricing. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Portland and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 27, 1972 trade: the Rockets sent Greg Smith to the Trail Blazers for Stan McKenzie. Ray Patterson's Houston executive record and Harry Glickman's Portland executive record preserve the same two-player structure. No draft choice, cash payment or future consideration appears in the reviewed primary transaction logs. The source-backed record therefore remains a direct player-for-player exchange. The Smith identity is the 1947-born Western Kentucky forward, not the later NBA center with the same common name.

sections.heading: Portland's Immediate Return
sections.body: Smith arrived after playing four games for Houston in 1972-73 and immediately became a regular member of Portland's rotation. He appeared in 72 games for the Trail Blazers that season, averaging 7.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 21.8 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,569 minutes, 533 points and 375 rebounds for Portland in that first season alone. Those totals already exceed the entire Houston production McKenzie would provide after the exchange, and Smith remained with the Blazers for several more seasons.

sections.heading: Three More Seasons in Portland
sections.body: Smith played 67 games for Portland in 1973-74 and another 55 in 1974-75, then made one final appearance in 1975-76. Across his Portland tenure, he totaled 195 regular-season games. His role diminished after the first season, but he still supplied 878 minutes in 1973-74 and 519 in 1974-75. Portland finally waived him on November 7, 1975. The move produced no trade return, yet the Blazers had already received roughly three full seasons of rotational value from a player acquired straight up for McKenzie.

sections.heading: Houston's McKenzie Return
sections.body: McKenzie had been a much larger scorer for Portland before the trade, averaging 13.5 points across his first three Trail Blazers seasons. That history gave Houston a reasonable basis for the deal, but the fit did not carry over. He played 26 games for the Rockets in 1972-73, averaging 3.3 points in 7.2 minutes. He returned for only 11 games in 1973-74, averaging 1.8 points in 10.2 minutes. Houston's total return was 37 regular-season appearances, 299 minutes and 106 points.

sections.heading: The Asset Chain Ends Quickly for Houston
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1973-74 Houston transaction page records the Rockets waiving McKenzie on November 9, 1973. That ended Houston's asset chain a little more than a year after the original trade. Unlike several neighboring archive transactions in which a player was later flipped for another asset, McKenzie did not generate a documented draft pick or player return when his Rockets tenure ended. His later professional career therefore does not add downstream value to Houston's side of this exchange.

sections.heading: Why the Legacy Grades Were Too Harsh
sections.body: The legacy Houston perspective had both teams in the D range, while the Portland perspective called the trade roughly even. The source-backed production record supports a wider gap. Portland received 195 games and multiple seasons from Smith; Houston received 37 low-minute games from McKenzie. Smith's Portland role was not star-level, and his efficiency and minutes declined after 1972-73, so the transaction does not justify an elite grade. It does, however, represent a useful straight-up roster win for the Blazers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, B+/D+. Portland receives a B+ because Greg Smith supplied 195 regular-season games over parts of four seasons, including a productive 72-game first year after the trade. Houston receives a D+ because McKenzie appeared in only 37 games, scored 106 points and was waived in November 1973 without a documented downstream return. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player identities, production totals and exit dates. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 31, 1972 trade: the Hawks sent Don Adams to the Pistons for Detroit's 1973 second-round pick. Edwin Coil's Detroit executive record confirms the same structure. Atlanta later used the selection at No. 27 on Villanova guard Tom Ingelsby. No cash, future consideration or additional player appears in the reviewed transaction logs, so the canonical record remains a direct player-for-pick deal.

sections.heading: Adams Immediately Becomes a Detroit Regular
sections.body: Adams had played only four games for Atlanta in 1972-73 before the trade. With Detroit, his role expanded sharply. He appeared in 70 games that season, averaging 9.3 points, 6.0 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 25.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,798 minutes, 649 points and 419 rebounds for the Pistons after the move. The production was not star-level, but Detroit converted one future second-round pick into an established frontcourt rotation player almost immediately.

sections.heading: His Best Pistons Season
sections.body: Adams became even more important in 1973-74. He played 74 games and averaged 10.3 points, 6.1 rebounds and 1.9 assists in 31.1 minutes. Detroit went 52-30 and reached the Western Conference semifinals, and Adams also appeared in seven playoff games at 36.6 minutes per contest. That season is the strongest evidence for Detroit's side of the trade: a second-round asset produced starter-level minutes on one of the league's better teams.

sections.heading: A Third Season Before the Waiver
sections.body: Adams remained with Detroit for 51 games in 1974-75, averaging 5.9 points and 4.8 rebounds in 27.0 minutes. On February 18, 1975, the Pistons waived him. His Detroit tenure therefore ended without a trade return, but by then the club had already received 195 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons. The absence of a downstream asset limits the ceiling on Detroit's grade, yet the quantity of direct play comfortably exceeds a typical second-round outcome.

sections.heading: Atlanta Uses the Pick on Tom Ingelsby
sections.body: The Hawks used the acquired selection on Tom Ingelsby with the 27th pick of the 1973 draft. Ingelsby played 48 games for Atlanta in 1973-74, averaging 2.7 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.8 assists in 8.3 minutes. His total NBA production for the Hawks was 398 minutes and 129 points. He did not appear for Atlanta again after that rookie season; his later professional games came in the ABA with the Spirits of St. Louis and San Diego Sails. Those games cannot be credited to the Hawks' side of this transaction.

sections.heading: Comparing the Realized Returns
sections.body: Atlanta did at least turn Adams into a real NBA player rather than a failed draft pick. Ingelsby reached the league and supplied 48 games, which keeps the Hawks from receiving the lowest possible grade. The difference is scale. Adams gave Detroit more than four times as many regular-season games, thousands more minutes and two seasons of substantial frontcourt responsibility. The 1973-74 Pistons also used him in a serious playoff rotation, while Ingelsby's Atlanta role never grew beyond limited reserve minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A-/C. Detroit receives an A- because Adams produced 195 regular-season games, a 10.3-point season and meaningful playoff minutes after being acquired for one second-round pick. Atlanta receives a C because No. 27 pick Tom Ingelsby reached the NBA but supplied only 48 games and one limited season for the Hawks before leaving the league. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, pick identity, player production and Adams' 1975 waiver. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction ledgers agree on the core event: on November 2, 1972, the Rockets sold Dick Gibbs' player rights to the Kings. Joe Axelson's executive record also lists Kansas City-Omaha acquiring the rights that day. The legacy archive entry correctly treats Houston's return as cash, but none of the reviewed ledgers reports a dollar amount. The source-backed record therefore keeps the payment as verified but unpriced instead of assuming it was trivial or assigning a modern equivalent.

sections.heading: A Complicated Rights Trail
sections.body: Gibbs appears in another transaction only a few weeks earlier. On October 9, Kansas City-Omaha's ledger says the Kings traded Jim Fox and Dick Gibbs to Seattle for Pete Cross and Don Kojis. Seattle's transaction page records the same deal. The November 2 Houston-to-Kansas City-Omaha entry is specifically phrased as an acquisition of Gibbs' player rights, and Gibbs then actually played for the Kings rather than Seattle during the remainder of 1972-73. The reviewed sources do not explain every contractual step between those entries, so this archive does not collapse them into a speculative three-team transaction.

sections.heading: Gibbs' Kansas City-Omaha Production
sections.body: The on-court outcome is clear. Gibbs played 66 games for Kansas City-Omaha in 1972-73, logging 733 minutes. He scored 207 points, grabbed 94 rebounds and recorded 61 assists. His averages were 3.1 points, 1.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 11.1 minutes per game. That is modest production, but it represents a full season of reserve availability from a player whose rights were purchased for cash rather than a draft pick or rotation player.

sections.heading: Houston's Side
sections.body: Houston had almost no 1972-73 on-court return from Gibbs before the sale. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Rockets appearance, two minutes and no points that season. His larger Houston contribution had come the year before, when he played 64 games in 1971-72, but those games predate the November 1972 transaction and should not be counted as value retained after the sale. Houston's realized return from this specific move is the cash payment, and the absence of a reported amount prevents a precise comparison in financial terms.

sections.heading: What Happened Next
sections.body: Gibbs played 71 games for Seattle in 1973-74, but the reviewed Kansas City-Omaha transaction page for that season does not list a corresponding transfer from the Kings to the SuperSonics. Because the documentary chain is incomplete, those Seattle games are not credited as a downstream Kansas City-Omaha asset return. The source-backed evaluation stops with the 66 Kings games directly supported by the 1972-73 roster and transaction records, while flagging the later Seattle appearance as unresolved disposition rather than inventing a missing transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- because the acquired rights produced 66 games and 733 minutes of immediate reserve value. Houston receives a C+ because it converted a lightly used player-rights asset into cash, but the amount is unknown and therefore cannot be credited as a major return. The edge is intentionally modest: Gibbs was a reserve, not a core player, and the later path to Seattle is not fully documented in the reviewed transaction logs. Confidence is high on the November 2 rights sale and Gibbs' Kings production, with moderate uncertainty around the cash amount and subsequent rights disposition. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 10, 1972 deal: the Cavaliers sent Dave Sorenson to the 76ers for Bob Rule. The transaction is a simple one-for-one player swap with no draft choices or cash attached in the reviewed logs. That makes the comparison unusually direct. Both players were frontcourt veterans whose roles had diminished from earlier peaks, and neither would generate a later trade asset for the team acquiring him.

sections.heading: Rule's First Cleveland Season
sections.body: Rule had appeared in only three games for Philadelphia before the trade. He then played 49 games for Cleveland in 1972-73, averaging 2.9 points and 2.2 rebounds in 9.0 minutes. The raw production was limited, but the Cavaliers at least received a regular reserve who remained available through most of the season. Rule's first Cleveland stint totaled 441 minutes, which already represented more team continuity than Philadelphia ultimately received beyond the remainder of that same season from Sorenson.

sections.heading: A Larger Role in 1973-74
sections.body: Rule returned for 26 games in 1973-74 and saw his role expand to 20.8 minutes per night. He averaged 7.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.8 assists, scoring 187 points in 540 minutes. Those 26 games were the strongest part of Cleveland's return. Rule was no longer the high-scoring Seattle center he had been earlier in his career, but he gave the Cavaliers a useful reserve stretch in a season when frontcourt depth remained thin. Across both Cleveland seasons, he appeared in 75 regular-season games.

sections.heading: Sorenson in Philadelphia
sections.body: Sorenson had played ten games for Cleveland before the trade and then appeared in 48 for Philadelphia. He averaged 5.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 0.6 assists in 13.0 minutes while shooting .456 from the field. Basketball-Reference credits him with 626 minutes and 283 points for the 76ers. Those numbers were respectable for a reserve on a rebuilding team, and his per-minute production was not dramatically worse than Rule's. The difference is that 1972-73 became Sorenson's final NBA season, so Philadelphia's return stopped after those 48 games.

sections.heading: Neither Side Creates a Second Asset
sections.body: Cleveland waived Rule on December 1, 1973. He later signed with Milwaukee as a free agent in July 1974, meaning the Cavaliers received no player, pick or cash return when his Cleveland tenure ended. Sorenson likewise did not create a documented 76ers trade return after his Philadelphia season. Because both asset chains end without a compensating transaction, the comparison should stay focused on direct games, minutes and role rather than speculative later value.

sections.heading: Why the Edge Is Modest
sections.body: The legacy perspectives disagreed sharply, with one side treating Rule as a decisive Cleveland win and another calling the exchange only slightly favorable to Philadelphia. The source-backed production falls between those extremes. Rule gave Cleveland 75 games and a useful 26-game second season. Sorenson gave Philadelphia 48 games and one decent reserve season. Rule's advantage is real, but neither player became a long-term starter, major trade chip or playoff centerpiece for the acquiring club.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, B/C+. Cleveland receives a B because Rule supplied 75 games across two seasons and expanded into a 20.8-minute role before being waived. Philadelphia receives a C+ because Sorenson provided 48 games and useful reserve scoring, but his NBA career ended after that season and the 76ers received no downstream asset. Confidence is high on the one-for-one trade mechanics, player production and Rule's December 1973 waiver. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree that the Suns acquired Walt Wesley on November 22, 1972 for a 1973 second-round pick later used on Allan Hornyak. Pro Sports Transactions adds cash to Phoenix's outgoing package and identifies the pick as No. 26. Jerry Colangelo's executive record confirms the pick-for-Wesley structure. Because Basketball-Reference omits the cash while the specialist transaction database records it explicitly, the source-backed record keeps the cash but marks the amount unpriced rather than treating the discrepancy as grounds to remove it.

sections.heading: Wesley's Direct Phoenix Production
sections.body: Wesley played 45 games for Phoenix in 1972-73 after appearing in 12 for Cleveland. His role was limited: 8.1 minutes per game, 3.2 points and 2.5 rebounds. Basketball-Reference credits him with 364 minutes, 144 points and 113 rebounds as a Sun. Those totals alone would make the trade modest. The important part of Phoenix's outcome came after the season, when the club retained enough value in Wesley to convert him into multiple future draft assets rather than simply losing him for nothing.

sections.heading: Phoenix Converts Wesley Again
sections.body: On October 9, 1973, Phoenix traded Wesley to the Capital Bullets for third-round picks in 1974 and 1975. The 1974 selection became No. 49 Earl Williams, and the 1975 selection became No. 54 Bayard Forrest. This downstream deal is directly linked in the Phoenix transaction ledger and Jerry Colangelo's executive record. It gives the original 1972 transaction a second stage: Phoenix received 45 Wesley games, then turned the same player into two draft selections.

sections.heading: The Two Downstream Draft Picks
sections.body: Williams played 79 regular-season games for Phoenix after being selected in 1974. Forrest later played 139 regular-season games for the Suns. Together they supplied 218 games. Neither became a star, and third-round selections carry inherently limited expected value, but both reached the NBA and contributed real minutes. That downstream production is much more than the original Hornyak selection produced for Cleveland and transforms Phoenix's side from a one-season rental into a multi-year asset chain.

sections.heading: Cleveland's Draft Return
sections.body: Cleveland used the acquired second-round pick on Ohio State guard Allan Hornyak with the 26th selection in the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference lists him as a Cavaliers draft choice but shows no NBA games or statistical line. Hornyak therefore produced zero NBA games from the pick. The cash component still has economic value, and its unknown amount prevents treating Cleveland's return as literally zero. Without a documented price, however, it cannot offset hundreds of realized NBA games on Phoenix's side with any precision.

sections.heading: Why the Old Even Grade Missed the Chain
sections.body: The legacy Phoenix perspective called the trade roughly even because it compared Wesley's modest 45-game Suns stint with Hornyak's failed draft outcome and unpriced cash. That stops the asset chain too early. Phoenix did not waive Wesley; it traded him for two picks, and both selected players reached the NBA for the Suns. source-backed evaluation must include that documented downstream conversion while avoiding the opposite error of crediting Phoenix with unrelated later moves.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A-/C. Phoenix receives an A- because Wesley provided 45 games and was then converted into two third-round selections that became Earl Williams and Bayard Forrest, who combined for 218 Suns games. Cleveland receives a C because Hornyak never played in the NBA and the cash amount remains unknown, though the verified payment keeps the return from being treated as empty. Confidence is high on the trade, draft identity and Wesley's later Capital deal, with only the cash amount unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the January 26, 1973 structure: the Hawks sent Jeff Halliburton to the 76ers for Philadelphia's 1973 third-round pick. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the same pick to No. 36 Ted Manakas. The deal contains no cash, secondary player or additional draft asset in the reviewed sources, making it a direct player-for-pick comparison. Atlanta was betting on future draft value; Philadelphia was acquiring a young guard who had already appeared in 61 NBA games for the Hawks.

sections.heading: Halliburton's Philadelphia Run
sections.body: Halliburton played 31 games for Philadelphia after the trade. Basketball-Reference credits him with 549 minutes, 294 points, 82 rebounds and 68 assists, equal to 17.7 minutes, 9.5 points, 2.6 rebounds and 2.2 assists per game. He did not start a game, but his scoring rate was useful for a 76ers roster that needed playable guards. The team itself finished 9-73, so Halliburton's production did not change the season's direction. It was still real, immediate NBA value directly tied to the acquired asset.

sections.heading: Atlanta Uses the Pick
sections.body: The Hawks selected Princeton guard Ted Manakas with the 36th pick of the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference and NBA.com both identify him as Atlanta's third-round selection. Atlanta signed him before the 1973-74 season but waived him in October. Basketball-Reference's Hawks transaction log records the October 8 waiver, and RealGM places his free-agent date two days later. He therefore produced zero regular-season games for Atlanta. The pick did reach the NBA, but not for the team that acquired it in this trade.

sections.heading: Manakas' Later Five Games Do Not Count for Atlanta
sections.body: Kansas City-Omaha signed Manakas as a free agent on November 16, 1973. He appeared in five games for the Kings, averaging 2.4 points in 9.0 minutes. Those five games confirm that Manakas was an NBA-caliber fringe roster player, but they are not downstream Atlanta value because the Hawks had already waived him and received no player or pick in return. The source-backed chain therefore stops Atlanta's realized return at zero Hawks games from the No. 36 selection.

sections.heading: Halliburton's Value Was Short but Direct
sections.body: Philadelphia's side is not a major long-term success. Halliburton's NBA career ended after the 1972-73 season, so the 76ers received only those 31 post-trade games. There is no documented later trade return to extend the asset chain. That limits Philadelphia's grade. Still, a half-season reserve guard scoring 9.5 points per game is materially more realized value than a draft pick whose selected player was waived before appearing for Atlanta.

sections.heading: Why the Legacy Even Grade Changes
sections.body: The legacy archive entry treated the transaction as even because both outcomes were modest. That framing missed the team-specific distinction between a player who actually contributed for Philadelphia and a drafted player who never appeared for Atlanta. Manakas' five Kansas City-Omaha games cannot be credited back to the Hawks. Once the asset chain is restricted to value realized by each acquiring team, Philadelphia has the clearer return even though neither side found a long-term rotation piece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B/D+. Philadelphia receives a B because Halliburton supplied 31 games, 549 minutes and 294 points immediately after the trade, including a 9.5-point scoring average. Atlanta receives a D+ because the No. 36 pick became Manakas, whom the Hawks waived before he played an NBA game for them. His later five games with Kansas City-Omaha are excluded from Atlanta's return because he signed there as a free agent. Confidence is high on the transaction, pick identity, Halliburton production, Atlanta waiver and later Kansas City-Omaha signing. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City-Omaha, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the January 26, 1973 structure: the Kings acquired John Block for Tom Van Arsdale and a 1974 third-round pick. Joe Axelson's executive record confirms the same package, and Pro Sports Transactions traces the pick to No. 42 Harvey Catchings. This is therefore a three-asset comparison rather than a simple veteran swap. Kansas City-Omaha received the best player Philadelphia had at that moment, but the 76ers received an established scorer plus a future pick that became a long-term NBA big man.

sections.heading: Block's Two-Part Kings Tenure
sections.body: Block joined Kansas City-Omaha after averaging 17.9 points and 9.2 rebounds in 48 games for the 76ers. His role fell immediately with the Kings, where he played 25 games in 1972-73 and averaged 9.0 points and 4.8 rebounds in 19.3 minutes. He returned for all 82 games in 1973-74, averaging 8.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 21.7 minutes. That gives the Kings 107 regular-season games from Block, including a full season of dependable rotation work. He was useful rather than a failed acquisition.

sections.heading: The Expansion Draft Ends Kansas City-Omaha's Chain
sections.body: On May 20, 1974, Kansas City-Omaha lost Block to the expansion New Orleans Jazz. The Kings did not receive a player or draft choice in exchange. Block later moved from New Orleans to Chicago for Rick Adelman, but that transaction belongs to the Jazz's asset chain, not Kansas City-Omaha's. For this trade, the Kings' realized return therefore stops at 107 Block games. That is a meaningful return for one transaction, but it has a firm endpoint after only a season and a half.

sections.heading: Van Arsdale Becomes Philadelphia's Primary Scorer
sections.body: Van Arsdale immediately took a much larger role than Block had with Kansas City-Omaha. He started all 30 of his Philadelphia games in 1972-73 and averaged 17.7 points, 6.2 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 34.3 minutes. In 1973-74 he started all 78 games and averaged 19.6 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.6 assists. He added nine games in 1974-75. In total, the 76ers received 117 regular-season games from Van Arsdale, and his 1973-74 scoring season alone supplied more offensive production than Block ever provided after the trade.

sections.heading: Van Arsdale Also Produced a Second Return
sections.body: Philadelphia did not simply lose Van Arsdale when his role ended. On November 8, 1974, the 76ers traded him to Atlanta for Clyde Lee and a 1975 third-round pick that became No. 39 Jimmie Baker. Lee then played 71 games for Philadelphia in 1974-75 and 79 more in 1975-76, giving the 76ers 150 games of additional frontcourt value from Van Arsdale's downstream trade. Baker never played an NBA game for Philadelphia, but the pick still represents another realized asset generated from the original Van Arsdale return.

sections.heading: The Third-Round Pick Becomes Harvey Catchings
sections.body: The 1974 third-round pick had even greater staying power. Philadelphia selected Catchings at No. 42. He played 37 games as a rookie, 75 in 1975-76, 53 in 1976-77, 61 in 1977-78 and 25 in 1978-79 before a February trade to New Jersey. That is 251 regular-season games for the 76ers. Catchings was primarily a defense-and-rebounding center, but he started 68 games in 1975-76 and remained in the rotation for five seasons. A third-round pick becoming a multi-year NBA big man is a strong draft outcome regardless of scoring totals.

sections.heading: Catchings' Later Trade Adds Context, Not Full Credit
sections.body: On February 7, 1979, Philadelphia traded Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash to New Jersey for Eric Money and Al Skinner. Because Catchings was only one component of that package, the entire Money-Skinner return cannot be assigned to the 1973 Kings trade. The transaction still proves that the Catchings asset retained trade utility after 251 Philadelphia games. That downstream durability is the opposite of Kansas City-Omaha's Block chain, which ended when the expansion draft removed him without compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, A+/B. Philadelphia receives an A+ because Van Arsdale produced 117 games and a 19.6-point season, later returned Clyde Lee plus another draft pick, and the original third-round pick became Catchings for 251 more 76ers games. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B because Block was genuinely useful across 107 games, including a full 82-game season, but the Kings lost him in the expansion draft and received no downstream return. Confidence is high on the trade structure, pick identity, direct production and documented follow-on transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Detroit and league transaction logs agree on the April 13, 1973 structure: the Hawks sent George Trapp to the Pistons for Detroit's 1973 first-round pick. Richie Guerin's executive record confirms the same deal. Atlanta used the acquired selection on Houston big man Dwight Jones. The legacy archive entry labels him as the No. 6 pick, but Basketball-Reference's draft and Atlanta transaction pages place Jones ninth overall. The source-backed record corrects the pick slot while preserving the underlying player identity. No cash or secondary asset appears in the reviewed trade logs.

sections.heading: Jones Gives Atlanta Three Productive Seasons
sections.body: Jones played 74 games as a rookie in 1973-74, averaging 8.0 points and 6.1 rebounds in 19.6 minutes. His role expanded the next season. In 75 games during 1974-75 he averaged 10.4 points and 9.3 rebounds in 27.8 minutes, giving Atlanta a legitimate frontcourt rebounder from the acquired pick. Jones then appeared in 66 games in 1975-76 and averaged 10.1 points with 7.9 rebounds. Across those three Hawks seasons he totaled 215 regular-season games. That is strong direct value from a first-round selection obtained for one veteran forward.

sections.heading: Trapp Becomes a Durable Detroit Rotation Forward
sections.body: Detroit also received real value. Trapp played all 82 games in 1973-74, scoring 765 points while averaging 9.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 18.2 minutes. He followed with 78 games in 1974-75 and 76 more in 1975-76. Trapp appeared in six games at the start of 1976-77 before Detroit waived him on October 20, 1976. His Pistons total was 242 regular-season appearances, more games than Jones played for Atlanta. The old D grade therefore understates the return badly: Detroit received three full seasons of dependable rotation availability.

sections.heading: Peak Value Favors Jones
sections.body: The difference is role and production rather than longevity. Jones developed into a larger rebounder and scorer, peaking at 10.4 points and 9.3 rebounds per game for Atlanta. Trapp's best Detroit scoring season was 9.3 points, and his rebounding stayed under four per game during each Pistons season. Trapp was useful, but Jones occupied a more valuable frontcourt role and was still only 24 when Atlanta moved him. That makes the direct player comparison lean toward the Hawks despite Detroit receiving 27 more regular-season games.

sections.heading: Atlanta Retains Trade Utility in 1976
sections.body: On June 7, 1976, Atlanta traded Jones and the No. 1 pick in the 1976 draft to Houston for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick. Houston used the top choice on John Lucas, while Atlanta selected Armond Hill at No. 9. That later deal shows Jones retained meaningful market value after three Hawks seasons. It would be incorrect to credit Atlanta with the entire Bailey-Meriweather-Hill package because the No. 1 pick was the dominant co-asset. The source-backed evaluation therefore treats the transaction only as evidence that Jones remained tradeable, not as a full downstream return from the 1973 deal.

sections.heading: Detroit's Asset Chain Ends with a Waiver
sections.body: Trapp's Detroit chain ends differently. RealGM's 1976 Detroit offseason ledger records the Pistons waiving him on October 20, 1976. He did not generate a player, pick or cash return for Detroit. That does not erase 242 useful regular-season appearances, but it means the Pistons received no additional asset after his playing contribution. Atlanta, by contrast, moved Jones inside a larger trade while he still had value. The distinction is modest because Atlanta also surrendered the first overall pick in that deal, but it supports the Hawks' side of an otherwise competitive comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge, A-/B+. Atlanta receives an A- because the acquired first-round pick became Jones, who supplied 215 games, three productive seasons and a 10.4-point, 9.3-rebound peak before retaining trade utility in the 1976 Houston deal. Detroit receives a B+ because Trapp played 242 games across parts of four seasons and was a durable rotation forward, but his peak impact was lower and his Pistons tenure ended with a waiver rather than a trade return. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, corrected No. 9 draft slot, player production and both players' later transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland and league transaction records agree on the April 24, 1973 structure. Cleveland sent John Johnson, Rick Roberson and its 1973 first-round pick to Portland. The Trail Blazers sent the second overall pick plus a third-round pick. Cleveland used those selections on Jim Brewer at No. 2 and Jim O'Brien at No. 37; Portland used the incoming first-rounder on Barry Parkhill at No. 15. Bill Fitch's executive record independently confirms the package. This was a major roster-and-draft exchange, not a simple pick swap.

sections.heading: Brewer Becomes Cleveland's Long-Term Core Return
sections.body: Brewer immediately made the Cavaliers and played all 82 games in each of his first three seasons. He then appeared in 81 games in 1976-77, 80 in 1977-78 and 55 more in 1978-79 before being traded. That is 462 Cleveland regular-season games. His offensive numbers were modest, but his rebounding and defense became central to the roster. Brewer averaged 10.9 rebounds in 1975-76, started all 82 games and earned All-Defensive Second Team honors. He repeated the defensive honor in 1976-77. He also played 17 playoff games for Cleveland across the 1976 and 1977 postseasons.

sections.heading: The Third-Round Pick Adds No Cleveland NBA Games
sections.body: Cleveland used the No. 37 pick on Maryland forward Jim O'Brien. O'Brien never appeared in an NBA game for the Cavaliers. His professional games came in the ABA, including time with Kentucky and San Diego, so those games cannot be credited to Cleveland. The second Cleveland asset therefore produced zero NBA games for the acquiring team. The strength of the Cavaliers' return rests overwhelmingly on Brewer rather than on the quantity of picks received.

sections.heading: John Johnson Gives Portland High-Level Immediate Production
sections.body: Portland received the best established player in the trade. Johnson played 69 games in 1973-74 and averaged 16.4 points, 7.5 rebounds and 4.1 assists. He followed with 80 games in 1974-75 at 16.1 points, 6.3 rebounds and 3.0 assists, then played nine more Portland games in 1975-76. In all, the Trail Blazers received 158 regular-season games from Johnson, with a 16.0-point scoring average across his Portland tenure. His direct production was considerably larger offensively than Brewer's, even though Brewer lasted much longer in Cleveland.

sections.heading: Johnson Also Produces Steve Hawes
sections.body: Portland retained value when Johnson left. On November 13, 1975, the Trail Blazers traded him to Houston for Steve Hawes. Hawes played 66 games for Portland that season, averaging 7.2 points and 7.3 rebounds in 20.6 minutes. The downstream transaction matters because Portland did not simply lose Johnson after 158 games; the original 1973 asset still produced another useful rotation big man. Hawes later left Portland, but the Johnson-to-Hawes exchange extends the direct trade tree beyond Johnson's own playing time.

sections.heading: Roberson Adds Another Productive Season and Return
sections.body: Rick Roberson also contributed immediately. He played 69 games for Portland in 1973-74, averaging 13.5 points and 10.2 rebounds in 29.9 minutes. On September 16, 1974, Portland traded Roberson to the expansion New Orleans Jazz for Barry Clemens and a 1976 second-round pick that became Major Jones. Clemens subsequently played for Portland, and the second-round pick became another roster asset. As with Johnson, Roberson therefore produced both direct games and a documented downstream return rather than ending as a sunk asset.

sections.heading: Parkhill Never Joins Portland
sections.body: The No. 15 pick did not add NBA value for the Trail Blazers. Portland drafted Virginia guard Barry Parkhill, but he chose the ABA and played for the Virginia Squires and Spirits of St. Louis instead. His 173 ABA games are part of his professional career but not realized Portland value. That weakens one piece of the Trail Blazers' package and is the main reason the trade does not become a clear Portland win despite Johnson and Roberson's immediate production.

sections.heading: Brewer Retains Some Cleveland Trade Value
sections.body: Cleveland also moved Brewer before his asset chain ended. On February 15, 1979, the Cavaliers traded Brewer and future considerations to Detroit for Earl Tatum. Because future considerations were bundled with Brewer, the entire Tatum return cannot be assigned to Brewer alone. The transaction still shows that Brewer remained a tradeable asset after 462 regular-season games and multiple playoff runs. That retained value helps offset Portland's two documented downstream player trades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A-/A-. Cleveland receives an A- because Brewer supplied 462 regular-season games, two All-Defensive Second Team seasons and meaningful playoff minutes, while remaining tradeable in 1979. Portland also receives an A- because Johnson and Roberson combined for 227 immediate games at much higher scoring rates and both later generated additional assets. Parkhill never played for Portland and O'Brien never played for Cleveland, effectively canceling the lesser draft outcomes. Brewer provided the longest single-team value; Portland received the stronger immediate veteran production and more branching downstream value. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, draft identities, direct production and major follow-on transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Seattle and league transaction ledgers all record the same July 25, 1973 exchange: the Warriors sent Walt Hazzard to the SuperSonics for Butch Beard. Seattle executive Bill Russell's transaction record independently confirms the deal. Hazzard had adopted the name Mahdi Abdul-Rahman, which explains why the legacy asset and internal player identifier use different versions of the same player's name. The source-backed record keeps one identity and records both names rather than treating them as separate players. No cash or draft choice appears in the trade.

sections.heading: Beard Immediately Becomes a Major Warriors Guard
sections.body: Beard played 79 games for Golden State in 1973-74 and averaged 10.2 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists in 27.0 minutes. He shot 51.2 percent from the field, an efficient mark for a guard in that era. The Warriors missed the playoffs, but Beard established himself as one of their primary backcourt pieces. His 2,134 minutes were among the heavier workloads on the roster, giving Golden State a much larger first-season return than Seattle received from Hazzard.

sections.heading: The Championship Season Defines the Trade
sections.body: Beard's second Warriors season is the central value in the deal. He appeared in all 82 regular-season games for the 1974-75 team, averaging 12.8 points, 4.2 assists, 3.9 rebounds and 1.6 steals in 30.7 minutes while shooting 52.8 percent. Golden State won 48 games, then went 12-5 in the playoffs and swept Washington in the NBA Finals. Beard played all 17 postseason games, averaging 9.1 points, 4.2 rebounds and 3.1 assists in 26.4 minutes. He was not the team's star, but he was a core guard throughout a championship season.

sections.heading: Hazzard's Seattle Return Is Short
sections.body: Seattle received a veteran with a much longer résumé, including an All-Star season for the original SuperSonics in 1967-68. His second Seattle stint was far smaller. Hazzard played 49 games in 1973-74, averaging 3.8 points, 2.5 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 11.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists no later NBA season for him. That makes the transaction a one-season, low-minute return for Seattle compared with two full seasons and a championship role for Golden State.

sections.heading: Beard's Downstream Trade Has to Be Handled Carefully
sections.body: Golden State moved Beard on May 29, 1975, trading him to Cleveland with a 1975 first-round pick and a 1975 second-round pick for Dwight Davis. That deal proves Beard remained a tradeable asset after the championship. It would be wrong, however, to credit the full Davis return to Beard because Golden State also surrendered two draft choices. The source-backed evaluation therefore treats the Cleveland trade as retained-asset evidence rather than assigning all of Davis' later Warriors value to this 1973 exchange.

sections.heading: Why the legacy Grades Were Too Close
sections.body: The inherited B+/B split understated the gap. Seattle did receive a real NBA contributor, but only for 49 games at 11.7 minutes per night. Golden State received 161 regular-season games, 4,655 regular-season minutes, a full championship season and 17 playoff appearances. Beard also remained valuable enough to be included in a subsequent multi-asset trade. The difference is not merely team success; it is direct availability, role, production and asset life.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, A/D+. Golden State receives an A because Beard supplied two full seasons, became a high-minute backcourt contributor and played every game of the 1974-75 championship run before retaining trade value in 1975. Seattle receives a D+ because Hazzard supplied 49 low-minute games and 186 points in what became the final season of his NBA career. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, the Walt Hazzard/Mahdi Abdul-Rahman identity, both players' production and Beard's later Cleveland transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Virginia Squires and league transaction ledgers agree on the July 31, 1973 structure: Virginia sent Julius Erving and Willie Sojourner to New York for George Carter, Kermit Washington and cash. Roy Boe's Nets executive record and Al Bianchi's Squires executive record preserve the same package. Washington had just been selected fifth overall by the Los Angeles Lakers in the 1973 NBA draft, so Virginia acquired his ABA rights rather than a player who was under contract to join the Squires. The reviewed sources do not preserve the cash amount, leaving that component verified but unpriced.

sections.heading: Erving Changes the Nets Immediately
sections.body: Erving transformed New York in his first season. He played all 84 games in 1973-74 and averaged 27.4 points, 10.7 rebounds and 5.2 assists while winning the ABA MVP. The Nets improved from 30-54 the previous year to 55-29 and won the ABA championship. Erving then played all 84 games again in 1974-75 and all 84 in 1975-76, winning the league MVP in each season. Across the three years New York received 252 consecutive regular-season appearances from the best player in the league.

sections.heading: Two Championships and Three MVPs
sections.body: The postseason return is even more important than the regular-season durability. Erving led the Nets to the 1974 championship in his first year with the club, then to another title in 1976, the ABA's final season. Basketball-Reference lists him as playoff leader in both championship runs, and his 1975-76 regular-season line reached 29.3 points, 11.0 rebounds and 5.0 assists per game. A transaction that produces three MVP seasons and two league titles is not merely a strong star acquisition; it changes the competitive history of the franchise.

sections.heading: Sojourner Adds Real Supporting Value
sections.body: Sojourner was not a throw-in who disappeared. He played 82 games for New York in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75, giving the Nets 161 regular-season appearances across two seasons. In the first championship year he averaged 5.6 points and 4.1 rebounds in 16.0 minutes and appeared in the postseason. New York waived him in October 1975, so his direct asset chain ended before the second championship season, but the initial trade still produced two usable players rather than Erving alone.

sections.heading: Virginia's Best Return Was George Carter
sections.body: Carter gave the Squires substantial short-term production. In 1973-74 he played 80 games and averaged 19.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and 1.7 assists in 35.2 minutes. He also averaged 20.8 points across five playoff games, which happened to come against the Nets. Virginia later traded Carter and Mike Barr to the Memphis Sounds for Glen Combs and Mike Jackson in August 1974. That means Carter retained some downstream transaction value after his strong Squires season, even though Virginia did not keep him long enough to build a multi-year core around the return.

sections.heading: Washington's Rights Never Become Squires Production
sections.body: Washington is important to distinguish from Carter. The Lakers drafted him fifth overall in 1973, and Basketball-Reference shows him beginning his NBA career with Los Angeles that fall. He played 45 games for the Lakers in 1973-74 and never appeared for Virginia. The Squires therefore received an ABA rights asset that produced zero direct games. Whatever strategic leverage those rights may have represented at the time, the reviewed transaction history does not show Virginia converting them into a later player or pick.

sections.heading: The Cash Cannot Close the Gap
sections.body: Virginia also received cash, which mattered for a financially strained ABA club, but the amount is not identified in the reviewed ledgers. This archive does not invent a figure or convert an unknown payment into fictional player value. Carter's 80-game season plus the later Memphis trade give Virginia a real return, and the cash keeps the package from being treated as empty. None of those assets, however, approaches three Erving MVP seasons, two championships and 252 games from a franchise-defining player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/C+. New York receives an A+ because Erving delivered 252 regular-season games, three consecutive ABA MVP awards and championships in 1974 and 1976, while Sojourner added 161 games over two seasons. Virginia receives a C+ because Carter supplied an excellent 80-game scoring season and later trade utility, plus unpriced cash, but Washington's ABA rights produced zero Squires games and the package did not replace the superstar value sent away. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player production and Washington's zero-game Squires outcome, with only the cash amount unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
