sections.heading: The Verified September 4 Package
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Buffalo and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that the Bulls and Braves completed this trade on September 4, 1974. Chicago sent veteran guard Bob Weiss to Buffalo. The Bulls received Matt Guokas, Buffalo's 1977 second-round pick and another future second-round draft choice. The core player movement is clear, but one legacy pick label needs correction before the deal can be graded responsibly. The inherited record calls the unspecified future second a 1975 pick that became No. 34 Larry Fogle. The historical pick chain does not support that attribution.

sections.heading: Why Larry Fogle Does Not Belong to This Trade
sections.body: Chicago's own transaction ledger shows that the Bulls had already obtained Buffalo's 1975 second-round pick in September 1973. On May 28, 1974, months before the Guokas-Weiss trade, Chicago sent that pick to New York in the Maurice Lucas rights transaction. The 1975 draft later shows New York using No. 34 on Larry Fogle. A pick that had already left Chicago in May cannot also have arrived from Buffalo in September. The source-backed archive therefore keeps the September 4 asset as an unresolved future second-round pick rather than repeating the legacy Fogle attribution.

sections.heading: Guokas Gives Chicago an Immediate Full Season
sections.body: Guokas became a dependable Bulls rotation guard immediately. He played all 82 regular-season games in 1974-75, averaging 25.5 minutes, 7.2 points and 2.2 assists. Chicago won 47 games and reached the Western Conference Finals. Guokas also appeared throughout the postseason. The Bulls therefore received a full season of real rotation value from the principal player in the return, not merely draft assets whose outcomes would be determined later.

sections.heading: Chicago Also Preserved Downstream Value
sections.body: Guokas remained with the Bulls into 1975-76 before Chicago traded him to Kansas City in December 1975 for draft compensation. That later move extended the asset chain beyond his direct Chicago games. The exact value of every later selection should not be inflated, but the key point is that Guokas was still tradable after supplying a full season of useful minutes. Chicago did not simply use him for one year and lose the asset for nothing.

sections.heading: Buffalo Gets Two Seasons from Bob Weiss
sections.body: Weiss also produced meaningful value. He played 76 games for Buffalo in 1974-75, averaging 17.6 minutes, 3.4 points and 3.4 assists, and appeared in seven playoff games. He returned for 66 games in 1975-76, again serving as a reserve ball-handler, and made seven more playoff appearances. Buffalo waived him in September 1976. The Braves therefore received two useful seasons and should receive a solid grade rather than being treated as a clear loser with no return.

sections.heading: The 1977 Pick Adds Little
sections.body: Buffalo's 1977 second-round pick became No. 24 overall Larry Johnson. His NBA career consisted of only four games, so that branch did not add much realized value for Chicago. The other future second-round pick remains unresolved in the strongest reviewed transaction ledgers and is not assigned a fabricated player outcome. Even with those limitations, Guokas' larger 1974-75 role and his later trade value give Chicago more documented return than the two reserve seasons Buffalo received from Weiss.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A-/B. Chicago receives an A- because Guokas played every game in 1974-75, contributed during a Western Conference Finals run and retained downstream trade value, while the 1977 second-rounder adds a small additional asset. Buffalo receives a B because Weiss gave the Braves 142 regular-season games over two seasons plus playoff depth. The trade was useful for both clubs, but Chicago's package created the larger verified asset chain. Confidence is high on the player movement and 1977 pick, while the second future pick remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 4 Package
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA league transaction ledgers all agree on the September 4, 1974 structure. Denver sent rookie guard Darrell Elston and a first-round draft choice to the Virginia Squires for veteran point guard Fatty Taylor. Carl Scheer's executive transaction record independently preserves the same package. The first-rounder is important because the 1975 ABA draft record identifies Virginia's No. 10 selection of Mel Bennett as coming from Denver. This is therefore a three-asset trade for hindsight purposes, not merely Taylor for Elston.

sections.heading: Taylor Immediately Helps a 65-Win Denver Team
sections.body: Taylor gave Denver exactly the kind of veteran guard depth the new Larry Brown group could use. He appeared in 76 regular-season games in 1974-75 and averaged 8.4 points, 4.4 assists and 2.9 rebounds in 26.6 minutes. Denver's depth chart places him behind Mack Calvin at point guard but still credits Taylor with 2,018 minutes, the sixth-highest total on the roster. The Nuggets went 65-19, won the ABA Western Division and reached the Western Division Finals. Taylor also appeared in all 13 playoff games, so the acquisition produced immediate value on a contender rather than only regular-season depth.

sections.heading: Virginia Gets a Full Season from Darrell Elston
sections.body: Elston was not a throw-in. The 22-year-old guard played 72 games for Virginia in 1974-75 and averaged 26.0 minutes, 8.3 points, 2.8 assists and 2.3 rebounds. The Squires were one of the ABA's weakest teams, but trade grading should separate a player's realized contribution from the club's overall record. Elston logged 1,869 minutes and became a regular part of Virginia's backcourt. His ABA tenure did not extend into 1975-76, limiting that branch to one season, but it was still a meaningful first half of the return.

sections.heading: The Pick Becomes Mel Bennett
sections.body: Virginia's second asset matured a year later. The 1975 ABA draft record lists Bennett as the No. 10 overall selection by the Squires from Denver. Virginia signed him in June 1975, and he became a substantial frontcourt contributor immediately. Bennett played 75 games in 1975-76 and averaged 12.1 points and 7.0 rebounds in 29.2 minutes. The depth chart credits him with more than 2,100 minutes at power forward. That production matters because it means the first-round pick was not theoretical value; the Squires turned it into one of their more heavily used players in the franchise's final season.

sections.heading: Denver Extends Taylor's Value Once
sections.body: Denver did preserve some downstream value when it moved Taylor back to Virginia on October 21, 1975 for Chuck Williams. Williams later appeared in 21 games for Denver in 1976-77 before the Nuggets included him with Gus Gerard in the December trade for Jim Price. Because Gerard was also part of that later package, Price's full value cannot fairly be assigned to the original Taylor acquisition. The direct Taylor-for-Williams step is still legitimate downstream value and keeps Denver's side above an ordinary one-season rental. Taylor's return to Denver in August 1976 does not extend this chain because Denver paid Philadelphia a new 1977 second-round pick to reacquire him.

sections.heading: Why Virginia Holds the Hindsight Edge
sections.body: Denver's side worked. Taylor was a regular guard on a 65-win team and participated in a deep playoff run, then returned another veteran guard when Denver traded him away. The difference is volume. Virginia received 72 games from Elston and then 75 games from Bennett, with Bennett carrying a larger scoring and rebounding role than either Elston or Taylor. The Squires' financial and franchise collapse after 1975-76 prevented a longer asset chain, but that does not erase the production already realized from the Denver pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Squires Win, A-/B+. Virginia receives an A- because Elston supplied a full 72-game season and the acquired first-round pick became Bennett, who delivered 75 games of 12.1-point, 7.0-rebound production. Denver receives a B+ because Taylor gave the Nuggets 76 games, meaningful minutes on a 65-win contender and 13 playoff appearances, then was converted into Chuck Williams. Both clubs received useful value, but Virginia realized two substantial player-seasons from the package. Confidence is high on the transaction date, the No. 10 Bennett pick and the player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified September 6 Deal
sections.body: Phoenix, Washington and the NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same September 6, 1974 exchange. The Suns sent Clem Haskins to the Bullets and received Dave Stallworth plus Washington's 1975 second-round draft choice. Bob Ferry's Washington executive record and Jerry Colangelo's Phoenix executive record independently preserve the same package. Phoenix's historical media guide adds a useful detail: on October 10 the Suns waived Stallworth and formally acquired the rights to Washington's 1975 second-rounder to complete the Haskins deal. The pick later became No. 35 overall Allen Murphy.

sections.heading: Stallworth Never Reached the Phoenix Regular Season
sections.body: Stallworth had been a useful veteran earlier in his career, but Phoenix received no regular-season production from him. The Suns waived him on October 10, before their 1974-75 regular season began. He became a free agent and signed with the New York Knicks later that month, where he appeared briefly before being waived again in November. Because he never played a regular-season game for Phoenix and the Suns did not receive compensation when he left, the Stallworth branch of the return ended without realized on-court or downstream trade value.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Became Allen Murphy
sections.body: Phoenix did use Washington's second-round choice. The 1975 NBA Draft ledger shows the Suns selecting Louisville guard Allen Murphy at No. 35 overall. That verifies the legacy pick outcome and gives the transaction a traceable draft branch. The problem for Phoenix is that Murphy never played for the Suns. He instead joined the Kentucky Colonels in the ABA for 1975-76, appearing in 29 games as a reserve. After the ABA season and the merger period, Murphy signed with Chicago as a free agent in August 1976, and the Bulls later traded him to the Lakers. Those later moves were not Phoenix transactions, so they do not create downstream value for the Suns' 1974 asset chain.

sections.heading: Haskins Gives Washington Two Useful Seasons
sections.body: Haskins was already 31 when Washington acquired him, but he still supplied two seasons of dependable reserve play. In 1974-75 he appeared in 70 regular-season games, averaging 10.0 minutes and 4.0 points. Washington reached the NBA Finals, and Haskins appeared in 13 playoff games. He returned in 1975-76 for 55 more regular-season games, raising his scoring to 6.4 points in 13.4 minutes, and he appeared in five more playoff games. Across the two seasons, the Bullets received 125 regular-season games and 18 postseason appearances.

sections.heading: The Role Was Modest, but the Value Was Real
sections.body: Haskins was not a star in Washington. His usage had fallen sharply from his Phoenix peak, and he played behind the Bullets' primary guards. That limits Washington's grade and keeps this from being treated like a franchise-changing steal. Still, two seasons of available NBA depth on playoff teams is materially more than zero Phoenix appearances from either acquired asset. The comparison is especially direct because Stallworth was waived almost immediately and Murphy never signed with the Suns. There is no need to inflate Haskins' role to establish the direction of the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, A-/D+. Washington receives an A- because Haskins delivered 125 regular-season games and 18 playoff appearances across two seasons, including a reserve role on the 1975 NBA Finals team. Phoenix receives a D+ because Stallworth never played a regular-season game for the Suns and the acquired No. 35 pick became Murphy, who chose the ABA and never appeared for Phoenix. The Suns correctly converted the pick into a real prospect, but neither branch produced team value. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, October 10 completion detail, draft outcome and player histories. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Correcting the Date and Package
sections.body: Portland's legacy archive entry used September 15, 1974, but the stronger transaction record points to September 16. Basketball-Reference's Portland, New Orleans and NBA league ledgers all use September 16, and the Trail Blazers' official historical media guide does the same. The official Portland guide also preserves a cash component omitted from Basketball-Reference: New Orleans sent Barry Clemens, Kansas City-Omaha's 1976 second-round pick and cash for Rick Roberson. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the pick to No. 20 Major Jones. The canonical date is therefore corrected to September 16 while retaining cash as an officially documented part of the package.

sections.heading: Clemens Gives Portland Two Seasons
sections.body: Barry Clemens became the most durable realized asset in the transaction. He appeared in 77 games for Portland in 1974-75, averaging 12.4 minutes, 4.9 points and 2.1 rebounds. He returned for 49 more games in 1975-76, giving the Trail Blazers 126 regular-season appearances across two seasons. His role was reserve-level rather than central, but availability across two full roster cycles has genuine value, especially compared with an outgoing player whose tenure with New Orleans lasted only a fraction of one season. Portland waived Clemens in September 1976, ending his direct asset chain.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Became Major Jones
sections.body: The future consideration was not generic forever. New Orleans' obligation became Kansas City-Omaha's 1976 second-round pick, which Portland used at No. 20 on Major Jones. NBA.com and Basketball-Reference both preserve Jones as Portland's second-round selection. The pick did not create regular-season Trail Blazers production: Portland signed Jones in 1976 and waived him before the season. He eventually reached the NBA with Houston in 1979 and played six seasons, but those later games do not belong to Portland's realized return because the Trail Blazers had already released him. The pick still had option value at the draft, but its on-court Portland value was zero.

sections.heading: Roberson's New Orleans Return Was Brief
sections.body: Rick Roberson had just averaged 13.5 points and 10.2 rebounds in 69 games for Portland in 1973-74, so New Orleans was acquiring a center with recent starting-level production. The outcome changed quickly. Roberson played only 16 games for the Jazz in 1974-75, averaging 7.4 points and 7.4 rebounds in 21.2 minutes. New Orleans' roster and depth chart place him behind a crowded center group, and the Jazz eventually waived him on October 22, 1975. His next NBA season came with Kansas City, so New Orleans did not recover a later trade asset when the relationship ended.

sections.heading: Cash Adds Value Without Creating False Precision
sections.body: The Portland media guide explicitly lists cash in the return. The amount is not stated, so it should not be converted into an invented dollar value or a grade bump large enough to dominate the trade. It is still legitimate consideration. In this case Portland does not need the cash to establish a directional advantage because Clemens' 126 games already exceed Roberson's 16-game New Orleans tenure. The payment simply reinforces that Portland received more than one usable asset for a player who did not remain with the Jazz long.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, B+/C. Portland receives a B+ because Clemens supplied 126 games over two seasons, the club also received the No. 20 pick used on Major Jones, and official team history confirms additional cash. The grade stops below the top tier because Jones never played for Portland and Clemens was a reserve rather than a major starter. New Orleans receives a C because Roberson produced 16 games before his Jazz tenure ended without a downstream return. Confidence is high on the September 16 date, the player movement, the Major Jones pick chain and the cash component documented by Portland. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified October 7 Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland and league-wide transaction ledgers agree on the structure and date: Cleveland sold Lenny Wilkens' playing rights to Portland on October 7, 1974. The Trail Blazers' historical material also preserves the rights transfer for cash. This was not a conventional player-for-player trade or a free-agent signing with draft compensation. Cleveland controlled Wilkens' NBA playing rights after his two seasons with the Cavaliers and monetized those rights when Portland wanted him available as a player.

sections.heading: The Coaching Job Predated the Transaction
sections.body: One important correction to the legacy analysis is that Portland did not acquire Wilkens' coaching services through the October rights sale. The Trail Blazers hired him as head coach on May 24, 1974, more than four months earlier. He therefore entered training camp already responsible for the team from the bench. The October transaction only resolved his ability to continue playing. That distinction matters for hindsight grading because Portland's later 38-44 coaching record was not purchased from Cleveland and should not inflate the value of the rights transaction.

sections.heading: Portland Still Received Real On-Court Value
sections.body: Even after separating the coaching role, the acquired playing rights produced a useful season. Wilkens appeared in 65 games in 1974-75 and averaged 17.9 minutes, 6.5 points, 3.6 assists and 1.8 rebounds. At age 37 he was no longer the All-Star-level guard who had led the league in assists earlier in his career, but he remained a dependable secondary ball-handler behind Portland's younger core. His 1,161 minutes are a meaningful realized return from a cash-only acquisition, especially because no player or draft choice left Portland in the transaction.

sections.heading: It Was His Final NBA Playing Season
sections.body: The Portland season also marked the end of Wilkens' 15-year NBA playing career. He did not create a later player trade asset for the Trail Blazers, and the club did not receive compensation when his playing career ended. That limits the transaction to one season of direct court value. The acquisition should therefore be graded as useful rather than transformative. Portland received a veteran contributor for 65 games, not a long-term starter or a multi-year asset chain.

sections.heading: Cleveland's Cash Is Real but Unpriced
sections.body: Cleveland's side should not be treated as zero. The Cavaliers sold rights to a 37-year-old player they no longer planned to use and received cash rather than carrying an inactive asset. That is rational roster management. The problem for retrospective grading is that the reviewed sources do not disclose the payment amount. Without a figure, the archive cannot compare the cash precisely with Portland's 1,161 minutes of veteran guard play. Still, the known on-court return is substantial enough to support a modest Portland edge while keeping Cleveland's grade respectable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, B/C+. Portland receives a B because the rights purchase produced 65 games of reliable veteran guard depth in Wilkens' final NBA season. Cleveland receives a C+ because it converted unused playing rights into cash, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable downstream basketball asset. The coaching role is explicitly excluded from the trade valuation because Portland had hired Wilkens months before the sale. Confidence is high on the date, transaction structure and playing outcome, with uncertainty limited to the cash amount. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified October 8 Transaction
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, New Orleans and league transaction ledgers agree on the structure and date. The Bucks sent Russ Lee and their 1975 first-round pick to the expansion Jazz for Steve Kuberski and New Orleans' 1975 second-round pick. Wayne Embry's Milwaukee executive record and Bill Bertka's New Orleans executive record independently match the package. The archive maps the historical New Orleans Jazz to the modern Utah Jazz franchise key, so the transaction remains under utah-jazz even though every contemporary source uses New Orleans.

sections.heading: Russ Lee Was a Short-Term Jazz Piece
sections.body: The legacy archive entry called him Russell Lee, but the verified player identity is Russ Lee, Basketball-Reference ID leeru01. New Orleans used him in only 15 regular-season games in 1974-75. He averaged 9.3 minutes, 4.3 points and 2.1 rebounds, then the Jazz waived him on November 27. Lee therefore supplied little direct value and did not create a later trade asset. His part of the package matters mostly because it accompanied the first-round pick that became the trade's dominant Jazz return.

sections.heading: Rich Kelley Became the Difference Maker
sections.body: New Orleans used Milwaukee's 1975 first-round pick at No. 7 on Rich Kelley. He immediately became a productive center, playing 75 games as a rookie and averaging 7.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.1 assists. His role grew each season. Kelley played 76 games in 1976-77, all 82 in 1977-78 and 80 in 1978-79. In that final New Orleans season he averaged about 15.7 points and 12.8 rebounds, giving the franchise 313 regular-season games across four years from the acquired pick.

sections.heading: Kelley's Value Continued After the Move to Utah
sections.body: The franchise moved to Utah in 1979, and Kelley still carried trade value. On October 2, the Jazz sent him to New Jersey for Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan. That downstream return should not be credited entirely as if the original Milwaukee pick alone created every later win, but it demonstrates that Kelley remained a substantial asset after four productive seasons. The trade therefore generated both direct on-court value and a later three-player return for the Jazz franchise.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Useful but Limited Depth
sections.body: Steve Kuberski appeared in 59 games for Milwaukee in 1974-75 and averaged 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds in 8.8 minutes. The Bucks kept him into the next preseason, but Buffalo claimed him on waivers on October 16, 1975. Milwaukee's draft return was No. 22 Clyde Mayes. Mayes played 65 games for the Bucks in 1975-76, averaging 4.4 points and 4.0 rebounds in 14.6 minutes. He did not become a long-term Milwaukee rotation piece, and his later NBA appearances came with other franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A+/C+. The Jazz franchise receives an A+ because Milwaukee's first-round pick became Rich Kelley, who supplied four productive seasons and later brought back Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan. Russ Lee added only 15 games, but the pick outcome alone makes the return excellent. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Kuberski and Mayes combined to provide one season each of reserve depth, but neither became a durable asset. Confidence is high on the October 8 date, player identities, draft outcomes and downstream Kelley trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified November 8 Trade
sections.body: Atlanta, Philadelphia and the NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the November 8, 1974 structure. The Hawks sent Clyde Lee and their 1975 third-round pick to the 76ers for Tom Van Arsdale. William Wilcox's Atlanta executive record and Pat Williams' Philadelphia record independently preserve the same deal. The pick became No. 39 in the 1975 draft, where Philadelphia selected Jimmie Baker. The legacy archive entry uses Jim Baker, but Basketball-Reference's player record identifies him as Jimmie Baker Jr.; the source-backed record retains Jim Baker as an alias while linking the draft outcome to the verified player identity.

sections.heading: Van Arsdale Immediately Became a Major Atlanta Scorer
sections.body: Van Arsdale had appeared in nine games for Philadelphia before the trade, averaging 14.0 points. His role expanded sharply in Atlanta. He played 73 games for the Hawks in 1974-75 and averaged 18.9 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 35.2 minutes. That was not reserve value; he became one of Atlanta's principal offensive players. He returned for 75 games in 1975-76, averaging 10.9 points and 2.6 assists. Across the two post-trade seasons, Atlanta received 148 games from a veteran wing who was still capable of carrying substantial offensive responsibility.

sections.heading: Atlanta Also Preserved Downstream Value
sections.body: The Hawks did not lose Van Arsdale for nothing when his Atlanta tenure ended. On June 16, 1976, they traded him to the Buffalo Braves for Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash. The later return does not automatically make every component of that Buffalo package equal to the original 1974 acquisition, but it proves Van Arsdale still had trade value after two seasons in Atlanta. That downstream conversion separates the Hawks' side from a simple two-year rental and adds another layer of realized value to the original transaction.

sections.heading: Clyde Lee Gave Philadelphia Real Frontcourt Production
sections.body: Philadelphia's return should not be minimized. Lee played 71 games for the 76ers after the trade in 1974-75, starting 35 and averaging 32.1 minutes, 5.8 points and 9.7 rebounds. He remained with the club for 79 games in 1975-76, contributing another 5.7 rebounds in 18.0 minutes per game. That is 150 regular-season appearances over two seasons from a useful veteran big man. The first season in particular gave Philadelphia a substantial rebounding presence while the roster was still being rebuilt around younger players.

sections.heading: The Jimmie Baker Pick Added Little NBA Value
sections.body: Philadelphia used Atlanta's third-round pick at No. 39 on Jimmie Baker. Baker did play professionally, appearing in five ABA games for Kentucky during 1975-76, but he never recorded an NBA regular-season game for the 76ers. The pick therefore added draft optionality without adding direct Philadelphia NBA production. In a close comparison between Van Arsdale and Lee, that unused draft outcome is not enough to erase Atlanta's advantage in scoring impact and Van Arsdale's later trade return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A/B+. Atlanta receives an A because Van Arsdale produced 148 games, delivered high-level scoring immediately after the trade and was later converted into Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Lee supplied 150 useful games and strong rebounding across two seasons, but the third-round pick did not become an NBA contributor for the 76ers. This was a productive trade for both sides rather than a lopsided failure; Atlanta's edge comes from Van Arsdale's stronger offensive impact and retained asset value. Confidence is high on the date, package, player outcomes and downstream Van Arsdale transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified November 8 Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 8, 1974 structure: the Lakers acquired Lucius Allen and sent Jim Price to the Bucks. Wayne Embry's Milwaukee executive record independently preserves the same player-for-player trade. There were no draft picks or cash in the original exchange, so the retrospective comparison begins with two guards whose direct production can be measured cleanly before following what each club later received when it moved them again.

sections.heading: Allen Became a Major Lakers Guard Immediately
sections.body: Allen stepped into a large role in Los Angeles. He played 56 games for the Lakers after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 19.5 points, 5.7 assists and 4.4 rebounds in 35.9 minutes. He returned for 76 games in 1975-76 at 14.7 points and 4.7 assists, then 78 games in 1976-77 at 14.6 points and 5.2 assists. That is 210 regular-season games over three seasons, with starter-level usage throughout most of the run. The first post-trade season alone supplied more offensive creation than the legacy B-minus grade suggested.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Preserved Downstream Value
sections.body: On June 1, 1977, the Lakers traded Allen to Kansas City for Ollie Johnson plus 1978 first- and second-round picks. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Kings and league transaction ledgers all preserve that package, with the draft assets later associated with Purvis Short and Ron Carter. The Lakers should not be credited with those players' careers simply because the picks later became their selections, but the package proves Allen still carried substantial transaction value after three productive Los Angeles seasons. That downstream return raises the value of the original acquisition beyond Allen's direct box-score production.

sections.heading: Price Was Productive for Milwaukee Too
sections.body: Jim Price also gave his new team substantial immediate value. He played 41 games for Milwaukee after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 14.9 points, 5.4 assists and 3.8 rebounds in 37.3 minutes. He then played 80 games in 1975-76 at 11.7 points and 4.9 assists before appearing in six more games for the Bucks in 1976-77. Across the Milwaukee portion of his career, Price produced 127 regular-season appearances and handled a meaningful share of the club's backcourt creation. That direct return supports a high grade even though Allen's Lakers tenure was longer.

sections.heading: Price's Downstream Pick Helped Milwaukee Reach Marques Johnson
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Price to Buffalo on November 2, 1976 for a 1977 first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong. On June 7, 1977, the Bucks packaged Swen Nater and that same first-round asset to Buffalo for the No. 3 pick, which Milwaukee used on Marques Johnson. It would be incorrect to attribute Johnson's later Bucks career entirely to Price because Nater was also a major part of the exchange. Still, the Price-derived first-rounder clearly contributed to obtaining one of Milwaukee's most important late-1970s players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge, A+/A. Los Angeles receives an A+ because Allen gave the club 210 games of high-minute guard production and later returned Ollie Johnson plus two draft assets. Milwaukee receives an A because Price supplied 127 productive games and was converted into a first-round pick that became part of the package used to acquire the No. 3 Marques Johnson selection. Both franchises extracted major value from the same one-for-one trade. The Lakers' edge comes from Allen's larger direct body of work and broader downstream package, not from Milwaukee receiving a poor return. Confidence is high on the original exchange and the major downstream transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified November 11 Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, New Orleans and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 11, 1974 deal: the Bulls sent Rick Adelman to the expansion Jazz for John Block. Dick Motta's Chicago executive record and Bill Bertka's New Orleans record independently preserve the same one-for-one swap. The archive maps the historical New Orleans Jazz to the modern Utah Jazz franchise key, so the source-backed verdict is stored under utah-jazz even though every contemporary record properly identifies New Orleans.

sections.heading: Block Helped a Contender Immediately
sections.body: John Block had played only four games for New Orleans before the trade, but Chicago gave him a steady frontcourt role. He appeared in 50 regular-season games for the Bulls in 1974-75 and averaged 17.6 minutes, 8.1 points and 4.3 rebounds while shooting 47.3 percent. Chicago won 47 games, finished first in the Midwest Division and reached Game 7 of the Western Conference Finals. Block was not one of the team's stars, but he supplied useful scoring and rebounding depth during a deep playoff season.

sections.heading: Chicago's Return Was Mostly a One-Season Asset
sections.body: Block's Chicago value was concentrated in that first year. He appeared in only two games for the Bulls in 1975-76, totaling seven minutes, and that season became the end of his NBA career. That does not erase the value of 50 useful appearances for a contender, but it limits the long-term return. There was no later Chicago trade package or draft asset created from Block, so the Bulls' side can be evaluated almost entirely from his direct 1974-75 production.

sections.heading: Adelman Gave New Orleans a Short-Term Backcourt Piece
sections.body: Rick Adelman played 28 games for the Jazz after the trade and averaged 21.9 minutes, 6.3 points, 2.5 assists and 2.0 rebounds. He was not a long-term building block for an expansion team that was still changing personnel rapidly, but he gave New Orleans a credible veteran guard during the franchise's difficult first season. His direct Jazz production was smaller than Block's Chicago contribution, so the New Orleans side needs its downstream transaction to justify the overall edge.

sections.heading: Adelman Became Part of the Nate Williams Deal
sections.body: On February 1, 1975, New Orleans traded Adelman and Ollie Johnson to Kansas City-Omaha for Nate Williams. Williams immediately averaged 14.3 points in 35 games for the Jazz, then played 81 games in 1975-76, 79 in 1976-77 and 27 more in 1977-78 before moving on. The Jazz should not receive full credit for Williams as though Adelman alone bought him, because Ollie Johnson was also part of the package. Still, Adelman clearly retained enough transaction value to help New Orleans acquire a player who became a regular scorer across multiple seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A-/B+. The modern Utah franchise receives an A- for the historical New Orleans side because Adelman supplied 28 games and then helped form the package that brought back Nate Williams, a productive multi-season Jazz rotation scorer. Chicago receives a B+ because Block gave the Bulls 50 useful regular-season games during a conference-finals season plus two more appearances the next year, but he produced no further downstream asset value. The edge is narrow and depends on giving Adelman partial, not full, credit for the Williams acquisition. Confidence is high on the original trade and direct statistics, and medium-high on the allocation of downstream value because Ollie Johnson shared that outgoing package. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified November 27 Package
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Suns and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the November 27, 1974 exchange. Los Angeles received Corky Calhoun, while Phoenix received the Lakers' 1976 second-round pick and 1977 third-round pick. Jerry Colangelo's executive transaction record independently preserves the same package. The two draft assets followed very different paths, which is important for hindsight grading: Phoenix traded the 1976 selection before draft night but kept and used the 1977 pick itself.

sections.heading: Calhoun Gave Los Angeles Two Useful Seasons
sections.body: Calhoun immediately entered the Lakers' rotation after playing only 13 games for Phoenix that season. He appeared in 57 Los Angeles games in 1974-75, averaging 22.3 minutes, 5.0 points and 4.1 rebounds. In 1975-76 he played 76 games and averaged 23.9 minutes, 5.4 points and 4.5 rebounds. That is 133 regular-season games of dependable wing and forward depth across two seasons. The production was modest, but Calhoun was a real rotation player rather than a fringe acquisition.

sections.heading: The Lakers' Asset Chain Ends With a Waiver
sections.body: Los Angeles did not turn Calhoun into a later player or draft return. The 1976-77 league transaction ledger records the Lakers waiving him in October 1976. Portland then became the beneficiary of his next productive seasons, but those games cannot be credited to Los Angeles because the Lakers received no compensation when he left. The original trade therefore produced exactly the two Lakers seasons Calhoun played and no documented downstream asset beyond them.

sections.heading: Phoenix Converted the 1976 Pick Before the Draft
sections.body: The first Lakers pick did not become Jacky Dorsey for Phoenix. On June 9, 1975, the Suns sent the 1976 second-round selection to Portland for Phil Lumpkin. Portland later moved the pick to New Orleans, which ultimately used No. 26 on Dorsey. For Phoenix's side of this trade, Lumpkin is the relevant realized return. He played 34 regular-season games for the 1975-76 Suns and appeared in all 17 playoff games as Phoenix reached the NBA Finals. His regular-season role was small, but the pick clearly became usable roster value on a Finals team.

sections.heading: Mike Bratz Made the Third-Round Pick the Difference
sections.body: Phoenix kept the Lakers' 1977 third-rounder and selected Mike Bratz at No. 66. Bratz then played 80 regular-season games as a rookie, 77 in 1978-79 and all 82 in 1979-80. His scoring rose from 4.7 points per game to 8.1 and then 8.5, and he appeared in 25 playoff games across those three seasons. In total, the third-round pick produced 239 Phoenix regular-season games before Bratz was lost to Dallas in the 1980 expansion draft. That sustained rotation value is the largest single return in the original transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A+/B+. Phoenix receives an A+ because the two picks became two separate useful assets: the 1976 second-rounder was converted into Lumpkin for the 1976 Finals run, while the 1977 third-rounder became Bratz for 239 regular-season games and 25 playoff appearances. Los Angeles receives a B+ because Calhoun supplied 133 useful games over two seasons, but the Lakers waived him without a downstream return. The trade was not a failure for Los Angeles; Phoenix simply extracted more total and postseason value from the two draft assets. Confidence is high on the package, Calhoun tenure, pick routing and Bratz outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Reconciling the December Date
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Lakers, New Orleans and NBA league transaction ledgers all date the Stu Lantz trade to December 6, 1974. Pro Sports Transactions' 1975 draft-trade ledger records the deal one day earlier, December 5. The package itself is consistent across the sources: Los Angeles received Lantz and New Orleans received the Lakers' 1975 third-round draft asset, later used at No. 38 on Jim McElroy. The specialist draft ledger also lists cash, while Basketball-Reference does not. The source-backed record therefore uses December 6 as the canonical transaction date, preserves the one-day source conflict in audit metadata and treats the cash amount as unresolved rather than inventing a value.

sections.heading: Lantz Gave the Lakers Two Useful Seasons
sections.body: Lantz had played 19 games for the expansion Jazz before the trade. In Los Angeles he immediately moved into a larger role, appearing in 56 games in 1974-75 and averaging 9.3 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 25.5 minutes. He returned for 53 games in 1975-76 at 4.7 points and 1.4 assists in 16.1 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 109 regular-season games for the Lakers across those two seasons. The first year supplied meaningful rotation value, while the second was a smaller bench role.

sections.heading: The Lakers Did Not Create a Downstream Asset
sections.body: Lantz did not play in 1976-77 because of a back injury and never returned to an NBA regular-season game. That means Los Angeles received two seasons of direct production but no later trade return, draft compensation or sale value from the asset. The trade should not be treated as a failure for the Lakers because Lantz was a real contributor, yet its value ended with the 109 games he played. The absence of a downstream conversion becomes important when compared with what New Orleans received from the draft pick.

sections.heading: McElroy Became a Four-Year Jazz Guard
sections.body: New Orleans used the acquired third-round pick at No. 38 on Jim McElroy, a Central Michigan guard. He played 51 games as a rookie in 1975-76 and then 73, 74 and 79 games over the next three seasons. Basketball-Reference's franchise trade comparison credits McElroy with 277 regular-season games for New Orleans, averaging 11.5 points, 2.4 rebounds and 4.0 assists in those Jazz games. That is a substantial return from a third-round pick and clearly exceeds the direct volume Los Angeles received from Lantz.

sections.heading: The Cash Note Only Strengthens the Jazz Side
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions also records cash going from Los Angeles to New Orleans, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed record. Because the cash cannot be priced, it should not be converted into a fictional player-equivalent value or used to inflate a grade numerically. It still matters directionally: if the specialist ledger is correct, New Orleans received additional consideration on top of the pick that became McElroy. The verdict does not depend on that cash, however, because McElroy's four-season Jazz tenure already provides the stronger realized basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A+/B. New Orleans receives an A+ because a third-round pick became McElroy, who supplied 277 regular-season games and four years of guard production, with an additional unresolved cash component listed by the specialist draft ledger. Los Angeles receives a B because Lantz gave the Lakers 109 useful games across two seasons, especially a productive first year, but the asset ended with his back injury and retirement from NBA play. Confidence is high on the package, player identities and outcomes, and medium-high on the exact transaction date because of the December 5 versus December 6 source conflict. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified January 8 Transaction
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that the Hawks traded Jim Washington to the Buffalo Braves on January 8, 1975 for a 1976 fifth-round draft pick. The later draft record identifies that selection as No. 82, which Atlanta used on Connie White. The archive maps historical Buffalo to the modern Los Angeles Clippers franchise key, so the source-backed record remains under los-angeles-clippers even though every contemporary transaction source correctly names the Braves. The package is unusually straightforward: one veteran player for one future fifth-round selection.

sections.heading: Washington Supplied Immediate Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Washington joined a Buffalo team that finished 49-33 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. After the trade he appeared in 42 regular-season games, averaging 16.0 minutes, 4.2 points and 4.7 rebounds while shooting 47.5 percent from the field. His per-36 rebounding rate was 10.5, which reflects the skill that had kept him in NBA rotations throughout the previous decade. He was not a featured scorer for Buffalo, but he provided experienced frontcourt minutes during a winning season and gave the club real on-court value from an otherwise distant fifth-round pick.

sections.heading: His Buffalo Tenure Was Brief
sections.body: The limitation is duration. Washington played only one additional game for Buffalo in 1975-76, logging seven minutes, and that was the final NBA regular-season appearance of his career. The Braves therefore received 43 games in total from the transaction and did not preserve a meaningful later trade asset. That keeps the return from earning an elite grade even though it clearly beats a pick that never produced NBA minutes. The value is best described as useful short-term depth rather than a transformational acquisition.

sections.heading: Atlanta Waited Until the 1976 Draft
sections.body: The Hawks' consideration did not convey for more than a year. Atlanta retained the fifth-rounder and used it on Connie White with the 82nd overall selection in the 1976 NBA Draft. The Hawks' transaction page and franchise draft history both preserve that outcome. White was a 6-foot-4 guard from California, and Basketball-Reference lists him as Atlanta's fifth-round selection. Because the pick did turn into a named player, the relationship should remain explicit rather than being left as generic future consideration.

sections.heading: White Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's player page contains White's draft information but no NBA season statistics, and Atlanta's franchise draft table likewise shows no NBA games for the No. 82 selection. That means the Hawks realized no regular-season production from the draft asset. A late-round pick still carries some optionality at the moment of the trade, so the return should not be graded as though Atlanta received literally nothing. In hindsight, however, the option did not convert into an NBA roster contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, B+/D+. Buffalo receives a B+ because Washington supplied 42 useful games during a 49-win season plus one final appearance the next year. His role was limited and the tenure was short, so the return stops below the A range. Atlanta receives a D+ because the fifth-round pick was retained and used on a real prospect, but White never played an NBA regular-season game. The outcome is clear without exaggerating Washington's impact: Buffalo converted a low future pick into immediate rotation depth, while Atlanta's eventual selection produced no NBA minutes. Confidence is high on the transaction date, package, Washington statistics and White draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The February 1 Package Is Well Documented
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Jazz and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the core February 1, 1975 exchange: New York received Jim Barnett and Neal Walk, while New Orleans received Henry Bibby and Detroit's 1975 first-round pick. The official Jazz media guide and Pro Sports Transactions add one more piece that Basketball-Reference omits: cash from New York to New Orleans. The Detroit pick had reached the Knicks in the Howard Porter trade, so this transaction continues the same asset chain already established in the source-backed archive.

sections.heading: New York Received Two Rotation Players
sections.body: Barnett played 28 games for the Knicks after the trade in 1974-75 and another 71 in 1975-76, giving New York 99 regular-season games. His role was modest by that stage of his career, but he still averaged 6.5 points in the first partial season and 5.9 the next year. Walk gave the Knicks more frontcourt volume. He played 30 games after the trade, all 82 in 1975-76 and 11 more in 1976-77, for 123 regular-season games in New York. His best Knicks season was 1975-76, when he averaged 7.4 points and 4.7 rebounds in 16.3 minutes.

sections.heading: Bibby Became a Useful Jazz Guard
sections.body: Henry Bibby immediately entered the New Orleans rotation. He played 28 games for the Jazz after the trade in 1974-75 and 79 more in 1975-76, totaling 107 regular-season games. In 1975-76 he averaged 9.3 points and 2.8 assists while playing 22.4 minutes per game. New Orleans then sold Bibby's player rights to Philadelphia on September 17, 1976. The sale amount is not preserved in the reviewed Basketball-Reference ledger, so the downstream financial value should be acknowledged without being assigned an invented number.

sections.heading: The Detroit Pick Became Another Trade Asset
sections.body: New Orleans also did not simply draft Bill Robinzine. On May 28, 1975, the Jazz traded the No. 10 pick to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Behagen and a 1976 second-round pick. Kansas City-Omaha used No. 10 on Robinzine. That distinction matters because Robinzine's NBA production belongs to the Kings' side of the later transaction, not directly to New Orleans. For the Jazz, the realized return from the pick is Behagen plus the later second-round selection, not Robinzine himself.

sections.heading: Behagen Gave New Orleans Two Productive Seasons
sections.body: Behagen played 66 games for the Jazz in 1975-76 and averaged 11.5 points and 8.4 rebounds. He returned for 60 games in 1976-77, adding 8.6 points and 7.2 rebounds per game. That is 126 regular-season games of direct frontcourt production created from the Detroit pick before considering the additional 1976 second-round asset. The second-rounder became No. 20 Major Jones, but Jones did not play an NBA regular-season game for New Orleans, so the pick's meaningful realized Jazz value rests primarily with Behagen.

sections.heading: Comparing the Two Returns
sections.body: New York's side was not poor. Barnett and Walk combined for 222 regular-season games, and Walk in particular gave the Knicks dependable reserve-center minutes. New Orleans, however, received 107 Bibby games plus 126 Behagen games from the downstream pick trade, along with cash in the original deal and later compensation when Bibby's rights were sold. The Jazz therefore generated slightly more total asset depth and comparable or better on-court production despite moving the first-round pick before draft night.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A/B+. New Orleans receives an A because Bibby and Behagen combined for 233 regular-season games, the original deal also included cash, and Bibby's rights later retained sale value. New York receives a B+ because Barnett and Walk combined for 222 games and filled real rotation roles, but neither created a comparable downstream asset. Bill Robinzine is preserved as the eventual draft identity of the No. 10 pick without falsely crediting his Kings production to the Jazz. Confidence is high on the transaction date, package and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The February 1 Trade Is Straightforward
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City-Omaha, New Orleans and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the February 1, 1975 exchange. The Kings sent Nate Williams to the Jazz and received Rick Adelman plus Ollie Johnson. No draft choice or cash belongs to the original transaction, which makes the first stage of the comparison unusually direct. The historical team keys in the archive map Kansas City-Omaha to the modern Sacramento Kings franchise and New Orleans to the modern Utah Jazz franchise, but the analysis preserves the contemporary team names when describing what happened.

sections.heading: Adelman Was a Short-Term Piece
sections.body: Rick Adelman had just arrived in New Orleans from Chicago in November 1974. After moving to Kansas City-Omaha, he appeared in 18 regular-season games and averaged 6.7 minutes and 1.7 points. Those were the final NBA games of his playing career. Adelman later became far more important as an NBA coach, but that coaching career cannot be credited to this player transaction. For trade-value purposes, the Kings received only the 18 games he actually played after the deal.

sections.heading: Ollie Johnson Supplied the Real Kings Return
sections.body: Ollie Johnson was the durable piece. He played 30 games for Kansas City-Omaha after the trade in 1974-75, then 81 games in 1975-76 and another 81 in 1976-77. That is 192 regular-season games for the franchise, including a 1975-76 season in which he averaged 10.1 points and 4.4 rebounds in 26.2 minutes. Combined with Adelman's 18 games, the Kings received 210 regular-season appearances from the two incoming players. Johnson was a legitimate multi-year rotation forward and keeps the Kings side from being graded as a poor outcome.

sections.heading: Johnson Still Had Trade Value in 1977
sections.body: On June 1, 1977, Kansas City sent Johnson, a 1978 first-round pick and a 1978 second-round pick to the Lakers for Lucius Allen. That later move shows Johnson retained value, but the full Allen return cannot responsibly be assigned to Johnson because two draft picks were also in the package. A source-backed archive should record the continuing asset chain without pretending one component purchased the entire downstream player. The original deal therefore gets credit for Johnson's direct Kings production and only limited qualitative credit for his later inclusion in a larger trade.

sections.heading: Williams Became the Best Player in the Deal
sections.body: Nate Williams immediately took on a larger scoring role in New Orleans. He played 35 games after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 14.3 points, then appeared in 81 games in 1975-76 at 12.8 points and 79 games in 1976-77 at 12.3 points. He added 27 more Jazz games in 1977-78 before being traded. Across those four partial seasons, Williams played 222 regular-season games for New Orleans. His scoring role and durability made him the strongest directly attributable basketball asset on either side of the transaction.

sections.heading: New Orleans Also Preserved Downstream Value
sections.body: The Jazz did not simply lose Williams when his role ended. On January 5, 1978, New Orleans traded him to Golden State for a 1978 second-round pick that became No. 35 Tommie Green. Green did not become a meaningful NBA player for the Jazz, so the later pick did not add major realized production. It still matters that Williams remained tradeable after 222 games. New Orleans received both the best direct player outcome and an additional asset at the end of the tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A/B+. New Orleans receives an A because Williams gave the franchise 222 regular-season games, three consecutive double-figure scoring seasons after the trade and a later second-round pick. Kansas City receives a B+ because Johnson supplied 192 useful games and Adelman added 18 more, but the combined package never matched Williams' offensive role or downstream value. The Kings side was productive enough that this is not a lopsided deal; the Jazz simply received the best player and kept value alive longer. Confidence is high on the date, package, direct production and downstream transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Pick Chain Starts Before This Trade
sections.body: The first-round pick Kansas City acquired had already moved twice. Detroit originally owned the 1975 No. 10 selection, sent it to New York for Howard Porter, and the Knicks then moved it to New Orleans in the February 1 Jim Barnett-Neal Walk trade. On May 28, New Orleans sent that same pick to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Behagen and a 1976 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Kings and Jazz transaction pages and Pro Sports Transactions all preserve the package. The Kings used No. 10 the next day on Bill Robinzine.

sections.heading: Robinzine Gave Kansas City Four Full Seasons
sections.body: Robinzine immediately became a useful frontcourt piece. He played 75 games as a rookie in 1975-76 and averaged 8.0 points and 4.7 rebounds. He played another 75 games the next season, all 82 in 1977-78 and all 82 again in 1978-79. That is 314 regular-season games for the Kings franchise in four seasons. His scoring climbed into double figures and his rebounding remained useful throughout the run. A first-round pick becoming a four-year rotation forward is a strong realized return even without All-Star honors.

sections.heading: Behagen Was a Real Return for New Orleans
sections.body: New Orleans did not give away the pick for nothing. Ron Behagen played 66 games for the Jazz in 1975-76 and averaged 11.5 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 26.3 minutes. He returned for 60 games in 1976-77 at 8.6 points and 7.2 rebounds. Across those two seasons, Behagen gave the Jazz 126 regular-season games and substantial frontcourt production. His first year in particular was good enough that the deal cannot be treated as a one-sided failure for New Orleans.

sections.heading: The Major Jones Pick Was Already Owed to Portland
sections.body: The legacy archive entry makes the 1976 second-round pick look like a simple future Jazz selection that became Major Jones. The chain is more complicated. New Orleans had traded Rick Roberson to Portland in September 1974 for Barry Clemens, future consideration, and cash. The Jazz later used the Kansas City second-rounder acquired in this Behagen trade to satisfy that future-consideration obligation. Portland ultimately held the No. 20 pick and drafted Major Jones. The official Jazz media guide explicitly describes the pick as sent to Portland under the earlier Roberson transaction.

sections.heading: That Means Major Jones' NBA Career Is Not Jazz Production
sections.body: Major Jones eventually played six NBA seasons, but he did not do so for New Orleans. Portland drafted him, and his NBA debut came later with Houston after several seasons in other professional leagues. The Jazz should receive transaction value for acquiring an asset that helped satisfy an existing obligation, but Jones' later NBA statistics cannot be credited to New Orleans. This is an important distinction between a pick's final draft identity and the actual realized production a franchise received from the asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A/B+. Kansas City receives an A because the acquired No. 10 pick became Robinzine, who supplied 314 regular-season games over four full seasons. New Orleans receives a B+ because Behagen delivered 126 productive games and the 1976 second-rounder had real value as the asset used to complete the prior Portland obligation. The Jazz did not actually receive Major Jones' NBA production, so that career is not counted in their grade. Kansas City gets the edge through the longer directly attributable player return. Confidence is high on the May 28 package, pick chain and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Sale Is Preserved Best in the Draft-Trade Ledger
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records a May 29, 1975 exchange in which Seattle sent cash to Atlanta for the Hawks' second-round pick, No. 21 overall. The same specialist database repeats the deal in its transaction-search results. Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Seattle and league transaction pages do not list the cash sale itself, although they do confirm that Seattle selected Bruce Seals with the 21st pick that day. Because the specialist source supplies the missing ownership chain while the draft outcome is independently verified, the source-backed record can preserve the trade with medium-high confidence rather than pretending every database carries identical historical detail.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned the Pick Into an Immediate Rotation Player
sections.body: Seals arrived with professional experience from the ABA and stepped directly into a substantial Seattle role. He played 81 games in 1975-76 and averaged 30.1 minutes, 11.8 points and 6.3 rebounds. That was not marginal second-round production. He also appeared in six playoff games during Seattle's postseason run. The next season he again played 81 games and averaged 11.0 points and 4.4 rebounds. In 1977-78 he added 73 games at 7.8 points and 3.1 rebounds. Across those three seasons, Seattle received 235 regular-season games from the acquired pick.

sections.heading: Seals' First Two Seasons Carry Most of the Value
sections.body: The strongest part of the return came early. Seals was a significant rotation forward in both 1975-76 and 1976-77, averaging double figures in scoring each year. His role declined in the third season, but he still played 73 games. That gives Seattle both volume and useful peak production from a second-round selection. Even without a star-level outcome, a three-year contributor who played more than 2,400 minutes as a rookie represents a strong conversion of a purchased draft asset.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Return Was Cash, but the Amount Is Unknown
sections.body: The Hawks received cash rather than a player or future draft asset. The reviewed specialist source does not provide the amount, and the major team transaction ledgers omit the sale entirely. That prevents a precise financial comparison. Cash can have legitimate value to a franchise, especially when ownership and roster economics differ from modern conditions, but a historical grade should not invent a dollar figure or assume the payment was trivial. Atlanta therefore receives credit for monetizing the pick while carrying a lower-confidence valuation than Seattle's measurable player return.

sections.heading: The Missing Entry in Basketball-Reference Matters
sections.body: The omission from Basketball-Reference is worth preserving in the audit trail because it limits certainty about transaction mechanics, not about who drafted Seals. Seattle's 1975 draft record clearly shows Seals at No. 21, and Pro Sports Transactions explicitly traces that pick from Atlanta to Seattle for cash. The appropriate response is not to erase the transaction or overstate confidence; it is to retain the specialist chain, cite the independent draft confirmation, and mark the cash amount as unresolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because the purchased second-round pick became Seals, who supplied 235 regular-season games and two double-figure scoring seasons. Atlanta receives a C+ because it converted the pick into cash, but the amount is unknown and no further basketball asset can be traced from the payment. The result is a clear realized-basketball advantage for Seattle without pretending the Hawks received nothing of value. Confidence is medium-high because the pick outcome is verified while the sale mechanics rely primarily on the specialist transaction ledger. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The First Correction Is the Package
sections.body: New York and San Antonio made two separate transactions on June 3, 1975. Basketball-Reference's ABA league ledger lists them independently: the Nets sold Mike Gale to San Antonio for cash, and in a second move the Nets traded Larry Kenon to the Spurs for Swen Nater. Roy Boe's Nets executive record and John Begzos' Spurs record repeat the same separation. The legacy this review record had pulled cash into the Kenon-Nater exchange, creating a false three-asset package. That cash item is removed from this trade and remains attributable only to the separate Mike Gale transaction that follows in the chronology.

sections.heading: Kenon Became a Long-Term San Antonio Star
sections.body: Kenon was already an ABA All-Star with New York before the trade, but San Antonio received the prime of his career. Contemporary Spurs history summarizes his five-season run at roughly 20.7 points and 10.3 rebounds per game. He made three All-Star teams during that span and became one of the franchise's core scorers and rebounders alongside George Gervin. The transaction therefore produced exactly the kind of durable high-end return that retrospective grading should reward: immediate performance, multiple seasons of continuity and major-team relevance.

sections.heading: The Spurs' Competitive Window Benefited Directly
sections.body: Kenon's value was not isolated to box-score accumulation. He remained part of San Antonio through the franchise's transition from the ABA into the NBA and helped the Spurs reach the 1979 Eastern Conference finals, where they came within one game of the NBA Finals. That does not make every team success his alone, but it confirms that the trade acquired a player who remained central throughout one of the franchise's earliest strong NBA periods. The fact that he stayed for five seasons also eliminates the attribution problems that often appear in short rental trades.

sections.heading: Nater Was Useful but Short-Lived in New York
sections.body: The Nets did receive a real player. Nater appeared in 43 games for New York in 1975-76 and averaged 8.7 points and 10.3 rebounds in 23.6 minutes. His per-36 rebounding rate was 15.6, so the move clearly gave the Nets a strong glass presence. The limitation was duration. On January 27, 1976, New York traded Nater and Billy Schaeffer to the Virginia Squires for Jim Eakins. Nater therefore did not remain through the entire Nets title run and did not create a long direct tenure comparable to Kenon's in San Antonio.

sections.heading: The Eakins Return Adds Some Nets Value
sections.body: Jim Eakins played 34 regular-season games for the Nets after the January trade and was on the roster that won the 1976 ABA championship. Because Billy Schaeffer was bundled with Nater, Eakins cannot be credited entirely to the original Kenon trade, just as multi-asset downstream deals elsewhere in the archive are not assigned to one component. The branch still matters: New York extracted some continuing value from Nater rather than losing him for nothing. It is not enough to close the enormous gap created by Kenon's five seasons of star production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, A+/B-. San Antonio receives an A+ because Kenon became a five-season franchise pillar, averaged approximately 20 points and 10 rebounds, made three All-Star teams and helped anchor a contender through the ABA-to-NBA transition. New York receives a B- because Nater provided 43 strong rebounding games and then contributed to the package that brought back Eakins, but the tenure was short and the downstream return required another player. The cash error is removed because authoritative transaction ledgers place that payment in the separate Mike Gale sale. Confidence is high on the June 3 date, straight player-for-player structure and realized outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Separating the Two June 3 Transactions
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's San Antonio and New York transaction ledgers list two distinct June 3, 1975 deals. In one, New York traded Larry Kenon for Swen Nater. In the other, the Nets sold Mike Gale to the Spurs for cash. Roy Boe's executive record preserves the same separation. That distinction is important because the legacy archive had previously blurred the cash into the Kenon-Nater transaction. This review removed the cash from that record; this review now preserves it only where the authoritative ledgers place it: in the Gale sale.

sections.heading: Gale Immediately Became a Full-Season Spurs Guard
sections.body: Gale played 78 games for San Antonio in the final ABA season of 1975-76. He averaged 6.8 points, 3.1 assists and 2.7 rebounds while appearing in every regular-season role the club needed from its backcourt. The Spurs then entered the NBA with Gale still in the rotation. In 1976-77 he played all 82 games and averaged 10.3 points, 5.8 assists and 2.3 steals, turning the cash purchase into an immediate NBA starter-level return rather than a short-term depth move.

sections.heading: The Value Continued for Years
sections.body: Gale remained in San Antonio for 70 games in 1977-78, 82 in 1978-79 and 67 in 1979-80. He appeared in 35 more games for the Spurs in 1980-81 before being traded in December. Across the ABA and NBA portions of his San Antonio tenure, that is 414 regular-season games. His scoring role fluctuated, but his minutes, assists and steals show a guard who remained usable across multiple coaches, league structures and roster iterations. That durability is the central reason the original cash purchase grades so well for the Spurs.

sections.heading: San Antonio Also Retained Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: On December 19, 1980, San Antonio traded Gale and a 1982 first-round pick to Portland for Ron Brewer. The first-round pick later became Ricky Pierce, so Brewer cannot be credited to Gale alone; the draft asset was an important component of the package. Still, Gale remained valuable enough to be included in a meaningful NBA trade more than five years after San Antonio acquired him for cash. The downstream deal therefore supports, but does not dominate, the verdict on the original transaction.

sections.heading: New York's Financial Return Is Unpriced
sections.body: The Nets did receive real consideration. The transaction ledgers explicitly say San Antonio sent cash, so New York converted Gale into financial value instead of waiving him or losing him without return. The problem is that the reviewed sources do not preserve the amount. Without that figure, the archive cannot compare the payment directly with Gale's six seasons of Spurs service or assign a precise economic win-loss calculation. The grade should recognize the verified sale while keeping confidence below the level used for trades where both sides' basketball assets are fully measurable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, A+/C+. San Antonio receives an A+ because a cash purchase produced 414 regular-season games across the ABA-to-NBA transition, including several seasons of substantial guard minutes, and Gale retained some trade value through December 1980. New York receives a C+ because it monetized the player through a verified cash sale, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable basketball asset on the Nets side. The verdict is clear on realized court value while the financial comparison remains incomplete. Confidence is medium-high because the transaction structure and Gale outcome are well documented but the cash amount is not. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The June 24 Rights Sale Completes an Unusual Pick Loop
sections.body: Indiana's transaction ledger and Pro Sports Transactions agree that the Pacers sold Jim Lee's ABA rights to San Antonio for cash on June 24, 1975. The path to that sale began almost a year earlier. In July 1974 Indiana sent Donnie Freeman to the Spurs for cash and San Antonio's 1975 second-round pick. The Pacers used that pick at No. 18 on Lee in the 1975 ABA draft, then sold the rights back to the same San Antonio franchise eight days after draft day. The source-backed record therefore treats this review as the final step of a previously verified asset chain rather than an isolated cash transaction.

sections.heading: Lee Was a Legitimate Two-League Draft Prospect
sections.body: Lee was a 6-foot-2 guard from Syracuse and was selected in both major professional drafts in 1975. Indiana used the No. 18 ABA pick on him, while Cleveland selected him in the fifth round at No. 79 of the NBA draft. Basketball-Reference preserves the Cleveland selection and identifies Lee as a Syracuse guard. The dual selections show that the rights had genuine prospect value at the moment Indiana sold them, even though Lee never established a top-league regular-season career. That context prevents the San Antonio side from being treated as a nonsensical acquisition simply because the eventual statistical return was zero.

sections.heading: San Antonio Did Not Receive Regular-Season Production
sections.body: The realized outcome is much less favorable for the Spurs. Lee does not appear in San Antonio's 1975-76 ABA regular-season player statistics, and Basketball-Reference's player page contains no NBA or ABA season line. A secondary ABA roster archive lists Lee with San Antonio during the 1975 offseason and later with the Baltimore Claws, but records no regular-season games for either team. The Claws folded before the 1975-76 regular season, so there is no later Baltimore production to treat as a downstream return from San Antonio's purchase.

sections.heading: Indiana's Cash Is Real but Cannot Be Priced
sections.body: The Pacers received cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed transaction records. That limits how aggressively the sale can be graded. A rights sale can be useful even when the player never reaches the floor: Indiana converted an asset it did not retain into immediate financial consideration during the ABA's financially unstable final years. Still, without a dollar figure the archive cannot compare the payment to player salary, roster cost or another transaction asset. The correct approach is to acknowledge a positive realized return without inventing economic precision.

sections.heading: The Prior Donnie Freeman Trade Adds Context, Not Extra Credit
sections.body: Because the No. 18 pick originally came from San Antonio in the Donnie Freeman deal, it is tempting to describe the Pacers as receiving Freeman's earlier return and then cashing the same asset back to the Spurs. That is historically useful context, but this review should be graded only on the June 24 exchange itself. Indiana's earlier compensation belongs to this review. Here the Pacers gave up Lee's ABA rights and received an unpriced cash payment. Keeping those transaction boundaries separate avoids double-counting the same draft choice across multiple verdicts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, B-/D+. Indiana receives a B- because it monetized freshly drafted rights that ultimately produced no ABA or NBA regular-season value for San Antonio. The grade stops below the B-plus or A range because the cash amount is unknown and Lee was a legitimate prospect when purchased. San Antonio receives a D+ because the rights did not yield a regular-season game or a verified downstream basketball asset. The original legacy Spurs-win verdict is reversed by the realized record. Confidence is high on the date and transaction structure, and medium-high on the full post-sale rights history because secondary roster evidence preserves Lee's later Baltimore connection without a complete transfer mechanism. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The July 14 Blockbuster Is Straightforward
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction ledgers agree that Denver acquired George Irvine and the rights to David Thompson on July 14, 1975, sending Mack Calvin, Mike Green and Jan van Breda Kolff to the Squires. The timing is essential: Atlanta had selected Thompson first overall in the 1975 NBA draft, but Denver controlled the ABA route that ultimately secured his professional services. This was therefore not an ordinary veteran swap. It was a bet that Thompson could become the face of Denver basketball.

sections.heading: Thompson Immediately Justified the Price
sections.body: Thompson's 1975-76 rookie season made the deal's direction obvious almost immediately. He averaged 26.0 points, 6.3 rebounds and 3.7 assists for Denver, made the ABA All-Star team and earned All-ABA First Team honors. He remained with the franchise through the ABA-NBA merger and became one of the NBA's most explosive scorers. In 1977-78 he averaged 27.2 points and finished third in NBA MVP voting. Thompson later entered the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. No other asset in this transaction approached that combination of peak value, franchise importance and longevity.

sections.heading: Irvine Added Real Secondary Value
sections.body: George Irvine was not merely attached to Thompson's rights. He gave Denver two useful seasons, appearing in 76 games in 1975-76 and 74 more in 1976-77. His scoring role was modest, but 150 regular-season appearances strengthened the return beyond the star acquisition. That matters for grading because Denver did not simply trade three rotation players for one prospect; it received one of the era's most important young stars plus a functional veteran wing who helped bridge the ABA and NBA versions of the franchise.

sections.heading: Virginia Received Proven Talent
sections.body: The Squires did receive meaningful players. Mack Calvin had just made the 1975 ABA All-Star team for Denver and finished third in MVP voting. Mike Green was also a 1975 ABA All-Star and had produced two strong Denver seasons. Jan van Breda Kolff had played all 84 games for Denver in 1974-75. On paper, Virginia was acquiring immediate veteran competence in exchange for rights and a role player. The problem is that the franchise's financial instability and short remaining life prevented those assets from generating a durable return comparable to Thompson.

sections.heading: The Squires' Collapse Limits the Realized Return
sections.body: Virginia finished 15-68 in 1975-76 and folded before the ABA-NBA merger. Calvin, Green and van Breda Kolff therefore could not become long-term Squires assets. Their careers continued elsewhere, but those later seasons do not count as Virginia return once the franchise ceased operations. The trade should not be graded as though the Squires received worthless players; Calvin and Green in particular were high-level ABA veterans. Hindsight evaluation, however, must use realized franchise value, and the short runway of the Squires sharply limits what their side produced.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A+/C+. Denver receives an A+ because Thompson became a franchise-defining superstar and Hall of Famer while Irvine added 150 useful games. Virginia receives a C+ because it acquired three established players, including recent All-Stars Calvin and Green, but the franchise collapsed after one season and could not convert that talent into lasting value. The grade gap reflects realized organizational outcome rather than dismissing the quality of the veterans sent to Virginia. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Thompson rights chain and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
