sections.heading: The July 30 Trade Is Clear
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Washington and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the basic exchange: the Braves received Dick Gibbs, and the Bullets received Buffalo's 1976 first-round pick. Bob Ferry's executive record confirms the same deal. Pro Sports Transactions adds cash to Washington's side, a detail omitted from Basketball-Reference. The pick later became the 13th selection in the 1976 NBA draft, where Washington chose Mitch Kupchak. The archive therefore keeps the cash as an undisclosed secondary asset while treating the first-round pick as the dominant return.

sections.heading: Gibbs Gave Buffalo One Reserve Season
sections.body: Gibbs played 72 regular-season games for Buffalo in 1975-76, totaling 866 minutes and 335 points. He averaged 4.7 points and 1.5 rebounds in 12.0 minutes per game. That is legitimate depth on a 46-win playoff team, but it is not a high-impact return for a future first-round pick. Gibbs had already been a larger scorer in Seattle two seasons earlier, yet Buffalo used him almost exclusively as a reserve. He did not become a long-term Braves asset and did not create a later trade return.

sections.heading: Kupchak Immediately Outperformed the Cost
sections.body: Washington used the acquired pick at No. 13 on Mitch Kupchak in 1976. He played all 82 games as a rookie and averaged 10.4 points and 6.0 rebounds while shooting 57.2 percent from the field. His role expanded in 1977-78, when he averaged 15.9 points and 6.9 rebounds in 67 games. Kupchak became a core frontcourt contributor for a Bullets team that won the 1978 NBA championship and returned to the Finals in 1979. The pick therefore produced both immediate regular-season value and postseason relevance at the highest level.

sections.heading: Washington Kept the Asset for Multiple Seasons
sections.body: Kupchak remained with Washington through 1980-81. Injuries reduced portions of his later Bullets tenure, but the broader value chain is straightforward: the franchise received several seasons from a first-round talent who became an important part of its championship-era rotation. That is far more durable than Gibbs' one Buffalo season. Even without assigning any value to the cash component, the realized basketball return strongly favors Washington.

sections.heading: The Cash Makes an Already Strong Return Better
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records cash moving from Buffalo to Washington along with the first-round pick. The amount is not preserved, so the archive should not pretend to know its financial significance. It still matters directionally because Washington did not merely receive a premium draft asset for Gibbs; the specialist transaction ledger indicates additional consideration as well. Since the pick alone became Kupchak, the verdict does not depend on pricing the cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, A+/C. Washington receives an A+ because the Buffalo pick became Kupchak, a multi-year frontcourt contributor and member of the 1978 championship team, with additional undisclosed cash also listed in the specialist ledger. Buffalo receives a C because Gibbs supplied 72 games of reserve depth on a playoff team but only one season of modest production and no downstream asset. The gap is large without overstating Gibbs' shortcomings: Buffalo obtained a usable player, while Washington turned his departure into a championship-era building block. Confidence is high on the date, pick outcome, Gibbs production and Kupchak career path. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The August 8 Trade Is Fully Traceable
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and NBA transaction ledgers agree that the Hawks acquired Connie Hawkins from the Lakers on August 8, 1975 for a 1976 third-round pick. The draft record later identifies that selection as No. 36, which Los Angeles used on Rutgers guard Mike Dabney. Unlike several nearby 1975 transactions with unresolved future consideration, this asset chain is complete enough to grade directly: one veteran player went to Atlanta, one named draft pick went to Los Angeles, and both outcomes can be measured.

sections.heading: Hawkins Still Had Useful NBA Value
sections.body: Hawkins was 33 and well past the peak that made him one of basketball's most celebrated forwards, but Atlanta still received a genuine rotation player. He appeared in 74 games in 1975-76, logged 1,907 minutes and averaged 8.2 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He shot 44.7 percent from the field and started 25 games. On a rebuilding Hawks team, those minutes represented real veteran production rather than a ceremonial final season.

sections.heading: The Atlanta Season Was Hawkins' NBA Finale
sections.body: The 1975-76 campaign was Hawkins' final NBA season. He did not create a downstream trade return for Atlanta, so the value chain ends with those 74 games. That prevents the Hawks' grade from reaching the very top tier despite the famous name involved. The transaction should be evaluated on what Atlanta actually received in 1975-76, not on Hawkins' earlier ABA and Phoenix accomplishments or his later Hall of Fame induction. Even on that narrower basis, the Hawks got meaningful value for a third-round selection.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Used the Pick on Mike Dabney
sections.body: The Lakers retained Atlanta's third-rounder and selected Dabney 36th overall in the 1976 NBA draft. Basketball-Reference identifies him as a 6-foot-4 guard from Rutgers and confirms the Lakers as the drafting team. The draft decision therefore gives Los Angeles a definite asset outcome rather than an unresolved pick. The problem for the Lakers is what happened next: Dabney's Basketball-Reference page contains draft information but no NBA regular-season statistical line.

sections.heading: No Lakers NBA Production Came From the Pick
sections.body: Because Dabney never logged an NBA regular-season game, the Lakers realized no measurable on-court return from the acquired selection. A third-round pick still had option value when the trade was made, and selecting a legitimate college guard was not inherently irrational. Hindsight grading, however, focuses on realized franchise value. Atlanta received 74 games and nearly 1,900 minutes from Hawkins; Los Angeles received no NBA games from the player chosen with the pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A-/D+. Atlanta receives an A- because one third-round pick produced a full season of useful veteran forward play, including 74 games and substantial minutes. The grade stops below A or A+ because Hawkins' Atlanta tenure lasted only one season and produced no later asset. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the pick was used on a real prospect but did not yield an NBA regular-season appearance. Confidence is high on the August 8 date, the No. 36 pick chain and both player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The August 28 Structure Is Clear
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Washington and league transaction ledgers agree on the core exchange: Detroit sent Dave Bing and a 1977 first-round pick to the Washington Bullets for Kevin Porter on August 28, 1975. The legacy archive record had incorrectly flattened the future pick into a traded player named Tree Rollins. That is not what happened. Washington received a draft asset, not Rollins' playing rights, and the distinction is important because the Bullets moved that pick before the 1977 draft. This repair restores the first-round pick as the actual asset and preserves Rollins only as its eventual selection outcome.

sections.heading: Bing Gave Washington Two Useful Seasons
sections.body: Bing immediately remained a high-level NBA guard after leaving Detroit. He played all 82 regular-season games for Washington in 1975-76, averaging 16.2 points and 6.0 assists in 35.9 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with an All-Star selection, the 1976 All-Star Game MVP award and a sixth-place finish in league MVP voting. He returned for 64 games in 1976-77, averaging 10.6 points and 4.3 assists in a reduced role. Across the two Washington seasons, Bing supplied 146 regular-season appearances before his career moved to Boston. That direct return alone gave the Bullets dependable veteran value from the player side of the trade.

sections.heading: Porter Was Productive but His Detroit Tenure Was Shorter
sections.body: Detroit did not come away empty-handed. Porter was already one of the league's premier passers, and in his first Pistons season he averaged 12.6 points and 10.2 assists across 19 games. In 1976-77 he appeared in 81 games and averaged 8.9 points and 7.3 assists in 26.1 minutes. He then played eight more Detroit games in 1977-78 before the Pistons packaged Kevin Porter, Howard Porter and cash to New Jersey for Al Skinner and two future second-round picks. Because Kevin Porter was only one component of that later package, this verdict credits him with retained trade utility without assigning the entire Skinner-and-picks return to the 1975 transaction.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Did Not Stay in Washington
sections.body: The largest correction concerns the future first-rounder. On January 20, 1977, Washington traded Truck Robinson and the Detroit-origin first-round pick to Atlanta for Tom Henderson and Atlanta's own 1977 first-round selection. The Bullets later used the Atlanta pick at No. 4 on Greg Ballard. The Hawks kept the Detroit-origin choice and selected Tree Rollins at No. 14. The 1977 draft record confirms Rollins as an Atlanta selection. Washington therefore cannot receive evaluative credit for Rollins' long NBA career; he was drafted by a later holder. What Washington can receive is credit for carrying the Detroit pick forward as one of two meaningful assets in the January swap.

sections.heading: Washington's Downstream Credit Must Stay Proportional
sections.body: The Robinson-Henderson exchange prevents a simplistic claim that Detroit's pick alone produced Henderson and Ballard. Washington also surrendered Truck Robinson, an established frontcourt player, while Atlanta sent both Henderson and its higher first-round choice. The defensible treatment is the same provenance rule used elsewhere in the archive: record the full factual chain, but grade only value the team directly received or demonstrably retained when it moved the asset. Detroit's first-rounder helped Washington execute a later trade, yet Ballard's entire career cannot be assigned to this 1975 deal. That keeps the verdict source-backed rather than inflating downstream value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, A-/B-. Washington receives an A- because Bing produced 146 regular-season games, remained an All-Star in the first season and the acquired first-round pick retained enough value to be used in a later first-round swap. Detroit receives a B- because Porter was a productive distributor, supplied 108 regular-season games over parts of three seasons and still had enough value to be included in a later multi-asset trade. The gap comes from Washington receiving both the stronger direct veteran run and an additional first-round asset. Confidence is high on the August 28 transaction structure, Bing and Porter production, and the 1977 pick chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 5 Exchange Is Fully Traceable
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cleveland and league transaction ledgers all record the same structure on September 5, 1975: the Bulls acquired Fred Foster and sent the Cavaliers a 1976 eighth-round draft pick. Bill Fitch's executive transaction record confirms the Cleveland side of the deal, while Dick Motta's executive record confirms Chicago's. Cleveland's draft history later identifies that exact selection as the No. 123 pick used on Dale Koehler. Unlike transactions in this era involving unspecified future considerations, the complete pick outcome is known.

sections.heading: Foster Never Reached a Bulls Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Chicago received an established NBA player rather than an unproven prospect. Foster had already played eight NBA seasons, including 131 games for Cleveland across 1973-74 and 1974-75. The Bulls nevertheless did not keep him into the regular season. Chicago's transaction ledger and the league ledger both show the club waiving Foster on October 22, 1975. His Basketball-Reference career page lists 1975-76 as a season in which he did not play after being traded to and waived by Chicago. The direct Bulls return therefore produced zero regular-season games, minutes or points.

sections.heading: Cleveland Converted the Veteran Into a Draft Asset
sections.body: The Cavaliers did preserve some option value by taking a future pick instead of simply waiving Foster themselves. On June 8, 1976, Cleveland used the acquired eighth-round selection on Wisconsin forward Dale Koehler at No. 123 overall. The Cavaliers' transaction ledger, franchise draft record and the 1976 NBA draft page all identify Koehler at that slot. In process terms, Cleveland successfully converted a veteran roster decision into a real draft choice. That is better asset management than receiving nothing at all, even though the later result still needs to be judged on what actually reached the NBA.

sections.heading: Koehler Produced No NBA Regular-Season Return
sections.body: Koehler's Basketball-Reference page confirms the draft information but contains no NBA regular-season statistical line. The 1976 draft table likewise shows no NBA games or seasons for him. That means Cleveland's acquired pick did not turn into measurable NBA production. Because the archive grades realized franchise value rather than the abstract possibility attached to a late pick, the Cavaliers cannot receive a high grade merely for having converted Foster into an eighth-round selection. The pick existed, was exercised and is fully traceable, but it produced no NBA game value.

sections.heading: Neither Side Created a Downstream Asset Chain
sections.body: Chicago waived Foster without receiving documented compensation, so the Bulls' branch ends in October 1975. Cleveland's branch ends when Koehler failed to reach an NBA regular-season game. There is no later trade return, retained player right or compensation chain to extend either side's value. This makes the transaction unusually simple to grade despite the complete historical documentation: one side received a veteran who never played for the club, and the other received a draft pick that never produced an NBA player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. Chicago receives a C because Foster cost only an eighth-round pick, but he never appeared in a Bulls regular-season game and was waived roughly seven weeks after the trade. Cleveland also receives a C because the Cavaliers converted Foster into a legitimate draft asset and used it at No. 123 on Koehler, yet the selection produced no NBA regular-season return. Neither franchise realized enough value to justify a meaningful hindsight edge. Confidence is high on the transaction date, waiver date, draft-pick identity and lack of NBA production from the two direct outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 8 Trade Is Fully Documented
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, San Antonio Spurs and ABA transaction ledgers all identify the same exchange: New York sent Billy Paultz to San Antonio for Rich Jones, Chuck Terry, Bob Warren and Kim Hughes. The Roy Boe and John Begzos executive transaction records independently preserve the deal from each franchise's side. The legacy archive entry was dated September 7, but the authoritative transaction ledgers consistently list September 8, 1975, so the source-backed repair corrects the transaction date while preserving the same five-player structure.

sections.heading: Paultz Was Immediately Excellent for San Antonio
sections.body: San Antonio received far more than a short-term rental. Paultz played 83 games in 1975-76 and averaged 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 3.0 blocks in 35.6 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star team and became one of the Spurs' major frontcourt pieces alongside George Gervin and Larry Kenon. His value did not end with the ABA season: Paultz remained with the franchise into its NBA years, making this a durable return rather than a one-season outcome.

sections.heading: New York Received Two Immediate High-Minute Contributors
sections.body: Rich Jones and Kim Hughes became important pieces immediately. Jones played 83 games for the 1975-76 Nets, averaging 13.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 29.2 minutes. Hughes appeared in all 84 games, averaged 8.2 points and 9.2 rebounds, and later earned All-Rookie recognition. Both also played throughout the postseason as New York won the final ABA championship. That direct production alone makes the package much stronger than the old summary suggested.

sections.heading: Terry Added Depth and Warren Became Tim Bassett
sections.body: Chuck Terry supplied another 66 regular-season appearances for New York in 1975-76 and remained with the franchise for the first NBA season. Bob Warren never became a Nets regular because New York traded him to the San Diego Sails on September 22 for Tim Bassett. Bassett then played all 84 regular-season games and 13 playoff games for the champion Nets, averaging 6.3 rebounds in the postseason. The archive should not pretend Warren alone created Bassett's entire later career value, but this is a direct one-for-one downstream conversion and therefore belongs in the original asset chain.

sections.heading: The Championship Context Matters Without Deciding the Trade by Itself
sections.body: New York finished 55-29, defeated San Antonio in a seven-game ABA semifinal and then beat Denver for the 1976 ABA championship. The championship does not automatically make every incoming player more valuable, but Jones, Hughes, Terry and Bassett all supplied real regular-season or postseason minutes on that title team. San Antonio also benefited heavily from Paultz, who was an All-Star and productive starter. This is therefore a strong return on both sides rather than a case where one team received value and the other did not.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/A. New York receives an A+ because the four-player package produced two major rotation players, additional depth, a direct Warren-to-Bassett conversion and substantial championship-season value, with several assets continuing into the NBA. San Antonio receives an A because Paultz was immediately an ABA All-Star, averaged a double-double with strong passing and rim protection, and remained a long-term Spurs center. The margin is narrower than the old grading suggested, but the combined volume and downstream value of New York's package gives the Nets the stronger hindsight return. Confidence is high on the corrected September 8 date, the five-player structure and the principal player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 22 One-for-One Trade Is Clear
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York transaction ledger records the Nets trading Bob Warren to the San Diego Sails for Tim Bassett on September 22, 1975. The two-player structure also fits the direct downstream chain from New York's September 8 Billy Paultz trade, because Warren had arrived from San Antonio only two weeks earlier. This record therefore represents a separate one-for-one transaction while preserving the fact that Warren was an incoming asset from the prior deal.

sections.heading: Bassett Became an Immediate Championship Contributor
sections.body: Bassett played all 84 regular-season games for New York in 1975-76, averaging 4.8 points and 6.3 rebounds in 21.3 minutes. He also appeared in all 13 playoff games and collected 93 postseason rebounds as the Nets defeated San Antonio and Denver to win the final ABA championship. Bassett was not the star of that team, but the combination of availability, rebounding and playoff minutes gave New York a direct and useful return immediately after the trade.

sections.heading: The Value Continued After the ABA-NBA Merger
sections.body: Bassett remained with the franchise when the Nets entered the NBA. In 1976-77 he played 76 games, averaged 9.0 points and 8.4 rebounds, and logged more than 2,400 minutes. He then played 65 games in 1977-78 and all 82 games in 1978-79. That gives New York multiple seasons of durable frontcourt value from a player acquired for someone who had not yet played a Nets regular-season game.

sections.heading: Warren Was Productive but San Diego's Window Was Extremely Short
sections.body: Warren did provide legitimate production for the Sails. He played 10 of the club's 11 games, averaging 10.1 points, 5.9 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 26.5 minutes. The problem was structural rather than individual: San Diego ceased operations after an 11-game start, so the franchise could not retain or build on the return. Warren's 1975-76 Sails stint was also the final season of his eight-year professional career.

sections.heading: The Franchise Survival Difference Decides the Hindsight Gap
sections.body: A transaction involving a folding team requires care because San Diego's inability to create long-term value was not caused by Warren. Even so, realized-value grading still measures what each franchise actually received. New York got a full championship season from Bassett and then carried him into the NBA for three more seasons. San Diego got ten productive games from Warren before the team disappeared. That is a large outcome gap even after giving Warren full credit for playing well in the brief Sails schedule.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A/C-. New York receives an A because Bassett played every regular-season game for the 1976 ABA champions, contributed throughout the playoffs and remained a multi-year NBA rotation player after the merger. San Diego receives a C- because Warren was productive in ten games, but the return ended when the Sails ceased operations and produced no further franchise value. The verdict does not blame Warren for the team's collapse; it simply reflects the duration and depth of the realized returns. Confidence is high on the date, one-for-one structure, Bassett's New York production and Warren's ten-game San Diego stint. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 23 Exchange Is Clear, and the legacy Identity Was Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bucks and league transaction ledgers all record the same transaction on September 23, 1975: Los Angeles sent Milwaukee a 1976 fifth-round pick for Ron Williams. Pete Newell's executive record confirms the Lakers side. The legacy archive entry incorrectly displayed the incoming player as Ron Williams with Fritz Williams in parentheses and attached the Fritz Williams player identity. That is an archive identity error. The actual player was Ron Williams, the veteran guard who had already spent two seasons with Milwaukee after five years with the Warriors.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Los Angeles Nine Games
sections.body: Ron Williams played nine regular-season games for the Lakers in 1975-76. Basketball-Reference credits him with 158 minutes, 44 points and 21 assists, which works out to 4.9 points and 2.3 assists per game in 17.6 minutes. He was a reserve behind the Lakers' established backcourt and did not develop into a lasting rotation piece. Those nine games were also the final NBA appearances of Williams' eight-year career, so Los Angeles received a real but very short return.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Converted the Trade Into the No. 77 Pick
sections.body: The Bucks held the Lakers' 1976 fifth-round selection and used it at No. 77 overall on Arizona guard James Rappis. Milwaukee's transaction ledger and the 1976 NBA draft record agree on the pick outcome. Rappis was therefore a fully traceable draft result rather than an unresolved future consideration. That gives the Bucks a concrete asset path to grade, but the pick's value still depends on what happened after the selection.

sections.heading: Rappis Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value
sections.body: Rappis' Basketball-Reference player page confirms his fifth-round draft position but contains no NBA regular-season statistical line. The draft table likewise shows no NBA games or seasons. The Bucks therefore converted Williams into a legitimate draft choice but did not receive measurable NBA production from that choice. This is not the same as receiving nothing on trade day, because the pick itself had optionality, but the realized basketball outcome ended at the draft.

sections.heading: The Hindsight Gap Is Small
sections.body: Neither franchise found durable value. Los Angeles received nine games from a veteran who was near the end of his career, while Milwaukee received a fifth-round selection that never reached an NBA regular-season game. The Lakers' nine games are enough to create a slight realized-value advantage, but not enough to justify a strong grade. Milwaukee also deserves some credit for extracting a draft asset from a player whose NBA career ended immediately after the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ because Ron Williams did provide nine regular-season appearances and some backcourt minutes, even though the stint was brief and ended his NBA career. Milwaukee receives a C because the Bucks converted Williams into a real fifth-round pick and selected James Rappis, but Rappis never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The source-backed correction matters more than the grade gap: the incoming player was Ron Williams, not Fritz Williams. Confidence is high on the September 23 date, the player identity, the No. 77 pick outcome and the limited realized value on both sides. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The September 25 Trade Is Clear
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Seattle and league transaction ledgers agree on the structure: the Pistons sent a 1978 first-round pick to the SuperSonics for Archie Clark on September 25, 1975. Oscar Feldman's Detroit executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle record confirm the same deal. The legacy archive entry was dated September 24 and mislabeled Seattle under the modern Oklahoma City franchise name in its prose. The source-backed repair corrects the transaction date while preserving the franchise key used by the archive.

sections.heading: Clark Gave Detroit One Useful Season
sections.body: Archie Clark played 79 regular-season games for Detroit in 1975-76 and averaged 7.6 points, 2.8 assists and 1.7 rebounds in 20.1 minutes. He also appeared in all nine of the Pistons' playoff games, averaging 8.0 points in 21.3 minutes. Clark was no longer the All-Star-level scorer he had been earlier in the decade, but he was a legitimate veteran rotation player on a playoff team. Detroit's return therefore deserves more credit than a low-end rental grade.

sections.heading: The Detroit Pick Stayed Valuable for Seattle
sections.body: Seattle held the acquired first-round pick for more than two years. On November 11, 1977, the SuperSonics traded that Detroit-origin 1978 first-rounder and a 1979 second-round pick to Portland for Wally Walker. This distinction matters because Seattle never used the first-rounder to draft Ron Brewer. Portland became the later holder and selected Brewer at No. 7 in 1978. The archive should record Brewer as the eventual pick outcome but should not assign his NBA career directly to Seattle.

sections.heading: Walker Produced Real Downstream Value
sections.body: The defensible downstream credit is Wally Walker. After the November 1977 trade, Walker played 68 regular-season games for Seattle in 1977-78 and all 20 playoff games during the SuperSonics' run to the NBA Finals. He returned for 60 regular-season games in 1978-79 and appeared in 13 playoff games as Seattle won the NBA championship. Walker remained with the franchise into 1979-80. Because Seattle also surrendered a second-round pick in the Walker trade, the Detroit first-rounder cannot receive full credit for Walker's entire tenure, but it was a major component of the acquisition.

sections.heading: Detroit's Branch Ended Quickly
sections.body: Clark's Pistons tenure ended after the 1975-76 season. Detroit waived him on July 28, 1976, and he did not play another NBA regular-season game. That leaves the Pistons with one season of useful veteran depth and playoff minutes but no later trade return or retained asset. Seattle, by contrast, carried the first-round value forward and converted it into part of a package for a younger rotation player who contributed across multiple playoff runs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A-/B. Seattle receives an A- because a first-round pick acquired for a veteran nearing the end of his career retained enough value to help acquire Wally Walker, who contributed to the 1978 Finals run and 1979 championship. The grade stops short of an A or A+ because Seattle also surrendered a 1979 second-round pick in the Walker trade and did not itself draft Ron Brewer. Detroit receives a B because Clark gave the Pistons 79 regular-season games and nine playoff appearances, a useful one-season return even though the team waived him the next summer. Confidence is high on the September 25 date, Clark's Detroit production and the pick's later use in the Walker trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The legacy Player Identity Was Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers all record the September 30, 1975 trade as Earl Williams to Detroit for a 1976 second-round pick. The Willie Norwood reference belongs to a different transaction attempt on May 28, when Phoenix originally agreed to send Williams to Detroit for Norwood. That earlier deal was cancelled. Norwood therefore remained a Piston and was waived on October 8. This review corrects the live September record to Earl Williams while preserving the cancelled May transaction only as historical context.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Detroit a Short Reserve-Center Stint
sections.body: Williams appeared in 46 games for the 1975-76 Pistons. He averaged 3.7 points and 5.5 rebounds in 12.2 minutes, with Detroit using him as a reserve frontcourt piece rather than a major rotation anchor. The Pistons waived him on February 23, 1976, so the return ended before the postseason. Williams later appeared in only one more NBA game, with the Nets in 1976-77. Detroit therefore received real regular-season minutes but no sustained multi-season or playoff value from the acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix Preserved the Pick and Used It in Another Trade
sections.body: Phoenix did not hold the Detroit-origin second-round pick until draft night. On November 3, 1975, the Suns sent John Roche and that 1976 second-round selection to the Los Angeles Lakers for Pat Riley. The Lakers' transaction ledger identifies the same pick as the one later used at No. 21 on Earl Tatum. The important source-backed distinction is that Tatum's NBA career belongs to Los Angeles, not Phoenix. Phoenix's realized benefit was the pick's role as part of the package that brought Riley to the Suns.

sections.heading: Riley Supplied More Immediate Team Value Than Williams
sections.body: Riley played 60 regular-season games for Phoenix in 1975-76, averaging 4.6 points in 13.2 minutes. He also appeared in five playoff games during the Suns' run through Seattle and Golden State to the NBA Finals. Riley was a reserve and the original pick was not the only asset Phoenix surrendered, so the Detroit pick should receive only proportional downstream credit. Even with that limitation, the pick clearly remained useful enough to help Phoenix turn John Roche into a rotation guard for a conference champion.

sections.heading: Earl Tatum Is the Pick Outcome, Not a Phoenix Player Outcome
sections.body: Los Angeles used the acquired second-round selection at No. 21 in the 1976 draft on Earl Tatum. Tatum went on to play 262 NBA games, but assigning that full career to Phoenix would overstate the Suns' return because Phoenix had traded the pick away seven months earlier. The correct asset-chain treatment is to record Tatum as the eventual draft outcome while stopping Phoenix's realized-value credit at the Riley transaction. This keeps the archive consistent with the proportional downstream treatment used elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, B-/C+. Phoenix receives a B- because the second-round pick retained enough value to function as a meaningful component of the Pat Riley trade, and Riley then played 60 regular-season games plus five playoff games on the 1976 Western Conference champions. The grade stays below a full B because Phoenix also had to include John Roche and Riley was a reserve. Detroit receives a C+ because Earl Williams supplied 46 games and rebounding depth, but his stint ended with a February waiver and produced no playoff or downstream value. Confidence is high on the player-identity correction, the cancelled May transaction, the September 30 trade, the November Riley trade and the No. 21 Earl Tatum pick outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The October 7 Exchange Is Verified, but the Pick Is Not Fully Identified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland, Atlanta and league transaction ledgers all record the same October 7, 1975 transaction: the Trail Blazers sent a future draft pick to the Hawks for Greg Lee. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bud Seretean's Atlanta record independently repeat that structure. None of those authoritative ledgers supplies a year, round, protection condition or eventual player for the future pick. The legacy archive entry described the asset as conditional and not exercised, but the source-backed audit could not verify those extra details. The repaired record therefore preserves only what the historical record establishes and marks the pick outcome unresolved.

sections.heading: Portland Acquired Rights and Immediately Signed Lee
sections.body: RealGM's transaction archive identifies the move as Portland acquiring Lee's draft rights from Atlanta and then signing him on October 7. Atlanta had originally selected Lee in the seventh round of the 1974 NBA draft after his UCLA career, but he had spent the 1974-75 season in the ABA with San Diego rather than playing for the Hawks. The October transaction thus functioned as a rights transfer that allowed Portland to place Lee on its roster immediately, not as a trade for an established Atlanta rotation player.

sections.heading: Lee's Portland Return Was Extremely Short
sections.body: Lee appeared in five games for the Trail Blazers during the 1975-76 season. Basketball-Reference credits him with 35 total minutes, six points, two rebounds and 11 assists. Portland waived him on November 11, barely five weeks after the trade, and those five games became the only NBA appearances of his career. He had also played five ABA games the previous season, leaving him with ten total major-league professional appearances. Portland therefore received a real player outcome, but the scale of the return was minimal.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Pick Cannot Be Assigned an Invented Outcome
sections.body: The future pick is the difficult side of the transaction. Standard Basketball-Reference transaction records often identify later selections when a traded pick can be traced, including many surrounding 1975 deals. This entry does not. The Atlanta-Portland trade-partner page likewise lists the transaction without naming a later draftee or attaching future player production to the Hawks. That absence is not proof that the pick was formally cancelled or never exercised, so the archive should not convert missing provenance into a definite claim. The defensible status is unresolved future draft pick, with no attributable player outcome found in the sources reviewed.

sections.heading: The Realized-Value Gap Is Too Small to Force a Winner
sections.body: Portland can point to five NBA games from Lee, but five games and 35 minutes are not enough to create a meaningful franchise advantage. Atlanta can point to having received a future-pick asset, yet the archive cannot responsibly price that asset or credit a later player without a traceable chain. A slight Portland edge would overstate the value of Lee's brief stint, while an Atlanta win would require assumptions about an unidentified selection. Treating the exchange as even is the most conservative hindsight result until additional primary or archival evidence resolves the pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. Portland receives a C because acquiring Lee's rights produced only five games, 35 minutes and a waiver roughly one month later. Atlanta also receives a C because the Hawks did receive a future draft pick, but the reviewed authoritative transaction sources do not establish its year, round, conditions or eventual player. The grade deliberately avoids repeating the legacy claim that the pick was not exercised because that specific outcome has not been verified. Confidence is high on the October 7 transaction and Lee's Portland stint but medium on the complete asset chain, so the record's overall confidence is medium. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The October 8 Deal Happened During the Claws' Collapse
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and ABA transaction ledgers record Denver sending Dave Robisch and cash to the Memphis/Baltimore franchise for Dan Issel on October 8, 1975. The transaction note explains that the Memphis Sounds had become the Baltimore Claws and that the Claws never played a regular-season game that season. The legacy archive entry's basic player structure is therefore correct, but the opposing franchise should be understood historically as Baltimore rather than as an active Memphis team.

sections.heading: Issel Became an Immediate Denver Star
sections.body: Issel played all 84 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76 and averaged 23.0 points, 11.0 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 34.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star team and then averaged 20.5 points and 12.0 rebounds across 13 playoff games as Denver reached the final ABA Finals. This was not a speculative acquisition that needed years to mature. The return became elite immediately and arrived at exactly the moment Denver was preparing to move from the ABA into the NBA.

sections.heading: The Value Extended Far Beyond the Final ABA Season
sections.body: Issel stayed with Denver after the merger and remained one of the franchise's defining frontcourt players for the rest of his career. Basketball-Reference lists a 15-year professional career, seven All-Star selections and Hall of Fame induction, with the Denver portion spanning the club's final ABA season and many NBA seasons. The source-backed verdict does not need to assign every later team accomplishment to this trade; simply retaining a high-level scorer and rebounder through the league transition creates enormous realized value.

sections.heading: Robisch Never Produced a Baltimore Regular-Season Return
sections.body: Baltimore's side cannot be graded like a normal player-for-player exchange because the Claws folded before the regular season. Robisch therefore never logged a regular-season game for the franchise that acquired him. On October 21, San Diego selected Robisch in the Baltimore dispersal draft. He played all 11 games the Sails completed, then Indiana selected him in the November 12 dispersal draft after San Diego also ceased operations. Robisch went on to have a substantial career, but those later games belonged to San Diego, Indiana and other franchises, not Baltimore.

sections.heading: The Cash Component Matters, but Its Exact Amount Is Not Required to Grade the Basketball Outcome
sections.body: The authoritative Basketball-Reference transaction ledger identifies cash as part of Denver's outgoing package but does not state an amount. Historical ABA accounts often describe the payment as $500,000 and connect it to Baltimore's earlier obligation in the Issel acquisition from Kentucky. The archive can preserve that context in research notes without pretending the standard transaction ledger independently verifies the figure. Even treating the cash as meaningful consideration, Baltimore never converted either Robisch or the cash into a sustainable on-court return before the franchise disappeared.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A+/D. Denver receives an A+ because Issel immediately delivered an All-Star 23-and-11 season, helped the Nuggets reach the ABA Finals and remained a long-term franchise cornerstone through the NBA transition. Baltimore receives a D rather than an F because it did receive Robisch plus cash and the cash had real economic value, but the franchise folded before Robisch could play a regular-season game and therefore realized no durable basketball return. Confidence is high on the October 8 transaction, Issel's Denver production, Baltimore's collapse and Robisch's dispersal path. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The October 10 Movement Was a Waiver Claim, Not a Nets Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 ABA transaction ledger states that the Virginia Squires claimed Gerald Govan on waivers from the Utah Stars on October 10, 1975. Virginia's team transaction page records the same claim, and Utah's page records the same player leaving through waivers. Those three ledgers agree on both the mechanism and the clubs involved. None places the New York Nets in the transaction. The legacy archive entry therefore cannot be repaired simply by changing a draft-pick detail; its entire trade structure is unsupported.

sections.heading: Utah Had Already Waived Govan in September
sections.body: The Utah Stars waived Govan on September 17, more than three weeks before Virginia claimed him. That chronology matters because a waiver claim does not create a trade package and does not require the claiming club to send a player or draft asset to another team. The legacy record's future draft pick was therefore not merely unresolved. It was attached to a transaction type that did not happen. Treating the draft-pick language as unverified would still leave a false Nets-Squires exchange in the archive, so the safer correction is structural supersession.

sections.heading: New York's Transaction Ledger Has No Matching October 10 Deal
sections.body: The 1975-76 New York Nets transaction log lists the club's September Billy Paultz and Bob Warren trades, the October 16 Ed Manning deal with Indiana, later waivers, and the January 27 transaction with Virginia involving Swen Nater, Billy Schaeffer and Jim Eakins. It does not list an October 10 Gerald Govan trade or a future draft pick received from Virginia. That absence is especially persuasive when combined with the affirmative Utah and Virginia waiver records, because the correct transaction is already documented elsewhere rather than merely missing from one team page.

sections.heading: Govan Did Play for Virginia, but That Does Not Validate the legacy Package
sections.body: Govan's 1975-76 player record confirms 24 games for the Squires. He averaged 5.7 points, 6.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 27.4 minutes, and Virginia's roster page carries the same 24-game line. The Squires later waived him on December 16. Those facts explain why the legacy archive record may have looked plausible: Govan genuinely ended up in Virginia. The error was assigning that roster move to New York and inventing a reciprocal draft-pick asset. His Virginia production belongs to the waiver claim, not to a Nets trade verdict.

sections.heading: The Correct Archive Treatment Is Superseded Provenance
sections.body: TradeVerdicts keeps malformed historical imports when they are useful for explaining how a bad record entered the archive, but they should not remain eligible for a graded trade history, player-history links or verdict. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. The unsupported future-pick asset is explicitly labeled as a legacy claim rather than a real draft asset, and the Nets-to-Virginia player movement is marked unsupported.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. No winner and no team grades are assigned because there was no verified Nets-Squires trade to evaluate. Confidence is high: the ABA league ledger, Utah Stars ledger and Virginia Squires ledger independently align on a September 17 Utah waiver followed by Virginia's October 10 claim, while New York's transaction history contains no corresponding deal. Govan's 24 Virginia games and December 16 waiver are also directly supported. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The October 21 Transaction Is Unusually Well Documented
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Denver sent Fatty Taylor to the Squires for Chuck Williams on October 21, 1975. Carl Scheer's Denver executive record and Jack Ankerson's Virginia record repeat the deal. The timing adds important context. Earlier that day Virginia selected Williams from the Baltimore Claws in the dispersal draft after the Claws folded before playing a regular-season game. The Squires then immediately moved him to Denver for Taylor.

sections.heading: Williams Became a Major Part of Denver's Final ABA Team
sections.body: Williams played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 4.7 assists and 2.7 rebounds in 32.0 minutes. Basketball-Reference also marks him as an ABA All-Star that season. Denver finished with the league's best regular-season record and reached the final ABA Finals, so Williams' value was not empty-volume production on a losing club. He was a substantial guard on a contender during the exact season when the franchise was preparing to enter the NBA.

sections.heading: Taylor Was Productive for Virginia, but the Team Had No Future
sections.body: Fatty Taylor also gave his new club legitimate minutes. He played 76 games for Virginia and averaged 8.2 points, 5.3 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 2.7 steals in 32.7 minutes. Those numbers make the old C-minus Denver grade too harsh on the deal's balance because Virginia did receive a real starting guard. The problem is organizational context: the Squires went 15-68, missed the playoffs and disappeared after the season. Taylor's one year therefore produced no retained franchise value beyond the final Virginia campaign.

sections.heading: Denver Retained Williams Through the ABA-NBA Transition
sections.body: Williams remained with the Nuggets when the ABA clubs entered the NBA. He appeared in 21 games for Denver in 1976-77 before the club traded him and Gus Gerard to Buffalo for Jim Price on December 15, 1976. That later deal means Williams generated a second layer of value beyond his strong 1975-76 season. The original October trade should not receive full credit for Price because Gerard was also part of the package, but Williams was a real component of the acquisition and therefore carried measurable downstream utility.

sections.heading: The Trade Also Illustrates Denver's Rapid Guard Reconfiguration
sections.body: Denver's later moves add an unusual wrinkle. In August 1976 the Nuggets reacquired Fatty Taylor from Philadelphia for a 1977 second-round pick after the Virginia franchise had disappeared. Taylor then played 79 NBA games for Denver in 1976-77. That later reacquisition is a separate transaction and should not be credited to the Squires side of this October deal, but it shows that Denver still valued Taylor. The key point for this review is narrower: on October 21, 1975 Denver exchanged one useful veteran guard for another who immediately became an All-Star-level contributor and later retained trade value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A-/B. Denver receives an A- because Williams delivered 79 games, 11.0 points and 4.7 assists for an ABA Finals team, earned All-Star recognition, stayed through the NBA transition and later helped form the package for Jim Price. Virginia receives a B because Taylor was genuinely useful, starting most of the Squires' final season and supplying playmaking, rebounding and defensive activity. The gap comes from team context and retained value rather than from Taylor failing individually. Confidence is high on the transaction, both players' 1975-76 production and Williams' later Buffalo trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The legacy Pick Round and Cash Claim Were Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Seattle SuperSonics and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the October 22, 1975 exchange as Herm Gilliam to Seattle for a 1976 third-round draft pick. Bill Russell's Seattle executive record repeats the same structure. None of those authoritative ledgers includes cash. This review therefore corrects two material import errors: the No. 46 selection was a third-round pick, not a second-rounder, and the extra cash asset is removed rather than preserved as an unsupported part of the package.

sections.heading: Gilliam Gave Seattle a Full Rotation Season
sections.body: Herm Gilliam appeared in 81 regular-season games for the 1975-76 SuperSonics, averaging 8.5 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 20.3 minutes. He was no longer the 14-point starting guard he had been in Atlanta two years earlier, but he remained a durable veteran contributor. Seattle therefore converted a third-round pick into immediate usable depth for essentially an entire season, a much stronger realized outcome than the old database wording captured.

sections.heading: Atlanta Used the Pick on Larry Cooke at No. 46
sections.body: Atlanta retained the pick and used it in the 1976 NBA draft on Larry Cooke, a Virginia Tech guard selected 46th overall. The Hawks' transaction page, the league draft table and Cooke's Basketball-Reference profile all align on that identity. Cooke never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The pick outcome is therefore fully traceable but produced no major-league playing value for Atlanta, making this one of the cleaner historical comparisons in the 1975 chronology.

sections.heading: Seattle Still Had a Small Downstream Asset After the Season
sections.body: Gilliam did not simply leave Seattle as a free agent. Bill Russell's executive ledger records the SuperSonics selling his player rights to Portland on September 2, 1976. The standard transaction record does not provide a sale amount in the material reviewed here, so the source-backed grade does not assign a specific dollar value. The sale nevertheless confirms that Seattle retained at least some transactional value after Gilliam's 81-game season rather than receiving a one-year return that vanished without compensation.

sections.heading: Gilliam's Portland Championship Is Not Seattle Value
sections.body: Gilliam later played 80 regular-season games for Portland in 1976-77 and was part of the Trail Blazers' championship roster, but those games belong to Portland, not Seattle. This distinction is important because a downstream player path can easily inflate a trade grade if later production is attributed to the wrong franchise. Seattle's realized return stops at Gilliam's 1975-76 SuperSonics season plus whatever economic value came from the later rights sale. That is already enough to win the trade without borrowing his Portland accomplishments.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/D+. Seattle receives a B+ because a third-round pick produced 81 games of useful veteran rotation play and a later rights sale. The grade stays below A territory because Gilliam was a complementary player and Seattle kept him for only one season. Atlanta receives a D+ because the Hawks did obtain the exact draft asset promised and used it at No. 46, but Larry Cooke never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the package correction, Gilliam's Seattle production and the Cooke draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: This Was a Player-Rights Sale, Not a Draft-Rights Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles Lakers, Milwaukee Bucks and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that Milwaukee sold the player rights to Cornell Warner to Los Angeles on October 22, 1975. The legacy archive entry broadly captured the cash-for-rights structure, but its asset type labels the return as draft rights. Warner was already an established NBA player with two Milwaukee seasons behind him, so this review corrects the asset to player rights and preserves the cash consideration without inventing an amount.

sections.heading: Warner Immediately Became a Major Lakers Rebounder
sections.body: Warner played 81 games for Los Angeles in 1975-76 and averaged 7.3 points, 8.9 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 31.0 minutes. Only Kareem Abdul-Jabbar averaged more rebounds for the club. Warner's 722 total rebounds and 2,512 minutes make the acquisition materially different from a speculative rights purchase. Los Angeles converted cash into a high-usage frontcourt role for almost an entire season, and the production arrived immediately rather than requiring a development period.

sections.heading: The Lakers Also Retained Warner Into the NBA's 1976-77 Season
sections.body: Warner returned for 14 games in 1976-77, averaging 3.9 points and 4.9 rebounds in 12.1 minutes. His role diminished sharply, so the second season adds only modest value, but it pushes the Los Angeles return to 95 regular-season appearances across two years. The core of the grade remains the 1975-76 season, when Warner played 31 minutes per game and supplied the rebounding support around Abdul-Jabbar on a team that improved to 40 wins.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Return Is Real but Economically Opaque
sections.body: The Bucks received cash, and a cash return should not be treated as zero. The problem for a retrospective basketball archive is that the standard transaction ledgers reviewed here do not state the amount, and no player or draft asset emerged from the deal that can be followed through a later transaction chain. That makes Milwaukee's realized basketball value impossible to quantify with the same precision as Warner's games and production. The grade therefore gives Milwaukee credit for completing a sale rather than pretending the cash had no value, but it does not award unsupported downstream value.

sections.heading: Warner's Milwaukee Tenure Provides Important Context
sections.body: Milwaukee was not giving up an unknown reserve. Warner had played 67 games for the Bucks in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75, averaging 7.0 points and 8.2 rebounds across his two Milwaukee seasons. His 1974-75 workload reached 31.9 minutes per game. Selling his rights therefore represented a real roster decision, not merely clearing an inactive name. Los Angeles correctly identified that Warner could still handle a substantial role and immediately gave him one of the heaviest frontcourt workloads on the team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B+/C. Los Angeles receives a B+ because a cash purchase delivered 81 games at 31 minutes per night in the first season, 8.9 rebounds per game and 95 total appearances across two seasons. The grade stays below A territory because Warner's second Lakers season was brief and the acquisition did not create a long multi-year asset chain. Milwaukee receives a C because the Bucks did receive cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard transaction record and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the transaction type and Warner's production, while the unreported cash amount is explicitly left unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified Package Was Jim Fox for One Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Milwaukee, Seattle, the NBA league transaction ledger, Wayne Embry's executive record and Bill Russell's executive record all align on the same October 22, 1975 structure: the Bucks received Jim Fox and Seattle received a 1976 second-round draft pick. None of those ledgers lists cash. This review therefore removes the legacy cash component from the verified package and simplifies the pick language to what the primary records actually support. The pick was later used at No. 19 on Bayard Forrest.

sections.heading: The Pick Had Come to Milwaukee Through the Atlanta Penalty
sections.body: Milwaukee's 1974-75 transaction ledger shows that on June 5, 1975 the Bucks received two 1976 second-round picks from Atlanta as a league remedy tied to the Hawks' earlier signing of Milwaukee draft pick Julius Erving. Basketball-Reference identifies those two picks as the selections later used on Alex English and Bayard Forrest. By October, Milwaukee moved the Forrest pick to Seattle for Fox. That provenance is important because the legacy phrase about the most favorable Bucks pick is unnecessary and is not how the authoritative October transaction ledgers describe the deal.

sections.heading: Fox Gave Milwaukee One Useful Reserve Season
sections.body: Jim Fox played 70 games for the 1975-76 Bucks, averaging 3.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 13.1 minutes. He also appeared in all three games of Milwaukee's first-round playoff series against Detroit. The production was modest compared with his earlier Seattle seasons, but it was real roster value for a Milwaukee team in transition after the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar trade. Fox should not be treated as a failed acquisition simply because his role had shrunk; the Bucks received a durable veteran backup for the entire regular season.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned the Pick Into Bayard Forrest and Then Another Pick
sections.body: Seattle selected Bayard Forrest with the No. 19 pick in the 1976 draft. Forrest never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics, but that did not end the asset chain. On March 18, 1977 Seattle traded Forrest to Phoenix for a 1979 second-round pick. The transaction record identifies that future pick as the one later used on Paul Mokeski after Seattle sent it onward. Forrest himself later played 139 NBA games for Phoenix, but those Suns games are not credited to Seattle; Seattle's realized value is the replacement draft asset it received for him.

sections.heading: The Forrest Pick Helped Seattle Acquire John Johnson
sections.body: On October 22, 1977 Seattle sent the Phoenix-derived 1979 second-round pick and a 1980 second-round pick to Houston for John Johnson. Because two picks were required, the original Fox trade deserves only partial credit for Johnson rather than full credit for the entire acquisition. Even with that discount, the downstream value is substantial. Johnson played 76 games for Seattle in 1977-78 as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals, then started all 82 games in 1978-79 and averaged 11.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 4.4 assists for the NBA champions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because a single second-round pick retained value through multiple transactions and became part of the package for a starting forward on consecutive Finals teams, including the 1979 champion. The grade stops short of a full A because the Johnson acquisition also required another second-round pick. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Fox supplied 70 regular-season games and three playoff appearances as a dependable reserve, but the Bucks surrendered the more durable asset and received no comparable downstream return. Confidence is high on the corrected package, Fox's Milwaukee production, Forrest's No. 19 selection and the later Forrest-to-Phoenix and Johnson transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: Two legacy archive entrys Describe One Haywood Transaction
sections.body: The Seattle import and the New York import contain the same core package: Spencer Haywood moved to the Knicks, while Gene Short and a future first-round pick moved to the SuperSonics. The pick later became the No. 6 selection used on James Bailey. The only major structural difference is the date, with the Seattle record showing October 23 and the Knicks record showing October 24. There is no evidence of two separate Haywood transactions between the clubs on consecutive days.

sections.heading: Basketball-Reference Supports October 24 as the Completed Transaction Date
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 New York Knicks transaction page lists the trade on October 24, as does Seattle's team transaction page. The NBA league transaction ledger and Eddie Donovan's executive history also use October 24. Those independently maintained Basketball-Reference surfaces agree on the effective transaction date and package. That makes the Knicks-side October 24 record the stronger canonical record for TradeVerdicts.

sections.heading: The October 23 Date Is Still Explainable as Announcement Provenance
sections.body: A contemporary Black World article dated October 30 says the Haywood trade was announced Thursday afternoon. October 23, 1975 was a Thursday, while October 24 was Friday. That gives the earlier import date a plausible origin: it may reflect the public announcement rather than the completed league transaction entry. The same article describes the return as rookie Eugene Short plus cash estimated at $1.5 million, while later transaction databases also describe the conditional 1979 first-round component. Preserving the duplicate as provenance keeps that historical wrinkle without creating a second trade page.

sections.heading: Gene Short and Eugene Short Are the Same Player
sections.body: Basketball-Reference identifies Gene Short as Eugene Short Jr., the Knicks' No. 9 pick in the 1975 draft. Seattle's legacy archive entry uses Gene Short, while the Knicks import uses Eugene Short. That naming variation does not create a different asset. Short played only seven games for Seattle before being waived on November 24, and the Knicks signed him as a free agent two days later. This review therefore treats the two names as identity variants inside the same transaction history.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Also Confirms the Duplicate
sections.body: The future first-round asset is not merely similar between the two rows. Both identify a 1979 conditional first-round pick that ultimately became James Bailey at No. 6. Seattle used that selection on Bailey in the 1979 draft. Matching player movement, matching future-pick outcome and matching counterpart clubs make the duplicate diagnosis decisive even before considering the one-day date discrepancy.

sections.heading: Why Supersession Is Better Than Date Correction Alone
sections.body: Simply changing the Seattle record from October 23 to October 24 would leave two canonical records with the same clubs, players and draft-pick outcome. That would duplicate the transaction across public records, player histories and historical counts. Supersession is therefore the safer structural repair. It preserves the original Seattle import for audit history, records why its date differed, and directs all reader-facing evaluation to one canonical transaction without erasing the provenance that produced the duplicate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. No winner or grades are assigned to the October 23 Seattle import because evaluating it independently would double-count the same Spencer Haywood transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high because the team, league and executive ledgers align on October 24 and the contemporary October 23 announcement context explains rather than contradicts the earlier provenance date.
