sections.heading: The November 22 Move Was a Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix Suns transaction page states that Phoenix sold the player rights to Mike Bantom to Seattle on November 22, 1975. Seattle's transaction page records the same acquisition, and the NBA league ledger describes the same rights sale. The legacy archive entry correctly captured the broad cash-for-player structure, but this review makes the rights language explicit and avoids inventing a sale amount that the standard ledgers do not provide.

sections.heading: Bantom Immediately Rebounded From a Small Phoenix Role
sections.body: Bantom had played only seven games for Phoenix at the start of 1975-76, averaging 3.0 points in 9.7 minutes. After the sale he appeared in 66 games for Seattle and averaged 8.4 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 22.8 minutes. He also produced 2.8 win shares for the SuperSonics. That is a meaningful first-year return for a transaction in which Seattle did not surrender a player or draft pick.

sections.heading: Seattle Received a Second Season of Rotation Value
sections.body: Bantom returned in 1976-77 and played 44 more games for Seattle. His role declined to 18.1 minutes per game, but he still averaged 7.5 points and 4.2 rebounds while shooting 48.8 percent from the field. Across the two seasons, Seattle received 110 regular-season games from Bantom. The total workload matters because the transaction was not a brief rental or a player who failed to report; it produced sustained frontcourt depth across two roster cycles.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Return Was Economic Rather Than Basketball-Specific
sections.body: Phoenix received cash, and that consideration should not be treated as worthless. The problem for a hindsight basketball grade is that the amount is not stated in the standard Basketball-Reference transaction records reviewed here, and no player or draft asset returned to Phoenix that can be followed through a later basketball chain. Bantom had been the No. 8 pick in the 1973 draft and had averaged 12.5 points and 6.7 rebounds for Phoenix in 1974-75, so the Suns were selling the rights to a player who had already demonstrated rotation value.

sections.heading: The Later Career Does Not Need to Be Borrowed to Make Seattle's Case
sections.body: Bantom later produced a strong 33-game run for the New York Nets in 1976-77 and continued his career with Indiana, Philadelphia and other teams. Those later games should not be credited to Seattle unless a verified transaction return links them back to the SuperSonics. The source-backed grade does not need that extra reach. Seattle's own 110 games, 923 points and substantial rebounding output are enough to establish the value of the original rights purchase.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/C. Seattle receives a B+ because an unquantified cash payment produced 110 regular-season games, one full 66-game post-trade season and useful frontcourt production over two years. The grade stops below A territory because Bantom was a rotation player rather than a star and no major downstream Seattle asset is assigned to the transaction. Phoenix receives a C because cash had real economic value, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the rights-sale structure and Bantom's Seattle production, while the cash amount remains explicitly unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The November 27 Four-Player Exchange Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cleveland and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the same structure: the Bulls sent Nate Thurmond and Rowland Garrett to the Cavaliers for Steve Patterson and Eric Fernsten. The four-player construction in the legacy archive entry is correct. This review focuses on fixing the thin analysis, adding verified player identities and grading the realized value rather than treating every roster appearance as equivalent.

sections.heading: Thurmond Was the Deal's Transformative Piece
sections.body: Nate Thurmond played 65 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade and averaged 4.6 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in 17.4 minutes. Those regular-season numbers look modest, but his postseason role was much larger. Thurmond appeared in all 13 playoff games, averaged 28.8 minutes, 8.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks, and gave Cleveland an experienced defensive center during the franchise's run to the Eastern Conference Finals. That playoff workload is the central reason the Cavaliers' side grades so well.

sections.heading: Cleveland Also Retained Thurmond and Garrett Into 1976-77
sections.body: Thurmond returned for 49 more regular-season games in 1976-77, averaging 5.5 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in 20.3 minutes. Garrett played 41 games for Cleveland immediately after the trade and another 29 the next season before moving to Milwaukee. Garrett's role was small, but he still gave the Cavaliers additional roster depth beyond Thurmond. The combination produced two seasons of value rather than a single playoff rental.

sections.heading: Chicago Received Two Rotation Bigs but Little Lasting Value
sections.body: Steve Patterson played 52 games for the Bulls after the trade, averaging 3.2 points and 3.8 rebounds in 15.0 minutes. Eric Fernsten appeared in 33 games, averaging 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds in 7.8 minutes. Both contributed real regular-season minutes, so Chicago's return should not be graded as if the Bulls received nothing. The problem is scale: neither player approached Thurmond's postseason impact, and neither developed into a lasting Chicago asset. Patterson left the NBA after the season for Italy, while Fernsten's later NBA career unfolded elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Team Context Strengthens Cleveland's Hindsight Case
sections.body: Cleveland finished 49-33 and reached the 1976 Eastern Conference Finals, the breakthrough postseason remembered as the franchise's first deep playoff run. Thurmond was not the Cavaliers' leading scorer, but his 375 playoff minutes and 117 rebounds made him a major part of the rotation. Chicago, meanwhile, fell to 24-58 after having reached the conference finals the year before. A trade should not receive full credit or blame for team records, yet the actual roles matter: Cleveland acquired a player who materially participated in a long playoff run while Chicago received two reserves on a rebuilding season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, A/C+. Cleveland receives an A because Thurmond delivered 65 regular-season games, a major 13-game playoff run at 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks per game, and another 49 games the next season, with Garrett adding depth across parts of two years. Chicago receives a C+ because Patterson and Fernsten combined for 85 regular-season appearances after the trade and filled rotation minutes, but neither matched Thurmond's impact or produced meaningful downstream value. Confidence is high on the four-player package and the principal outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Was Marin for Chicago's 1977 First-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Buffalo and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the November 27, 1975 structure: Buffalo sent Jack Marin to the Bulls for Chicago's 1977 first-round draft choice. The pick ultimately landed at No. 13 in the 1977 draft and Tate Armstrong was selected there, but Buffalo did not hold the pick continuously until draft night. That distinction is important because the legacy archive entry made Armstrong look like a direct Braves draft return when the actual asset chain was more complicated.

sections.heading: Marin Gave Chicago 121 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Marin immediately stepped into a real role for the Bulls. He played 67 games after the trade in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 24.3 minutes. He returned for 54 games in 1976-77 and averaged 6.8 points in 16.1 minutes. Across the two Chicago seasons he supplied 121 regular-season appearances and more than 2,400 minutes. He was not a star by that stage of his career, but Chicago received dependable veteran wing production rather than a short rental.

sections.heading: Buffalo Converted the Pick Into Jim Price, Then Gerard and Williams
sections.body: On November 2, 1976 Buffalo traded the 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. Price played 20 games for the Braves before Buffalo moved him to Denver on December 15 for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard then appeared in 41 Buffalo games that season, while Williams played 44. That chain gave the Braves 105 combined regular-season appearances from Price, Gerard and Williams during 1976-77. The original pick therefore produced tangible roster value even before the asset later returned to Buffalo.

sections.heading: The No. 13 Pick Later Returned to Buffalo and Then Back to Chicago
sections.body: Milwaukee held the pick until June 7, 1977, when the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the No. 13 selection to Buffalo for the No. 3 pick that became Marques Johnson. Three days later Buffalo traded the No. 13 pick back to Chicago for the No. 24 second-round pick that became Larry Johnson; a secondary draft-transaction ledger also reports $150,000 cash going to Buffalo. Chicago then used No. 13 on Tate Armstrong. Because Buffalo had to surrender the No. 3 pick to reacquire No. 13, that later return cannot be credited solely to the 1975 Marin transaction, but it explains why Armstrong was ultimately a Bull rather than a Brave.

sections.heading: Armstrong's Career Should Not Be Treated as Buffalo's Direct Realized Outcome
sections.body: Armstrong played 92 NBA games, all for Chicago, averaging 3.8 points per game across two seasons. His modest career is relevant to the value of the No. 13 selection, but Buffalo never rostered him. The Braves' directly traceable basketball return from the original asset was the Price-to-Gerard-and-Williams chain, plus whatever value Buffalo received when the reacquired No. 13 pick was moved back to Chicago. That makes the transaction more competitive than a simple Marin-versus-Armstrong comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, B+/B. Chicago receives a B+ because Marin gave the club 121 regular-season games and meaningful veteran production over parts of two seasons without requiring another player in the original package. Buffalo receives a B because the first-round pick became a useful trade asset: it brought back Jim Price, who was then converted into Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, producing substantial 1976-77 roster value. The later No. 13 pick loop is documented but not over-credited because Buffalo spent the No. 3 selection to reacquire it. Confidence is high on the original transaction, Marin's Chicago production and the pick's documented path through Milwaukee and back to Chicago. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified December 3 Package Was Tom Owens for Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana Pacers transaction page states that Indiana traded cash to Kentucky for Tom Owens on December 3, 1975. Kentucky's transaction page records the mirror image, and the ABA league ledger uses the same structure. None of those standard ledgers includes future considerations. This review therefore removes the legacy future-considerations language from the verified package and retains cash as the only confirmed outgoing asset from Indiana.

sections.heading: Owens Gave Indiana a Short but Legitimate Rotation Stint
sections.body: Owens appeared in 16 games for the Pacers after the trade. He averaged 6.5 points, 4.3 rebounds and 0.7 blocks in 15.2 minutes while shooting 51.2 percent from the field and 80.0 percent from the line. In a limited role, that is useful frontcourt production rather than an empty roster transaction. Indiana was not acquiring a long-term starter, but Owens supplied real minutes during the final ABA season and gave the club another experienced center option.

sections.heading: The Pacers Recycled Owens Back Into Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana and San Antonio transaction logs record a January 1976 sale of Owens to the Spurs for cash. That means Indiana did not simply spend cash for 16 games and lose the asset for nothing. The Pacers received several weeks of production and then recovered another cash return. The exact amounts paid to Kentucky and received from San Antonio are not listed in the standard transaction records, so the two cash legs cannot be compared dollar for dollar. The grade must stay conservative rather than assuming Indiana made or lost money on the resale.

sections.heading: Kentucky's Return Cannot Be Overstated Without a Cash Figure
sections.body: The Colonels received cash and had already used Owens for 19 games earlier in 1975-76. Selling a reserve center for cash may have been sensible roster management, especially for a club that was also reshaping its frontcourt through the Caldwell Jones and Maurice Lucas transaction later that month. Still, there is no traceable player or draft asset coming back from the Owens sale itself. In a realized-value model, an undisclosed cash return has to be acknowledged but cannot be treated as equal to a documented player contribution without evidence.

sections.heading: Owens' Later San Antonio Production Belongs to the Next Transaction
sections.body: After leaving Indiana, Owens played 39 games for the Spurs and averaged 5.8 points and 4.0 rebounds in 13.8 minutes. Those games demonstrate that he still had rotation value, but they belong to San Antonio's acquisition rather than Indiana's December deal with Kentucky. The Pacers should receive credit for recognizing a usable player, getting 16 games from him and preserving some residual value through the later cash sale, not for the production he delivered after he left.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pacers Edge, B-/C+. Indiana receives a B- because a cash-only acquisition produced 16 games of efficient reserve-center work and was later converted back into cash. Kentucky receives a C+ because the Colonels did receive confirmed cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no basketball asset can be traced from the return. The grade gap remains small because the entire Indiana tenure lasted only 16 games and both cash figures are unresolved. Confidence is high on the December 3 cash-for-Owens structure and his Indiana production. The unsupported future-considerations claim is explicitly excluded. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The December 18 Transaction Was a Cash Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, Spirits of St. Louis and ABA league transaction pages all record the same December 18, 1975 move: Denver sent cash to St. Louis for Gus Gerard. Carl Scheer's executive record confirms the transaction. None of the standard ledgers reviewed states the amount. This review therefore preserves the cash consideration but does not invent a dollar figure or assign financial value that cannot be verified.

sections.heading: Gerard Immediately Became a Useful Denver Rotation Forward
sections.body: Gerard played 60 regular-season games for Denver after the trade in 1975-76. He averaged 9.9 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 19.8 minutes while shooting 43.4 percent from the field. Basketball-Reference lists him as an ABA All-Star that season. The minutes and production are meaningful for a midseason cash purchase: Denver received a regular rotation forward rather than a fringe reserve or a short emergency stint, and Gerard remained available throughout the stretch run.

sections.heading: He Also Contributed Throughout Denver's 1976 Playoff Run
sections.body: Gerard appeared in all 13 of Denver's playoff games after the acquisition. His postseason role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game, but he still contributed 4.6 points and 2.5 rebounds while the Nuggets advanced through the ABA playoffs. That postseason availability adds value beyond the regular-season line and confirms that Gerard remained part of Denver's working rotation during the final ABA postseason.

sections.heading: Gerard Returned After the ABA-NBA Merger
sections.body: Denver retained Gerard for the franchise's first NBA season. He played 24 games in 1976-77, started 21, scored 240 points and produced 1.1 win shares in 456 minutes before being traded in December. Combining the two Denver seasons gives the club 84 regular-season games from the original cash acquisition, with useful production on both sides of the league merger. That durability makes the original legacy C-minus grade too low for the realized return.

sections.heading: Denver Later Used Gerard in the Jim Price Package
sections.body: On December 15, 1976 Denver traded Gerard and Chuck Williams to Buffalo for Jim Price. Because Williams was also required, the original Gerard purchase cannot receive full credit for Price. Still, Gerard retained enough value to function as half of the outgoing player package one year after Denver bought him for cash. Price then played 55 games for Denver in 1976-77. That downstream use strengthens the acquisition without turning it into a one-player chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+/C. Denver receives a B+ because an undisclosed cash payment produced 84 regular-season games across the ABA and NBA, 13 playoff appearances, an ABA All-Star selection and partial downstream value in the Jim Price trade. The grade stops below A territory because Gerard was a rotation-level forward and Chuck Williams was also needed to acquire Price. St. Louis receives a C because cash had real economic value but the amount is unresolved and no basketball asset can be traced from it. Confidence is high on the sale structure and Gerard's Denver production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Transaction Date Is January 15, 1976
sections.body: The legacy archive record carried January 6, 1976, but Basketball-Reference's Indiana Pacers transaction page, San Antonio Spurs transaction page and ABA league transaction ledger all identify January 15 as the date Indiana sold Tom Owens to San Antonio for cash. This review corrects the canonical trade date to January 15 while preserving the original record ID for continuity. The package itself is straightforward: Owens to San Antonio, cash to Indiana.

sections.heading: Owens Gave San Antonio 39 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Owens appeared in 39 games for the Spurs after the purchase. He averaged 5.8 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 13.8 minutes per game while shooting 49.5 percent from the field. That is modest production, but it is meaningful for a midseason cash acquisition. San Antonio received a dependable reserve center for the final portion of the ABA season rather than a player who barely appeared or failed to report.

sections.heading: He Also Appeared in Every Spurs Playoff Game
sections.body: Owens played in all seven San Antonio playoff games in 1976. His role stayed limited at 12.7 minutes per game, but he remained part of the postseason rotation and averaged 3.3 points and 3.4 rebounds. A cash purchase that contributes through the entire playoff run carries more realized value than a short regular-season-only stint, even if the player is not a starter or a major scorer.

sections.heading: Indiana's Return Was Cash After a Six-Week Trial
sections.body: Indiana had acquired Owens from Kentucky for cash on December 3, 1975 and used him in 16 games before selling him to San Antonio. The Pacers therefore got a short stretch of reserve production and then recovered cash. That makes the sequence more nuanced than a simple loss for Indiana. The problem for retrospective grading is that the standard ledgers do not state either cash amount, so there is no defensible way to determine whether Indiana made money, broke even or took a financial loss on the two transactions.

sections.heading: The Date Correction Also Keeps this review and this review Distinct
sections.body: this review covers Indiana's December 3 purchase of Owens from Kentucky. This review is the separate January 15 sale to San Antonio. Correcting the second date prevents the archive from implying a January 6 transaction that the primary Basketball-Reference ledgers do not support, while preserving the real six-week Indiana tenure between the two moves. The player source reference is updated to the same corrected date so the player-history links and canonical record stay aligned.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because cash produced 39 regular-season games and seven playoff appearances from a usable reserve center. The grade stays modest because Owens averaged fewer than fourteen minutes per game and did not become a long-term Spurs asset. Indiana receives a C because the Pacers did receive cash after using Owens for 16 games, but the amount is unresolved and no later basketball asset can be traced from the return. Confidence is high on the January 15 date, cash-sale structure and San Antonio production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The January 27 Three-Player Package Is Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Virginia Squires and ABA league transaction ledgers all record the same January 27, 1976 exchange: New York sent Swen Nater and Billy Schaeffer to Virginia for Jim Eakins. This review also corrects the legacy Bill Schaeffer label to the Basketball-Reference identity Billy Schaeffer. There is no cash or draft component in the authoritative ledger, so the evaluation can focus directly on what the three players produced after the trade.

sections.heading: Eakins Became a Championship Rotation Center for the Nets
sections.body: Eakins played 34 regular-season games for New York after the trade, averaging 6.2 points, 3.5 rebounds and 0.6 blocks in 13.6 minutes while shooting 50.3 percent from the field. His role expanded in the playoffs. He appeared in all 13 postseason games, averaged 21.6 minutes, 6.8 points and 6.0 rebounds, and was part of the rotation as the Nets defeated San Antonio and Denver to win the final ABA championship. That postseason contribution materially changes the hindsight value of the deal.

sections.heading: Virginia Received the Best Regular-Season Player in Nater
sections.body: Swen Nater was clearly the strongest regular-season performer in the package after the trade. He played 33 games for Virginia and averaged 11.3 points, 9.8 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 23.5 minutes while shooting 49.8 percent. Nater had already been a major rebounder in the ABA, and his Squires production confirms that he remained a starting-caliber interior player. If the trade were judged only by regular-season box-score output, Virginia would have the stronger case.

sections.heading: Schaeffer Added Another 31 Games for the Squires
sections.body: Billy Schaeffer also contributed immediately, playing 31 games for Virginia at 6.6 points and 2.9 rebounds in 16.7 minutes. His role was smaller than Nater's, but the two outgoing Nets combined for 64 Squires appearances after the deal. That is substantial short-term volume and prevents the transaction from being graded as a New York landslide. Virginia received two usable players, not one star plus a throw-in who never appeared.

sections.heading: The Championship Context Breaks the Near Tie
sections.body: New York gave up the better regular-season package, but Eakins filled a role that mattered during the most important games of the season. He played every playoff game and increased his rebounding from 3.5 per game in the regular season to 6.0 in the postseason. The Nets did not acquire a star, yet they acquired a center who could handle more than twenty playoff minutes per night on the team that won the ABA title. That kind of direct postseason utility is a legitimate realized outcome and should not be erased by Nater's superior regular-season averages.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge, B+/B. New York receives a B+ because Eakins supplied 34 regular-season games and then became a 21.6-minute postseason rotation center across all 13 games of the 1976 ABA championship run. Virginia receives a B because Nater was the best regular-season player in the transaction and Schaeffer added useful depth, combining for 64 Squires appearances. The margin is intentionally narrow: the Squires won the regular-season production comparison, while the Nets received the more consequential postseason result. Confidence is high on the package and direct 1975-76 outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified Package Was Shumate for Heard and One 1976 Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo Braves, Phoenix Suns and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the February 1, 1976 structure: Buffalo sent Gar Heard and a 1976 second-round pick to Phoenix for John Shumate. The pick became No. 30 Al Fleming. None of those authoritative ledgers includes the legacy 1978 second-round pick that was labeled as No. 41 Jerome Whitehead. This review therefore removes that unsupported asset from the verified package and disconnects Whitehead from this trade's player-history linkage.

sections.heading: Heard Became a Major Part of Phoenix's 1976 Finals Run
sections.body: Gar Heard played 36 regular-season games for Phoenix after the trade, averaging 12.4 points and 9.9 rebounds in 33.9 minutes. His postseason role was even more important. Heard appeared in all 19 Suns playoff games, averaged 13.9 points, 10.4 rebounds, 2.1 steals and 1.9 blocks, and helped Phoenix reach the NBA Finals. That immediate two-way playoff production is the strongest single realized outcome in the deal.

sections.heading: Phoenix Kept Heard for Two More Seasons
sections.body: Heard returned for 46 games in 1976-77 and 80 in 1977-78, giving Phoenix 162 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons from the original transaction. His scoring declined after the Finals run, but he continued to rebound, defend and play substantial minutes. The extra longevity separates the return from a short postseason rental and gives Phoenix a strong multi-year case even before considering the draft pick.

sections.heading: The Al Fleming Pick Produced No Suns Games
sections.body: Phoenix used the acquired second-round pick at No. 30 on Al Fleming in the 1976 draft. Fleming did not play for the Suns and is listed as not playing after being waived in 1976-77. He later reached the NBA with Seattle in 1977-78, but those games are not Phoenix value. The pick therefore adds draft optionality to the transaction but no realized Suns production. Heard, not Fleming, carries the Phoenix grade.

sections.heading: Shumate Was an Excellent Buffalo Return
sections.body: John Shumate immediately became a major Braves frontcourt player. He appeared in 32 games after the trade at 12.2 points and 9.8 rebounds, then played 74 games in 1976-77 at 15.1 points and 9.5 rebounds and another 18 in 1977-78. He also averaged 14.1 points and 8.6 rebounds across nine playoff games in 1976. Buffalo therefore received 124 regular-season games of strong production, making this a competitive trade rather than a one-sided Phoenix win.

sections.heading: Shumate Retained Some Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: On November 23, 1977 Buffalo included Shumate, Gus Gerard and a 1979 first-round pick in a larger deal with Detroit for Marvin Barnes and two 1978 draft picks. Because Gerard and a first-rounder were also required, this review gives Shumate only partial downstream credit. The later package still shows that he retained trade value after nearly two productive Braves seasons. It also reinforces why Buffalo's side remains close to Phoenix's despite Heard's superior longevity and deeper 1976 playoff run.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Heard delivered 162 regular-season games, three seasons of frontcourt value and a major 19-game playoff run to the 1976 NBA Finals. The No. 30 pick produced no Suns games, so the grade is driven by Heard rather than draft luck. Buffalo receives a B+ because Shumate gave the Braves 124 regular-season games, strong scoring and rebounding, nine playoff appearances and partial downstream trade value. The margin stays narrow, but Heard's longer Phoenix tenure and much deeper 1976 postseason role break the tie. Confidence is high on the corrected package and direct outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Verified Return Was Cash, Not Future Considerations
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets transaction page, Kentucky Colonels transaction page and ABA league ledger all place the move on February 15, 1976 and describe the same structure: Kentucky sent Ted McClain to New York for cash. None of those sources lists future considerations. This review therefore replaces the legacy future-considerations asset with a verified cash return while leaving the amount unresolved because the standard ledgers do not publish it.

sections.heading: McClain Immediately Became a Regular Nets Guard
sections.body: McClain played 30 regular-season games for New York after the purchase. He averaged 11.3 points, 3.5 assists, 2.4 rebounds and 1.9 steals in 23.2 minutes while shooting 42.2 percent from the field and 81.2 percent from the line. Those are meaningful rotation numbers for a mid-February acquisition. The Nets were not buying an end-of-bench player; they added a veteran guard who could handle more than twenty minutes per night during the final stretch of the ABA season.

sections.heading: He Also Contributed During the 1976 Championship Run
sections.body: McClain appeared in eight playoff games for New York, including five games in the semifinal series against San Antonio and three in the ABA Finals against Denver. His postseason role was smaller than his regular-season role, but he remained part of the active rotation on the team that won the final ABA championship. That direct championship-season contribution gives the transaction more realized basketball value than a simple cash purchase with no postseason impact.

sections.heading: Kentucky's Side Is Economically Real but Basketball-Opaque
sections.body: The Colonels received cash, and the sale should not be treated as if Kentucky got nothing. The difficulty is that the surviving standard transaction ledgers do not state the dollar amount, and no named player or draft asset came back in the transaction that can be followed through a later chain. Kentucky had already received 43 games from McClain earlier in the season, where he averaged 7.7 points and 4.7 assists, before converting him into cash in February.

sections.heading: The Timing Favors New York's Competitive Window
sections.body: New York was preparing for a championship push and added a veteran backcourt contributor without surrendering a roster player or draft choice. McClain's 30 regular-season games and eight playoff appearances fit that short-term objective well. Kentucky's financial motivation may also have been reasonable, but the retrospective basketball archive can measure McClain's Nets role much more precisely than it can measure an undisclosed cash return. That asymmetry is why the grading advantage belongs to New York without pretending the Colonels' side had zero value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ because a cash-only acquisition produced 30 regular-season games at 11.3 points and 3.5 assists per game plus eight playoff appearances during the 1976 ABA championship run. The grade stays below A territory because McClain was a rotation guard rather than a primary star and the Nets' postseason core was led elsewhere. Kentucky receives a C because cash had real economic value, but the amount is unresolved and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the date, cash-sale structure and McClain's direct New York production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The June 3 Deal Was a Straight Second-Round Pick Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland Trail Blazers, New Orleans Jazz and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Portland sent its 1976 second-round pick to New Orleans for the Jazz's 1977 second-round pick. New Orleans used the 1976 selection at No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey, while Portland later used the 1977 selection at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. The legacy structure is correct; this review adds the actual player outcomes and distinguishes later NBA careers from value realized by the teams that owned the picks.

sections.heading: New Orleans Selected Jacky Dorsey but Received No NBA Games
sections.body: The Jazz selected Dorsey No. 26 in the 1976 draft. Basketball-Reference lists him as playing in the Eastern Basketball Association rather than the NBA in 1976-77, and he never appeared in a regular-season game for New Orleans. Dorsey did eventually reach the NBA in 1977-78, but his first games came with Denver and later Portland. Those appearances demonstrate that the pick identified an NBA-caliber player, yet they cannot be credited to the Jazz because New Orleans did not realize that production.

sections.heading: Portland Waited a Year for Kim Anderson
sections.body: Portland used the incoming 1977 second-round pick at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. Anderson spent 1977-78 playing professionally in Italy rather than joining the Trail Blazers immediately. He reached Portland in 1978-79 and appeared in 21 games, averaging 3.0 points, 2.1 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 10.7 minutes. The production was limited and his field-goal percentage was only 31.2 percent, but the pick did eventually generate real NBA minutes for the team that acquired it.

sections.heading: The Later Dorsey Career Does Not Reverse the Jazz Outcome
sections.body: Dorsey played 11 NBA games across Denver and Portland in 1977-78 and later appeared for Houston. Those games matter to his career history but not to the realized return from this New Orleans trade. A draft pick's hindsight value should follow the team that actually retained and used the player, not automatically inherit every game the drafted player later produced elsewhere. That rule prevents the Jazz from receiving credit for Dorsey's Denver, Portland or Houston appearances after he failed to play for New Orleans.

sections.heading: The Difference Remains Small Because Anderson's Portland Role Was Small
sections.body: Portland's 21 games from Anderson are enough to separate the outcomes, but not enough to make this a major win. Anderson totaled only 224 minutes in his lone Trail Blazers season and scored 63 points. New Orleans received no direct NBA games from Dorsey, but the Jazz did secure a second-round prospect one year earlier than the pick they surrendered. The swap therefore remains a low-value transaction where the grade gap should be compressed rather than inflated.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge, C+/C. Portland receives a C+ because the 1977 No. 28 pick eventually produced 21 Trail Blazers games from Kim Anderson, even though the contribution was modest and delayed by a season in Italy. New Orleans receives a C because the 1976 No. 26 pick became Jacky Dorsey, who never played an NBA regular-season game for the Jazz. Dorsey's later NBA career belongs to other teams and does not erase that zero-game New Orleans outcome. Confidence is high on the pick swap and draft outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Package and Draft Outcomes Are Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and Houston transaction records agree on the June 7, 1976 structure: Atlanta sent Dwight Jones and the 1976 No. 1 pick to Houston for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick. Houston used No. 1 on John Lucas Jr.; Atlanta used No. 9 on Armond Hill the next day. This review preserves that five-asset structure and attaches the direct player and draft-outcome identities.

sections.heading: Houston Received a Starting Guard and a Durable Big
sections.body: Lucas played all 82 games as a rookie, averaging 11.1 points, 5.6 assists and 1.5 steals in 30.9 minutes while earning All-Rookie recognition. He returned in 1977-78 and again played all 82 games, this time averaging 12.4 points and 9.4 assists. Dwight Jones supplied frontcourt depth across three Houston seasons, appearing in 74 games in 1976-77, 82 in 1977-78 and 81 in 1978-79. The Rockets therefore received immediate help from both the established player and the premium pick.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned the No. 9 Pick Into a Multi-Year Point Guard
sections.body: Armond Hill played 81 games as a rookie and averaged 5.0 assists, then started all 82 games in both 1977-78 and 1978-79. He added 79 more games in 1979-80, giving Atlanta 324 appearances over his first four seasons alone. Hill was not the same caliber of prospect as the No. 1 selection, but he became a stable backcourt piece for several years and gave the Hawks substantial realized value from the pick swap.

sections.heading: Meriweather Was Also a Strong Immediate Return
sections.body: Joe Meriweather played 74 games for Atlanta in 1976-77 and averaged 11.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 27.9 minutes. He produced 4.8 win shares before moving on the next season. Gus Bailey did not play for Atlanta and was waived, so the Hawks' player return is driven overwhelmingly by Meriweather rather than Bailey. Even so, Meriweather plus Hill created a productive two-part return that balances much of Houston's Lucas-and-Jones package.

sections.heading: The Trade Worked for Both Sides for Different Reasons
sections.body: Houston received the best single draft slot and turned it into a guard who immediately played major minutes, while also adding a useful veteran big. Atlanta moved down eight spots but landed Hill and added a starting-caliber center in Meriweather. The draft-position gap is real, yet the Hawks converted their lower pick well enough that the practical results remained competitive rather than one-sided.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A-/A-. Houston receives an A- for two full seasons of major Lucas production plus three years of Dwight Jones frontcourt minutes. Atlanta receives an A- because Armond Hill became a multi-year starter and Joe Meriweather delivered a strong 74-game season immediately after the trade. Bailey contributed no Atlanta games, which keeps the Hawks from grading higher, while Lucas leaving Houston after only two seasons prevents the Rockets from separating decisively. Confidence is high on the package, draft outcomes and first-stage realized production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The June 16 Package Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Buffalo Braves and NBA transaction ledgers agree that Atlanta sent Tom Van Arsdale to Buffalo for Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash on June 16, 1976. Executive records for Bud Seretean and Bob MacKinnon repeat the same structure. This review therefore preserves the legacy four-asset package and replaces the thin evaluation with the actual realized outcomes.

sections.heading: Ken Charles Became Atlanta's Main Return
sections.body: Charles played all 82 games for the Hawks in 1976-77 and averaged 11.1 points, 2.0 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals in 30.3 minutes. He returned for 21 more games in 1977-78, giving Atlanta 103 regular-season appearances and more than 3,000 minutes from the deal. His first Hawks season was a genuine full-time rotation role rather than a reserve cameo.

sections.heading: Dick Gibbs Added No Atlanta NBA Games
sections.body: Gibbs had played 72 games for Buffalo in 1975-76, but his NBA career ended after that season. He did not appear in a regular-season game for Atlanta following the June trade. That makes him a zero-game basketball return in this transaction. The Hawks still received cash in addition to Charles, but the amount is not stated in the standard transaction ledgers and is not assigned unsupported value.

sections.heading: Buffalo Immediately Recycled Van Arsdale
sections.body: Van Arsdale never played a regular-season game for the Braves. On August 25, 1976, Buffalo traded him to Phoenix for a 1977 second-round pick. That means Buffalo did preserve some asset value rather than losing the veteran for nothing, but the June trade itself produced no on-court Buffalo contribution. The later pick should be recognized as downstream value without being overstated, especially because the 1977 second-round draft chain around Buffalo and Milwaukee contains multiple transactions. The important source-backed point is simpler: Buffalo never received on-court production from Van Arsdale, while Atlanta received a full season of meaningful guard play from Charles. That contrast is firm even if the exact downstream value of Buffalo's later pick is treated conservatively.

sections.heading: Atlanta Clearly Received the Better Immediate Basketball Return
sections.body: Charles' 103 Hawks games provide a straightforward realized return, and the cash component adds some unquantified value. Buffalo used Van Arsdale as a trade chip rather than a player, so the Braves' success depends on what the later Phoenix pick became. That is a weaker and less direct return than a productive full season plus additional games from Charles, especially in a realized-value model centered on documented NBA contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, B+/C+. Atlanta receives a B+ because Ken Charles delivered 103 games, including an 82-game season at 11.1 points and 3.6 assists, while the Hawks also received cash. The grade stops below A territory because Gibbs produced no Atlanta games and the cash amount is unresolved. Buffalo receives a C+ because Van Arsdale never played for the Braves but was successfully flipped to Phoenix for a future second-round pick. Confidence is high on the package and direct player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The August 5 Structure Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree that the Nuggets sent a 1977 second-round pick to the 76ers for Fatty Taylor on August 5, 1976. Carl Scheer's executive record confirms the same exchange, and Denver's own media guide lists Taylor as an August 5 acquisition for the pick that became Herm Harris. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the selection to No. 43 in the 1977 draft.

sections.heading: Denver Received a Real Rotation Guard Immediately
sections.body: Taylor played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1976-77 and averaged 19.6 minutes, 3.8 points, 2.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals. He was no longer the high-usage ABA guard he had been earlier in the decade, but he still gave the Nuggets a steady defensive and ball-handling option throughout their first NBA season. Denver finished 50-32 and first in the Midwest Division, and Taylor was available almost every night.

sections.heading: The Postseason Contribution Was Minimal but the Regular Season Was Not
sections.body: Taylor appeared in only one playoff game and logged a single minute, so this review does not inflate his value by treating him as an important postseason piece. The trade's Denver case rests on the 79-game regular-season body of work. That distinction matters because the acquisition was useful without being transformative. Denver still received a full regular-season rotation player for the price of one future second-round selection. Taylor filled a role for one season, then Denver waived him in October 1977.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Pick Became Herm Harris at No. 43
sections.body: The 76ers used the acquired second-round pick on Herm Harris, a 6-foot-5 forward from Arizona, with the 43rd overall selection in the 1977 NBA draft. Basketball-Reference's draft page lists no NBA seasons or games for Harris. In a realized-value model, the pick therefore produced no NBA on-court return for Philadelphia. The draft choice still had legitimate option value when acquired, but hindsight grading must reflect what actually materialized in NBA competition.

sections.heading: The Rights Language Is Historically Accurate
sections.body: Secondary transaction records often describe Denver as acquiring Taylor's draft rights because Philadelphia had originally selected him in the 12th round of the 1969 NBA draft even though he built his career in the ABA. RealGM and Denver's historical records both preserve that rights-based framing. Taylor then signed with Denver on the same August 5 date and entered the Nuggets' 1976-77 roster, so the practical outcome is straightforward: Denver converted the rights into an active player immediately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B/D+. Denver receives a B because one second-round pick produced 79 games of dependable rotation play during a 50-win season, including useful passing and steal production, even though Taylor lasted only one NBA season with the club and barely played in the postseason. Philadelphia receives a D+ because the pick became Herm Harris at No. 43 and Harris never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Taylor's Denver production and the draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

sections.heading: The Martin Trade and the Gilliam Sale Were Separate Transactions
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all list two distinct September 2, 1976 moves between the same clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, and Portland separately traded LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle executive record preserve the same separation. This review therefore evaluates only Martin for future considerations and does not fold Gilliam into the exchange.

sections.heading: The Future Consideration Was Conditional on Martin Making the Team
sections.body: The standard Basketball-Reference ledgers do not identify the future consideration by round, but an archival Portland account of a September 3 report quotes Russell clarifying that Seattle had not traded a first-round pick. Russell said the consideration would be a 1977 draft pick and that it was conditional on Martin making Seattle's opening-day roster. That detail resolves the legacy "not exercised" note: the draft asset existed only if the roster condition was satisfied.

sections.heading: Seattle Waived Martin Before the Regular Season
sections.body: RealGM records Seattle acquiring Martin on September 2, placing him on waivers on October 12 and Martin becoming a free agent on October 14. Basketball-Reference's career page lists four NBA seasons, all with Portland, ending in 1975-76. Martin therefore produced zero regular-season games, minutes or points for Seattle. The SuperSonics took a low-cost look at a former No. 1 overall pick, but the basketball return from the transaction was zero.

sections.heading: Portland's Return Also Finished at Zero
sections.body: Because Martin did not make Seattle's opening-day roster, the conditional 1977 pick never became an exercised Portland asset. No draft selection or player outcome should be assigned to the Trail Blazers from this transaction. Herm Gilliam did appear in 18 games for Portland in 1976-77, but that value came from the separate same-day rights sale and cannot be used to improve Portland's grade on the Martin deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, D/D. Seattle receives a D because Martin never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics and was waived before opening day. Portland also receives a D because the conditional 1977 draft consideration did not trigger, leaving the Trail Blazers with no realized asset from this specific exchange. The transaction was inexpensive for Seattle and allowed Portland to move on from Martin, so neither side warrants an F, but neither side generated measurable on-court or draft value from the deal itself. Confidence is high on the transaction, the separate Gilliam sale, Martin's waiver and the zero-game outcome; the exact round of the conditional 1977 pick remains unspecified.

sections.heading: The Gilliam Rights Sale Was Separate From the LaRue Martin Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers list two distinct September 2, 1976 transactions between the clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, while Portland separately sent LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Bill Russell's Seattle executive record and Harry Glickman's Portland executive record preserve the same separation. This review therefore grades Gilliam for cash on its own and does not import Martin or the conditional 1977 pick into this exchange.

sections.heading: Gilliam Became a Real Rotation Piece in Portland
sections.body: Gilliam had already played for Seattle in 1975-76 before the rights sale. With Portland in 1976-77, Basketball-Reference credits him with 80 regular-season games and 1,665 minutes. He averaged 9.3 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 20.8 minutes per game while shooting 43.8 percent from the field. That is substantial realized value for an acquisition whose documented outgoing asset is cash rather than a player or draft pick.

sections.heading: The Value Extended Into Portland's Championship Run
sections.body: The regular season was not the end of Gilliam's contribution. Basketball-Reference's postseason record shows him appearing in 18 playoff games for Portland, totaling 295 minutes and averaging 6.4 points. Portland won the 1977 NBA championship, and Gilliam was part of that playoff rotation. The title should not turn every reserve into an elite trade return, but it is legitimate hindsight value when the acquired player actually appeared throughout the postseason run.

sections.heading: Seattle's Cash Return Is Real but Unpriced
sections.body: Seattle's side of the transaction is documented as cash. None of the reviewed Basketball-Reference or RealGM records identifies the amount, so this review does not invent a dollar figure or pretend to know how materially it affected the club. Cash has genuine transaction value, especially for a veteran whose rights Seattle was willing to move, but an unpriced financial return cannot be credited like a productive player season. The conservative approach is to give Seattle some value without equating the unknown cash with Gilliam's documented NBA production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, B+/C. Portland receives a B+ because Gilliam delivered 80 regular-season games, meaningful reserve scoring and 18 playoff appearances during a championship season for a cash-only cost. Seattle receives a C because it converted Gilliam's rights into financial consideration, but the amount is unverified and there is no player or draft asset to trace forward. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Gilliam's Portland production, while the unknown cash amount keeps Seattle's side from being graded more precisely.

sections.heading: The Primary Record Shows McNeill for a 1977 Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and NBA transaction ledgers all record the September 9, 1976 exchange as Larry McNeill to the Nets for a 1977 third-round draft pick. The Nets' own historical media guide says the same thing and identifies the eventual selection as Bill Paterno. None of those primary-style records lists cash. Pro Sports Transactions does preserve a UPI-based note that cash was also included, while also flagging conflicting reporting around the transaction date. This review therefore keeps the cash report visible as secondary evidence but does not treat it as a fully verified primary-ledger asset.

sections.heading: McNeill Gave New York Only a Brief Regular-Season Return
sections.body: McNeill had been a useful Kansas City reserve and part-time starter before the trade, appearing in all 82 games in 1975-76. His New York stint was much shorter. Basketball-Reference credits him with eight Nets games, 93 total minutes, 60 points and 26 rebounds in 1976-77. On a per-game basis he averaged 7.5 points and 3.3 rebounds in 11.6 minutes. That is real realized value, but the sample is too small to treat the acquisition as a successful long-term rotation move.

sections.heading: The Nets Waived Him in December
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's league and Nets transaction pages show New York waiving McNeill on December 13, 1976. RealGM independently records the same waiver, followed by free agency two days later. He did not return to the Nets. Golden State signed him on February 24, 1977, so his later 16-game Warriors stint belongs to a separate free-agent transaction and cannot be credited to New York here. This review grades only the eight games the Nets actually received from the September trade.

sections.heading: Kansas City Used the Pick on Bill Paterno at No. 45
sections.body: The pick outcome is fully traceable. Kansas City selected Notre Dame forward Bill Paterno with the first pick of the third round, No. 45 overall, in the 1977 NBA Draft. Basketball-Reference's Kings transaction log and Paterno player page both identify that selection. Paterno has no NBA regular-season statistical record, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value for Kansas City. The draft asset had option value when acquired, but its completed on-court outcome was zero.

sections.heading: The Cash Report Does Not Create a Measurable Kings Advantage
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions says a UPI report included cash in addition to the third-rounder. Because the amount is not identified and the Basketball-Reference ledgers plus the Nets' historical media guide omit cash entirely, this review discounts that component heavily. It is reasonable to preserve the possibility that Kansas City received some financial consideration, but there is not enough verified information to price it or use it to overturn the direct basketball comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge, C+/C. New York receives a C+ because McNeill at least produced eight regular-season games and 93 minutes before being waived. Kansas City receives a C because the acquired third-round pick became Bill Paterno, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game; the secondary cash report adds some possible transaction value but cannot be measured confidently. The margin is intentionally small. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure, McNeill's Nets production and the Paterno draft outcome, while the cash component remains secondary-source-only.

sections.heading: The Exchange Is One of the Deepest Packages of the Merger Era
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 10, 1976 structure. The Kings sent Tiny Archibald to the Nets for Jim Eakins, Brian Taylor, New York's 1977 first-round pick and its 1978 first-round pick. Those selections became Otis Birdsong at No. 2 in 1977 and Phil Ford at No. 2 in 1978. Joe Axelson's Kansas City executive ledger and Roy Boe's Nets ledger record the same package. Unlike several nearby 1976 trades, there is no material source conflict over the core assets.

sections.heading: Brian Taylor Was an Immediate High-Level Return
sections.body: Taylor gave Kansas City 72 games in 1976-77 and immediately became one of the club's best guards. He averaged 17.0 points, 4.4 assists and 2.8 steals in 34.6 minutes while shooting 50.4 percent from the field, and he earned NBA All-Defensive Second Team honors. That is substantial direct value before the draft picks even enter the equation. Kansas City then used Taylor in a May 1977 package with another first-round pick to acquire Tom Burleson and a second-round selection, so Taylor also retained transaction value beyond his one Kings season. Because that later deal contained another premium asset, this review credits the downstream return only partially.

sections.heading: Jim Eakins Added a Full Season of Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Eakins was less valuable than Taylor but still produced a complete NBA season. He appeared in all 82 games for Kansas City in 1976-77, averaging 6.0 points and 4.4 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. His role was modest, yet it matters in a trade that already delivered two future No. 2 picks. The Kings did not have to wait for the draft assets to mature before receiving useful rotation minutes from the incoming veterans.

sections.heading: Otis Birdsong Became a Multi-Year Kansas City Star
sections.body: The 1977 first-round pick became Birdsong at No. 2 overall. Across four Kansas City seasons he played 308 regular-season games and developed from a 15.8-point rookie into one of the league's top scoring guards. He made the All-Star team in 1979, 1980 and 1981, averaged 24.6 points in 1980-81 and earned All-NBA Second Team honors that season. In June 1981 Kansas City traded Birdsong and a second-round pick to New Jersey for Cliff Robinson, adding another traceable asset conversion after four strong seasons of production.

sections.heading: Phil Ford Made the Second First-Rounder Pay Off Immediately
sections.body: The 1978 first-round pick also landed at No. 2, where Kansas City selected Phil Ford. Ford played 79 games as a rookie, averaged 15.9 points and 8.6 assists, won Rookie of the Year and made All-NBA Second Team. He remained the Kings' starting-level point guard beyond that first season. Two consecutive No. 2 selections turning into Birdsong and Ford is the central reason Kansas City's hindsight grade reaches the top tier: the draft portion of the return produced two major backcourt pieces rather than merely retaining theoretical pick value.

sections.heading: Archibald Still Produced Star-Level Numbers for the Nets
sections.body: New York's direct return was shortened, not empty. Archibald played 34 games in 1976-77 and averaged 20.5 points and 7.5 assists in 37.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists his next season as missed because of an Achilles injury, but the Nets had already moved him before that 1977-78 season began. On September 1, 1977 New Jersey traded Archibald to Buffalo. The Nets' historical media guide identifies the return as George Johnson, Houston's 1978 first-round pick and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick. That distinction is important: Archibald did not simply leave New York for nothing.

sections.heading: New Jersey Recovered Substantial Downstream Value
sections.body: The two Buffalo-trade picks continued to produce value, although not in a straight line. The Houston-origin 1978 first was the No. 4 selection later used on Micheal Ray Richardson, but New Jersey did not make that pick. In June 1978 the Nets packaged it with another 1979 first in a settlement with the Knicks and received Phil Jackson plus the No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes, so only part of that later return belongs to the Archibald asset chain. Buffalo's 1979 first stayed with New Jersey and became No. 11 Cliff Robinson. Robinson averaged 13.6 points as a rookie and 19.5 in his second season. In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Birdsong and a second-round pick, bringing one of the original Kings assets back to New Jersey through the Archibald exit chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A+/A-. Kansas City receives an A+ because the return produced a full season from Taylor, 82 games from Eakins, four high-level Birdsong seasons and a Rookie of the Year/All-NBA start from Ford. New York receives an A- rather than the legacy F because Archibald was still a 20-point, seven-assist player in his 34 Nets games and, more importantly, retained enough market value to bring back Johnson and two first-round assets. One of those picks became part of a later settlement package and the other became Robinson, who eventually brought Birdsong back to the Nets. The Kings still generated the deeper direct return and the best combined draft outcome, but the source-backed asset chain shows that both franchises realized substantial value.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree This Was a Cash Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, New York and NBA transaction pages all record the same September 10, 1976 structure: the Braves sold the player rights to Jim McMillian to the Knicks. The New York page describes the acquisition of McMillian's rights, while the Buffalo and league ledgers explicitly use the word "sold." No player or draft pick is listed going back to Buffalo. The legacy cash asset is therefore directionally correct, but the reviewed records do not state an amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than inventing a figure.

sections.heading: McMillian Became an Immediate Knicks Starter
sections.body: McMillian was not merely an end-of-bench veteran. In 1976-77 he played 67 games, started 60 and averaged 32.2 minutes, 9.9 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists while shooting 46.4 percent from the field. New York finished 40-42, so the acquisition did not create a major team-level jump, but the Knicks received more than 2,100 regular-season minutes from him in the first year alone. That is substantial realized value for a transaction whose only documented outgoing consideration is cash.

sections.heading: The Second Season Added Durability and Playoff Minutes
sections.body: McMillian returned for 81 games and 63 starts in 1977-78. He averaged 8.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 24.4 minutes, giving New York another full season of wing depth. The Knicks reached the 1978 playoffs, and McMillian started all six postseason games, averaging 8.8 points and 3.5 rebounds in 22.3 minutes. Across the two regular seasons, New York received 148 games and 123 starts. The scoring role had declined from McMillian's Buffalo years, but the volume of usable NBA minutes is clear.

sections.heading: New York Also Recovered a Compensatory Pick
sections.body: McMillian became a restricted veteran free agent after the 1977-78 season. Portland signed him in December 1978, and Basketball-Reference records New York receiving a 1979 second-round pick as compensation. The Knicks used that selection at No. 34 on San Diego State forward Kim Goetz. Goetz never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the downstream draft outcome added no on-court value, but the Knicks still extracted a second asset after two seasons of McMillian production. That preserved value strengthens the acquisition even though the pick itself did not hit.

sections.heading: Buffalo's Return Cannot Be Valued Beyond the Cash Proceeds
sections.body: The Braves' side is straightforward but difficult to quantify. Buffalo converted McMillian's rights into cash and did not surrender a draft asset or player in addition to those rights. Cash has legitimate franchise value, yet the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed transaction ledgers and there is no basketball asset to trace forward. This review therefore does not assign Buffalo a failing grade simply because New York got useful production, but it also cannot credit an unknown financial return as if it matched 148 games and later pick compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ because McMillian supplied two full seasons of meaningful minutes, 123 starts and six playoff starts, then generated a 1979 second-round compensation pick when he left for Portland. The pick became Kim Goetz and produced no NBA games, which keeps the return below the highest grades. Buffalo receives a C because it obtained cash in a documented rights sale without taking back a basketball obligation, but the amount is unverified and cannot be compared directly with McMillian's realized production. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and player outcome, with only the cash valuation remaining unknown.

sections.heading: The Ledgers Resolve the Future Considerations as a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Washington and league transaction pages all record the September 13, 1976 exchange as Tom Kropp to the Bulls for a 1977 third-round draft pick. Chicago's official historical media guide uses the broader phrase "future considerations" for the same acquisition. Those descriptions are not mutually exclusive: the league and team transaction ledgers identify the specific draft asset that later satisfied the consideration. This review therefore keeps the pick as the verified outgoing Chicago asset rather than leaving the return unresolved.

sections.heading: Kropp Gave Chicago One Useful Bench Season
sections.body: Kropp was a fringe Washington player before the trade, appearing in 25 games but only 72 total minutes for the Bullets in 1975-76. Chicago gave him a much larger role. In 1976-77 he played 53 games and 480 minutes, scoring 174 points while shooting 48.0 percent from the field. His per-game line was modest at 3.3 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 9.1 minutes, but the Bulls received a full season of usable reserve minutes rather than an empty roster transaction.

sections.heading: His Chicago Tenure Ended After One Season
sections.body: The return did not develop into a long-term rotation piece. Basketball-Reference credits Kropp with only two minutes in one 1977 playoff appearance, and Chicago's official media guide records the Bulls waiving him on October 17, 1977. RealGM independently lists the waiver and his move to free agency two days later. Kropp never appeared in another NBA regular-season game. That ceiling keeps Chicago's grade below the stronger historical trades where a low draft pick produced multiple seasons or a starter-level role.

sections.heading: Washington Used the Pick on Steve Puidokas
sections.body: The Bullets kept and exercised the acquired third-rounder. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger shows Washington selecting Washington State center Steve Puidokas at No. 57 overall, and the Bullets transaction page lists the same selection. Puidokas never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Contemporary Washington Post draft coverage described him as a productive four-year college center, but his professional career continued outside the NBA. The pick therefore had legitimate option value on draft night without creating realized NBA production for Washington.

sections.heading: The Margin Should Stay Narrow
sections.body: Chicago did not acquire a major contributor, and Washington did receive a real draft asset rather than nothing. The distinction is realized outcome: Kropp supplied 53 games and nearly 500 regular-season minutes, while Puidokas supplied no NBA games. That supports a Bulls edge, but not the legacy B+ grade. A third-round pick in this era carried enough uncertainty that one season of reserve play is a modest win rather than a major value event.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, B-/C. Chicago receives a B- because Kropp delivered 53 regular-season games and useful bench minutes for the cost of a third-round pick, even though he was gone before the next season began. Washington receives a C because the acquired pick was fully exercised at No. 57 but Steve Puidokas never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction and draft outcome. The source wording differs only in specificity: Chicago's media guide says future considerations, while the Basketball-Reference ledgers identify the consideration as the 1977 third-round pick.

sections.heading: The Package Is Verified, With a One-Day Date Conflict
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, New York and league transaction ledgers record the Nuggets sending 1978 third- and fourth-round picks to the Nets for Ted McClain on September 15, 1976. Denver's official franchise history also uses September 15 and explicitly adds cash to the package. RealGM dates McClain's acquisition one day earlier, September 14, matching the canonical TradeVerdicts record. This review preserves September 14 as the canonical date but treats the package itself as high confidence: McClain for the two identified picks plus cash.

sections.heading: McClain Became a Major Rotation Guard for Denver
sections.body: McClain immediately took on a real role in Denver's first NBA season. He appeared in 72 regular-season games and logged 2,002 minutes, averaging 8.2 points, 4.5 assists, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 steals in 27.8 minutes per game. Denver won 50 games and finished first in the Midwest Division. McClain was not the team's star, but he was a genuine rotation guard on one of the league's better teams rather than a short-term roster flier.

sections.heading: He Also Played Meaningful Postseason Minutes
sections.body: Denver's season ended in a six-game conference semifinal loss to Portland, and McClain appeared in all six games. He averaged 28.3 minutes, 7.3 points, 4.5 assists and 1.7 steals in the series. Those postseason minutes strengthen the realized return because they show his regular-season role carried into the playoffs. The Nuggets received exactly the kind of immediate veteran depth a contending team could use during the ABA-to-NBA transition.

sections.heading: Denver Recovered a Pick When McClain Left
sections.body: McClain's Denver tenure lasted one season, but his departure still produced an additional asset. Buffalo signed him as a veteran free agent in October 1977 and sent Denver a 1978 third-round pick as compensation. The Nuggets used that selection at No. 46 on Hollis Copeland. Copeland did not play a regular-season game for Denver and was later an NBA player with New York, so this review does not credit his 93 career games as Nuggets production. Even so, the compensation shows Denver retained some asset value after already receiving a full season from McClain.

sections.heading: New Jersey's Two Picks Produced No Nets Games
sections.body: The Nets used Denver's original 1978 third-round pick at No. 62 on Dave Batton and the fourth-rounder at No. 84 on Walter Jordan. Both eventually reached the NBA, but neither played a regular-season game for New Jersey. Batton did not debut until 1982 and finished with 58 career games. Jordan spent two seasons outside the NBA before playing 30 games for Cleveland in 1980-81. Those later careers belong to other teams. For this trade, the Nets' draft return created option value but no direct on-court production.

sections.heading: The Cash Helps New Jersey but Is Not Priced
sections.body: Denver's official media guide explicitly says cash accompanied the two picks. Basketball-Reference's transaction ledgers omit the cash component, and the amount is not identified in the reviewed record. This review therefore recognizes cash as a documented part of the package without assigning it a speculative dollar value. It raises the Nets' return above a pure two-pick miss, but it cannot offset a full season and playoff role from McClain on realized basketball value alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+/C. Denver receives a B+ because McClain played 72 games, logged more than 2,000 regular-season minutes, contributed throughout the playoffs and later generated a third-round compensation pick when Buffalo signed him. New Jersey receives a C because it obtained two real draft assets plus documented cash, but Dave Batton and Walter Jordan produced no Nets regular-season games and the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes; the only structural uncertainty is whether the transaction should be dated September 14 or September 15, 1976.
