sections.heading: The Transaction Is a Straight Cash Sale in the Primary Ledgers
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New Orleans and NBA transaction pages all record the September 17, 1976 move as the Jazz selling Henry Bibby to the 76ers. The legacy TradeVerdicts structure is therefore correct: Philadelphia received Bibby and New Orleans received cash. The reviewed transaction ledgers do not identify the amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than creating a speculative value for the Jazz.

sections.heading: Bibby Immediately Became Philadelphia's Starting Point Guard
sections.body: The acquisition had an instant basketball effect. Bibby played 81 games in 1976-77, started 80 and averaged 32.6 minutes, 10.2 points, 4.4 assists and 3.4 rebounds. Philadelphia won 50 games and the Atlantic Division. In the playoffs Bibby appeared in all 19 games, averaging 36.4 minutes and 11.1 points as the 76ers won the Eastern Conference before losing the NBA Finals to Portland. That first season alone made the cash purchase a meaningful competitive return.

sections.heading: The Value Continued for Two More Full Seasons
sections.body: Bibby's Philadelphia tenure was not a one-year peak. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, started all 82 and averaged 30.7 minutes with 10.3 points and 5.6 assists per game. He appeared in all 10 playoff games. In 1978-79 he again played all 82 regular-season games, starting 38 as rookie Maurice Cheeks took over more of the point-guard role. Bibby still averaged 12.2 points, 4.5 assists and 31.0 minutes, then appeared in all nine postseason games. Across the three seasons, Philadelphia received 245 regular-season games and 38 playoff appearances.

sections.heading: The Acquisition Bridged Two Different 76ers Backcourts
sections.body: Bibby's role also had timing value. In 1976-77 and 1977-78 he handled the primary starting point-guard assignment for teams built around Julius Erving, George McGinnis and Doug Collins. By 1978-79, Cheeks had arrived and immediately started all 82 games, but Bibby remained a high-minute guard rather than becoming disposable depth. That transition allowed Philadelphia to keep veteran ballhandling and scoring while bringing a younger long-term point guard into the lineup.

sections.heading: New Orleans' Return Cannot Be Traced Beyond Cash
sections.body: The Jazz moved a player who had appeared in only 12 games for them after arriving from New York during the prior season. Receiving cash for a veteran outside the club's long-term core has legitimate financial value, but the amount is not reported in the reviewed source set and there is no incoming player or draft asset to follow. The Jazz therefore receive credit for a documented sale without being treated as if an unknown cash payment matched three seasons of playoff-caliber guard production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, A-/C. Philadelphia receives an A- because Bibby gave the club 245 regular-season games, 200 starts and 38 playoff appearances over three seasons, including a starting role on the 1977 Finals team. New Orleans receives a C because the Jazz obtained cash without taking back another basketball obligation, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable on-court or draft return. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Bibby's production. The only unquantified element is the cash consideration.

sections.heading: The Official Franchise Histories Say Terry Went to Buffalo for Future Considerations
sections.body: Denver's official franchise history lists the September 21, 1976 transaction as Claude Terry to Buffalo for future considerations. The historical Clippers media guide, which preserves the Buffalo Braves' transaction history, independently records the same date and structure. RealGM likewise lists Buffalo acquiring Terry from Denver in a trade on September 21. Those records resolve the core package more clearly than the legacy archive entry. This review therefore removes the unsupported 1977 draft-pick language and records Denver's return only as future considerations whose eventual form remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Basketball-Reference Preserves a Conflicting Transaction Path
sections.body: Basketball-Reference does not list the September 21 trade on the Denver, Buffalo or league transaction ledgers. Its Buffalo page instead says the Braves signed Terry as a free agent on October 21, 1976. That conflict cannot simply be ignored. Two official franchise histories and RealGM agree on the September 21 trade, so TradeVerdicts keeps that date and structure as the canonical interpretation, but confidence is medium rather than high. The disagreement also reinforces why this review should not invent a draft pick or pretend the future consideration has been fully traced.

sections.heading: Terry Gave Buffalo 33 Games of Bench Minutes
sections.body: Terry's Buffalo stint was modest but real. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 games, 304 minutes and 116 points for the 1976-77 Braves. He averaged 9.2 minutes and 3.5 points per game while adding 28 rebounds, 33 assists and 11 steals. That is not starter-level or long-term value, but it is enough to distinguish Buffalo's return from an empty roster transaction. Terry provided several months of usable reserve minutes before the club moved his rights again.

sections.heading: Buffalo Recovered Another Financial Return When Terry Left
sections.body: The historical Buffalo/Clippers record says the Braves sold Terry to Atlanta on February 1, 1977. Basketball-Reference also records Buffalo selling Terry's player rights to the Hawks on that date. The amount is not identified in the reviewed sources, so this review does not assign a speculative dollar value. Still, Buffalo received 33 games from Terry and then converted his rights into another financial return. That downstream sale adds a little value to the acquisition even though the cash cannot be compared precisely with a player or draft asset.

sections.heading: Denver's Future Consideration Cannot Be Traced
sections.body: The reviewed records do not identify a player, draft pick or other basketball asset that Denver ultimately received from the future-considerations clause. The legacy archive entry's 1977 draft-pick language is therefore removed rather than carried forward as an unresolved guess. Denver still receives credit for a documented consideration in the official franchise histories, but without a traceable realization there is no basis to grade the Nuggets as though they received a usable draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Braves Edge, C+/C. Buffalo receives a C+ because Terry delivered 33 regular-season games and 304 minutes, then generated another unpriced financial return when his rights were sold to Atlanta. Denver receives a C because the official franchise histories document future considerations, but the reviewed record does not reveal what those considerations became. The edge stays narrow because Terry's role was small and the downstream cash amount is unknown. Confidence is medium because Basketball-Reference conflicts with the September 21 trade structure preserved by the two franchise histories and RealGM.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Murphy for a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Los Angeles and NBA transaction pages all record the October 4, 1976 exchange the same way: the Bulls sent Allen Murphy to the Lakers for a future draft pick. Bill Sharman's Lakers executive record and Jon Kovler's Chicago record repeat that package, while the Lakers' official all-time transaction history independently confirms the future-pick wording. The legacy archive entry is therefore directionally correct, but its question-mark placeholders can be replaced with a cleaner description of what the record actually establishes.

sections.heading: The Pick's Year and Outcome Remain Unresolved
sections.body: The authoritative transaction sources do not identify a year, round, protection condition or eventual draftee for the future pick. Unlike many surrounding deals, Basketball-Reference does not attach a later selection to this transaction. The reviewed draft-trade sources also do not provide a supported player chain for the Murphy pick. That absence does not prove the pick was cancelled or never exercised. This review therefore records a future draft pick with an unresolved outcome and does not invent a year or player for Chicago.

sections.heading: Murphy Played Only Two Games for the Lakers
sections.body: Los Angeles received almost no on-court return. Basketball-Reference credits Murphy with two games and 18 total minutes for the 1976-77 Lakers. He scored five points, collected four rebounds and did not record an assist. Those appearances were his only NBA games that season and his only games for Los Angeles. The Lakers had acquired a young guard with ABA experience, but he never established a role in Jerry West's rotation.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Waived Him Less Than a Month Later
sections.body: The Lakers' transaction ledger and official franchise history both record Murphy being waived on November 2, 1976. That ended his Los Angeles tenure just 29 days after the trade. Murphy did not create a later Lakers trade return or compensation asset. His two games and 18 minutes therefore represent the complete realized basketball value Los Angeles received from the original transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago's Asset Has Option Value but No Traceable Realization
sections.body: A future draft pick carried real value even when its exact slot was not known on trade day, so Chicago cannot be graded as though it received nothing. The problem is retrospective attribution: without a verified year, round or selected player, TradeVerdicts cannot credit the Bulls with production that may belong to an unrelated pick. The responsible grade recognizes the existence of the asset while stopping short of assigning an invented downstream outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. Chicago receives a C because the Bulls converted Murphy into a legitimate future draft asset, but the reviewed record does not establish what that pick became. Los Angeles also receives a C because Murphy produced only two games and 18 minutes before being waived less than a month after the trade. Neither side generated enough verified realized value to justify a directional edge. Confidence is high on the October 4 package and Murphy's brief Lakers stint but medium on the complete pick chain, so the record's overall confidence is medium.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on an October 12 Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland, Boston and NBA transaction pages all record the same October 12, 1976 move: Portland sold the player rights to Sidney Wicks to the Celtics. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Red Auerbach's Boston record independently preserve that structure. This review therefore treats the transaction as Wicks's rights for cash and does not repeat the false October 5 Portland-New Orleans record that has now been superseded. The cash amount is not identified in the reviewed ledgers.

sections.heading: Wicks Immediately Became a Major Boston Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Wicks played all 82 regular-season games for Boston in 1976-77 and logged 2,642 minutes. He averaged 15.1 points, 10.0 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 32.2 minutes per game while shooting 45.8 percent from the field. That was not fringe production from an aging name. Wicks was one of Boston's highest-minute frontcourt players and delivered a full season of double-figure scoring and double-figure rebounding after the cash acquisition.

sections.heading: The First Season Also Carried Into the Playoffs
sections.body: Boston reached the 1977 postseason and Wicks appeared in all nine playoff games. He averaged 29.0 minutes, 13.1 points and 9.2 rebounds while shooting 51.9 percent from the field. The Celtics beat San Antonio in the opening round before losing a seven-game conference semifinal to Philadelphia. Wicks's role therefore survived into the postseason rather than disappearing when the rotation tightened.

sections.heading: The Value Continued for a Second Full Season
sections.body: Wicks remained a substantial part of Boston's 1977-78 team even as the Celtics fell out of the playoffs. He played 81 games and another 2,413 minutes, averaging 13.4 points, 8.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 29.8 minutes. Across the two Boston seasons, the rights purchase produced 163 regular-season games, 5,055 minutes, 2,321 points and 1,497 rebounds. That volume is enough to make the acquisition materially better than a short-term cash flier.

sections.heading: Wicks Still Had Trade Utility in the 1978 Blockbuster
sections.body: On August 4, 1978, Boston sent Wicks, Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington and Freeman Williams to the San Diego Clippers for Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two future second-round picks. Wicks was only one component of that multi-player package, so this review does not assign the entire later return to him. His inclusion still shows that Boston retained transaction value after already receiving two full seasons of production from the original cash purchase.

sections.heading: Portland's Cash Return Is Real but Cannot Be Priced
sections.body: Portland moved on from a player who had spent five seasons with the franchise and received cash in return. That financial consideration has legitimate value, particularly as the Trail Blazers reshaped the roster that would win the 1977 championship. The problem is that the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed source set and there is no separate incoming player or draft asset to trace. This review therefore gives Portland credit for the sale without pretending an unknown cash figure can be measured against Wicks's documented Boston production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, B+/C. Boston receives a B+ because Wicks produced 163 regular-season games, more than 5,000 minutes, two productive frontcourt seasons and nine playoff appearances before remaining part of a major 1978 trade package. Portland receives a C because the Trail Blazers obtained cash and cleared Wicks from the roster before their championship season, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable basketball asset to measure against Boston's return. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Wicks's production, with only the cash valuation unquantified.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Hackett for a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, New York Nets and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: Denver sent Rudy Hackett to New York for a future draft pick. Carl Scheer's executive transaction record and Roy Boe's Nets record independently preserve that structure. RealGM also lists Hackett as a New York trade acquisition on the same date. No reviewed source adds cash or a second player to the package.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Cannot Be Traced Responsibly
sections.body: The transaction ledgers stop at the phrase "future draft pick." They do not identify a year, round, protection, overall selection or player outcome. Pro Sports Transactions likewise lists the pick as unknown. This review therefore preserves the draft asset without assigning it to a later Denver selection. That matters because a hindsight archive should not turn an unidentified future consideration into a named player simply because Denver later owned other picks.

sections.heading: Hackett Played One Game for the Nets
sections.body: Hackett's New York tenure was extremely short. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Nets regular-season appearance in 1976-77: eight minutes, two points and three rebounds. The Nets waived him on October 29, only eleven days after the trade. That gives New York a measurable basketball return, but it is about as small as an acquired player's realized value can be.

sections.heading: New York Did Not Preserve a Downstream Asset
sections.body: After the waiver, Hackett became a free agent and signed with Indiana in November. The Pacers used him in five games before waiving him in December. Because New York received no player, pick or compensation when Hackett left, none of his later Indiana activity belongs to the Nets side of this trade. New York's attributable return ends with the single game he played for the franchise.

sections.heading: Denver Turned a Short-Term Signing Into Draft Consideration
sections.body: RealGM records Denver signing Hackett in September 1976 before moving him roughly six weeks later. The Nuggets therefore converted a recent free-agent addition into a future draft asset without giving up another documented basketball piece in this transaction. The unidentified pick keeps the return from earning a strong grade, because its eventual use cannot be verified, but the exchange still left Denver with more traceable asset value than New York received on the court.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, C+/D+. Denver receives a C+ because it converted Hackett into a future draft pick, but the pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed sources. New York receives a D+ because Hackett appeared in only one game before being waived and generated no downstream return. The deal is minor rather than disastrous for the Nets, yet one eight-minute appearance is too little to justify an average grade. Confidence is high on the transaction and Hackett's one-game tenure, but medium on the complete asset chain because the future pick cannot be identified.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Lock the Three-Team Routing
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Boston, Denver, Detroit and NBA transaction ledgers all preserve the same October 20, 1976 structure. Boston sent Paul Silas to Denver. Denver sent Ralph Simpson to Detroit. Detroit sent Curtis Rowe to Boston. Red Auerbach's, Carl Scheer's and Oscar Feldman's executive records repeat that routing. This review therefore repairs the canonical asset ledger by adding Simpson as Denver's outgoing asset and Detroit's incoming asset instead of leaving Detroit with an empty return.

sections.heading: Curtis Rowe Gave Boston Three Seasons of Real Value
sections.body: Rowe became an immediate Celtics rotation piece. He played 79 games in 1976-77, totaling 2,190 minutes, 800 points and 563 rebounds. Boston reached the playoffs, and Rowe started all nine postseason games, including the seven-game conference semifinal against Philadelphia. He then played 51 games in 1977-78 and 53 more in 1978-79. Across the three Boston seasons, Rowe appeared in 183 regular-season games and supplied more than 1,400 points and 1,000 rebounds. The return was not star-level, but it was far stronger than the old C-minus grade implied.

sections.heading: Paul Silas Helped Denver Immediately
sections.body: Silas played 81 games for the Nuggets in 1976-77 and averaged 7.5 rebounds in 24.2 minutes. He also appeared in all six Denver playoff games. That gave the Nuggets a veteran frontcourt contributor during a 50-win season. Denver did not simply lose Silas after one year: on May 24, 1977, the Nuggets included him with Marvin Webster and Willie Wise in the trade that brought Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a second-round pick from Seattle.

sections.heading: Denver's Downstream Return Must Be Shared Across a Larger Package
sections.body: The Seattle trade created additional value, but this review does not assign the entire return to Silas because Webster and Wise were also outgoing assets. Denver then moved Burleson and the acquired second-rounder to Kansas City for Brian Taylor and a 1977 first-round pick that became Tom LaGarde. That downstream chain shows Silas retained trade utility after his Denver season, but the multi-player package prevents treating LaGarde or Taylor as a one-for-one Silas return.

sections.heading: Ralph Simpson Produced for Detroit and Then Became Another Package
sections.body: Simpson played 77 games for Detroit in 1976-77, averaging 11.0 points, then appeared in 32 more Pistons games the following season at 10.6 points per game. Detroit therefore received 109 regular-season games from the player it acquired in the three-team deal. On February 1, 1978, the Pistons traded Simpson back to Denver for Jim Price and a 1979 first-round pick. That second transaction is where Detroit's side of this review separates from the others.

sections.heading: The Simpson Exit Produced Jim Price and Phil Hubbard
sections.body: Price played 34 games for Detroit after the February 1978 trade, averaging 11.5 points and 3.0 assists. More important for the long-term asset chain, the 1979 first-round pick became No. 15 Phil Hubbard. Hubbard played 64 games for Detroit as a rookie, 80 in 1980-81 and 52 more before his 1981-82 move, giving the Pistons 196 regular-season games from the draft asset created by Simpson's exit. Detroit received useful production from Simpson first and then converted him into another player plus a first-round pick that produced several additional seasons of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A/B+/B. Detroit receives an A because Simpson supplied 109 games and then became Jim Price plus the first-round pick used on Phil Hubbard, extending the transaction's value well beyond the original player. Denver receives a B+ because Silas contributed to a 50-win team for 81 games and retained value in the later Seattle package, although that downstream return cannot be credited to Silas alone. Boston receives a B because Rowe delivered 183 regular-season games and nine playoff starts across three seasons. All three teams received meaningful basketball value; Detroit simply created the strongest verified downstream chain. Confidence is high on the three-team routing and the traced player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Sources Disagree on Which Franchise Sent Lamar to Los Angeles
sections.body: this review has an important source conflict. Basketball-Reference's 1976-77 NBA and Lakers transaction ledgers say the Indiana Pacers traded Bo Lamar to Los Angeles for future considerations on October 20, 1976. Bill Sharman's executive record repeats Indiana. Official Lakers media guides, however, state that Los Angeles acquired Dwight "Bo" Lamar from Detroit for future consideration, and the 1978 draft-pick transaction chain ties Detroit to the Lakers' future second-round selection. Because the canonical record represents the Detroit rights transaction, this review keeps that record but explicitly preserves the disagreement rather than pretending every source says the same thing.

sections.heading: The Future Consideration Became the No. 38 Pick
sections.body: The historical 1978 draft-pick chain identifies the consideration as the Lakers' second-round pick, eventually No. 38. Pro Sports Transactions cites contemporary draft reporting that the choice originally belonged to Los Angeles and had been traded for Bo Lamar. Detroit later sent that pick, along with Marvin Barnes and another draft asset, to Buffalo in November 1977. Buffalo then traded the No. 38 pick back to Los Angeles for Tom Abernethy on June 7, 1978.

sections.heading: Lamar Gave the Lakers a Full Rotation Season
sections.body: Whatever the rights-routing ambiguity, Lamar's Los Angeles outcome is clear. Basketball-Reference credits him with 71 regular-season games in 1976-77. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 7.1 points and 2.5 assists while shooting 40.6 percent. The Lakers won 53 games and finished first in the Pacific Division. Lamar was not a star, but 71 appearances and more than 1,100 minutes represent legitimate rotation value from an acquisition made immediately before the season.

sections.heading: He Also Appeared Throughout the 1977 Playoffs
sections.body: Lamar played in all 10 Lakers playoff games in 1977. His role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game and 3.3 points, but Los Angeles used him in both postseason rounds as the club beat Golden State before losing to Portland in the Western Conference Finals. That playoff participation reinforces that the Lakers received more than an expendable camp body from the transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit Used the Pick in a Larger Marvin Barnes Package
sections.body: Detroit did not simply hold the future second-rounder until draft night. On November 23, 1977, the Pistons sent Marvin Barnes, the No. 38 pick and a 1978 fourth-round pick to Buffalo for Gus Gerard, John Shumate and a 1979 first-round pick that later became Roy Hamilton. That gives the Lamar consideration real transactional utility. This review does not assign the full Gerard-Shumate-Hamilton return to the second-rounder, however, because Barnes and another pick were also necessary outgoing assets.

sections.heading: The Pick Eventually Returned to Los Angeles and Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: Buffalo subsequently sent the No. 38 selection back to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Los Angeles used the pick on UNC Charlotte guard Lew Massey. Basketball-Reference lists Massey as the No. 38 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. That terminal outcome prevents Detroit's original consideration from receiving a strong standalone grade even though the pick had value as part of the Barnes package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B/C+. Los Angeles receives a B because Lamar played 71 regular-season games, contributed useful reserve scoring and appeared in all 10 playoff games during a 53-win season. Detroit receives a C+ because the future consideration became a real second-round asset and was used in the larger Marvin Barnes package, but the pick eventually returned to Los Angeles and became Lew Massey, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is medium rather than high because Basketball-Reference attributes Lamar's October 20 transfer to Indiana while Lakers media guides and the traced draft-pick chain identify Detroit's rights involvement.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Price for Buffalo's 1977 First
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Milwaukee and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same November 2, 1976 exchange. Buffalo sent its 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. The selection ultimately landed at No. 13. No additional player or cash component is needed to explain the canonical trade.

sections.heading: Price Stayed in Buffalo for Only 20 Games
sections.body: Price's Braves stint was brief. He appeared in 20 games, averaging 5.3 points and 1.9 assists in 16.7 minutes per game. On December 15, only six weeks after the Milwaukee deal, Buffalo moved him again. The short stay limits the direct value of the acquisition, but it does not end the asset chain.

sections.heading: Buffalo Flipped Price for Two Rotation Players
sections.body: The Braves sent Price to Denver for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard played 41 games for Buffalo in 1976-77, while Williams appeared in 44 games that season and 73 more in 1977-78. Williams became a regular backcourt contributor, averaging 5.7 assists per 36 minutes in 1977-78. That secondary return keeps Buffalo's side from being judged as 20 games of Price and nothing else.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Pick as Trade-Up Currency
sections.body: Milwaukee did not simply make the No. 13 selection. On June 7, 1977, the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the acquired No. 13 pick back to Buffalo for the Braves' own higher first-rounder. That incoming pick became No. 3 overall. The original Buffalo selection therefore became part of a direct draft-night value upgrade.

sections.heading: The No. 3 Pick Became Marques Johnson
sections.body: Milwaukee used the third pick on Marques Johnson. Johnson went on to make five All-Star teams and three All-NBA teams, and Basketball-Reference credits him with a 20.1-point career scoring average. His Milwaukee tenure became one of the strongest outcomes tied to the 1977 draft. This review does not assign all of that value to the No. 13 pick because Nater was a major outgoing asset in the trade-up.

sections.heading: Nater's Value Prevents Over-Crediting the Pick
sections.body: Nater had averaged 13.0 points and 12.0 rebounds for Milwaukee in 1976-77 before the Bucks included him in the June trade. He then averaged 15.5 points and 13.2 rebounds for Buffalo in 1977-78. That production matters when grading the downstream branch. The No. 13 pick helped Milwaukee reach Johnson, but the trade-up required a productive starting center as well.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Edge, A-/B-. Milwaukee receives an A- because turning Price into a first-round asset and then using that asset in the package that produced No. 3 Marques Johnson created excellent long-term value. Buffalo receives a B- because Price himself lasted only 20 games, but his resale brought back Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, with Williams contributing across two seasons. The gap favors Milwaukee, though the later Johnson outcome cannot be credited to the original pick alone. Confidence is high on the package and downstream transaction chain.

sections.heading: The Core Transaction Is Bob Love for a 1977 Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, New York Nets, league and executive transaction ledgers all agree on the November 30, 1976 core exchange. Chicago sent Bob Love to the Nets for New York's 1977 second-round pick, which became No. 23 overall. The Bulls' official all-time transaction history and Pro Sports Transactions add cash to the Nets' outgoing package. This review keeps that cash component while distinguishing the sources that actually record it.

sections.heading: Love's Nets Tenure Lasted 13 Games
sections.body: Love had been one of the defining Bulls scorers of the previous decade, but by the time of this trade he was 34. With New York he appeared in 13 games, averaging 10.1 points, 2.9 rebounds and only 17.5 minutes. The Nets did receive immediate veteran offense, but the relationship ended quickly. Love was waived in January 1977 and finished the season with Seattle.

sections.heading: Chicago's Pick Became Mike Glenn
sections.body: The incoming second-rounder landed at No. 23 in the 1977 draft. Chicago used it on Mike Glenn out of Southern Illinois. Glenn eventually played 593 NBA games across ten seasons and finished with a 54.2 percent career field-goal rate, so the selection itself identified a legitimate long-term NBA player.

sections.heading: The Bulls Did Not Receive Glenn's NBA Career
sections.body: That career cannot be credited to Chicago. The Bulls waived Glenn on December 8, 1977, six days before his NBA debut with Buffalo. He never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago. The pick therefore had real draft value at the moment of the trade, but its realized on-court return to the Bulls was zero. This review credits Chicago for obtaining and exercising the No. 23 asset, not for the production Glenn later supplied to Buffalo, New York or Atlanta.

sections.heading: The Cash Keeps Chicago's Side From Being Empty
sections.body: The official Bulls media guide and Pro Sports Transactions both record cash in addition to the pick, although the amount is not specified in the sources used here. That financial consideration matters because the pick did not become Chicago production. At the same time, an unspecified cash payment cannot be treated as though it created a known player or draft branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C+/C+. The Nets receive a C+ because Love supplied only 13 games before being waived, but those games at least produced immediate NBA rotation value. Chicago also receives a C+ because the Bulls obtained a top second-round pick plus cash, yet the selected player was waived before his NBA debut and produced no Chicago games. The transaction created optionality for the Bulls and short-term production for the Nets without a durable franchise return on either side. Confidence is high on the package and the realized player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on a Straight Player Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Washington and league transaction pages all record the same December 13, 1976 deal. The SuperSonics sent Leonard Gray to the Bullets for Nick Weatherspoon. There were no draft picks or cash components in the recorded package, making this review a direct comparison of the two forwards' realized value after the exchange.

sections.heading: Weatherspoon Became a Productive Seattle Regular
sections.body: Weatherspoon had appeared in only 11 games for Washington before the trade. In Seattle he played 51 games, totaling 652 points and 404 rebounds. That works out to 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per game, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 2.8 win shares during the Seattle portion of the season. He was not a star, but he immediately became a meaningful rotation scorer and rebounder.

sections.heading: Gray Gave Washington More Games but a Smaller Role
sections.body: Gray played 58 regular-season games for the Bullets after arriving from Seattle. He totaled 347 points, 186 rebounds and 69 assists, averaging 6.0 points and 3.2 rebounds in 17.2 minutes per game. Washington went 48-34 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Gray also appeared in eight playoff games, though his postseason role was limited to 6.5 minutes and 1.5 points per game.

sections.heading: The Longer-Term Return Vanished on Both Sides
sections.body: Neither team turned the trade into a durable multi-season asset. Gray did not play in 1977-78 because of injury and never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Seattle kept Weatherspoon through the end of the 1976-77 season but waived him on September 28, 1977. He continued his career with Chicago and later San Diego, so those later seasons are not credited to the SuperSonics.

sections.heading: The Timing Makes Seattle's Edge Clear but Modest
sections.body: Seattle received fewer games than Washington, but Weatherspoon's 51-game stretch was much more productive. He more than doubled Gray's points per game and delivered over twice as many rebounds per game. Washington can still point to 58 regular-season appearances and a small playoff contribution, which keeps the trade from becoming a one-sided failure. The difference is mainly the quality of the one-season rotation value each club received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle Edge, B/C+. Seattle receives a B because Weatherspoon produced 51 solid games with 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per night before the relationship ended. Washington receives a C+ because Gray supplied 58 games and appeared in the playoffs, but his role was smaller and injury ended his NBA career after that season. With no picks or downstream assets attached, the comparison stays focused on those direct 1976-77 results. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Correct the Date to January 8
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, New York Nets, NBA league and executive ledgers all record the Dave Wohl trade on January 8, 1977. The existing canonical record used January 7. This review corrects the stored date while preserving the stable canonical trade ID. The package itself is straightforward: Houston sent Wohl to the Nets for New York's 1978 fourth-round pick.

sections.heading: Wohl Immediately Became a Nets Rotation Guard
sections.body: Wohl had appeared in only 14 Houston games before the trade in 1976-77. With the Nets he played 37 games, averaging 25.0 minutes, 7.4 points and 3.4 assists. He totaled 275 points and 127 assists in that post-trade stretch. The Nets were a struggling team, but the transaction still produced a regular rotation player rather than a brief end-of-bench appearance.

sections.heading: He Added a Small Second Season
sections.body: Wohl returned after the franchise moved to New Jersey in 1977-78. He appeared in 10 more games, adding 35 points and 13 assists before the Nets waived him on November 19, 1977. That gives the franchise 47 regular-season games from the acquisition. The second season was minor, but it confirms the return lasted beyond the closing months of 1976-77.

sections.heading: Houston's Pick Became Jackie Robinson
sections.body: The fourth-round selection conveyed at No. 67 in the 1978 draft. Houston selected Jackie Robinson from UNLV. Basketball-Reference's draft record shows Robinson eventually played 22 NBA games over three seasons, so the pick did identify a player capable of reaching the league.

sections.heading: Robinson Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Houston
sections.body: The important realized-value distinction is that Robinson's NBA career did not occur with the Rockets. Houston waived him on October 11, 1978, months before his March 1979 NBA debut. His later 22-game career therefore belongs to other teams for franchise-value purposes. This review credits Houston for the draft selection but not for production the Rockets never received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Edge, C+/C. The Nets receive a C+ because Wohl supplied 47 regular-season games and became a usable rotation guard immediately after the trade. Houston receives a C because the fourth-rounder became an NBA player, but Robinson was waived before debuting and produced zero Rockets games. The difference is modest because Wohl's tenure was not long or high-impact, yet the Nets clearly received more realized basketball value from the direct exchange. Confidence is high on the corrected date, package, draft identity and player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Transaction Is a Straight Johnson-for-First Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Golden State and league transaction ledgers all record the January 18, 1977 deal the same way. The Braves sent their 1977 first-round pick to the Warriors for George Johnson. The pick became No. 18 overall and Golden State used it on Wesley Cox in the 1977 draft.

sections.heading: Johnson Immediately Became Buffalo's Starting Center
sections.body: Johnson had played 39 games for Golden State before the trade, mostly in a reserve role. Buffalo changed his usage immediately. He started all 39 of his Braves games after the deal and averaged 27.1 minutes, 7.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 2.7 blocks. That is meaningful direct value from a midseason acquisition, especially because his rebounding and rim protection were substantially larger contributions than his scoring average suggests.

sections.heading: Johnson Also Retained Trade Utility
sections.body: Buffalo did not keep Johnson into the next season. On September 1, 1977, the Braves traded him with their 1978 and 1979 first-round picks to the New Jersey Nets for Tiny Archibald. Johnson therefore remained a useful transaction asset after his 39-game Buffalo stint. This review does not credit Buffalo with Archibald's entire value because Johnson was only one of three outgoing assets, but his inclusion in that package is legitimate downstream evidence that the Braves had not exhausted his value.

sections.heading: Cox Became a Two-Year Warriors Reserve
sections.body: Golden State selected Cox at No. 18 in 1977. He played 43 games as a rookie and 31 more in 1978-79, giving the Warriors 74 regular-season games in total. Cox averaged 4.6 points and 2.8 rebounds for his career while playing roughly 11 minutes per game. He was a real NBA return from the pick, but he never became a major rotation piece and his NBA career ended after those two Warriors seasons.

sections.heading: The Direct Comparison Favors Buffalo
sections.body: The Braves received only half a season of Johnson before moving him again, but those 39 games included starting-center production at 10.3 rebounds and 2.7 blocks per night. Golden State received more total games from Cox, yet in a much smaller role. The later Archibald package adds modest extra value to Buffalo's side because Johnson was still useful enough to be included in a major trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves Edge, B/C+. Buffalo receives a B because Johnson provided strong starting-center production immediately and retained downstream trade utility. Golden State receives a C+ because the first-round pick became Cox, who supplied 74 games but only limited reserve production over two seasons. The outcome is a clear Buffalo edge rather than a franchise-altering result, and the grading avoids assigning Archibald's full later value to Johnson alone. Confidence is high on the package, pick identity and direct player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Confirm a Player-and-First-Round-Pick Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Washington and league transaction ledgers agree on the January 20, 1977 structure. Atlanta sent Tom Henderson and its 1977 first-round pick to Washington for Truck Robinson and Washington's 1977 first-round pick. The Bullets' incoming pick became No. 4 Greg Ballard. Atlanta's incoming pick became No. 14 Tree Rollins.

sections.heading: Robinson Was Excellent Immediately for Atlanta
sections.body: Robinson played 36 games for the Hawks after the trade and produced star-level numbers: 806 points and 462 rebounds, or 22.4 points and 12.8 rebounds per game. He did not remain in Atlanta after the season. New Orleans signed Robinson as a veteran free agent in August 1977, and the Hawks received Ron Behagen and cash as compensation. That gives Atlanta both a high-end half-season and a legitimate downstream return.

sections.heading: Rollins Became the Long-Term Atlanta Anchor
sections.body: The No. 14 pick became Tree Rollins, whose value dwarfed a typical mid-first-round outcome. Rollins spent eleven seasons with Atlanta, developed into one of the league's premier shot blockers, led the NBA in blocks in 1982-83 and earned two All-Defensive selections. The trade therefore gave the Hawks both immediate star production from Robinson and a durable defensive center from the pick.

sections.heading: Henderson Became Part of Washington's Championship Backcourt
sections.body: Henderson played 41 games for Washington after the trade in 1976-77, then 75 games in 1977-78 and 70 in 1978-79. That is 186 regular-season games for the Bullets. More important than the raw total, he played 21 postseason games during Washington's 1978 championship run and averaged 9.6 points and 5.0 assists in those playoffs. His contribution was not merely regular-season depth.

sections.heading: Ballard Became an Eight-Year Washington Fixture
sections.body: Washington used the No. 4 pick on Greg Ballard. He played 76 games as a rookie on the 1978 championship team and remained with the franchise through 1984-85. Across eight Washington seasons he appeared in 643 regular-season games, growing from a reserve into a full-time starting forward and double-figure scorer. The pick produced far more than a short rookie-contract contribution.

sections.heading: Henderson Created One More First-Round Asset
sections.body: Houston signed Henderson as a veteran free agent in July 1979. Under the compensation rules of the era, Washington received a 1980 first-round pick that became No. 14 Wes Matthews. This review credits that specific compensation because it was directly tied to Henderson's departure, while avoiding any unrelated later asset chains.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Edge, A+/A. Atlanta receives an A because Robinson delivered an elite half-season, Rollins became a long-term defensive anchor, and Robinson's departure produced compensation. Washington receives an A+ because Henderson and Ballard both contributed to the 1978 championship, Ballard supplied eight seasons and 643 games, and Henderson later generated another first-round pick. This is a high-value trade for both teams; Washington's championship impact and extra draft return create only a narrow hindsight advantage. Confidence is high on the package, draft identities and realized outcomes.

sections.heading: The Nets Media Guide Preserves the Full Package
sections.body: The clearest package source is the New Jersey Nets' historical media guide. It records that New York obtained Mike Bantom from Seattle on January 27, 1977 in exchange for the Nets' 1979 fourth-round pick, which became James Donaldson, plus cash. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same media-guide account while flagging conflicting historical descriptions. Basketball-Reference's team and league ledgers record New York selling the rights attached to Donaldson to Seattle on that date, and Bantom's player ledger records Seattle selling his rights to New York. Taken together, the sources support the canonical Bantom-for-pick-and-cash package while explaining why individual ledgers describe the two sides as sales.

sections.heading: Bantom Was Excellent for 33 Nets Games
sections.body: Bantom played 33 games for New York after the transaction. He totaled 614 points and 285 rebounds, which works out to 18.6 points and 8.6 rebounds per game, while logging 33.8 minutes. That was strong immediate production for a Nets team going through a difficult first NBA season.

sections.heading: The Nets Did Not Keep Him Beyond the Season
sections.body: Bantom became a veteran free agent after the season and signed with Buffalo on September 1, 1977. New Jersey received a future fourth-round pick as compensation. Because the primary compensation ledger used here does not identify the eventual selection, this review credits the Nets with the existence of that downstream draft asset without inventing a player outcome.

sections.heading: The Fourth-Round Pick Became James Donaldson
sections.body: Seattle's incoming 1979 fourth-round pick landed at No. 73 and became James Donaldson. Donaldson spent 1979-80 playing professionally in Italy before joining the SuperSonics in 1980-81. He appeared in 68 games as a rookie, then played all 82 games in both 1981-82 and 1982-83. Across those three Seattle seasons he logged 232 regular-season games.

sections.heading: Donaldson Became a Useful Seattle Center
sections.body: His role grew each year. Donaldson averaged 5.3 points and 4.5 rebounds in 1980-81, 8.1 points and 6.0 rebounds in 1981-82, then 8.9 points and 6.1 rebounds in 1982-83. The late fourth-round pick therefore became a durable rotation center rather than a player who never reached the roster.

sections.heading: He Also Retained Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: In August 1983 Seattle included Donaldson, Greg Kelser, Mark Radford and two draft picks in the trade that brought back Tom Chambers, Al Wood and additional picks from San Diego. Donaldson's inclusion demonstrates continued transaction value, but this review does not assign the full Chambers return to him because the package contained several other substantial assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sonics Win, A-/B. Seattle receives an A- because a fourth-round pick plus cash cost produced 232 games from Donaldson and preserved later trade utility. New York receives a B because Bantom was highly productive in 33 games and his free-agent departure generated another draft asset, but the Nets did not retain his services beyond that season. The source record is unusually messy, so the package explanation explicitly distinguishes the Nets media-guide account from the Basketball-Reference rights-sale presentation. Confidence is high on the player movement and pick identity and medium-high on the exact package mechanics.

sections.heading: The February Date Comes From the Team Media Guides
sections.body: The historical ledgers require care. Indiana's official media guide records February 1, 1977 as the date the Pacers acquired John Williamson from the Nets for Darnell Hillman and a first-round pick. The Nets' own historical media guide separates the mechanics: New York traded Williamson on February 1 for Indiana's 1977 first-round pick and a player to be named, then received Hillman in April to complete the deal. Basketball-Reference lists the completed transaction under April. This review preserves February 1 as the parent-trade date while treating Hillman's April delivery as part of the same exchange.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Became Bernard King
sections.body: New Jersey used the No. 7 pick on Bernard King. His impact was immediate. King played 79 games as a rookie and averaged 24.2 points and 9.5 rebounds, finishing third in Rookie of the Year voting. He followed with all 82 games in 1978-79 and scored 1,769 points, or 21.6 per game. Across two Nets seasons he played 161 games and scored 3,678 points.

sections.heading: Hillman Added Another Useful Nets Piece
sections.body: Hillman did not join the Nets until the following season, but he supplied real frontcourt production once he arrived. In 1977-78 he played 45 games for New Jersey and averaged 13.1 points and 7.5 rebounds. The Nets then traded him to Denver in January 1978 for a 1979 second-round pick that became Clint Richardson. Because Hillman directly produced that pick, this review credits the draft asset as downstream value without assigning unrelated later moves to him.

sections.heading: Williamson Was a High-Volume Indiana Scorer
sections.body: The Pacers did not receive a marginal player. Williamson played 30 games after the trade in 1976-77, started 28 and averaged 20.7 points. He returned for 42 more Pacers games in 1977-78 and averaged 19.1 points. Across the two partial seasons he scored 1,424 points in 72 regular-season games.

sections.heading: Indiana Then Recycled Williamson Into Three More Assets
sections.body: On January 27, 1978, Indiana traded Williamson back to New Jersey for Bob Carrington, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick. Carrington played 35 games for the Pacers that season. The 1980 pick became Louis Orr, who played all 82 games as a rookie and 80 more in 1981-82 while averaging 10.5 and 11.5 points. The 1981 pick became Brian Jackson, who did not play an NBA regular-season game. That downstream package materially improves Indiana's side of the original evaluation.

sections.heading: King's Nets Tenure Was Great but Not Permanent
sections.body: New Jersey traded King in October 1979 with Jim Boylan and John Gianelli to Utah for Rich Kelley. This review does not credit the full Kelley return to King because two other players were included. The trade still demonstrates that King's value had not disappeared after his two high-scoring Nets seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Edge, A/B+. New Jersey receives an A because the No. 7 pick became an immediate 20-plus-point scorer in King, while Hillman added 45 productive games and another second-round asset. Indiana receives a B+ because Williamson was a 20-point scorer for 72 games and his resale produced Carrington plus the pick that became Louis Orr, a useful two-year Pacers forward. King's peak scoring gives the Nets the stronger realized return, but Indiana's downstream value makes the gap moderate rather than overwhelming. Confidence is high on the assets and outcomes, with the parent date anchored to the team media guides.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Describe a Player-Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and NBA transaction pages agree on February 1, 1977. Buffalo sold Claude Terry's player rights to Atlanta. The Braves had signed Terry as a free agent on October 21, 1976, so the February transaction converted a player the club had held for a little more than three months into financial consideration.

sections.heading: The Cash Amount Is Not Identified in the Primary Ledgers
sections.body: Atlanta's canonical record represents the outgoing side as cash, which is consistent with Basketball-Reference's sale language. The amount is not specified in the primary transaction ledgers used for this review. That means Buffalo receives credit for a real financial return, but the grade does not invent a dollar value or treat the cash as though it became a later player or draft asset.

sections.heading: Terry Immediately Received a Larger Atlanta Role
sections.body: Terry had played 33 games for Buffalo in 1976-77, averaging 9.2 minutes and 3.5 points. After the sale, he appeared in 12 games for Atlanta and averaged 20.1 minutes and 9.3 points while shooting 54.0 percent from the field. The Hawks therefore received more immediate on-court use from him than Buffalo had been getting before the transaction.

sections.heading: His Second Atlanta Season Was Smaller
sections.body: Terry returned for 27 games in 1977-78, but his role dropped to 6.1 minutes per game and 2.2 points. Across the two Atlanta seasons he appeared in 39 regular-season games, played 407 minutes and scored 171 points. Those totals establish a genuine but limited basketball return.

sections.heading: There Is No Major Downstream Asset Chain
sections.body: Terry's NBA career ended after the 1977-78 season. Atlanta did not turn him into a documented later player or draft pick in the source set used here. Buffalo's side is similarly limited to the sale proceeds. This review therefore remains a narrow comparison between two seasons of modest Atlanta production and an unspecified cash return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Edge, B-/C+. Atlanta receives a B- because a cash-only acquisition produced 39 games, including a productive 12-game stretch immediately after the sale, without costing a basketball asset. Buffalo receives a C+ because selling Terry created financial value and removed a player who had been playing only 9.2 minutes per game for the Braves, but the unidentified cash amount cannot be credited with a known basketball outcome. The gap is small and the stakes are low. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Terry's Atlanta production, while the precise cash value remains unknown.

sections.heading: The Core Package Was Forrest for a 1979 Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the March 18, 1977 core exchange. Phoenix sent its 1979 second-round pick to Seattle for Bayard Forrest. Pro Sports Transactions' 1979 draft ledger also records cash going from Phoenix to Seattle. The cash amount is not specified in the sources used for this review.

sections.heading: Forrest Did Not Play Until the Following Season
sections.body: Forrest had been Seattle's second-round selection in the 1976 draft but did not play in the NBA during 1976-77. His Phoenix career began in 1977-78. He appeared in 64 games that season, averaging 13.9 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.9 rebounds. He also appeared in one playoff game.

sections.heading: His Second Suns Season Was More Durable
sections.body: Forrest played 75 games in 1978-79, averaging 16.6 minutes, 4.0 points and 4.2 rebounds. He appeared in 14 playoff games as Phoenix reached the Western Conference Finals, including the seven-game series against Seattle. Across two regular seasons with the Suns, Forrest totaled 139 games, 569 points and 565 rebounds.

sections.heading: A Back Injury Ended the Phoenix Return
sections.body: Basketball-Reference lists Forrest as missing the entire 1979-80 season with a back injury. He never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Phoenix therefore received two seasons of reserve-center production and meaningful playoff availability, but no longer-term asset branch.

sections.heading: Seattle Reused the Incoming Pick Before the Draft
sections.body: The 1979 second-rounder later landed at No. 42, where Paul Mokeski was selected. Mokeski never played for Seattle because the SuperSonics had already traded the pick. On October 22, 1977, Seattle sent that 1979 second-rounder plus a 1980 second-round pick to Houston for John Johnson. Pro Sports Transactions' draft ledger confirms the Phoenix-to-Seattle and Seattle-to-Houston chain.

sections.heading: Johnson Became a Major Seattle Rotation Piece
sections.body: Johnson played 76 games for Seattle in 1977-78, then started all 82 games in 1978-79 as the SuperSonics won the NBA championship. He remained with Seattle through 1981-82, totaling 333 regular-season appearances across five seasons. Because the Forrest-derived pick was only one of two second-rounders used to acquire Johnson, this review does not assign all of Johnson's production to this transaction. The pick still had clear downstream utility as one half of a successful trade package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sonics Edge, B+/B. Seattle receives a B+ because the incoming second-round pick and cash retained enough value for the pick to become part of the John Johnson acquisition, which supported a championship core. Phoenix receives a B because Forrest supplied 139 games and 15 playoff appearances across two seasons before injury ended his career. The Seattle edge is meaningful but not overwhelming because the Johnson return required an additional second-round pick. Confidence is high on the core trade, Forrest's production and the pick's downstream path, while the cash amount remains unspecified.

sections.heading: The Core Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Seattle and league transaction ledgers all record the May 24, 1977 exchange the same way. Denver sent Paul Silas, Marvin Webster and Willie Wise to Seattle for Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and Seattle's 1977 second-round pick, which became No. 30 Steve Sheppard. The structure is unusually useful for hindsight analysis because nearly every major asset produced either direct playing time or a traceable downstream branch.

sections.heading: Denver Immediately Recycled Burleson and the Pick
sections.body: The Nuggets did not hold Burleson or the Sheppard pick through the draft. One day later Denver traded both to Kansas City for Brian Taylor and a 1977 first-round pick that became No. 9 Tom LaGarde. That means Burleson and the incoming second-rounder should be evaluated together as one downstream package rather than as separate Denver tenures. Taylor played 39 regular-season games for Denver in 1977-78, while LaGarde played 77. The two incoming assets therefore became another useful two-player package almost immediately.

sections.heading: Wilkerson Was the Long-Term Denver Piece
sections.body: Bob Wilkerson became the clearest direct return for the Nuggets. He played 81 games in 1977-78, 80 in 1978-79 and 75 in 1979-80. Across those three seasons he appeared in 236 regular-season games for Denver and scored 2,358 points. He also played 16 playoff games for the Nuggets over the first two seasons. Denver therefore received both durable direct production and a successful next-day asset conversion.

sections.heading: Silas Became a Three-Year Seattle Rotation Mainstay
sections.body: Paul Silas played all 82 games in each of his first three Seattle seasons, giving the SuperSonics 246 regular-season appearances from 1977-78 through 1979-80. He also appeared in 54 playoff games during that stretch. Most importantly, Silas was part of the 1978-79 championship team and appeared in all 17 playoff games during Seattle's title run.

sections.heading: Webster Powered the 1978 Finals Run
sections.body: Marvin Webster played all 82 regular-season games for Seattle in 1977-78 and then appeared in 22 postseason games as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals. His playoff workload included every game of the first round, conference semifinals, conference finals and seven-game Finals. Webster left after the season as a veteran free agent, but that departure produced another traceable branch.

sections.heading: The Webster Compensation Branch Added More Value
sections.body: When Webster signed with the Knicks in September 1978, Seattle and New York completed an arranged compensation exchange. Seattle sent a 1981 first-round pick to New York and received Lonnie Shelton plus a 1979 first-round pick that became Vinnie Johnson. Shelton immediately played 76 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the 1979 champions. Johnson later played 119 regular-season games for Seattle across two seasons. This review credits that compensation branch while also acknowledging that Seattle surrendered a future first-round pick to complete it.

sections.heading: Wise Was the Smallest Seattle Asset
sections.body: Willie Wise played only two games for Seattle before being waived in November 1977. His minimal contribution does not materially change the evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A+/A. Denver receives an A because Wilkerson supplied 236 games and the Burleson-Sheppard branch quickly became Taylor plus LaGarde. Seattle receives an A+ because Silas provided three full seasons and championship value, Webster helped drive a Finals run, and Webster's departure produced Shelton and the pick used on Vinnie Johnson through a documented compensation exchange. Both teams extracted real value, but Seattle's combination of Finals impact, a championship contributor and downstream compensation gives it the stronger realized outcome. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Core Trade Is Clear, but the Second-Round Pick Needs a Source Note
sections.body: Denver, Kansas City and the NBA transaction ledgers agree on the May 25, 1977 framework: Denver sent Tom Burleson plus a 1977 second-round pick and received Brian Taylor plus Kansas City's 1977 first-round pick. The first-rounder became No. 9 Tom LaGarde. The second-rounder is commonly attached to No. 30 Steve Sheppard in the transaction ledger, but Chicago's own history lists the Bulls as the team that drafted Sheppard and Sheppard's player ledger traces a prior Kansas City-to-Chicago future-pick obligation from 1975. This review preserves that conflict and does not award Sheppard's NBA production to the Kings.

sections.heading: Taylor Was Valuable but Short-Lived in Denver
sections.body: Brian Taylor played 39 games for Denver in 1977-78 and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. His direct tenure was short, but it retained downstream value. Taylor later signed with San Diego as a veteran free agent, and Denver received two 1979 second-round picks as compensation. Those picks became Lawrence Butler and Gary Garland. Butler never produced NBA regular-season value for Denver, but Garland played 78 games for the Nuggets in 1979-80.

sections.heading: LaGarde Produced One Season and Another First-Round Asset
sections.body: Denver used the No. 9 pick on Tom LaGarde. He played 77 regular-season games as a rookie and appeared in nine playoff games during Denver's run to the 1978 Western Conference Finals. In June 1978 the Nuggets traded LaGarde to Seattle for a 1978 first-round pick that became No. 17 Rod Griffin. Griffin was drafted by Denver but never played an NBA regular-season game, so the LaGarde branch generated draft capital without a later NBA player return.

sections.heading: Burleson Gave Kansas City Three Seasons
sections.body: Tom Burleson played 76 games for Kansas City in 1977-78, 56 in 1978-79 and 37 in 1979-80. That is 169 regular-season appearances and 1,884 points across three seasons. His role declined over time, but the Kings received substantially more direct service from him than Denver received from either Taylor or LaGarde individually.

sections.heading: Burleson's Departure Produced the Biggest Downstream Asset
sections.body: Atlanta signed Burleson as a veteran free agent in July 1980. Kansas City received a 1981 second-round pick as compensation, and that pick became No. 29 Eddie Johnson. Johnson immediately became a major franchise asset. He played 74 games as a rookie, then 82 games in each of the next five seasons spanning Kansas City and Sacramento. Across those six franchise seasons he appeared in 483 regular-season games and scored 9,027 points, including three consecutive seasons above 19 points per game from 1982-83 through 1984-85.

sections.heading: The Sheppard Ledger Conflict Stays Uncredited
sections.body: The canonical trade record and several transaction pages associate the outgoing second-round pick with Sheppard, but Chicago's draft history shows the Bulls selecting him at No. 30 and his player ledger contains an older Kansas City-to-Chicago pick transaction. Because the historical routing is internally inconsistent, this review records the discrepancy instead of assigning Sheppard's 86 career games to Kansas City.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A+/B+. Kansas City receives an A+ because Burleson delivered 169 games and, more importantly, his free-agent compensation became Eddie Johnson, a six-season franchise scorer with 9,027 points. Denver receives a B+ because Taylor was an All-Defensive guard, his departure yielded two second-rounders with Garland providing 78 games, and LaGarde supplied a full rookie season before becoming another first-round asset. The long-term Johnson branch creates the decisive separation. Confidence is high on the player movement and downstream compensation, with the Sheppard pick-routing conflict explicitly isolated.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Cavaliers and league transaction logs agree that New York sent Cleveland a 1972 second-round pick and a future draft choice for Luther Rackley. The 1972 pick became Steve Hawes at No. 24. Pro Sports Transactions and a Knicks media guide add cash to Cleveland's return, while the surviving Basketball-Reference entry does not list the cash. Because the media guide and transaction database independently support it, the source-backed record preserves cash as real but unpriced consideration. The additional future draft pick remains unidentified by year, round and outcome.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: Rackley gave the Knicks a full useful season as a reserve center. He played 62 regular-season games after the trade, totaling 618 minutes, 233 points and 187 rebounds while averaging 10.0 minutes per game. He also appeared in all 11 of New York's 1972 playoff games, including the NBA Finals run, although his postseason role was tiny at 29 total minutes. Rackley returned for one regular-season game in 1972-73 before the Knicks waived him in October and he moved to the ABA. That is not star value, but it is concrete rotation depth for a contender and a traceable postseason contribution.

sections.heading: Cleveland Return
sections.body:
Cleveland's most visible return was the 1972 second-round pick used on Hawes. Hawes eventually had a 10-year NBA career, but none of that production belongs to the Cavaliers because he spent 1972-73 and 1973-74 in Italy and Cleveland traded his NBA rights to Houston on September 22, 1972 before his league debut. In exchange, the Cavaliers received Houston's 1973 third-round pick, which they used on James Lister at No. 41. Basketball-Reference and RealGM list no NBA games for Lister. Pro Sports Transactions also reports cash in the Hawes-rights trade, but Basketball-Reference does not, so any financial return is preserved as source-supported but unpriced rather than turned into invented basketball value.

The second future pick from New York is even less traceable. The Knicks and Cavaliers transaction ledgers confirm that it existed, but neither identifies its year, round or drafted player. That unresolved asset means Cleveland's return cannot be treated as zero. It also means the old A grade overstates what the surviving record can actually prove. The only fully traceable draft chain runs from the 1972 No. 24 pick to Hawes's rights and then to Lister, with no NBA games realized by Cleveland from that chain.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: New York's side produced 62 regular-season games, 618 minutes and 11 playoff appearances from Rackley during a Finals season. Cleveland's known draft chain produced no Cavaliers games, while the unidentified future pick and cash retain some unresolved value. That makes the deal much closer to a modest Knicks win than the legacy Cavaliers blowout. Hawes's later NBA career should not be credited to Cleveland simply because the Cavaliers drafted him; the club moved his rights away before he ever appeared in the league. That distinction is exactly why the source-backed pass follows realized team value rather than player-name prestige.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, B-/C+. New York receives a B- because Rackley gave the club dependable reserve-center minutes and appeared throughout the 1972 postseason run. Cleveland receives a C+ because it acquired multiple real assets, including a second-round pick and cash, but the known pick chain ended with James Lister and no NBA games for the Cavaliers while the additional future pick remains unresolved. Confidence is medium-high on the exchange, Rackley production and Hawes-to-Lister chain, but only medium on the full Cleveland outcome because the second future pick and cash amount cannot be completed from the surviving ledgers.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records the core agreement on March 12, 1972: Boston sent Charlie Scott's NBA rights to Phoenix for cash and future considerations, later fulfilled by Paul Silas. Basketball-Reference dates the rights transaction March 14 and says Silas agreed to terms with Boston in September; the Phoenix media guide lists Silas as sent on September 19, while the legacy Boston source record uses September 18. The exact day varies across otherwise consistent transaction ledgers, so the canonical March 12 date is preserved with the discrepancy documented rather than silently rewritten. The basketball substance is clear: Phoenix obtained Scott's rights, Boston eventually received Silas plus cash, and the cash amount is not identified.

sections.heading: Boston Return
sections.body: Silas gave Boston four high-value seasons. From 1972-73 through 1975-76 he played 325 regular-season games, including 80 or more in every season, and became one of the league's strongest rebounding forwards. He made the 1975 All-Star team, earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition in 1973 and First Team honors in both 1975 and 1976. The championship value is especially important. Boston won the 1974 and 1976 NBA Finals with Silas in the rotation, and he appeared in 60 postseason games across his four Celtics seasons. His role was not decorative: his rebounding and defensive work complemented Dave Cowens and gave the Celtics a durable frontcourt piece through two title runs. When Boston moved Silas in October 1976, the three-team transaction brought Curtis Rowe to the Celtics. Rowe then supplied 183 more regular-season games over three Boston seasons, so Silas also retained some traceable downstream value after the championship years.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body:
Scott's Phoenix value was also immediate and substantial. After leaving the ABA he played six late-season games for the Suns in 1971-72, then became a three-time NBA All-Star for Phoenix from 1972-73 through 1974-75. Across those four partial or full Phoenix seasons he appeared in 208 regular-season games and averaged more than 24 points in each of the final three. The rights therefore became a genuine star rather than a speculative asset. Phoenix then preserved that value instead of losing Scott for nothing.

On May 23, 1975 the Suns traded Scott to Boston for Paul Westphal plus Boston's 1975 and 1976 second-round picks. The picks became Jimmy Dan Conner and Butch Feher, but Westphal is the central downstream return. Westphal played five full Phoenix seasons from 1975-76 through 1979-80, appearing in 406 regular-season games, helping the Suns reach the 1976 NBA Finals and making four consecutive All-Star teams from 1977 through 1980. He also earned four straight All-NBA selections, including three First Team honors. Phoenix then traded Westphal to Seattle on June 4, 1980 for Dennis Johnson. That conversion extends the Scott-rights chain well beyond Scott's own scoring peak and makes the original acquisition one of the more productive rights transactions of the era.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Calling the trade even understates how well both organizations converted the assets. Boston received the more championship-specific direct return: Silas was a core rebounding and defensive contributor on two title teams, played 325 regular-season games and 60 playoff games, then still returned Curtis Rowe in a later three-team trade. Phoenix received the more expansive star-value chain. Scott was a three-time Suns All-Star, then became Westphal and two picks; Westphal produced five high-level seasons, four All-Star selections, four All-NBA selections and a Finals run before becoming Dennis Johnson. Because downstream credit is shared with the later packages rather than assigned entirely to Scott, the margin should remain narrow. Phoenix does not erase Boston's two championships, but the Scott-to-Westphal-to-Johnson path adds enough durable value to move the verdict beyond a pure tie.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ for turning Scott's rights into three All-Star seasons from Scott, then Westphal, two second-round picks and eventually Dennis Johnson. Boston receives an A because Silas gave the Celtics four durable seasons, elite rebounding and defense, an All-Star appearance, three All-Defensive selections and major minutes on the 1974 and 1976 championship teams, with Curtis Rowe arriving downstream. Confidence is high on the player identities, production and later trade chains. The only meaningful source uncertainty is the exact transaction date: Pro Sports Transactions uses March 12 and September 18, while Basketball-Reference and Phoenix media guides use March 14 and September 19 for the two stages.

sections.heading: What the Sources Actually Establish
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Virginia and Denver transaction pages agree that the Squires traded Jan van Breda Kolff to Denver during June 1974. They do not preserve an exact day. Virginia's ledger lists the move as 'June ?, 1974,' while Denver's ledger shows the same month and records the outgoing asset only as TO_TRADE. Denver then signed van Breda Kolff on June 25. The legacy archive record used June 1 and labeled the return as future considerations, but the source-backed review could not verify either the exact day or that specific compensation description. The record therefore keeps June 1 only as an ordering placeholder and marks the actual date precision as month-known.

sections.heading: Virginia Had Drafted Him First
sections.body: The Squires had selected van Breda Kolff in the 1974 ABA draft on March 6. He was also chosen by Portland in the NBA draft, but his professional path began in the ABA with Denver. The rights transfer is therefore a genuine Virginia-to-Denver transaction even though the surviving ledger does not resolve what Denver surrendered. That distinction matters because the asset itself is well documented while the consideration is not. The correct archive treatment is to separate verified player movement from unverified compensation rather than carrying a speculative future-considerations label forward as fact.

sections.heading: Denver Gets a Full Season
sections.body: Van Breda Kolff played all 84 regular-season games for Denver in 1974-75. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,639 minutes, 487 points, 358 rebounds and 181 assists. He averaged 5.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 19.5 minutes while shooting .453 from the field. He also appeared in 12 playoff games, averaging 5.3 points in 16.0 minutes. Those numbers make the rights acquisition more than a paper transaction: Denver received a full year of rotation availability on a 65-win team that reached the ABA Western Division Finals.

sections.heading: The Asset Still Had Trade Value
sections.body: Denver retained value in van Breda Kolff after that season. On July 14, 1975, the Nuggets traded him with Mack Calvin and Mike Green to Virginia for George Irvine and the rights to David Thompson. The transaction is independently recorded by the Virginia ledger, Denver ledger, league transaction page and Virginia's 1976 media guide. Because Calvin and Green were substantial co-assets, the archive does not credit van Breda Kolff alone with acquiring Thompson. It does credit the original rights purchase with preserving a movable player asset that became one part of a franchise-changing package.

sections.heading: Virginia's Original Return Cannot Be Scored
sections.body: The unresolved issue is the other side of the June 1974 transaction. No reviewed authoritative ledger identifies a draft pick, cash amount, named player or later consideration that Virginia received from Denver. Basketball-Reference literally preserves the Denver outgoing side as TO_TRADE. That is not enough to grade the Squires. It is also not evidence that Virginia received nothing. Assigning a losing grade would convert missing documentation into a basketball judgment, which this source-backed review standard is designed to avoid.

sections.heading: Date Handling
sections.body: The canonical record remains dated June 1 because changing an legacy placeholder without a verified replacement day would create false precision in a different direction and disturb chronological processing. The record now explicitly records that the exact June date is unknown, with June 25 separately documented as Denver's signing date. Any future source that identifies the actual transaction day can replace the placeholder cleanly without changing the source-backed evaluation or player lineage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, Denver B+ / Virginia N/A. Denver's side earns a B+ for 84 regular-season games, 12 playoff appearances and retained trade utility in the later David Thompson package. Virginia remains ungraded because the outgoing Denver consideration cannot be verified. Confidence is high on van Breda Kolff's transfer, Denver production and 1975 downstream trade, but low on the exact June day and original compensation.
