sections.heading: The Public Ledger Describes a Sale
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records New Jersey selling Edgar Jones' player rights to Detroit on June 11, 1981.

The legacy canonical record describes the Nets' return as future considerations or cash. The reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the financial term without inventing a value for it.

sections.heading: Jones Played 97 Games for Detroit
sections.body:
Jones became a useful Detroit reserve and part-time starter in 1981-82. He played 48 games, started 19 and averaged 7.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 1.9 blocks in 16.7 minutes.

He remained with the Pistons for most of 1982-83, appearing in 49 games and starting 25. That season he averaged 8.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.6 blocks in 21.1 minutes.

Across the two seasons, Jones gave Detroit 97 regular-season games and 44 starts.

sections.heading: Detroit Later Recovered Two Draft Picks
sections.body:
On February 10, 1983, Detroit traded Jones to San Antonio for a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick.

The 1984 selection landed at No. 32 and became Eric Turner. The 1985 selection landed at No. 60 and became Andre Goode.

Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season statistics for either Turner or Goode. The picks therefore did not add direct NBA playing value after the Jones tenure ended.

sections.heading: The Nets' Cash Return Is Unquantified
sections.body:
New Jersey's side cannot be treated as zero value because the transaction was a sale and the club received financial consideration.

The problem is that the reviewed sources do not identify the amount or any later basketball asset tied to that payment. This review therefore grades the Nets conservatively rather than pretending the cash can be compared precisely with 97 games of on-court production.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Detroit received two seasons of useful frontcourt play from Jones, including 44 starts, and then converted him into two draft selections.

Neither draft pick reached an NBA regular-season floor, so the downstream branch does not transform the deal into a major win. The direct Jones tenure remains the core of Detroit's value.

New Jersey received real financial consideration, but without a documented amount or a basketball branch it cannot match Detroit's identifiable return in a realized-value archive.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, B+/C. Detroit receives a B+ for 97 Jones games, 44 starts and two later draft opportunities. New Jersey receives a C because the cash consideration was real but is not quantified in the reviewed public record.

sections.heading: Kansas City Bought Five Seasons of Larry Drew
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Kansas City and league transaction ledgers agree on the August 26, 1981 terms. Detroit sent Larry Drew to the Kings for Kansas City's 1982 second-round pick, later No. 28 Dave Magley, and 1984 second-round pick, later No. 34 Tony Costner.

The original canonical record treated Magley as if Detroit directly received the player. That is not what happened. Both incoming assets were draft picks, and Detroit traded each pick before it was exercised.

sections.heading: Drew Became a Long-Term Kings Starter
sections.body:
Drew played 81 games for Kansas City in 1981-82, then moved into a much larger role. In 1982-83 he started 74 of 75 games and averaged 20.1 points and 8.1 assists.

He remained with the franchise through the move to Sacramento in 1985-86. Across five Kings seasons, Drew played 376 regular-season games and started 263.

That is a large direct return for two second-round picks, especially because Drew was only 23 when Kansas City acquired him.

sections.heading: Detroit Rerouted the 1982 Pick
sections.body:
The 1982 second-rounder became the No. 28 selection, which Cleveland ultimately used on Dave Magley.

Detroit had already moved that pick on February 16, 1982. The Pistons sent Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, a 1982 first-round pick and this second-round pick to Cleveland for Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer.

Because the pick was one component of a four-asset package, this review does not credit the entire Laimbeer-Carr return to the Drew trade. It does, however, credit the pick with retaining real transaction value.

sections.heading: Detroit Rerouted the 1984 Pick Too
sections.body:
The second Kansas City pick became No. 34 in 1984, when Washington selected Tony Costner. Detroit never made that selection.

On February 13, 1983, the Pistons sent the 1984 second-rounder and a 1985 second-rounder to Atlanta in a three-team trade that brought Ray Tolbert from Seattle to Detroit. Tolbert played 77 regular-season games for the Pistons across parts of two seasons.

Again, the incoming pick was only one part of the later package, so Tolbert cannot be assigned entirely to this branch.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Wins
sections.body:
Detroit extracted meaningful trade utility from both second-round picks, which prevents this from being a one-sided failure. One pick helped complete the package for Laimbeer and Carr, while the other helped bring Tolbert.

Kansas City still received the clearest standalone asset. Drew gave the franchise 376 games, 263 starts and multiple seasons as a productive starting point guard.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A/B-. Kansas City receives an A for turning two second-rounders into five productive seasons of Drew. Detroit receives a B- because both picks retained downstream trade value, including use in the Laimbeer-Carr package, but neither pick created a clean direct return comparable to Drew's Kings tenure.

sections.heading: Washington Got the Best Direct Return
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Golden State transaction ledger records the October 19, 1981 package clearly. The Warriors sent John Lucas to Washington for two second-round picks, one in 1982 and one in 1984.

Golden State eventually used those choices on Derek Smith at No. 35 in 1982 and Steve Burtt at No. 30 in 1984.

sections.heading: Lucas Became Washington's Starting Point Guard
sections.body:
Lucas played 79 regular-season games for the Bullets in 1981-82 and started 53. He averaged 24.6 minutes, 8.4 points and 7.0 assists while helping Washington finish 43-39 and reach the Eastern Conference semifinals.

He returned for 35 games in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 4.1 points and 2.9 assists. Washington waived him on January 25, 1983.

That gives the Bullets 114 regular-season games and 53 starts from the trade, including one season in which Lucas handled a major portion of the point-guard workload.

sections.heading: Derek Smith Produced 27 Warriors Games
sections.body:
Golden State used the 1982 pick at No. 35 on Louisville wing Derek Smith. He appeared in 27 Warriors games as a rookie, all off the bench, averaging 5.7 minutes and 2.2 points.

The Warriors waived Smith on September 8, 1983. He later became a productive NBA starter with the Clippers, but that later success came after Golden State had released him and cannot be credited to this trade.

sections.heading: Steve Burtt Added 47 More Games
sections.body:
The second incoming pick became No. 30 in the 1984 draft, where Golden State selected Steve Burtt.

Burtt played 47 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 8.9 minutes and 4.2 points. His later NBA seasons came with other franchises.

Together, the two draft branches produced 74 Golden State games and zero starts.

sections.heading: Why Washington Wins
sections.body:
Golden State did identify two players who reached the NBA, and that gives the picks more value than unused selections. The problem is that neither player produced much for the Warriors themselves.

Washington received 114 games, 53 starts and a full season of starting point-guard play from Lucas. On direct franchise value, that outweighs 74 reserve appearances and no starts from Smith and Burtt combined.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, B+/C+. Washington receives a B+ because Lucas supplied a useful starting season plus additional reserve time. Golden State receives a C+ because both picks became NBA players, but their combined Warriors contribution stayed below Lucas's Washington value and produced no starts.

sections.heading: San Antonio Bought a Full Season of Backcourt Depth
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's San Antonio transaction ledger records the October 28, 1981 trade clearly. The Spurs sent Cleveland a 1983 third-round pick and received Mike Bratz.

That pick eventually became No. 66 Les Craft, but Cleveland did not simply keep Craft as its final return.

sections.heading: Bratz Played 81 Games for a Conference Finalist
sections.body:
Bratz appeared in 81 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1981-82 and started three. He averaged 20.0 minutes, 7.7 points and 5.4 assists while serving as a reserve point guard behind the Spurs' veteran backcourt.

San Antonio finished 48-34, won the Midwest Division and reached the Western Conference Finals. Bratz also appeared in all nine Spurs playoff games, averaging 20.0 minutes and 5.3 assists per game in the postseason.

His San Antonio tenure lasted one season, but it was a complete and useful one.

sections.heading: Cleveland Used the Pick on Les Craft
sections.body:
The Cavaliers exercised the incoming third-round selection at No. 66 in the 1983 NBA Draft and selected Kansas State center Les Craft.

Craft never played a regular-season game for Cleveland. On the same draft day, the Cavaliers packaged his rights with No. 56 pick Larry Anderson and sent both players to San Diego for a 1985 second-round pick.

That means the original Bratz return retained transaction value even though Craft himself never suited up for Cleveland.

sections.heading: The Downstream Pick Became Calvin Duncan
sections.body:
The 1985 second-rounder acquired from San Diego became No. 30 Calvin Duncan.

Cleveland then included Duncan with Charles Oakley in a draft-night trade with Chicago for Keith Lee and Ennis Whatley. Duncan never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

This review does not credit the entire Lee-Whatley return to the Bratz trade because Craft was packaged with Larry Anderson to acquire the 1985 pick, and Duncan was later packaged with Oakley. Those other assets were essential parts of both downstream transactions.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Wins
sections.body:
The Spurs received 81 regular-season games, three starts and nine playoff appearances from Bratz. Cleveland received a third-round pick that retained some trade utility but never produced a direct Cavaliers game through Craft or Duncan.

The downstream chain prevents Cleveland from receiving a failing grade, but the direct realized basketball value is clearly on San Antonio's side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B+/C. San Antonio receives a B+ for a full season of useful guard depth on a division champion and conference finalist. Cleveland receives a C because the pick retained later transaction utility, but its direct player outcomes produced zero Cavaliers regular-season games.

sections.heading: New Jersey Bought Two Seasons of Len Elmore
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, New Jersey and league transaction ledgers all record the November 2, 1981 move as a sale of Len Elmore's player rights from the Bucks to the Nets. The legacy canonical package identifies the return as future considerations in cash.

The public sources reviewed for this review do not specify the dollar amount, so the Milwaukee side cannot be valued precisely. The basketball return to New Jersey is much easier to measure.

sections.heading: Elmore Started 70 Games in His First Nets Season
sections.body:
Elmore appeared in 81 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82 and started 70. He averaged 25.9 minutes, 9.1 points, 5.4 rebounds, 1.1 steals and 1.1 blocks.

The Nets finished 44-38 and reached the playoffs after going 24-58 the previous season. Elmore was not the only reason for that turnaround, but 70 starts and more than 2,100 minutes make him a substantial part of the rotation.

He also appeared in both New Jersey playoff games that spring.

sections.heading: He Added a Second Full Season
sections.body:
Elmore returned for 74 regular-season games in 1982-83. His role shrank to 13.2 minutes per game and he did not start, but he still supplied frontcourt depth for a 49-win playoff team.

Across the two seasons, Elmore played 155 regular-season games for the Nets. He accumulated 983 points and 679 rebounds during that New Jersey tenure.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Cash, Not a Player Asset
sections.body:
The Bucks sold Elmore's rights rather than receiving a player or draft pick. That gives Milwaukee a tangible return, but the lack of a public cash figure limits how strongly the outcome can be graded.

Elmore had played 72 games for Milwaukee the previous season, so this was not a meaningless set of rights. The Bucks chose to monetize a veteran they were moving away from, and that decision produced some value even if the amount cannot be reconstructed from the reviewed public record.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins
sections.body:
The Nets received two seasons and 155 regular-season games from Elmore, including 70 starts in his first year. Milwaukee received an unquantified cash return.

Without a known large cash figure, the realized basketball value clearly favors New Jersey. The transaction was not franchise-changing, but it was a useful low-cost acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New Jersey receives a B+ for two seasons of frontcourt depth, 155 games and 70 starts. Milwaukee receives a C for converting player rights into cash, with the unknown amount preventing a stronger or more exact grade.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Dandridge Reunion Lasted Less Than a Month
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Washington transaction ledgers agree on the core November 2, 1981 restricted-veteran-free-agent mechanism. Milwaukee signed Bob Dandridge, and Washington received the Bucks' 1982 fifth-round pick as compensation.

The legacy canonical package also includes cash going to Washington. The reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning it a speculative financial value.

sections.heading: Dandridge Played Only 11 Games
sections.body:
Dandridge returned to the franchise where he had spent his first nine NBA seasons, but the reunion was brief. He appeared in 11 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 1981-82, made no starts and averaged 15.8 minutes.

His production was modest: 4.7 points, 1.5 rebounds and 1.2 assists per game while shooting 38.2 percent from the field.

Milwaukee waived Dandridge on November 25, only twenty-three days after signing him. Those 11 games were the final appearances of his NBA career.

sections.heading: Washington's Pick Became Jerry Davis
sections.body:
The fifth-round compensation pick became No. 112 in the 1982 NBA Draft, where Washington selected Detroit Mercy forward Jerry Davis.

Basketball-Reference lists Davis as the No. 112 selection, while RealGM's draft history gives him zero NBA years of service. The pick therefore produced no regular-season games for Washington.

That prevents the draft branch from creating a meaningful basketball advantage by itself.

sections.heading: Cash Separates Two Small Returns
sections.body:
If the transaction consisted only of Dandridge against the fifth-round pick, the realized result would be close to even: 11 low-minute games for Milwaukee versus zero NBA games from the pick for Washington.

The cash component gives the Bullets an additional tangible return. Because the amount is not publicly identified in the reviewed sources, it should not be treated as a large asset or used to justify an aggressive grade.

sections.heading: Why Washington Gets a Slight Edge
sections.body:
Milwaukee received a famous franchise veteran, but the actual 1981-82 return was only 11 reserve games before a waiver. Washington's pick failed to produce an NBA player, yet the Bullets also received cash.

The difference is small, but Washington extracted more realized value from a veteran it was losing anyway.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, C+/C-. Washington receives a C+ because the fifth-round pick produced no NBA games but the cash component gave the franchise a tangible return. Milwaukee receives a C- because Dandridge played only 11 games, never started and was waived before the end of November.

sections.heading: Kansas City Received a Long-Term Scorer Plus a First-Round Pick
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Kansas City records agree on the November 12, 1981 package. The Nets received Sam Lacey, while the Kings received Mike Woodson and a 1982 first-round pick that became No. 17 Brook Steppe.

The pick was conditional on the more favorable of the Lakers and Suns choices available through New Jersey's prior transactions. It ultimately landed in the middle of the first round.

sections.heading: Woodson Became the Centerpiece
sections.body:
Woodson had played only seven games for New Jersey before the trade. In Kansas City he immediately moved into a much larger role, appearing in 76 games in 1981-82 and starting 74 while averaging 16.1 points.

He followed with 81 games and 18.2 points per game in 1982-83. Woodson then played 71 games in 1983-84, 78 in 1984-85 and 81 in the franchise's first Sacramento season in 1985-86.

Across those five Kings seasons, Woodson played 387 regular-season games and started 143. He scored more than 6,000 points for the franchise during that stretch and remained a reliable scoring guard through the move from Kansas City to Sacramento.

sections.heading: Steppe Added Another NBA Player
sections.body:
Kansas City used the No. 17 pick on Georgia Tech guard Brook Steppe.

Steppe played 62 games for the Kings as a rookie in 1982-83, made six starts and averaged 4.0 points in 9.8 minutes. He moved to Indiana the following season, so this review credits only that original Kansas City tenure.

The pick did not become a star, but it still produced a rotation player on top of Woodson's much larger contribution.

sections.heading: Lacey's Nets Tenure Was Brief
sections.body:
Lacey played 54 regular-season games for New Jersey after the trade and started six. He averaged 8.6 points, 5.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists in a reduced role.

He did not return to the Nets the following season, instead finishing his NBA career with Cleveland in 1982-83. New Jersey therefore received less than one full season from the veteran center.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Wins Decisively
sections.body:
Woodson alone makes the trade heavily favor the Kings. He provided five seasons of scoring value, including several years as one of the franchise's most productive guards.

Steppe's 62 games add another useful branch. Kansas City received 449 direct regular-season games from the two incoming assets, while Lacey produced 54 for New Jersey.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A+/D. Kansas City receives an A+ because Woodson became a five-season franchise fixture and the first-round pick also produced an NBA rotation player. New Jersey receives a D because Lacey's useful but brief 54-game tenure was nowhere close to the value surrendered.

sections.heading: The Canonical Date Needed Correction
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry carried November 21, 1981, but Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Seattle, league and Jack McCloskey transaction ledgers all place the trade on November 23. RealGM independently lists the same November 23 date.

This review therefore corrects the canonical date rather than preserving the earlier value. The package itself is undisputed: Detroit received Vinnie Johnson and Seattle received Greg Kelser.

sections.heading: Johnson Became a Ten-Year Pistons Fixture
sections.body:
Johnson played 67 regular-season games for Detroit in 1981-82 and started 15. He immediately became useful, averaging 7.7 points and 2.4 assists while shooting 49.3 percent from the field.

His role expanded the following season to 82 games and 51 starts, but his long-term value came from becoming one of the defining reserve scorers of Detroit's rise. Across ten Pistons seasons, Johnson played 798 regular-season games, started 164 and scored 10,146 points.

He stayed with the franchise through both championship seasons. Detroit won the 1989 and 1990 NBA titles with Johnson as a core member of the backcourt rotation, and his postseason résumé with the Pistons reached 108 games.

sections.heading: Kelser Gave Seattle Two Solid Seasons
sections.body:
Kelser was not a zero-value return. He played 49 regular-season games for Seattle in 1981-82, started ten and averaged 4.9 points and 3.1 rebounds.

He then appeared in 80 games in 1982-83, made nine starts and averaged 8.3 points and 5.0 rebounds. That gives Seattle 129 regular-season games and 19 starts from Kelser before the franchise moved him again.

For a player who had battled knee trouble in Detroit, two mostly healthy Seattle seasons represent a credible return.

sections.heading: Seattle Later Used Kelser in a Much Larger Trade
sections.body:
On August 18, 1983, Seattle included Kelser with Mark Radford, James Donaldson, a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick in the multi-asset deal that brought Tom Chambers, Al Wood and two draft picks from San Diego.

That downstream move gives Kelser some additional transaction utility. This review does not assign the entire Chambers return to him because the package included several other meaningful players and picks.

The direct comparison is still the cleanest measure: Seattle received two useful seasons from Kelser, while Detroit received a decade from Johnson.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Wins by a Wide Margin
sections.body:
Johnson's 798 Detroit games alone dwarf Kelser's 129 Seattle games. The gap becomes even larger when Johnson's 10,146 Pistons points, 164 starts, 108 playoff games and two championship seasons are included.

Seattle did not get nothing, and Kelser's later inclusion in the Chambers trade keeps the grade above failing. The outcome simply was not close.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A+/C+. Detroit receives an A+ because Johnson became a ten-year franchise fixture and championship rotation cornerstone. Seattle receives a C+ because Kelser supplied two useful seasons and later retained package value, but the direct and historical returns fall far short of Johnson's Pistons career.

sources.title: Detroit Pistons feature on the Vinnie Johnson acquisition

sections.heading: Seattle Received Two Useful NBA Players
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Seattle transaction ledgers agree on the November 25, 1981 package. The Nets received James Bailey, while the SuperSonics received Ray Tolbert and New Jersey's 1984 second-round pick.

That pick eventually landed at No. 39 and became Danny Young.

sections.heading: Bailey Gave New Jersey 73 Games
sections.body:
Bailey played 67 regular-season games for the Nets in 1981-82, all off the bench. He averaged 8.9 points, 5.1 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 19.2 minutes while shooting 52.3 percent from the field.

He returned for only six games in 1982-83 before New Jersey traded him to Houston on November 10. Across his Nets tenure, Bailey therefore produced 73 regular-season games and zero starts.

New Jersey did not lose the asset for nothing. The Houston trade returned a 1983 second-round pick that became Horace Owens and a 1985 second-round pick that became Yvon Joseph.

Those downstream picks had limited direct NBA outcomes. Owens never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, although New Jersey later included him in the package that acquired Reggie Johnson from Philadelphia. Joseph played one regular-season game for the Nets.

sections.heading: Tolbert Played 97 Games for Seattle
sections.body:
Ray Tolbert appeared in 52 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1981-82 and 45 more in 1982-83. He made two starts across those seasons.

His role was modest, but he gave the SuperSonics 97 games of frontcourt depth before being moved in a three-team transaction in February 1983. Seattle received Steve Hawes in that later structure, although this review does not assign the entire Hawes return to Tolbert because multiple teams and draft assets were involved.

sections.heading: Danny Young Became the More Important Seattle Return
sections.body:
Seattle used the incoming 1984 second-round pick on Wake Forest guard Danny Young at No. 39.

Young appeared in only three games as a rookie, then became a regular rotation player. He played all 82 games in 1985-86 with 29 starts, followed with 73 games and 26 starts in 1986-87, and added 77 games in 1987-88.

That gives Seattle 235 regular-season games and 55 starts from Young across four seasons. His strongest year was 1985-86, when he averaged 6.9 points and 3.7 assists while shooting 50.6 percent from the field.

Seattle valued Young enough that in June 1988 it sent Miami a second-round pick in exchange for the Heat agreeing not to select him in the expansion draft. The SuperSonics waived him later that October, but the protection transaction confirms that he remained a meaningful roster asset deep into his Seattle tenure.

sections.heading: Why Seattle Wins
sections.body:
The direct player accounting strongly favors the SuperSonics. Tolbert and Young combined for 332 Seattle regular-season games and 57 starts. Bailey produced 73 Nets games and zero starts.

New Jersey's later Bailey trade preserved some transaction utility through two second-round picks, which keeps the result from being a severe loss. The downstream player outcomes from those picks, however, were limited.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/C+. Seattle receives a B+ because Tolbert supplied useful depth and the second-round pick became a four-season rotation guard in Young. New Jersey receives a C+ because Bailey was productive in a reserve role and later returned two second-round picks, but the direct realized player value fell well short of Seattle's package.

sections.heading: San Diego Won the Immediate Production Exchange
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the January 20, 1982 package. Atlanta sent Charlie Criss and Al Wood to the Clippers for Freeman Williams.

On direct post-trade production alone, the deal favors San Diego. Williams played 23 regular-season games for Atlanta, all off the bench, and averaged 4.8 points in only 8.2 minutes.

Criss immediately became San Diego's starting point guard for much of the remainder of the season. He played 28 games for the Clippers, started 20 and averaged 12.9 points and 4.0 assists in 30.0 minutes.

sections.heading: Wood Gave the Clippers a Longer Return
sections.body:
Al Wood played 29 games for San Diego after the trade in 1981-82 and made five starts. He averaged 12.5 points while shooting 51.8 percent from the field.

His role grew substantially in 1982-83. Wood appeared in 76 games, started 47 and averaged 10.9 points, 3.1 rebounds and 1.8 assists.

That gives San Diego 105 regular-season games and 52 starts from Wood, plus 28 games and 20 starts from Criss. Combined, the two incoming players produced 133 Clippers games and 72 starts.

Criss left after the season and signed with Milwaukee. Wood remained one more year before becoming part of a larger transaction.

sections.heading: Wood Later Carried Additional Trade Utility
sections.body:
On August 18, 1983, San Diego included Wood with Tom Chambers, a 1984 third-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick in the multi-asset trade with Seattle that brought James Donaldson, Greg Kelser, Mark Radford, a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick to the Clippers.

That gives Wood additional downstream value, but this review does not assign the full Seattle package to him. Chambers and the draft assets were substantial pieces of the same transaction.

sections.heading: Williams' Atlanta Tenure Was Short but Strategically Important
sections.body:
Williams' direct Hawks production was minimal. He played only 23 games, made no starts and never returned for another Atlanta regular-season appearance.

The importance comes from what Atlanta did next. On September 2, 1982, the Hawks traded John Drew and Williams to Utah for the draft rights to Dominique Wilkins.

Wilkins became one of the defining players in franchise history, eventually playing 882 regular-season games for the Hawks and becoming the franchise's career leader in games played. He was a nine-time All-Star overall, won the 1985-86 scoring title and later entered the Hall of Fame.

This review does not credit the entire Wilkins career to Williams because John Drew was the other major asset in the Utah package. Williams should instead receive strong transaction-utility credit for being one required component of a franchise-altering acquisition.

sections.heading: Why Atlanta Gets the Hindsight Edge
sections.body:
San Diego clearly received more direct value from the January trade. Criss and Wood combined for 133 games and 72 starts, while Williams gave Atlanta only 23 reserve appearances.

The downstream branches change the comparison. Wood later helped San Diego in the Chambers trade, but Williams was part of the package that brought Wilkins to Atlanta. Even with conservative shared-credit treatment, participating in that acquisition carries more long-term franchise consequence than the original 23-game stint suggests.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Edge, A-/B+. Atlanta receives an A- because Williams' direct contribution was small but his later use in the Dominique Wilkins trade created exceptional transaction utility. San Diego receives a B+ because Criss and Wood supplied 133 games and 72 starts, and Wood retained later trade value. The margin is not wide enough to treat Wilkins' full career as Williams-only value, but the downstream Atlanta outcome is still the most consequential branch.

sections.heading: The Date Differs Across Major Sources
sections.body:
this review preserves a documented source-date conflict instead of forcing false precision. RealGM lists Armond Hill as acquired by San Diego on February 12, 1982, matching the canonical record. Basketball-Reference's San Diego, Seattle and league transaction ledgers place the full Hill-for-Phil Smith trade on February 16.

Because the team and league ledgers agree on February 16 while RealGM supports February 12, this review retains the canonical February 12 date but lowers confidence to medium and records the four-day discrepancy explicitly.

sections.heading: San Diego Got a Short Starting Look at Armond Hill
sections.body:
Hill played 19 regular-season games for the Clippers after the trade and started 14. He averaged 25.3 minutes, 4.7 points and 4.3 assists.

He did not return to San Diego the following season. RealGM's roster turnover lists Hill becoming a free agent on July 1, 1982 before later joining Milwaukee.

That makes Hill a useful but short-lived direct return.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Retained Trade Utility
sections.body:
Seattle's 1982 second-round pick was the choice that ultimately became No. 42 Jeff Taylor, but San Diego did not use it on Taylor. On June 28, the Clippers packaged that pick with Joe Bryant and sent both to Houston for the 1982 No. 32 pick that became Richard Anderson.

This review does not credit the full Anderson return to this one pick because Bryant was also required in the package. The correct value is narrower: the acquired second-rounder retained enough transaction utility to help San Diego move up ten spots in the draft.

The canonical source package also includes cash to San Diego. The reviewed public primary ledgers do not specify the amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning a speculative dollar value.

sections.heading: Phil Smith Gave Seattle Two Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Smith played 26 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1981-82, started two and averaged 8.2 points. He also appeared in all eight of Seattle's playoff games that spring.

He returned for 79 games in 1982-83, starting 17 and averaging 5.7 points and 2.7 assists.

Across the two seasons, Smith gave the SuperSonics 105 regular-season games and 19 starts. That is substantially more direct team production than Hill's 19 games for San Diego.

sections.heading: Why Seattle Gets the Edge
sections.body:
San Diego did not come away empty. Hill started 14 games, the pick remained useful in a later draft-day trade and the canonical package includes cash.

Seattle still received the stronger direct realized basketball value. Smith stayed for parts of two seasons, played 105 games and remained a usable rotation guard after Hill had already left San Diego.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/B. Seattle receives a B+ for 105 games and 19 starts from Smith across parts of two seasons. San Diego receives a B because Hill started 14 games and the pick retained downstream transaction value, with cash providing additional but unquantified consideration. Confidence is medium because authoritative sources disagree on the exact trade date and the public primary ledgers do not quantify the cash component.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Was Only the Beginning
sections.body:
Phoenix's media guide and Basketball-Reference transaction records identify the June 21, 1982 trade clearly. Denver received veteran center Rich Kelley, while Phoenix received Denver's 1982 first-round pick.

The Suns used No. 15 on David Thirdkill. Evaluating only Kelley against Thirdkill would make the deal look minor and perhaps Denver-favored. The source-backed downstream chains change the picture dramatically.

sections.heading: Kelley Played 38 Games Before Denver Converted Him Again
sections.body:
Kelley appeared in 38 regular-season games for Denver in 1982-83, all off the bench. He averaged 14.9 minutes, 4.6 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists.

On February 7, 1983, Denver traded Kelley one-for-one to Utah for Danny Schayes and cash. Because Kelley was the sole outgoing asset, this review can credit the Schayes branch directly to the original acquisition.

sections.heading: Schayes Became a Long-Term Nugget
sections.body:
Schayes played 32 Denver games immediately after the trade, then remained with the Nuggets for eight seasons in total.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 536 regular-season games and 229 starts for Denver. He became a durable interior rotation player through the 1980s and appeared in 48 playoff games for the franchise.

That downstream conversion transforms Denver's side from a 38-game rental into a long-running positive asset chain.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Pick Became David Thirdkill
sections.body:
Phoenix selected Thirdkill at No. 15 in the 1982 draft. He played 49 regular-season games for the Suns as a rookie, started twice and averaged 4.0 points in 10.6 minutes.

That direct rookie return was modest. Phoenix, however, did not let the asset chain stop there.

sections.heading: Thirdkill Became Two Future Second-Round Picks
sections.body:
On October 17, 1983, Phoenix traded Thirdkill to Detroit for a 1986 second-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick. Thirdkill was the sole outgoing Suns asset, so both picks belong directly to this branch.

The 1986 pick became No. 46 Jeff Hornacek. The 1987 pick became No. 46 Bruce Dalrymple, who did not play in the NBA.

sections.heading: Hornacek Changed the Entire Value of the Trade
sections.body:
Hornacek played 468 regular-season games for Phoenix across six seasons and started 343. He averaged 13.7 points and 5.4 assists across his Suns tenure while shooting 51.0 percent from the field.

He developed into an All-Star and averaged 20.1 points in 1991-92. Phoenix then included Hornacek with Andrew Lang and Tim Perry in the 1992 trade for Charles Barkley.

This review does not credit the entire Barkley return to Hornacek because Lang and Perry were also part of that package. It does credit Hornacek's six high-level Suns seasons and the fact that he remained a major trade asset at departure.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Gets the Edge Despite Denver's Excellent Return
sections.body:
Denver's branch was genuinely strong. Kelley became Schayes plus cash, and Schayes delivered 536 games and 229 starts over eight seasons.

Phoenix's branch produced fewer raw franchise games if Thirdkill and Hornacek are combined, but the quality of Hornacek's peak was much higher. He became a long-term starter, an All-Star and a 20-point scorer while remaining valuable enough to become a central component in a later superstar trade.

This is not a one-sided outcome. Both teams turned their original asset into much more than the first-year return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ because the No. 15 pick became Thirdkill, then directly became the future pick used on Hornacek, who delivered 468 games, 343 starts and All-Star production. Denver receives an A because Kelley was converted one-for-one into Schayes and cash, producing 536 Schayes games and 229 starts across eight seasons. Phoenix wins on peak impact rather than volume.

sections.heading: The Draft Labels Need Routing, Not Literal Credit
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the June 23, 1982 exchange as Chicago sending a 1982 second-round pick, later No. 38 Wayne Sappleton, to Golden State for a 1983 second-round pick, later No. 31 Doc Rivers.

Those draft labels describe where the picks eventually landed, not which franchise actually received those players. Treating Rivers as a Bulls player from this trade would be incorrect, and treating Sappleton as a Warriors contributor would be equally misleading.

sections.heading: Golden State Routed the Sappleton Rights to New Jersey
sections.body:
Golden State's executive ledger and the Nets' media guide show that the Warriors sent the rights to Sappleton to New Jersey for a 1983 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference dates that rights transaction June 19, four days before the Chicago pick-swap entry, while other draft-trade ledgers place the rights routing around draft week. This review records the chronology discrepancy but follows the consistent asset chain.

The incoming New Jersey pick became No. 43 Pace Mannion in 1983. Mannion played 57 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84, made no starts and averaged 2.1 points in 8.2 minutes.

That gives Golden State a real realized player return from the Chicago branch, but only a modest one.

sections.heading: Chicago Did Not Draft Doc Rivers
sections.body:
The No. 31 pick eventually belonged to Atlanta, not Chicago. The Hawks used it on Doc Rivers in the 1983 draft.

Contemporary and later accounts identify the pick as compensation connected to Chicago's hiring of former Hawks coach Kevin Loughery. Rivers himself later recalled that Atlanta received the selection because Loughery left the Hawks for the Bulls.

This review therefore credits Chicago with the coaching return attached to the asset, not with Rivers' NBA career.

sections.heading: Loughery Coached Two Bulls Seasons
sections.body:
Loughery coached Chicago in 1983-84 and 1984-85. His Bulls record was 65-99 across 164 regular-season games.

The first season ended 27-55. The second improved to 38-44 and produced a playoff berth, with Chicago losing 3-1 to Milwaukee in the first round.

That is not star-level value, but it is substantially more organizational use than 57 low-minute games from Mannion.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Wins Without Getting Doc Rivers Credit
sections.body:
The old shorthand makes the trade look like Chicago acquired Rivers while Golden State acquired Sappleton. Neither statement reflects the realized franchise outcome.

Golden State converted the No. 38 branch into Mannion, who played 57 reserve games. Chicago converted the future No. 31 asset into coaching compensation tied to Loughery, who ran the team for two full seasons and reached one postseason.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, B/C+. Chicago receives a B because the acquired pick became compensation in a two-season coaching hire that included a playoff appearance. Golden State receives a C+ because the Sappleton-rights branch became Pace Mannion and 57 reserve games. Rivers' Atlanta career is not credited to Chicago, and Sappleton's later Nets career is not credited to Golden State.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought Two Full Starting Seasons
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Dallas and Milwaukee transaction records identify the June 28, 1982 deal as Pat Cummings to the Mavericks for the No. 27 pick in the 1982 draft.

Dallas used Cummings as a major frontcourt piece immediately. He played 81 regular-season games in 1982-83, started 71 and averaged 12.5 points and 8.2 rebounds.

He returned for all 80 games he played in 1983-84 and started every one. Cummings averaged 13.1 points and 8.2 rebounds while Dallas reached the playoffs for the first time in franchise history.

That gives the Mavericks 161 regular-season games and 151 starts from the acquisition across two seasons.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Pick on Fred Roberts
sections.body:
The Bucks selected BYU forward Fred Roberts at No. 27.

Roberts ultimately had a long NBA career, but Milwaukee did not receive that career. Basketball-Reference lists 1982-83 as a season in which Roberts played in Italy, and his NBA debut came the following year with San Antonio.

He never appeared in a regular-season game for the Bucks.

That distinction matters for a franchise-specific trade grade. Drafting a player who later becomes useful elsewhere is not the same as receiving that value.

sections.heading: Dallas Got the Production It Needed
sections.body:
Cummings was not merely a bench piece. He started 151 games in two seasons, averaged double-figure scoring both years and provided durable frontcourt minutes during the Mavericks' transition from expansion team to playoff club.

The timing adds weight to the return. Dallas was building around Rolando Blackman, Mark Aguirre and Derek Harper, and Cummings supplied stability while that young core matured.

Milwaukee's branch produced no direct basketball return before Roberts' NBA career began elsewhere.

sections.heading: Why Dallas Wins Clearly
sections.body:
The Bucks can receive some scouting credit because Roberts became a legitimate NBA player, eventually lasting 13 seasons. That career, however, was realized by San Antonio, Utah, Boston and other teams, not Milwaukee.

Dallas received 161 games, 151 starts and two full seasons of dependable production. Milwaukee received zero regular-season games from the player selected with the pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, A-/F. Dallas receives an A- because a late first/early second-round-level asset turned into two full starting seasons and immediate playoff-era value. Milwaukee receives an F because Roberts never played an NBA game for the Bucks, regardless of the respectable career he later had elsewhere.

sections.heading: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Luke Kennard from Atlanta at the February 5, 2026 trade deadline. In return, the Hawks received Gabe Vincent and the Lakers' 2032 second-round pick. NBA.com's official 2025-26 trade tracker and its transaction report confirm those three assets. The future pick wasn't a 2026 draft choice, and its eventual selection position is unknown; calling it a high second-rounder would invent value that hasn't been established. The league's report also describes an approximately $11 million trade exception created for Atlanta in the transaction. That financial tool can matter to subsequent roster construction, but it isn't a player or an additional draft selection. Keeping those distinctions intact is the starting point for judging the two teams.

sections.heading: Why the Lakers Targeted Kennard
sections.body: Kennard offered Los Angeles a specific shooting skill it had been missing. NBA.com reported that he led the league in 3-point percentage at 49.7% when the deal was arranged, connecting on 74 of 149 attempts as a reserve. The Lakers ranked 25th in 3-pointers made and attempted at that point, so the acquisition targeted a measurable offensive weakness rather than adding an unrelated scorer. Kennard was averaging 7.9 points with 2.2 rebounds and 2.1 assists before the trade. The fit beside players who attract defensive attention was straightforward: another reliable floor-spacing option could punish defenders for collapsing into the paint. Los Angeles nevertheless paid both a veteran guard and a future draft asset to acquire that specialist, which keeps the early grade below an outright bargain.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Return Was More Than Vincent Alone
sections.body: Vincent had a defined NBA résumé before moving to Atlanta. He'd contributed during Miami's 2023 Finals run, but injuries had restricted his time with the Lakers, according to the league's transaction report. By February 5, he was averaging 4.8 points while shooting 34.6% from the field. Those numbers didn't suggest he would immediately replace Kennard's elite perimeter accuracy. The Hawks received something else, though: a 2032 second-round draft claim and the reported trade exception. That combination offered a short-term veteran backcourt option while preserving an opportunity to make a future selection or include the pick in another transaction. The eventual value depends on Vincent's availability, Atlanta's use of the exception and the ultimate draft position, none of which should be presented as a known success.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Grades and the Limits of Hindsight
sections.body: The exchange had clear but different purposes. The Lakers sacrificed depth and a distant second to add one of the league's most efficient long-range shooters for a roster trying to contend immediately. Atlanta converted a useful specialist into a veteran, future draft flexibility and a financial mechanism for roster moves. Both sides gained an asset that could serve their own timeline, and both accepted obvious trade-offs. The original C+ grades for each team are reasonable provisional marks because the short-term fit is plausible without a demonstrated major gain. A more conclusive evaluation would need Kennard's actual Lakers impact, Vincent's Hawks availability and the real uses of the pick and trade exception; simply counting a future second as a guaranteed NBA player would overstate Atlanta's outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Provisional Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, provisionally. The Lakers get C+ for exchanging Gabe Vincent and a distant second for Luke Kennard’s verified elite perimeter shooting; the Hawks get C+ for Vincent, the 2032 pick and financial flexibility. Neither team can claim the unplayed future pick as proven player production, and any final grade should consider the realized post-trade impact rather than a trade-day prediction.

sections.heading: Houston Received Two NBA Contributors
sections.body:
The June 28, 1982 transaction sent Joe Bryant and San Diego's No. 42 draft pick to Houston for the Rockets' No. 32 selection. Both draft picks became NBA players, which makes the deal more useful to grade through direct franchise production rather than draft reputation.

Houston received immediate value from Bryant plus a second rotation player from the later pick.

sections.heading: Joe Bryant Started 56 Games for Houston
sections.body:
Bryant played 81 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 25.4 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

Houston struggled to a 14-68 record, so Bryant's season did not translate into team success. Still, he was a regular starter and one of the more experienced players on a rebuilding roster.

That was Bryant's only NBA season in Houston and the final NBA season of his playing career before he continued professionally overseas.

sections.heading: Jeff Taylor Added 44 Games
sections.body:
Houston used the No. 42 pick on Texas Tech guard Jeff Taylor.

Taylor appeared in 44 regular-season games as a rookie, started five and averaged 17.6 minutes, 3.6 points and 2.5 assists. He was waived the following season, so his Houston contribution was limited to that one year.

Even so, the pick produced a real rotation player rather than a zero-game branch.

sections.heading: Richard Anderson Gave San Diego One Season
sections.body:
The Clippers used No. 32 on UC Santa Barbara big man Richard Anderson. He played 78 regular-season games for San Diego in 1982-83, made five starts and averaged 5.2 points and 3.5 rebounds.

Anderson later had a six-year NBA career, but only that rookie season belongs to San Diego for this trade. He played for Denver in 1983-84 and never returned to the Clippers.

The direct Clippers return was therefore 78 games and five starts.

sections.heading: Why Houston Wins
sections.body:
Bryant and Taylor combined for 125 regular-season games and 61 starts in Houston. Anderson gave San Diego 78 games and five starts.

The Clippers selected a player who ultimately had the longest NBA career of the three, but most of that career happened elsewhere. Franchise-specific realized value favors the Rockets because Bryant supplied a full starting season and Taylor added another 44 appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B for extracting one season of starting production from Bryant plus 44 games from Taylor. San Diego receives a C+ because Anderson was a useful rookie rotation player, but his later career cannot be credited to the Clippers and the direct return was smaller.

sources.title: 1982-83 San Diego Clippers roster and stats

sections.heading: Both Sides Rerouted the Asset They Acquired
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the June 30, 1982 trade as Atlanta receiving Jim Johnstone's draft rights from Kansas City for a 1984 second-round pick. The Hawks' official media guide adds an important detail: the pick originally belonged to Seattle and had reached Atlanta in the 1980 Armond Hill trade.

Neither Atlanta nor Kansas City ultimately used its incoming asset as a long-term player piece.

sections.heading: Johnstone Never Played for Atlanta
sections.body:
Kansas City had selected Johnstone at No. 51 in the 1982 draft. Atlanta acquired his rights the next day but never used him in a regular-season game.

On September 27, 1982, the Hawks sent Johnstone, a 1983 second-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick to San Antonio for George Johnson.

Johnstone later appeared in seven games for San Antonio and sixteen for Detroit in 1982-83. Those games cannot be credited to Atlanta because they occurred after the Hawks had traded him again.

His rights did retain transaction value, but they were only one of three outgoing assets in the George Johnson deal. This review therefore does not assign Atlanta the entire value of Johnson.

sections.heading: Kansas City Also Moved the Pick Again
sections.body:
The Kings held the acquired 1984 second-round pick until June 28, 1983. Kansas City then sent the pick to Chicago together with the draft rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux.

Chicago ultimately exercised the pick at No. 37 in 1984 and selected Ben Coleman.

Coleman did not play in the NBA until 1986-87 after two seasons in Italy, and he never played for Kansas City. His later five-year NBA career belongs to other franchises for direct realized-value purposes.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Gets a Small Edge
sections.body:
Atlanta and Kansas City both converted the acquired asset into a later transaction instead of direct on-court production. That makes this a much closer comparison than the terminal player names suggest.

The difference is asset portability. Kansas City's second-round pick remained a discrete draft asset that could be packaged in a later deal and ultimately became a useful NBA player after reaching Chicago. Atlanta's Johnstone rights also carried value, but they were moved only months later as one piece of a three-asset package.

No original team received a direct NBA game from Johnstone or Coleman. The Kings' advantage is therefore limited to the continuing value of the pick, not Coleman's later career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, C+/C. Kansas City receives a C+ because the 1984 second-rounder remained useful in a later trade and eventually became No. 37 Ben Coleman after leaving the Kings. Atlanta receives a C because Johnstone never played for the Hawks and his rights were only one component of a later multi-asset deal. The margin is modest.

sources.title: Atlanta Hawks historical transactions media guide

sections.heading: Both Teams Received Starting Forwards
sections.body:
The July 7, 1982 swap was straightforward: New York received Truck Robinson, and Phoenix received Maurice Lucas.

Unlike many historical trades in this archive, both incoming players immediately became regular starters and stayed beyond a single season. The question is therefore not whether either side got value, but which veteran produced more of it.

sections.heading: Robinson Gave New York Two Full Starting Seasons
sections.body:
Robinson played 81 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1982-83, starting 76. He averaged 30.0 minutes, 9.5 points and 8.1 rebounds.

He returned for 65 games in 1983-84 and started 63, averaging 10.8 points and 8.4 rebounds. Robinson also appeared in 18 playoff games across those two seasons, starting all of them.

His final Knicks season was brief: two games and one start in 1984-85.

That gives New York 148 regular-season games and 140 starts from Robinson.

sections.heading: Lucas Became an All-Star in Phoenix
sections.body:
Lucas made an even larger immediate impact. In 1982-83 he played 77 regular-season games, started 71 and averaged 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists.

He earned an All-Star selection that season and received MVP votes. Phoenix got both high-end production and heavy minutes from him right away.

Lucas returned for 75 games and 69 starts in 1983-84, averaging 15.9 points and 9.7 rebounds. He then played 63 more games in 1984-85, starting 22 and averaging 13.4 points and 8.8 rebounds.

Across three Phoenix seasons, Lucas played 215 regular-season games and started 162.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got the Higher Peak and More Volume
sections.body:
Robinson was a useful Knicks starter and helped New York reach the playoffs in both 1982-83 and 1983-84. His return was legitimate enough that this trade cannot be treated as a bad move for New York.

Lucas, however, gave Phoenix 67 more regular-season games, 22 more starts and substantially more scoring. His 1982-83 All-Star season also produced a level of individual recognition Robinson did not match in New York.

The Suns therefore received both the better peak and the longer direct tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A-/B. Phoenix receives an A- for three productive seasons, 215 games, 162 starts and an All-Star year from Lucas. New York receives a B because Robinson was a durable two-year starter and playoff contributor, but his direct value was lower in both volume and peak impact.

sources.title: 1982-83 New York Knicks roster and stats

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid a First-Round Pick and Cash for a Starting Center
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Philadelphia transaction records identify the August 27, 1982 package as Darryl Dawkins to the Nets for a 1983 first-round pick and cash. The canonical package specifies the cash at $700,000.

The pick later landed at No. 17, where Philadelphia selected Leo Rautins.

sections.heading: Dawkins Immediately Became New Jersey's Starting Center
sections.body:
Dawkins played 81 regular-season games for the Nets in 1982-83 and started all 81. He averaged 12.0 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks while shooting 59.9 percent from the field.

He was even better in 1983-84, starting 80 of 81 games and averaging 16.8 points on 59.3 percent shooting. New Jersey reached the playoffs and upset defending champion Philadelphia in the first round.

That second season alone supplied more top-end basketball value than the draft return ultimately produced for the 76ers.

sections.heading: He Stayed With the Nets for Five Seasons
sections.body:
Injuries reduced Dawkins' availability after 1983-84, but he still remained a meaningful part of New Jersey's frontcourt. He played 39 games in 1984-85, 51 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across five Nets seasons, Dawkins appeared in 258 regular-season games, started 196 and scored 3,687 points.

This review credits only his New Jersey production. His prior Philadelphia career and later appearances elsewhere do not affect the Nets' realized return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Pick Became Leo Rautins
sections.body:
The 76ers used the No. 17 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Syracuse forward Leo Rautins.

Rautins played 28 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1983-84, started three and averaged 7.0 minutes, 1.7 points, 1.2 rebounds and 1.0 assist.

He played only four more NBA games, all with Atlanta the following season. Philadelphia therefore received just one limited NBA season from the first-round component.

sections.heading: The $700,000 Cash Component Matters
sections.body:
Unlike many historical cash considerations, the amount here is known. Philadelphia received $700,000 in addition to the first-round pick, so its side should not be evaluated as Rautins alone.

The cash provided tangible financial value and raises the 76ers' grade. It still does not produce on-court value comparable to several seasons from a starting-caliber center.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins
sections.body:
The Nets accepted the cost of a first-round pick and substantial cash, but the acquired player immediately became a starter and stayed for five seasons. Dawkins gave New Jersey 258 games and nearly 200 starts.

Philadelphia's draft branch produced 28 games and three starts. Even with the $700,000 payment, the realized basketball gap is too large to call the transaction even.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for acquiring five seasons of center production, including two high-volume starting years. Philadelphia receives a C+ because it obtained a first-round pick and a meaningful known cash payment, but the selected player produced only 28 games for the franchise.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Three Seasons of Useful Guard Depth
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee transaction ledger records the September 9, 1982 exchange directly: the Bucks sent Quinn Buckner to Boston for Dave Cowens, who had been retired since 1980.

Buckner immediately became a major rotation guard for a title contender, while Cowens gave Milwaukee one final NBA season.

sections.heading: Buckner Played 226 Regular-Season Games for Boston
sections.body:
Buckner appeared in 72 games for the Celtics in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 7.9 points, 3.8 assists and 1.5 steals while playing 21.7 minutes per game.

He returned for 79 games in 1983-84 and all 75 games he was available for in 1984-85. Across three Boston seasons, Buckner played 226 regular-season games and started 62.

His role declined over time, but his availability and defensive backcourt depth gave Boston repeated value well beyond the first season.

sections.heading: He Was Part of the 1984 Championship Rotation
sections.body:
Buckner appeared in 23 playoff games during Boston's 1984 title run. He averaged 11.7 minutes in the postseason and served as a reserve behind the Celtics' established starting backcourt.

That championship contribution is not treated as if Buckner were one of the team's primary stars. It still matters because Boston received a dependable playoff rotation player from the trade.

sections.heading: Cowens Gave Milwaukee One Useful Comeback Season
sections.body:
Cowens had not played in either 1980-81 or 1981-82. Milwaukee acquired his rights and convinced him to return for the 1982-83 season.

He played 40 regular-season games, started 34 and averaged 25.4 minutes, 8.1 points, 6.9 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The Bucks won 51 games and reached the Eastern Conference Finals.

Cowens therefore was not an empty return. Milwaukee received legitimate frontcourt minutes from a Hall of Fame veteran during a strong season.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Duration and Championship Value
sections.body:
Cowens retired again after 1982-83, ending Milwaukee's return after 40 regular-season games. Buckner stayed in Boston through 1984-85 and played 226 regular-season games plus 45 playoff games across those three seasons.

The Celtics did not acquire a star, but they received far more durable value and a contributor to a championship team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A/C+. Boston receives an A for three seasons, 226 regular-season games, 62 starts and meaningful playoff depth during the 1984 championship run. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Cowens supplied one credible comeback season on a 51-win team, but the return lasted only 40 games before he retired again.

sections.heading: Atlanta Got One Reserve Season From George Johnson
sections.body:
The September 27, 1982 deal sent George Johnson from San Antonio to Atlanta for Jim Johnstone plus second-round picks in 1983 and 1985.

Johnson was a veteran defensive center, but his Atlanta return was limited. He played 37 regular-season games in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 12.5 minutes, 1.7 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.6 blocks.

He did not play in 1983-84 after refusing to attend Hawks training camp without a guaranteed contract. He later resumed his career with New Jersey, so Atlanta receives credit only for those 37 games.

sections.heading: Johnstone and Lockhart Barely Played for San Antonio
sections.body:
Johnstone appeared in seven regular-season games for the Spurs in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 7.7 minutes and 1.0 point. His San Antonio tenure ended quickly.

The 1983 second-round pick landed at No. 35, where San Antonio selected Darrell Lockhart. Lockhart played only two regular-season games for the Spurs, made no starts and was waived on November 4, 1983.

Those two branches produced just nine direct Spurs games.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Became a Useful Trade Asset
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry identifies the 1985 second-round pick as No. 31 Manute Bol. That terminal draft result is correct, but it does not mean Bol played for San Antonio.

On January 20, 1984, the Spurs traded the future second-round pick to Golden State for Ron Brewer. Brewer then played 40 games for San Antonio in 1983-84 and nine more in 1984-85, starting five total and averaging 8.7 points in his first Spurs stint.

That gives San Antonio 49 regular-season games from the direct downstream conversion of the pick.

sections.heading: Manute Bol Belongs to the Later Washington Branch
sections.body:
Golden State later moved the pick to Washington, and the Bullets used No. 31 in the 1985 draft on Manute Bol.

This review preserves Bol as the terminal pick identity but does not credit his Washington career to San Antonio. The Spurs had already converted the asset into Brewer more than a year before the draft.

This distinction avoids overstating San Antonio's return while still recognizing that the 1985 pick carried real transaction value.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Wins Slightly
sections.body:
Atlanta received 37 reserve games from Johnson. San Antonio received seven games from Johnstone, two from Lockhart and 49 from Brewer through the directly traceable second-round-pick conversion.

The total Spurs basketball return was still modest, but it was broader and lasted longer than Johnson's single Atlanta season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because the original player and 1983 pick produced little, but the 1985 pick was successfully converted into 49 games of Ron Brewer. Atlanta receives a C because Johnson supplied useful shot-blocking depth for 37 games but never played a second season for the Hawks.

sections.heading: Houston Received a Second-Round Pick for Bill Willoughby
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Houston, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 18, 1982 mechanism. Willoughby signed with the Spurs as a veteran free agent, and Houston received San Antonio's 1985 second-round pick as compensation.

That pick is commonly labeled as the selection later used on Yvon Joseph, but Houston did not retain it until the 1985 draft.

sections.heading: Willoughby Gave San Antonio 52 Reserve Games
sections.body:
Willoughby appeared in 52 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1982-83 and made no starts. He averaged 20.4 minutes, 6.1 points and 3.7 rebounds while shooting 46.1 percent from the field.

The Spurs were a 53-win Midwest Division champion and eventually reached the Western Conference Finals. Willoughby therefore supplied real rotation minutes on a contender even though he was not a starter.

His San Antonio stay ended on February 10, 1983, when the Spurs waived him. New Jersey later signed him on March 25, so this review credits only the 52 Spurs games produced directly from this compensation transaction.

sections.heading: Houston Rerouted the Pick Within Three Weeks
sections.body:
On November 10, 1982, Houston traded the 1985 second-round pick together with the 1983 second-round pick received from San Antonio in the Mike Dunleavy compensation transaction to New Jersey for James Bailey.

The Nets ultimately used the 1985 selection at No. 36 on Yvon Joseph. That draft outcome belongs to New Jersey, not Houston, so this review should not score Joseph's NBA career as the Rockets' realized result.

For Houston, the relevant value is that the pick helped complete the Bailey acquisition.

sections.heading: Bailey Produced Two Useful Rockets Seasons
sections.body:
Bailey played 69 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83, started 39 and averaged 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds. He returned for 73 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds.

His two-year Houston total was 142 games and 39 starts. That is a strong downstream outcome from the two-pick package.

This review does not assign all of Bailey's value to the Willoughby pick. The Dunleavy compensation pick was equally necessary, so the proper conclusion is that this 1985 second-rounder carried meaningful partial transaction value rather than becoming Bailey by itself.

sections.heading: Why Houston Gets a Modest Edge
sections.body:
San Antonio received 52 reserve games and useful regular-season minutes from Willoughby before waiving him. That is a real return, especially on a 53-win team.

Houston received an asset that became half of the package for a player who produced 142 games and 39 starts over two seasons. Even with conservative attribution, the downstream value of the pick slightly exceeds Willoughby's shorter Spurs tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B because the compensation pick became an important part of the James Bailey acquisition without requiring this review to credit the entire Bailey return to one asset. San Antonio receives a C+ for 52 useful reserve games before Willoughby was waived in February.

sections.heading: Indiana Received One Season From Brad Branson
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction ledger records the October 25, 1982 exchange directly: the Cavaliers sent Brad Branson to Indiana for a 1983 second-round pick.

Branson played 62 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1982-83 and made two starts. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 5.5 points and 2.8 rebounds while shooting 42.5 percent from the field.

Those 62 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Indiana therefore received one season of reserve frontcourt production and no longer-term branch from the player.

sections.heading: Cleveland Did Not Draft Scooter McCray
sections.body:
The incoming pick ultimately became No. 36 in the 1983 NBA Draft, where Seattle selected Scooter McCray.

That draft label can be misleading if treated as Cleveland's realized player outcome. On June 27, one day before the draft, Cleveland traded the pick to Seattle for Lonnie Shelton.

Basketball-Reference records the pick-for-Shelton transaction, while Pro Sports Transactions also lists cash going from Cleveland to Seattle. Because the Cavaliers added cash, this review cannot assign Shelton's entire later Cleveland career to the Branson pick by itself.

sections.heading: The Pick Helped Bring Lonnie Shelton to Cleveland
sections.body:
Shelton played 79 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84 and started 78. He averaged 26.6 minutes, 10.8 points, 4.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

He returned for 57 games and 14 starts in 1984-85, then 44 games and one start in 1985-86.

Across those three Cavaliers seasons, Shelton appeared in 180 regular-season games and started 93. The first season alone gave Cleveland a near full-time starter from a package built around the acquired second-round pick plus cash.

sections.heading: Scooter McCray's Career Belongs to Seattle
sections.body:
Seattle used No. 36 on McCray, who played 53 regular-season games for the SuperSonics across two seasons before later appearing for Cleveland as a free agent in 1986-87.

Those later Cleveland games are not credited to this 1982 trade. McCray reached Cleveland years later through an independent free-agent signing, after the original pick had already been spent in the Shelton transaction.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Indiana obtained 62 reserve games and two starts from Branson. Cleveland converted the second-round pick, together with additional cash, into a veteran who supplied 180 games and 93 starts over three seasons.

The cash component prevents the pick from receiving full credit for Shelton, but the transaction chain still shows that Cleveland preserved and then leveraged the asset for much more roster value than Branson produced in Indiana.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, B/C+. Cleveland receives a B because the acquired second-round pick became a central part of the Lonnie Shelton package and helped produce three seasons of frontcourt value. Indiana receives a C+ for 62 useful reserve games from Branson, with no additional NBA return after his lone Pacers season.

sections.heading: The Canonical Player Name Needed a Correction
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger identifies the incoming veteran as Mickey Johnson, not Wallace Johnson. The 1982-83 Nets roster confirms Johnson played 42 games for New Jersey after the trade.

This review corrects that asset identity while preserving the rest of the package: New Jersey received Mickey Johnson and the rights to 1982 second-round pick Fred Roberts, while Milwaukee received Phil Ford and New Jersey's 1983 second-round pick.

sections.heading: Mickey Johnson Gave New Jersey 42 Games
sections.body:
Johnson played 42 regular-season games for the Nets, started seven and averaged 23.8 minutes, 13.4 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists.

His Nets stay lasted only until February 6, 1983, when New Jersey traded Johnson and Sleepy Floyd to Golden State for Micheal Ray Richardson. This review credits only the 42 direct Nets games from this transaction and does not assign the later Richardson return entirely to Johnson because Floyd was a major co-asset.

sections.heading: Fred Roberts Never Played for the Nets
sections.body:
Roberts had been Milwaukee's No. 27 pick in the 1982 draft but spent 1982-83 in Italy. New Jersey held his NBA rights rather than receiving immediate on-court value.

On June 7, 1983, the Nets sent Roberts and another 1983 second-round pick to San Antonio as compensation for signing Stan Albeck as head coach. Roberts therefore produced zero New Jersey regular-season games.

His later 818-game NBA career cannot be credited to the Nets because it began with San Antonio after New Jersey had moved his rights.

sections.heading: Phil Ford Became a Milwaukee Starter
sections.body:
Ford had appeared in only seven games for New Jersey before the trade. With Milwaukee he played 70 regular-season games in 1982-83 and started 56.

He averaged 20.7 minutes, 6.8 points and 3.6 assists while the Bucks went 51-31 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. That gave Milwaukee a full season of real rotation and starting value.

sections.heading: The No. 41 Pick Became Ted Kitchel
sections.body:
Milwaukee used the 1983 second-round pick on Indiana forward Ted Kitchel at No. 41. Kitchel never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That means the pick branch itself produced zero direct Bucks games, but Ford's 70-game season still outweighs New Jersey's shorter Johnson return.

sections.heading: Why Milwaukee Wins
sections.body:
New Jersey received 42 games and seven starts from Johnson, plus Roberts' rights, which never turned into a Nets appearance. Milwaukee received 70 games and 56 starts from Ford, while Kitchel produced no NBA games.

The gap is meaningful but not enormous because Johnson was productive during his short New Jersey stay and Roberts retained some transaction utility as a rights asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee receives a B+ for 70 games and 56 starts from Ford at a modest cost, even though Kitchel did not reach the NBA. New Jersey receives a B- because Johnson gave the Nets 42 useful games and Roberts' rights retained value, but neither incoming asset lasted long enough to match Ford's direct Milwaukee contribution.
