sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Detroit and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the February 24, 1988 package: the Pistons received James Edwards and sent Ron Moore plus a future second-round pick. That pick did not convey until 1991, when Phoenix used No. 46 on Richard Dumas. The long delay is central to the hindsight comparison. Detroit received an established veteran immediately for a title push, while Phoenix's most meaningful return arrived more than three years later through the draft.

sections.heading: Detroit Return
sections.body: Edwards joined a Pistons team already moving toward the top of the Eastern Conference and fit a role Detroit needed: experienced frontcourt scoring behind and alongside Bill Laimbeer and Rick Mahorn, and later as a larger offensive piece as the roster evolved. He appeared in Detroit's 1988 postseason run to the NBA Finals, then remained part of the rotation for the back-to-back championship teams in 1988-89 and 1989-90. He gave Detroit multiple seasons of regular-season and playoff availability rather than a short rental. In 1989-90, Edwards averaged double figures and became an especially useful interior scorer during a championship season. The key grading point is not that he was a franchise star; he was not. It is that Detroit converted a marginal player and a future second into several seasons of dependable frontcourt production during the exact competitive window that produced two titles.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Ron Moore was not the value center of the Suns side. His Phoenix stay was brief and did not approach Edwards' Detroit impact. The future second-round pick, however, became much more important. Phoenix selected Richard Dumas at No. 46 in the 1991 draft. After missing the 1991-92 NBA season, Dumas emerged in 1992-93 as one of the league's most productive rookies, averaging roughly 16 points per game in 48 regular-season appearances and starting for stretches on a Suns team that went 62-20 and reached the NBA Finals. He also supplied athletic scoring in the postseason. That is legitimate realized value from the draft asset and prevents the Phoenix grade from falling into the failing range. His Suns tenure was also short and unstable, though, and he never developed into a durable multi-season cornerstone.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Phoenix deserves substantial credit because the pick was not merely theoretical: it became Dumas, and Dumas contributed to a Finals team. But Detroit received the more durable and better-timed return. Edwards helped three consecutive Finals teams, won two championships with the Pistons and remained useful across several seasons. Dumas' peak was exciting and meaningful, yet much shorter. Moore adds little to Phoenix's side. The trade therefore is not a landslide, but Detroit clearly captured more total realized value and did so during a championship window.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit Pistons Win. Detroit earns an A because Edwards became a multi-year championship rotation piece and provided strong timing value without costing a premium first-round asset. Phoenix earns a B because the second-round pick became a genuinely productive Finals-team contributor in Richard Dumas, even though the return was delayed and short-lived. The grade does not credit Detroit for Edwards' pre-trade career or Phoenix for anything Dumas did outside the Suns; it measures only realized value tied to this exchange.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix drafted St. John's forward-center Jayson Williams with the No. 21 pick in the 1990 draft, but the relationship stalled before his rookie season. Contemporary Associated Press reporting said Williams preferred an East Coast team, had considered Europe and was offered only a one-year minimum contract by Phoenix after missing the club's rookie camp. On October 28, Phoenix moved his draft rights to Philadelphia for a future first-round pick. Basketball-Reference records that pick as the 1994 first that later became No. 6 Sharone Wright, while the draft-trade ledger describes the obligation as lottery-protected in 1993 before it rolled into 1994.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Williams did become an NBA player immediately, so this was not an empty rights acquisition. He played 52 games with one start as a rookie, averaging 3.5 points and 2.1 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. In 1991-92 he played another 50 games with eight starts, averaging 4.1 points and 2.9 rebounds. Across two Philadelphia seasons that is 102 games and nine starts: real depth value, but not first-round-caliber production. Philadelphia also preserved some downstream value. On October 8, 1992 the 76ers traded Williams to New Jersey for two future second-round choices, later listed as the 1994 No. 41 pick and the 1997 No. 35 pick. That conversion keeps the Philadelphia return above a failing grade, even though Williams' later All-Star career with the Nets cannot be credited back to the 76ers.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The Suns received the more valuable asset: a future first that eventually landed sixth overall. Phoenix did not wait for the pick to convey. On December 7, 1990, only forty days after the Williams trade, the Suns sent Eddie Johnson, their 1991 first-round pick and this acquired future first to Seattle for Xavier McDaniel. The 1994 first therefore had immediate trade-market value inside a major veteran acquisition. The pick later moved through additional transactions and eventually became Sharone Wright, but Wright's career belongs to the team that ultimately exercised the selection, not to Phoenix. The source-backed credit here is the premium first-round asset Phoenix obtained and then successfully used as trade capital.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Philadelphia got two useful reserve seasons, then recovered two second-round assets. That is a legitimate return and explains why the deal is not a disaster. The problem is the price. A future first that ultimately landed at No. 6 was substantially more valuable than Williams' direct 76ers contribution, and Phoenix demonstrated that value almost immediately by using the pick in the McDaniel package. The legacy slight Philadelphia edge had the direction backwards because it focused on Williams becoming an NBA player without weighing the eventual position and transaction utility of the outgoing first.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix Suns Win, A- to C+. Phoenix turned the rights to an unsigned No. 21 pick into a premium future first and quickly used that asset in a major trade. Philadelphia received 102 games of reserve value and later two second-round picks, enough to avoid a harsh grade, but not enough to match the first-round asset it surrendered.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix and Boston transaction logs resolve the structure more precisely than the legacy generic 'future considerations' wording. Boston sent Charlie Scott to Phoenix on March 14, 1972 for Paul Silas and cash, with Silas agreeing to terms with Boston in September to complete the transaction. Scott was still playing in the ABA when the deal was arranged, so Phoenix was initially acquiring NBA rights rather than an active Celtics roster player. He joined the Suns late in the 1971-72 season and immediately became the centerpiece of their offense.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Scott played six Suns games at the end of 1971-72, then became an All-Star in each of his next three full Phoenix seasons. In 1972-73 he played 81 games and averaged 25.3 points, 6.1 assists and 4.2 rebounds. He followed with 25.4 points and 5.2 assists in 52 games in 1973-74, then 24.3 points and 4.5 assists across 69 games in 1974-75. That is three consecutive All-Star scoring seasons from a player acquired as rights. Phoenix also preserved enormous transaction value. On May 23, 1975, the Suns traded Scott to Boston for Paul Westphal plus second-round choices in 1975 and 1976. Westphal became a franchise star in Phoenix. That later trade is a separate evaluation, so its entire outcome should not simply be copied backward, but it proves the Scott asset remained premium when Phoenix eventually moved him.

sections.heading: Boston Return
sections.body: Silas fit Boston's championship core almost perfectly. He played 80 games in 1972-73, 82 in 1973-74, 82 in 1974-75 and 81 in 1975-76. He was named All-Defensive Second Team in his first Celtics season, All-Defensive First Team in 1975 and 1976, and an All-Star in 1975. His rebounding was especially valuable for a team built around John Havlicek, Dave Cowens and Jo Jo White: Silas collected more than 1,000 rebounds in both 1974-75 and 1975-76. Most importantly, he was a major rotation piece on Boston's 1974 and 1976 NBA championship teams. The Celtics received four full seasons of high-end defense, rebounding and postseason value from the future-consideration component, while the cash piece was secondary.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: This is one of the rare trades where forcing a winner makes the analysis worse. Phoenix received three full All-Star seasons from Scott, then converted him into the package that included Westphal. Boston received four durable Silas seasons, three All-Defensive selections, an All-Star appearance and two championships. The teams extracted different kinds of value but both outcomes were elite relative to the assets they surrendered. The legacy B-/B- grades dramatically undersell the transaction because they ignore Scott's sustained All-Star peak, Silas's championship defense and the fact that Scott remained a premium trade asset. An A+ for Phoenix and an A+ for Boston better reflect the realized outcomes without double-counting the full downstream Westphal career. Final verdict: Even Trade.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Atlanta's and San Antonio's official releases agree on the core deal: the Hawks received Dejounte Murray and Jock Landale; the Spurs received Danilo Gallinari, a protected Charlotte first, Atlanta's unprotected 2025 and 2027 first-round picks, and the right to swap 2026 firsts. That package looked expensive in 2022 and has become easier to value because two of the Atlanta-controlled draft mechanisms have now converted into actual Spurs selections.

sections.heading: Atlanta Return
sections.body: Murray was productive. He played 74 games in 2022-23 and 78 in 2023-24, averaging 20.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 6.1 assists in his first Hawks season and 22.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 6.4 assists in his second. Atlanta reached the 2023 playoffs but lost to Boston in the first round, then lost in the 2024 Play-In Tournament. The Murray-Trae Young pairing therefore supplied high-level individual production without producing the contender jump the trade was designed to create. Landale never played for Atlanta; the Hawks sent him to Phoenix for cash on July 6, 2022. Murray did retain substantial transaction value. In July 2024 Atlanta traded him to New Orleans for Dyson Daniels, Larry Nance Jr., E.J. Liddell, Cody Zeller and two future first-round picks. That later trade should be judged separately, but it prevents the original Hawks return from being treated as a dead-end asset.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: Gallinari was waived, so the Spurs' basketball value was always in the draft package. The 2025 unprotected Atlanta first became No. 14, which San Antonio used on Carter Bryant. The 2026 swap also became real value: San Antonio ended up with Atlanta's No. 20 slot and selected Jayden Quaintance. The protected Charlotte first never became a Spurs draft selection, but San Antonio preserved its market value and included that conditional first in the February 2025 package for De'Aaron Fox. The largest unresolved piece is still ahead: Atlanta's 2027 first remains unprotected and belongs to San Antonio. That means the Spurs have already realized two first-round selections plus transaction value from the Charlotte asset while another unprotected first remains outstanding.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio wins clearly. Atlanta did not receive nothing: Murray delivered 152 regular-season games of high-level guard play and later brought back a meaningful package from New Orleans. That makes a D-range grade too harsh. But the Spurs converted one outgoing All-Star into a long asset runway that has already produced Carter Bryant, Jayden Quaintance and a piece of the De'Aaron Fox trade, with the unprotected 2027 Atlanta first still to come. An A+ for San Antonio reflects both realized and remaining draft value. A B- for Atlanta recognizes Murray's strong individual production and retained resale value while accounting for the lack of team-level breakthrough and the extraordinary draft cost. Final verdict: San Antonio Spurs Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Los Angeles and Phoenix swapped four veterans on January 10, 1997. The Lakers sent Cedric Ceballos and Rumeal Robinson to the Suns for Robert Horry and Joe Kleine. Contemporary reporting described the move as a fit change as much as a talent exchange: Ceballos had been a high-volume scorer before Shaquille O'Neal arrived, while Horry offered defense, size and a lower-usage role that fit the Lakers' new roster construction. The transaction logs for both franchises record the same four-player exchange, so the asset ledger is unusually straightforward.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: Horry is the asset that decides the long-term evaluation. He joined the Lakers during the 1996-97 season and immediately supplied frontcourt versatility, three-point range and playoff experience from Houston's championship teams. The Lakers' season history notes that Horry provided an immediate spark and set a playoff record by making seven three-pointers without a miss against Utah that spring. More important, he remained with Los Angeles through the franchise's 2000, 2001 and 2002 championships. His box-score production was modest for a starter-level player, but his value was tied to lineup fit and high-leverage postseason possessions. The most famous example came in Game 4 of the 2002 Western Conference finals against Sacramento, when Horry hit the game-winning three that tied the series. Los Angeles eventually won that series in seven games and completed its third straight championship. Kleine was a secondary piece and was traded again in February 1997, so almost all of the Lakers' enduring value came from Horry.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Ceballos gave Phoenix real short-term offense. Basketball-Reference lists him at 15.3 points and 6.6 rebounds per game in 42 appearances for the Suns after the trade, and contemporary coverage showed that he quickly regained a larger scoring role after being reduced in Los Angeles. That production helped a Phoenix team that recovered from a poor start to reach the playoffs. The problem is duration. Ceballos played only 35 games for Phoenix the next season before being traded to Dallas in February 1998. Robinson supplied almost no return value and was waived by the Suns on February 14, 1997, barely a month after the transaction. Phoenix therefore received a useful scorer, but not a lasting building block.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The trade looks much different when measured across the full life of the assets rather than the first few months. Phoenix can defend the move as a short-term roster correction because Ceballos was productive immediately and Horry had not fit cleanly during his brief Suns tenure. Los Angeles, however, acquired a player whose role scaled with a championship roster. Horry did not become an All-Star, yet he stayed through six full Lakers seasons, won three titles with the club and produced several postseason moments that made his reputation. That combination of longevity, fit and championship leverage overwhelms the Suns' shorter Ceballos return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A+/C+. Los Angeles receives an A+ because Horry became a durable playoff rotation piece across three championships and supplied direct high-leverage postseason value. Phoenix receives a C+ because Ceballos was genuinely productive after returning, but the second stint was short and Robinson added almost nothing. The Suns did not receive zero value, so this is not a failed transaction in the immediate sense. Over the full timeline, though, the Lakers acquired the one player whose contribution became part of a championship-era identity.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, Washington and league transaction logs all record the June 22, 1979 deal the same way: Washington sent Phoenix its 1979 first-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick for the rights to Steve Malovic. Contemporary Washington Post reporting adds useful context. The Bullets were the defending Eastern Conference champions, had just lost the 1979 NBA Finals, and believed the 6-foot-10 Malovic could help immediately; general manager Bob Ferry said Malovic had already agreed to contract terms. The first-round choice was No. 22 overall only three days later, while the future third became No. 59 in 1980.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Phoenix used the No. 22 pick on Kentucky guard Kyle Macy. Macy stayed in college for 1979-80, then joined the Suns and became a durable five-year rotation and starting guard. He played all 82 regular-season games in each of his first four NBA seasons, started 72 games in 1981-82, and later started 52 games in 1984-85. Across his Phoenix tenure he appeared in 393 regular-season games with 178 starts, scored 4,180 points, handed out 1,555 assists and recorded 491 steals. His shooting efficiency was also a real asset: his five Suns seasons included field-goal percentages of .511, .514, .517, .501 and .485, plus elite free-throw shooting. Macy was not a franchise superstar, but he was a long-term NBA guard who gave Phoenix years of rotation stability and significant starting value. The 1980 third-round pick became Clemson forward John Campbell at No. 59. Campbell never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so that second draft asset produced no realized league value. That miss does not change the overall return because the first-round pick alone became a productive five-year Suns player.

sections.heading: Washington Return
sections.body: Malovic's Washington outcome was almost empty. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Bullets appearance in 1979-80, totaling six minutes and one point. He then played 28 games for San Diego and 10 for Detroit in the same season, finishing his NBA career after 39 total games. Washington therefore traded a first-round pick and a future third for a player who contributed a single regular-season game to the franchise. The move made more sense in process terms than the raw hindsight result suggests because Washington was a veteran contender trying to add immediate frontcourt depth, and Malovic was a 6-foot-10 prospect who had delayed his NBA arrival to preserve college eligibility. Still, TradeVerdicts grades realized value, and the realized Bullets return was negligible.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins decisively. The Suns converted rights to a player who never became part of their NBA rotation into a first-round pick that produced five full seasons of Kyle Macy plus an additional draft chance. Washington received only one Malovic game. An A for Phoenix reflects the extraordinary asset conversion without inflating Macy into a star he was not. A D for Washington is severe but fair: the Bullets at least acquired a legitimate prospect rather than receiving nothing, yet the first-round pick they surrendered became a useful long-term guard while Malovic's Washington career lasted six minutes. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: NBA.com's draft tracker and Phoenix's official release agree on the package. Philadelphia selected Mikal Bridges at No. 10 and traded his rights to Phoenix for the rights to No. 16 pick Zhaire Smith plus Miami's unprotected 2021 first-round selection, an asset Phoenix had acquired earlier in the Goran Dragic trade. The 2021 pick was especially notable because it carried no protection. It later landed at No. 18 and ultimately became Tre Mann after moving through additional transactions, but Philadelphia had already used the asset in a different trade long before draft night 2021.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Bridges became one of the NBA's most durable two-way wings. He played all 82 games as a rookie, all 73 in the shortened 2019-20 season, all 72 in 2020-21, all 82 in 2021-22 and all 56 Suns games before the 2023 deadline. That is 365 regular-season games and 298 starts without missing a Suns game. He grew from a low-usage defender into a 13-to-17-point scorer, started all 22 playoff games during Phoenix's 2021 run to the NBA Finals and earned All-Defensive First Team in 2022 while finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting. Phoenix then retained significant exit value. In February 2023, Bridges was one of the central players sent to Brooklyn in the Kevin Durant trade. Durant's entire acquisition cannot be credited to Bridges because Phoenix also sent Cam Johnson, Jae Crowder and a large draft package, but Bridges' inclusion shows that the 2018 asset remained premium currency after four and a half productive Suns seasons.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Smith's career never developed. He suffered a foot fracture before his rookie season and then a severe food-allergy complication during recovery. He eventually appeared in six games as a rookie and seven more in 2019-20, finishing his Philadelphia tenure with only 13 NBA games and two starts. The 2021 Miami first was the meaningful portion of the return. In February 2019, Philadelphia included that unprotected pick in the multi-asset package that acquired Tobias Harris, Boban Marjanovic and Mike Scott from the Clippers. The Sixers also sent Landry Shamet, Wilson Chandler, Mike Muscala, their own protected 2020 first and two second-round picks, so the Harris return cannot be assigned entirely to the Miami selection. Still, the pick demonstrably carried enough market value to function as a major component of a win-now trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins clearly because Bridges delivered 365 consecutive regular-season appearances, elite defense, a Finals run and premium downstream trade value. That supports an A+ grade. Philadelphia's player outcome was poor, but grading the Sixers as a D ignores the unprotected Miami first and the leverage it supplied in the Harris deal. A B- better reflects a return consisting of one failed prospect plus one genuinely valuable first-round asset that Philadelphia converted into veteran help. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Utah's official all-time transaction history confirms the June 28, 2005 deal: Portland sent the No. 3 pick, which became Deron Williams, for No. 6 Martell Webster, No. 27 Linas Kleiza and a conditional 2006 first-round pick that ultimately became No. 30 Joel Freeland. Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction log independently matches the package. The trade was not simply Williams for Webster; Portland received three first-round assets and immediately used one of them in another draft-night move.

sections.heading: Utah Return
sections.body: Williams became the franchise-level point guard Utah was paying to reach. He appeared in 439 regular-season games for the Jazz from 2005-06 through the 2011 trade to New Jersey, became a full-time starter in his second season, and developed into one of the league's top playmakers. He made the All-NBA Second Team in 2007-08 and 2009-10 and was an All-Star in 2010 and 2011. Utah also reached the 2007 Western Conference finals with Williams averaging 19.2 points and 8.6 assists in that postseason. Those are direct Jazz results, so no later Nets or Cavaliers production is needed to justify an elite grade.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Portland's side was better than the legacy D- suggests. Webster played 301 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers across five seasons and started 164 of them, including 70 starts in 2007-08 and 49 in 2009-10. The No. 27 pick became Linas Kleiza, whose rights Portland packaged with its own No. 35 pick Ricky Sanchez to acquire No. 22 Jarrett Jack from Denver. Because another Portland asset was required, only part of Jack's three-season, 240-game Portland value should be credited back to this Utah trade. The protected 2006 first-rounder conveyed at No. 30 as Joel Freeland, who later played 151 games for Portland from 2012-13 through 2014-15.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland converted the package into multiple useful rotation seasons, so the deal was not a barren return. The gap is still large: Utah obtained a two-time All-NBA point guard who drove a four-year playoff run and a conference-finals appearance, while Portland's assets produced depth and secondary starters rather than a comparable centerpiece. Utah receives an A+ because the aggressive move up landed a genuine franchise lead guard. Portland receives a C+ because Webster, partial downstream Jarrett Jack value and Freeland created real utility, but the combined realized return fell well short of Williams' Utah peak. Final verdict: Utah Jazz Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Toronto's official release and the NBA trade tracker confirm the February 9, 2023 package: Jakob Poeltl to the Raptors for Khem Birch, Toronto's 2023 second-round pick, its 2025 second-round pick and a protected 2024 first. The first was protected 1-6 and conveyed in 2024 when Toronto landed at No. 8. Basketball-Reference maps the two seconds to No. 44 in 2023 and No. 37 in 2025, but those pick labels should not be confused with players who necessarily stayed with San Antonio. The transaction has to be graded through the actual asset chain.

sections.heading: Toronto Return
sections.body: Poeltl immediately returned to a starting-center role and gave Toronto the interior size and screening the roster had lacked. The Raptors re-signed him in July 2023, so the return was not a short rental. His value is real and multi-year: Toronto acquired a proven center who already understood the organization and remained part of the core beyond the trade-deadline season. The cost became much steeper once the protected first conveyed at No. 8. Toronto did not surrender an abstract future first; it surrendered a top-ten selection after a 25-win 2023-24 season.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: The 2023 second became No. 44, which San Antonio used on Sidy Cissoko. The 2024 first became No. 8. The Spurs selected Rob Dillingham and immediately traded his rights to Minnesota for an unprotected 2031 first-round pick and a 2030 first-round swap protected only for the No. 1 pick. That draft-night conversion is the most important downstream result because it turns the original Toronto first into two pieces of distant first-round equity. The 2025 Toronto second later became No. 37, but San Antonio had already routed that pick to Dallas in the 2023 Grant Williams transaction; Detroit eventually selected Chaz Lanier after another trade. That later player should not be counted as Spurs value from the Poeltl deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio receives an A- because it turned a veteran center into a top-eight first, two seconds and additional future first-round leverage through the Dillingham draft-night trade. Toronto receives a C+ because Poeltl has provided legitimate multi-year starter value, but the No. 8 pick was a high price for a team that did not become a contender after the acquisition. The final verdict is San Antonio Spurs Win. The grade recognizes that the 2030 and 2031 assets remain future value as of 2026 and therefore stops short of treating them as already realized star production.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix's and Sacramento's transaction logs confirm the June 21, 1987 package: Eddie Johnson to the Suns for Ed Pinckney and a 1988 second-round pick. The pick was later identified as the selection that became No. 30 Fennis Dembo, but Sacramento did not actually make that selection. On October 15, 1987, the Kings traded the pick to New York for center Jawann Oldham. New York later moved it to Detroit, which drafted Dembo. The source-backed return for Sacramento is therefore Pinckney plus the value Sacramento itself realized by converting the pick into Oldham—not Dembo's Pistons career.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Johnson immediately became a major scorer. He played 73 games with 59 starts in 1987-88 and averaged 17.7 points. In 1988-89 he moved primarily to the bench, played 70 games, averaged 21.5 points on 49.7 percent shooting and won NBA Sixth Man of the Year. In 1989-90 he played 64 games and averaged 16.9 points, then appeared in 15 more Suns games in 1990-91 before moving to Seattle. Across those Phoenix seasons he scored thousands of points, delivered three straight years of high-volume offense and provided postseason scoring during the club's late-1980s resurgence. His 1988-89 award season is especially important because it shows the trade produced more than raw volume: Phoenix acquired a player who became one of the NBA's best reserves and a major offensive piece.

sections.heading: Sacramento Return
sections.body: Pinckney gave Sacramento legitimate rotation value. He played 79 games with seven starts in 1987-88, averaging 6.2 points and 2.9 rebounds in 14.9 minutes, then played 51 more Kings games with 24 starts in 1988-89 before being traded to Boston. The second-round pick also produced a realized Kings return before draft night. Sacramento sent the pick to New York for Jawann Oldham. Oldham played 54 games with 13 starts for the 1987-88 Kings, averaging 5.5 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.5 minutes. He missed 1988-89 with a knee injury, so the downstream pick conversion delivered only one useful Sacramento season. That is meaningful depth from two separate pieces, but neither return approached Johnson's Phoenix scoring peak or longevity.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins clearly. The Suns acquired a player who gave them more than two hundred regular-season games, a 21.5-point Sixth Man of the Year season, and three consecutive years as a major scorer. Sacramento received two seasons of Pinckney and one season of Oldham through the pick conversion, so the Kings deserve more than a failing grade. Their package provided useful frontcourt minutes and retained value instead of disappearing. A for Phoenix reflects Johnson's award-level production and sustained scoring impact. A C+ for Sacramento recognizes real rotation value from Pinckney and Oldham but also the large gap between that depth and the star-level scorer the Kings surrendered. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, Seattle and league transaction logs all place the deal on June 4, 1980: Phoenix sent Paul Westphal to Seattle and received Dennis Johnson. The date correction is important because the legacy archive record carried June 3. Both players arrived with major credentials. Westphal had just averaged 21.9 points for Phoenix and made the 1980 All-NBA First Team, while Johnson was coming off a 19.0-point season for Seattle with All-NBA Second Team and All-Defensive First Team honors.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Johnson immediately supplied the stronger sustained return. In 1980-81 he played 79 games, averaged 18.8 points, made the All-Star team, earned All-NBA First Team and All-Defensive First Team honors, and helped Phoenix win the Pacific Division. He followed with 80 games, 19.5 points per game, another All-Star appearance and another All-Defensive First Team selection in 1981-82. In 1982-83 he played 77 games, started 74, averaged 14.2 points and 5.0 assists, and again made All-Defensive First Team. That is three seasons of high-level two-way guard play directly realized by Phoenix. Johnson's later championships with Boston confirm his longevity, but they are not credited as Suns value in this transaction.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body: Westphal was still a real player, so Seattle did not receive an empty return. He averaged 16.7 points and 4.1 assists in 36 games and was selected as an All-Star in 1980-81. The problem was availability. Basketball-Reference shows only 36 appearances, and contemporary transaction research plus UPI reporting document a right-foot problem that repeatedly removed him from the lineup. He did not play another regular-season game for Seattle after that season. That makes the Sonics return meaningful but brief: one productive partial season from a decorated guard rather than multiple years of dependable top-end play.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The direct club value favors Phoenix by a wide margin. Johnson gave the Suns 236 regular-season games across three seasons and remained an elite defender throughout that run; Westphal gave Seattle 36 games in one injury-disrupted season. Phoenix receives an A- for converting an outgoing star into a younger guard who immediately produced All-NBA and repeated All-Defensive value. Seattle receives a C- because Westphal still produced at an All-Star level when available, preventing the return from being treated as a total loss. The final verdict is Phoenix Suns Win, based on realized value with later Boston accomplishments excluded from Phoenix's grade.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix's official announcement and Basketball-Reference agree on the July 20, 2007 structure. The Suns sent Kurt Thomas plus their own 2008 and 2010 first-round picks to Seattle for a conditional 2009 second-round pick. Phoenix also received an $8 million trade exception, not the $9 million figure carried by the legacy archive entry. The Suns openly framed the move around salary relief and roster flexibility, while Seattle was rebuilding around Kevin Durant and Jeff Green.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body:
The first 2008 pick became No. 24, Serge Ibaka. That alone creates substantial realized value: Ibaka developed into a long-term defensive anchor for the Oklahoma City core and played 14 NBA seasons. Basketball-Reference credits the No. 24 pick to Seattle, and the Thunder's own historical profile describes the organization selecting Ibaka at No. 24 after scouting him internationally. The 2010 first became No. 26, Quincy Pondexter, adding another first-round asset to the return.

Kurt Thomas also was not dead salary from Seattle's perspective. He gave the club part of the 2007-08 season and was then traded to San Antonio on February 20, 2008 for Brent Barry, Francisco Elson and a 2009 first-round pick. Seattle waived Barry, but the ability to turn Thomas into another first shows that the veteran component retained transaction value beyond his short stay. The original deal therefore produced both immediate optionality and multiple draft assets rather than relying entirely on one lucky pick outcome.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The Suns received the conditional 2009 second-round pick that Basketball-Reference later maps to No. 57, Emir Preldžić, along with the $8 million trade exception and the intended financial relief. Contemporary Associated Press reporting described the move as a salary-cutting decision after Phoenix signed Grant Hill and while the team was already carrying a high payroll. That context explains the transaction, but financial flexibility does not erase the basketball assets surrendered.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle receives an A+ because it converted cap capacity into Thomas, two first-round picks and eventually Ibaka, then extracted more value from Thomas in a later trade. Phoenix receives a D+ because the club achieved the intended salary relief but surrendered the best long-term basketball asset and an additional first to do it. The verdict remains Seattle SuperSonics Win. The grade credits only traceable assets from this transaction and its direct downstream chain rather than unrelated Oklahoma City success.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Chicago's own historical archive and Basketball-Reference both describe the October 2, 1995 transaction as Dennis Rodman to the Bulls for Will Perdue. The legacy archive entry's vague 'other considerations' asset is not supported by those primary and high-quality transaction records and is removed rather than treated as hidden value. At the time, Chicago was specifically looking for the rebounding and defensive presence lost when Horace Grant departed, while San Antonio was ready to move on from a highly productive but difficult fit.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Rodman became exactly the specialized piece the Bulls needed. He played 64 regular-season games in 1995-96 and averaged 14.9 rebounds, 55 games in 1996-97 at 16.1 rebounds, and 80 games in 1997-98 at 15.0. He led the NBA in rebounding in all three seasons, made the All-Defensive First Team in 1995-96, and started 177 regular-season games across the three-year stint. Chicago won the championship in every one of those seasons. NBA.com's Rodman retrospective describes him as the missing piece alongside Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, which matches the realized team result without requiring any speculative value calculation.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: Perdue was not remotely as impactful as Rodman, but the legacy F grade ignores four seasons of useful center depth. He appeared in 80 games with 22 starts in 1995-96, then 65 games with 34 starts during the injury-ravaged 1996-97 season, 79 games with 30 starts in 1997-98, and 37 games in the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season. That totals 261 regular-season games and 87 starts. Perdue averaged 8.7 points and 9.8 rebounds in 1996-97 when San Antonio needed him most, then remained a reserve on the 1999 championship roster. The Spurs did not receive a star, but they did receive durable frontcourt innings and eventually a title-season contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago wins decisively because Rodman's rebounding, defense and fit were instrumental to a three-title run. The Bulls earn an A+ because a one-for-one trade turned a useful center into an elite role player whose strengths matched the roster perfectly. San Antonio earns a B rather than an F: Perdue delivered four seasons, 261 games, 87 starts and a place on the 1999 title roster. The gap is still enormous at the top end, but the Spurs return had legitimate basketball value. Final verdict: Chicago Bulls Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Chicago's official all-time transaction history and Basketball-Reference agree on the source-safe package: Steve Kerr went to San Antonio for Chuck Person and a future first-round pick. The conditional pick conveyed in 2000 at No. 24 and became Dalibor Bagaric. A secondary transaction database lists vague 'other considerations,' but the Bulls' official ledger and both Basketball-Reference executive records omit that item, so it should not be treated as a confirmed asset.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: Kerr was a reserve rather than a centerpiece, which keeps this trade below the top grade range. He appeared in 44 games during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season, then 32 in 1999-00 and 55 in 2000-01, for 131 regular-season games in the stint created by this transaction. He also appeared in 11 playoff games during the Spurs' 1999 championship run. His box-score role was modest, but San Antonio acquired a trusted shooter with championship experience at the precise moment the Duncan-Robinson team broke through. Kerr's famous four-three-pointer burst against Dallas in the 2003 Western Conference finals belongs to a later Spurs stint after an intervening Portland season, so it is not credited to this 1999 trade.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Person produced no Bulls regular-season value. Chicago waived him on January 25, four days after acquiring him, and Charlotte signed him the next day. The real long-term return was the first-round pick. Bagaric played 95 games for Chicago across three seasons, never started, averaged 2.6 points and 2.5 rebounds, and shot 36.1 percent from the field. That is actual roster value from a late first-round selection, but it never became a core piece or a comparable contributor to Kerr's championship-era role in San Antonio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Spurs win, but the result should be graded more modestly than the legacy A-to-D split. Kerr was a useful reserve on a title team and supplied three seasons of depth, not a star acquisition. Chicago at least converted the deal into a first-round pick, even though Bagaric's 95-game tenure was inefficient and Person contributed nothing before being waived. San Antonio earns a B+ for obtaining a useful championship guard at a manageable cost. Chicago earns a C- because the pick conveyed and produced NBA games, but the realized return remained limited. Final verdict: San Antonio Spurs Win.

sources.title: AP report on Chuck Person signing with Charlotte

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago transaction log identifies this as veteran free-agent compensation rather than a conventional player trade. Chicago signed Kyle Macy on October 4, 1985 and sent Phoenix second-round picks in 1986 and 1990. The Phoenix record describes the Suns' side as agreeing not to exercise their right of first refusal on Macy. The picks later became No. 39 Rafael Addison in 1986 and No. 50 Milos Babic in 1990. That structure means the hindsight comparison is one Chicago season of Macy against the direct and downstream value Phoenix created from two second-round assets.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Macy became the Bulls' primary point guard immediately. He played all 82 games in 1985-86 and started 79, averaging 29.6 minutes, 8.6 points and 5.4 assists while shooting 48.3 percent from the field and 41.1 percent from three. Chicago's season was disrupted by Michael Jordan's foot injury and ended at 30-52, so Macy did not transform the team's record, but he supplied stable full-season guard play when the roster needed it. He left for Indiana after the season, making the Bulls return useful but short-lived.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The 1986 second-rounder became Rafael Addison at No. 39. Addison played 62 games with 12 starts as a Phoenix rookie, averaging 5.8 points in 11.5 minutes. He then spent four seasons outside the NBA before returning with New Jersey, so Phoenix received only that one season of his eventual six-year NBA career. The 1990 second-rounder became Milos Babic at No. 50. Phoenix did not retain Babic's rights: on draft night the Suns traded him to Cleveland for the rights to Stefano Rusconi, selected two spots later. Rusconi did not join Phoenix immediately and eventually appeared in only seven Suns games in 1995-96, totaling 30 minutes. The two picks therefore produced one modest Addison season and a rights chain that yielded almost no NBA court value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago has the better realized return, but the margin is not large enough for an extreme grade. Macy gave the Bulls one full season as a starting point guard and played every game. Phoenix received two legitimate draft assets, one of which produced a 62-game rookie season from Addison and the other of which remained movable until it became Rusconi's rights. The Suns did not receive nothing; they simply failed to turn either second-round opportunity into durable rotation value. A B for Chicago reflects the immediate 82-game starting return from a free-agent signing. A C+ for Phoenix recognizes that the compensation was reasonable in form and produced some NBA value, but less than Macy gave Chicago directly. Final verdict: Chicago Bulls Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix and Portland transaction logs agree on the June 14, 1985 deal: the Suns sent a 1987 second-round choice to the Trail Blazers for Bernard Thompson. Thompson had been Portland's 1984 first-round pick at No. 19 and had just completed a 59-game rookie season. Two years later Portland used the acquired second-rounder at No. 30 overall on LSU forward Nikita Wilson. Because both assets produced NBA results, this is a straightforward realized-value comparison rather than a rights or conditional-pick problem.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Thompson immediately became a useful Suns reserve. In 1985-86 he played 61 games with 20 starts, averaged 8.5 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists, and shot 48.9 percent from the field. His role declined in 1986-87, when he appeared in 24 games with two starts, but he returned for 37 games and seven starts in 1987-88. Across those three Phoenix seasons he totaled 122 regular-season games, 29 starts, 819 points, 248 rebounds, 201 assists and 83 steals. That is not star production, but it is a meaningful amount of real rotation value for the cost of one future second-round pick. Thompson later played briefly for Houston, so Phoenix received essentially the prime NBA portion of his career after the trade.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: The Trail Blazers waited two years for the pick and selected Nikita Wilson at No. 30 in the 1987 draft. Wilson made the 1987-88 roster but appeared in only 15 games, never started, and logged 54 total minutes. He scored 19 points, grabbed 11 rebounds and recorded three assists before his NBA career ended after that one season. Portland therefore converted a recent first-round wing who still had three NBA seasons ahead of him into a second-round selection that produced only 15 low-minute games. The process was defensible—Thompson had been a low-efficiency rookie and a future second was a normal asset for a player outside the core—but the realized outcome was poor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins clearly while the stakes remain modest. Thompson was never a foundational Suns player, so an elite grade would overstate the deal. He did, however, give Phoenix 122 games, nearly thirty starts and one genuinely useful 61-game season. Portland's return became a player who barely reached the floor and was out of the NBA after 15 games. A B for Phoenix reflects strong value extraction from a second-round cost. A D+ for Portland recognizes that the Blazers received a legitimate draft asset and made an ordinary second-round bet, but that bet produced almost no NBA value. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's San Antonio and Philadelphia transaction logs agree on the June 26, 2002 package: the Spurs sent veteran Mark Bryant and the rights to first-round pick John Salmons and second-round pick Randy Holcomb for Speedy Claxton. Contemporary reporting explains the roster logic. Philadelphia had Allen Iverson, Eric Snow and Aaron McKie ahead of Claxton, while San Antonio wanted a backup point guard behind Tony Parker. The trade therefore exchanged future depth for an immediate positional need.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: Claxton missed much of the 2002-03 regular season and appeared in only 30 games, averaging 5.8 points and 2.5 assists in 15.7 minutes. His value rose sharply in the playoffs. He became a trusted change-of-pace guard during the championship run and was especially important in the NBA Finals. In the clinching Game 6 against New Jersey, Claxton played 23:44, scored 13 points on 5-of-8 shooting, added four assists and finished plus-21 as San Antonio closed out the title. He left for Golden State after the season, so the direct Spurs return was short but unusually leveraged.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Salmons supplied the durable side of the package. He played 64 games as a rookie, 77 in 2003-04, 58 in 2004-05 and all 82 in 2005-06, totaling 281 regular-season games for Philadelphia. His role grew from deep reserve to a useful multi-position guard and wing, including 24 starts in 2003-04 and another 24 in 2005-06. Bryant added 11 Philadelphia games in 2002-03. Holcomb never produced meaningful 76ers NBA value, but Salmons alone makes this a legitimate return rather than a failed package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: This is a slight San Antonio edge rather than a one-sided win. Philadelphia received far more regular-season volume, and Salmons became a genuine rotation player over four seasons. San Antonio received only one season from Claxton, but the value of that season peaked at exactly the right time: he provided real minutes in a championship postseason and delivered one of his best performances in the title-clinching game. The Spurs earn a B+ for converting three expendable assets into immediate title-run help. Philadelphia earns a B for obtaining four seasons of Salmons plus a small Bryant contribution. Final verdict: slight San Antonio Spurs edge.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix did not trade an active player contract to Chicago in the usual sense. Dudley Bradley signed with the Bulls as a veteran free agent, and the Suns agreed to waive their right of first refusal in exchange for Chicago's 1983 third-round pick. Phoenix's 1982-83 transaction log records the free-agent move and compensation, while Pro Sports Transactions maps the pick to No. 52 overall in the 1983 draft. That distinction matters because the correct hindsight comparison is one Chicago season of Bradley versus the draft asset Phoenix received, not Bradley versus a player Phoenix drafted directly.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Bradley played 58 games for the 1982-83 Bulls and started 11. He averaged 3.5 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 11.8 minutes per game while shooting 51.6 percent from the field. His role was clearly secondary, but it was real NBA rotation value over most of the season. Chicago finished 28-54, so Bradley did not alter the franchise's competitive direction, and he was not retained as a long-term core piece. After that season his career continued in Washington, Milwaukee and New Jersey, meaning Chicago received only the one-year portion of his later NBA longevity.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The compensation became the 1983 third-round pick at No. 52. Phoenix did not actually make the selection. On June 27, 1983, the Suns included that pick with Dennis Johnson and the No. 21 first-round choice in the trade that brought Rick Robey and two second-round picks from Boston. Boston ultimately used No. 52 on East Tennessee State guard Winfred King, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. For this Bradley transaction, Phoenix deserves credit for receiving a movable draft asset, not for any later player that another team selected with it. The pick's inclusion in the Johnson-Robey package proves it had some transaction utility, but it was still a third-rounder with limited standalone value. The later Dennis Johnson trade has its own much larger hindsight story and should not be legacy into this grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Neither side created a major advantage from the original free-agent compensation. Chicago obtained a 58-game reserve season from Bradley. Phoenix obtained a low-cost draft chip that was useful enough to include in a later package but ultimately corresponded to a player who never logged an NBA game. Calling Phoenix the loser would ignore the fact that the Suns received exactly the kind of modest compensation expected when declining to retain a veteran reserve. Calling Chicago the clear winner would overstate one season from a player who averaged 3.5 points. An Even Trade with C+ grades reflects two modest but legitimate returns: one year of rotation depth for Chicago and one transferable third-round asset for Phoenix.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix and Washington transaction logs agree on the September 28, 1990 structure: the Suns sent Mike Morrison to the Bullets for a conditional 1993 second-round pick. The important part is the condition. Contemporary reporting described Morrison as a training-camp candidate who still had to earn a roster spot, and the official transaction sequence shows Washington waiving him on October 22. Basketball-Reference explicitly marks the conditional 1993 second-rounder as not conveyed. This means the final realized package was much smaller than the original trade shell suggests.

sections.heading: Washington Return
sections.body: Morrison was a Washington-area guard who had been Phoenix's second-round pick in 1989. He played 36 NBA games for the Suns in 1989-90, averaging 2.0 points in limited minutes, but those Phoenix games happened before this trade and cannot be credited to Washington. After the September 1990 deal, the Bullets brought him to camp and evaluated him alongside other guards competing for roster spots. Washington waived him on October 22, before the 1990-91 regular season. He never appeared in a Bullets regular-season game and never played another NBA season. Washington therefore received no realized regular-season production.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The Suns' return existed only if the trade condition was satisfied. It was not. Both Phoenix's and Washington's transaction pages identify the 1993 second-round pick as conditional and state that it did not convey. Phoenix therefore did not receive a draft selection, a player or another basketball asset from the deal. The transaction may have created roster flexibility by moving Morrison before camp decisions were complete, but TradeVerdicts does not invent value for unrecorded financial or roster effects when the explicit return failed to materialize.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The legacy slight Washington edge incorrectly treats Morrison as if he provided more value than Phoenix's conditional pick. He did not make the team. Once the non-conveyance is handled correctly, both sides finish at the same place: Washington received no regular-season player contribution, and Phoenix received no draft pick. The trade was essentially a conditional preseason audition that expired without a realized basketball return for either franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. The grades reflect zero realized regular-season value on both sides rather than poor execution of a major asset exchange. Washington got a short evaluation period with Morrison; Phoenix got no pick because the condition was not met. Neither outcome deserves a positive or punitive grade beyond neutral.

sources.title: Washington Post Bullets camp report, October 2 1990

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix and San Antonio transaction logs agree on the November 8, 1993 structure: the Suns sent Negele Knight to the Spurs for San Antonio's 1994 second-round choice. The pick landed at No. 29 and Phoenix used it on Duke forward Antonio Lang. That clean one-player-for-one-pick structure makes the hindsight comparison unusually direct because both teams realized the acquired asset themselves rather than routing it through another trade first.

sections.heading: San Antonio Return
sections.body: Knight stepped into a real rotation role immediately. He played 64 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1993-94 and started 18 of them, averaging 22.3 minutes, 9.3 points and 3.1 assists while shooting 47.6 percent from the field. That was substantially more responsibility than a typical end-of-roster acquisition. The value did not last beyond the season: San Antonio released Knight on July 6, 1994, and he never played another game for the Spurs. Still, one productive 64-game season with 18 starts is meaningful direct return for a future second-round pick.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: The Suns converted the pick into Antonio Lang at No. 29 in the 1994 draft. Lang made the 1994-95 Phoenix roster, but his role was extremely small. He appeared in 12 games, did not start, averaged 4.4 minutes and 0.9 points, and totaled only 53 minutes for the Suns. Lang later played additional NBA seasons with Cleveland, Miami, Toronto and Philadelphia, but those later games cannot be credited to Phoenix because the Suns no longer controlled his career. The trade's realized Phoenix value is therefore the 12-game rookie stint, not Lang's six-year NBA résumé.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The old Even Trade framing understated the difference. Knight was not a star and San Antonio did not retain him past one season, so this is not an A-level win. But the Spurs received a functioning backup point guard who played nearly 1,500 minutes and started 18 times. Phoenix's draft return produced 53 minutes and 11 points in 12 games. When the acquired assets are credited only for the teams that actually received their production, the gap is substantial.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio Spurs Win, B to D+. Knight supplied one solid season of rotation and spot-starting value. Phoenix correctly converted the second-round pick into an NBA player, but Lang's Suns tenure was too brief and too small to balance the exchange.

sections.heading: The Trade Is Clear, but Dallas' Return Is Not
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's 1980-81 transaction records show Dallas sending Austin Carr to Washington on November 6, 1980.

The Mavericks received future considerations. The reviewed team and league transaction sources do not identify what those considerations ultimately became.

sections.heading: Carr Played 39 Games for Washington
sections.body:
Carr had played eight games for Dallas before the trade. After joining the Bullets, he appeared in 39 regular-season games.

He averaged 4.9 points, 1.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.9 minutes. The role was small, but Washington received a real veteran guard contribution.

Those 39 games were the final regular-season appearances of Carr's NBA career. There is no later Washington transaction branch from Carr that materially changes the trade.

sections.heading: Dallas' Future Considerations Stay Unresolved
sections.body:
The key evaluation problem is the Dallas side. "Future considerations" can represent cash, a conditional right, a player to be named later or another form of transaction value, but the reviewed records do not specify the outcome here.

This review therefore leaves that asset unresolved. It is not treated as zero, but it also cannot be credited with an invented player, pick or cash amount.

sections.heading: The Known Return Was Small but Real
sections.body:
Carr's 39 Washington appearances came after he had played only eight games for expansion Dallas. The Bullets did not acquire a long-term starter, but they did receive the only traceable NBA playing value attached to the transaction in the reviewed record.

The uncertainty on Dallas' side is important to preserve. A future-considerations clause proves that Dallas did not simply give Carr away, yet source-backed grading has to distinguish a documented but unidentified asset from a player, pick or cash amount that can actually be measured. That is why the Dallas grade stays above a complete zero-return outcome while remaining below Washington's documented 39-game return.

sections.heading: Why Washington Gets Only a Narrow Edge
sections.body:
Washington's return is modest: 39 games from a veteran near the end of his career.

Dallas may have received some useful value through the future-considerations term, but there is not enough documentation to measure it. The fairest source-backed approach is to grade only the known realized return while keeping confidence below high.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bullets Edge, C+/D+. Washington receives a C+ for 39 Carr games. Dallas receives a D+ because an incoming asset is documented but unresolved, preventing either a zero-value grade or a stronger realized-value claim.

sections.heading: Boston Reacquired a Former Celtic
sections.body:
Kevin Stacom had played 55 games for Boston in 1977-78 before signing with Indiana as a veteran free agent in July 1978. The Pacers sent Boston a 1979 third-round pick as compensation for that signing.

On February 9, 1979, Indiana sold Stacom's player rights back to Boston. The Boston ledger records the rights acquisition, while Indiana's ledger describes the transaction as a sale. The reviewed records do not state the cash amount.

sections.heading: Stacom Played 24 Games After the Deal
sections.body:
Stacom appeared in 24 regular-season games for Boston after returning. He averaged 10.8 minutes, 4.9 points and 1.5 assists while shooting 39.1 percent from the field.

That is limited production, but it is real roster value from a transaction in which Boston surrendered only an unspecified cash payment.

sections.heading: There Was No Long Boston Tail
sections.body:
Stacom did not play in 1979-80 and Basketball-Reference notes that he was considered retired while working as an inn manager. He remained out in 1980-81, then returned for seven games with Milwaukee in 1981-82.

Boston therefore received one short late-season stint rather than a multi-year asset. There was no later Celtics trade branch to increase the return.

sections.heading: Indiana's Cash Return Is Unquantified
sections.body:
The Pacers had already gotten 44 games from Stacom before selling his rights. For this February transaction specifically, their return was cash. Because the amount is not documented in the reviewed sources, this review does not assign speculative value to it.

That uncertainty keeps Boston's edge small rather than turning a 24-game reserve stint into a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Edge, B-/C. Boston receives a B- because Stacom gave the team 24 games of usable guard depth for an unspecified cash payment. Indiana receives a C because the cash return cannot be evaluated and produced no traceable basketball asset in the reviewed record.

sections.heading: Houston Received Steve Francis and a Future First
sections.body: Houston emerged from the August 27, 1999 three-team trade with Steve Francis, Tony Massenburg, Don MacLean and Orlando's 2001 first-round choice, eventually identified as No. 18 Jason Collins. Francis had refused to play for the Vancouver Grizzlies, creating the circumstances for the expanded transaction. He became the defining incoming piece for Houston, making the Rockets' return quite different from a normal exchange of four equal-value players. The first-round pick was a separate asset branch; the Rockets' grade doesn't need to attribute the whole career of the eventual selection to Houston.

sections.heading: Francis Became the Best Direct Team Return
sections.body: Francis shared the 1999-2000 Rookie of the Year honor and later made three All-Star teams with Houston. Over five Rockets seasons he averaged 19.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 6.2 assists per game. Houston subsequently used him as a centerpiece of its 2004 Tracy McGrady transaction, retaining another form of exchange value after his own high-level seasons. That combination of immediate star production and later asset utility provides the strongest completed franchise result of the three participants. Massenburg and MacLean were recorded incoming players, but neither was responsible for the A+ grade.

sections.heading: Vancouver Obtained a Real Package in a Difficult Situation
sections.body: Vancouver received Michael Dickerson, Othella Harrington, Brent Price, Antoine Carr, a future first-round asset recorded with No. 13 Marcus Banks in 2003 and a 2002 second associated with No. 46 Matt Barnes. Dickerson averaged 18.2 points in 1999-2000 for Vancouver; Harrington added 13.1 points and 6.9 rebounds. Those two were substantial direct NBA returns for a team that could not retain Francis. The draft names specify later asset outcomes, not automatic Vancouver career credit. Vancouver's B reflects that the franchise secured meaningful production and options despite surrendering the eventual top player.

sections.heading: Orlando Sacrificed Picks for a Weaker Group
sections.body: Orlando obtained Lee Mayberry, Makhtar N'Diaye, Rodrick Rhodes and Michael Smith. Its outgoing compensation included Don MacLean, a 2001 first-round pick and the second-round selection that entered the Vancouver portion of the deal. The players Orlando acquired did not turn into a comparable long-term Magic core, so the organization's return ranks behind both Houston's star and Vancouver's productive contributors. These distinctions matter in a three-team comparison: the eventual talents selected with later routed choices can't all be credited as minutes played for the franchises that previously owned those picks.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston earns A+ for Steve Francis' five highly productive seasons and retained trade value, alongside its other incoming assets. Vancouver/Memphis gets B for Michael Dickerson, Othella Harrington and multiple draft opportunities in difficult circumstances. Orlando receives D because its four-player return did not match the players and draft choices it surrendered. The verdict evaluates direct returns, not unrelated later player careers.

sections.heading: Ariza and a First Made Houston the Largest Winner
sections.body: Houston obtained Trevor Ariza from Washington as part of the July 15, 2014 three-team agreement. The Rockets also received Alonzo Gee, Scotty Hopson and a protected 2015 first-round pick from New Orleans. The choice ultimately conveyed at No. 18 and became Sam Dekker. Ariza supplied an established wing defender and floor spacer who became a four-year starter, while the first created additional value beyond his contract. The three-team routing must be preserved: Ariza came from the Wizards, while the pick and two other players arrived from the Pelicans.

sections.heading: Ariza Helped Houston in Two Conference Finals Runs
sections.body: Ariza held a regular Houston starting role across four seasons and played on teams that reached the Western Conference Finals in 2015 and 2018. This is an identifiable competitive return rather than hypothetical improvement inferred from his reputation. The No. 18 first-round selection was a distinct draft result Houston could use or convert, though any later unrelated transaction should not be automatically counted twice. The combined player production and first-round asset support the Rockets' A- without suggesting all of the success of those teams was caused by this single trade.

sections.heading: New Orleans Bought a Starting Center for 2014-15
sections.body: The Pelicans received Ömer Aşık, Omri Casspi and cash considerations. Aşık started 76 games in his first New Orleans season and averaged 9.8 rebounds, contributing to a 45-win team that reached the 2015 playoffs. That was meaningful short-term performance, not an empty return. His value declined afterward, and New Orleans later included him with another first-round pick in the 2018 Nikola Mirotić trade. The original 2015 first sent to Houston was a real cost. Casspi and cash belong to the return, but the immediate center role supplies its strongest documented basketball benefit.

sections.heading: Washington Used a Trade Exception to Recover Value
sections.body: Washington did not retain Ariza, yet it avoided letting his free-agent departure pass with no incoming transaction consideration. The Wizards received Melvin Ely and a trade exception through the three-team structure, then used the exception to assist in acquiring Kris Humphries. That is a concrete secondary asset conversion, even though it isn't equivalent to acquiring a starting star. Washington's B+ and New Orleans' C+ describe different outcomes: one team monetized a departure and another bought short-term interior minutes. Houston's long Ariza tenure plus the first-round pick earned the strongest practical return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston receives A- for four seasons of Trevor Ariza's starting role and the No. 18 first that became Sam Dekker. Washington earns B+ for converting Ariza's exit into a trade exception later used toward Kris Humphries. New Orleans receives C+ for Aşık's 76-start 2014-15 season, Casspi and cash, against the cost of a protected first. All three franchises got something identifiable, but Houston realized the most durable combined return.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired a Ready-to-Play Center
sections.body: Detroit sent Phoenix a 1996 second-round pick and a conditional 1999 second-round choice on August 1, 1994 for Mark West. The later 1999 choice never conveyed, so the Suns' actual return was narrower than the two-pick headline suggests. The 1996 selection eventually landed at No. 39 and became Russ Millard. Neither the 1999 contingency nor the existence of a drafted player should be confused with a second NBA contributor reaching the Suns.

sections.heading: West Played, Started and Filled a Frontcourt Need
sections.body: West appeared in 114 games for Detroit across two seasons, with 79 starts. In 1994-95 alone, he averaged 7.5 points and 6.1 rebounds, useful center production obtained without surrendering a first-round asset. This wasn't a future-star acquisition. It was a trade for an established rotation big who could occupy real frontcourt minutes immediately. His actual Pistons performance explains why the franchise received the stronger return even if those teams didn't build a title run around this transaction.

sections.heading: Phoenix Had a Second-Round Shot, Not Matching NBA Minutes
sections.body: The Suns used the conveyed 1996 pick on Millard, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The conditional 1999 pick did not convey, leaving Phoenix without another selection from this deal. Its return therefore had draft opportunity rather than confirmed game production. Detroit's existing 114 games from West contrast directly with that outcome; this isn't an inference about Millard's potential or anything West achieved for other clubs before the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit earns B for West's immediate center minutes and 79 starts across 114 games without using a first-rounder. Phoenix receives C- for the 1996 No. 39 selection of Russ Millard, who never played in the NBA, plus a 1999 conditional second that did not convey. The grades reflect the very different realized returns.

sections.heading: A One-for-One Veteran Trade in February
sections.body: On February 21, 1990, Denver acquired Joe Barry Carroll from New Jersey in exchange for Michael Cutright. The transaction sources identify a direct swap rather than a larger multi-team chain or additional supported draft compensation. That matters when judging the outcome: neither side needs to be credited with a later pick or cash payment outside the source record. Denver was buying an immediately usable frontcourt player at the approach of the postseason.

sections.heading: Carroll Supplied 30 Games in Denver
sections.body: Carroll played 30 regular-season games after arriving with 27 starts. He averaged 11.9 points and 6.4 rebounds in that short Nuggets stretch, then appeared in the club's 1990 playoff series. Those numbers are not a full-season breakout or a new franchise core, but they do show that the deal filled a real rotation and starting position for the specific period Denver acquired him. The contribution was concentrated and measurable.

sections.heading: Cutright Never Produced a Nets NBA Appearance
sections.body: New Jersey received Cutright but got no subsequent NBA game appearances from him. That leaves the Nets with no realized regular-season production from the known incoming player, while Denver can point to Carroll's 27 starts. There's no verified additional asset in the canonical record to balance that difference. The trade still shouldn't be assessed as though it were a high-stakes star swap: its actual value was a late-season starting center against a player who never reached an NBA court for the buyer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver receives B for thirty Carroll appearances, twenty-seven starts, and a playoff contribution. New Jersey earns C- because Michael Cutright provided no NBA playing return. The source-backed record identifies no additional compensation that would change that player-for-player comparison.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent a Conditional Choice for Ed Nealy
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Ed Nealy from Phoenix on October 5, 1989 for a conditional 1996 second-round selection. Seven years of potential separation between the trade and the nominal pick could make the return sound more elaborate than it actually became. The condition was never exercised; no draft pick conveyed to the Suns. This leaves an identifiable player on one side and an unfulfilled draft contingency on the other.

sections.heading: Nealy Supplied Modest Real Games
sections.body: Nealy appeared in 46 Chicago games during 1989-90. He wasn't the sort of high-minute scorer who would turn a transaction into a defining season, but forty-six NBA appearances are direct roster value. Chicago received useful frontcourt depth at the time it needed bodies to complete the rotation. The narrow scale of that output is also why a modest edge describes the outcome better than an overwhelming win.

sections.heading: Phoenix Ultimately Did Not Receive a Draft Asset
sections.body: Phoenix's hypothetical compensation would have been a 1996 second-round pick only if its conditions were met. Since the pick did not convey, the Suns cannot receive credit for a selection, a drafted player or subsequent development. They may have viewed the original condition as acceptable compensation for a marginal veteran, but hindsight shows no realized pick from this transaction. The comparison rests on Nealy's 46 games against no conveyed selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago earns C+ for Nealy's 46 appearances, a modest but direct role. Phoenix receives C because its conditional 1996 second-rounder never conveyed. The decision to make the exchange had limited stakes, so the grades acknowledge a small advantage without claiming major franchise consequences.

sections.heading: The Money Was the Main Incoming Asset
sections.body: On October 25, 2002, Chicago took Erick Barkley and $1 million from San Antonio. In exchange, the Spurs received a protected conditional second-round choice that was nominally tied to 2007. The conditions were never satisfied, and the pick did not convey. Unlike an ordinary player-for-player deal, this transaction transferred a contract and a substantial cash payment while the future draft asset proved hypothetical.

sections.heading: Chicago Waived Barkley Instead of Using Him
sections.body: The Bulls immediately waived Barkley after receiving him. Chicago's basketball return therefore wasn't a new guard entering its rotation; it was the cash paired with the opportunity to process the contract. There was also no eventual outgoing draft pick after the 2007 condition failed. That combination is why the Bulls benefited financially despite adding no on-court production from the named player.

sections.heading: San Antonio Exchanged Cash for Contract Relief
sections.body: San Antonio paid $1 million and did not end up with the protected draft choice. Contemporary transaction context describes the move as a way of removing Barkley's contract and addressing luxury-tax exposure. The Spurs' benefit was avoiding costs and freeing roster or payroll space, not collecting picks or players. Those aims make the club's return different from Chicago's cash receipt; judging either organization by eventual player scoring would miss why the trade happened.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Chicago earns C+ for $1 million in cash, no conveyed 2007 second-rounder and immediate ability to waive Barkley. San Antonio also receives C+ for successfully moving the contract despite paying the cash. Neither club collected meaningful game production, but both accomplished the financial purposes documented in the transaction.

sections.heading: Houston Purchased the Rights to K.J. Martin
sections.body: Houston acquired K.J. Martin's draft rights from Sacramento on November 25, 2020. The Rockets sent cash and a 2021 second-round pick that ultimately became No. 52 Luka Garza. This was not a trade in which both franchises exchanged established NBA players. One acquired a particular young forward's rights immediately; the other accepted cash and a later draft opportunity. Comparing the rights outcome to the actual later selection is more informative than treating either pick as a proven prospect on the date of the deal.

sections.heading: Martin Gave the Rockets a Rotation Forward
sections.body: Martin developed into an NBA rotation contributor for Houston and later became a reusable trade asset. That is a concrete return for an acquisition financed with a second-round pick and cash. His production wasn't equivalent to landing a franchise centerpiece, but it supplied roster minutes that the Rockets could evaluate and eventually convert into other options. The rights were valuable specifically because Martin played and retained an identifiable market rather than remaining an unused draft placeholder.

sections.heading: Sacramento Took Cash and the Garza Selection
sections.body: Sacramento's second-rounder became Luka Garza at No. 52 in the 2021 draft. Garza reached the NBA, so the pick can't be called a dead asset, and the cash was an immediate separate return. Even so, that combined package did not reproduce the basketball and subsequent transaction value Martin produced for Houston. The comparison stays tied to which team acquired which asset rather than assuming Sacramento received Martin's future contributions simply because it had held his rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston receives B+ for developing K.J. Martin into a rotation player and useful subsequent asset. Sacramento earns C for cash and the 2021 No. 52 choice that became Luka Garza. Both pieces had identifiable worth, but Martin produced the stronger direct return for his new club.

sections.heading: The Olajuwon Departure Was a Sign-and-Trade
