These were draft-night rights rather than veteran contracts, with neither team buying a known immediate starter.

sections.heading: Kleiza Became a Useful Nuggets Scorer
sections.body: Kleiza developed into a credible Denver rotation scorer and contributed across several Nuggets playoff seasons. That on-court return gave his rights substantially more value to Denver than a pick that never turned into a usable player. Sánchez was a second incoming developmental asset, though the Nuggets' positive historical grade is primarily supported by Kleiza's contribution. His specific Denver minutes explain why the team viewed the package as a suitable trade for a guard prospect.

sections.heading: Jack Was the Strongest Overall Career of the Group
sections.body: Portland obtained Jarrett Jack's rights, and Jack ultimately had a longer and more productive overall NBA career than the other incoming prospects. Acknowledging that fact prevents the verdict from being written as if Portland received nothing. The existing Nuggets-centered grades instead value how Kleiza filled a Denver scoring need during the club's playoff window. Those two different viewpoints explain how the rights trade produced genuine player value on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver earns A- for Linas Kleiza's playoff-era scoring contribution plus Ricky Sánchez's rights. Portland receives C+ for Jarrett Jack's rights; Jack had the stronger overall NBA career but did not reproduce Kleiza's specific Denver role. The Nuggets' advantage reflects their own completed team fit rather than denying Jack's value.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Exchanged Smrek for a Future Second
sections.body: The Lakers sent Mike Smrek to San Antonio on November 2, 1988 for a 1990 second-round draft choice. That pick eventually became No. 51 Tony Smith. The deal exchanged an existing frontcourt player's NBA rights for a later, comparatively low draft opportunity, not a player of equal professional standing. Los Angeles was trading away a center who had already been part of its roster in favor of a future backcourt or roster development chance.

sections.heading: The Pick Became a Named Lakers Guard
sections.body: Los Angeles eventually used the received 1990 selection on Tony Smith at No. 51. That was a real draft outcome rather than a conditional choice that was never exercised. Smith developed into an NBA guard and had a playing role with the Lakers, giving the franchise some recognizable return for surrendering Smrek. The late position of the choice limited its expected value, which makes the B grade a credit for a useful conversion rather than a claim of exceptional draft capital.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received a Veteran Center
sections.body: Smrek had NBA championship-era experience when the Spurs acquired him. He provided San Antonio a frontcourt option instead of a prospect waiting for a future draft. That was a legitimate reason to make the deal, but the recorded comparison assigns his Spurs return less value than the Lakers obtained from their No. 51 selection. The Spurs' C grade acknowledges a real acquired player while the Lakers' higher mark reflects turning the later pick into an NBA contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles gets B for the 1990 No. 51 draft choice that became Tony Smith, who provided identifiable guard value for the team. San Antonio receives C for veteran center Mike Smrek. Both incoming pieces had NBA uses, but the Lakers' eventual draft outcome gave them the better completed return.

sections.heading: Dallas Sent Solomon Alabi’s Rights for Pick and Cash
sections.body: Dallas traded the rights to Solomon Alabi to Toronto on June 24, 2010 for cash considerations and a protected future second-round selection. That choice eventually converted into the 2013 No. 41 pick, associated with Jamaal Franklin. This was not an exchange of two established players; both teams were using draft rights and financial considerations to adjust their future options. Dallas accepted two assets rather than keeping Alabi's developmental rights.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Ultimately Conveyed
sections.body: Unlike many heavily protected second-round trades, the future selection here became an actual 2013 draft asset. Its specified top-40 protection left Dallas with the No. 41 outcome, which became Franklin. The pick was a concrete return distinct from the incoming cash, although its later use should not be treated as if Franklin necessarily produced a long Mavericks career. The Dallas B grade credits getting both a usable selection and money for the rights it moved.

sections.heading: Toronto Received a Developmental Center
sections.body: Toronto acquired Alabi's rights, giving the Raptors a prospect with size and an opportunity for roster development. That outcome had value, but Alabi didn't become a long-term franchise center. The Mavericks' cash payment and actual later pick created more varied compensation than the sole rights asset Toronto acquired. The narrow scope keeps this from becoming a major historical trade, though Dallas's side can point to two received components.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns B for the protected second-round choice that conveyed as the 2013 No. 41 pick tied to Jamaal Franklin, plus cash. Toronto receives C for Solomon Alabi's rights. The Mavericks acquired two distinct items and the more flexible completed package.

sections.heading: Sacramento Acquired a Young Wing in Chris Duarte
sections.body: Sacramento received Chris Duarte from Indiana on July 6, 2023. The Pacers took two future second-round selections, scheduled for 2028 and 2030, in exchange. Because those drafts remain in the future, the exact players ultimately taken using the picks cannot yet be known. This is a useful case for separating the trade's actual completed player component from the still-outstanding selection rights, rather than inventing hindsight results for unmade picks.

sections.heading: Duarte Was a Defined Current Basketball Asset
sections.body: Duarte arrived in Sacramento with NBA wing experience, outside shooting potential and the ability to compete for rotation minutes. Those were immediate options unavailable from a selection several years away. The Kings' B grade reflects adding a player they could evaluate during their existing competitive window. It does not assert a major Sacramento postseason breakthrough caused by Duarte, and it allows for the possibility that the Pacers' future picks will later grow in value.

sections.heading: Indiana Retained Two Long-Dated Second-Round Rights
sections.body: The Pacers received separate picks in 2028 and 2030, not a current first-rounder or a pair of already named prospects. That package provides flexibility in later draft years and possible trade uses, but its completed playing return cannot be graded from future player careers today. Indiana's C+ therefore recognizes the known rights without assuming the selections have conveyed and developed. Sacramento held the clearer near-term player asset while the future Indianapolis return is still pending.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win on the current recorded evaluation. Sacramento receives B for acquiring Chris Duarte as an NBA-ready wing. Indiana earns C+ for its two future second-round picks in 2028 and 2030. Those selections remain unresolved; the verdict evaluates established assets today rather than assigning them fictional future players.

sections.heading: Memphis Exchanged Bonzi Wells for Two Veterans
sections.body: The Grizzlies sent Bonzi Wells to Sacramento on August 2, 2005, receiving Bobby Jackson and Greg Ostertag. Memphis took two established players with different assignments, Jackson as a guard and Ostertag as a big man. Sacramento received the single versatile scoring wing in Wells. This was a basketball-role exchange rather than a swap of future protected draft choices, and the specific incoming veterans explain why Memphis didn't simply pursue another scorer with the same profile.

sections.heading: Jackson and Ostertag Supplied Distinct Rotation Roles
sections.body: Jackson offered Memphis veteran guard depth, while Ostertag brought interior experience and size. Both players had already shown they could function in NBA rotations. Their combined return provided an alternative to keeping Wells and concentrated fewer possessions in one wing scorer. Neither should be credited for the entirety of his career elsewhere, and the B- grade acknowledges a useful but relatively short-term two-player package rather than a foundational roster rebuilding move.

sections.heading: Sacramento Obtained Wells’s Scoring and Wing Versatility
sections.body: Wells had a demonstrated ability to create offense and rebound from the wing. Sacramento's acquisition added a different immediate role than either of the veterans going to Memphis, and he remained a recognizable NBA contributor. The clubs therefore both obtained real rotation talent, but the canonical evaluation assigns Memphis the small advantage from securing two positional pieces. Sacramento's C+ still recognizes the value of receiving a player who could help the Kings.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge. Memphis earns B- for Bobby Jackson and Greg Ostertag, two usable veterans providing guard and frontcourt depth. Sacramento receives C+ for Bonzi Wells, a capable scoring wing. The exchange was competitive, but the more varied Memphis package produced a modest edge in the recorded grading.

sections.heading: Golden State Moved No. 34 for No. 44 and Cash
sections.body: The Warriors traded a 2010 second-round choice that became No. 34 Armon Johnson to Portland on June 21, 2010. In return they acquired the No. 44 second-round pick ultimately associated with Jerome Jordan and cash considerations. The trade consisted of a move ten draft positions down within the second round plus financial compensation, not a transfer of established NBA players. The position difference is the principal basketball cost of Golden State receiving cash.

sections.heading: Portland Kept the Earlier Selection
sections.body: The Blazers received No. 34 and used the position on guard Armon Johnson. An earlier second-round pick offered Portland a better opportunity to select its preferred prospect before the Warriors' later slot came due. That advantage was modest rather than star-level, but it provided the team with a clear draft asset. Portland's C grade recognizes the stronger relative pick position without crediting every unrelated development in Johnson's later career as a Blazers result.

sections.heading: The Warriors Received a Later Pick and Immediate Money
sections.body: Golden State obtained No. 44 Jerome Jordan and the cash payment. Both were genuine compensation, and the team didn't leave empty-handed. The later selection simply carried less draft leverage than No. 34, while cash can't be converted into points or rebounds for a drafted player. Golden State's C- grade captures the lower potential basketball impact of trading down even after acknowledging the money that accompanied the pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge. Portland earns C for the 2010 No. 34 choice that became Armon Johnson. Golden State receives C- for No. 44 Jerome Jordan and cash considerations. The Warriors collected two real items, but the Blazers acquired the stronger draft position and earned the narrow historical advantage.

sections.heading: New Orleans Converted Tim Frazier Into the No. 52 Pick
sections.body: New Orleans sent reserve point guard Tim Frazier to Washington before the 2017 draft and received the 52nd overall selection. Frazier had averaged 7.1 points and 5.2 assists for the Pelicans in 2016-17, so this wasn't the disposal of an inactive player. Washington was seeking an experienced backup to John Wall. New Orleans chose a second-round asset over keeping that particular source of guard depth.

sections.heading: The Sumner Pick Was Traded Again on Draft Night
sections.body: The incoming No. 52 pick was used to select Edmond Sumner, but the Pelicans moved that selection to Indiana during the same draft. Sumner's later Pacers games can't be credited as playing production for New Orleans. The asset's value to the Pelicans was its ability to be transferred, not a long-term Sumner development story. That distinction keeps the C+ grade modest rather than treating a future Indiana player as a New Orleans contributor.

sections.heading: Washington Purchased a Defined Backcourt Role
sections.body: For Washington, Frazier supplied an experienced reserve behind Wall rather than a new starting guard. He was already a proven distributor and made more immediate basketball sense than waiting on the last nine picks of a draft. His limited ceiling and the temporary nature of the role constrain the Wizards' C. The choice was understandable for a club that wanted bench help, but it also surrendered a pick with some remaining transaction value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pelicans Edge. New Orleans receives C+ for exchanging Frazier for No. 52 and using the selection as another draft-night asset. Washington earns C for obtaining an actual backup point guard. Neither side landed an enduring franchise piece, and Sumner's subsequent Pacers career isn't assigned to the Pelicans.

sections.heading: Portland Consolidated Two First-Round Rights Into No. 10
sections.body: The Trail Blazers acquired Zach Collins' rights from Sacramento on June 22, 2017. Collins had been taken 10th overall after one season at Gonzaga. Sacramento received the rights to No. 15 Justin Jackson and No. 20 Harry Giles instead. Portland traded two separate opportunities to develop young players for one higher selection, a conscious choice to pursue the specific frontcourt prospect rather than maintain a wider group of draft bets.

sections.heading: Collins Gave the Blazers a Real Defensive Frontcourt Option
sections.body: Collins provided size and interior defense during Portland's playoff-era roster, including its run to the 2019 Western Conference finals. That team-specific contribution matters even though injuries later interrupted his continuity with the club. The C+ recognizes useful rotation value without assuming that drafting 10th delivered a durable All-Star. Portland spent two first-round opportunities on Collins and therefore needed his actual contribution, not just his pre-draft reputation, to support the grade.

sections.heading: Sacramento Split Its Investment Between Jackson and Giles
sections.body: Jackson offered a wing prospect with college scoring credentials, while Giles represented a frontcourt development swing complicated by earlier knee injuries. Both rights conveyed to Sacramento, and neither became the long-term Sacramento building block that would clearly outweigh Collins' Portland role. The Kings received two recognizable NBA prospects, so the return can't be treated as empty. Their D reflects how little lasting value the pairing produced for that particular club in the years following the draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win. Portland earns C+ for the No. 10 Zach Collins rights and the defensive minutes he supplied. Sacramento receives D for Justin Jackson and Harry Giles at Nos. 15 and 20. The Kings obtained two players, but Portland realized the more useful contribution to its own roster.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Matt Bonner’s Draft Rights Into a Future Pick
sections.body: The Bulls selected Matt Bonner 45th overall in the 2003 draft, then moved his rights to Toronto for a second-round pick in 2004. That future choice became No. 38 Chris Duhon. Chicago traded away the rights to one newly selected forward in exchange for a later opportunity that yielded a point guard. The exchange was therefore a draft-rights decision, not a swap of two veterans already under contract.

sections.heading: Duhon Became a Regular Contributor for the Bulls
sections.body: Duhon developed into a dependable Chicago guard after the 2004 draft, handling ball movement and perimeter defense through several seasons with the team. His role was considerably more durable than the uncertainty associated with a future second-rounder at the time of this trade. The Bulls' A- grade reflects the useful guard they ultimately obtained with Toronto's pick, not the abstract value of holding an unspecified future choice for another year.

sections.heading: Toronto Received a Shooter Whose Career Extended Beyond the Raptors
sections.body: Bonner developed a recognizable perimeter-shooting role and did play for Toronto, so the Raptors received a real player rather than a wasted selection. Much of Bonner's later, longer NBA career occurred in San Antonio, however, and doesn't all belong on Toronto's side of the ledger. The Raptors' C recognizes Bonner's early contribution but doesn't equal the sustained Bulls value that emerged from Duhon's selection. Both clubs got actual players; the duration and team fit differed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago grades A- for turning Bonner's 2003 rights into the 2004 No. 38 selection used on Chris Duhon. Toronto gets C for Bonner, a viable shooting forward whose most enduring team tenure came later. The Bulls secured the more sustained contribution within their own roster.

sections.heading: Orlando Acquired Doug Christie for Two Players
sections.body: On January 10, 2005, the Magic sent Cuttino Mobley and Michael Bradley to Sacramento in exchange for Doug Christie. Orlando had added Mobley before the season, so the move quickly altered its guard rotation again. Christie brought a defensive résumé from Sacramento's successful teams, but was an older player changing clubs midway through the season. The Kings instead acquired a more active scorer in Mobley and a second player in Bradley.

sections.heading: Christie’s Magic Tenure Never Recreated His Sacramento Role
sections.body: Christie had supplied perimeter defense and playmaking to Sacramento's earlier playoff groups, but his Orlando stint was brief and affected by physical problems. The Magic didn't get the long run of effective wing play that had made him desirable. Their D- grade reflects the difference between acquiring a well-regarded veteran name and receiving meaningful production from that player after the exchange. Moving Mobley was a real cost to Orlando's immediate offense.

sections.heading: Mobley Scored for Sacramento Before Leaving That Summer
sections.body: Mobley started 43 games for the Kings in the rest of 2004-05 and averaged 16.6 points per game. His shooting immediately mattered more to Sacramento's playoff push than Christie's short Orlando contribution did for the Magic. Bradley wasn't a long-term Kings fixture and was included in the club's later Chris Webber trade, so he shouldn't be mistaken for another lasting core player. The C grade credits the useful Mobley stint while acknowledging that the return was temporary.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento receives C after obtaining 43 starts and 16.6 points per game from Cuttino Mobley, plus Bradley as a movable roster piece. Orlando grades D- for the brief Doug Christie experiment. Both clubs made a midseason change, but the Kings received the stronger immediate basketball return.

sections.heading: Sacramento Acquired James Johnson for a Conditional Second
sections.body: Sacramento traded a conditional 2014 second-round selection to Toronto on July 16, 2012, receiving forward James Johnson. The Kings' announcement stressed Johnson's size, defense and ability to play multiple frontcourt positions. He had started 40 games for the Raptors in 2011-12, making him an established NBA option rather than an unknown developmental prospect. Sacramento chose to use a future pick to address a near-term roster need.

sections.heading: Johnson Brought Versatility but Was Not a Long-Term King
sections.body: Johnson gave Sacramento a defensive forward who could help across several positions, but he did not establish a prolonged tenure with the franchise. His value in this trade sits between a total miss and a foundational acquisition: the Kings obtained a player they could use while parting with a future second-round opportunity. That limited but tangible return supports Sacramento's C, even without crediting Johnson's later work for other teams.

sections.heading: Toronto’s Pick Eventually Became DeAndre Daniels at No. 37
sections.body: The conditional 2014 second transferred to the Raptors and resolved as the 37th overall choice associated with DeAndre Daniels. That created a measurable draft asset for Toronto, though Daniels did not become a sustained NBA rotation player for the Raptors. The pick carried an opportunity cost for Sacramento, yet its specific outcome limits how much Toronto actually realized. The Raptors' D reflects the disappointing conversion rather than claiming they received nothing of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento earns C for taking James Johnson into its frontcourt in 2012. Toronto receives D for the conditional second-round pick that eventually became No. 37 DeAndre Daniels. Johnson's Sacramento stay was short, but it offered more immediate NBA utility than Toronto realized from the selection.

sections.heading: Orlando Split Its Ibaka Investment Into Ross and a First
sections.body: Orlando sent Serge Ibaka to Toronto on February 14, 2017, and acquired Terrence Ross plus the Raptors' 2017 first-round selection. Ibaka had joined the Magic the previous summer, but the team changed direction before reaching another offseason with the veteran forward. Ross was an established NBA wing who could shoot and defend in the backcourt, while the first-round pick created a second asset beyond the immediate roster addition. Toronto accepted that price to strengthen its frontcourt for the playoffs.

sections.heading: Ross Supplied Years of Magic Wing Production
sections.body: Ross stayed in Orlando for multiple seasons and became an important perimeter scoring option, notably as a bench scorer during the Magic's 2019 playoff return. The incoming pick became No. 25 Anžejs Pasečņiks, whose later development did not create a comparable playing contribution for Orlando. The Magic's A- recognizes the substantial Ross tenure rather than pretending that both incoming assets became successful rotation players. That distinction makes the return more useful than a simple two-for-one asset count suggests.

sections.heading: Ibaka Helped Toronto Build a Championship Frontcourt
sections.body: Toronto wanted a frontcourt defender who could also stretch the floor next to its established guards. Ibaka provided that role for several Raptors seasons and was part of the 2019 NBA championship team, giving the acquisition a distinct team-specific outcome. The Raptors paid Ross and a first to add a player who could contribute to their near-term title ambitions. Their A grade reflects the championship-era contribution, not merely Ibaka's reputation before arriving in Toronto.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Raptors Edge. Toronto grades A for Serge Ibaka's multi-season frontcourt contribution, including the 2019 championship run. Orlando receives A- for Terrence Ross's lengthy wing role and a first-round selection that became Anžejs Pasečņiks. Both teams received tangible value, but Ibaka's Toronto championship role earns the narrow advantage.

sections.heading: Toronto Sent Steve Novak and a Future Second for Garrett
sections.body: On July 10, 2014, Toronto dealt Steve Novak and the rights to New York's 2017 second-round selection to Utah for guard Diante Garrett. The Jazz's own announcement identifies the future pick as a New York selection, making the draft obligation more precise than a generic future second. Toronto used the exchange to move Novak's contract while taking back another guard option. Utah instead acquired a specialist shooter and a draft asset with three years before its final selection.

sections.heading: Garrett Did Not Become a Raptors Rotation Player
sections.body: Garrett had appeared in 71 games for Utah in 2013-14, averaging 3.5 points, but that prior experience did not convert into lasting Toronto production. The Raptors waived him later in July 2014 rather than building a new backcourt role around him. Their C grade must therefore be read as limited direct basketball value from the player received, with any salary or roster-management benefit considered separately. Garrett's earlier Jazz season cannot be counted as a Raptors return.

sections.heading: Utah Added Novak and the Pick That Became No. 36
sections.body: Novak had established himself as a high-percentage NBA three-point shooter, giving Utah an identifiable specialist to try in its rotation. The accompanying second-round pick later resolved as the 2017 No. 36 selection associated with Jonah Bolden. That is an actual named draft outcome, even though Bolden's later NBA work should not be assigned to a Utah roster that did not develop him. The Jazz's B+ credits the combination of shooter and transferable draft value, rather than claiming that either became a franchise cornerstone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah earns B+ for acquiring Steve Novak and the future second-rounder that became No. 36 Jonah Bolden. Toronto grades C after receiving Diante Garrett and waiving him that month. The Jazz obtained a useful specialist and additional draft flexibility; the Raptors realized little direct playing production from Garrett.

sections.heading: Seattle Exchanged Bobby Simmons Rights for Drobnjak
sections.body: On the night of the 2001 draft, Seattle selected DePaul forward Bobby Simmons with the No. 42 pick and sent his draft rights to Washington. The SuperSonics instead received the rights to Predrag Drobnjak, whom Washington had originally drafted in 1997 while he was playing overseas. The Wizards wanted a fresh American wing prospect, while Seattle chose an international big man it could bring into an NBA frontcourt. Neither side received an established NBA veteran as part of the rights exchange.

sections.heading: Drobnjak Became a Real Seattle Frontcourt Contributor
sections.body: Drobnjak joined the SuperSonics and appeared in 72 games as a rookie in 2001-02 before taking on an expanded role the next season. That concrete Seattle playing time is the central reason the team's C+ grade is defensible: the exchanged draft rights yielded immediate NBA minutes rather than only speculative overseas value. His tenure did not produce an elite starting center, which limits the victory margin. The stronger local return was a working rotation big, not an unfulfilled promise.

sections.heading: Washington Developed Simmons but His Peak Came Later
sections.body: The Wizards acquired a second-round forward who had averaged 16.7 points at DePaul during his junior year, and Simmons later established himself in the NBA. His most notable scoring production, however, came with other franchises after the Washington phase of his career. The Wizards' C recognizes that they acquired a legitimate professional player without treating every later season as a Washington accomplishment. That team-specific distinction helps explain why Seattle receives the slight edge despite Simmons's wider career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Seattle SuperSonics Edge. Seattle gets C+ for turning No. 42 Bobby Simmons' rights into Predrag Drobnjak's early-2000s frontcourt minutes. Washington receives C for Simmons, who later developed into a capable NBA wing. The Sonics realized the more direct return in their own uniform, though neither acquisition became a franchise star.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Jake Voskuhl for Samake and a Future Pick
sections.body: On October 29, 2001, Chicago sent center Jake Voskuhl to Phoenix for Soumaila Samake and a 2003 second-round pick. The future selection mattered more than the immediate center exchange: Chicago waived Samake the same day, according to its transaction ledger. The Bulls were therefore not acquiring Samake as a lasting rotation piece. They had turned Voskuhl's rights into draft capital while Phoenix chose a center it could retain and use on its own roster.

sections.heading: The Future Selection Became Matt Bonner at No. 45
sections.body: Chicago's incoming second-rounder ultimately became the No. 45 choice in the 2003 draft, used to select Matt Bonner. The Bulls later traded Bonner's rights to Toronto rather than enjoying his eventual NBA shooting career directly. Nevertheless, the selection was a tangible asset Chicago could move in another draft-rights transaction. The B+ grade rests on acquiring and ultimately using transferable draft value, not on crediting the Bulls for seasons Bonner played in Toronto and San Antonio.

sections.heading: Phoenix Obtained a Center, Not a Future Draft Choice
sections.body: Voskuhl gave the Suns a conventional center option at the start of the 2001-02 season. That was a more immediate roster addition than the pick Phoenix gave up, and he stayed with the franchise beyond that season. The Suns' C+ credits his actual center minutes without pretending that the return transformed the team. Phoenix gave up a future second-round option, while Chicago deliberately traded away immediate center depth to obtain a different long-term asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives B+ for the 2003 second-round pick that became No. 45 Matt Bonner and was subsequently usable in another transaction. Phoenix grades C+ for the center minutes supplied by Jake Voskuhl. Samake was immediately waived, so the Bulls' advantage comes from the acquired pick, not from his NBA contribution.

sections.heading: Portland Added Ruffin Amid the 2009 Deadline Shuffle
sections.body: On February 18, 2009, Portland sent forward Ike Diogu and cash to Sacramento for Michael Ruffin. The deal followed the larger Chicago-Sacramento exchange that briefly routed Ruffin through the Kings. Portland was making a small frontcourt roster change rather than trading a featured scorer or starter. Ruffin was known for rebounding and defensive effort, while Diogu was a former first-rounder still looking for a durable NBA role. The cash component made Sacramento's return more than just another big man.

sections.heading: Ruffin Was a Short-Term Defensive Depth Option
sections.body: Portland acquired a veteran whose value was tied to physical frontcourt work and role-specific bench minutes, not to producing a high scoring average. Ruffin was not a long-term Trail Blazers centerpiece, so Portland's C+ cannot reasonably be justified by an extended future contribution. The move fit the club's immediate playoff-season roster requirements at relatively low basketball cost. Its limited scope explains why the verdict is a slight edge instead of a sweeping evaluation of a major franchise turning point.

sections.heading: Sacramento Received Diogu and Cash Instead
sections.body: Diogu arrived in Sacramento with prior NBA experience and the hope that a change of setting might revive his development. The Kings also received cash, an immediate financial return separate from the player's court production. Diogu's Sacramento stint was too limited to turn this into a durable talent win, even though his draft pedigree gave the incoming player some appeal. The Kings' C reflects a plausible low-cost transaction, with Portland narrowly favored because Ruffin answered its more immediate frontcourt need.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge. Portland gets C+ for acquiring Michael Ruffin as immediate veteran frontcourt depth during a playoff season. Sacramento earns C for Ike Diogu plus cash. Neither player produced a lasting transformation for his new club, leaving a narrow outcome based on role fit and the short-term utility of the exchanged players.

sections.heading: Chicago Brought Charles Oakley Back in a Toronto Deal
sections.body: Chicago reacquired veteran forward Charles Oakley from Toronto during the summer of 2001. The Bulls also received a 2002 second-round draft choice, sending Brian Skinner to the Raptors. Oakley was already an established rebounding and defensive presence from his earlier Chicago years, making this a recognizable immediate frontcourt move. The draft choice was a second asset, not a throwaway detail, and gave the Bulls flexibility during the following season. Toronto chose a younger frontcourt option in Skinner instead.

sections.heading: Oakley Supplied Experience During the Rebuilding Season
sections.body: Oakley returned to a Bulls franchise very different from the playoff team he once supported. He brought veteran leadership and frontcourt physicality, rather than a promise of another long prime. The Bulls' A- grade reflects what they received through the combined player and selection package, not an assumption that Oakley recreated his earlier All-Star-era contribution. Chicago used him as an immediate frontcourt option while retaining the ability to move the draft asset in a separate transaction.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Later Went to Portland
sections.body: The incoming second-round pick eventually became the No. 42 selection in 2002 associated with Jason Jennings. Chicago did not use that pick to draft Jennings; it sent the rights to the future selection to Portland in a separate Greg Anthony trade later in the offseason. Toronto's C recognizes Skinner as a real NBA player, but the Bulls gained both Oakley's near-term experience and draft flexibility. Those two identifiable forms of value explain the source-side advantage without double-counting the subsequent deal as a second pick created from nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago grades A- for adding Charles Oakley and the second-round pick later used in the Greg Anthony exchange. Toronto receives C for Brian Skinner. Oakley's veteran minutes and the pick's subsequent transaction value make the Bulls' return more useful than the single young frontcourt piece surrendered.

sections.heading: Houston Paid Cash to Acquire Vince Edwards at No. 52
sections.body: During the 2018 NBA draft, Utah selected Purdue forward Vince Edwards with the 52nd pick and transferred his rights to Houston for cash considerations. NBA.com's draft-night tracker confirms the cash-for-rights structure. The Rockets received a low-cost developmental prospect; the Jazz obtained money without sacrificing a featured rotation player or a first-round selection. The trade's purpose was therefore draft-rights acquisition rather than a conventional player-for-player exchange.

sections.heading: Edwards Did Not Develop Into a Houston Rotation Piece
sections.body: Edwards entered the league after a four-year college career and gave Houston a chance to evaluate a versatile forward. He later spent time on a two-way arrangement, but his NBA role with the Rockets was extremely limited. The D grade reflects that modest return relative to the cash paid, rather than counting every G League appearance as productive NBA rotation value. Houston acquired someone it could develop, yet the initial rights did not translate into a significant first-team contribution.

sections.heading: Utah Received Immediate Financial Value
sections.body: Utah's compensation was cash, not another draft choice that would mature later. The Jazz therefore realized its side of the deal immediately, while the Rockets carried the uncertainty of Edwards' development. A cash return can be useful for an organization even though it doesn't generate points or rebounds on its own. Utah's C reflects that direct financial benefit against the limited NBA impact of the selected player. The verdict shouldn't be mistaken for evidence that the Jazz acquired a future star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah receives C for converting the No. 52 draft rights to Vince Edwards into cash. Houston earns D after using the acquired rights on a prospect with little NBA rotation impact for the Rockets. The exchange was small, but Utah realized more direct value from its side.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Boozer Through a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: In July 2010, Chicago reached a sign-and-trade arrangement with Utah for two-time All-Star forward Carlos Boozer. The Bulls also received a protected future second-round selection. Utah obtained a traded-player exception worth roughly $13 million, which created flexibility under the salary-cap rules rather than adding an active player to the Jazz roster. The second-round obligation eventually resolved as the 2011 pick used at No. 43 on Malcolm Lee. Both sides were making decisions about roster construction rather than exchanging two equal-profile players.

sections.heading: Boozer Delivered Several Seasons as a Bulls Starter
sections.body: Boozer became a productive Chicago frontcourt scorer and rebounder on multiple playoff teams, including the 2010-11 Bulls who reached the Eastern Conference finals. He did not provide every year of his contract at peak value, but the Bulls received far more than an empty salary commitment. Their B+ grade acknowledges a useful veteran in a winning period while taking account of the expense and eventual decline attached to the deal. The future second-round pick was a secondary part of the exchange.

sections.heading: Utah Retained Salary-Cap Trade Flexibility
sections.body: The Jazz had to replace Boozer's frontcourt contribution, but a traded-player exception allowed them to acquire future salary in another permitted trade without a matching outgoing salary at that moment. The exception was not a conventional roster asset and it wasn't worth treating as a guaranteed future star. Still, the financial flexibility was genuine compensation for cooperating in a sign-and-trade rather than losing Boozer through an ordinary free-agent departure. Utah's B+ reflects that negotiated value against Chicago's direct on-court benefit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Chicago earns B+ for several productive seasons from Carlos Boozer and an additional second-round pick. Utah also receives B+ for the roughly $13 million traded-player exception generated by the sign-and-trade. The Bulls secured immediate frontcourt production while the Jazz preserved meaningful financial flexibility.

sections.heading: Cleveland Exchanged Allen Crabbe for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: Cleveland selected California guard Allen Crabbe 31st overall in the 2013 draft and traded his rights to Portland. The Cavaliers received second-round selections in 2015 and 2016 instead of bringing the wing to training camp. Those two choices ultimately resolved as No. 53 Sir'Dominic Pointer and No. 48 Paul Zipser, respectively. The exchange let Cleveland break a single immediate prospect into two future draft assets, while Portland secured the right to develop a particular shooter.

sections.heading: Crabbe Became a Productive Portland Perimeter Player
sections.body: Crabbe earned a lasting rotation role with the Trail Blazers and provided outside shooting during several seasons with the club. That return gave Portland more direct NBA playing value than it would have received from a prospect who never reached the roster. The C+ grade recognizes a useful second-round acquisition without exaggerating it into a franchise-altering star. His Portland work should be judged separately from contracts and production acquired with other franchises later in his career.

sections.heading: Cleveland Used the Picks as Assets Before Draft Day
sections.body: Cleveland later included the two incoming second-round choices in its January 2014 trade with Chicago for Luol Deng. That matters when evaluating the original 2013 exchange: the Cavaliers did not themselves draft and develop Pointer or Zipser with these selections. They held transferable options that helped assemble a more immediate veteran acquisition. Cleveland's C+ reflects that subsequent draft-capital utility, rather than attributing Pointer's or Zipser's playing time on unrelated NBA teams to the Cavaliers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Cleveland gets C+ for two future seconds eventually incorporated into the Luol Deng trade. Portland also earns C+ for Allen Crabbe's useful wing tenure after receiving his rights at No. 31. The Cavaliers realized transferable draft value, while the Blazers obtained direct perimeter production.

sections.heading: Chicago Moved a Second-Rounder for Greg Anthony
sections.body: Chicago sent Portland a conditional second-round choice during July 2001 and acquired veteran point guard Greg Anthony. The selection had been part of an earlier transaction with Toronto and ultimately resolved as No. 42 Jason Jennings in the 2002 draft. Anthony was an established defensive-minded guard whose short-term availability suited a young rebuilding Bulls team. The Blazers were willing to exchange his experience for another future draft opportunity.

sections.heading: Anthony Supplied a Veteran Guard Option, Briefly
sections.body: Anthony played for Chicago during the 2001-02 season but did not become a long-term foundation for the franchise. The Bulls waived him in March 2002, according to their transaction log. The B- grade recognizes the limited yet identifiable value of veteran guard minutes at a time when the roster needed experienced direction. Chicago did not obtain a franchise point guard, so his brief stint can't be treated as evidence of a major personnel victory.

sections.heading: Portland Received a Real Selection That Became Jennings
sections.body: The second-round pick sent to Portland carried conditional protection and eventually became No. 42 in 2002, the selection used on Jason Jennings. That gave the Blazers an identifiable draft result rather than an unexercised option. Jennings did not become an established NBA rotation player, which limits the realized basketball return from that pick. Portland's C+ acknowledges that it acquired draft flexibility while Chicago actually used Anthony for a short stretch. This was one pick conveyed through consecutive transactions, not a second pick created by the Bulls.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago receives B- for the short-term point guard minutes supplied by Greg Anthony. Portland earns C+ for a conditional second-rounder that converted into the 2002 No. 42 Jason Jennings selection. Both returns were modest, but Chicago obtained a more immediate NBA role from its asset.

sections.heading: San Antonio Chose Daye Over De Colo at the Deadline
sections.body: San Antonio sent guard Nando De Colo to Toronto for Austin Daye on February 20, 2014. De Colo had been in the Spurs' system for almost two seasons but was not part of the regular backcourt rotation that would lead the club into the postseason. Daye offered a taller, perimeter-oriented forward option for the end of the bench. Toronto used the exchange to test another ball-handler rather than continue with a forward it had barely played.

sections.heading: Daye Joined a Title Team Without Becoming a Main Rotation Player
sections.body: The Spurs won the 2014 championship after this trade, but Daye's part in that achievement needs precision. He appeared in 14 San Antonio regular-season games and played 115 total minutes after the exchange, with one brief postseason appearance. He was on the roster, not a central contributor to the playoff run. San Antonio's C- reflects a depth acquisition with limited direct court production, rather than awarding him the value created by Tim Duncan, Tony Parker and the rest of the rotation.

sections.heading: De Colo Offered Toronto a Short Guard Trial
sections.body: The Raptors were looking for backcourt insurance during a season that ended with a first-round playoff series against Brooklyn. De Colo played part of the stretch run and made one brief postseason appearance. His later success overseas doesn't count as NBA production for Toronto, but the club acquired a usable ball-handler without surrendering an established rotation wing. The Raptors' C acknowledges a small practical return, marginally better than San Antonio's very limited Daye minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Raptors Edge. Toronto earns C for acquiring Nando De Colo and using him briefly behind its established guards. San Antonio gets C- for Austin Daye, whose place on the eventual championship roster wasn't the same as major postseason impact. Neither club obtained a long-term NBA starter.

sections.heading: Golden State Moved Injured Chriss and Cash for Draft Rights
sections.body: On March 25, 2021, Golden State traded Marquese Chriss and cash considerations to San Antonio, receiving the draft rights to Cady Lalanne. Chriss had played only twice that season after suffering a leg injury, so the move wasn't an exchange of two active frontcourt rotation players. The Warriors also generated a trade exception, as their transaction ledger records. San Antonio was compensated financially while taking on an injured player whose season was already over.

sections.heading: Lalanne’s Rights Never Produced Warriors NBA Minutes
sections.body: Lalanne had been a 2015 second-round pick whose professional career was based largely outside the NBA. Golden State acquired his rights rather than a player who was expected to report immediately and play meaningful minutes. That distinction accounts for the Warriors' D in the completed trade record: the incoming basketball asset didn't become a useful Golden State rotation contributor. The related salary-management flexibility was real, but it wasn't the same thing as receiving a healthy frontcourt replacement for Chriss.

sections.heading: The Spurs Kept the Cash and Quickly Waived Chriss
sections.body: San Antonio waived Chriss on March 28, only three days after the transaction. The Spurs therefore should not be credited with a later stretch of NBA production from him. Their actual return was the cash accompanying his contract, balanced against the temporary roster and accounting consequences of accepting him. The C reflects a defined financial benefit in a low-stakes trade, not an attempt to portray Chriss as a successful on-court acquisition for San Antonio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio receives C because the deal produced cash, while injured Marquese Chriss was waived three days later. Golden State grades D for acquiring unused Cady Lalanne draft rights; the accompanying trade exception supplied flexibility but no replacement frontcourt performance. The narrow transaction created little new basketball talent for either roster.

sections.heading: Cleveland Paid Utah Cash for Damian Jones
sections.body: Cleveland acquired center Damian Jones from Utah on July 8, 2023, sending cash considerations in the transaction. Both teams announced the terms, so the incoming asset wasn't a draft choice or a protected selection that might convey years later. Jones had played for the Jazz after arriving from the Lakers the previous February. The Cavaliers wanted another experienced big man behind their established frontcourt, while Utah chose immediate cash rather than retaining a reserve center.

sections.heading: Jones Supplied 39 Regular-Season Appearances
sections.body: Jones saw action in 39 games for the Cavaliers in 2023-24, all as a reserve. He averaged 6.9 minutes and 2.7 points, providing a small but identifiable amount of center depth. Those numbers explain why this wasn't a deal for a new starter, even though the player had prior championship experience with Golden State. Cleveland's B in the canonical grading reflects an inexpensive way to add a proven NBA body, not a claim that Jones became one of the team's principal contributors.

sections.heading: Utah Took a Certain Cash Return Instead of Bench Minutes
sections.body: The Jazz had used Jones for 19 games after acquiring him in February 2023, averaging 4.6 points during that prior Utah tenure. The July exchange converted his contract into cash instead of holding him for another season. Cash has real organizational use but doesn't make a basket or rebound, so Utah's C is best read as an immediate financial outcome. In this comparison, Cleveland extracted actual bench minutes while Utah chose money over a continuing reserve role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B for acquiring Damian Jones at a cash-only cost and getting 39 reserve appearances in 2023-24. Utah earns C for a guaranteed financial return. The Cavaliers' advantage reflects usable NBA depth, though Jones's 6.9 minutes per appearance keep the sporting contribution in perspective.

sections.heading: The Warriors Exchanged Whitehead for Shelton Jones
sections.body: Golden State sent center Jerome Whitehead to San Antonio on November 22, 1988, receiving young forward Shelton Jones. The swap happened shortly after the season began, with the Warriors looking at another athletic frontcourt option and the Spurs taking an experienced interior player. Neither incoming asset was a draft choice, and the deal did not involve cash or a star under a long-term commitment. The eventual value depends on what each player actually did in his new uniform.

sections.heading: Jones Was Waived Less Than a Month After Arriving
sections.body: Jones never established a lasting Warriors role. Golden State's transaction ledger shows the club waiving him on December 15, just over three weeks after the exchange. Even if his youth gave the deal a development rationale, the team gained little direct rotation use from the player it acquired. Golden State's C- captures that unsuccessful audition rather than counting Jones's subsequent appearances for Philadelphia as a Warriors benefit. Trading an established center for a temporary roster look carried a modest opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Whitehead Played 52 Games for the Spurs
sections.body: Whitehead appeared in 52 San Antonio games during the 1988-89 season, starting four and averaging 11.2 minutes with 3.2 points and 2.5 rebounds. Those aren't star numbers, but they document an actual reserve-center role that San Antonio received from the transaction. The Spurs' C reflects usable interior minutes without treating one partial season as a major building block. Compared with Golden State's quick release of Jones, Whitehead gave San Antonio the more tangible short-term basketball contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge. San Antonio earns C after getting 52 games of reserve-center work from Jerome Whitehead. Golden State receives C- for Shelton Jones, whom it waived within a month of the swap. The Spurs obtained useful short-term depth while the Warriors' incoming player barely lasted.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Swapped Two Draft Assets for Krejci and Schofield
sections.body: In the 2020 draft sequence, the Thunder acquired the rights to Vit Krejci, selected No. 37, and forward Admiral Schofield from Washington. The Wizards received Cassius Winston's rights at No. 53 plus a future second-rounder ultimately associated with the 2024 No. 37 selection of Bobi Klintman. The two sides weren't simply exchanging two current rotation players. Oklahoma City prioritized a higher-positioned 2020 prospect, while Washington diversified its return between an immediate guard pick and a later draft opportunity.

sections.heading: Krejci Gave the Thunder a Chance to Develop a Young Wing
sections.body: Krejci had international experience and was recovering from a serious knee injury at the time of the 2020 draft. Oklahoma City held his rights as part of a patient roster-building period, and he later played NBA games for the Thunder. Schofield was a separate incoming player but didn't become a long-term OKC rotation centerpiece. The Thunder's B+ reflects control of a developmental player who reached its own court, not an assertion that either incoming asset immediately turned the franchise into a contender.

sections.heading: Washington Got Winston and a Pick With a Later Life
sections.body: Winston was a productive Michigan State point guard, but his NBA role with Washington remained limited. The second-round pick conveyed alongside his rights was valuable chiefly as a future transaction resource; it later became linked to the No. 37 Bobi Klintman selection in 2024. Washington shouldn't automatically receive credit for Klintman's later NBA work elsewhere merely because the pick appears in the original asset chain. The Wizards' C- acknowledges the received draft opportunities while distinguishing them from meaningful Washington playing production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder earn B+ for Krejci's developmental rights and subsequent NBA appearances, plus Schofield. Washington receives C- for the rights to Cassius Winston and the future second-rounder that became No. 37 in 2024. The Thunder converted more of this package into its own NBA roster use.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Dan Roundfield for Two Washington Frontcourt Players
sections.body: On June 17, 1985, Detroit sent Dan Roundfield to the Washington Bullets and acquired Rick Mahorn and Mike Gibson. Both the Pistons' transaction ledger and contemporary league records identify the same three players. Roundfield had spent only one season in Detroit, while Mahorn was an established defensive and rebounding presence for Washington. The Pistons were rebuilding their frontcourt around a developing contender; the Bullets chose a veteran who could contribute immediately. It wasn't a straight player-for-player exchange, and Gibson should remain part of the recorded package even though Mahorn would later define its reputation.

sections.heading: Mahorn's Value Developed Into a Championship Role
sections.body: Mahorn wasn't a finished answer in Detroit on arrival. A Pistons retrospective notes he started only 12 games in his first season and six the next, before becoming a trusted physical presence under Chuck Daly. That later transformation is central to the A grade: Mahorn ultimately played an important role on Detroit's 1989 championship club and became a recognizable part of the Bad Boys' interior defense. The grade reflects sustained team-specific impact that wasn't obvious from his first months after the swap. Gibson was an additional incoming piece, but the lasting difference in this trade was Mahorn, not an imagined equal contribution from both players.

sections.heading: Washington Got a Productive Year Before Roundfield Declined
sections.body: The Bullets didn't get nothing. At age 32, Roundfield appeared in 79 Washington games in 1985-86, starting 21, averaging 11.6 points and 8.1 rebounds. He supplied tangible frontcourt production in the season immediately after the trade, rather than an empty roster slot. His role shortened sharply the following season, when he played 36 games. Washington's C+ grade recognizes that one useful veteran campaign but discounts its limited duration. Detroit's advantage emerges from what Mahorn became over several playoff runs, not from pretending Roundfield failed to play for the Bullets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit earns A for bringing in Rick Mahorn and Mike Gibson in exchange for Dan Roundfield; Mahorn developed into a central defensive contributor to the 1989 championship team. Washington receives C+ because Roundfield produced 11.6 points and 8.1 rebounds per game in 1985-86 but offered a shorter return. The Pistons secured the longer-lasting value.

sections.heading: Chicago Moved From Keith Lee to Charles Oakley on Draft Night
sections.body: On June 18, 1985, Cleveland drafted Virginia Union forward Charles Oakley ninth and VCU guard Calvin Duncan 30th. Chicago selected Memphis State big man Keith Lee 11th, then sent Lee's rights and guard Ennis Whatley to the Cavaliers for Oakley and Duncan. A contemporaneous United Press International dispatch described the four-player exchange, and both clubs' transaction histories corroborate it. Chicago preferred Oakley's rebounding and defensive profile to the higher-profile college scoring pedigree of Lee. Cleveland accepted two players with immediate roster potential, but the pick numbers alone weren't a reliable measure of what either team would receive.

sections.heading: Oakley Became a Major Part of Chicago's Frontcourt
sections.body: Oakley's value to the Bulls was substantial in his own Chicago tenure, not just in the reputation he developed elsewhere. After a rookie campaign in which he averaged 8.6 rebounds, he played all 82 games in 1986-87 and averaged 14.5 points and 13.1 rebounds. He followed that with 13.0 rebounds per game in 1987-88. Those seasons gave Michael Jordan's early Chicago teams durable interior rebounding and a physical frontcourt partner. Chicago later traded Oakley to New York for Bill Cartwright in a separate 1988 move, so Cartwright's subsequent accomplishments shouldn't be credited as direct Oakley playing production. The Bulls' A+ reflects the immediate and sustained impact of their 1985 acquisition.

sections.heading: Lee and Whatley Never Matched That Cleveland Return
sections.body: Cleveland's gamble on Lee didn't yield an equivalent long-term NBA contributor. The Cavaliers used him for a limited portion of two seasons, while Whatley's role shrank sharply: he played eight Cleveland games in 1985-86, totaling 66 minutes and averaging 2.8 points. That was markedly less useful guard production than he had supplied for Chicago before the trade. Duncan, the second-round right obtained by the Bulls, wasn't the reason Chicago won this exchange; Oakley's development drove the gap. Cleveland's D grade records the short and disappointing return from its two incoming assets rather than assuming every college star would eventually become an NBA starter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives A+ for securing Charles Oakley's rights and getting three productive seasons of elite rebounding before a separate 1988 trade. Cleveland grades D for Keith Lee's limited Cavaliers tenure and Ennis Whatley's eight-game stay. Calvin Duncan was part of Chicago's package, but Oakley supplied the defining value.

sections.heading: Cleveland Turned Paul Thompson Into Two Conditional Draft Returns
sections.body: On February 12, 1985, Cleveland sent forward Paul Thompson to Milwaukee for the Bucks' 1985 second-round selection and a conditional 1987 choice. The first pick became No. 45 in 1985, used on John 'Hot Rod' Williams. The later obligation was a second-rounder if Thompson appeared on Milwaukee's roster that season, and a third-rounder otherwise; it ultimately became the 1987 No. 41 selection of Kannard Johnson. Those conditions matter because the Cavaliers secured two defined draft opportunities rather than a vague promise of future compensation. Milwaukee wanted a wing who had played a much larger role in Cleveland, but accepted the future-draft cost for a midseason roster addition.

sections.heading: No. 45 Became a Long-Term Cavaliers Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Williams didn't join Cleveland's NBA rotation until 1986-87, so the deal shouldn't be described as an instant 1985 breakthrough. His delayed arrival proved worth waiting for. Williams started all 80 of his Cleveland games in 1986-87 and averaged 14.6 points, 7.9 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. He played for the Cavaliers throughout the next several seasons, including the developing playoff era that followed, and recorded 16.8 points and 8.1 rebounds per game in 1989-90. This sustained, directly attributable production from the acquired second-round pick is why Cleveland's A+ has a concrete foundation. Johnson's later selection is a separate, smaller incoming asset, not a second Hot Rod Williams.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received a Short Reserve Stint
sections.body: Thompson had started 27 of his 33 Cavaliers games in 1984-85, averaging 10.5 points before the trade. Milwaukee instead used him as a reserve in 16 regular-season games, where he averaged 6.6 points and 2.6 rebounds. He was with Philadelphia the following season. That narrow Bucks return is real enough to record, but far short of the multi-season Cleveland value created by Williams. Milwaukee's D doesn't imply that Thompson had no NBA ability; it reflects the specific bargain the Bucks made by sending away a pick that turned into a long-serving Cavaliers forward.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives A+ after trading Paul Thompson for a 1985 second-round pick that became Hot Rod Williams and a conditional 1987 pick later used on Kannard Johnson. Milwaukee gets D for 16 games of reserve production from Thompson. Williams' substantial Cavaliers career gives Cleveland the decisive advantage.

sections.heading: The Kings Sent a Veteran Scorer to the Spurs for a Young Center
sections.body: On December 11, 1984, Kansas City traded Billy Knight to San Antonio for Mark McNamara. This was the Kings' final season in Kansas City before their move to Sacramento, so the modern archive team name shouldn't obscure which franchise made the decision. Knight was a veteran wing with a long ABA and NBA scoring history, while McNamara was a younger center whose size appealed to a team needing different bench options. The trade was a direct two-player exchange. Neither franchise acquired a draft selection, extra cash, or another contractual asset as part of the recorded terms.

sections.heading: Knight Added Measurable Depth to San Antonio
sections.body: Knight played 52 regular-season games for the Spurs in 1984-85, averaging 11.8 minutes and 6.0 points, according to San Antonio's season ledger. He also appeared five times in the playoffs, though his scoring and minutes were modest there. The Spurs didn't gain an All-Star or a new full-time starter. They did obtain an experienced small forward who could fill a real reserve shift for most of the year. Their A- grade in the canonical record is a favorable relative verdict on the exchange, not an assertion that those minutes constituted franchise-level value. The near-term contribution was clear enough to establish an advantage over the alternative.

sections.heading: McNamara's Kansas City Rotation Opportunity Stayed Small
sections.body: McNamara suited up for 33 Kings games following the move, playing 6.4 minutes per appearance and averaging 2.4 points and 1.7 rebounds. He didn't start a game for Kansas City during that stint. The club briefly gained another available center but received little frontcourt production and no enduring role from the acquisition. San Antonio had received 52 games of veteran wing depth in return, a more tangible one-season contribution. Kansas City's D+ reflects that limited outcome rather than blaming McNamara for every difficulty the team faced that year. Both players were complementary roster pieces, yet Knight provided materially more regular playing time after the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio gets A- for Billy Knight's 52 games of reserve work and five postseason appearances. The Kansas City Kings earn D+ after Mark McNamara managed 33 games at only 6.4 minutes per night. The Spurs received the stronger short-term return in a modest veteran-for-center exchange.

sections.heading: The Bullets Bought Immediate Scoring with a Future First
sections.body: Washington acquired Dallas forward Jay Vincent on September 3, 1986, by sending the Mavericks its first-round choice in 1990. Bullets general manager Bob Ferry explained at the time that the roster needed another scoring forward alongside Moses Malone and Jeff Malone. Dallas faced a crowded forward rotation and accepted a draft asset whose precise slot was still four years away. The exchange therefore traded present certainty for future flexibility. Contemporary reporting and the clubs' transaction ledgers corroborate the basic terms: Vincent went to Washington, and the future Washington first went to Dallas.

sections.heading: Dallas Converted the Pick Rather Than Drafting Willie Burton
sections.body: The Washington-origin selection eventually became No. 9 in 1990, but Willie Burton never played for the Mavericks. Dallas included the choice alongside another first-round pick in a June 21, 1990 deal bringing Fat Lever from Denver. The Nuggets then moved No. 9 and their No. 15 to Miami for the No. 3 selection. Miami selected Burton ninth. Official Denver and Miami media guides document that chain. Dallas deserves partial credit for using the Washington pick as consideration for Lever, but not direct credit for Burton's career and not the entire value of Lever, who cost another first as well. Lever's Mavericks stint was later hampered by injuries, including just four games in 1990-91.

sections.heading: Vincent Delivered a Useful but Short Washington Return
sections.body: Vincent filled a legitimate scoring role for the Bullets in 1986-87, playing 51 regular-season games with 13.3 points and 4.1 rebounds per appearance. He also appeared in three playoff games. Those numbers provided a return more immediate than Dallas could collect from a pick that would not convey until 1990. But he wasn't a long-term answer for Washington. Dallas eventually gained transaction utility from the choice, and Washington gained a rotation scorer when it wanted one. This is why B- grades for both sides and an even verdict are defensible: the pick had value despite its indirect outcome, while Vincent's direct production was measurable but brief.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Washington receives B- for Jay Vincent's immediate 1986-87 scoring. Dallas also receives B- for a first-round asset later used alongside another choice to acquire Fat Lever. Miami, not Dallas, drafted Willie Burton with the Washington-origin No. 9 pick.

sources.title: Bullets Get Vincent for No. 1 Pick

sections.heading: Denver and Washington Exchanged Four Different Rotation Fits
sections.body: On November 2, 1987, Denver acquired guard Michael Adams and forward Jay Vincent from Washington in exchange for guard Darrell Walker and forward Mark Alarie. The trade followed the Bullets' signing of Bernard King and reflected two separate roster priorities. Washington wanted a different combination of guard defense, ball movement and frontcourt depth. Denver wanted scoring and a point guard who could play at the Nuggets' pace. Contemporary reporting described all four named players, and the NBA's dated transaction ledger confirms the exchange. It was not a simple Adams-for-Walker swap: Vincent and Alarie were real parts of the roster calculation.

sections.heading: Adams Developed Into Denver's Long-Term Difference
sections.body: Adams became the most productive player involved after the swap. In his first Denver season, 1987-88, he played all 82 regular-season games, starting 75, and averaged 13.9 points, 6.1 assists and 2.0 steals. His game fit the Nuggets' fast offense, and his scoring climbed to 18.5 points per game in 1988-89. He remained an important Denver guard as the team changed around him. The A+ grade reflects a player who developed into a durable offensive contributor, not just a promising backup who briefly filled minutes. Vincent also came to Denver in the package, but his career there wasn't the chief reason the deal tilted the Nuggets' way.

sections.heading: Washington Still Obtained Two Usable Players
sections.body: The Bullets didn't surrender Adams and Vincent for nothing. Darrell Walker played 52 regular-season games in 1987-88 and added five playoff appearances, offering defense and backcourt experience. Alarie appeared in 63 regular-season games that year and later grew into a larger rotation role, averaging 10.5 points across 82 games in 1989-90. He supplied Washington with several seasons of frontcourt availability. These concrete contributions justify Washington's A grade rather than a harsh verdict based only on Adams' Denver breakout. The edge is slight because the Bullets acquired meaningful depth, but Adams' longer high-level perimeter production supplies Denver with the highest-impact player in this four-person exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge. Denver receives A+ for turning Michael Adams into a productive long-term guard, with Jay Vincent also acquired. Washington earns A for the contributions of Darrell Walker and Mark Alarie. Both clubs secured genuine NBA rotation players, but Adams gave the Nuggets the best individual return.

sections.heading: Chicago Gave Indiana a Veteran Guard for Two Future Choices
sections.body: On September 18, 1986, the Bulls traded Kyle Macy to Indiana for a 1988 second-round pick and another second-round selection that eventually conveyed in 1992. The Pacers' official franchise transaction history verifies the two-pick price. Macy had been a full-time Chicago starter in 1985-86, but moving him allowed the Bulls to pursue a different guard mix without losing the value of his expiring role entirely. Indiana sought an experienced reserve, while Chicago obtained two draft opportunities with different arrival dates. The 1988 pick later became No. 37 and the 1992 selection No. 39; neither was a first-round asset.

sections.heading: The Earlier Pick Helped Chicago Acquire Rory Sparrow
sections.body: Chicago didn't use the 1988 second-round selection to draft Greg Butler. On November 12, 1987, the Bulls sent that choice to the Knicks for guard Rory Sparrow. Contemporary UPI reporting specified that New York received the lower of Chicago's two second-rounders, tracing the pick back to the Indiana transaction. Sparrow played 55 Bulls regular-season games in 1987-88 and averaged 4.5 points and 2.9 assists. That was reserve production, not a star acquisition, but it represents a basketball use for the asset. Chicago held its other pick until 1992, selected Litterial Green at No. 39, and traded his draft rights to Orlando for a 1993 second-rounder. The two branches should be evaluated as different transactions, not double-counted as Bulls player careers.

sections.heading: Macy Delivered One Season of Indiana Backup Minutes
sections.body: Macy appeared in 76 games for the 1986-87 Pacers, starting none and averaging 16.4 minutes, 4.9 points and 2.6 assists. He also played in four playoff games. Those totals document a useful but limited veteran presence behind Indiana's regular guards. The Pacers' B- grade reflects the stability of having another experienced option for that season, with no later extended run for the team. Chicago's B+ advantage is modest in raw on-court production but reflects two separate assets that the front office could reuse. The verdict doesn't require claiming Butler or Green became Chicago rotation players: neither did, and only Sparrow's later Bulls minutes flowed from the first pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ for two future second-round picks, one used to acquire Rory Sparrow and the other eventually traded after the Litterial Green selection. Indiana receives B- for one reserve season from Kyle Macy. The Bulls retained more opportunities to exchange their assets for additional roster help.

sections.heading: Miami Converted an Expansion Pick Into a Future Selection
sections.body: The Heat drafted Darnell Valentine from the Los Angeles Clippers in the June 23, 1988 expansion draft, then traded him to Cleveland that day for a second-round pick that could convey in 1990 or 1992. Miami was building its first NBA roster and could exchange one of its new selections for a later opportunity instead of keeping every expansion player. Cleveland sought an experienced guard who could help immediately. Reporting from that day's draft and both franchises' transaction histories establish the deal; it wasn't a direct Clippers-to-Cavaliers trade because Miami acquired Valentine first. The eventual second-round pick became No. 41 in 1990, associated with Steve Bardo.

sections.heading: Valentine Played Two NBA Seasons for Cleveland
sections.body: Valentine gave the Cavaliers usable guard depth, although his two Cleveland seasons were interrupted by a year outside the league. In 1988-89 he played 77 games, starting four, averaging 4.8 points and 2.3 assists in 14.1 minutes. He wasn't on an NBA roster in 1989-90, then returned to Cleveland in 1990-91 for 65 games with 60 starts, averaging 9.4 points and 5.4 assists. Those 142 Cavaliers appearances represent concrete value from a future second-round investment. The B grade recognizes his considerable playing time, particularly as a starter on his return, without mistaking him for a long-term cornerstone of the franchise.

sections.heading: Miami Used the Pick in Another Trade Before the 1990 Draft
sections.body: The second-rounder wasn't worthless to Miami simply because Valentine never played a regular-season game for the expansion Heat. A 1990 draft-pick ledger traces the Cleveland-origin choice to Miami's October 1989 exchange with Golden State for Tellis Frank; that pick then moved through another Warriors transaction before the Hawks used No. 41 on Steve Bardo. Miami therefore obtained a negotiable future asset, not Bardo's later playing production. The Heat's B- grade reflects the pick's utility and the limited long-term basketball return through that transaction chain. Cleveland's slightly higher grade is based on actual minutes from Valentine, not hypothetical development of the player eventually taken with the selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B for obtaining Darnell Valentine and using him in 142 games across two seasons, including 60 starts in 1990-91. Miami receives B- for a conditional second-round pick that became a later trade asset. The Cavaliers got the clearer on-court benefit.
