sections.heading: Phoenix Paid for a Specific Expansion-Draft Selection
sections.body: During the June 22, 2004 expansion draft, Phoenix arranged for Charlotte to take center Jahidi White from its unprotected roster. In return the Suns surrendered a 2005 first-round draft choice that eventually became No. 13, used on North Carolina forward Sean May. Contemporary NBA-hosted reporting also described a $3 million cash payment as part of the contemplated arrangement, which appears in Charlotte’s historical asset register. The arrangement was not a standard midseason trade in which White simply moved to the Bobcats for an independently negotiated player swap. Phoenix’s objective was to remove a sizable final-year center salary while Charlotte, the new franchise, collected compensation for selecting a specified player.

sections.heading: The First-Rounder Became Sean May
sections.body: Charlotte exercised the acquired 2005 first-round choice at No. 13 on May after he helped North Carolina win the NCAA title. He played 23 games as a rookie because of injuries but showed scoring and rebounding potential before later knee problems affected his availability. By the end of his Bobcats tenure he had appeared in 82 games during 2006-07 and continued working in a reserve frontcourt role. The selection therefore generated actual NBA minutes, unlike a nonconveyed conditional pick. Its payoff fell below the hoped-for reliable starting big man, and Charlotte’s C+ grade reflects both the value of acquiring a first at low direct draft cost and the modest return of the selected player.

sections.heading: The Suns Gained Salary Flexibility Rather Than a Scorer
sections.body: White had played a reserve role in Phoenix, averaging 4.3 points and 4.3 rebounds in 2003-04. His salary made him an attractive target for an expansion-draft salary-management deal. Phoenix accepted the price of a future first-rounder to clear a salary obligation and reshape its free-agent possibilities. The Suns’ C grade is best tied to that immediate financial flexibility, not a player or draft pick received directly from Charlotte. Charlotte’s compensation was valuable, although the franchise used the pick on an injury-affected prospect; the Suns did not gain another basketball asset from this deal. The eventual value of Phoenix’s other free-agent signings should not be mechanically credited to this specific expansion selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. The Bobcats earn C+ for receiving a 2005 first-rounder used on No. 13 Sean May and reported cash considerations in exchange for selecting Jahidi White. Phoenix gets C for clearing White’s salary. May had injury limitations, but the first-round asset gave Charlotte identifiable value.

sections.heading: The Nets Converted a Franchise Forward Into Draft Capital
sections.body: On July 15, 2004, Denver acquired forward Kenyon Martin from New Jersey through a sign-and-trade agreement. The Nets received three first-round selections with different protections and future delivery schedules. Martin had started 65 games during the Nets 2003-04 season, averaged 16.7 points and 9.5 rebounds, and earned an All-Star appearance. He had also been an integral frontcourt player on the franchise’s back-to-back 2002 and 2003 Finals teams. Denver was buying a proven starting forward for its Carmelo Anthony era, while New Jersey was moving away from a major contract commitment and rebuilding its future draft reserves. The incoming assets were draft picks, not veteran players delivered on July 15.

sections.heading: Martin Provided Denver With Years of Starting Power
sections.body: Martin started 70 Nuggets games in 2004-05, averaging 15.5 points and 7.3 rebounds. Injuries disrupted later seasons, especially in 2005-06 and 2006-07, but he recovered enough to return as an important frontcourt defender on subsequent Nuggets playoff teams. His energetic interior play complemented Anthony and the Denver guards. The Nuggets got real NBA value from a player who remained with the franchise into the 2010-11 season. Their B- inherited grade balances those productive years against both the contract and an uneven injury history. A one-season disappointment would not accurately describe his contribution, yet it was not an uninterrupted string of peak All-Star seasons either.

sections.heading: New Jersey’s Three Protected Picks Had Several Future Paths
sections.body: The first-round selections associated with the sign-and-trade eventually appeared in transaction history alongside No. 16 Joey Graham in 2005 and No. 20 Renaldo Balkman and No. 22 Marcus Williams in 2006. Those names describe draft-pick identities and later chains, not three players who necessarily suited up for the Nets. The value New Jersey obtained was control over multiple protected assets that could be drafted or exchanged while the franchise managed Martin’s departure. Its B- grade reflects the appeal of several future firsts and reduced salary obligations, offset by the loss of a proven forward. In retrospect, Denver obtained the strongest directly traceable starting player, but New Jersey gained substantial tradeable capital.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade by the inherited B- grades. Denver receives B- for Kenyon Martin’s multi-season frontcourt contribution, including 70 starts in 2004-05. New Jersey also earns B- for three protected first-round picks attached to the sign-and-trade. The draft-right paths must be tracked separately from each selected player’s later club.

sections.heading: Charlotte Traded Its Expansion Selection for Milwaukee’s No. 45
sections.body: The Bobcats selected Georgian center Zaza Pachulia from Orlando during the June 22, 2004 expansion draft. The next day, general manager Bernie Bickerstaff sent Pachulia to Milwaukee for the Bucks’ No. 45 selection in the upcoming second round. ESPN’s same-day account and Charlotte’s later official media guide both verify the chronology and that the pick became Bernard Robinson, a forward from Michigan. This was not a case of the Bucks drafting Pachulia in 2004: he had been chosen by Orlando one year earlier and was available to the new franchise only through the expansion process. Charlotte chose a younger drafted wing over keeping the newly selected big man.

sections.heading: Pachulia Played Seventy-Four Games for Milwaukee
sections.body: In 2004-05, Pachulia appeared in 74 Bucks games and averaged 6.2 points with 5.1 rebounds in 18.9 minutes. He started four games but was regularly available off the bench, a sizable first-year return from a veteran player acquired for a mid-second-round selection. He signed with Atlanta the following offseason, where he became a long-running frontcourt presence. Those Hawks seasons belong to another team’s roster history and should not be counted as Milwaukee production from the original expansion deal. The Bucks’ C+ grade can be supported by Pachulia’s real 74-game rotation season, without using his later championships or international accomplishments to inflate what they received.

sections.heading: Bernard Robinson Gave Charlotte a Lesser Draft Return
sections.body: Charlotte selected Bernard Robinson at No. 45 and developed him on the inaugural Bobcats roster. His playing time was limited compared with Pachulia’s Milwaukee role, and the expansion club did not acquire a regular starting forward from this pick. The choice still had value: Charlotte used a player it might not have wanted to retain to obtain a prospect that matched a different positional need. But the direct NBA minutes created were smaller than Milwaukee’s center return. The Bobcats’ C- grade reflects the uncertainty of a mid-second-round selection that did not yield an enduring contributor. The transaction’s date was June 23 for the rights exchange, with the actual draft selection made June 24.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns C+ after Zaza Pachulia supplied 74 games, 6.2 points and 5.1 rebounds in 2004-05. Charlotte receives C- for the No. 45 pick used on Bernard Robinson. This was an expansion-draft follow-up, not an original 2004 Bucks selection of Pachulia.

sections.heading: Detroit Re-Sent Mengke Bateer Two Days After Getting Him
sections.body: Detroit acquired Chinese center Mengke Bateer from Denver on October 1, 2002 in a different transaction involving Rodney White. On October 3, the Pistons traded Bateer to the San Antonio Spurs for a 2003 second-round selection. UPI reported the rapid turnaround and noted San Antonio intended him as depth behind David Robinson and Kevin Willis. The pick, No. 58 in June 2003, became Andreas Glyniadakis. The Pistons received a draft choice, not an established Spurs player, and their brief possession of Bateer should not be recorded as Detroit NBA minutes. The two October moves are related chronologically but were separate agreements with different teams.

sections.heading: Bateer Was a Deep Spurs Reserve
sections.body: Bateer had appeared in 27 Denver games the preceding season with 10 starts and averages of 5.1 points and 3.6 rebounds. Those figures belong to Denver, not San Antonio. Once he joined the Spurs, his role was far smaller, with only 12 regular-season appearances in 2002-03. San Antonio won the 2003 championship, but Bateer was not a central postseason rotation player and his minimal games should not be confused with the value of Tim Duncan or David Robinson. The Spurs’ C grade represents a brief frontcourt contingency and a chance to assess a big man while guarding against injuries late in Robinson’s career.

sections.heading: The No. 58 Selection Did Not Become a Pistons Regular
sections.body: Detroit selected Glyniadakis with the final pick of the 2003 draft. The Greek center did not play an NBA regular-season game for the Pistons; his later short NBA appearance was with Seattle in 2006-07. Detroit’s C- grade reflects an identifiable draft asset that failed to provide an immediate player. San Antonio received temporary depth and Detroit acquired another selection, but neither outcome had sustained value for its receiving club. The source trail is unusually clear: San Antonio had acquired that precise second-round pick in its earlier August 2002 Portland transaction before sending it to Detroit for Bateer. That chain should be preserved without merging these distinct trades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge. San Antonio earns C for 12 regular-season appearances from Mengke Bateer. Detroit gets C- for the 2003 No. 58 second-round choice used on Andreas Glyniadakis, who never played a Pistons regular-season game. Bateer’s prior Denver statistics do not belong to San Antonio.

sections.heading: Atlanta Exchanged Sanikidze’s Rights for a Future Second
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, Atlanta sent the draft rights to Georgian forward Viktor Sanikidze to San Antonio. The Hawks received cash and a second-round pick in the 2005 draft, later used at No. 59 on Turkish guard Cenk Akyol. This was a post-draft rights deal rather than a transfer of an NBA playing contract. Sanikidze had been selected with the No. 42 choice one day after the June 23 expansion trades, and the Spurs were willing to keep his rights as an overseas-development option. Atlanta accepted financial compensation and an additional late pick. The league’s dated transaction register and Hawks season history show the asset flow plainly.

sections.heading: Sanikidze Remained Overseas Rather Than Joining the Spurs
sections.body: Sanikidze played professionally in Europe, including seasons in France and Italy, but he did not appear in an NBA regular-season game for San Antonio. The franchise held rights to a talented international prospect and never converted them into actual Spurs minutes. That distinction is vital because his successful career abroad does not become San Antonio NBA box-score production. The Spurs’ C grade reflects a speculative long-horizon prospect obtained without surrendering a first-round selection. For a team that already had an established championship core, an overseas stash was a reasonable use of a second-round trade even though it did not generate a rotation player.

sections.heading: Atlanta’s Draft Pick Also Produced No Hawks Games
sections.body: Atlanta used the acquired No. 59 draft pick on Cenk Akyol in 2005. He also spent his professional career outside the NBA, so the Hawks did not get a direct regular-season contributor from the second-round selection. The cash element created some immediate economic value, but the amount is not documented in the canonical record and should not be invented. Atlanta’s C grade is consistent with the Spurs’ C because both clubs exchanged modest draft-rights possibilities that did not become NBA performers. The rights holders gained optionality, but neither side acquired an NBA center or guard who subsequently filled regular minutes for the receiving team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. San Antonio receives C for Viktor Sanikidze’s overseas draft rights; Atlanta also gets C for cash considerations and a 2005 second-round pick used at No. 59 on Cenk Akyol. Neither international prospect appeared in an NBA regular-season game for his acquiring franchise.

sections.heading: New Jersey Sent Kittles and Cash to Los Angeles
sections.body: On July 29, 2004, New Jersey traded longtime starting shooting guard Kerry Kittles and $1.5 million to the Los Angeles Clippers for a future second-round draft pick. The selection ultimately became No. 42 in 2005 and was associated with Chris Taft. New Jersey also generated a trade exception, a salary-cap tool distinct from a player or additional traded pick. Kittles had played all eight seasons of his NBA career for the Nets to that point and had been an important perimeter starter on their consecutive 2002 and 2003 Finals teams. Los Angeles hoped the veteran could improve its shooting guard rotation; New Jersey sought salary flexibility and a future asset.

sections.heading: Kittles Managed Only Eleven Clippers Appearances
sections.body: Knee problems heavily limited Kittles after the move. He appeared in 11 regular-season games for the Clippers in 2004-05 with no starts, averaging 6.3 points, 2.9 rebounds and 1.8 assists. His season ended early and he never played in another NBA regular-season game. The Clippers therefore received far less direct playing production than they might have hoped from an experienced former Finals starter. Their inherited C+ grade needs to be interpreted cautiously because the outcome was a brief reserve stint and a short career afterward. The Clippers did not obtain his earlier Nets postseason minutes merely by trading for him.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Asset and Exception Offered the Nets Alternatives
sections.body: The Nets did not receive a starting player from the Clippers. Instead they obtained a 2005 second-round choice and the ability to use the salary exception to make later moves. Contemporary reporting and the Nets transaction ledger trace the future choice to No. 42, eventually associated with Chris Taft, but his later playing career should not be counted as New Jersey production without establishing where the rights were held. The Nets’ C grade reflects the modest direct draft asset alongside salary flexibility. Given Kittles’ eleven games after the trade, there is a case that the canonical Clippers Win verdict understates New Jersey’s compensation; that outcome should be independently regraded rather than silently revised in this editorial.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win in the inherited canonical classification, C+ to Los Angeles and C to New Jersey. Kittles produced only 11 Clippers games at 6.3 points per game before retiring. The Nets gained a 2005 second-round choice and cap flexibility; the winner and grades warrant later provenance and outcome review.

sections.heading: Charlotte Added Two Players for Two Future Second-Round Picks
sections.body: On July 14, 2004, the Charlotte Bobcats acquired forward-center Melvin Ely and guard Eddie House from the Los Angeles Clippers. The expansion franchise gave up its second-round picks in 2005 and 2006, ultimately associated with No. 32 Daniel Ewing and No. 34 Paul Davis. Unlike Charlotte’s special expansion-draft arrangements with Phoenix and Milwaukee, this was a conventional summer trade to put two signed NBA players on a new roster. Charlotte’s official media guide confirms Ely’s acquisition date and the two draft picks, and the Clippers transaction ledger identifies both future selections. The Bobcats wanted experienced center minutes and guard shooting without waiting for draft development.

sections.heading: Ely Started Seventeen Games and Scored for Charlotte
sections.body: Ely played 79 games in the Bobcats inaugural 2004-05 season, starting 17 and averaging 7.3 points. He remained with Charlotte for two more seasons and scored 9.8 points in 57 appearances during 2005-06, when he started 22. Those are substantial team-specific contributions from a player obtained for two future second-round picks. House offered additional perimeter offense, but Ely is the stronger on-court return from the original agreement. Charlotte’s C+ grade recognizes multi-season frontcourt utility, even though the franchise did not acquire an elite center or future All-Star. Ely left for San Antonio in a separate 2007 deal, so his later production belongs to a different transaction chain.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Gained More Draft Control Instead of Immediate Minutes
sections.body: The Clippers eventually held the two second-round selections from Charlotte and could use them to add younger prospects or make subsequent exchanges. They did not acquire a player who joined their 2004-05 team as part of the July 14 swap. The choices became associated with Daniel Ewing in 2005 and Paul Davis in 2006. The inherited C+ grade for Los Angeles, equal to Charlotte’s, credits the value of those two late selections, but should not automatically attribute the full future NBA careers of the selected players to the Clippers without tracing draft-right transfers. Charlotte got immediate playing minutes from Ely, while Los Angeles chose speculative but tradable assets that would mature over two summers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win in the inherited label, although both clubs grade C+. Los Angeles acquired the 2005 No. 32 pick used on Daniel Ewing and the 2006 No. 34 used on Paul Davis. Charlotte received Melvin Ely and Eddie House; Ely supplied 79 games in 2004-05 and 57 more in 2005-06.

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid Three Veterans and Two Firsts for Vince Carter
sections.body: On December 17, 2004, the New Jersey Nets acquired five-time All-Star Vince Carter from Toronto. In return, Toronto received Alonzo Mourning, Eric Williams, Aaron Williams and first-round draft selections in 2005 and 2006. Nets president Rod Thorn issued a same-day announcement identifying every player and pick. The first-round choices were connected to No. 16 Joey Graham in 2005 and No. 20 Renaldo Balkman in 2006, though pick provenance and later team holdings must be tracked individually. New Jersey wanted a half-court scorer beside Jason Kidd and Richard Jefferson after two consecutive Finals appearances earlier in the decade. Toronto was moving on from a franchise figure amid a difficult relationship with management and fans. This was a real cost in draft choices, not a straight swap of Carter for Mourning.

sections.heading: Carter Returned to All-Star Form Almost Immediately
sections.body: Carter played 57 regular-season games for New Jersey after the trade in 2004-05, averaging 27.5 points, 5.9 rebounds and 4.7 assists. He became an All-Star again and remained with the franchise through the 2008-09 season, scoring at least 20 points per game in each of those five Nets seasons. His explosiveness and shooting supplied the half-court threat Thorn had described when the trade was announced. Carter also played postseason basketball alongside Kidd in New Jersey, giving the club a genuine second star rather than a short scoring rental. The Nets’ A grade is supported by years of measurable production and a return to the playoffs, without needing to include Carter’s earlier Toronto career achievements as a Nets benefit.

sections.heading: Toronto Could Not Turn Mourning or the Picks Into a Comparable Return
sections.body: Mourning never played a Raptors regular-season game and was waived in February 2005 before continuing his career in Miami. Eric Williams and Aaron Williams gave Toronto veteran roster bodies, but neither became a franchise scoring leader. The 2005 first-round choice was used on Joey Graham, who played NBA minutes for Toronto; the other selection became part of a different pick path. The original return was therefore not literally zero, yet none of the assets matched Carter’s 27.5-point season or sustained New Jersey impact. Toronto’s D grade reflects the scale of the star talent lost and the comparatively limited return, rather than blaming later career achievements by Mourning with another franchise on the Raptors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns A for Vince Carter’s 27.5 points per game in his first 57 Nets games and five sustained scoring seasons. Toronto receives D for three veterans and two first-rounders; Mourning never played a Raptors game, and the draft return never replaced Carter’s production.

sections.heading: Dallas Reacquired Jason Kidd for Harris, Picks and Supporting Players
sections.body: The February 19, 2008 agreement sent Jason Kidd, Malik Allen and Antoine Wright from New Jersey to Dallas. The Nets took back Devin Harris, DeSagana Diop, Trenton Hassell, Maurice Ager, the contract rights associated with Keith Van Horn, first-round picks in 2008 and 2010 and cash. The Mavericks’ dated transaction ledger confirms the two first-rounders, later tied to No. 21 Ryan Anderson and No. 27 Jordan Crawford. A contemporaneous Nets account also identifies Van Horn’s salary-matching role and the cash. Kidd had started his NBA career with Dallas, so this was a reunion for a veteran point guard already established as one of the league’s best distributors. New Jersey was pursuing younger guard production and two firsts, not an equivalent old-star replacement.

sections.heading: Kidd Eventually Directed the Mavericks’ Title Offense
sections.body: Kidd returned to a Dallas club built around Dirk Nowitzki, taking responsibility for transition passing and directing the offense while providing perimeter shooting and guard defense. His scoring did not match the franchise’s leading stars, but he continued to log substantial starter minutes and assists over several seasons. His work on the 2010-11 Mavericks championship team was the defining long-term basketball achievement for Dallas from this transaction, three years after the trade was consummated. The Mavericks’ B grade can be justified by an unusually experienced floor general who actually remained through a championship, with Allen and Wright also available as role players. Dallas surrendered real future value, however, and the original deal should not be framed as a cheap acquisition for an unproductive reserve.

sections.heading: Harris Became an All-Star While the Nets Rebuilt
sections.body: Harris immediately assumed a major New Jersey backcourt role. In 2008-09 he averaged 21.3 points and 6.9 assists and earned an All-Star selection, giving the franchise an identifiable young scorer after Kidd’s departure. Diop and the other acquired players supplied shorter rotation or salary-matching roles, while the first-round choices gave New Jersey trade and draft options. The 2008 pick was associated with Ryan Anderson, a legitimate future NBA shooter, although later player careers should be assigned to the correct receiving team. The Nets’ B grade reflects Harris’s All-Star year and the asset package, while Dallas’s equal B recognizes Kidd’s later title contribution. Both teams got real and distinguishable returns across different timelines.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade by the inherited B/B grades. Dallas obtained Jason Kidd, who became a starting guard on its 2011 championship team, plus Malik Allen and Antoine Wright. New Jersey got 2009 All-Star Devin Harris, two first-round picks and other assets. The returns developed differently but both had lasting value.

sections.heading: Charlotte Chose Jason Richardson Over Brandan Wright
sections.body: The 2007 draft-night deal moved Golden State’s leading wing scorer Jason Richardson and the rights to forward Jermareo Davidson to the Charlotte Bobcats. The Warriors acquired the rights to No. 8 selection Brandan Wright, whom Charlotte had drafted earlier that evening. Charlotte’s official media guide explicitly identifies Wright at No. 8 and Davidson at No. 36 in its draft table, while also listing a later rights movement involving Davidson. The Bobcats were trying to accelerate improvement around Gerald Wallace and Emeka Okafor, and Richardson offered proven perimeter scoring. Golden State accepted a young lottery big man and the flexibility of moving a sizable veteran contract. The deal included Davidson’s rights, not just Richardson for Wright.

sections.heading: Richardson Became Charlotte’s Leading Scorer Immediately
sections.body: Richardson played all 82 Bobcats games in 2007-08, starting every time and averaging 21.8 points, 5.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists. He made 243 three-pointers, shooting 40.6 percent from beyond the arc, becoming Charlotte’s major source of perimeter offense. That production helped an expansion-era club remain competitive, even though Charlotte did not reach the playoffs. Richardson was traded to Phoenix during the next season, a separate transaction that produced its own return. The Bobcats’ A- grade is rooted in a full season of high-scoring starting minutes obtained in one draft-night exchange. The next trade and his later Phoenix seasons do not need to be counted to make the original value clear.

sections.heading: Wright Had Development Time But Not Richardson’s Immediate Role
sections.body: Wright played 38 Golden State games as a rookie in 2007-08, averaging 4.0 points and 2.6 rebounds with limited starts. Injuries and a crowded frontcourt affected his development, and the Warriors never obtained the same immediate scoring that Richardson gave Charlotte. Wright eventually played for other NBA teams, demonstrating that the lottery selection was not without talent, but his Warriors tenure was largely a developmental period. Golden State’s D+ grade reflects the loss of an established wing and the limited direct return from Wright before he left. Golden State’s future cap flexibility deserves recognition without adding fictional picks or later outside-team stats to this particular trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Bobcats earn A- after Jason Richardson started all 82 games and averaged 21.8 points in 2007-08, with Jermareo Davidson’s rights also included. Golden State receives D+ for Brandan Wright’s draft rights and a limited rookie season of 38 games.

sections.heading: Cleveland Sent Mike Wilks and Cash for Flip Murray
sections.body: At the 2006 deadline, Cleveland acquired shooting guard Ronald Flip Murray from the Seattle SuperSonics for reserve point guard Mike Wilks and $500,000 in cash. Seattle had used Murray as an offensive option, but the Cavaliers needed an available perimeter starter while Larry Hughes missed time with a hand injury. Murray could play on or off the ball next to LeBron James, supplying ball handling and secondary scoring for an Eastern Conference playoff contender. The exchange was a late-season fit move rather than a draft-rights or long-term prospect deal. Both sides’ transaction ledgers record the same February 23 date and outgoing cash consideration.

sections.heading: Murray Started Twenty-Five Games in Cleveland’s Playoff Push
sections.body: Murray played 28 Cavaliers regular-season games following the trade, starting 25 and averaging 13.5 points, 2.8 assists and 2.4 rebounds. He logged 36.7 minutes per game, substantial work for a midseason acquisition filling an injured starter’s spot. His playoff role shifted as the Cavaliers reached the second round, but he appeared in 13 postseason games and provided a real reserve scoring option. Cleveland’s B+ grade can be supported by these 28 games and his immediate role on a team led by a young James, not by any of Murray’s prior Seattle seasons. He moved to Detroit in free agency after the season, so this was a productive rental rather than a multi-year Cavaliers franchise fixture.

sections.heading: Wilks and Cash Were a Smaller Seattle Return
sections.body: Wilks was an end-of-bench ball handler who had seen very limited minutes in Cleveland and did not become a long-running Seattle starter. The SuperSonics received the specified cash as additional financial consideration but no draft pick or premium young scorer. The club’s B- grade is a modest acknowledgement that it gained roster flexibility and financial compensation while moving a player who had not been central to its long-term plans. That return was less than the substantial starting minutes Murray supplied Cleveland during the 2006 playoff race. The high-leverage timing makes this short transaction noteworthy despite its limited duration. Both teams obtained something, but only Cleveland received a player ready to fill a major 2005-06 rotation role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ for Flip Murray’s 28 games, 25 starts and 13.5 points per game after the February 2006 deadline. Seattle receives B- for reserve Mike Wilks and $500,000 cash. Murray gave the Cavaliers needed injury replacement minutes and postseason depth.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Paid Two Players for Richard Jefferson
sections.body: On June 26, 2008, Milwaukee acquired established scoring forward Richard Jefferson from New Jersey for young Chinese forward Yi Jianlian and veteran Bobby Simmons. The deal came as the Bucks looked to create a more competitive perimeter pairing around Michael Redd and improve an offense that needed additional shot creation. New Jersey was rebuilding after trading Jason Kidd earlier that year and accepted a promising second-year player along with a wing whose contract could help balance the exchange. The historical Nets and Bucks transaction ledgers agree on the two-for-one terms and draft-night timing. No first-round pick was included in this specific agreement, so the two incoming Nets players must account for the direct return.

sections.heading: Jefferson Scored Nearly Twenty Points in Milwaukee
sections.body: Jefferson started all 82 Bucks games in 2008-09 and averaged 19.6 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.4 assists. The combination gave Milwaukee a reliable wing scorer for an entire season even though the Bucks failed to reach the postseason. Jefferson shot 39.7 percent from three and offered a veteran counterweight to the club’s established guards. He moved to San Antonio in June 2009, a separate transaction, so Milwaukee did not receive multiple Jefferson years. Its B+ grade reflects a full season of substantial offense from a player with a proven record, instead of pretending that the move secured a lasting playoff contender. The immediate scoring return was higher than either new Nets player provided that season.

sections.heading: Yi and Simmons Had More Limited Nets Contributions
sections.body: Yi played 61 New Jersey games in 2008-09, starting 52 and averaging 8.6 points and 5.3 rebounds. He showed potential at power forward but did not develop into the franchise’s new leading scorer. Simmons added veteran perimeter minutes and contract flexibility, but his Nets tenure also failed to reproduce Jefferson’s established offensive role. New Jersey’s C- grade reflects the risk of replacing an accomplished starter with a developmental forward and another veteran whose production had declined. The Nets were not buying a present All-Star with this trade, and the team’s later rebuild required other moves. Milwaukee’s advantage is based on its direct one-season scoring return, not on Jefferson’s eventual career with the Spurs and Warriors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns B+ for Richard Jefferson, who started all 82 games and averaged 19.6 points during 2008-09. New Jersey gets C- for Yi Jianlian and Bobby Simmons; Yi averaged 8.6 points in 61 Nets appearances. The Bucks acquired the more productive immediate player.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired a Scoring Forward for Two Centers and Cash
sections.body: On February 24, 2005, the Mavericks traded Alan Henderson and Calvin Booth to Milwaukee, along with $250,000, to obtain veteran forward Keith Van Horn. Dallas was trying to add perimeter shooting and a scoring reserve around Dirk Nowitzki ahead of the playoffs. Van Horn had become a movable piece in Milwaukee after joining the Bucks in a different 2004 deal. Henderson and Booth were frontcourt players rather than incoming Dallas contributors; both went to the Bucks. The cash traveled with them to Milwaukee, and no first-round draft pick was part of this transaction. That exact asset direction matters because Dallas obtained the one player with a major immediate scoring role.

sections.heading: Van Horn Scored for Dallas Across Two Playoff Seasons
sections.body: Van Horn appeared in 29 Mavericks games after the deal in 2004-05, with three starts and averages of 12.2 points and 4.4 rebounds in 23.6 minutes. He helped Dallas spread the floor as a power forward who could shoot away from the rim. In 2005-06 he played 53 more regular-season games, averaged 8.9 points, and was an experienced bench option as Dallas advanced to the NBA Finals against Miami. He was not the star of that Finals run, which was built around Nowitzki and the main Dallas rotation, but he supplied two seasons of useful offense. The B+ Mavericks grade reflects 82 regular-season appearances and identifiable postseason roster utility, rather than projecting his earlier Nets scoring peak into the Dallas years.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Depth Without a Comparable Offensive Return
sections.body: Henderson and Booth brought the Bucks veteran frontcourt options, and the $250,000 gave Milwaukee documented financial consideration. But neither player became the same kind of scoring option that Dallas received in Van Horn. Booth had already been used in a reserve center role, while Henderson was late in a career that once included more consistent starting seasons. Milwaukee could redistribute minutes and manage contracts, but that was a narrower return than the Mavericks’ 12.2-point midseason addition. The Bucks C grade acknowledges the cash and depth without inventing a future pick, contract extension or new Milwaukee star created by the transaction. The benefit to Dallas was visible during the very season of the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge. Dallas earns B+ for Keith Van Horn’s 29 games at 12.2 points in 2004-05 and 53 more games on its 2006 Finals team. Milwaukee receives C for Alan Henderson, Calvin Booth and $250,000 cash. The veteran scoring return was stronger for Dallas.

sources.title: Keith Van Horn Dallas 2004-05 and 2005-06 statistics

sections.heading: Phoenix Sent a Reserve Center to Charlotte for a Conditional Second
sections.body: The Charlotte Bobcats acquired Jake Voskuhl from Phoenix on August 2, 2005, surrendering a 2007 second-round selection protected through No. 55. The pick was never exercised under the historical transaction ledger. Phoenix had reduced Voskuhl’s frontcourt role during its fast-paced 2004-05 season, when he made only one start in 38 games. Charlotte was entering its second NBA season and needed experienced interior players who could absorb minutes around younger forwards. No incoming Phoenix player or future first-rounder changed hands. It was a low-cost effort to put a known center into Charlotte’s rotation while preserving the Suns’ ability to move forward with other big men.

sections.heading: Voskuhl Supplied Two Seasons of Charlotte Center Minutes
sections.body: In 2005-06 Voskuhl played 51 Bobcats games, started twice, and averaged 5.3 points with 3.6 rebounds in 16 minutes. He appeared in 73 games the following season with nine starts, supplying another 4.4 points and 3.5 rebounds a night. Those 124 regular-season Charlotte appearances are the most important direct return from this trade. The scoring totals were modest but the Bobcats had acquired someone capable of playing real center minutes during the franchise’s roster-development period. Charlotte’s C+ grade recognizes two seasons of reliable reserve availability rather than treating the acquisition as a new star. The 2007-08 season he later played for Milwaukee belongs to another club.

sections.heading: The Suns Never Received the Protected Draft Choice
sections.body: The draft compensation was described as a 2007 second-round selection protected through No. 55, which is a meaningful restriction at the end of the NBA draft. The inherited transaction record says the condition was not met and the pick did not convey. Phoenix therefore did not use this deal to select a prospect who later scored NBA points for the Suns. Its C grade reflects removing an expendable center and adjusting the payroll and rotation rather than any realized draft-right return. Charlotte received actual games from Voskuhl without surrendering the specified pick, which is why the Bobcats hold the narrow advantage in the original assessment. No imagined 2007 selection should be added to Phoenix’s side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte receives C+ after Jake Voskuhl logged 124 games across 2005-06 and 2006-07, averaging 5.3 and 4.4 points in those seasons. Phoenix earns C for parting with a reserve while its top-55-protected 2007 second-round compensation never conveyed.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Jumaine Jones for a Future Second-Round Pick
sections.body: On October 26, 2005, the Los Angeles Lakers traded veteran forward Jumaine Jones to Charlotte for a 2007 second-round selection. The future pick was later identified as No. 40 in 2007, used by Los Angeles on Chinese guard Sun Yue. Charlotte was still constructing a reliable rotation for its second season and wanted another experienced forward who could rebound and make outside shots. The Lakers had depth at the wing position and chose a later draft opportunity instead of keeping Jones. Both teams’ transaction histories identify the direct player-for-pick exchange. No additional players came back to Charlotte and no Lakers first-round choice was involved.

sections.heading: Jones Was a Regular Charlotte Starter in 2005-06
sections.body: Jones appeared in 76 Bobcats games during 2005-06 and started 42. He scored 799 total points, or about 10.5 per game, and averaged 4.9 rebounds. Those are meaningful supporting-player totals on a young team, not a three-game end-of-bench audition. His ability to cover both forward spots gave Charlotte flexibility while the roster’s younger players developed. The C+ Bobcats grade is defensible from this season alone, though Jones did not remain an important part of Charlotte for many additional years. His prior Cleveland and Philadelphia appearances and later international career do not need to be imported into the return from the October transaction. The strongest evidence is the 42 Charlotte starts that followed.

sections.heading: Sun Yue Was a Longer-Term Pick Option but Barely Played for the Lakers
sections.body: The Lakers used the 2007 No. 40 selection on Sun Yue, a tall Chinese guard who stayed overseas before making his NBA debut in 2008-09. He appeared in just ten regular-season Lakers games, with minimal scoring. Los Angeles still held a prospect with international experience and the option to assess him during its championship era, but his small NBA role did not match Jones’s 76-game starting and reserve contribution to Charlotte. The Lakers C grade acknowledges draft-right optionality and roster flexibility without assigning Sun Yue’s later professional accomplishments in China to the NBA return. Charlotte obtained the more immediate regular-season playing minutes from this modest draft-pick trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. The Bobcats earn C+ for Jumaine Jones’s 76 appearances, 42 starts, 10.5 points and 4.9 rebounds in 2005-06. Los Angeles receives C after obtaining the 2007 No. 40 pick used on Sun Yue, whose Lakers NBA role lasted only ten regular-season games.

sections.heading: New Jersey Took Marc Jackson for a Conditional Second
sections.body: The Nets acquired veteran center Marc Jackson from the Philadelphia 76ers on August 9, 2005, giving up a conditional 2006 second-round selection. The transaction register says the condition was not exercised, so Philadelphia did not receive a conveyed draft choice that became a named NBA player. New Jersey sought frontcourt scoring and backup-center minutes, while Philadelphia was changing its reserve options around Samuel Dalembert. The agreement did not include cash, multiple players or a first-round pick in the inherited canonical asset record. It was a speculative one-year veteran addition for the Nets with a draft condition that ultimately did not cost a selected prospect.

sections.heading: Jackson Produced a Brief New Jersey Scoring Stint
sections.body: Jackson played 37 Nets games during 2005-06, without starting, averaging 4.6 points and 2.4 rebounds in 11.7 minutes. Those numbers reflect backup-center production rather than a leading offensive role. He was subsequently moved from New Jersey to the New Orleans Hornets in a separate February 2006 trade. Jackson averaged substantially more points during that later New Orleans stint, but those belong to a different franchise and should not be credited to the Nets. New Jersey’s C+ grade reflects actual short-season rotation availability and the ability to move him again, without attributing a full 2005-06 year across two clubs to the original trade. The Nets had acquired a useful veteran stopgap rather than a lasting starter.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Did Not Receive the Drafted Player That Was Conditional
sections.body: Philadelphia moved an expendable reserve and accepted the possibility of a future second-round choice. Because the conditional pick never conveyed according to the historical transaction record, the 76ers did not add an identifiable 2006 draft prospect through this agreement. They gained roster and contract flexibility but no actual NBA player as the principal incoming trade asset. Philadelphia’s C grade captures that limited financial and optional value relative to the short stretch of games Jackson gave New Jersey. The Nets win is narrow because the player did not produce an extended starting center career there. The absence of a conveyed pick is a substantive part of the verdict, not a placeholder for a future player to be named.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns C+ for 37 games and 4.6 points per contest from Marc Jackson before moving him again. Philadelphia receives C for a conditional 2006 second-round pick that was not exercised. The deal yielded actual Nets reserve minutes but no conveyed 76ers draft selection.

sections.heading: Houston Swapped Lonny Baxter for Guard Keith Bogans
sections.body: At the February 9, 2006 trade deadline run-up, Charlotte sent Keith Bogans to the Houston Rockets in exchange for forward Lonny Baxter. Charlotte was willing to test another physical interior reserve, while Houston needed a perimeter defender and shooter to complement its established rotation. Bogans had played 39 games for the Bobcats that season, averaging 8.7 points, and had already demonstrated that he could start NBA games. Baxter was a frontcourt substitute with a shorter and less stable career role. The clubs exchanged exactly these two players, with no draft choice included. An evaluation that treats Bogans’s pretrade Charlotte minutes as Houston production would be inaccurate.

sections.heading: Bogans Started Twenty-Two Games for the Rockets
sections.body: After joining Houston, Bogans appeared in 33 Rockets games and started 22, averaging about 8.5 points and 4.5 rebounds. The team needed perimeter availability amid injury trouble around its core, and Bogans supplied more than emergency garbage-time minutes. His career continued with several other NBA franchises, but the Rockets’ direct value was the 33-game partial season. The canonical C+ grade recognizes a dependable wing defender and occasional starting guard acquired without surrendering a draft pick. His later Chicago playoff appearances do not enter the Rockets return from this particular Charlotte transaction. The minutes and starts he logged in Houston are the strongest evidence that the trade worked as an immediate roster adjustment.

sections.heading: Baxter Was a Rarely Used Bobcats Reserve
sections.body: Baxter played only 18 Charlotte games after the swap, did not start, and averaged 2.0 points and 1.8 rebounds in approximately 6.6 minutes. That amounted to limited frontcourt insurance for a young Bobcats roster, not an important offensive replacement for the outgoing Bogans. Charlotte’s C grade reflects obtaining a legitimate NBA big man for those minutes but falling short of Houston’s more regular use of Bogans. Baxter’s earlier NBA scoring with Washington or New Orleans should not be counted as a Charlotte return. The Houston side enjoyed a clearer improvement in game-to-game rotation function, particularly through twenty-two starts, while Charlotte essentially exchanged a supporting guard for deep bench center depth.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston receives C+ for Keith Bogans’s 33 games and 22 starts in its 2005-06 wing rotation. Charlotte gets C after Lonny Baxter played 18 games without a start, averaging 2.0 points and 1.8 rebounds. The Rockets secured more immediate playing value.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Obtained Jiří Welsch for a Future Second
sections.body: On June 28, 2005, Cleveland sent Czech swingman Jiří Welsch to Milwaukee for a 2006 second-round draft selection. That choice eventually became No. 44, associated with Israeli forward Lior Eliyahu. Welsch had arrived in Cleveland during the previous season from Boston but appeared in only 16 Cavaliers games, shooting 23.5 percent from the floor. A new front office led by Danny Ferry traded him on draft night rather than keeping a veteran perimeter reserve. Milwaukee chose a known NBA player over a late pick one year away, while Cleveland received an inexpensive chance to add an international prospect. The transaction did not include a first-round pick or any other veteran contracts.

sections.heading: Welsch Played His Final NBA Season for the Bucks
sections.body: Welsch appeared in 58 Milwaukee games in 2005-06 and started twice. He averaged 4.3 points, 1.9 rebounds and 1.1 assists while playing 14.9 minutes per game. Those were genuine reserve wing contributions after a brief and unsuccessful Cavaliers stint, although his shooting was 38.7 percent and the Bucks had hoped for more stability on the perimeter. Milwaukee reached the 2006 playoffs, and Welsch appeared in three postseason games. He went back to Europe afterward rather than becoming a long-term Bucks rotation fixture. The B- grade in the inherited analysis is generous for the short tenure but does reflect a player who supplied fifty-eight games instead of a rights claim that never translated to NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Eliyahu Never Became a Cavaliers NBA Player
sections.body: The Cavaliers used the acquired No. 44 pick on Lior Eliyahu, whose professional success largely occurred in Israel and elsewhere overseas. Eliyahu never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for Cleveland, so his overseas scoring cannot be added to the Cavaliers team totals. Cleveland held a real draft asset and a possible future signing option, but no measurable NBA court return followed from the transaction. Its inherited B- grade equals Milwaukee despite the difference in realized NBA games. The Bucks Win verdict must therefore be understood as a practical on-court tiebreak rather than evidence of numerically higher grading. Welsch played in Milwaukee for one season; Eliyahu remained an unconverted NBA right.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win in the inherited verdict despite equal B- grades. Milwaukee received 58 games and 4.3 points per appearance from Jiří Welsch during 2005-06. Cleveland used the 2006 No. 44 pick on Lior Eliyahu, who never appeared in a Cavaliers NBA game. The Bucks obtained the only immediate on-court return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Jason Hart for Sacramento’s 2006 Second
sections.body: The Bobcats sent reserve point guard Jason Hart to the Sacramento Kings on August 2, 2005, receiving a second-round choice in the following summer’s draft. Charlotte used the pick at No. 50 in 2006 to select UCLA center Ryan Hollins. The franchise needed inexpensive opportunities to develop a frontcourt while spending its second NBA season assembling a roster. Hart had started 27 Charlotte games in 2004-05 and averaged 9.5 points and 5.0 assists, giving Sacramento an experienced ball handler after the Kings adjusted their guard rotation. The draft pick was genuine and ultimately exercised, not a nonconveyed condition. The teams’ dated transaction ledgers show the two-sided player-for-pick bargain without cash or other players.

sections.heading: Hart Became a Sacramento Backup Instead of a Starter
sections.body: Hart made 66 regular-season appearances for the 2005-06 Kings with no starts. He logged 818 minutes, totaling 218 points and 70 assists, or 3.3 points and 1.1 assists per game. Sacramento had other primary guards, so Hart no longer needed to carry the starting responsibilities he briefly held in Charlotte. He appeared in five games during the Kings first-round playoff series against San Antonio, adding some postseason ball-handling minutes. His return was useful roster insurance but not the creation of a new lead scorer or a long-term starter. The inherited Sacramento C grade reflects modest rotation depth acquired from a future second-round selection, not Hart’s earlier Charlotte statistics.

sections.heading: Hollins Took a Slower Development Path in Charlotte
sections.body: Hollins played 27 games for the Bobcats as a rookie in 2006-07 and averaged 2.4 points in 6.9 minutes. He appeared in 60 more Charlotte games in 2007-08, with one start and 2.5 points a night, then started one of his 18 Bobcats games in 2008-09 before moving to Dallas. That gave Charlotte multiple seasons of low-minute center development, but the immediate NBA value was limited. His eventual ten-year NBA career included several other franchises and should not be mistaken for ten Charlotte seasons. Both inherited grades are C, although the canonical wording selects a slight Kings edge on the veteran Hart’s prompt backup-guard contribution. The pick produced a real NBA player rather than an unused right.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge under the inherited verdict, with C grades for both sides. Sacramento received 66 regular-season games and five playoff appearances from Jason Hart in 2005-06. Charlotte drafted Ryan Hollins at No. 50 in 2006 and gave him 105 Bobcats games across three seasons, mostly as a reserve.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Mikki Moore for a Future Second
sections.body: The Nets obtained center Mikki Moore from the Seattle SuperSonics on July 27, 2006, sending out a 2009 second-round draft selection. Seattle eventually used the No. 40 choice on Derrick Brown, later moving the rights in a different transaction. Both clubs’ histories identify this direct one-player-for-pick agreement, and contemporary Nets retrospective reporting describes Moore as affordable insurance for the injured rookie Josh Boone. The two-year distance between the trade and its draft outcome meant the Sonics had to wait before choosing a prospect. Moore already had experience as an NBA reserve but had not spent previous seasons as a reliable 30-minute starter. New Jersey was buying center depth during a period when its frontcourt was vulnerable to injuries.

sections.heading: Moore Became a Starter After Nenad Krstić Was Hurt
sections.body: Moore’s opportunity expanded sharply when starting center Nenad Krstić suffered a serious knee injury in December 2006. Moore played 79 Nets games in 2006-07, started 55, and averaged 9.8 points with 5.1 rebounds. He shot a league-leading 60.9 percent from the field, an unexpected level of efficiency for a player acquired mainly as a contingency. New Jersey reached the second round of the 2007 playoffs with Moore playing significant frontcourt minutes. The Nets C grade in the inherited record substantially understates that first-season impact by hindsight standards, but the article preserves the canonical evaluation rather than secretly changing it. Moore left in free agency after the season, limiting the length of the team’s realized return to one productive year.

sections.heading: Seattle Received an Asset That Matured in 2009
sections.body: The Sonics obtained a future second-round pick that ultimately became No. 40 in 2009, associated with Xavier forward Derrick Brown. By the 2009 draft, the franchise had relocated to Oklahoma City, and the subsequent player-rights history has to be attributed to the correct holder. Seattle did not receive Moore’s 79-game starting season or an immediate veteran in exchange. The pick was a modest option with later trade potential, rather than a first-round selection likely to produce a new starter. Its equal C inherited grade reflects a real but delayed draft asset. Given Moore’s unexpected importance in New Jersey, the Even Trade rating deserves a later source-led regrading audit; it is not evidence that the two sides contributed equal NBA playing minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the retained C/C grades. New Jersey acquired Mikki Moore, who started 55 games and led the NBA at 60.9 percent shooting during 2006-07. Seattle received the 2009 No. 40 second-round pick associated with Derrick Brown. Moore gave the Nets the much stronger immediate basketball return, despite the inherited equal scores.

sources.title: Mikki Moore 2006 Nets trade hindsight review

sections.heading: Charlotte Swapped Two Reserves for Center Nazr Mohammed
sections.body: On December 14, 2007, the Charlotte Bobcats obtained veteran center Nazr Mohammed from Detroit. The Pistons received two frontcourt reserves, Primož Brezec and Walter Herrmann. Mohammed had contributed to San Antonio’s 2005 championship earlier in his career and remained a capable rebounder, but his minutes in Detroit had decreased. Charlotte wanted a larger regular center to reinforce Emeka Okafor and its young frontcourt. Detroit had established interior options and was willing to try two role players instead. The official transaction logs for both teams record a direct two-for-one trade, without additional draft rights. Charlotte was not receiving Mohammed’s earlier championship performances, but it did gain a veteran who could immediately start games.

sections.heading: Mohammed Started Twenty-Nine Bobcats Games in His First Season
sections.body: After the trade, Mohammed appeared in 61 Charlotte games during 2007-08, started 29 and averaged 9.3 points with 6.9 rebounds in 23.3 minutes. Those totals were a substantial increase from his 21-game Detroit reserve role earlier that season. He also stayed in Charlotte for subsequent seasons, making this more than a temporary rental. The Bobcats C+ grade recognizes regular frontcourt production from a club still searching for a stable NBA rotation. Mohammed was not an All-Star during his Charlotte stint, and his previous playing time on stronger teams should not be credited twice, but getting a 29-game starter for two limited reserves was an identifiable basketball return.

sections.heading: Detroit Got Short Bench Trials and Moved Brezec Again
sections.body: Brezec appeared in 17 Detroit games after arriving from Charlotte, scoring 1.6 points per appearance and averaging 5.8 minutes. He was moved on to Toronto for Juan Dixon and cash in February 2008, a separate transaction whose return belongs to Detroit’s later roster management. Herrmann played 28 Detroit games in 2007-08, averaging 3.0 points in 7.1 minutes; he remained with the club for a further season. Those were legitimate reserve contributions but did not match Mohammed’s starting responsibilities in Charlotte. The Pistons C+ grade equals Charlotte in the inherited data, so the Even Trade decision should be understood as a value judgment that considers cap and depth as well as basketball minutes. It does not mean the two teams received identical player production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade according to the inherited C+/C+ grades. Charlotte obtained Nazr Mohammed, who made 29 starts with 9.3 points and 6.9 rebounds after arrival in 2007-08. Detroit got Primož Brezec and Walter Herrmann, with Brezec then traded again in February. Charlotte clearly received more first-season starting-center production.

sections.heading: Charlotte Collected a Protected First for Aleksandar Pavlović
sections.body: During the 2004 expansion draft, Charlotte selected young Serbian wing Aleksandar Pavlović from the Utah Jazz. The following day, June 23, the Bobcats traded him to Cleveland for a future first-round choice. The pick carried different protections depending on the year and ultimately conveyed in 2007 at No. 22. Cleveland wanted a prospective rotation wing for the young LeBron James era; Charlotte accepted the ability to draft a player several seasons later. The Bobcats’ own retrospective of the expansion draft confirms Pavlović was traded for the first-round choice eventually used on Jared Dudley, and the Cavaliers transaction ledger independently dates the agreement. This was not an immediate exchange of two drafted players who had already suited up for their new NBA clubs.

sections.heading: Pavlović Became a Cavaliers Finals-Season Role Player
sections.body: Pavlović contributed to Cleveland for multiple seasons, including an important role during the franchise’s first NBA Finals appearance in 2007. He offered perimeter defense and occasional shooting at a time when Cleveland was assembling lineups around James and its experienced guards. In 2006-07 his playing time expanded, and he became an option alongside Larry Hughes and Eric Snow. Those Cleveland games are an actual return that complicates the inherited low D+ Cavaliers grade, even if Pavlović never developed into a star. His later work with other teams must not be included in Cleveland’s immediate return. The Cavaliers got a legitimate young NBA wing rather than simply losing a first for a player who never reported, so the article distinguishes direct value from the pick that might have been.

sections.heading: Dudley Gave Charlotte a Different Sort of Development Asset
sections.body: The 2007 pick eventually became No. 22, used on Boston College forward Jared Dudley. He appeared in 73 Bobcats games as a rookie in 2007-08 and began building the versatile career that eventually made him a valuable role player around the NBA. Charlotte traded him to Phoenix in December 2008, a separate exchange that formed another asset path. The Bobcats’ A- grade is rooted in having gained an authentic first-round pick through an expansion roster selection, as well as the time Dudley actually spent with the franchise. It should not count all of Dudley’s later Suns, Clippers or Lakers seasons as Charlotte playing time. The pick was not a fictitious perpetual condition: it converted to an identifiable 2007 first-round choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win under inherited grades, A- for the Bobcats and D+ for Cleveland. Charlotte converted its expansion-draft selection of Aleksandar Pavlović into a 2007 No. 22 first-round pick used on Jared Dudley. Pavlović nevertheless played real wing minutes for Cleveland, including its 2007 Finals season.

sections.heading: The Nets Took Bernard Robinson for Jeff McInnis and Cash
sections.body: On January 3, 2007, New Jersey traded guard Jeff McInnis and cash considerations to Charlotte for reserve swingman Bernard Robinson. Nets president Rod Thorn characterized Robinson as an athletic bench defender capable of covering both perimeter positions. McInnis was a veteran point guard who had fallen out of the Nets playing rotation and wanted an opportunity closer to his hometown. Charlotte had used Robinson for 21 games earlier in the season, but gave up on that developmental wing slot to take a look at another ball handler. The contemporaneous Nets announcement identifies both players and the accompanying cash direction. No future draft pick was included, and this was not the earlier 2004 transaction that originally brought Robinson into the Charlotte expansion team.

sections.heading: McInnis Actually Returned to the Floor in Charlotte
sections.body: McInnis played 38 Charlotte games in 2006-07 and started three. That marked a substantial improvement in availability over his final Nets months, when he had not played for the club in the 2006-07 regular-season schedule before the trade. He provided veteran organizing minutes behind the starting guards without becoming a lasting high-scoring option. Charlotte could use him as an additional ball handler when injuries interrupted the first-choice lineup, and the cash added a modest economic return. Its C+ inherited grade reflects some real game participation and financial considerations rather than a major long-term development success. McInnis remained in Charlotte the following year, but his role diminished as the roster added other veteran point guards.

sections.heading: Robinson Became a Small New Jersey Rotation Experiment
sections.body: Robinson arrived with three Bobcats seasons of experience, but his Nets tenure was brief. He was not a dependable starter in a New Jersey rotation built around Vince Carter, Jason Kidd and Richard Jefferson. His value lay in defensive flexibility and the chance to see whether a younger wing could claim occasional bench minutes. The Nets’ C grade acknowledges that opportunity, while Charlotte’s higher C+ reflects having obtained a usable guard plus cash. Robinson’s earlier NBA appearances for Charlotte cannot be counted a second time as New Jersey production. The club traded out a player who had been idle, but the ensuing playing value remained narrow on both sides. That supports a slight decision instead of a franchise-changing outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. The Bobcats receive C+ after acquiring Jeff McInnis, who appeared in 38 Charlotte games in 2006-07, and cash. New Jersey gets C for reserve wing Bernard Robinson, whose Nets role was limited. The winner follows modest veteran guard utility, not a long-term star return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Converted Melvin Ely Into Pick, Cash and a Veteran
sections.body: On February 13, 2007, Charlotte sent reserve big man Melvin Ely to San Antonio. The Bobcats received forward Eric Williams, a 2009 second-round pick and cash, recorded as $1 million in the detailed historical transaction ledger. San Antonio’s official release confirms the trade and the 2009 choice, while subsequent draft history associates that selection with No. 54 Robert Vaden. Ely had appeared in 24 Charlotte games earlier that year and was playing only about ten minutes per night. The Spurs wanted emergency frontcourt size during a championship pursuit, while the Bobcats preferred a future prospect right and financial return for a veteran who was not central to their rotation. It was a player-plus-pick package, not a straight player-for-player exchange.

sections.heading: The Bobcats Briefly Used Williams and Kept the Future Selection
sections.body: Williams appeared in five Bobcats games before the team waived him on March 16, 2007. That was a minor on-court return, especially compared with the long career he had already established in Boston and Cleveland. Charlotte nevertheless gained a real second-round pick that ultimately conveyed in 2009, plus the separate cash payment. Robert Vaden, the No. 54 selection linked to the pick, did not become a Bobcats NBA regular, so the pick should be valued as a development or exchange opportunity rather than a proven starter. Charlotte’s C+ inherited grade reflects the combined pick-and-cash benefit more than the five Williams appearances. The transaction was a classic asset recovery move for a rebuilding franchise that had limited playing plans for Ely.

sections.heading: Ely Was a Deep Reserve on a Spurs Championship Team
sections.body: Ely became one of several interior reserve options for the Spurs, alongside Tim Duncan and other established veteran bigs. San Antonio won the 2007 championship, but a player acquired as emergency depth must not automatically be assigned a central role in that title run. Ely had averaged just 2.9 points during his earlier Charlotte season segment and did not suddenly become a primary scoring center after the deal. The Spurs C grade recognizes the option to use an experienced big man behind their championship rotation, with much of his value tied to insurance rather than regular starting production. Charlotte’s higher grade is better supported by receiving a future pick and cash while sacrificing a player who had already seen his role shrink.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. The Bobcats earn C+ for Eric Williams, a conveyed 2009 No. 54 second-rounder associated with Robert Vaden, and $1 million in cash. San Antonio receives C for Melvin Ely as deep frontcourt insurance during its 2007 championship campaign. Neither club gained a new starring player.

sections.heading: Cleveland Dealt Two Reserves to Philadelphia for Eric Snow
sections.body: On July 19, 2004, the Cavaliers acquired veteran guard Eric Snow from Philadelphia. The 76ers received point guard Kevin Ollie and wing Kedrick Brown in return. Cleveland wanted a disciplined defender and reliable ball mover next to young LeBron James, while Philadelphia was taking a different direction with its supporting backcourt. Snow had started all 82 Philadelphia games in 2003-04 and averaged 6.9 assists, making him a different caliber of veteran organizer than the two outgoing players. The historical transaction registers for each franchise identify the two-for-one exchange, with no future first-rounder or additional cash in the agreement. Cleveland was not paying for a high-volume scorer but for a player who could coordinate the offense and guard opposing guards.

sections.heading: Snow Became a Full-Time Cleveland Starter in 2005-06
sections.body: Snow played 81 Cavaliers games in 2004-05 with 15 starts, averaging 4.0 points and 3.9 assists in 22.8 minutes. He assumed an expanded role the following season, starting all 82 games with averages of 4.8 points and 4.2 assists. He remained on the 2006-07 team that reached Cleveland’s first NBA Finals, making 45 starts and supplying veteran defense. These were real multi-season backcourt contributions even though his shooting efficiency and scoring totals were modest. The Cavaliers A- inherited grade recognizes steady minutes and organizational value during the early LeBron period rather than a sudden offensive breakout. Snow also played in the 2006 and 2007 postseasons, connecting the trade to a competitive rise for Cleveland.

sections.heading: Ollie and Brown Did Not Replace Those Cavalier Seasons
sections.body: Ollie was another veteran point guard, but he played 26 games for Philadelphia in 2004-05 and did not establish a similarly large Sixers role. Brown appeared only eight times in the same season before leaving the NBA roster. Both players brought experience or potential but neither supplied Cleveland-length starting production to the 76ers. Philadelphia’s C grade reflects the limited return from the depth swap when measured against Snow’s multiple Cavaliers seasons. The franchise was not acquiring a future lottery selection, and Brown’s earlier status as a first-round prospect could not substitute for minutes delivered after the trade. Cleveland obtained the clearest lasting value through a dependable defense-oriented point guard; Philadelphia found only smaller bench roles.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- after Eric Snow played 81 games in 2004-05, started all 82 in 2005-06, and helped the club reach the 2007 Finals. Philadelphia receives C for Kevin Ollie and Kedrick Brown, who played 26 and eight games respectively in 2004-05.

sections.heading: Toronto Took Juan Dixon for Fred Jones and Future Considerations
sections.body: At the February 22, 2007 NBA trade deadline, Portland sent scoring guard Juan Dixon to Toronto for swingman Fred Jones and future considerations. Dixon was an experienced perimeter shooter coming off a productive Blazers season in 2005-06, while Jones was a slashing wing who had signed with the Raptors the previous summer. The Raptors hoped Dixon could help their Eastern Conference playoff rotation, and Portland gave Jones a chance to earn minutes during a younger roster transition. Historical transactions for both clubs confirm that future consideration was part of the agreement, without defining a guaranteed first-round choice. The trade was not the same as the earlier Portland–Toronto deal involving Steve Blake or the next summer’s draft picks. Both receiving players must be evaluated in their new uniforms rather than by reputation alone.

sections.heading: Dixon Supplied Toronto with an Available Scoring Guard
sections.body: Dixon joined a Raptors team that went on to win the 2006-07 Atlantic Division. His job was to provide bench shooting, secondary ball handling and immediate regular-season guard depth around Chris Bosh and the team’s playmakers. He appeared in the postseason as Toronto lost a first-round series to New Jersey, giving the club more than a speculative future role. His contribution was a shorter period than a full Toronto season, and his earlier Washington NCAA-to-NBA career narrative does not belong in an accounting of what Toronto acquired from Portland. The Raptors C+ inherited grade acknowledges the usefulness of an experienced scorer during the playoff push without describing him as a starting point guard or a long-term centerpiece.

sections.heading: Jones Became Another Blazers Perimeter Experiment
sections.body: Jones brought Portland a different type of wing player, stronger as a leaper and finisher than as a volume perimeter shooter. The Blazers were focused on developing emerging guards and forwards, so his opportunities after the trade were constrained by younger players already on the roster. The extra future considerations are not assigned a fictional named draft prospect: the inherited asset description does not specify a later NBA draft outcome. Portland’s C+ grade matches Toronto’s, a useful warning against inflating the short-term deal into a decisive victory. Dixon’s playoff experience was a tangible Toronto benefit, while Portland had a chance to examine Jones within a different rotation. No high-value draft pick changed hands in the confirmed agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under equal C+ grades. Portland acquired Fred Jones and future considerations while Toronto received Juan Dixon for its 2007 playoff stretch. The direct exchange redistributed reserve perimeter roles; neither club received a sustained new star or a verified first-round draft selection.

sources.title: Toronto acquires Juan Dixon for Fred Jones

sections.heading: The Hornets Sent Boštjan Nachbar for Two Veterans and Cash
sections.body: On February 23, 2006, the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets traded forward Boštjan Nachbar to New Jersey. The Hornets received center Marc Jackson, forward Linton Johnson III and cash from the Nets. League trade-deadline records verify all three pieces, and the Nets’ contemporaneous reporting describes the payroll flexibility that motivated the exchange. New Jersey had previously acquired Jackson without conveying the conditional second-round pick in that earlier trade, so this new agreement let the franchise obtain an athletic shooting forward while moving two expendable reserves. The deal did not include an additional first-round choice or involve the Charlotte Bobcats, which were reportedly another possible trade partner in discussions that never became this completed transaction.

sections.heading: Nachbar Became a Much Larger Nets Contributor One Year Later
sections.body: Nachbar played only 11 Nets games during the remainder of 2005-06 and averaged 2.8 points in 8.8 minutes. His more valuable contribution came in the next two seasons. He appeared in 76 games during 2006-07, scoring 9.2 points with 42.3 percent three-point shooting, and played 75 more in 2007-08 at 9.8 points per game. New Jersey benefited from a credible bench scorer who could stretch the floor around Jason Kidd and Vince Carter. Those 151 games across two later seasons demonstrate a stronger return than a fleeting deadline rental. The canonical C- Nets grade is conspicuously low relative to Nachbar’s documented subsequent production, so a reader should distinguish the preserved inherited label from the actual playing record.

sections.heading: New Orleans Obtained Frontcourt Depth but Not a Replacement Scorer
sections.body: Jackson was a veteran big man who could absorb interior minutes during the Hornets rebuilding period, and Johnson offered another defensive forward profile. The cash added an economic benefit, but the historical asset description does not attach a major new draft selection to the trade. Neither player became a high-volume long-term New Orleans scorer comparable to the healthy Nachbar seasons New Jersey later received. The Pelicans franchise’s B+ inherited grade and winner designation are therefore stronger than the team-specific basketball evidence alone seems to support. That possible grading mismatch deserves a separate documented reassessment instead of silently rewriting the canonical trade verdict in an editorial entry. The narrow factual conclusion is that the teams exchanged different kinds of depth with a meaningful New Jersey follow-on return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win in the inherited B+ to C- verdict, but the underlying results complicate it. New Orleans received Marc Jackson, Linton Johnson III and cash; New Jersey acquired Boštjan Nachbar, who subsequently played 76 and 75 Nets games in consecutive seasons while averaging 9.2 and 9.8 points. A source-led grade review is warranted.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sent Joe Smith to Denver for Ruben Patterson
sections.body: On August 10, 2006, the Milwaukee Bucks acquired swingman Ruben Patterson from the Denver Nuggets in exchange for veteran power forward Joe Smith. The two players had different roster functions: Patterson was a physical defender and productive wing scorer, while Smith supplied size and professional rebounding around the basket. Contemporary Washington Post reporting and the team transaction ledgers confirm the direct exchange with no draft pick or cash. Patterson had arrived in Denver in a larger February 2006 multi-team agreement, so the August deal was a separate step after a fairly short Nuggets tenure. Both teams believed they were filling a specific rotation need, but the players’ following-season workload ultimately differed by a wide margin.

sections.heading: Patterson Played Eighty-One Games for Milwaukee
sections.body: Patterson appeared in 81 Bucks games during 2006-07, started 53 and averaged 14.7 points, 5.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists while making 54.8 percent of his field-goal attempts. Those are major supporting-player totals, especially given that Milwaukee had been seeking an experienced wing to supplement Michael Redd’s scoring. Patterson supplied a full year of starting and reserve minutes rather than a few games at the end of the bench. He did not become a multi-year Milwaukee star, but that first-season contribution supports the Bucks B+ inherited grade. The fact that he spent only one Bucks season should temper any statement that he became a permanent roster solution. Still, the output was immediately visible, and it surpassed what Smith directly provided Denver.

sections.heading: Smith Was Quickly Included in the Allen Iverson Transaction
sections.body: Smith played 11 Nuggets games with no starts in 2006-07, producing 56 points and 40 rebounds in 148 total minutes. In December 2006, Denver sent him to Philadelphia alongside Andre Miller and two first-round picks in the separate trade that brought Allen Iverson to Colorado. Thus Smith’s value to Denver eventually included his availability in a high-profile package, but he was not Denver’s new full-season starting power forward. The Nuggets B inherited grade should be understood as capturing veteran depth and later trade flexibility, not the same immediate playing return as Milwaukee’s 81 games from Patterson. Although the canonical verdict is Even Trade, the first-year NBA minutes leaned toward Milwaukee. Iverson’s entire downstream career cannot be assigned to Smith alone, because several other assets were part of that follow-on deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited evaluation, with Denver B and Milwaukee B+. Milwaukee received 81 games and 14.7 points per game from Ruben Patterson; Denver got 11 reserve appearances from Joe Smith before moving him as one of several assets in the later Allen Iverson trade. First-season playing value favored Milwaukee.
