sections.heading: The Timberwolves Bought a Reserve Wing with a Distant Pick
sections.body: On October 31, 2005, Minnesota acquired Ronald Dupree from Detroit for a future second-round draft pick. The Timberwolves retained the right to specify a second-round selection between 2006 and 2009 under the inherited transaction description, and the eventual choice came in 2009 at No. 35. Detroit used that pick on Georgetown forward DaJuan Summers. This was a minor depth transaction rather than a trade involving a first-rounder or a regular-season NBA starting guard. Minnesota wanted another athletic forward for the bench alongside Kevin Garnett; Detroit preferred a flexible future selection after Dupree had played a limited role on a successful Pistons team. League transaction records independently confirm the 2005 date and later draft outcome.

sections.heading: Dupree Played Thirty-Six Games for Minnesota
sections.body: Dupree appeared in 36 Timberwolves regular-season games during 2005-06 with no starts and a total of 265 minutes. He scored only modestly as a reserve, but his rebounding and wing size provided insurance on a roster struggling to build the right supporting cast around Garnett. He had played 47 Detroit games the previous season, yet those belonged to his earlier team and should not be counted as Minnesota value. The new club received a part-time defensive forward, not a franchise-changing perimeter scorer. Minnesota’s inherited C grade reflects those limited appearances and the relatively small draft-pick cost it initially expected. His time with the Timberwolves ended after one season, while Detroit held a pick that did not become selectable until four years after the transaction.

sections.heading: The Later Pick Gave Detroit a Real Second-Round Prospect
sections.body: Detroit used No. 35 of the 2009 draft on DaJuan Summers, a versatile forward who went on to appear in NBA games for the Pistons and other teams. The value of this selection was more concrete than a conditional pick that never conveyed, but Summers was a second-round development bet rather than an established starter. Detroit’s inherited B- grade is higher than Minnesota’s C, while the canonical headline says Slight Wolves Edge. Those judgments conflict numerically and warrant a separate provenance and grading review, rather than hiding the discrepancy. The key asset chain remains straightforward: Dupree moved to Minnesota in 2005, and Detroit’s compensation turned into the No. 35 pick in 2009. Both clubs had measured returns without an enduring centerpiece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge is the inherited winner, but grades of Detroit B- and Minnesota C point in the opposite direction. Minnesota obtained 36 games from Ronald Dupree in 2005-06, while Detroit received the eventual 2009 No. 35 draft pick used on DaJuan Summers. The disagreement between winner label and numeric grades requires a dedicated grade audit.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Juan Dixon for Brezec and Cash
sections.body: On February 21, 2008, Detroit acquired guard Juan Dixon from Toronto, sending reserve center Primož Brezec and cash considerations to the Raptors. The Pistons were seeking an additional backcourt option ahead of a playoff run, and Toronto was exploring more frontcourt depth. Brezec had been acquired by Detroit from Charlotte only two months earlier in the Nazr Mohammed trade, so his move to Toronto was the second leg of a short asset path. The teams’ transaction logs independently confirm this swap and its date. There was no first-round selection attached, and it was not part of the separate large multi-team Cavaliers trade that occurred the same day. The agreement exchanged an expendable reserve big man for a veteran scorer who could cover guard minutes.

sections.heading: Dixon Had a Brief but Measurable Pistons Scoring Role
sections.body: Dixon played 17 Detroit regular-season games after the transaction, with no starts, averaging 6.5 points and 1.9 assists in 14.4 minutes. He shot 48.0 percent from the floor and 39.4 percent from three during that short span, making him a usable offense-first reserve. Detroit had an established backcourt built around Chauncey Billups and Richard Hamilton, so a trade deadline addition was never expected to displace either starter. Dixon’s contribution was a narrow scoring bench role during a season the Pistons went on to reach the Eastern Conference Finals. The Detroit C inherited grade reflects those minutes without overstating him as an essential scorer or a new long-term rotation fixture. His earlier Portland and Toronto games do not belong to the Detroit portion of this trade.

sections.heading: Toronto Added a Center with Limited Playing Time
sections.body: Brezec made 13 Toronto appearances after the trade in 2007-08 and did not start, averaging 3.7 points and 1.4 rebounds. He was a limited bench-center addition rather than a replacement for the Raptors principal interior scorer Chris Bosh. The Raptors also received cash, whose exact amount is not specified in the canonical transaction record. Toronto’s C+ grade exceeds Detroit’s C, even though the inherited headline describes an Even Trade. That can be interpreted as a small economic or positional preference, but the grade discrepancy should be visible rather than rounded away. Both players produced only part-season contributions for their new clubs, with Dixon supplying more immediate perimeter scoring and Brezec offering a different positional option.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited classification, although Detroit grades C and Toronto C+. The Pistons received 17 games and 6.5 points per game from Juan Dixon. The Raptors acquired Primož Brezec, who played 13 games at 3.7 points, plus unspecified cash. Both were brief reserve transactions, with differing grade assessments.

sources.title: Detroit February 21 trade and earlier Brezec acquisition

sections.heading: Cleveland Acquired Draft Rights to Sasha Kaun for Cash
sections.body: The Cavaliers obtained the NBA draft rights to Kansas center Sasha Kaun from the Seattle SuperSonics on June 26, 2008. Seattle had selected Kaun at No. 56 earlier in the draft, and Cleveland sent cash for the opportunity to retain him as an overseas prospect. Kaun was a senior member of the Kansas team that won the 2008 NCAA championship, giving the Cavaliers a known college basketball defender without using their own first-round selection on him. Cleveland’s dated transaction history confirms the rights acquisition, while the canonical trade record lists cash on the Seattle side. The amount is not specified and should not be invented. Neither franchise expected a ready NBA starting center on the night of this minor second-round rights transaction.

sections.heading: Kaun Played Several Seasons Overseas Before His NBA Debut
sections.body: Kaun returned to Europe and played professionally for CSKA Moscow, where he gained substantial high-level experience. His NBA rights did not immediately produce Cavaliers playing time. In September 2015 Cleveland signed him for what became his only NBA season. He appeared in 25 regular-season games during 2015-16, averaging 0.9 points and 1.0 rebound in 3.8 minutes. The official Cavaliers media guide independently confirms both those numbers and his original 2008 Seattle draft selection. Cleveland went on to win the 2016 NBA championship, but Kaun was a deep reserve rather than a major postseason contributor. His eventual Cleveland appearances establish a small realized on-court return after an unusual seven-year wait, not a hidden multi-season Cavaliers starting career.

sections.heading: The Seattle Franchise Collected Cash and Surrendered an Unused Prospect
sections.body: Seattle acquired cash without retaining Kaun’s rights or adding another pick through this specific move. The franchise relocated to Oklahoma City before the 2008-09 season, meaning the receiving side is the historical Seattle club even though the modern team label reads Oklahoma City Thunder. Cash was a legitimate return for a No. 56 selection, especially when the player was expected to remain overseas. The club’s B- inherited grade values the low-cost financial return, while Cleveland’s equal B- acknowledges the rights and eventual reserve NBA appearances. Calling this an Even Trade is reasonable for a late second-round prospect and undisclosed money; neither team gained a future All-Star or franchise-building player from the agreement. The delayed NBA debut, not immediate draft-night playing time, is the distinguishing detail.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with B- grades on both sides. Cleveland obtained Sasha Kaun’s No. 56 draft rights in 2008 and eventually signed him for 25 NBA games in 2015-16 at 0.9 points a night. The Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise received undisclosed cash. The draft-right investment had a small, delayed payoff.

sections.heading: Phoenix Pursued Scoring with a Six-Player Deal and a Pick
sections.body: On December 10, 2008, Phoenix acquired scoring guard Jason Richardson and young wing Jared Dudley from Charlotte. The Suns also received a 2010 second-round selection, later No. 46 Gani Lawal. The Bobcats obtained Boris Diaw, defensive guard Raja Bell and rookie Sean Singletary. Contemporary Associated Press reporting explains Phoenix’s desire for a more explosive scorer around Steve Nash, while Charlotte coach Larry Brown wanted additional defense and playmaking. The transaction was larger than a Richardson-for-Diaw swap, because Dudley became an important later Suns contributor and Bell arrived with a substantial perimeter-defense reputation. The future second mattered as a separate draft opportunity. The teams’ official transaction records agree on all six players and the 2010 pick.

sections.heading: Diaw and Bell Started Right Away for Charlotte
sections.body: Diaw became a central Charlotte forward after leaving Phoenix’s bench. He started all 59 Bobcats games he played during 2008-09, averaging 15.1 points, 5.9 rebounds and 4.9 assists while shooting 41.9 percent from three. His ability to pass from the frontcourt gave Charlotte a new playmaking dimension. Bell started 44 of his 45 Bobcats appearances that season, scoring 13.0 points per game and supplying the veteran wing defense the team had sought. Singletary’s role was much smaller, but the two principal arrivals immediately filled large rotation assignments. The Bobcats’ B- inherited grade acknowledges that improvement without suggesting that Charlotte reached the playoffs because of the trade alone. Diaw stayed several years and later found additional NBA success elsewhere, which belongs to separate team contexts.

sections.heading: Richardson Helped Phoenix, and Dudley Became a Long-Term Asset
sections.body: Richardson remained a proven high-volume scorer after the move, pairing his perimeter attack with Nash and Amar’e Stoudemire. Phoenix advanced to the 2010 Western Conference Finals with Richardson as a notable offensive contributor. Dudley developed into a reliable shooting forward and stayed on the Suns beyond Richardson’s stint, extending the trade’s value well past the first season. The acquired 2010 second-round choice added another asset, though Gani Lawal’s eventual NBA minutes were limited and cannot account for the whole trade. Phoenix’s B+ grade exceeds Charlotte’s B- because the Suns obtained both a useful veteran scorer and a younger wing with multi-year impact. The Bobcats nonetheless received significant immediate production from Diaw and Bell. Both sides addressed real basketball needs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win under the inherited B+ Phoenix versus B- Charlotte assessment. Phoenix gained Jason Richardson, Jared Dudley and a 2010 second-round pick used on Gani Lawal. Charlotte obtained Boris Diaw, Raja Bell and Sean Singletary; Diaw started 59 games at 15.1 points and 4.9 assists in 2008-09, making this a productive trade on both sides.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned Radmanović into Two Young Wings
sections.body: On February 7, 2009, the Lakers traded forward Vladimir Radmanović to Charlotte for Adam Morrison and Shannon Brown. Lakers general manager Mitch Kupchak explained that Radmanović had slipped behind Trevor Ariza and Luke Walton in the team’s forward rotation and carried a relatively expensive contract. Morrison had struggled to meet expectations attached to his 2006 No. 3 selection, while Brown offered defense and athleticism on the perimeter. Los Angeles sought cheaper roster flexibility and a different kind of wing depth before the postseason. Charlotte gained an experienced forward capable of shooting from distance and filling reserve minutes. There were no draft picks in the agreement, so the value on both sides comes from the players and salary situation rather than an invented future draft asset.

sections.heading: Brown Became a Regular on Two Lakers Championship Teams
sections.body: Brown played 18 Lakers games in the remainder of 2008-09, then became a much larger contributor. He appeared in all 82 regular-season games in 2009-10, averaging 8.1 points in 20.7 minutes, and played in every game again during 2010-11. His athletic defense and ability to provide a fast break spark helped Los Angeles’ guard rotation as the club won consecutive NBA championships in 2009 and 2010. Morrison remained a deeper bench option and did not become the leading scorer once projected at Gonzaga. Still, the Lakers’ B grade rests on genuine Brown minutes, postseason utility and the different contract profile obtained for Radmanović. Brown’s later Phoenix and other franchise seasons cannot be added to the Lakers’ direct return, though his two title years clearly belong here.

sections.heading: Radmanović Provided Charlotte Shooting Without a Major Breakthrough
sections.body: Radmanović gave the Bobcats another experienced forward in their attempts to build a more competitive lineup around Gerald Wallace, Boris Diaw and Raymond Felton. He could space the floor and cover minutes at both forward positions, but did not become Charlotte’s leading scorer or provide the enduring guard impact Brown ultimately offered Los Angeles. Charlotte’s C+ inherited grade recognizes roster utility while discounting the cost and limited ceiling of the incoming player. The transaction also had a financial angle: removing a longer contract was a stated Lakers motivation, not a claim that Brown alone had been expected to be a future star on the day of the trade. From a hindsight perspective, Los Angeles obtained the more meaningful on-court contribution to championship seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B for Adam Morrison and especially Shannon Brown, who appeared in all 82 games in 2009-10 while averaging 8.1 points on a second straight championship team. Charlotte receives C+ for Vladimir Radmanović, who offered veteran forward shooting but not a comparable postseason contribution.

sections.heading: Charlotte Got Stephen Jackson and Acie Law for Two Veterans
sections.body: The Bobcats acquired Stephen Jackson and Acie Law from Golden State on November 16, 2009. The Warriors took back experienced shooting guard Raja Bell and forward Vladimir Radmanović. Charlotte general manager Rod Higgins announced the two-for-two agreement, emphasizing Jackson’s scoring and defense and Law’s potential as additional point-guard depth. Golden State moved Jackson after friction surrounding his role with the club and took on two veterans whose contracts and minutes could be managed differently. Charlotte was in pursuit of its first playoff appearance, not simply accumulating young draft rights. The transaction did not include a first-round pick or cash, and it was separate from the Bobcats earlier acquisitions of Bell and Radmanović from Phoenix and the Lakers. Their asset paths converge in this deal.

sections.heading: Jackson Was Charlotte’s Leading Scorer During Its First Playoff Year
sections.body: Jackson appeared in 72 Charlotte games after the trade during 2009-10, started every time and averaged 21.1 points, 5.1 rebounds and 3.6 assists. He played alongside Gerald Wallace as the Bobcats reached the NBA playoffs for the first time in franchise history. That clear immediate effect is the reason Charlotte earned an A- in the inherited verdict. Jackson returned in 2010-11 for 67 appearances, all starts, with another 18.5 points per game. These two seasons demonstrate a far larger return than a short-term rental. His defensive intensity and willingness to assume difficult shots helped a Bobcats roster that had struggled to find a dependable second scorer. Law’s Charlotte stint was shorter, and he moved in a separate trade months later, but Jackson alone delivered multiple years of substantial playing value.

sections.heading: Bell and Radmanović Did Not Replicate Jackson in Golden State
sections.body: Golden State’s incoming players could supply outside shooting, experienced defense and some lineup flexibility, but neither gave the Warriors the same two-season lead-scoring output Jackson produced in Charlotte. Bell’s available minutes were limited after the transaction, while Radmanović became a supporting forward on a rebuilding roster. The Warriors’ D+ inherited grade captures this gap between established star-level offense leaving and supplementary rotation value arriving. It would be wrong to credit Golden State with Bell’s earlier first-team All-Defensive seasons or Radmanović’s Los Angeles performances after they had already happened. The Warriors pursued a workable contract and chemistry adjustment but did not receive an obvious on-court replacement for Jackson. Charlotte got both a primary scorer and the club’s first postseason appearance during his tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Bobcats receive A- after Stephen Jackson started 72 games at 21.1 points per night in 2009-10 and helped deliver the franchise’s first playoff berth, with Acie Law also acquired. Golden State earns D+ for Raja Bell and Vladimir Radmanović; neither replaced Jackson’s sustained Charlotte scoring.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Tyson Chandler and Alexis Ajinça
sections.body: On July 13, 2010, the Dallas Mavericks obtained defensive center Tyson Chandler and young big man Alexis Ajinça from Charlotte. The Bobcats received center Erick Dampier, shooting guard Matt Carroll, forward Eduardo Nájera and cash. The official Charlotte announcement confirms the complete five-player agreement, while contemporary ESPN reporting details the major role of Dampier’s largely non-guaranteed contract. Charlotte had explored a different Chandler trade involving Toronto before reaching terms with Dallas, but that proposal was not the completed transaction. Dallas wanted more athletic rim protection alongside Dirk Nowitzki and could not acquire the much larger star it had pursued. The deal did not involve an additional first-round pick, and Charlotte’s main incoming bargaining tool was Dampier’s contract rather than an expectation of elite new scoring.

sections.heading: Chandler Became the Defensive Center Dallas Needed to Win a Title
sections.body: Chandler started 74 Mavericks games in 2010-11, giving Dallas rim protection and interior rebounding beside Nowitzki. His ability to defend pick-and-rolls and protect the basket helped the Mavericks win the 2011 NBA championship over Miami. He was a markedly different player from the aging Dampier and offered defensive versatility without demanding many offensive touches. Ajinça supplied a younger center prospect who could develop or be exchanged, although Chandler was clearly the central return. Dallas’s inherited A+ grade is supported by the title-winning season of the player it received directly in this trade, not by attributing all of Nowitzki’s scoring or the coaching staff’s work to the transaction. The defensive improvement had an observable effect in the very next season.

sections.heading: Charlotte Waived Dampier and Could Not Match the Mavericks’ Return
sections.body: Charlotte subsequently waived Dampier without him appearing in a regular-season Bobcats game. His contract had financial flexibility, but it did not yield sustained center play to the franchise. Carroll and Nájera offered veteran bench minutes and the accompanying cash created a limited economic benefit, yet the roster did not gain a new anchor comparable to Chandler. Charlotte’s F inherited grade reflects sacrificing a future championship center without a strong playing return from the main incoming contract. The decision looks especially harsh in hindsight because the Bobcats did not retain a comparable rim protector through the next season. Dallas effectively converted a difficult contract package into the defensive starting center who was central to a championship run.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns A+ for Tyson Chandler and Alexis Ajinça, with Chandler starting 74 regular-season games and anchoring the 2011 championship defense. Charlotte receives F for Erick Dampier, Matt Carroll, Eduardo Nájera and cash; Dampier was waived before providing Bobcats regular-season minutes. The team-specific on-court difference was substantial.

July 13 2010 Dallas acquires Chandler and Ajinca for Dampier package

sections.heading: The Jazz Moved Deron Williams for Two Players and Two Firsts
sections.body: On February 23, 2011, Utah traded All-Star point guard Deron Williams to New Jersey. The Jazz received guard Devin Harris, young forward Derrick Favors, a 2011 first-round pick that became No. 3 Enes Kanter and another first-round selection that was later No. 21 in 2013, associated with Gorgui Dieng. The inherited transaction record also includes cash considerations. Williams was an established elite pick-and-roll operator who had averaged more than ten assists in multiple Utah seasons. New Jersey needed a franchise-level point guard to headline its rebuilding effort before the later move to Brooklyn. Utah accepted a package that paired a current NBA guard with a very young power forward and two draft opportunities. The teams’ histories identify the asset flow, though each later pick transfer requires independent tracing.

sections.heading: Williams Was Productive for the Nets but Never Restored Their Former Finals Standing
sections.body: Williams played at an All-Star level after the move, supplying scoring and playmaking in both New Jersey and Brooklyn. He helped the relocated Nets reach the postseason in multiple seasons, including the second round in 2014. That is genuine basketball value; the inherited Nets F grade should not be read as a claim that Williams never played effectively for the franchise. His later large contract and uneven health reduced the value of the acquisition relative to its high price, however, and the Nets did not return to the Finals during his tenure. New Jersey’s immediate gamble was to secure a star point guard; its longer-term opportunity cost was the loss of two firsts and Favors. The gap between professional production and the price of acquiring it explains the harsh retrospective assessment.

sections.heading: Favors and the Kanter Pick Anchored Utah’s Rebuild
sections.body: Favors developed into a starting Utah frontcourt player over several seasons, with major rebounding and defensive responsibilities. Harris supplied a veteran guard during the initial transition. Utah also selected Enes Kanter at No. 3 in 2011, obtaining another young interior prospect who played regular NBA minutes for the Jazz before a later trade. The 2013 No. 21 pick connected to Gorgui Dieng followed its own rights chain, so Dieng’s entire NBA career should not be credited as Utah games. The Jazz’s A+ inherited grade reflects a package of long-term roster-building assets rather than a single replacement guard matching Williams’s past All-Star stats. Utah traded an established star yet obtained several different usable pieces, while New Jersey concentrated its future resources in one veteran.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah earns A+ for Derrick Favors, Devin Harris and two first-round assets tied to No. 3 Enes Kanter in 2011 and No. 21 Gorgui Dieng in 2013, plus cash considerations. New Jersey receives F despite Deron Williams’s productive Nets years because the high acquisition cost and later contract reduced the lasting payoff.

sources.title: February 2011 Deron Williams trade franchise analysis

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired DeSagana Diop for Two Players
sections.body: On January 16, 2009, Charlotte acquired defensive center DeSagana Diop from Dallas. The Bobcats sent shooting guard Matt Carroll and center Ryan Hollins to the Mavericks. Charlotte general manager Rod Higgins emphasized Diop’s rebounding, shot blocking and ability to guard big men, while Dallas wanted a different combination of perimeter shooting and athletic reserve size. The Charlotte official announcement confirms the entire two-for-one package; there was no first-round pick involved. Diop had been a Mavericks rotation center during the club’s 2006 Finals appearance before leaving for New Jersey and later returning to Dallas. He had appeared in 34 Mavericks games earlier in 2008-09, but those pretrade appearances do not belong to Charlotte’s direct return.

sections.heading: Diop Provided Reserve Center Minutes but Limited Scoring
sections.body: Diop was primarily a rim protector and rebounder rather than an offensive focal point. He arrived averaging only 1.6 points and 3.5 rebounds in 13.3 minutes for Dallas that season, so Charlotte should not have expected another high-volume scoring big man. He could absorb center minutes while allowing Emeka Okafor and other forwards to take different assignments, but his offensive ceiling and contract were limiting. He stayed with Charlotte beyond this trade, making it more than a brief tryout, yet the Bobcats had not acquired a starting center who would dramatically improve the offense. The inherited C- grade reflects a narrow value from his defense and availability rather than a playoff-transforming addition. His earlier Dallas championship-contender work should not inflate his Bobcats impact.

sections.heading: Dallas Gained Two Different Rotation Tools
sections.body: Carroll returned to Dallas as an experienced outside shooter who could help stretch the floor in bench lineups. Hollins, acquired in his third NBA season, was a young seven-footer whose mobility gave the Mavericks more athletic center depth. Neither should be credited with Diop’s prior shot-block totals, and neither instantly became a franchise star. But Dallas had the option to use two complementary reserves rather than carry Diop’s bigger frontcourt commitment. Its B+ inherited grade reflects the additional lineup and payroll flexibility alongside the players’ modest direct contributions. The difference in grades is larger than the players’ raw scoring production, so the deal is best viewed as a basketball and contract management decision for a playoff hopeful. The later careers of Carroll or Hollins with other clubs are separate from the Dallas return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas receives B+ for Matt Carroll and Ryan Hollins, two role-specific rotation options obtained for DeSagana Diop. Charlotte gets C- for a defense-first center who provided size and rebounding but little scoring. The immediate result was a rotation and contract trade, not the arrival of a leading scorer.

sections.heading: The Thunder Acquired Thabo Sefolosha for a Future First
sections.body: On February 19, 2009, Chicago traded wing defender Thabo Sefolosha to Oklahoma City for a 2009 first-round draft selection. The Thunder’s official announcement specified the least favorable of two picks it held from Denver and San Antonio, while Chicago’s own release confirmed the basic terms. The selection eventually became No. 26 and was used to draft USC forward Taj Gibson. Chicago was replenishing its young frontcourt while Oklahoma City sought a defensive-minded perimeter player to accompany Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook. There was no major existing scorer coming back to the Bulls on the day of the trade; its principal return was a future draft opportunity, not a guaranteed veteran rotation player. The teams were building different complementary pieces for their developing cores.

sections.heading: Gibson Became a Durable Bulls Frontcourt Contributor
sections.body: The Bulls selected Gibson at No. 26 in the 2009 draft. He made an immediate impression with rebounding, defensive effort and reliable frontcourt minutes, later becoming a key member of Chicago’s competitive Derrick Rose-era teams. His Chicago career extended across many seasons, including deep postseason runs. Gibson was particularly useful as a reserve power forward and occasional starter, providing interior defense while more prominent scorers handled the offense. That long-term Chicago production supports an A+ inherited grade without requiring that the second-half 2009 trade itself produced a scorer right away. It is the drafted player’s sustained team-specific contribution that distinguishes this deal. The selection did not become an unexercised conditional pick: No. 26 was used on an actual NBA forward with significant Chicago playing time.

sections.heading: Sefolosha Also Helped Oklahoma City Become a Contender
sections.body: Sefolosha was far from a wasted Thunder acquisition. He became a regular starting guard or wing on a roster built around Durant and Westbrook, defending opposing perimeter scorers while providing lower-volume offense. Oklahoma City advanced to the 2012 NBA Finals during his tenure, with Sefolosha part of the main rotation. The inherited D grade for the Thunder therefore seems unusually harsh compared with his long tenure and role on a Finals team. That does not erase the value Chicago obtained from Gibson, but it makes the winner less one-sided than the grade gap implies. A complete hindsight analysis must distinguish the future pick’s Chicago impact from Sefolosha’s real Oklahoma City games instead of treating the Thunder’s side as no return. The record still identifies Chicago as the winner in the original evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win in the inherited A+ Chicago to D Oklahoma City assessment. Chicago drafted Taj Gibson at No. 26 with the received first-round pick, securing years of frontcourt production. The Thunder obtained Thabo Sefolosha, a meaningful defender on their 2012 Finals team, so the existing grade gap may overstate the difference.

sections.heading: Charlotte Surrendered Two Guards and a Protected First for Tyrus Thomas
sections.body: The Bobcats obtained athletic power forward Tyrus Thomas from Chicago on February 18, 2010. In return, Chicago received veteran scorer Ronald Murray, young guard Acie Law and a future first-round selection with protections through 2016. The draft choice eventually became No. 16 in 2014, associated with Jusuf Nurkić. The Bulls’ transaction record confirms the 2014 selection, and Charlotte’s record identifies Thomas as the only player received. Thomas had been the No. 4 selection in the 2006 draft and offered explosive shot-blocking talent, but his Bulls development had been uneven. Charlotte was attempting to strengthen a team about to reach its first postseason, while Chicago accepted immediate guard depth and a long-term asset. The protected first was a material cost, not a minor second-round option.

sections.heading: Thomas Contributed at First but Never Justified the Later Contract
sections.body: Thomas supplied energetic reserve minutes for Charlotte following the deadline and gave the Bobcats more athleticism near the basket. He could block shots and finish above the rim, but offensive limitations and later injuries complicated his future. Charlotte subsequently committed to a large multi-year contract, and his performance did not develop into the expected dependable starting power forward production. His playing role shrank before the franchise eventually waived him, leaving substantial salary costs and the traded draft asset as the lasting effects of the experiment. The Bobcats F inherited grade reflects the entire value proposition, not merely his initial short stint during the 2010 playoff push. It would be misleading to claim Thomas never appeared for Charlotte: the issue was whether he justified the combined pick and contract commitment over the long term.

sections.heading: Chicago Retained a Valuable First-Round Asset
sections.body: Chicago received two guards who could provide immediate backcourt minutes and later held rights connected to the protected first-round pick. That selection eventually materialized in 2014 as No. 16, linked to Jusuf Nurkić. The full draft-rights path needs to be traced rather than assigning all of Nurkić’s eventual NBA seasons to the Bulls if the rights were subsequently traded. Even without a long Bulls career from the selected player, an actual mid-first-round choice had meaningful exchange value in 2014. The Bulls A inherited grade recognizes obtaining tradable future draft capital for a young forward whose expensive Charlotte tenure disappointed. Thomas’s best Charlotte highlights were not enough to offset the pick and later contract burden, explaining the extreme grade difference in the retrospective verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A after acquiring Ronald Murray, Acie Law and a protected future first-round selection that became the 2014 No. 16 choice associated with Jusuf Nurkić. Charlotte receives F after Tyrus Thomas failed to justify the later long-term investment, despite initially providing shot blocking during the 2010 playoff push.

sections.heading: Golden State Obtained the Pick That Became Draymond Green
sections.body: On February 23, 2011, New Jersey sent veteran forward Troy Murphy and a future 2012 second-round draft selection to Golden State. The Warriors sent big man Dan Gadzuric and young forward Brandan Wright to the Nets. The traded selection eventually became No. 35 in 2012, used on Michigan State forward Draymond Green. Both franchises’ transaction histories confirm the players, date and draft outcome. Golden State was not acquiring an existing NBA star in this exchange; it obtained a player who was quickly waived and the right to select a prospect in the following year. New Jersey wanted immediate frontcourt changes and let go of a second-round option. That seemingly minor asset became the decisive long-run value.

sections.heading: Green Became a Multi-Championship Defensive Leader
sections.body: Green joined the Warriors as a rookie in 2012-13, then developed into an indispensable defensive organizer and passing forward for their championship era. He later won NBA Defensive Player of the Year and multiple NBA championships, providing far greater return than would ordinarily be expected from the 35th pick. His versatility allowed Golden State to use smaller, faster lineups around Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson without losing interior defensive coordination. This playing value directly connects to the future draft selection acquired from New Jersey in 2011. The Warriors A- inherited grade reflects getting an exceptionally productive player from a low pick while giving up two comparatively expendable bigs. Murphy never supplied a new Golden State regular-season career after being acquired: he was waived within days, underscoring that the draft right was the true winning asset.

sections.heading: Neither Incoming Nets Forward Matched the Draft Outcome
sections.body: Gadzuric and Wright were legitimate NBA frontcourt players, but their New Jersey stays were limited. Neither became a long-term Nets defensive cornerstone. New Jersey also gave up the opportunity to use the No. 35 pick or exchange it for another future asset, an enormous missed value in hindsight. The Nets D+ grade is tied to that opportunity cost rather than claiming its two acquired players had no professional basketball skills. Green’s later career cannot be credited to Murphy, who did not play significant Warriors minutes, but it can be traced to the actual selection Golden State obtained. This trade also occurred on the same date as the Nets blockbuster Deron Williams acquisition; the two agreements are distinct and must not be combined into a fictional single package. The overlooked second-round pick is the central narrative.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns A- for the 2012 No. 35 second-round pick it used on Draymond Green, a future Defensive Player of the Year and championship cornerstone. New Jersey receives D+ for Brandan Wright and Dan Gadzuric, whose limited Nets tenure did not match the long-term value of the traded pick.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Kris Humphries and Shawne Williams
sections.body: On January 11, 2010, the Nets traded veteran forward Eduardo Nájera to Dallas for young frontcourt player Kris Humphries and wing Shawne Williams. The Mavericks had previously used Nájera as an energetic defender during his first stint with Dallas and wanted him back in a reserve role. New Jersey sought younger players and more rebounding opportunities during a rebuilding season. Both franchises’ transaction registers describe a direct two-for-one exchange, without cash or a future first-round choice. The transaction would prove more productive for the Nets than the low-profile player names suggested at the time, particularly as Humphries was given increased minutes when New Jersey’s roster changed. Williams did not become an equally important long-term contributor for the franchise, so the two incoming players should not receive equal credit.

sections.heading: Humphries Became a Double-Digit Nets Rebounder
sections.body: Humphries improved considerably after joining New Jersey. In 2010-11 he became a regular frontcourt starter and averaged a double-double, contributing both inside scoring and more than ten rebounds per game. He repeated that level of rebounding during the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season, before the franchise moved to Brooklyn. Those were genuine Nets seasons arising from the January 2010 acquisition, not production borrowed from his later Boston, Washington or Atlanta teams. New Jersey’s C+ inherited grade is conservative compared with the number of games and rebounds Humphries ultimately delivered. The club obtained a useful starting power forward in exchange for a veteran reserve, a favorable result that does not require inventing a lottery pick or other compensation. Humphries was also available during the team’s broader effort to add star talent through subsequent trades.

sections.heading: Nájera Returned to Dallas for Veteran Bench Minutes
sections.body: Nájera helped Dallas with veteran defense and hustle, but this second Mavericks stint was not equivalent to Humphries becoming a full-time Nets rebounder. Dallas had other power forwards and centers capable of taking the main rotation minutes, so its use of Nájera was more specialized. Shawne Williams did not become a major New Jersey scorer from this particular acquisition, but the long-term value of Humphries was enough to justify the narrow inherited Nets winner. Dallas’s C grade reflects legitimate depth from a known reserve, and the franchise went on to become a championship team in 2011 through other major roster changes. The Mavericks’ later championship season should not be wholly credited to Nájera or counted as a direct return from this trade. The teams made different calculations about experience and development.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey receives C+ for Kris Humphries and Shawne Williams, with Humphries subsequently developing into a double-double rebounder over multiple Nets seasons. Dallas gets C for Eduardo Nájera’s reserve contribution. The frontcourt production New Jersey received was more durable than the initial transaction suggested.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Sent Two Forwards for Nazr Mohammed
sections.body: On February 24, 2011, Charlotte acquired forward D.J. White and veteran wing Morris Peterson from Oklahoma City in exchange for center Nazr Mohammed. The Bobcats official announcement confirmed both incoming players, with Mohammed having already played 51 Charlotte games that season. Oklahoma City wanted a reliable reserve big man behind its developing core as the playoffs approached, while Charlotte took the chance to develop White, a former first-round pick. Peterson had already spent years as a Toronto starter, but that résumé did not guarantee a Bobcats role. The two-for-one exchange did not contain an additional draft choice. It happened on the same date as Charlotte's larger Gerald Wallace deal with Portland, a completely separate asset package that should not be conflated with this transaction.

sections.heading: White Scored for Charlotte but Peterson Was Waived Almost Immediately
sections.body: White appeared in 24 Bobcats games after the trade in 2010-11, all as a reserve, averaging 8.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 19.4 minutes. He returned for 58 games in the abbreviated 2011-12 season, with 6.8 points and 3.6 rebounds per game. Those are real Charlotte contributions from a forward acquired for a veteran center, although White did not become the franchise's long-term primary scorer. Peterson played no Charlotte regular-season games and was waived on February 28, just four days after the acquisition, as the team's official release confirms. Crediting his earlier Toronto career to Charlotte would substantially exaggerate the on-court return. Charlotte's C+ grade is primarily grounded in White's 82 direct Bobcats games over two seasons.

sections.heading: Mohammed Brought Playoff Frontcourt Insurance to the Thunder
sections.body: Mohammed gave Oklahoma City an experienced interior reserve behind its younger starters. His post-trade contribution belongs to the Thunder's 2011 postseason push, not to Charlotte's prior 51 games that year. The team reached the Western Conference Finals before losing to Dallas, and it had a recognized defensive and rebounding center available for matchups requiring additional size. His later appearances for the Thunder were a shorter-term return than a prospective draft pick or long developmental deal. The inherited Oklahoma City Thunder Win wording stands alongside equal C+ grades for both teams, so it signals a preference for the veteran fit rather than a numerical grade advantage. White nonetheless supplied Charlotte a substantial reserve scoring return. The facts make this more balanced than a veteran-for-zero account.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win in the inherited verdict despite equal C+ grades. The Thunder added veteran center Nazr Mohammed for a playoff push. Charlotte received D.J. White, who produced 24 games at 8.5 points in 2010-11 and 58 games at 6.8 points the next season; Morris Peterson was waived after four days.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired the Rights to Bojan Bogdanović from Minnesota
sections.body: On June 24, 2011, New Jersey purchased draft rights to Croatian scorer Bojan Bogdanović from Minnesota, giving up cash and a 2013 second-round pick. That choice eventually became No. 52 Lorenzo Brown. Miami had selected Bogdanović at No. 31 before moving his rights to Minnesota in a separate draft-night agreement, so the Nets did not select him directly with their own pick. Contemporary Nets reporting confirms the cash-and-pick construction and his European scoring reputation. The Nets were able to hold his NBA rights while he continued developing abroad, an inexpensive form of delayed roster construction. Minnesota chose immediate financial compensation and another future selection over retaining an international prospect.

sections.heading: Bogdanović Eventually Became a Useful Brooklyn Starting Forward
sections.body: Bogdanović did not join the NBA immediately, spending the next three seasons playing professionally in Turkey before his Nets debut in 2014. In 2014-15 he appeared in 78 Brooklyn games, making 28 starts and scoring 9.0 points per outing. The next season he played 79 games with 39 starts and averaged 11.2 points. His shooting and size gave Brooklyn another regular scoring wing, and his presence proved to be much more than merely speculative international rights. Brooklyn used him during a playoff season and later moved him to Washington in a separate transaction. New Jersey's B+ inherited grade is supported by years of directly attributable Nets games from a player acquired using a second-rounder and cash rather than a premium first.

sections.heading: Minnesota Held a Future Pick, Not Bogdanović’s NBA Production
sections.body: The Timberwolves gained cash and a 2013 second-round selection tied to No. 52 Lorenzo Brown. The draft-right ledger shows the choice moving through later transactions, so it should not be treated automatically as a full Minnesota player tenure without verifying that later chain. Minnesota also could have retained Bogdanović, but chose the opportunity to use those resources for other roster needs. Its inherited C grade recognizes a legitimate late pick and financial consideration rather than a first-round asset or experienced starter acquired in 2011. As a direct return, the Nets gained the player who eventually scored NBA points for multiple seasons, while Minnesota acquired resources with more uncertain realized impact. The delay until 2014 does not erase his subsequent Brooklyn years.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn/New Jersey receives B+ after acquiring Bojan Bogdanović’s rights and getting 78 games at 9.0 points in 2014-15 and 79 games at 11.2 in 2015-16. Minnesota gets C for cash and a 2013 second-round choice tied to No. 52 Lorenzo Brown, whose later pick chain is distinct.

sections.heading: The Bulls Obtained C.J. Watson for a Second and a Trade Exception
sections.body: On July 22, 2010, Chicago acquired reserve point guard C.J. Watson from Golden State. The Warriors received a 2011 second-round pick, eventually No. 44 Charles Jenkins, and a traded-player exception according to the inherited asset record. Golden State had used Watson as a useful offensive guard behind its more established backcourt, but Chicago wanted a steady alternative to Derrick Rose. The Warriors' dated transactions confirm the pick and Watson's departure, while the Bulls' incoming point guard filled a clear need on a team preparing to compete at the top of the East. This was a backup guard and asset-flexibility transaction, not a transfer of a marquee first-round selection.

sections.heading: Watson Became a Frequent Bulls Reserve and Occasional Starter
sections.body: Watson appeared in all 82 regular-season Bulls games in 2010-11, including one start, scoring 405 points and distributing 186 assists. Chicago went 62-20 and reached the Eastern Conference Finals that season. When Rose missed games in the abbreviated 2011-12 season, Watson stepped into a bigger role: 49 appearances, 25 starts, 474 points and 200 assists. His backup playmaking and three-point shooting were direct benefits from the trade, not achievements from his previous Golden State years. Watson also gave Chicago an established reserve who could cover unexpectedly large minutes without completely changing the rest of its offense. The Bulls' B+ inherited grade reflects two seasons of dependable point-guard availability, rather than claiming he was a second All-Star scorer beside Rose.

sections.heading: The No. 44 Choice Yielded Limited Warriors Production
sections.body: Golden State used the 2011 second-round selection on Hofstra guard Charles Jenkins. He played 51 games for the Warriors as a rookie and produced some reserve guard minutes, but did not become the long-term backcourt partner Watson had been for Chicago. The traded-player exception represented salary-management flexibility, which should be considered separately from actual scoring output. The Warriors' C+ inherited grade acknowledges receiving a draft prospect and financial maneuverability for a player whose role had already become expandable. Chicago obtained the clearer immediate bench and injury-replacement return through Watson, who supplied substantially more games in two years than Jenkins managed in the Warriors' main rotation. Later Jenkins teams do not add to the original Golden State production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ after C.J. Watson played all 82 games in 2010-11 and made 25 starts during the next season. Golden State receives C+ for the 2011 No. 44 second-rounder used on Charles Jenkins and a traded-player exception. The established backup guard helped the Bulls immediately.

sections.heading: Anthony Morrow Changed Teams for a Protected Second
sections.body: On July 13, 2010, New Jersey acquired shooting guard Anthony Morrow from Golden State through a sign-and-trade in exchange for a conditional 2011 second-round pick. The pick carried top-55 protection and never conveyed, as the contemporary franchise transaction record explicitly notes. Morrow had established himself as a strong outside shooter with the Warriors, shooting 46.7 percent on threes as a rookie and 45.6 percent in his second season. The Nets were assembling a new perimeter rotation around Brook Lopez and future backcourt needs, while the Warriors did not retain the shooter. The exchange did not include a first-round pick or an existing Nets starter. The contract and conditional nature of the pick are crucial to the actual asset cost.

sections.heading: Morrow Started Forty-Seven Games in His First Nets Season
sections.body: In 2010-11, Morrow appeared in 58 Nets games, started 47, and averaged 13.2 points while shooting 42.3 percent from three. The following season he appeared in 62 games with 18 starts, scoring 12.0 points per contest and making 106 three-pointers. Those were substantial two-season shooting returns for a club that had surrendered only a second-round pick that ultimately did not transfer. His scoring was valuable even though New Jersey had an unsuccessful overall record and did not contend for a title. The Nets C+ inherited grade looks cautious relative to two seasons of useful regular minutes, but the source-grounded player record independently establishes the transaction's return. Morrow subsequently played for other franchises, whose later totals do not belong to the Nets.

sections.heading: Golden State Gained Flexibility but No Drafted Prospect
sections.body: Golden State allowed Morrow to leave and received a second-round condition that did not produce an actual selection. Thus there is no 2011 Warriors draftee to attribute to this transaction. The Warriors C inherited grade can reflect avoiding another contract obligation and redirecting their perimeter rotation toward developing stars Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson in later seasons, but it cannot claim Morrow was directly exchanged for a prospect who reached the NBA. New Jersey gained a starting-caliber shooter at a tiny realized draft cost. The trade took place before Golden State's subsequent title years, and those championships are not proof that this particular sign-and-trade returned substantial player value. The clearest direct comparison is 120 Nets appearances from Morrow against zero conveyed picks for the Warriors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey receives C+ after Anthony Morrow played 58 games at 13.2 points in 2010-11 and 62 games at 12.0 in 2011-12. Golden State earns C for a protected 2011 second-rounder that did not convey. The Nets got two seasons of shooting without surrendering a realized draft selection.

sections.heading: The Bucks Acquired Chris Douglas-Roberts for a Future Second
sections.body: On June 23, 2010, the New Jersey Nets traded scoring guard Chris Douglas-Roberts to Milwaukee for a 2012 second-round selection. The pick eventually became No. 60, used on center Robert Sacre, although its subsequent rights path needs to be tracked separately from the Nets' actual NBA playing return. Douglas-Roberts had been a Brooklyn/New Jersey prospect since 2008 and appeared in 67 games during 2009-10 with a larger scoring role. Milwaukee wanted an inexpensive perimeter scorer while the Nets were restructuring around new ownership and their future roster. The agreement had one outgoing NBA guard against one future second-round pick; no veteran Bucks player returned to New Jersey. The teams' dated transaction ledgers independently confirm the draft year and later pick identity.

sections.heading: Douglas-Roberts Played Forty-Four Bucks Games
sections.body: Douglas-Roberts appeared in 44 Milwaukee games during 2010-11, averaging 7.3 points with 2.0 rebounds and 1.1 assists. That is legitimate supporting-player production for a second-round pick surrendered two summers before it would be selected. He did not become the club's primary scorer or an enduring starter, so the Bucks C+ grade recognizes a moderate one-year guard contribution rather than a franchise centerpiece. His earlier 111 New Jersey appearances cannot be counted again as a Milwaukee return. The Bucks already had established perimeter personnel and were trying to widen the bench, a function Douglas-Roberts could serve when healthy. His later NBA seasons with other clubs did not make this a long-term Bucks investment. The return was practical and limited to a narrow portion of the rotation.

sections.heading: New Jersey Received a Distant Draft Opportunity
sections.body: The Nets obtained a 2012 second-round pick instead of an existing player. No. 60 Robert Sacre eventually appeared in NBA games for the Lakers, not for New Jersey, so it would be false to assign his Laker starts to the Nets merely because the trade ledger links him to the pick. The rights chain and later draft transactions determine where the selection actually landed. New Jersey C grade reflects modest future flexibility and a decision to move a guard who was not part of its long-term plans. Milwaukee earned the immediate advantage through 44 games of usable scoring while the Nets waited for a late second-round asset to mature. Neither side acquired a proven All-Star through this trade, which explains the moderate grading on both ends.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee receives C+ for Chris Douglas-Roberts, who played 44 games at 7.3 points per appearance during 2010-11. New Jersey earns C for the 2012 No. 60 draft choice associated with Robert Sacre; his subsequent Lakers NBA career cannot be credited directly to the Nets.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Gerald Wallace for Three Players and Two Firsts
sections.body: On February 24, 2011, Charlotte traded Gerald Wallace to Portland. The Bobcats received Dante Cunningham, Joel Przybilla, Sean Marks, cash and two protected future first-round selections. The picks ultimately became No. 19 Tobias Harris in 2011 and No. 24 Shabazz Napier in 2014. Both team transaction registers confirm the full package and its protections. Wallace had helped lead Charlotte to the postseason in 2010, making his departure a major franchise decision. Portland wanted an established two-way wing immediately, while Charlotte sought financial flexibility and multiple chances to develop a new roster. This was much more than Wallace for one reserve forward.

sections.heading: Wallace Gave Portland Immediate Playoff-Caliber Production
sections.body: After the trade, Wallace played 23 Portland regular-season games and started all 23, averaging 15.8 points, 7.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists. He joined the Blazers playoff lineup as the club lost to Dallas in the first round. In 2011-12, Wallace remained a prominent Portland option before being sent to New Jersey in another transaction. Portland therefore did receive valuable immediate wing play, not an empty trade return. Its inherited C grade recognizes that his stay ended relatively quickly after the original deal. The first-round picks it surrendered were meaningful future assets that might have supported its own youth movement. Portland accepted those costs for a veteran capable of helping in the present.

sections.heading: Charlotte Gained Real Draft Capital with Complex Later Chains
sections.body: Cunningham supplied young frontcourt minutes while Przybilla and Marks provided veteran depth. The larger future value was the pair of protected firsts, which could be traded or exercised separately. Tobias Harris and Shabazz Napier are associated with the final selection numbers, but their eventual NBA careers are not automatically Charlotte playing production: subsequent draft rights moved between clubs. The Bobcats also received cash in the completed deal. The inherited A- grade captures the quantity of assets received while the club rebuilt around younger players. Wallace was still effective for Portland, but Charlotte was obtaining a collection of options rather than gambling the entire transaction on one replacement veteran.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. Charlotte earns A- after acquiring Dante Cunningham, Joel Przybilla, Sean Marks, cash and two future first-round selections tied to No. 19 in 2011 and No. 24 in 2014. Portland receives C after Gerald Wallace started 23 games at 15.8 points following the trade and later departed.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Sent Byron Mullens for a Future Second
sections.body: On December 19, 2011, the Bobcats obtained former first-round center Byron Mullens from Oklahoma City for a 2013 second-round choice. The pick became No. 32, associated with Spanish wing Álex Abrines. The Thunder were growing into a title contender and had limited playing time for Mullens behind their established interior players. Charlotte was rebuilding and could give the young center real development minutes. Both franchise transaction histories date the move after the lockout shortened the season calendar. This was a straightforward player-for-pick agreement without incoming veteran contracts or a first-round choice going to the Thunder. The difference in timing mattered: Charlotte could immediately assess Mullens while Oklahoma City would wait another draft.

sections.heading: Mullens Became a Regular Bobcats Starter
sections.body: In 2011-12 Mullens played 65 Charlotte games with 25 starts and averaged 9.3 points and 5.0 rebounds. A season later he started 41 of 53 appearances with 10.6 points and 6.4 rebounds. That was substantial on-court production for an incoming center obtained with a second-round selection. He expanded his shooting range and scored from farther from the basket, although his overall field-goal percentage suffered as his offensive responsibilities grew. The Bobcats won few games during these years, so Mullens was not a transformative anchor, but his 66 starts across two seasons distinguish the return from an unused prospect right. The inherited C+ grade reflects development and partial starting utility rather than a franchise star.

sections.heading: Abrines Offered Oklahoma City a Delayed Overseas Return
sections.body: Oklahoma City held the pick until the 2013 draft, when it was used on Álex Abrines. He continued playing in Spain before joining the Thunder in 2016, later supplying three-point shooting as a reserve. This meant the acquiring franchise did not receive any immediate 2011-12 NBA playing minutes, but the selection eventually produced a prospect with a real professional role. The canonical winner says Oklahoma City Thunder Win even though Charlotte grades C+ and the Thunder grades C. That discrepancy deserves separate grading review rather than an unannounced change to historical data. Charlotte got starting center opportunities promptly; the Thunder obtained later outside scoring. Neither side traded an existing All-Star in 2011.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win in the inherited verdict despite Charlotte C+ exceeding Thunder C. Charlotte obtained Byron Mullens, who started 25 games in 2011-12 and 41 the next season. Oklahoma City acquired the 2013 second-round choice used on Álex Abrines, whose NBA contributions began several years later.

sections.heading: Charlotte Paid a Highly Protected Second for Theo Ratliff
sections.body: On February 18, 2010, Charlotte acquired veteran center Theo Ratliff from the San Antonio Spurs. The compensation was a conditional 2016 second-round pick protected through No. 55, and the historical transaction record confirms that it did not convey. Ratliff was a 36-year-old shot blocker who had played for several NBA teams. His reserve role in San Antonio was small, but Charlotte had a need for reliable size while pursuing its first playoff appearance. The agreed pick condition kept the eventual cost low, with no guaranteed first-round selection or additional Charlotte player changing hands. The six-year distance between the deal and pick expiration is central to the asset accounting.

sections.heading: Ratliff Played Twenty-Eight Bobcats Games with Twenty-Six Starts
sections.body: Ratliff played 28 regular-season games for the Bobcats after the trade, starting 26. He totaled 624 minutes and averaged roughly 5.1 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.5 blocks, supplying defensive presence near the basket. Charlotte reached the postseason and gave Ratliff four playoff appearances against Orlando. His job was not to replace the franchise leading scorer or create a long-term center development program. The value came from a known veteran starting most of his games during a late-season playoff push. His NBA career later continued with the Lakers, so those appearances do not belong to Charlotte. The inherited Bobcats C grade recognizes a useful but relatively brief rental rather than a permanent roster upgrade.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received No Actual Drafted Player
sections.body: The 2016 second-round pick was protected through No. 55 and extinguished when the conditions were not met. That means the Spurs did not receive an actual draft prospect from this agreement. Their C grade can acknowledge financial or rotation flexibility, but there was no player delivered and no future selection from this specific transaction to credit with NBA statistics. San Antonio still had other centers and forwards available at the time, making the reserve expendable. The Even Trade label and equal grades are a conservative inherited characterization despite Charlotte clearly getting the only direct post-trade playing minutes. The important distinction is between a promised conditional future pick and a pick that actually transferred.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with inherited C grades for both teams. Charlotte obtained Theo Ratliff, who made 26 starts in 28 games during its 2010 playoff push. San Antonio received a 2016 second-rounder protected through No. 55 that failed to convey. No Spurs drafted player can be assigned to the unexercised condition.

sections.heading: The Wizards Acquired Yi Jianlian and Cash for Quinton Ross
sections.body: On June 29, 2010, Washington obtained young seven-footer Yi Jianlian and $3 million in cash from New Jersey for defensive wing Quinton Ross. The Wizards made an official announcement that described Yi as a former sixth overall pick with development potential. The Nets wanted financial flexibility before the summer free-agent market, and contemporary reporting identified nearly $3 million of cap savings from replacing Yi with the lower-salary Ross. There were no draft picks in the agreement. The cash went from New Jersey to Washington, not the other way around. Those financial terms are crucial: the receiving Washington player had averaged 12.0 points and 7.0 rebounds for New Jersey in 2009-10, but his contract was also more expensive.

sections.heading: Yi Contributed a Season of Reserve Frontcourt Minutes
sections.body: Yi played 63 Wizards games in 2010-11, starting 11 and averaging 5.6 points and 3.9 rebounds. His production declined from the previous Nets season, but Washington gained a real rotation big man at a time when it was developing guard John Wall and rebuilding the frontcourt. The club did not obtain a future All-Star and did not retain Yi as a long-term core player. Its inherited B+ grade is relatively generous compared with the modest direct scoring, but the package included both an experienced prospect and substantial cash. The 63 games belong to Washington, while his earlier Milwaukee and New Jersey statistics do not. That team distinction keeps the retrospective focused on the actual trade return.

sections.heading: New Jersey Valued Cap Space Over Ross Scoring
sections.body: Ross had played a defensive specialist role in several NBA cities, and he was not expected to replace the scoring Yi had supplied for New Jersey. The Nets were changing their payroll before potential pursuit of more established stars. Acquiring a smaller contract while paying cash therefore fit their immediate financial strategy even though the on-court return was limited. New Jersey C- reflects that narrow benefit. The transaction did not yield a second-round selection or new star player for the Nets, so crediting it with subsequent unrelated free-agent signings would exaggerate the actual deal. Washington received the more tangible immediate basketball return and cash, while New Jersey made a salary-management decision. The inherited winner follows that difference in practical player value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington receives B+ for Yi Jianlian, who appeared in 63 games and started 11 in 2010-11, plus $3 million cash. New Jersey earns C- for Quinton Ross and about $3 million in cap flexibility. The cash traveled to Washington, and the direct Nets scoring return was limited.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought Draft Rights to Dominique Jones for Cash
sections.body: On June 24, 2010, the Mavericks obtained draft rights to South Florida guard Dominique Jones, the No. 25 first-round selection, from Memphis. Dallas paid $3 million in cash for the rights rather than surrendering a veteran player or another first-round pick. The Grizzlies had just selected Jones and chose a financial asset instead of developing him. Dallas was assembling a rotation around Dirk Nowitzki and hoped an aggressive young scorer could eventually supplement an experienced backcourt. The exchange did not involve NBA game statistics from Jones in Memphis because he was traded on draft night. It was a direct sale of a newly selected first-round right rather than a sign-and-trade of an established player.

sections.heading: Jones Was a Small Mavericks Reserve During the Championship Year
sections.body: Jones played 18 Dallas regular-season games in 2010-11, with no starts, averaging only 2.3 points in limited minutes. He remained with Dallas for the next season and appeared in 33 games, scoring 1.7 points per outing. Those were actual NBA appearances but did not establish him as a regular starting guard. The Mavericks won the 2011 NBA championship through a roster anchored by Nowitzki and its veteran starters, not because Jones had become a crucial scorer. The inherited Dallas B- grade recognizes the potential value of a first-round asset and some depth, though the realized on-court contribution was modest. He did not become the kind of long-term offensive playmaker that the late first-round selection could have provided.

sections.heading: Memphis Received Money Without a Later Player Claim
sections.body: The Grizzlies obtained the $3 million cash payment at the time of the 2010 draft and had no subsequent Jones games to show for it. That financial value was immediate and separate from any other draft selections made that year. No future draft choice should be invented as a Memphis return from this agreement. The inherited B- grade equals Dallas, while the canonical headline selects a Slight Mavericks Edge. That slight preference reflects the possibility of developing a first-round player rather than proof that Jones ultimately became a major scorer. In hindsight the decision is close because his Dallas NBA tenure remained limited, but the initial acquisition produced a contractual opportunity with more potential than a simple reserve signing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge by the inherited label, although Dallas and Memphis both grade B-. Dallas paid $3 million for 2010 first-round No. 25 Dominique Jones and received only limited bench minutes in two NBA seasons. Memphis got immediate financial compensation without adding a player or draft pick from the swap.

sections.heading: Detroit Paid a Protected First to Move Ben Gordon
sections.body: On June 26, 2012, Charlotte acquired veteran scorer Ben Gordon and a future protected first-round selection from Detroit in exchange for Corey Maggette. The pick protections changed over several seasons and eventually expired when the selection conveyed in 2014 at No. 9, which Charlotte used on Indiana forward Noah Vonleh. Both teams were adjusting contracts during rebuilding years, and Detroit was willing to give up a major asset to move the Gordon obligation. Charlotte accepted a scoring guard with an expensive contract while gaining a potentially valuable draft pick. This was not a player-for-player deal with a trivial second-round sweetener. The first was central to the transaction economics and to the eventual evaluation.

sections.heading: Gordon Scored for Charlotte but Lost His Role
sections.body: Gordon played 75 Bobcats games in 2012-13, all as a reserve, averaging 11.2 points while shooting 38.7 percent from three-point range. Those were tangible offensive minutes on a struggling young roster. His role diminished severely in 2013-14, when he played 19 Charlotte games and averaged only 5.2 points, before leaving the franchise. It would be wrong to count his earlier twenty-point Chicago seasons as Charlotte playing production or pretend he justified the entire salary cost on the court. The Bobcats were chiefly compensated with future draft value, and the guard was an interim scorer. Charlotte A- was supported more by the incoming first-round asset than by the durability of the Ben Gordon stint.

sections.heading: Vonleh Was a Real Selection, Not a Nonconveyed Condition
sections.body: The acquired first finally landed at the 2014 No. 9 overall selection, which Charlotte used on Noah Vonleh. That gave the club a legitimate lottery prospect and another future tradeable player. Vonleh did not become an immediate Charlotte star and was subsequently traded, so his later NBA seasons with other organizations should not inflate the actual Bobcats or Hornets return. Detroit received Corey Maggette, a former high-volume scorer whose Pistons role was severely limited and whose NBA career was nearing its end. The Pistons D+ inherited grade reflects the combination of weak direct player production and the premium future pick surrendered to shed salary. Both clubs entered the trade with financial motives, but Charlotte emerged with an asset that was far more durable than the veteran scoring in the agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. Charlotte earns A- for Ben Gordon and a protected first-rounder that became No. 9 Noah Vonleh in 2014. Gordon played 75 games and averaged 11.2 points in 2012-13. Detroit receives D+ for Corey Maggette and the salary-management benefit, having surrendered a valuable lottery selection.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Hakim Warrick for Josh McRoberts
sections.body: On February 21, 2013, Charlotte acquired forward Josh McRoberts from Orlando in exchange for veteran Hakim Warrick. The Magic had acquired McRoberts in the previous Dwight Howard blockbuster and used him as a reserve, while the Bobcats wanted passing and more versatile frontcourt offense. Warrick had provided athletic scoring on earlier NBA teams but was no longer a dependable lead option. Both team transaction histories confirm the simple player-for-player deadline swap, with no draft selections. The NBA historical trade-deadline ledger also reports cash sent with Warrick to Orlando, a term missing from the inherited canonical asset record and requiring reconciliation. The clubs were trying to solve different bench problems, but Charlotte would get more than a temporary replacement forward. McRoberts became an important organizing piece in a starting lineup that reached the playoffs the following season.

sections.heading: McRoberts Became a Frontcourt Playmaker
sections.body: After his arrival, McRoberts offered passing and outside shooting that helped Charlotte move the ball through the power forward position. In 2013-14 he became a regular Bobcats starter, appearing in 78 games while averaging about 8.5 points, 4.8 rebounds and 4.3 assists. Charlotte earned a playoff berth with Kemba Walker and Al Jefferson leading the team, and McRoberts provided a connective offensive role rather than volume scoring. That return is directly attributable to this February 2013 swap, not to his earlier Lakers or Magic career. He subsequently signed with Miami, preventing an extended Charlotte tenure, but the season of starting playmaking was still much more valuable than an ordinary minimum-contract reserve appearance. Charlotte C+ reflects that team-specific utility.

sections.heading: Orlando Did Not Keep a Long-Term Scoring Replacement
sections.body: Warrick had appeared for Charlotte in a limited reserve role before the deal, and Orlando did not convert him into a new long-term starting forward. The Magic instead continued building around younger players, while moving a passer whose abilities became more useful in the Bobcats lineup. Orlando C recognizes the option to try a different veteran and adjust its roster without giving up a first-round asset, but the immediate basketball return was comparatively small. The inherited Even Trade winner label conflicts somewhat with Charlotte C+ against Orlando C, a numerical preference that should be acknowledged rather than silently reversed. This was a minor deadline move whose significance only grew after McRoberts established himself as a Charlotte starting playmaker. The subsequent playoff season is the strongest evidence of the player value created.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited label, though Charlotte receives C+ and Orlando C. The Bobcats acquired Josh McRoberts, who became a 2013-14 starter averaging roughly 8.5 points and 4.3 assists on a playoff team. The Magic obtained Hakim Warrick, whose subsequent NBA role was much smaller.

sections.heading: Charlotte Paid Gerald Henderson and Noah Vonleh for Batum
sections.body: On June 24, 2015, the Hornets acquired established French wing Nicolas Batum from Portland. The Trail Blazers received veteran shooting guard Gerald Henderson and young forward Noah Vonleh. Charlotte general manager Rich Cho announced the deal and identified outside shooting, passing, and the ability to defend multiple positions as reasons for targeting Batum. At age 26, Batum had already played seven NBA seasons for Portland and was experienced without being near the end of his career. The Hornets were seeking more versatile offense beside Kemba Walker and Al Jefferson after a disappointing 2014-15 campaign. Portland was shifting its roster around Damian Lillard and gaining two players at different development stages. There was no first-round draft pick in this agreement.

sections.heading: Batum Helped Restore Charlotte to the Playoffs in 2015-16
sections.body: In his first Charlotte season, Batum appeared in 70 games and averaged 14.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 5.8 assists. The scoring and assists were career highs to that point. His playmaking from the wing helped Charlotte win 48 games and reach the postseason, where the Hornets pushed Miami to seven games. The franchise official season review credits his versatile role as a major factor in that return. Batum supplied real team-specific production rather than a reputation imported from Portland, and Charlotte later kept him on a substantial new contract. His subsequent injuries and fluctuating play should be considered in a full contract analysis, but the 2015 trade itself immediately delivered a forward who could create, shoot and defend. The inherited A- Charlotte grade reflects this high level of utility.

sections.heading: Portland Received Useful Pieces but No Equal Wing Creator
sections.body: Henderson supplied veteran guard defense and shot-making during his Portland tenure, while Vonleh was a lottery-selected forward still developing his offense and rebounding. The younger prospect received more minutes in a rebuilding frontcourt but did not become the same level of wing playmaker as Batum had been for Charlotte in 2015-16. Portland C grade recognizes legitimate player value, not a completely empty return. The trade also freed the Trail Blazers to reorganize their salary and positional needs around Lillard, which had financial and roster advantages. However, neither of the incoming players matched the balanced 14.9-point, 5.8-assist inaugural Hornets Batum season. Their later contracts and other-team careers belong to different decisions and cannot be retroactively treated as Portland returns from this June exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn A- for Nicolas Batum, who averaged 14.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 5.8 assists in 70 games during a 48-win 2015-16 season. Portland receives C for Gerald Henderson and Noah Vonleh, who supplied supporting roles but not an equivalent primary playmaking wing.
