sections.heading: The Hornets Replaced Lance Stephenson with Two Veterans
sections.body: On June 15, 2015, Charlotte sent guard Lance Stephenson to the Los Angeles Clippers for center Spencer Hawes and forward Matt Barnes. General manager Rich Cho explained that Hawes could shoot and pass at center while Charlotte would evaluate the options for Barnes. Stephenson had joined Charlotte on a high-profile contract the previous summer but struggled to deliver the expected playmaking and was moving on after one disappointing season. The Clippers wanted to take a chance on a versatile guard whose Indiana seasons had shown promise. No draft pick or cash accompanied the original two-for-one trade. The agreement should be separated from the subsequent Matt Barnes trade to Memphis, which Charlotte completed only ten days later.

sections.heading: Hawes Played Regular Bench Minutes in Charlotte
sections.body: Hawes appeared in 57 Hornets games during 2015-16, starting six and averaging 6.0 points, 4.3 rebounds and 1.9 assists. His ability to stretch the floor from the center position provided a different offensive option from traditional low-post players. The Hornets reached the 2016 playoffs, and Hawes had a supporting rotation role behind the principal starters. Barnes never became a Charlotte regular-season player: the team traded him to Memphis on June 25 for Luke Ridnour, a separate transaction. Charlotte B inherited grade reflects a useful veteran bench presence and the ability to recover another asset from Barnes, while acknowledging that Hawes was not a high-volume star. His later Milwaukee minutes are unrelated to the original direct Hornets return.

sections.heading: Stephenson Did Not Rediscover His Indiana Form in Los Angeles
sections.body: Stephenson appeared in 43 Clippers games during 2015-16, with no long-term path to becoming the starting lead guard. The team moved him to Memphis in February 2016 as part of another transaction involving Jeff Green. He was a worthwhile positional gamble because of his defense and passing reputation, but the realized Clippers tenure lasted only part of one season. Their C+ inherited grade reflects a short experiment that did not yield the consistent production the front office originally sought. Charlotte obtained more immediate rotation utility from Hawes and optionality from Barnes, while Los Angeles took on a contract to test whether a former high-level Indiana role player could rebound. The deal illustrates the value and limits of exchanging two known veterans for a declining trade asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade according to the inherited label, although Charlotte grades B and the Clippers C+. Charlotte obtained Spencer Hawes, who played 57 games with six starts at 6.0 points in 2015-16, and traded Matt Barnes again. Los Angeles received Lance Stephenson for a shorter experiment.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Traded Mason Plumlee for Hollis-Jefferson and Blake
sections.body: On the night of the June 25, 2015 NBA draft, Brooklyn traded center Mason Plumlee and the rights to No. 41 Pat Connaughton to Portland. The Nets received veteran point guard Steve Blake and rights to No. 23 Rondae Hollis-Jefferson. Nets general manager Billy King confirmed all four assets in an official release. Portland needed a young athletic center as it reorganized around Damian Lillard, while Brooklyn wanted a defense-first wing prospect. The transfer was not a single straight player trade; Connaughton and Hollis-Jefferson were freshly drafted rights. The pick numbers mattered because Brooklyn gave up an established NBA center plus a later second-round prospect to obtain a mid-first-round athlete and veteran contract.

sections.heading: Plumlee Was an Immediate Starting Center in Portland
sections.body: Plumlee started all 82 Trail Blazers games during 2015-16, averaging 9.1 points, 7.7 rebounds and 2.8 assists, and helped Portland reach the Western Conference semifinals. His passing from the center position and interior defense gave the team a functional frontcourt alongside its young guards. Connaughton developed more gradually in Portland and later became a dependable perimeter role player with other NBA clubs. The direct first-year value was dominated by Plumlee, who played a full season as the starting big man. The inherited Blazers Win label therefore has a strong practical rationale even with equal C+ grades assigned to both franchises. Portland did not keep Plumlee forever, moving him later to Denver in another transaction, but the starting center return was substantial.

sections.heading: Hollis-Jefferson Became a Nets Defensive Regular
sections.body: Hollis-Jefferson remained with Brooklyn and eventually developed into a regular starting defensive forward, providing steals, rebounding and frontcourt versatility. His rookie season was interrupted by injury, making his immediate playing impact smaller than that of Plumlee in Portland. Blake was moved again to Detroit in July 2015 for Quincy Miller, so he contributed no lasting Brooklyn playing tenure. The Nets therefore obtained a young defensive prospect and a briefly held veteran trade asset, not an established starting center. Their C+ grade reflects potential and later useful defense from Hollis-Jefferson. Portland gained more immediate NBA minutes and later had Connaughton available for development. The teams placed different values on present center production and longer-term wing growth, explaining the inherited winner label.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win in the inherited verdict, though both clubs grade C+. Portland received Mason Plumlee, who started all 82 games at 9.1 points and 7.7 rebounds in 2015-16, plus Pat Connaughton rights. Brooklyn got Rondae Hollis-Jefferson rights and Steve Blake, who was subsequently traded again.

sections.heading: Charlotte Obtained Jeremy Lamb for a Veteran and a Future Second
sections.body: On June 25, 2015, the Charlotte Hornets acquired shooting guard Jeremy Lamb from the Oklahoma City Thunder. Charlotte surrendered point guard Luke Ridnour and a conditional 2016 second-round pick later associated with No. 53 Petr Cornelie. Oklahoma City had used Lamb in a supporting wing role but was reducing its roster around Russell Westbrook and Kevin Durant. The Hornets saw an opportunity to develop a 23-year-old shooter who could complement Kemba Walker and new forward Nicolas Batum. The terms were not a first-round swap: Ridnour was a veteran point guard and the other outgoing asset was a protected future second. Charlotte executed the deal immediately after a sequence of other 2015 draft-night roster moves, so it must be kept distinct from those separate agreements.

sections.heading: Lamb Became a Four-Season Charlotte Scoring Wing
sections.body: Lamb played 66 Hornets games in 2015-16, averaging 8.8 points and 3.8 rebounds while shooting 45.1 percent from the field. The club reached the playoffs that season, although his minutes declined in the second half as other guards took larger roles. He continued developing and eventually averaged 15.3 points in 2018-19, his last Charlotte season, providing a much greater direct basketball return than an expected deep reserve. His outside shooting and ability to create shots gave the team a genuine long-term wing contributor rather than a brief audition. The inherited Charlotte B+ grade is well supported by those seasons. Lamb was not an All-Star, and later production for Indiana should not be imported into his Charlotte record, but the franchise received years of tangible rotation value from a low-cost trade.

sections.heading: The Thunder Held the Draft Asset While Ridnour Moved Again
sections.body: Ridnour was a veteran ball handler acquired mostly for contract or roster purposes. The Thunder subsequently changed his status rather than installing him as a long-running backup next to Westbrook. The conditional second-round asset is associated with 2016 No. 53 Petr Cornelie, but its final conveyance path must be traced separately from actual Oklahoma City NBA playing production. The inherited Thunder C- grade reflects how little direct player value the club received compared with the four Charlotte seasons Lamb later provided. A future second was a legitimate asset, yet not equivalent to an established starting wing. Charlotte exchanged a player it had only briefly acquired and a protected draft opportunity for someone with enough development time to become an important offensive piece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited label, despite Charlotte B+ versus Oklahoma City C-. Charlotte obtained Jeremy Lamb, who gave it 66 games at 8.8 points in 2015-16 and later averaged 15.3 in 2018-19. Oklahoma City received Luke Ridnour and a conditional 2016 second linked to No. 53 Petr Cornelie.

sections.heading: Minnesota Sent Two Guards and Cash for Gary Neal and a Pick
sections.body: On February 10, 2015, the Charlotte Hornets acquired veteran point guard Mo Williams, sharpshooter Troy Daniels and cash considerations from Minnesota. The Timberwolves received guard Gary Neal and a 2019 second-round selection that Charlotte originally held through Miami. The Hornets official announcement describes an immediate need for another ball handler while Kemba Walker was recovering from injury. Minnesota was rebuilding and preferred an inexpensive veteran scorer plus a distant future draft choice. The asset later became No. 43 in 2019, associated with Jaylen Nowell. The deal involved three forms of Charlotte compensation: two players and cash, not simply a point guard rental. The clubs were pursuing different timelines, with Charlotte trying to compete during the 2015 season and Minnesota valuing later roster options.

sections.heading: Williams Immediately Became a Charlotte Starting Guard
sections.body: Williams appeared in 27 Charlotte games in 2014-15 and started 14, averaging 17.2 points and 6.0 assists in 30.8 minutes. His scoring increased from his earlier Minnesota segment, and he helped carry a large backcourt responsibility during the Walker injury period. Daniels supplied outside shooting in a smaller rotation role, though his more durable Hornets contributions came later. Williams left for Cleveland in free agency after the season, preventing a second Charlotte campaign. His later 2016 championship as a Cavaliers reserve cannot be counted as a Hornets benefit. The inherited Charlotte C+ grade reflects a productive rental with a short life, weighed against the future second-round choice surrendered. The meaningful direct result was twenty-seven games of starting-caliber playmaking rather than a multi-year franchise cornerstone.

sections.heading: The Timberwolves Could Wait for the Draft Asset
sections.body: Neal had NBA scoring experience and offered temporary guard minutes for Minnesota, but he did not become a long-running Wolves leader. The more durable transaction asset was a 2019 second-round choice, later associated with Jaylen Nowell. Even though a second-round prospect comes with uncertainty, Minnesota did obtain a real future selection rather than a pick that expired unexercised. Its inherited B grade values that longer-term optionality over the Williams rental that Charlotte received. The Wolves Win label remains plausible if later pick value is emphasized, while the immediate posttrade statistics favor Charlotte. The article does not credit Minnesota with the 17.2-point Charlotte stretch from Williams or with the complete later career of any player whose draft rights were subsequently moved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win under the inherited B for Minnesota versus C+ Charlotte evaluation. Charlotte acquired Mo Williams, who averaged 17.2 points and 6.0 assists in 27 games while Walker was injured, along with Troy Daniels and cash. Minnesota received Gary Neal and a 2019 second-round pick tied to No. 43 Jaylen Nowell.

sections.heading: Charlotte Pursued Shooting in a Four-Player Deadline Swap
sections.body: On February 20, 2014, the Bobcats acquired guards Gary Neal and Luke Ridnour from Milwaukee. The Bucks received point guard Ramon Sessions and forward Jeff Adrien. Charlotte president Rod Higgins confirmed the two-for-two package and identified outside shooting and veteran point-guard depth as the goals during a push to return to the playoffs. Neal had shot well during his San Antonio seasons, while Ridnour offered another experienced ball handler behind Kemba Walker. Milwaukee wanted Sessions to cover a larger point-guard role and Adrien to reinforce its interior defense. The deal had no future first-round pick or cash, and the teams agreed on a direct swap of NBA players rather than draft rights.

sections.heading: Neal and Ridnour Added Charlotte Reserve Depth
sections.body: Neal became an additional outside shooter for a Charlotte team that lacked many reliable three-point threats. Ridnour covered backup point guard minutes during the closing weeks of the 2013-14 regular season and postseason, with Walker retaining the primary starting responsibility. The Bobcats qualified for the playoffs for only the second time in franchise history, although they lost in the first round to Miami. The two incoming guards were supporting players rather than the driving offensive stars. Charlotte C in the inherited evaluation accounts for the limited duration and bench utility instead of assuming that Neal replicated every Spurs playoff achievement after changing teams. Their experience had a defined use, but the transaction was not equivalent to acquiring a multi-year leading scorer.

sections.heading: Sessions Made a More Substantial Return to Milwaukee
sections.body: The Bucks official retrospective reported Sessions averaging 16.2 points, 4.7 assists and 3.1 rebounds over 27 appearances after the trade, including eleven starts. That was a sizeable immediate role for a point guard acquired in a roster reshuffle. Adrien gave Milwaukee additional forward depth during the end of a difficult 2013-14 season. The Bucks still finished at the bottom of the league standings, so the deal did not cure broader problems, but Sessions offered much stronger individual scoring than a typical deep reserve. Its inherited C grade is the same as Charlotte, and the Bucks Win label therefore reflects a small playing-value preference rather than superior numerical grading. The difference lies in the immediate 27-game Sessions workload compared with bench minutes in Charlotte.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win in the inherited winner label, while both clubs receive C. Milwaukee obtained Ramon Sessions, who averaged 16.2 points and 4.7 assists in 27 late-season games, and Jeff Adrien. Charlotte acquired shooting guard Gary Neal and point guard Luke Ridnour for its 2014 playoff push.

sections.heading: The Nets Purchased Draft Rights to Juan Pablo Vaulet
sections.body: On June 25, 2015, Brooklyn acquired rights to Argentine wing Juan Pablo Vaulet from Charlotte. The Bobcats/Hornets franchise received cash and two future second-round selections, eventually linked to No. 55 Arnoldas Kulboka in 2018 and No. 46 Talen Horton-Tucker in 2019. Contemporary transaction records document the substantial draft compensation for a player Brooklyn intended to keep developing internationally. Vaulet had been chosen at No. 39 earlier that same evening, and his transfer was a draft-rights transaction, not the sale of a contracted NBA player who already had Brooklyn or Charlotte appearances. The Nets were hoping to discover an international talent while Charlotte collected two future opportunities and cash without needing to sign another prospect immediately.

sections.heading: Vaulet Never Became a Nets NBA Rotation Player
sections.body: Vaulet continued playing outside the NBA rather than establishing a Brooklyn regular-season career. His basketball achievements overseas were legitimate, but cannot be counted as Nets points, games or starts. The Nets C- inherited grade reflects the fact that acquiring his rights did not ultimately produce meaningful NBA on-court value. Brooklyn may have considered the future option worthwhile in 2015, but the cost of two second-round selections and cash was substantial relative to the realized outcome. It would be misleading to praise the move based only on his overseas performance without checking that he ever appeared in a Brooklyn uniform in the NBA. This was a classic rights-stash gamble, with a longer delay and a much smaller payoff than the franchise hoped for when the picks were sent away.

sections.heading: Charlotte Secured Two Usable Draft Assets Instead
sections.body: Charlotte obtained actual second-round choices that matured in separate drafts three and four years later. The 2018 selection was tied to No. 55 Arnoldas Kulboka, and the 2019 selection to No. 46 Talen Horton-Tucker. The eventual NBA careers and subsequent draft-night movements of those players should be assigned to the teams where the rights ultimately landed, not mechanically treated as full Charlotte playing seasons. Nevertheless, the Hornets obtained tradable assets while relinquishing an unsigned prospect who did not make a Nets NBA roster. The cash also had an immediate value, with contemporary transaction reporting listing a payment of roughly $880,000. The inherited Charlotte B+ grade rewards the combination of financial and draft options; Brooklyn C- reflects the unrealized signing potential.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B+ for two second-round picks eventually connected to No. 55 Arnoldas Kulboka in 2018 and No. 46 Talen Horton-Tucker in 2019, plus cash. Brooklyn receives C- for Juan Pablo Vaulet rights that never produced Nets NBA appearances.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Swapped a Young Forward for Marquis Teague
sections.body: The Nets acquired former Kentucky point guard Marquis Teague from Chicago on January 21, 2014, sending Georgian forward Tornike Shengelia to the Bulls. Teague had been the No. 29 pick in 2012 but had not developed into an established Chicago rotation guard. Brooklyn wanted a younger backcourt option behind veterans on a team still trying to contend after an expensive summer. Shengelia had spent portions of his Nets tenure moving between the NBA roster and the developmental league, so he offered Chicago a different kind of youth gamble. The agreement was a direct player exchange, not a deal for a draft choice or salary-only consideration. The two clubs gave each prospect a change of setting without surrendering a frontline starter.

sections.heading: Teague Played Twenty-One Brooklyn Games, Mostly off the Bench
sections.body: Teague appeared in 21 Nets games during the remainder of 2013-14. He started just once, averaged 3.0 points and 1.4 assists, and played fewer than ten minutes per appearance. Those figures capture his actual Brooklyn opportunity, distinct from the 19 games he had already played for Chicago earlier that season. A former first-round guard was given a chance to improve his decision making, but established Nets backcourt players carried the larger jobs. Brooklyn did not retain him for a multi-season starting role. Teague was subsequently moved to Philadelphia in October 2014, demonstrating that this January exchange functioned more as a development trial than a commitment to the future at point guard. The Nets inherited C grade reasonably reflects that limited direct return.

sections.heading: Shengelia Brought Potential but Not an Established Chicago Starter
sections.body: Shengelia had shown flashes of offensive skill for Brooklyn in infrequent NBA appearances and developmental assignments. Moving to the Bulls gave the forward a chance to earn minutes on a different roster, yet he did not emerge as a lasting Chicago starter. The Bulls had competitive frontcourt options and were seeking manageable young contracts while preserving their main playoff rotation. Their inherited C grade matches the Nets grade, and the Even Trade classification is appropriate for the small-scale exchange of two prospects with restricted immediate roles. Neither incoming player can be credited with earlier college achievements or NBA statistics accrued on his old team. The transaction was a change-of-scenery attempt that did not produce a clear long-term on-court winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the retained C/C grades. Brooklyn got Marquis Teague for 21 games, one start, 3.0 points and 1.4 assists after the January 2014 swap. Chicago received Tornike Shengelia, another young player who did not develop into a sustained Bulls starter. Neither side acquired a dependable franchise contributor.

sections.heading: Sacramento Took Two Veterans for Scoring Guard Marcus Thornton
sections.body: On February 19, 2014, Brooklyn obtained Marcus Thornton from Sacramento in exchange for veteran guard Jason Terry and rebounding forward Reggie Evans. Official releases by both franchises confirmed the same two-for-one agreement, with no draft choice in the package. The Nets needed another scorer from the perimeter on a team relying heavily on aging veterans, while Sacramento wanted physical rebounding and the experience of a former Sixth Man of the Year. The Kings had been using Thornton intermittently, despite his earlier 18.7-point season, and Brooklyn offered a possible reset. Neither club obtained the former Dallas version of Terry merely because his career résumé included a championship. This transaction has to be judged by the 2014 roles and what came next.

sections.heading: Thornton Averaged 12.3 Points in Twenty-Six Nets Games
sections.body: Thornton played 26 Brooklyn regular-season games after the trade, starting once and averaging 12.3 points on 38.0 percent three-point shooting. Those were useful bench scoring numbers for a veteran club that reached the second round of the Eastern Conference playoffs. His production jumped from 8.3 points in 46 Sacramento games before the agreement, demonstrating that the Nets found a better immediate offensive fit. Brooklyn received a real scorer for the closing months rather than an unused contract. However, Thornton was moved to Boston in a subsequent trade during the summer, so the Nets did not retain several seasons of direct scoring. The inherited C grade reflects a productive but short rental, not the entirety of his later career.

sections.heading: Evans Played in Sacramento While Terry Rehabilitated
sections.body: Evans delivered the rebounding and physical interior presence Sacramento had wanted from the exchange. Terry, by contrast, did not suit up for the Kings during the remainder of 2013-14 because he was rehabilitating a knee injury, a distinction confirmed in contemporary reporting. Sacramento therefore did not receive a season of Terry outside shooting just because he had a decorated Dallas past. Its direct playing return was centered on Evans, with Terry functioning more as a veteran contractual addition. The Kings inherited C+ grade narrowly exceeds Brooklyn C, which explains the original Kings Win verdict despite Thornton supplying more points per game after the trade. Rebounding and short-term salary choices are distinct kinds of value from guard scoring, and both should be visible.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win under the retained C+ Sacramento versus C Brooklyn grades. Brooklyn acquired Marcus Thornton for 26 games at 12.3 points and 38.0 percent three-point shooting. Sacramento received Reggie Evans and Jason Terry, although Terry did not play for the Kings during the remainder of 2013-14 while recovering from injury.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Paid Cash for the 2014 No. 44 Pick
sections.body: The Nets acquired rights to Oklahoma State guard Markel Brown from Minnesota for cash on June 27, 2014, the local overnight transaction following the June 26 draft. Brown had been taken 44th overall and was one of three second-round draft prospects Brooklyn acquired through separate trades during that draft period. The Timberwolves obtained immediate financial consideration rather than another active roster player. Brooklyn wanted athletic backcourt depth and defensive potential from a rookie who could compete for minutes without costing a first-round pick. The cash amount does not appear in the canonical asset description, so it should not be assigned an invented number. The agreement had no additional veteran names or protected future selections. The modern Nets team received the player rights, not Minnesota team statistics from a previous professional season.

sections.heading: Brown Made Twenty-Nine Rookie Starts for the Nets
sections.body: Brown appeared in 47 Brooklyn games in 2014-15 and started 29, averaging 4.6 points and 2.3 rebounds in 16.6 minutes. His defensive athleticism gave the Nets a useful alternative on the wing, especially as the team adjusted veteran-heavy combinations. In 2015-16 he played 62 games with six starts, averaging 5.9 points and 1.5 assists. That totals 109 Nets regular-season games and 35 starts across two years directly resulting from the rights purchase. It was not a star-making development story, but the club obtained much more NBA court time than many second-round picks provide. Brooklyn C in the inherited grading is cautious when compared with those games, yet he remained a complementary player rather than a centerpiece.

sections.heading: Minnesota Chose Cash Without a Later Draft Return
sections.body: Minnesota received cash for a second-round draft right. It did not acquire a replacement guard or another drafted player through the agreement, so there are no later Wolves minutes to compare directly with Brown. The Timberwolves were assembling a younger roster and could use the proceeds or allocation flexibility elsewhere, which was a rational use of a lower selection. Brown did not become a long-term star in Brooklyn and spent parts of his development time in the D-League, limiting how far the deal should be elevated. The inherited Wolves Win designation sits alongside identical C grades and is best understood as a mild preference for financial certainty. From a basketball minutes standpoint, Brooklyn clearly received the only active player return for this specific draft-night cash transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win in the inherited winner label with C grades for both sides. Minnesota received cash for No. 44 Markel Brown rights. Brooklyn got 109 regular-season games and 35 starts across 2014-15 and 2015-16, with Brown averaging 4.6 and 5.9 points. The Nets received the only direct playing minutes.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Acquired the No. 60 Rights Through a Multi-Step Draft Chain
sections.body: The Nets obtained the rights to Baylor forward Cory Jefferson for cash during the 2014 NBA draft period. The original No. 60 selection belonged to San Antonio, which had drafted Jefferson and then transferred his rights to Philadelphia in a separate draft-night exchange involving Nemanja Dangubić and Jordan McRae. Philadelphia subsequently sent Jefferson to Brooklyn for cash. The canonical ledger identifies Philadelphia as the direct Nets counterparty, and detailed draft trade histories confirm this route. Some shorter transaction summaries describe Brooklyn as receiving Jefferson from San Antonio, reflecting the original selection; these should not erase the intermediate rights transfer. Brooklyn was attempting to find a usable NBA forward at minimal draft cost, while Philadelphia converted an asset received moments earlier into money.

sections.heading: Jefferson Earned Fifty Brooklyn Games and One Start
sections.body: Jefferson appeared in 50 Nets games during 2014-15, making one start and averaging 3.7 points, 2.9 rebounds and 0.4 blocks in 10.6 minutes. His playing role was modest but real for the final pick of the draft. He also had assignments to the developmental league as Brooklyn tried to improve his readiness, and his NBA tenure with the Nets ended after that rookie campaign. He later appeared briefly for Phoenix, but those minutes do not count as Brooklyn playing production. The Nets C grade in the inherited trade review acknowledges a cheap developmental return without overstating his impact on the playoff rotation. Jefferson was not a 2014 starting power forward for an entire season, nor was his NBA future completely hypothetical.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Financial Consideration, Not a Nets Player
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired cash from Brooklyn instead of keeping Jefferson draft rights. The 76ers were rebuilding through draft selection accumulation and asset management, so selling a lower second-round right was a routine financial decision. It did not add a veteran player or another guaranteed future pick to Philadelphia through this particular cash transfer. The inherited 76ers C+ grade, higher than Brooklyn C, values financial certainty and a willingness to move a limited prospect. The Slight 76ers Edge verdict is therefore based on a different form of return rather than a claim that Jefferson never played in the NBA. Brooklyn did receive measurable 2014-15 reserve games, while Philadelphia immediately recovered money. Tracing the Spurs-to-76ers-to-Nets rights path is essential to avoid conflating two separate draft-night transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge with inherited C+ Philadelphia and C Brooklyn grades. Philadelphia received cash for No. 60 Cory Jefferson rights after obtaining him from San Antonio in a separate draft trade. Brooklyn acquired Jefferson for 50 games, one start and 3.7 points per appearance during 2014-15.

sections.heading: Indiana Traded Two Guards to Acquire Ian Mahinmi
sections.body: The Pacers acquired center Ian Mahinmi from Dallas during July 2012 through a sign-and-trade, sending point guard Darren Collison and veteran wing Dahntay Jones to the Mavericks. Indiana publicly confirmed the two-player return and the intention to add a larger defensive reserve behind Roy Hibbert. Dallas needed backcourt depth after losing veterans Jason Kidd and Jason Terry in free agency. This was a practical roster adjustment between teams addressing different positional holes, not a direct exchange of first-round picks. Mahinmi had been a reserve on the Mavericks 2011 championship team, while Collison had started extensively for Indiana before a roster change. The sign-and-trade structure also meant Mahinmi arrived with a new contract, creating a longer time horizon for assessing his value.

sections.heading: Mahinmi Supplied Four Indiana Seasons of Center Depth
sections.body: Mahinmi became a regular interior defender and rebounder for the Pacers, backing Hibbert during playoff runs and later taking on a larger role. Indiana reached consecutive Eastern Conference Finals in 2013 and 2014, and Mahinmi supplied frontcourt minutes without demanding high shot volume. His ability to defend bigger players and cover the paint fit a team emphasizing physical half-court defense. He stayed with the Pacers through the 2015-16 season, giving the club several years of rotation stability from a single July transaction. Indiana B in the inherited grades reflects that lasting return. His eventual Washington contract and later injuries belong to different teams and should not be projected backward onto the Pacers evaluation. This was a long-term reserve center investment rather than a one-game rental.

sections.heading: Dallas Received Immediate Backcourt Rotation Help
sections.body: Collison gave the Mavericks a younger point guard option after Kidd departed, taking significant starts and ball-handling responsibility during 2012-13. Jones provided perimeter defense and emergency wing minutes. Dallas missed the playoffs in 2013, and both guards moved on afterward, so the combination did not become the permanent replacement for its outgoing veteran backcourt. The Mavericks C+ inherited grade captures the useful but shorter tenure and the lack of a lasting roster anchor. Indiana surrendered two recognizable NBA players, not just expiring contracts, but recovered multi-season size in Mahinmi. The Pacers Win winner and higher B grade are consistent with the longer on-court center contributions compared with Dallas one-season guard experiment. The championship history of Mahinmi with Dallas before the trade is not part of his later Pacers return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win. Indiana earns B for Ian Mahinmi, who supplied center depth across four seasons and participated in its 2013 and 2014 conference-finals runs. Dallas receives C+ for Darren Collison and Dahntay Jones, who addressed backcourt needs primarily during 2012-13. The Pacers gained the longer-running contributor.

sections.heading: The Nets Needed Mehmet Okur After Brook Lopez Was Hurt
sections.body: New Jersey acquired veteran Turkish center Mehmet Okur from Utah on December 22, 2011, giving up a 2015 second-round selection and generating a trade exception for the Jazz. Utah identified the future second and the exception in its official announcement. The choice would ultimately be tied to No. 41 Pat Connaughton, although later selection chains must be treated separately from the Jazz player statistics. The Nets needed experienced center minutes because Brook Lopez was recovering from a foot injury ahead of the shortened 2011-12 season. Okur had been an All-Star during his Utah tenure and was known for three-point shooting as a big man, but he had played only thirteen Jazz games in the previous season due to injuries. New Jersey was purchasing a possible short-term answer rather than a healthy young franchise centerpiece.

sections.heading: Okur Was a Brief Nets Center Before Another Trade
sections.body: Okur supplied center minutes at the beginning of the 2011-12 season but could not reproduce the durable scoring and rebounding he had once provided in Utah. His age and health limited the opportunity, and his tenure in New Jersey lasted only until March 2012. At that point the Nets included him with Shawne Williams and a first-round choice in a completely separate trade to Portland for Gerald Wallace. The Nets therefore used the veteran both as an interim frontcourt player and subsequently as part of another asset package. It would be incorrect to attribute the later Wallace acquisition entirely to Okur, since the first-rounder was a materially important outgoing asset in that next agreement. The inherited Nets C grade reflects a limited rental and some follow-on trade flexibility, not an entire new All-Star season.

sections.heading: Utah Gained Financial Room and a Future Second
sections.body: Utah moved an experienced but injury-limited center while obtaining a 2015 draft opportunity and a trade exception. Those were distinct resources: the pick allowed future selection or another rights exchange, while the exception created flexibility under NBA trade rules. The Jazz did not receive an active Nets center in the transaction, so a later unrelated Utah signing should not be presented as direct incoming trade consideration. A second-round selection associated with Connaughton was eventual evidence that the draft asset existed, but the player right required its own subsequent transaction tracking. The equal C inherited grades and Even Trade classification capture different returns across time rather than identical box-score numbers. New Jersey received temporary center minutes, while Utah preserved optional future draft and payroll tools during a roster transition following Deron Williams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades on both sides. New Jersey acquired Mehmet Okur for temporary center depth after the Brook Lopez injury and later included him in a separate Gerald Wallace package. Utah received a 2015 second-round selection associated with No. 41 Pat Connaughton and a trade exception, rather than an incoming NBA player.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Acquired Reggie Evans Through a Second-Round Swap
sections.body: In July 2012, the newly renamed Brooklyn Nets acquired hard-rebounding forward Reggie Evans from the Los Angeles Clippers in a sign-and-trade with complicated 2016 second-round swap rights. The teams did not exchange an established starting scorer. The transaction registers ultimately identify Brooklyn as receiving Evans and a 2016 choice associated with No. 55 Marcus Paige, while the Clippers received another 2016 second connected to No. 33 Cheick Diallo. Later trades changed who held the relevant picks, and the option took several years to resolve. Contemporary Nets coverage emphasized that Evans would fill a frontcourt role at a small initial cost. Brooklyn was about to launch its first season in its new arena and needed physically reliable rebounding next to a backcourt led by Deron Williams and Joe Johnson.

sections.heading: Evans Became One of the League Rebounding Leaders for the Nets
sections.body: Evans played 80 Brooklyn regular-season games in 2012-13 and started 56, averaging 11.1 rebounds despite scoring only 4.5 points per game. His offensive scoring was limited, but his work recovering missed shots and disrupting opponents provided a clearly defined value to a playoff team. He played another 30 Nets games in 2013-14 before the February 2014 deal that moved him to Sacramento with Jason Terry. That later transaction should not be folded into the 2012 agreement; it produced a separate return. For the original Clippers swap, the direct Brooklyn value was a player who could rebound at an elite rate during the first year of the franchise in Brooklyn. The inherited Nets C+ grade acknowledges productive rebounding despite his limited scoring and short total tenure.

sections.heading: The Clippers Eventually Obtained the More Favorable Pick
sections.body: Los Angeles traded a reserve it could replace within its frontcourt rotation and received the right to exchange second-round choices later. The eventual 2016 pick chain left the Clippers side associated with No. 33 Cheick Diallo, while Brooklyn held the less favorable No. 55 Marcus Paige selection. Those draft positions show that the option could become a legitimate later asset, not merely nominal compensation. Their inherited C grade still reflects that nothing on the immediate Clippers roster matched the 80-game Evans rebounding season in Brooklyn. The later Clippers decisions involving the acquired draft choice require separate tracing rather than attributing the entire NBA career of Diallo automatically to Los Angeles. The Nets acquired near-term rebounding, and the Clippers preserved a more advantageous draft-right outcome down the road.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. Brooklyn earns C+ for Reggie Evans, who appeared in 80 games with 56 starts and 11.1 rebounds per game in 2012-13. The Clippers receive C for 2016 second-round swap rights that eventually became the more favorable No. 33 Cheick Diallo selection versus No. 55 Marcus Paige.

sections.heading: New Orleans Exchanged an International Right for Tyshawn Taylor and Cash
sections.body: On January 21, 2014, Brooklyn sent point guard Tyshawn Taylor and cash to New Orleans for the NBA rights to Bosnian forward Edin Bavčić. Taylor had been a second-round Nets selection in 2012 but was stuck behind a veteran point-guard rotation that included Deron Williams. New Orleans was examining its reserve backcourt options, while Brooklyn was creating a roster opening and taking an international rights asset that did not require an immediate NBA contract. The official Nets transaction register records both Taylor and the direction of the cash, and a contemporary NBA transactions log confirms Bavčić as the incoming right. This was not the simultaneous, separate January 21 Brooklyn move involving Marquis Teague and Tornike Shengelia. The two deals had independent players and financial consideration.

sections.heading: The Nets Did Not Obtain a Playing NBA Forward from the Rights
sections.body: Bavčić had continued his professional career in Europe for years while his NBA rights changed hands. Brooklyn did not sign him into a regular-season Nets rotation after this deal, so there were no immediate NBA games, points or rebounds from the acquired prospect to count. Rights can still have value because they may be held or exchanged in other transactions, but that value is different from the playing output of a current reserve. The inherited Nets C grade is a recognition of possible roster and financial flexibility, not evidence that Bavčić developed into a Brooklyn starting forward. The transaction made it possible to move on from Taylor without claiming that New Jersey had received an active replacement point guard. That distinction keeps the retrospective grounded in what actually happened.

sections.heading: Taylor Provided a Small New Orleans Option
sections.body: Taylor had already appeared in NBA games for Brooklyn, but those earlier minutes cannot be assigned to New Orleans after the January transfer. New Orleans acquired him as a depth option rather than as an established primary ball handler, with cash supplied as part of the exchange. His career did not develop into a sustained Pelicans starting role, and he was released soon afterward. The New Orleans B- inherited grade can be understood as valuing financial consideration and relief from a long-held overseas draft right, while Brooklyn C reflects the speculative nature of the rights. The Pelicans Win assessment does not imply Taylor became an All-Star or that Bavčić was worthless as a professional overseas. The deal mattered mainly as short-term roster management for two clubs with different backcourt and rights priorities.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win under the inherited B- New Orleans and C Brooklyn grades. New Orleans received Tyshawn Taylor and cash for Edin Bavčić rights. Brooklyn held an international NBA prospect right without obtaining regular-season playing time from Bavčić. Neither franchise gained a new established starter through this January 2014 deal.

sections.heading: Charlotte Sold Semaj Christon Draft Rights to Oklahoma City
sections.body: The Charlotte Hornets selected Xavier guard Semaj Christon with the No. 55 pick in the June 26, 2014 NBA draft and then transferred his draft rights to Oklahoma City for cash. The Thunder announced the acquisition together with the selection of their own two first-round prospects, Mitch McGary and Josh Huestis. Christon had been a productive college guard but was not expected to step immediately into a veteran NBA rotation. Oklahoma City saw a potential depth point guard it could develop outside the main roster, while Charlotte preferred cash rather than a commitment to a second-round player. This agreement was separate from the other Hornets draft-night trades involving Shabazz Napier and P.J. Hairston. The exact pick was No. 55, with no future first-round selection or established NBA starter as part of the completed exchange.

sections.heading: Christon Took Two Years to Make the NBA Roster
sections.body: Christon spent the next two seasons developing with the Oklahoma City Blue of the NBA Development League and pursuing an eventual opportunity with the parent club. In 2016-17 he played 64 Thunder games, making one start and averaging 2.9 points, 2.0 assists and 1.4 rebounds in 15.2 minutes. Those are direct Thunder NBA contributions from the draft rights acquired in 2014, even though they were not delivered in the original season. He was not a long-term replacement for Russell Westbrook, but he supplied a modest second-unit ball-handling role when the club needed depth. The inherited Thunder C grade acknowledges an eventual player return while tempering expectations for a 55th overall choice. His developmental years should be described accurately rather than assumed to be Oklahoma City NBA starter seasons.

sections.heading: Charlotte Collected Cash Without Developing the Drafted Guard
sections.body: The Hornets received cash considerations, with no existing Thunder NBA player joining Charlotte through this sale. Financial value from a late second-round selection can be sensible when a team already has a young guard rotation to evaluate, but there was no Charlotte court contribution by Christon after he was moved on draft night. The cash amount is not specified in the canonical record and cannot be invented to support a stronger verdict. Charlotte C+ is numerically higher than Oklahoma City C even though the inherited winner says Oklahoma City Thunder Win. This discrepancy should be visible to readers rather than being changed secretly in a single editorial entry. The Thunder converted the right into 64 later appearances; Charlotte obtained immediate financial consideration and no future player option.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win in the inherited verdict, despite Charlotte C+ and Oklahoma City C grades. The Thunder acquired No. 55 Semaj Christon rights for cash, eventually receiving 64 NBA appearances, one start, 2.9 points and 2.0 assists per game in 2016-17. Charlotte held the financial return only.

sections.heading: Toronto Acquired Sebastian Telfair for Haddadi and a Future Pick
sections.body: Toronto traded reserve center Hamed Haddadi and a protected future second-round selection to Phoenix for veteran point guard Sebastian Telfair on February 21, 2013. The NBA historical trade deadline ledger confirms the players and the additional second-round right. The pick protections depended on the relative positions of Sacramento and Toronto choices and ultimately resolved as a 2014 pick associated with No. 48 Lamar Patterson. Toronto wanted emergency ball-handling depth behind Kyle Lowry and other guards, while Phoenix needed frontcourt size and the value of a future draft opportunity. Haddadi had been in Toronto only briefly through another roster move before this transaction, and neither team was exchanging a current All-Star. The different conditions in the pick made it materially more complex than a simple player-for-player swap.

sections.heading: Telfair Offered the Raptors Only a Short Trial
sections.body: Telfair had been an experienced NBA point guard since being drafted as a teenager, but Toronto was his latest opportunity to find a reserve role. He appeared in a small number of games after the 2013 trade while Lowry and other guards carried most of the playmaking load. Telfair did not become a regular Raptors starter or a long-term replacement for the lead guard spot, and his time with Toronto ended after that season. The team C inherited grade recognizes some emergency roster depth from a player with professional experience, not a new franchise centerpiece. Statistics he had produced for Phoenix before the deadline belong to the Suns, not to the Raptors. Evaluating the transaction properly also requires recognizing the future selection Toronto relinquished as separate from the short scoring contribution.

sections.heading: Haddadi Supplied Phoenix Center Minutes and a Draft Asset
sections.body: Haddadi arrived as a physical reserve center capable of rebounding and contesting shots. His NBA role with Phoenix was limited in duration and did not make him an established starter, but the Suns obtained an interior player while also holding a protected second-round opportunity. That pick ultimately became the No. 48 selection in 2014, associated with Lamar Patterson, though later rights movements must be traced before crediting any subsequent NBA team performance to Phoenix. The Suns C grade equals Toronto C, explaining the inherited Even Trade classification. The player contributions were small for both organizations, but Phoenix had an additional future asset whereas Toronto concentrated on immediate backup guard availability. No winner can be established by assigning another franchise player statistics to these short stints.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under identical C grades. Toronto obtained Sebastian Telfair for backup point-guard depth. Phoenix received reserve center Hamed Haddadi and a conditional second-round selection that eventually became No. 48 Lamar Patterson in 2014. Neither incoming player produced a major long-term starting tenure after the February 2013 deadline.

sections.heading: Charlotte Moved Matt Barnes and Used Ridnour to Acquire Lamb
sections.body: On June 25, 2015, Charlotte traded forward Matt Barnes to Memphis for veteran point guard Luke Ridnour. Both players had recently changed teams: Charlotte had received Barnes from the Clippers as part of the Lance Stephenson swap earlier that month, while Memphis acquired Ridnour from Orlando the day before in exchange for Janis Timma draft rights. The Grizzlies wanted Barnes as an actual perimeter defender for the coming season. Charlotte needed a tradeable contract and immediately sent Ridnour, along with a conditional 2016 second-round selection, to Oklahoma City for 23-year-old shooting guard Jeremy Lamb in a separate agreement. The initial Barnes–Ridnour transaction is a distinct deal, but the direct sequence explains why Charlotte would acquire a guard it never planned to play.

sections.heading: Barnes Was a Useful Memphis Rotation Wing
sections.body: Barnes joined a Memphis club with established defensive personnel and a strong veteran frontcourt. In 2015-16 he appeared in regular-season games as a starting and reserve wing, shooting from the perimeter and helping space the floor around Marc Gasol and Zach Randolph. His toughness and experience fit the Grizzlies on a team that fought through injuries during the season. The Grizzlies acquired a real player rather than an unused cash-only asset, and their C inherited grade acknowledges that modest but meaningful rotation value. The trade did not guarantee a new core star or a long multiyear Barnes tenure. Memphis later changed its roster direction, so the first season was the main direct playing return. Barnes previous Clippers minutes and his future playing years for other franchises are separate from this exchange.

sections.heading: Ridnour Was an Intermediate Hornets Asset, Not a Charlotte Player
sections.body: Ridnour never appeared in a regular-season game for Charlotte after this acquisition. He was redirected to Oklahoma City on the same draft day as part of the later Lamb transaction. That means the Hornets cannot count any NBA points or assists by Ridnour as a direct playing return from Barnes. The meaningful benefit was the ability to use his contract as part of a package for a younger wing with more growth potential. Charlotte's C grade reflects this financial and transactional function, not a season of veteran point-guard stability. The Grizzlies Win verdict follows the fact that Memphis kept Barnes and obtained immediate wing minutes, while Charlotte's longer-term value required another trade and an additional second-round selection. The separate downstream deal should not be misrepresented as a straight Barnes-for-Lamb agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win under equal C grades. Memphis obtained Matt Barnes for actual wing minutes in 2015-16. Charlotte received Luke Ridnour, then immediately sent him and a separate conditional second-round pick to Oklahoma City for Jeremy Lamb. Ridnour played no Hornets regular-season games; Lamb's future production belongs to the next transaction.

sections.heading: Cleveland Took Brendan Haywood and Dwight Powell Draft Rights
sections.body: On July 12, 2014, Cleveland obtained veteran center Brendan Haywood and rookie forward Dwight Powell draft rights from Charlotte in exchange for Scotty Hopson and cash. The move followed LeBron James's announcement that he would return to the Cavaliers and was part of a wider effort to acquire veteran big-man insurance. Haywood was recovering from a foot injury that had cost him the 2013-14 season, so this was not a swap for an available All-Star starting center. Powell had been selected No. 45 in the 2014 draft after four years at Stanford and represented a potential developmental option. The Hornets official July 13 report documents the exact outgoing and incoming assets, including the direction of cash. No additional draft selection accompanied this particular exchange.

sections.heading: Haywood Had More Contract Value Than NBA Court Time in Cleveland
sections.body: Haywood appeared in a limited role for Cleveland during 2014-15, behind other frontcourt contributors, as the Cavaliers advanced to the NBA Finals. His size and experience provided insurance, but his playing totals were small and he was not the center responsible for Cleveland's postseason success. A non-guaranteed component in his later contract also provided the Cavaliers with flexibility in further roster negotiations. Powell did not become a Cleveland regular-season contributor: his rights and contract moved through additional transactions before his long NBA career took hold in Dallas. The Cavaliers B+ inherited grade consequently describes the combined reserve and asset flexibility rather than years of Powell playing time in Cleveland. It is important to keep the 2014 transaction distinct from Powell's eventual Mavericks seasons.

sections.heading: Charlotte Quickly Sent Hopson Elsewhere for More Cash
sections.body: Charlotte acquired Hopson and cash from Cleveland on July 12 and then moved the guard to New Orleans the following day for additional cash considerations. The official Hornets announcement on July 13 directly confirms that second leg of the asset chain. Hopson therefore did not become a dependable Bobcats or Hornets roster player and did not provide Charlotte regular-season starts. The franchise used his contract and the two financial transactions to adjust its resources while parting with a veteran center and a second-round forward. Its C- inherited grade reflects the limited basketball return even though the transaction had a rational economic function. Cleveland gained a big-man contract and rookie rights that could be used or moved, while Charlotte got immediate funds but did not add a rotation player from this specific swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B+ for Brendan Haywood and Dwight Powell's 2014 No. 45 draft rights, valuable primarily as reserve or later transaction assets rather than substantial Cleveland game production. Charlotte gets C- for Scotty Hopson and cash; Hopson was traded again to New Orleans the next day without becoming a Hornets rotation player.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Paid Cash for the Last Pick of the 2014 Draft
sections.body: Toronto selected San Diego State point guard Xavier Thames with the No. 59 overall selection on June 26, 2014, then sold his draft rights to Brooklyn for cash on June 27. The Raptors transaction record shows the original selection and next-day transfer, while the Nets register also includes several other cash-for-rights deals in the same draft period. Thames had been a Mountain West Conference Player of the Year and an effective college scorer, giving Brooklyn a potential developmental guard for a low draft cost. He was not being acquired from Toronto as a contracted NBA veteran, and the deal did not include a second future draft pick. The Nets hoped to reserve an opportunity to sign him while Toronto chose immediate money rather than keeping another young guard in its pipeline.

sections.heading: Thames Did Not Translate the Rights into Brooklyn NBA Minutes
sections.body: Thames later pursued professional playing time outside the Nets regular-season rotation, including overseas opportunities. He never appeared in a Brooklyn NBA regular-season game from these draft rights. That absence is important to the on-court evaluation: his strong San Diego State senior season and later non-NBA work cannot be listed as Nets points, assists or starts. The club did acquire an internationally usable prospect right and the freedom to assess him in future camps, but he did not develop into a starting point guard for Brooklyn. The inherited Nets C grade reflects the inexpensive speculative opportunity rather than delivered NBA court production. Brooklyn had already built a veteran roster, so there was never a clear path to immediate extensive minutes from the 59th pick.

sections.heading: Toronto Collected Cash and Preserved Its Guard Rotation
sections.body: The Raptors received cash considerations and no NBA player through this exchange. Their roster had Kyle Lowry and other guards occupying available playing time, so selling a late second-round choice was financially sensible. No later Toronto player can be automatically credited to this transaction, and the cash value is not specified in the inherited canonical record. Toronto used the sale to obtain a predictable small return from a selection that carried substantial development risk. Its C grade matches Brooklyn C and the Even Trade label because the difference was between a speculative right and certain money rather than an obvious exchange of established player talent. The original June 26 draft and June 27 trade dates should also remain distinct; they were linked parts of the same draft-right acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades on both sides. Brooklyn obtained Xavier Thames's No. 59 draft rights but never received NBA regular-season games from him. Toronto received cash the day after drafting Thames. This low-cost draft-rights sale yielded an option for the Nets and immediate financial compensation for the Raptors.

sections.heading: Cleveland Paid Bynum's Contract and Draft Capital for Luol Deng
sections.body: On January 6, 2014, Cleveland acquired two-time All-Star Luol Deng from Chicago for center Andrew Bynum and multiple draft considerations. The return included a protected first-round selection originally associated with Sacramento, second-round choices later linked to Sir'Dominic Pointer in 2015, Paul Zipser in 2016 and Jordan Bell in 2017, and a conditional 2015 first-round swap that was never exercised. The protected first itself did not convey as a normal first and ultimately resolved through second-round terms. Chicago was reducing payroll and obtaining draft options rather than expecting Bynum to become a Bulls starter. Cleveland wanted an established two-way wing to help a developing team reach the playoffs. Keeping the many distinct pick conditions is essential to understanding the true cost of a veteran rental.

sections.heading: Deng Supplied Forty Cavaliers Starts Without a Playoff Berth
sections.body: Deng appeared in 40 Cleveland regular-season games after the trade and started all of them, averaging 14.3 points, 5.1 rebounds and 2.5 assists. Those were substantial wing contributions, but Cleveland still missed the 2014 playoffs. Deng signed with Miami later that summer, meaning Cleveland obtained only one partial season rather than a long-term cornerstone. The Cavaliers B inherited grade can be justified by forty starts and a genuine upgrade from their weaker wing options, but it must be weighed against the multiple future rights given up. His earlier Chicago All-Star seasons and subsequent Miami career cannot be double counted as Cleveland trade value. The team later added LeBron James and changed course, decisions separate from the January Deng experiment.

sections.heading: Chicago Waived Bynum and Gained Asset Flexibility
sections.body: The Bulls waived Bynum on January 7, 2014, one day after the trade, using the transaction to avoid keeping an injured big man's full contract. Chicago did not gain any Bynum regular-season game production from this deal. The financial flexibility and draft-right package were the direct returns. The first-round protection was complex and some expected swaps or high selections never came through, so the draft haul should not be presented as multiple guaranteed lottery players. Nevertheless, actual second-round rights including those associated with Zipser and Bell eventually existed, though rights and later NBA playing teams had separate chains. Chicago's inherited C+ grade reflects a modest return relative to the All-Star wing it gave up. The Cavaliers Win verdict emphasizes Deng's immediate availability, while Chicago prioritized future roster management and cap savings.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win in the inherited B versus Chicago C+ verdict. Cleveland obtained Luol Deng for 40 starts at 14.3 points, 5.1 rebounds and 2.5 assists but missed the playoffs and lost him in free agency. Chicago waived Andrew Bynum the next day and retained protected first-round, second-round and conditional swap considerations with different future outcomes.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took Two Veterans and Multiple Second-Round Rights
sections.body: On December 11, 2014, Brooklyn traded Andrei Kirilenko and Jorge Gutierrez to Philadelphia along with a 2020 second-round choice and the 76ers right to exchange second-round picks with Brooklyn in 2018. The Nets received forward Brandon Davies and acquired a pair of trade exceptions, worth roughly $3.4 million and $916,000. Brooklyn's own official announcement confirms the multiple terms. The acquired swap later connected to No. 38 Khyri Thomas for Philadelphia and No. 55 Arnoldas Kulboka for Brooklyn, while the 2020 second ultimately became No. 47 Yam Madar. This was a cap and second-round asset trade, not simply Kirilenko for Davies. Philadelphia had room to absorb veteran salaries while rebuilding through prospects and future draft rights, and Brooklyn sought financial roster flexibility.

sections.heading: Davies Played Just Seven Nets Games
sections.body: Davies had averaged 6.3 points in 20 Philadelphia games before the transaction, but his opportunity in Brooklyn was considerably smaller. He appeared in just seven Nets regular-season games in 2014-15, with no starts and averages of 2.3 points and 1.4 rebounds. Those are the statistics that count as the direct on-court return, not his 2013-14 Philadelphia season or previous BYU career. Brooklyn's C- inherited grade reflects short-term frontcourt insurance and the created trade exceptions, offset against the draft rights it surrendered. The roster had veteran big men already filling most of the minutes, so Davies never became a reliable Nets rotation regular. Brooklyn waived him later that month, ending the experiment quickly even though the financial restructuring remained in place.

sections.heading: Kirilenko Did Not Become a Sixers Player, but the Picks Were Real
sections.body: Kirilenko did not join the 76ers playing roster in a meaningful regular-season role, and the team later waived him. Gutierrez was a reserve guard, but Philadelphia placed most of the transaction's value in the incoming future picks and favorable swap option. The 2018 second-round swap was actually usable, and the 2020 selection added another developmental asset. The 76ers B+ inherited grade reflects collecting draft opportunities and financial flexibility from a team that wanted to reduce obligations, rather than new on-court production from Kirilenko. The Nets gave up multiple future options in return for a seven-game forward and exceptions that could be used elsewhere. The best explanation of the lopsided retrospective grading is asset control across future drafts, not a claim that Philadelphia acquired an immediate All-Star through this deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B+ after receiving Andrei Kirilenko, Jorge Gutierrez, a 2020 second-round choice tied to Yam Madar and favorable 2018 second-round swap rights. Brooklyn gets C- for Brandon Davies, whose Nets tenure lasted seven games at 2.3 points, and trade exceptions. The future picks were the most durable returns.

sections.heading: The Nets Added Chris Quinn and a Future Second-Round Choice
sections.body: New Jersey acquired guard Chris Quinn and a 2012 second-round draft selection from Miami on January 5, 2010. The Nets sent a top-50-protected 2010 second-rounder that ultimately did not convey. The 2012 pick became No. 57, associated with Turkish forward İlkan Karaman. The transaction occurred while New Jersey was experiencing a difficult season and sought low-cost roster opportunities, and Miami was managing the bottom of its backcourt ahead of a consequential free-agent summer. Quinn had been a reserve behind more prominent Heat guards and was not expected to become a new leading scorer. The trade involved an actual veteran player and future draft option in one direction, against a conditional pick that ultimately expired in the other. Those asset details distinguish it from a routine cash-only exchange.

sections.heading: Quinn Supplied Short-Term Backcourt Insurance
sections.body: Quinn was an experienced perimeter player whose previous Miami seasons included reserve ballhandling and three-point shooting. In New Jersey he saw limited minutes and did not displace Devin Harris as the main point guard. His short Nets stint was a roster-insurance contribution rather than an All-Star acquisition, but he gave the club another guard with NBA game experience during a difficult rebuild. New Jersey also retained the separate future second-round option, allowing the franchise to assess an international prospect years after the trade. The Nets B inherited grade should be understood as covering the two different forms of value: immediate reserve availability and a later draft right. Quinn continued his career elsewhere after leaving New Jersey, and those later team minutes are not part of this specific return.

sections.heading: The Miami Second-Round Condition Never Produced a Player
sections.body: Miami received a second-round selection protected through the first 50 picks in the 2010 NBA draft. Under the historical transaction ledger, the condition was not met and the choice did not convey. The Heat therefore did not obtain an NBA draftee through this particular return and should not be assigned the statistics of some unrelated 2010 second-round prospect. The club could still benefit from an available roster slot or reduced salary obligation, which explains a modest financial rationale, but that is smaller than a realized draft asset. Miami C+ versus New Jersey B reflects the Nets receiving both a reserve guard and a future pick while surrendering a condition that expired. The No. 57 Karaman right later had its own international and NBA-rights history; his non-Nets professional seasons cannot be counted as New Jersey points.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns B for reserve Chris Quinn and a 2012 No. 57 second-round pick tied to İlkan Karaman. Miami gets C+ for a top-50-protected 2010 second-round choice that did not convey. The direct trade produced Nets roster depth and a future right, not a Heat draft player.

sections.heading: The Nets Purchased Tornike Shengelia Draft Rights from Philadelphia
sections.body: On June 28, 2012, Brooklyn acquired the draft rights to Georgian forward Tornike Shengelia from the Philadelphia 76ers for cash considerations. Philadelphia had selected him with a late second-round choice, and Brooklyn used money rather than another draft selection or a veteran player to secure the rights. The deal occurred just before the franchise began its first NBA season in Brooklyn. Shengelia was a promising international forward with professional experience overseas, making him a developmental investment rather than an immediate projected starting scorer. The cash amount is not specified in the canonical asset ledger and should not be invented. Nor should Philadelphia be credited with a pick it never received in this transaction. The complete exchange consisted of the draft rights and cash, with each club taking a different approach to the second round.

sections.heading: Shengelia Became a Short-Term Brooklyn Reserve
sections.body: Shengelia eventually appeared in NBA games for Brooklyn, but his opportunities were narrow behind established forwards. His role was primarily developmental and suited to deep reserve minutes rather than handling major starting responsibilities. Later in his career he found more success playing professionally overseas, but achievements in other leagues are not Brooklyn NBA games. His stay with the Nets also became part of a subsequent January 2014 transaction that sent him to Chicago in exchange for Marquis Teague. The importance of that follow-up is that Brooklyn did have an actual player right that could be traded again, even though he never developed into a franchise-leading scorer. The Nets C inherited grade reflects the small on-court and later exchange value of a prospect purchased with cash rather than a high draft selection.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Financial Flexibility Instead of a Prospect
sections.body: The 76ers received cash immediately and could apply their roster flexibility to other draft choices and acquisitions. They did not retain Shengelia rights or obtain a different player as part of the June 2012 exchange. The inherited Slight 76ers Edge wording accompanies equal C grades for Philadelphia and Brooklyn, so the winner is a financial-value judgment rather than proof that the Sixers received superior numerical grading. In hindsight, Shengelia played some Nets NBA games and was later converted into a different roster asset, while the Sixers received immediate cash without developing the international forward. Both returns were modest. The original agreement was a legitimate draft-rights purchase, not a deal that delivered an established Philadelphia scorer to Brooklyn. That distinction preserves the actual level of risk involved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge under equal C grades. Philadelphia collected cash for the 2012 draft rights to Tornike Shengelia; Brooklyn received a developmental forward who played limited NBA minutes before being exchanged for Marquis Teague in January 2014. Neither side gained a long-running franchise star from the draft-night agreement.
