sections.heading: Portland Exchanged Tyshawn Taylor Rights for Cash
sections.body: On the night of the 2012 NBA draft, Brooklyn obtained the draft rights to Kansas point guard Tyshawn Taylor from Portland for cash considerations. Portland had selected Taylor in the second round before moving his rights, and Brooklyn was building a low-cost developmental backcourt for its debut season after relocating from New Jersey. Taylor had helped Kansas reach the 2012 NCAA championship game, giving him experience in high-pressure college contests, but second-round rookies do not come with a guaranteed NBA starting role. The historical transaction ledger contains no future first-rounder or active Brooklyn veteran being sent to Portland. Cash was the sole immediate Blazers return. This was a rights purchase separate from the Nets other second-round deal for international forward Tornike Shengelia on the same draft night.

sections.heading: Taylor Reached the Nets Roster but Had Few Minutes
sections.body: Taylor joined Brooklyn and appeared in regular-season NBA games, generally in reserve assignments behind experienced point guards Deron Williams and C.J. Watson. His value was as emergency ballhandling and a young player the team could evaluate in limited minutes. He did not develop into a regular Nets starting point guard or high-volume scorer. The franchise later moved him in a separate transaction, further limiting the original period of direct playing benefit. The Nets C inherited grade accounts for having acquired an actual rostered NBA guard rather than an unsigned draft right. Yet it also recognizes that his on-court role remained small and did not justify describing the transaction as a major backcourt upgrade. His college performances are useful background, not Brooklyn NBA statistics to be added to the return.

sections.heading: The Blazers Converted a Late Draft Selection into Money
sections.body: Portland chose financial compensation for the second-round rights instead of attempting to develop Taylor on a roster with other guard prospects. That was a normal late draft strategy, especially if the franchise valued roster space for higher-priority young players. The cash sum is not specified in the inherited asset record, so assigning an exact amount would be speculative. The Blazers received no NBA player through the agreement, while the Nets obtained one whose direct NBA contributions were limited. Both sides receive C under the canonical Even Trade evaluation, a defensible result for a minor draft-right sale. The distinction between realized NBA minutes and cash-only flexibility remains important, even though neither asset turned into an established All-Star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for both Brooklyn and Portland. The Nets paid cash for Tyshawn Taylor draft rights and used him as a reserve guard during the early Brooklyn seasons. Portland obtained immediate financial compensation but no incoming player. Neither return turned into a long-term starting NBA contributor.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Steve Blake as a Veteran Reserve Guard
sections.body: On July 13, 2015, Detroit acquired point guard Steve Blake from Brooklyn. The Nets received young forward Quincy Miller. The deal was a small but identifiable roster decision for teams at different points in their development. Detroit had recently added Reggie Jackson and wanted experienced guard insurance behind its starters, while Brooklyn was examining inexpensive younger wing and forward options. Blake had already played for multiple NBA franchises and had been acquired by Brooklyn on the June 2015 draft night in the Mason Plumlee agreement with Portland. This July swap was the next separate step in that contract path, not a part of the earlier four-player draft-rights trade. The transaction register contains only Blake and Miller, with no draft pick or cash amount to assign to either side.

sections.heading: Blake Filled Detroit Backup Point Guard Minutes
sections.body: Blake spent the 2015-16 season as one of the Detroit guard reserves, giving the franchise a veteran capable of directing possessions when Jackson was off the floor. His scoring role was small, but he could bring the ball up, make an entry pass and provide outside shooting. The Pistons finished the season with a playoff berth, and the main rotation depended on the starting backcourt and Andre Drummond for much of its offense. Blake did not become a starring guard or a long-term franchise building block. Detroit received a practical one-year veteran option for a developmental forward who had not established a dependable starting place in the NBA. Its inherited C grade captures modest but real playing value without assigning prior Los Angeles or Portland seasons to the Pistons return.

sections.heading: Miller Did Not Develop into a Brooklyn Starting Forward
sections.body: Quincy Miller brought youth and a chance to evaluate a different forward skill set, but he did not become a long-running Nets rotation starter. Brooklyn had obtained Blake from Portland only weeks earlier and was willing to redirect the veteran toward a younger player instead of filling another backup point guard spot. The former Denver prospect had already seen his NBA opportunities shrink before the exchange, making him a speculative reclamation option rather than a guaranteed scorer. Brooklyn C equals Detroit C in the inherited assessment, and the Even Trade label is consistent with two teams swapping end-of-rotation options. It would be inappropriate to credit Brooklyn with the Detroit guard minutes Blake played or Detroit with Miller later overseas performances. Neither club received a first-round choice or premium All-Star in this isolated agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for both teams. Detroit acquired Steve Blake and used him for backup point guard minutes during its 2015-16 playoff season. Brooklyn received young forward Quincy Miller, who did not become an established Nets starter. The agreement moved two lower-rotation pieces without draft compensation.

sections.heading: Detroit Swapped Tony Mitchell for Veteran Shooter Anthony Tolliver
sections.body: On December 24, 2014, Detroit acquired veteran power forward Anthony Tolliver from Phoenix in exchange for second-year forward Tony Mitchell. The Pistons were trying to find perimeter shooting and a better frontcourt fit during a difficult season, while Phoenix was adjusting its bench and exploring younger options. Tolliver had experience stretching the floor and defending across two forward positions; Mitchell was a former second-round draft selection who had struggled to earn regular playing time in Detroit. The dated transaction records for both teams confirm a direct player-for-player swap, without cash, future draft picks or other included veterans. Unlike a draft-night rights deal, both outgoing assets had NBA contracts and the teams had direct roster decisions to make. The Christmas Eve timing brought quick changes during the active season.

sections.heading: Tolliver Became a Useful Detroit Frontcourt Reserve
sections.body: Tolliver joined Detroit and provided outside shooting, defensive effort and rotation minutes at power forward for the rest of 2014-15. He appeared in more than fifty Pistons games after the trade and gave the club a perimeter threat from a position otherwise dominated by interior scorers. Tolliver returned for the following season, contributing to a Detroit team that reached the 2016 playoffs. This made his time with the Pistons more than a short emergency stint. He was not the main offensive star, but a veteran stretch four who helped balance lineups around Andre Drummond and other scorers. Detroit C in the inherited evaluation may understate that practical fit, although the canonical Even Trade label must be preserved pending a sourced regrading. His later years with other teams are not part of the Detroit return.

sections.heading: Phoenix Did Not Develop Mitchell into a Starting Forward
sections.body: Mitchell had athletic upside and was a sensible low-cost experiment for a Suns team that already had an established group of perimeter scorers and forwards. But he did not become a regular starting Phoenix power forward or a high-minute contributor after the transaction. The club later moved on, limiting its direct basketball return. Phoenix C in the inherited evaluation recognizes taking on a young prospect without sacrificing a core star, but the actual posttrade player contribution was modest relative to the steady veteran role Tolliver established in Detroit. The absence of a future pick also matters: Phoenix cannot be credited with a drafted star from an agreement that brought back one developmental forward. This was a direct depth exchange with a more visible veteran benefit on the Detroit side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited C/C scores. Detroit acquired Anthony Tolliver, who offered more than fifty games of stretch-forward rotation utility in 2014-15 and stayed through the 2016 playoffs. Phoenix received Tony Mitchell, whose direct Suns NBA role was much smaller. The immediate value favored Detroit despite equal historical grading.

sections.heading: Charlotte Swapped Matt Carroll for Forward Hakim Warrick
sections.body: On November 13, 2012, Charlotte acquired power forward Hakim Warrick from New Orleans in exchange for veteran shooter Matt Carroll. The Bobcats were beginning a rebuilding year after drafting Michael Kidd-Gilchrist, while the New Orleans franchise was trying to rebalance its guards and wings around a young Anthony Davis. Warrick had been a highly athletic forward since his Syracuse college career, but his role in New Orleans had become limited. Carroll had returned to Charlotte in an earlier Dallas trade and could shoot from distance, yet was no longer a high-minute starter. Both franchise transaction records confirm a straight one-player-for-one-player agreement with no draft selections or cash. This move was a reserve-depth exchange, not the arrival of an established All-Star for either rebuilding team.

sections.heading: Warrick Supplied Charlotte Frontcourt Depth for Part of a Season
sections.body: Warrick played regular-season games in Charlotte and gave the club a different athletic finisher at forward. His playing time and scoring were modest compared with more prominent Bobcats frontcourt players, and the team did not make him a multi-season building block. At the February 2013 deadline, Charlotte moved Warrick to Orlando in a separate trade for Josh McRoberts, with NBA historical records also identifying cash as part of that later Charlotte package. Thus Warrick was a transitional asset that eventually led to a more versatile passing forward for Charlotte. The original Warrick trade cannot be credited with every later McRoberts assist or playoff achievement, however, because another team and a second agreement intervened. The Bobcats C inherited grade captures direct reserve minutes and some later exchange value, not a new cornerstone on the court.

sections.heading: New Orleans Received Carroll but Did Not Secure a Long-Term Starter
sections.body: Carroll was a veteran guard whose outside shooting had once been a larger part of the Charlotte offense. He provided New Orleans a chance to add an experienced perimeter option without giving up a draft pick, but did not establish himself as a long-term starting scorer there. His previous high-volume Bobcats minutes belonged to another part of his career and should not be counted as a New Orleans return. The inherited Pelicans Win headline appears alongside equal C grades, suggesting a narrow preference for the positional or financial fit rather than a measurable grade advantage. Charlotte held Warrick briefly and then converted him in another move, while New Orleans made its own contract and depth adjustment. A neutral assessment recognizes modest returns to both clubs from a deliberately small transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win under the inherited headline, with Charlotte and New Orleans both graded C. Charlotte received Hakim Warrick, used him briefly and later traded him to Orlando for Josh McRoberts. New Orleans obtained Matt Carroll for reserve shooting and roster flexibility. Neither club received a future draft pick in this 2012 exchange.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Rights to Ricky Ledo for a Future Second
sections.body: At the 2013 NBA draft, Dallas obtained the rights to Providence shooting guard Ricky Ledo from Philadelphia. The 76ers received a 2014 second-round pick, later tied to No. 47 Russ Smith. Ledo was a first-year professional prospect with an unusual college résumé: he had practiced at Providence but did not play official games there because of NCAA eligibility restrictions. Dallas wanted a low-cost swing at a wing scorer without using another premium selection, while Philadelphia preferred a later draft opportunity. The trade involved draft rights rather than existing NBA player contracts; neither Ledo nor Smith had previously played a Dallas or Philadelphia NBA game. Both team transaction histories connect the 2013 rights move to the 2014 pick identity, although later rights transfers should be tracked separately.

sections.heading: Ledo Had a Limited Mavericks NBA Role
sections.body: Ledo eventually reached the Dallas roster but received few minutes behind a veteran backcourt led by Monta Ellis and other established guards. He appeared in a small number of NBA games over two seasons, splitting his development between the main roster and assignments intended to provide more playing time. His outside shooting potential did not translate into a regular Mavericks starting position, and the club eventually moved on. The Dallas B- inherited grade seems relatively favorable for a prospect with modest direct NBA output. It may reflect the original chance to control a talented young guard selected late in the draft, which carried more potential at the time than the eventual results showed. Ledo later played elsewhere, but his subsequent work cannot be counted as productive Dallas years.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received a Draft Selection for the Next Year
sections.body: Philadelphia obtained a genuine 2014 second-round selection, eventually recorded as No. 47 Russ Smith. The pick represented a future developmental right, not a starter immediately joining the 76ers in the summer of 2013. Smith was selected by Philadelphia and subsequently moved in another draft-night rights transaction, meaning all of his later NBA appearances cannot be credited to the original receiving team. Philadelphia B- equals Dallas B- in the inherited grades, while the verdict gives the Mavericks a slight edge. That is a small prospective preference rather than evidence of a large long-term advantage. Dallas gained rights to Ledo at a modest price, and Philadelphia kept another late draft opportunity. The actual on-court returns were limited for both original teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge in the inherited label, with B- assigned to both Dallas and Philadelphia. The Mavericks acquired 2013 draft rights to Ricky Ledo and received limited reserve minutes. Philadelphia obtained a 2014 No. 47 second-rounder tied to Russ Smith, whose subsequent rights movements must be separated from Philadelphia NBA production.

sections.heading: Minnesota Exchanged Three Assets for Point Guard Tyus Jones
sections.body: On June 25, 2015, Minnesota obtained the draft rights to Duke guard Tyus Jones from Cleveland. In return, the Cavaliers received rights to international forward Cedi Osman, forward Rakeem Christmas and a 2019 second-round draft selection eventually associated with No. 40 Justin James. Jones had just helped Duke win the NCAA national championship, establishing a reputation as an effective tournament floor general. Cleveland was coming off its first Finals appearance of the LeBron James return era and could wait for international development or shift draft assets later. Minnesota wanted a young point guard who could develop alongside its rebuilding group, including Karl-Anthony Towns and Andrew Wiggins. The exchange did not include a current All-Star player on either side. It was a draft-rights trade with both immediate and delayed developmental paths.

sections.heading: Jones Provided Minnesota Several Seasons of Guard Depth
sections.body: Jones joined Minnesota as a young ball handler who could organize an offense behind the established guard rotation. His scoring was modest in his first seasons, but he was dependable in distributing the ball and protecting possessions. He became a useful reserve during the 2017-18 Timberwolves playoff season, gaining NBA experience in meaningful games without being counted as a full-time star starter. His subsequent career in Memphis and elsewhere should not be attributed to Minnesota, but the original franchise still received multiple NBA seasons from him before his departure. The inherited Slight Wolves Edge verdict reflects the appeal of obtaining an actual NBA point guard without waiting for a second-round player to mature overseas. The player fit was concrete even if the raw scoring did not dominate the offense.

sections.heading: Osman Eventually Developed into a Cavaliers Starter
sections.body: Cleveland did not end up with only an unsigned international option. Osman made his NBA debut in 2017-18 and became a regular wing for the Cavaliers, including a larger scoring role after James left for Los Angeles. He contributed multiple seasons of NBA games and started regularly on the rebuilding Cleveland roster. Christmas supplied an additional prospect opportunity, and the later second-round selection added another asset to the return. The 2019 No. 40 Justin James right must be assessed through the later pick chain rather than assigning every future game to Cleveland without checking ownership. Cleveland B is equal to Minnesota B in the inherited grades, even though the headline leans toward the Wolves. Both clubs obtained meaningful basketball assets whose impact emerged on different schedules, making an overwhelming winner claim unwarranted.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge under the inherited winner despite equal B grades. Minnesota obtained Tyus Jones and several seasons of dependable point guard depth. Cleveland acquired Cedi Osman, later a Cavaliers starting wing, Rakeem Christmas rights and a future second tied to No. 40 Justin James in 2019. Both teams received real developmental value.

sections.heading: Washington Obtained Marcin Gortat in a Multi-Player Center Trade
sections.body: On October 25, 2013, Washington acquired center Marcin Gortat, Kendall Marshall, Shannon Brown and Malcolm Lee from Phoenix. The Suns received injured veteran center Emeka Okafor and a protected future first-round pick. The protection allowed it to convey in 2014 at No. 18, subsequently used on Syracuse point guard Tyler Ennis. Both franchise histories detail the agreement shortly before the regular season began. Washington was building around young guard John Wall and shooting guard Bradley Beal, and needed a dependable starting center to provide screens, rebounding and interior defense. Phoenix accepted the draft capital and the risk of carrying an injured player. This was not simply Gortat-for-Okafor, because three additional outgoing Suns contracts and a consequential first-round selection were involved.

sections.heading: Gortat Became a Five-Season Wizards Frontcourt Starter
sections.body: Gortat immediately became a regular starter in Washington, averaging 13.2 points and 9.5 rebounds in 2013-14 and helping the Wizards return to the playoffs in 2014. He played many games alongside Wall and Beal across five seasons, providing physical screens and rebounding that supported the perimeter offense. His return was direct, sustained and visible on a Washington team that advanced to the Eastern Conference semifinals in both 2014 and 2015. Marshall, Brown and Lee did not each have similarly large Wizards roles, but they were real components of the original package. Washington C+ is conservative when measured against the multiple seasons of starting center production. A later full regrade should compare that playing value with the first-round asset surrendered rather than treating all four incoming players as interchangeable reserves.

sections.heading: Phoenix Converted an Injured Contract into a First-Round Prospect
sections.body: Okafor had a serious neck injury and did not play a regular-season Suns game after the trade. Phoenix was primarily acquiring an expiring contract and a future first-round selection rather than a healthy veteran center to start immediately. The pick conveyed at No. 18 in 2014, and the Suns selected Tyler Ennis, who became another draft or trade asset as the team changed its guard rotation. Its B inherited grade values the pick and financial optionality, while the canonical Slight Wizards Edge headline favors Washington even though the recorded Wizards grade is only C+. That mismatch should remain visible for eventual grading review. The Suns did acquire a real first-rounder, but the Wizards obtained years of on-court Gortat production. Neither team should be credited with unrelated careers of players moved in subsequent transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wizards Edge under the inherited headline, despite Phoenix B exceeding Washington C+ numerically. Washington obtained Marcin Gortat, a five-season starting center, plus Kendall Marshall, Shannon Brown and Malcolm Lee. Phoenix acquired injured Emeka Okafor and a protected first that conveyed as 2014 No. 18 Tyler Ennis.

sections.heading: Washington Acquired Glen Rice Jr. Draft Rights from Philadelphia
sections.body: On June 27, 2013, Washington obtained the draft rights to Glen Rice Jr. from Philadelphia. The 76ers received rights to guard Nate Wolters and forward Arsalan Kazemi. This was a three-prospect draft-night exchange with no current NBA veteran or cash in the canonical asset ledger. Rice had gained experience in the NBA Development League after leaving Georgia Tech, showing enough scoring ability to attract interest as a second-round choice. Washington wanted another perimeter development option behind John Wall and Bradley Beal, while Philadelphia preferred two separate young players whose potential could be evaluated in different positions. None of the three had already compiled Wizards or Sixers regular-season NBA games before this agreement. Draft rights rather than veteran contracts were the economic assets.

sections.heading: Rice Jr. Had a Short NBA Opportunity in Washington
sections.body: Rice reached the Wizards roster but made only a limited number of NBA appearances, primarily in reserve situations when the team needed guard or wing depth. He was not a core starter during the Washington playoff runs in the middle of the decade. His longer professional path involved other leagues, which should not be counted as Washington NBA production simply because the original franchise selected his rights. The Wizards C inherited grade recognizes taking a reasonable draft risk without investing a first-round selection. Rice could score in development competition but did not establish a lasting role alongside the more prominent Washington perimeter players. The franchise did get a prospect who suited up in its uniform, distinguishing the return from a draft right that never produced an NBA appearance at all.

sections.heading: The Philadelphia Rights Package Followed Two Development Paths
sections.body: Wolters played NBA games after the 2013 draft, but his principal early-season action came with Milwaukee, not Philadelphia. Kazemi, an experienced college rebounder, also followed an international or developmental route without establishing a long 76ers NBA starting career. The two rights gave Philadelphia optionality to retain or move prospects as its roster rebuilding process changed direction, but their later team affiliation determines what on-court value can be credited directly. Philadelphia C matches Washington C, which supports the inherited Even Trade decision for a low-leverage second-round exchange. It would be misleading to treat the later NBA careers of all three young players as if they occurred with their original receiving clubs. The agreement itself was a swap of potential rather than immediate playoff depth.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for Washington and Philadelphia. The Wizards obtained draft rights to Glen Rice Jr., who logged limited reserve NBA minutes. Philadelphia acquired Nate Wolters and Arsalan Kazemi rights, with their later development split across other teams and leagues. No veterans or first-round selections were exchanged directly.

sections.heading: The Knicks Obtained Derrick Rose and Justin Holiday in a Five-Player Deal
sections.body: New York acquired former NBA MVP Derrick Rose and guard Justin Holiday from Chicago on June 22, 2016, along with a 2017 second-round selection. The Bulls received center Robin Lopez, young guard Jerian Grant and veteran point guard José Calderón. The pick was eventually used at No. 44 on Damyean Dotson in 2017. Rose had been the face of Chicago since the 2008 draft, but multiple knee injuries had complicated his tenure and the club was moving toward a different backcourt arrangement. New York wanted another scoring guard alongside Carmelo Anthony and Kristaps Porziņģis. Chicago emphasized interior depth, youth and financial flexibility while losing a recognizable franchise figure. This was not a straight swap of Rose for Lopez; Holiday, Grant, Calderón and the future second were all part of the actual agreement.

sections.heading: Rose Scored Eighteen Per Game but New York Missed the Playoffs
sections.body: Rose started all 64 Knicks games he played in 2016-17 and averaged 18.0 points with 4.4 assists. That was a substantial individual scoring contribution from a player whose prime Chicago seasons were interrupted by injury. It did not turn New York into a playoff team, and his first Knicks stint ended when he signed with Cleveland in the following offseason. Holiday appeared as a guard and wing reserve while New York assessed its perimeter options. The second-round pick produced a separate opportunity in Dotson, who later appeared in NBA games for the Knicks. The inherited B Knicks grade reflects an actual season of Rose starting and a draft option, not an immediate return to his 2011 MVP standard. Neither Rose later career revival nor his second Knicks stint belongs automatically to this single 2016 agreement.

sections.heading: Lopez Became Chicago Starting Center Across Multiple Seasons
sections.body: Lopez was the clearest immediate Bulls return. He started 81 games in 2016-17, averaging 10.4 points and 6.4 rebounds while giving a club led by Jimmy Butler and Dwyane Wade interior size and screens. He stayed in Chicago beyond that season and served as an experienced center during a further rebuild. Grant provided reserve guard minutes and developmental flexibility, while Calderón was moved again rather than occupying a lasting Bulls starting role. Chicago C is lower than New York B in the inherited grades, but its practical player return was not an empty roster slot. Lopez provided multiple seasons of dependable center play, an important distinction when comparing Rose short New York scoring stint with the long-term costs of the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win according to the inherited B New York versus C Chicago grades. New York received Derrick Rose, Justin Holiday and a 2017 second-rounder used on Damyean Dotson; Rose averaged 18.0 points and 4.4 assists over 64 starts. Chicago got Robin Lopez, Jerian Grant and José Calderón, with Lopez becoming its regular starting center.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Took a Draft-Night Bet on Caris LeVert
sections.body: On July 7, 2016, Brooklyn acquired the rights to Michigan guard Caris LeVert and a protected future second-round draft choice from Indiana in exchange for forward Thaddeus Young. Indiana had selected LeVert at No. 20 in the first round but moved his rights in an agreement finalized after the draft. LeVert had shown playmaking and shooting potential in college despite a history of foot injuries. The Nets were early in a major rebuild and could give a promising rookie development time, while Indiana wanted a proven athletic forward ready to contribute alongside Paul George and Myles Turner. The future second was later associated with the 2021 No. 44 selection used on Kessler Edwards, an asset whose subsequent ownership path should be distinguished from LeVert immediate signing. This was not a simple player-for-player veteran swap.

sections.heading: LeVert Developed Into a Primary Brooklyn Scoring Guard
sections.body: LeVert joined the Nets in 2016-17 and gradually expanded from a developing reserve into a starter who could create offense off the dribble. During 2019-20 he averaged 18.7 points and 4.4 assists in 45 games for Brooklyn, demonstrating the upside that made the original draft-night gamble attractive. He was a significant contributor to the franchise rebuilding process before joining the multi-team January 2021 James Harden transaction. Those Brooklyn playing seasons are directly traceable to the LeVert rights obtained from Indiana. His later production for the Pacers or Cavaliers belongs to different franchises and should not be added to the initial Nets return. Brooklyn B+ recognizes several seasons of useful guard offense from a player whose draft stock had been clouded by health uncertainty.

sections.heading: Young Gave Indiana Several Seasons of Dependable Frontcourt Play
sections.body: Young was a veteran who could defend both forward spots, rebound and finish near the rim. He became a steady Indiana starter over three seasons from 2016-17 through 2018-19 and helped the team adapt after the eventual Paul George departure. The Pacers did not receive an unproductive expiring contract: Young supplied real team-specific NBA minutes while LeVert developed elsewhere. Its inherited C grade appears cautious against that sustained veteran role. The canonical Even Trade label also does not align with Brooklyn B+ exceeding Indiana C, suggesting the original grading and headline deserve a future source-led reconciliation. Both teams had legitimate reasons for the deal and both received substantial direct basketball value along different timelines.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade is the inherited winner label despite Brooklyn B+ versus Indiana C grades. Brooklyn obtained Caris LeVert rights and a protected future second, and LeVert later averaged 18.7 points in 2019-20. Indiana received Thaddeus Young, a dependable three-season starting forward. The retained grades and winner require separate reconciliation.

sections.heading: The Wizards Acquired Bojan Bogdanović for a Protected First
sections.body: On February 22, 2017, Washington acquired wing scorer Bojan Bogdanović and forward Chris McCullough from Brooklyn. The Nets received forward Andrew Nicholson, guard Marcus Thornton and a protected future first-round pick that conveyed at No. 22 in the 2017 draft. Brooklyn ultimately selected center Jarrett Allen with that choice. Washington was seeking another scorer for its playoff push beside John Wall, Bradley Beal and Otto Porter Jr., while the Nets prioritized a premium future selection during a rebuild. Nicholson and Thornton were salaries and roster options rather than the principal long-term basketball return. The deal was more than Bogdanović for Allen directly, because Allen had not yet been drafted and the first had conditions attached. The agreement exchanged immediate wing offense for draft capital and veteran contracts.

sections.heading: Bogdanović Helped the Wizards Reach the Second Round
sections.body: Bogdanović averaged 12.7 points in 26 regular-season appearances with Washington following the trade. He supplied outside shooting and bench offense as the Wizards advanced to the Eastern Conference semifinals, where Boston beat them in seven games. He then signed with Indiana in free agency, so Washington did not receive multiple seasons of his production. McCullough was a younger forward available for development, though he did not become a long-term Washington starter. The Wizards C inherited grade acknowledges a useful playoff rental while discounting the first-round selection surrendered. Bogdanović later scored many points for Indiana, Utah and Detroit, but those performances cannot be counted as Washington franchise benefit from the February agreement. The direct return was a timely addition to an established Eastern contender.

sections.heading: Jarrett Allen Became the Rebuilding Asset for Brooklyn
sections.body: The Nets used the conveyed No. 22 draft choice on Texas center Jarrett Allen. He appeared in 72 games as a rookie in 2017-18, averaging 8.2 points and 5.4 rebounds, and developed into a much more substantial starting center over subsequent Brooklyn seasons. His defense, rebounding and rim finishing provided value beyond what is usually expected from a selection late in the first round. Brooklyn later moved him to Cleveland in the January 2021 James Harden package, another transaction that must be evaluated separately. Nicholson and Thornton did not represent an equivalent long-term core on their own; the pick was the decisive part of Brooklyn return. The Nets B+ inherited grade reflects converting a veteran scoring rental into a strong young center with tangible NBA production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn receives B+ for Andrew Nicholson, Marcus Thornton and a protected 2017 first-rounder that became No. 22 Jarrett Allen, a multi-season starting center. Washington gets C for Bojan Bogdanović, who averaged 12.7 points in 26 games during its 2017 playoff run, and Chris McCullough. The pick created the longer-term return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Marco Belinelli for Malachi Richardson Draft Rights
sections.body: On July 7, 2016, Charlotte acquired experienced Italian shooting guard Marco Belinelli from Sacramento in exchange for draft rights to Syracuse wing Malachi Richardson. Sacramento had selected Richardson at No. 22 in the 2016 first round. The Hornets had narrowly lost a seven-game playoff series to Miami earlier that year and wanted additional perimeter scoring. Belinelli had previously played on San Antonio 2014 championship team and brought a reputation for moving without the ball and making outside shots. The Kings preferred a younger draft option in Richardson, who would take time to develop behind other guards. There was no additional first-round pick or veteran player coming to Charlotte, and no cash consideration in the inherited asset record. This agreement converted a fresh rookie right into a proven rotation shooter.

sections.heading: Belinelli Gave Charlotte a Full Season of Bench Scoring
sections.body: Belinelli appeared in 74 games for the Hornets during 2016-17, averaging 10.5 points and contributing dependable outside shooting. He was not a permanent replacement for a starting star, but his ability to space the floor helped Charlotte rotate guards around Kemba Walker. His prior Spurs playoff success explained why the club sought him, but the specific 74-game Hornets season is the actual direct return from this trade. Charlotte did not return to the 2017 playoffs, and Belinelli moved to Atlanta in another transaction during the following summer. The Hornets B inherited grade reflects one substantial season of reliable bench offense rather than multiple years of new starter production. He was a low-risk veteran whose immediate playing value became more visible as the rookie Richardson struggled to establish an NBA role.

sections.heading: Richardson Did Not Become an Established Sacramento Starter
sections.body: Richardson had a promising NCAA tournament reputation after Syracuse reached the Final Four, giving Sacramento a legitimate young upside bet. But he made only limited NBA appearances for the Kings over his initial seasons, and the franchise traded him to Toronto in February 2018. His shooting and athleticism never turned him into Sacramento leading wing scorer. The Kings C+ inherited grade recognizes the financial and development appeal of a rookie contract, but the direct team-specific production fell short of Belinelli 74-game Charlotte contribution. Richardson later roster attempts elsewhere should not be credited as Kings minutes. Both teams pursued understandable goals, yet Charlotte enjoyed the clearer immediate basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets receive B for Marco Belinelli, who appeared in 74 games and averaged 10.5 points during 2016-17. Sacramento earns C+ after acquiring No. 22 Malachi Richardson draft rights; he did not develop into a long-term Kings starting guard. Charlotte got the proven single-season scoring return.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned a Lottery Point Guard Into Lopez and Kuzma
sections.body: On June 22, 2017, Brooklyn acquired D’Angelo Russell and center Timofey Mozgov from the Lakers for veteran Brook Lopez and the draft rights to No. 27 Kyle Kuzma. The Nets official release lists the exact four assets, while reporting from two days earlier makes clear the agreement was reached before the draft could be completed. Los Angeles wanted to move Mozgov’s sizable remaining contract while seeking a fresh roster direction before drafting Lonzo Ball. Brooklyn valued Russell’s potential as a former second overall pick who could become a primary creator. The franchise also had to take on Mozgov’s salary, which was a substantial cost rather than a minor throw-in. The outgoing Brooklyn first-round choice became a real basketball player in Los Angeles that season.

sections.heading: Russell Reached the All-Star Game as a Net
sections.body: Russell averaged 15.5 points and 5.2 assists in his first Brooklyn season, though injuries held him to 48 appearances. In 2018-19 he became an All-Star, starting 81 games and averaging 21.1 points and 7.0 assists on a Nets team that reached the playoffs. That was the clearest return for Brooklyn, making this much more than a salary-absorption maneuver. Mozgov played only a portion of one Nets season and did not become an extended starter, demonstrating that the incoming value was concentrated in Russell. Brooklyn later sent Russell to Golden State in a different transaction, so his subsequent production elsewhere should not be assigned to this trade. The inherited Brooklyn B grade captures an actual All-Star season but accounts for the salary obligation and eventual limits of the pairing.

sections.heading: Kuzma Made an Immediate Impact Before Lopez Left Los Angeles
sections.body: Kuzma played 77 games as a rookie with the Lakers, averaged 16.1 points and 6.3 rebounds, and continued developing into a key scoring forward over subsequent seasons. Lopez started 72 of his 74 Los Angeles appearances in 2017-18, scoring 13.0 points per game while adding rim protection. He left in free agency after that season, but both incoming players supplied meaningful direct on-court value. The inherited Slight Lakers Edge verdict coexists with grades of Brooklyn B and Los Angeles C+, a numerical contradiction worth flagging for later canonical review. The Lakers did clear Mozgov’s contract and obtain two useful players, though the Nets found an All-Star in Russell. Each team can demonstrate an identifiable return without pretending the grade conflict is resolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge is the inherited verdict, despite Brooklyn B and Lakers C+. Los Angeles received Brook Lopez and No. 27 Kyle Kuzma; Kuzma averaged 16.1 points as a rookie. Brooklyn acquired D’Angelo Russell, who made the 2019 All-Star team at 21.1 points and 7.0 assists, while also absorbing Timofey Mozgov’s contract.

sections.heading: Toronto Attached Two Draft Picks to Move DeMarre Carroll
sections.body: On July 13, 2017, Toronto sent veteran forward DeMarre Carroll, a future first-round draft choice and a future second-round selection to Brooklyn for center Justin Hamilton. The Raptors official announcement gives all four components, and contemporary reporting details the pressure of managing luxury-tax exposure while keeping a competitive team around Kyle Lowry and DeMar DeRozan. Brooklyn accepted the Carroll contract in exchange for younger draft options. The first became No. 29 in 2018, used on Džanan Musa, while the second became No. 40 Rodions Kurucs. Both selections were actual players rather than expired protections. Justin Hamilton had averaged 6.9 points for Brooklyn in 2016-17, but Toronto’s primary rationale was financial, not acquiring its next leading scorer.

sections.heading: Carroll Provided Brooklyn a Starting Veteran Wing
sections.body: Carroll joined a rebuilding Nets squad and occupied meaningful minutes on the perimeter. He supplied defensive experience, spacing and leadership for a team still developing its identity after the earlier Boston draft-pick trade. His direct Brooklyn seasons therefore count as more than a salary obligation, although the real long-term attraction was the two added draft rights. Musa and Kurucs each eventually appeared for the Nets, allowing the front office to assess young wings without spending an extra future first-rounder of its own. Those players did not all become stars, and Carroll’s subsequent NBA seasons with other franchises are not Brooklyn trade returns. The inherited Brooklyn A- grade values the combination of veteran service and two additional development chances obtained for a replaceable center.

sections.heading: Toronto Gained Payroll Flexibility More Than Playing Value
sections.body: Toronto received Hamilton but waived him later that summer rather than inserting him into its 2017-18 rotation. That is an important distinction: the center was the formal incoming player but the financial benefit from clearing Carroll’s contract was the central objective. The Raptors continued advancing toward a later championship through additional trades, none of which should be credited entirely to this one salary move. Toronto’s inherited C- grade reflects losing a veteran and two draft choices without receiving a significant direct playing return. Brooklyn had to absorb a larger contract but acquired the rights to No. 29 and No. 40, along with a credible veteran wing. A sound analysis separates immediate cap accounting from actual basketball production rather than treating Hamilton as a two-year Toronto starter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A- after taking DeMarre Carroll and two picks that became 2018 No. 29 Džanan Musa and No. 40 Rodions Kurucs. Toronto receives C- for Justin Hamilton and financial relief; Hamilton did not become its next regular starting center. The Nets used available cap space to collect legitimate development assets.

sections.heading: The Nets Took Two Former Lottery Picks and a Second for Booker
sections.body: On December 7, 2017, Brooklyn acquired former top-three draft choice Jahlil Okafor, shooter Nik Stauskas and a future 2019 second-round pick from Philadelphia. The 76ers received veteran forward Trevor Booker. Philadelphia had already built its frontcourt around Joel Embiid, leaving Okafor without a reliable role, and was seeking a tougher reserve who could defend and rebound. Booker had averaged 10.1 points for the Nets before the transaction. Brooklyn could examine two younger players for very little veteran cost while acquiring a genuine future draft opportunity. The official 2017 reporting confirms the full package; reducing it to Okafor for Booker would miss both Stauskas and the late first-selection-in-the-second-round asset.

sections.heading: Okafor and Stauskas Offered Smaller Brooklyn Returns Than Expected
sections.body: Okafor needed a fresh start after injuries and limited opportunity with Philadelphia. In Brooklyn he remained a supporting center rather than rediscovering the high-scoring form of his rookie 2015-16 76ers season. Stauskas had been drafted eighth overall in 2014 and still offered outside shooting, but his Nets role was also a shorter experiment rather than a sustained starting guard tenure. The opportunity to evaluate two former first-round talents made sense for a rebuilding team, even if neither became a core member. Their earlier Philadelphia numbers cannot be transferred to the Brooklyn ledger. The eventual draft choice became the much more consequential asset, so the retrospective should acknowledge that the highest-impact return was delayed until 2019.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Became Nic Claxton
sections.body: Brooklyn selected Georgia center Nic Claxton at No. 31 in 2019 with the second-round choice tied to this deal. Claxton developed into an important long-term Nets defender and rim protector, supplying substantially more sustained team value than either Okafor or Stauskas. That explains the inherited Brooklyn A- grade despite the modest initial player performance. Philadelphia’s C- reflects the comparatively short tenure it received from Booker; the 76ers were buying depth for an immediate playoff push, not a future starter. The later success of Claxton belongs to Brooklyn’s actual draft investment, not to an unexercised pick or another unrelated trade. This deal illustrates why tracing the draft asset matters as much as comparing the players who changed uniforms in December 2017.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A- for Jahlil Okafor, Nik Stauskas and the 2019 second-round pick used on No. 31 Nic Claxton. Philadelphia gets C- for Trevor Booker, who offered shorter-term reserve frontcourt depth. Claxton’s later long-term defense provided the most durable Nets return from the full package.

sections.heading: New Orleans Secured Nikola Mirotić After the Cousins Injury
sections.body: On February 1, 2018, New Orleans traded Omer Asik, Tony Allen, Jameer Nelson and a protected first-round pick to Chicago for scoring forward Nikola Mirotić and a 2018 second-round selection. The Bulls also obtained a conditional right to swap 2021 second-round picks. Both teams’ official releases describe the complete terms, and the Pelicans had lost center DeMarcus Cousins to an Achilles injury only days earlier. Mirotić offered the rebounding, three-point shooting and scoring that might help compensate for that absence around Anthony Davis. Chicago was pursuing a younger roster and wanted an additional first-round draft opportunity while moving on from a strained relationship with the forward. This was a carefully negotiated exchange that involved future draft rights as well as four veterans.

sections.heading: Mirotić Helped New Orleans Win a Playoff Series
sections.body: Mirotić contributed frontcourt spacing and scoring to a Pelicans group that beat Portland in a first-round sweep in spring 2018. His outside shooting helped Davis find room inside and gave New Orleans a plausible lineup without Cousins. That was genuine near-term playing value and the main rationale for the Pelicans’ decision, even though Mirotić did not remain on their roster through multiple additional seasons. The club gained an active scoring forward rather than only an expiring contract. The inherited New Orleans C grade appears conservative for the playoff contribution, but it also weighs the protected first-round pick surrendered. The second-round selection Chicago sent out became a separate development right rather than a replacement for the immediate Mirotić output.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned the Protected First Into No. 22 Chandler Hutchison
sections.body: Chicago used the 2018 first-round pick acquired from New Orleans at No. 22, selecting Boise State wing Chandler Hutchison. The Bulls’ official year-end summary confirms both the trade and that exact draft result. Hutchison did not become a franchise scoring centerpiece, but the selection was a real first-round opportunity. Chicago also took the salaries of Asik, Allen and Nelson, and later moved or waived those players. The inherited Chicago A- grade values draft assets and flexibility, while the canonical Even Trade label conflicts with the numerically lower Pelicans C. That grading discrepancy should be visible instead of quietly changing either side. Each club gained something: New Orleans a useful playoff contributor and Chicago a first-round choice. The lasting balance depends on the relative value assigned to each.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade is the inherited headline although Chicago grades A- and New Orleans C. The Pelicans acquired Nikola Mirotić and a 2018 second; Mirotić helped sweep Portland in 2018. Chicago received Asik, Allen, Nelson, a 2018 first used on No. 22 Chandler Hutchison and a 2021 second-round swap right.

sections.heading: The Cavaliers Sent Dwyane Wade Home for a Protected Second
sections.body: On February 8, 2018, Cleveland traded veteran guard Dwyane Wade to Miami for a heavily protected 2024 second-round selection. The Heat official release and public remarks from Pat Riley confirm the terms. Wade had returned to Cleveland on a minimum-style veteran contract to play alongside LeBron James, but the Cavaliers made extensive deadline changes around a struggling supporting cast. Miami wanted to bring back its longtime franchise star for another playoff push and to give him a proper farewell period. The future second was top-55 protected and was never exercised, so it did not become an incoming NBA player for Cleveland. This was a player-return decision with personal meaning as well as basketball timing, rather than a major draft asset sale.

sections.heading: Wade Contributed to Two Additional Miami Seasons
sections.body: Wade returned to Miami and supplied scoring, ball handling and experienced leadership off the bench. The Heat reached the 2018 postseason, where he had notable contributions against Philadelphia. He then played a final 2018-19 NBA season for Miami, giving the franchise another year of the player whose earlier career had included three championship victories. Those appearances are real team-specific return from Cleveland’s deadline decision, though Wade was no longer the 2006 Finals MVP version of himself. Miami C in the inherited grade system recognizes a short-term but meaningful reserve contribution rather than a new long-term starting guard. His career before 2018 was established long before this deal and cannot count as a fresh player acquisition return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Did Not Receive an Exercised Draft Choice
sections.body: Cleveland agreed to the protected future second, which the transaction history later records as nonconveyed. The Cavaliers still benefited from greater roster flexibility and Wade’s stated preference to return to Miami, but they did not draft a player with a pick gained in this agreement. Cleveland proceeded to the 2018 NBA Finals with other players after its deadline overhaul, which should not be credited solely to Wade’s departure. The inherited Cleveland B- and Miami B- grades are equal, yet the record says Heat Win, reflecting the short-term basketball and goodwill value to Miami instead of a formal numerical grading lead. The distinction between an identified future pick and a selection that actually transfers is essential here. The final accounting favors Miami for the player it received and used.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win in the inherited assessment despite equal B- grades. Miami received Dwyane Wade for the 2018 postseason and his final 2018-19 NBA season. Cleveland obtained a top-55-protected 2024 second that did not convey. The on-court return was therefore concentrated on Miami, while Cleveland gained roster flexibility.

sections.heading: Charlotte Drafted Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Immediately Traded His Rights
sections.body: On June 21, 2018, Charlotte selected Kentucky guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at No. 11 and sent his rights to the Clippers for the rights to No. 12 Miles Bridges and two future second-round selections. The NBA draft tracker confirms both players and the two picks, which the historical ledger later connects to Vernon Carey Jr. at No. 32 in 2020 and Scottie Lewis at No. 56 in 2021. The Hornets valued a young explosive forward to develop alongside Kemba Walker, while Los Angeles wanted the guard they had targeted one pick earlier. Neither prospect had played an NBA game for the team that drafted him when the rights moved, making this a draft-slot and development transaction rather than a veteran swap.

sections.heading: Gilgeous-Alexander Helped the Clippers in His Rookie Season
sections.body: The new Clippers guard played in all 82 regular-season games during 2018-19 and started 73, averaging 10.8 points and 3.3 assists. He also gained playoff experience in a difficult first-round series with Golden State. Los Angeles then included him in its 2019 trade with Oklahoma City to acquire Paul George, using his newly established value as part of a much larger superstar package. The later scoring titles and MVP-level performance belong to his Thunder playing career, not the Clippers record, but the 2018 rights acquisition created an unusually valuable piece. That is the main rationale behind the inherited Clippers A+ grade. The value exists in his actual rookie minutes and later trade capital, rather than assigning his entire peak NBA career to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Bridges Produced for Charlotte but the Opportunity Cost Was Huge
sections.body: Bridges also became a genuine NBA starter and scorer for the Hornets over several seasons, so an F grade must not be interpreted as proof that the franchise got no court time from the exchange. His scoring and athleticism improved while Charlotte continued developing its roster. The additional second-round choices created more opportunities, but Carey and Lewis did not become comparable league-leading guards. The Clippers gained the player with greater career upside and the prospect eventually used in the Paul George deal, while Charlotte retained a usable forward. The inherited Clippers Win verdict focuses on the elite guard lost in a one-slot trade down. A proper accounting can acknowledge meaningful Bridges production without inventing a Charlotte career for Gilgeous-Alexander or a Clippers career for his Thunder achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A+ for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, an 82-game rookie who later became a key outgoing asset in the Paul George trade. Charlotte receives F for Miles Bridges and future seconds associated with Vernon Carey Jr. and Scottie Lewis, reflecting the much greater lost guard upside even though Bridges played substantial NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Used Cap Room to Collect Two Picks from Denver
sections.body: On July 13, 2018, Brooklyn accepted forward Kenneth Faried, veteran Darrell Arthur, a protected 2019 first-round pick and a 2020 second-round choice from Denver for reserve guard Isaiah Whitehead. The Nets official announcement identifies all four incoming assets and the player the Nuggets received. Denver was facing a difficult payroll situation with an expensive frontcourt, while Brooklyn had the space to take on salaries while rebuilding. The first became No. 27 in 2019, associated with Mfiondu Kabengele, and the second No. 55 Jay Scrubb in 2020. The pick rights followed their own later movements, but the draft selections were actual assets rather than theoretical options that never conveyed. The exchange was principally an asset-and-salary transaction, not a claim that Whitehead was Denver’s preferred new star.

sections.heading: The Two Big Men Did Not Supply Long Nets Careers
sections.body: Faried had been an effective Denver rebounder in earlier seasons, but his tenure in Brooklyn was short before he continued with Houston. Arthur did not establish himself as a regular Nets starter, and Brooklyn soon moved him to Phoenix in a separate deal for Jared Dudley and another pick. The original Denver transaction mattered because the Nets could make multiple roster decisions after acquiring those contracts and draft opportunities. Counting Faried’s earlier Nuggets career or later Rockets offense as Brooklyn playing time would wildly overstate the return. Brooklyn’s inherited A- grade rewards the first- and second-round assets obtained at a time when the franchise had lost many future draft choices in earlier decisions. The value of the picks should still be measured through the correct subsequent rights chain.

sections.heading: Denver Exchanged Future Choices for Financial Space
sections.body: Whitehead had played in 89 Nets games across two seasons and offered some defensive guard potential, but he did not become a major long-term Nuggets starter. Denver mainly reduced salary obligations, which created room for other roster investments around Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. The inherited Nuggets C- grade reflects having surrendered valuable draft capital for financial flexibility, even when salary relief was a legitimate operational objective. The eventual first- and second-round selections made the opportunity cost visible years after the July 2018 trade. Neither Kabengele nor Scrubb should be credited with an entire Brooklyn playing career without checking their rights movements; the picks themselves are the directly documented returns. The Nets obtained two distinct draft opportunities while Denver prioritized removing large veteran contracts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A- for Kenneth Faried, Darrell Arthur, a protected 2019 first associated with No. 27 Mfiondu Kabengele and a 2020 second associated with No. 55 Jay Scrubb. Denver gets C- for Isaiah Whitehead and payroll relief, having surrendered future pick value.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Justin Holiday into Two Guards and Two Picks
sections.body: The Bulls traded Justin Holiday to Memphis on January 3, 2019 for MarShon Brooks, Wayne Selden Jr., a 2019 second-round draft choice and a 2020 second-round choice. Both teams announced the exact package, and the selected players became No. 38 Daniel Gafford in 2019 and No. 44 Marko Simonović in 2020. Holiday had started all 38 of his Chicago appearances that season, averaging 11.6 points and 4.4 rebounds while providing perimeter defense. Memphis wanted a reliable veteran wing alongside Mike Conley and Marc Gasol, while the rebuilding Bulls could absorb a short-term roster change and wait for new prospects. The draft compensation was not conditional cash: both seconds became actual selections. Chicago also waived Cameron Payne in a separate roster move connected to making space for the incoming guards.

sections.heading: Gafford Became the Bulls Most Productive Long-Term Asset
sections.body: Chicago used its 2019 No. 38 pick on athletic Arkansas center Daniel Gafford. He immediately provided vertical finishing and shot blocking, becoming a regular contributor before his later trade to Washington. His entire subsequent career with Washington and Dallas should not be assigned to Chicago games, but the original 2019 pick produced an identifiable NBA big man with substantial professional value. The 2020 selection led to Marko Simonović, whose NBA impact was comparatively limited. Selden supplied additional wing minutes in the remainder of 2018-19, while Brooks was waived early rather than becoming a long-term scorer. The inherited Bulls A grade is supported by obtaining multiple resources for a veteran whose team was not contending. It is more accurate to credit Gafford and the picks than to claim all four acquired assets were equally successful on the court.

sections.heading: Memphis Got a Real Veteran but Paid a Future Development Cost
sections.body: Holiday gave the Grizzlies another experienced defender and occasional outside shooter during the 2018-19 season. His NBA role was legitimate, although Memphis was changing direction soon after the trade as its older core was broken up. The inherited Grizzlies C grade reflects the limited tenure compared with two selections that Chicago could develop or exchange. That is not a claim Holiday was useless, only that a short veteran assignment was a smaller return than having future picks that ultimately conveyed. The deal does not include the unrelated Marshon Brooks and Dillon Brooks name-confusion report from the preceding month as a completed part of this trade. The official January 3 transaction identifies MarShon Brooks and Selden as the two incoming Bulls players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A for MarShon Brooks, Wayne Selden Jr. and two picks that became No. 38 Daniel Gafford in 2019 and No. 44 Marko Simonović in 2020. Memphis gets C for Justin Holiday, an experienced wing with a shorter remaining Grizzlies tenure.

sections.heading: Detroit Took a Rookie Shooter and a Second for Reggie Bullock
sections.body: On February 6, 2019, Detroit traded veteran guard Reggie Bullock to the Lakers for rookie Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk and a future second-round selection. The 2021 pick ultimately became No. 52 Luka Garza. The official NBA deadline tracker and both team transaction lists identify the completed agreement. Detroit executive Ed Stefanski explained that he preferred the combination of a named young player and a future second to offers consisting of two picks. Bullock had averaged 12.1 points earlier that season for the Pistons, giving Los Angeles an available perimeter shooter during an injury-disrupted playoff chase. The exchange contained no premium first-round pick and no additional starting veteran, so the return must be evaluated through Bullock’s short Lakers stint and Detroit’s two developmental pieces.

sections.heading: Bullock Was a Short-Term Shooter on a Lakers Team That Missed the Playoffs
sections.body: Bullock joined LeBron James and a team trying to stabilize a thin guard rotation while Lonzo Ball was injured. He provided spot-up shooting and experience defending on the wing, but could not resolve the much broader problems that led Los Angeles to miss the 2019 postseason. Bullock left in the summer, and his later career with New York and Dallas should not be credited as Lakers games obtained from the February agreement. The inherited Lakers B grade reflects real rotation use of a veteran sharpshooter, not a durable new scoring star. A player who had averaged more than twelve points for Detroit could still be useful, but his pretrade Pistons production does not belong in the Los Angeles statistical return. The trade was a rental aimed at the current season.

sections.heading: Mykhailiuk and Garza Offered Detroit More Development Time
sections.body: Mykhailiuk had been the No. 47 draft choice in 2018 and could shoot from distance. His Detroit role expanded during later seasons as the Pistons sought inexpensive prospects to complement a veteran roster. The added 2021 second became Iowa center Luka Garza, who appeared in actual NBA games for Detroit after the draft. Neither player instantly replaced the established Bullock scoring role, but the return provided two separate chances to develop contributors. The inherited Pistons B+ grade over Lakers B matches the Slight Pistons Edge verdict. Those grades reflect both the potential longevity of Mykhailiuk and the later draft result, rather than Bullock’s short-term usefulness being zero. The Pistons gained another inexpensive contract and a second selection while the Lakers acquired one wing for immediate minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit earns B+ for Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk and a 2021 second-round pick used on No. 52 Luka Garza. Los Angeles gets B for Reggie Bullock as a veteran perimeter option during the 2018-19 stretch run. The Lakers missed the postseason, while Detroit retained two development assets.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Traded Darrell Arthur for Dudley and a Protected Second
sections.body: On July 20, 2018, Brooklyn acquired veteran forward Jared Dudley and a protected 2021 second-round draft selection from Phoenix in exchange for Darrell Arthur. The Suns official release confirms all three assets and the NBA reported roughly $2.1 million in expected Phoenix salary savings. Brooklyn had acquired Arthur only one week earlier in the larger Denver cap-absorption agreement, demonstrating that the forward served as a tradeable contract rather than a new long-term Nets starter. Dudley could space the floor and advise a young Brooklyn team, while the second-round pick offered additional future flexibility. The later selection became No. 59 in 2021, associated with RaiQuan Gray. This was not the separate Richaun Holmes deal between Phoenix and Philadelphia completed that day, so its terms should not be mixed into the Brooklyn transaction.

sections.heading: Dudley Had a Useful Role on the 2019 Nets Playoff Team
sections.body: Dudley appeared in 59 Brooklyn regular-season games during 2018-19. His scoring totals were small compared with the franchise leading scorers, but his passing, outside shooting and experienced defense were relevant on a Nets group that reached the postseason. He also played in the first-round series against Philadelphia, where the veteran forward became a visible part of the competitive confrontation. Those are actual NBA appearances for the team that received him in the July trade, not a purely financial return. Brooklyn later allowed Dudley to join the Lakers, so his subsequent championship experience belongs to a different club. The inherited Nets B+ grade can be supported by a capable rotation veteran and a future pick, without claiming he became the primary reason the team improved. The trade created both immediate depth and longer-horizon draft value.

sections.heading: Phoenix Paid a Second to Achieve Financial Flexibility
sections.body: Arthur had already played numerous Denver and Memphis seasons as a power forward, but he did not establish a significant new Suns tenure after this exchange. Phoenix planned to buy out or waive the contract and gain the salary savings from moving Dudley. The protected 2021 selection represented a tangible future cost, even though a late second is not a guarantee of a new NBA starter. The inherited Suns C grade acknowledges that financial rationale and the limited basketball return from Arthur, while Brooklyn collected the pick and got Dudley for a playoff year. RaiQuan Gray’s later professional appearances must be credited to their proper rights holder rather than automatically assigning every career game to Brooklyn. The Nets Win result is grounded in documented on-court minutes plus an actual future draft option.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn receives B+ for Jared Dudley and the protected 2021 second-rounder associated with No. 59 RaiQuan Gray. Phoenix earns C for Darrell Arthur and estimated payroll savings; Dudley contributed to the Nets 2018-19 playoff run while Arthur did not become an ongoing Suns rotation fixture.

sections.heading: Chicago Sold the No. 38 Rights Instead of Developing Jordan Bell
sections.body: On June 22, 2017, the Bulls drafted Oregon forward Jordan Bell with the 38th selection and moved his rights to the Golden State Warriors for $3.5 million in cash. The agreement did not involve an established NBA player moving to Chicago or a future first-round pick. Golden State had just won the NBA championship and was looking for inexpensive defensive depth around Draymond Green and its other veteran stars. Bell had shown unusual shot-blocking and passing ability for a college forward, making his athletic profile attractive to the Warriors. Chicago had other roster priorities and chose immediate financial consideration rather than committing a second-round roster spot to his development. That cash amount, not an unnamed draft choice, is the direct Chicago return.

sections.heading: Bell Contributed to Golden State as a Rookie
sections.body: Bell appeared in 57 Warriors regular-season games in 2017-18, starting 13 and averaging 4.6 points and 3.6 rebounds in fewer than 15 minutes. His ability to defend in space made him an interesting reserve on a team that already had elite offensive creators. Golden State won another NBA championship in 2018, and Bell appeared in postseason games, giving the defending champions cheap rotation insurance from a second-round selection. His role diminished in subsequent seasons, so the acquisition was not the creation of a long-term franchise star. Nevertheless, he supplied immediate NBA games and title-season frontcourt minutes, which is more basketball value than Chicago could obtain directly from cash in the same agreement. The inherited Warriors A- grade emphasizes that favorable cost-to-contribution relationship.

sections.heading: The Bulls Received Cash but No Direct Player Development
sections.body: Chicago collected $3.5 million and did not have to sign Bell. That consideration had financial value, yet no NBA games, rebounds or blocks can be credited as an incoming Bulls player return from this transaction. The Bulls D inherited grade reflects the opportunity cost of giving a useful young defender to a championship rival for a cash payment. It should not be exaggerated into an argument that Bell eventually became an All-Star or that all Warriors championships were his doing. His specific reserve contribution in 2017-18 is enough to establish why the Warriors benefited. The draft-night rights chain is simple and complete: Chicago chose Bell, Golden State purchased his rights and the Bulls retained the money. This deal illustrates how a modest draft prospect can have more practical roster value than immediate cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns A- for No. 38 Jordan Bell, who played 57 games and provided reserve defense on its 2018 championship team. Chicago receives D for $3.5 million cash. The Bulls got financial consideration, while the Warriors acquired an inexpensive player who actually filled frontcourt minutes.

sections.heading: Charlotte Took Miles Plumlee and Cash for Two Veteran Big Men
sections.body: On February 2, 2017, Charlotte acquired reserve center Miles Plumlee and cash considerations from Milwaukee for veteran centers Roy Hibbert and Spencer Hawes. Plumlee had signed a substantial long-term contract with the Bucks the preceding summer but had not secured the playing role envisioned. Charlotte was seeking a younger, more mobile reserve to complement its existing frontline, while Milwaukee wanted to reduce its future salary obligations. The three-player deal was a contract and roster restructuring transaction, not a move for a first-round draft selection. Both franchise transaction records show the asset direction, including two outgoing Charlotte centers. Any later player drafted by either team must not be assigned to this deal without another separate trade.

sections.heading: Plumlee Delivered a Brief Charlotte Trial Rather Than a New Core Center
sections.body: Plumlee appeared in just 13 Hornets games over the remainder of 2016-17, starting none and averaging approximately 2.4 points and 3.2 rebounds. Those totals represented emergency frontcourt depth rather than the reliable backup center contribution Charlotte had hoped to buy. The Hornets moved him again that summer as part of a much bigger trade with Atlanta to acquire Dwight Howard, so this February agreement is one link in a larger contract path. Plumlee did not become a regular long-term Charlotte starter. The inherited D grade reflects how little basketball return the franchise initially received while accepting significant future salary commitments. His earlier seasons with Phoenix and Milwaukee do not count as Bobcats or Hornets performance.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Found Roster Flexibility Without Retaining Both Arrivals
sections.body: Hibbert and Hawes carried experience as NBA starting centers but were past their most productive seasons. Hibbert did not establish a significant Milwaukee playing tenure before being traded again to Denver, while Hawes was used in a small reserve role. The most valuable return for Milwaukee was the ability to move the contract owed to Plumlee and regain options for future roster construction around Giannis Antetokounmpo. The Bucks A- inherited grade is partly an assessment of that contract management, not a claim that Hibbert and Hawes scored like elite big men after the deal. Charlotte received a center who quickly left, while Milwaukee reduced its longer-term salary risk. That mismatch in financial commitments explains the pronounced difference between the inherited team grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- after moving the Miles Plumlee contract and receiving Roy Hibbert and Spencer Hawes. Charlotte gets D for Plumlee and cash; he played only 13 Hornets games before being traded again. The larger value to the Bucks was salary flexibility, not an All-Star acquired in the swap.

sections.heading: Charlotte Sent Johnny O’Bryant and Two Seconds for Hernangómez
sections.body: At the February 7, 2018 trade deadline, the Charlotte Hornets acquired young Spanish center Willy Hernangómez from the New York Knicks. New York received reserve forward Johnny O’Bryant III and second-round selections in 2020 and 2021. Those choices later became associated with No. 38 Saben Lee and No. 42 Isaiah Livers, although the draft-right chains and subsequent owners are separate from the original agreement. Hernangómez had played meaningful rookie minutes for New York in 2016-17 but lost his place in its developing frontcourt rotation. Charlotte sought a low-cost younger big man with touch around the basket and good rebounding instincts. The Hornets were not surrendering a current first-rounder, but two future seconds were real draft assets.

sections.heading: Hernangómez Became a Productive Hornets Reserve
sections.body: After the deal, Hernangómez played 22 Charlotte games to finish 2017-18. His next season featured a larger bench role, and he averaged 7.3 points and 5.4 rebounds across 58 appearances in 2018-19. Those were genuine Hornets contributions from an incoming big man who had been squeezed out in New York. He did not develop into a multi-year All-Star or regular thirty-minute starter for Charlotte, but he offered usable center offense and rebounding. His later New Orleans NBA seasons and work for the Spanish national team do not belong to Charlotte’s direct return. The inherited Hornets C+ grade credits a developing reserve but discounts the two future second-round choices surrendered and the relatively modest ceiling achieved.

sections.heading: New York Obtained Two Future Draft Opportunities
sections.body: O’Bryant supplied short-term frontcourt depth but was not the main long-term Knicks return. The two second-round selections were more important to future roster optionality, ultimately associating with No. 38 in 2020 and No. 42 in 2021. Both rights passed through additional draft decisions, so the complete NBA output of Saben Lee and Isaiah Livers should not automatically be treated as Knicks playing time. New York’s B inherited grade values the ability to convert an underused center into multiple choices over different years. Charlotte obtained the more visible immediate playing return; the Knicks chose flexibility and potential replacement players. The Knicks Win conclusion reflects the premium placed on two selections relative to a reserve center’s Charlotte tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B for Johnny O’Bryant III and 2020 and 2021 second-round assets linked to No. 38 Saben Lee and No. 42 Isaiah Livers. Charlotte receives C+ for Willy Hernangómez, who provided 22 games immediately and later averaged 7.3 points in 58 Hornets games in 2018-19.
