sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Corliss Williamson for Two Older Big Men
sections.body: On August 4, 2004, the defending champion Detroit Pistons traded Sixth Man of the Year winner Corliss Williamson to Philadelphia. The 76ers sent veteran power forward Derrick Coleman and center Amal McCaskill in return. Both teams were trying to reposition their frontcourt rotation before the 2004-05 season. Detroit had recently signed Antonio McDyess and already relied on Ben Wallace and Rasheed Wallace for significant interior minutes. Philadelphia was looking for scoring and experience beside Allen Iverson. The team transaction lists agree on the two-for-one player exchange. The inherited asset ledger also describes cash with Philadelphia; the Detroit chronological record lists the player exchange without a cash amount, so that supplementary consideration should not be assigned an invented figure.

sections.heading: Detroit Waived Both Incoming Players Within Five Months
sections.body: The Pistons quickly decided not to retain the two men acquired for Williamson. Detroit waived McCaskill on October 1, 2004, before the regular season, and waived Coleman on January 5, 2005. Neither developed into an extended starting frontcourt role for the team. In the months after the deal, Detroit continued to rely on its established championship-era big men and reached the 2005 NBA Finals, but that later success does not mean the Williamson trade supplied a key playoff rotation center. Its inherited C+ grade appears generous in light of the short tenure of the acquired players. The waiver dates are verifiable from Detroits own transaction ledger and should not be obscured by the players’ earlier NBA reputations. This was largely a payroll and roster adjustment for the Pistons, not a source of durable direct playing value.

sections.heading: Williamson Supplied Philadelphia Bench Scoring
sections.body: Williamson was no longer the sixth man of Detroit’s 2004 championship team when he arrived in Philadelphia, but he could still provide low-post scoring and strength as a forward. He appeared in the 2004-05 76ers rotation while Iverson remained the central offensive option. Philadelphia C+ grade is equal to Detroit in the historical record, resulting in an inherited Even Trade label. Yet the direct receiving-team basketball payoff leaned toward Philadelphia because Williamson actually played while both Pistons returnees were soon waived. The transaction was not a first-round draft asset swap. It also should not be confused with Philadelphia’s older 2001 trades involving Derrick Coleman and Robert Traylor; those were separate developments with their own asset chains. The outcomes illustrate why equal inherited grades should be checked against the later team-specific records.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade according to the inherited C+ scores for Detroit and Philadelphia. The Pistons received Derrick Coleman and Amal McCaskill but waived both by January 2005. Philadelphia acquired Corliss Williamson, a veteran scorer with a 2004 championship background, and obtained the more durable playing contribution. The historical numerical grade tie deserves further review.

sections.heading: The Nuggets Acquired Renaldo Balkman for Two Players and a Pick
sections.body: On July 28, 2008, Denver acquired defensive-minded forward Renaldo Balkman and cash from New York. The Knicks received guard Taurean Green, forward Bobby Jones and a 2010 second-round draft selection that eventually became No. 38, used on Syracuse guard Andy Rautins. Executive transaction histories corroborate all four principal assets and the money traveling to Denver. Balkman had been a 2006 first-round selection for New York, valued for hustle and defense more than outside shooting. The Nuggets hoped he could help defend larger wings beside Carmelo Anthony. The Knicks were reducing their forward depth and wanted additional optionality under a front office led by Donnie Walsh. No current NBA star came to New York, and the final pick was a second-round selection, not a lottery asset.

sections.heading: Balkman Became a Rotation Forward on a Deep Denver Team
sections.body: Balkman provided energy, rebounding and versatile defense in Denver’s rotation during the 2008-09 season, when the Nuggets reached the Western Conference Finals. His own scoring was modest, but his athleticism offered a different complement to the team’s main offensive stars, Anthony and Chauncey Billups. He remained with Denver beyond the initial season, although injuries and changing lineup needs eventually reduced his impact. The Nuggets B- inherited grade credits that defensive availability without calling him a future franchise-leading forward. Cash was an additional part of their incoming consideration. Balkman’s later professional seasons with New York and other clubs cannot be counted twice as Denver value. Denver used him as a supporting piece in a competitive team context rather than a primary offensive acquisition.

sections.heading: The Second-Rounder Became a Knicks Development Attempt
sections.body: New York moved two fringe players and the second-round selection ultimately tied to No. 38 Andy Rautins, creating draft-right value despite limited direct NBA games from the players entering the 2008 Knicks roster. Taurean Green and Bobby Jones were not long-term starting guards for New York. Rautins arrived in 2010 and played a small NBA role, but the pick itself was a real asset rather than a conditional choice that failed to convey. New York A+ inherited grade is substantially higher than Denver B- even though the immediate basketball production of Balkman was more identifiable for the Nuggets. A grade review should consider the cash direction and the later utilization of the selection; the Knicks Win label should not be described as proof that New York obtained a new star from the deal. Both franchises sought salary and positional flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge according to the inherited A+ for New York and B- for Denver. The Knicks gained Taurean Green, Bobby Jones and the 2010 No. 38 second-round pick used on Andy Rautins. Denver obtained Renaldo Balkman and cash; Balkman later supplied reserve defense for a team that reached the 2009 Western Conference Finals.

sections.heading: Toronto Sold the Rights to an International Second-Round Pick
sections.body: On June 28, 2006, the Toronto Raptors selected Bosnian forward Edin Bavčić in the second round of the NBA draft and transferred his signing rights to Philadelphia for cash considerations. The Sixers June 2006 transaction ledger confirms the club acquired Bavčić’s rights from Toronto. This was a rights transaction involving an unsigned international prospect, not a deal in which Toronto sent an established NBA player under contract. Philadelphia was looking for low-cost future roster possibilities while Toronto preferred immediate financial compensation to carrying another overseas draft-rights prospect. The amount of cash is not established in the canonical record and should not be guessed. No first-round pick and no veteran player moved to Toronto from the 76ers in the completed trade.

sections.heading: Bavčić Continued Playing Abroad Instead of Joining the NBA
sections.body: Bavčić continued his professional career with European clubs after the draft rather than entering an NBA regular-season lineup. Philadelphia therefore obtained a chance to evaluate and retain his NBA rights without realizing actual 76ers points, rebounds or starts. The inherited Philadelphia C grade represents optionality from a late selection, not proof the prospect developed into an NBA starter. Treating his overseas games as if they occurred in the NBA would materially distort the historical trade analysis. The 76ers had made other draft-night moves involving Rodney Carney and Thabo Sefolosha, but those were separate transactions and their roster value should not be assigned to the Bavčić purchase. This small financial agreement could have made sense as a low-risk developmental bet even without later NBA appearances.

sections.heading: Toronto Obtained Cash Without Waiting for a Development Result
sections.body: The Raptors received cash consideration immediately, turning a late second-round selection into a financial resource rather than tying up a long-term roster place. Since the underlying amount is unspecified, Toronto’s direct return cannot be expressed as an exact salary savings or equivalent player value. The inherited C grade for Toronto is equal to Philadelphia’s, consistent with a modest economic transaction without measurable NBA playing contributions for the new rights holder. Neither franchise obtained a future All-Star through this specific agreement. The winner label is Even Trade because both sides exchanged a small certain benefit for a larger but uncertain development option. The outcome should be judged on that scale, not against the much more prominent Toronto draft selection of Andrea Bargnani on the same night.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Toronto and Philadelphia both receive C: the Raptors gained cash considerations, and the 76ers obtained Edin Bavčić draft rights in 2006. Bavčić never appeared in a Philadelphia NBA regular-season game. The exchange was a financial and international-scouting option rather than a trade for immediate rotation production.

sections.heading: The Bulls Exchanged Larry Hughes for Three Knicks Contracts
sections.body: On February 19, 2009, Chicago traded veteran scoring guard Larry Hughes to New York. The Knicks sent back forwards Tim Thomas and Anthony Roberson and center Jerome James. The agreement was one of two Chicago transactions on the deadline day, with the Bulls separately sending Thabo Sefolosha to Oklahoma City for the pick later used on Taj Gibson. Those two trades must not be merged. Hughes had struggled to secure a lasting place in a backcourt being reorganized around rookie Derrick Rose, while New York wanted another player capable of handling the ball and scoring from the perimeter. The Bulls accepted three contracts, including James, who had been sidelined with an Achilles injury. No draft choice changed hands in the Hughes agreement.

sections.heading: Chicago Received Limited On-Court Value but Altered Its Payroll
sections.body: Thomas returned to Chicago as a veteran forward who had previously spent time with the Bulls. His offensive role was smaller than it had been in his best earlier seasons, and the club waived him during the following summer. Roberson did not develop into a long-term starting wing for Chicago, while James was injured and did not supply sustained Bulls center minutes. Contemporary reporting emphasized insurance recovery associated with the injured James contract, a potential business consideration beyond direct playing production. The Bulls inherited C+ grade reflects roster adjustments and limited frontcourt use rather than a new high-level scorer. Chicago made other acquisitions that week which contributed more directly to its postseason push, especially John Salmons and Brad Miller in the separate Sacramento trade. None of those players were part of the Knicks package.

sections.heading: Hughes Supplied New York More Immediate Guard Production
sections.body: Hughes appeared in a regular New York rotation role during the remainder of 2008-09 and returned for part of the next season. He was experienced as a defender and scoring guard, although his peak Cleveland and Washington performances were behind him. The Knicks inherited B+ grade is higher than Chicago C+, but the canonical Bulls Win label contradicts those scores. The article preserves that inconsistency for later source-led grading review instead of describing the verdict as numerically unanimous. Direct player value from Hughes in New York was more observable than James and Roberson in Chicago, while the Bulls gained different salary and positional options. The transaction was a veteran contract exchange during two rebuilding projects, not a permanent solution at point guard for either team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win according to the inherited winner wording, although New York grades B+ against Chicago C+. Chicago acquired Tim Thomas, Jerome James and Anthony Roberson for Larry Hughes; James was already injured. The Knicks gained a veteran scoring guard, while the Bulls reorganized contracts and frontcourt depth. The disagreement between headline and grades warrants review.

sections.heading: Washington Sent Dominic McGuire and Cash for a Conditional Pick
sections.body: At the February 18, 2010 deadline, Washington traded reserve forward Dominic McGuire and cash considerations to Sacramento. The Wizards were promised a 2010 second-round selection with protection covering the first 41 picks in the round-order numbering, but the condition did not result in a conveyed choice. Both teams dated transaction logs document the same asset flow. Washington was reorganizing around a major rebuilding effort while Sacramento wanted inexpensive athletic depth. McGuire had played a reserve role for the Wizards and was not an established lead offensive option, though his length and defensive energy had value. The deal was not part of the complicated Kings, Knicks and Rockets three-team trade on the same date that featured Kevin Martin and Tracy McGrady. It was a separate two-team transaction with its own conditional terms.

sections.heading: McGuire Was a Limited Kings Reserve Before Moving Again
sections.body: Sacramento added McGuire as a player who could defend forwards and cover bench minutes without needing a high-volume scoring role. His contribution to the Kings remained brief, and he did not establish a long-running starting assignment there. He later spent NBA seasons with other organizations, but those subsequent games belong to the contracts and team decisions that followed. Sacramento also received documented cash, with the precise figure not available in the canonical ledger. That consideration gave the Kings an immediate economic return even if the acquired forward was not a franchise-building piece. The Kings inherited B+ grade reflects getting an actual NBA reserve plus money while surrendering a draft condition that ultimately expired. The transaction was low-profile compared with the club larger deadline activity but had an identifiable asymmetry in realized value.

sections.heading: Washington Did Not Receive the Protected Draft Selection
sections.body: The promised 2010 second-round pick never conveyed, as both the Wizards and Kings historical transaction records explicitly state. No actual 2010 Washington draftee should therefore be attributed to this deal. Washington may have valued clearing a roster spot, but it also included cash in the outgoing package and did not obtain measurable NBA player production from the conditional choice. Its inherited C- grade reflects that weak final return. The Kings Win verdict is supported by the direct comparison between a received player and cash on one side and no realized pick on the other. Both clubs were rebuilding in different ways, yet Sacramento ended up with the only concrete assets from the agreement. The hypothetical future pick should remain a condition, not be converted into an invented prospect.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento earns B+ for Dominic McGuire and cash while the conditional 2010 second-round selection sent to Washington failed to convey. The Wizards receive C- after surrendering a reserve forward and money without receiving a new NBA player or draft selection from this particular trade.

sections.heading: The Lakers Acquired Maurice Evans for Cheikh Samb Rights
sections.body: On June 28, 2006, Detroit traded guard-forward Maurice Evans to the Los Angeles Lakers. Detroit obtained the NBA draft rights to Senegalese center Cheikh Samb, who had been selected in the second round. Both clubs were looking for different kinds of inexpensive roster help. Los Angeles wanted another veteran wing capable of guarding opposing perimeter players and making open shots beside Kobe Bryant. Detroit held an established veteran rotation but hoped Samb could become a long-term interior prospect after additional development outside the NBA. The teams used rights rather than another signed veteran on the Pistons side. No first-round pick or cash was part of the historical canonical transaction record, making this a direct experienced-player-for-international-draft-option swap.

sections.heading: Evans Immediately Became a Dependable Lakers Wing
sections.body: Evans appeared regularly for the Lakers after arriving, giving the team athletic defense and occasional scoring from the perimeter. His 2006-07 role was much more immediate than an overseas center waiting to be evaluated, and he remained available as the club tried to regain its competitive footing in the West. Evans later continued his career with other NBA teams, but those seasons are not Lakers playing time arising from the original transaction. Los Angeles inherited C grade reflects an affordable supporting player rather than a new All-Star beside Bryant. The canonical Lakers Win conclusion recognizes the reality that Evans supplied NBA rotation minutes right away. His arrival was also separate from the Lakers decisions involving established point guards and power forwards that summer, which had their own roster implications.

sections.heading: Samb Never Became a Detroit Starting Center
sections.body: Samb eventually reached the NBA and made a small number of Pistons appearances before the franchise moved on. Much of his development occurred outside Detroits main NBA lineup, and he did not become the kind of regular rebounder or rim protector that the club might have imagined in 2006. The Detroit C+ inherited grade is numerically higher than the Lakers C even though the winner label favors Los Angeles. That inconsistency should be documented for later assessment instead of disappearing behind an apparently clear grade difference. Detroit did receive authentic NBA draft rights and kept the option of developing a seven-foot prospect, but realized playing contributions remained modest. The immediate advantage was with the Lakers, who acquired an experienced NBA wing for a player whose future had not yet been determined.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win by the inherited winner designation, even though Detroit grades C+ against Los Angeles C. The Lakers added Maurice Evans for immediate wing depth. Detroit obtained Cheikh Samb draft rights, but he never became a long-term Pistons center. The numerical grade and winner discrepancy deserves a source-led revisit.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Kyle Weaver Rights for a Future Second
sections.body: On August 11, 2008, the Charlotte Bobcats sent the rights to young Washington State guard Kyle Weaver to the Seattle SuperSonics franchise. Charlotte received a 2009 second-round choice that later became No. 40 Derrick Brown. Seattle had not yet started play in Oklahoma City, so the historical counterparty is the SuperSonics even though the modern data model uses the Thunder identifier. A contemporary executive transaction record confirms the date and draft consequence. Weaver had been a second-round prospect whose ball handling and perimeter defense interested a young roster, while Charlotte chose to wait for another draft to select a player with a different position profile. The agreement involved two second-round opportunities rather than cash or a first-round selection.

sections.heading: Weaver Played for Oklahoma City During the First Thunder Season
sections.body: Weaver joined the newly relocated team and appeared in its regular-season backcourt rotation during 2008-09. His offensive impact was modest, but he gained valuable NBA experience as a defensive-minded wing behind developing young guards. The Thunder moved on from him after a limited tenure, and he did not establish himself as a long-term starting partner to Russell Westbrook. The inherited C grade recognizes actual NBA games from a late-draft asset, not a draft right that sat unused forever. Weaver also played professionally overseas later, but those appearances should not be credited as additional Oklahoma City NBA games. The club had traded a future pick for the chance to assess him immediately during the franchises first season in its new city.

sections.heading: Derrick Brown Gave Charlotte Real Forward Minutes
sections.body: Charlotte used its 2009 No. 40 choice on Xavier forward Derrick Brown, who appeared for the Bobcats in the following season and provided athletic reserve minutes. He had a different positional profile from Weaver, making the exchange more about fit and development than an obvious talent mismatch. The Charlotte C grade mirrors the Thunder C, which matches the inherited Even Trade decision. Neither player became an All-Star for the franchise that initially acquired his rights. The pick was not protected into nonconveyance or used to select another named prospect in a later class; it matured on schedule in 2009. Charlotte gained a young forward and Oklahoma City gained a young wing, with both sides obtaining some actual NBA playing contributions. The larger rebuilding success of the Thunder belongs to other roster decisions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte and Oklahoma City both earn C. Charlotte acquired the 2009 No. 40 second-round pick used on Derrick Brown, while the Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise gained Kyle Weaver draft rights. Both players saw NBA rotation minutes, but neither became an enduring leading scorer for his receiving team.

sections.heading: Portland Received Viktor Khryapa Rights in a Draft-Night Exchange
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, Portland acquired the draft rights to Ukrainian forward Viktor Khryapa from New Jersey. The Nets received veteran guard Eddie Gill and cash considerations in exchange. Historical NBA draft-day transaction registers establish that direction, with the rights moving to the Blazers and the player plus money going to the Nets. Khryapa had been selected late in the first round by New Jersey, but the transfer came before he ever took the court in a Nets NBA game. Portland was willing to develop a young forward who could defend and play in transition, while New Jersey wanted immediate roster or salary flexibility. The transaction did not include a later first-round pick or a conditional second-round selection, so the actual return consists of the named guard, rights and cash.

sections.heading: Khryapa Became a Real Portland Rotation Option
sections.body: Khryapa joined Portland and spent portions of two NBA seasons with the club. He could defend different forward positions and contribute rebounding, though he was not a leading scorer in the Blazers offense. His second season provided a longer look at what he could do on a rebuilding team before the franchise traded him to Chicago in a separate 2006 agreement. Portland received actual NBA games from a prospect acquired on draft night, rather than a right that remained permanently overseas. Its inherited C grade reflects development and roster use that fell short of an elite starter. The later Chicago tenure and career with the Russian national team were genuine achievements but are not Portland basketball production from this original deal. The Blazers saw a prospect at the beginning of his NBA development curve.

sections.heading: Eddie Gill and Cash Were a More Limited Nets Return
sections.body: Gill was a veteran point guard used as a depth option by several NBA franchises. His New Jersey role was much smaller than the time Khryapa later spent in Portland, and he did not become a long-running Nets starter. The accompanying cash created economic value immediately, which helps explain why New Jersey might have accepted the agreement rather than keeping the forward prospect. The Nets inherited C+ grade is higher than Portland C, despite the Even Trade winner designation and the more substantial Blazers player minutes. The difference may reflect financial terms, but the original data does not provide a cash figure that could justify a definitive calculation. The narrow verdict should be understood as a historical grade assignment rather than proof that a veteran backup guard outperformed every later Khryapa season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade in the inherited verdict, with New Jersey C+ and Portland C. The Nets gained Eddie Gill and cash while the Trail Blazers obtained Viktor Khryapa rights. Khryapa later gave Portland multiple seasons of developmental forward minutes, whereas Gill was a shorter Nets reserve opportunity. The cash amount is not documented.

sections.heading: Denver Turned Keon Clark Into a Four-Asset Package
sections.body: On January 12, 2001, Denver acquired Kevin Willis, Aleksandar Radojevic, Garth Joseph and a second-round selection from Toronto. The Raptors obtained center Keon Clark, scorer Tracy Murray and rookie Mamadou N’diaye. The second-rounder eventually became the 2001 No. 47 overall (No. 46 among actual selections after a forfeited pick) choice associated with Ousmane Cisse, an asset that requires draft-rights tracing rather than being counted as an immediately signed Nugget. The swap combined veteran depth, young players and a future pick instead of operating as a simple one-for-one center exchange. Denver was rebuilding its frontcourt while Toronto was preparing to compete in the Eastern Conference playoffs with Vince Carter. Each side was trying to cover different needs before the deadline, so the number of incoming contracts should not alone determine the winner.

sections.heading: Toronto Gained an Athletic Center for Its Playoff Push
sections.body: Clark supplied Toronto with frontcourt athleticism and shot-blocking ability. He became a useful member of the 2001 Raptors playoff roster, which reached the Eastern Conference semifinals and narrowly lost to Philadelphia. Murray could provide perimeter offense, and N’diaye offered another developmental center, though their contributions were smaller. The Toronto A+ inherited grade reflects a franchise receiving multiple options while adding a shot blocker for a competitive team. Clark was not a permanent Raptors franchise star; he moved on after a short period. Toronto’s actual benefit was a relevant center during a playoff window, not the sum of all of Clark’s later NBA career appearances. The fact that Toronto made a deeper postseason run after the acquisition is useful context but does not make the trade solely responsible for the team’s success.

sections.heading: Denver Collected Veteran Size and a Future Selection
sections.body: Willis was a long-established rebounding center who could contribute NBA rotation minutes, while Radojevic and Joseph were younger big men with less certain future roles. The Nuggets also held the incoming second-round asset, which offered another avenue for later roster construction. The pick’s connection to Ousmane Cisse is a draft outcome, not automatically a Denver player who logged NBA games. Denver A+ in the inherited evaluation equals Toronto A+, though the canonical winner is Nuggets Win. The equal scores underline that both teams received multiple legitimate types of value. Denver’s roster was not made into a contender by the move, and the package included several speculative elements. Toronto bought shorter-term playoff defense, while Denver spread its return across depth and assets. That difference is a more grounded comparison than treating one organization as having received no return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win according to the inherited headline, although Denver and Toronto both have A+ grades. Denver received Kevin Willis, Aleksandar Radojevic, Garth Joseph and a second-round asset tied to 2001 No. 47 overall (No. 46 among actual selections after a forfeited pick) Ousmane Cisse. Toronto obtained Keon Clark, Tracy Murray and Mamadou N’diaye for an immediate playoff-window frontcourt adjustment.

sections.heading: The Hornets Bought Overseas Rights with a Late Second
sections.body: On June 14, 2001, Charlotte exchanged its 2001 second-round selection with Chicago for the NBA signing rights to Spanish center Roberto Dueñas. The pick became No. 45 overall (sometimes numbered No. 44 when the forfeited pick is excluded), used by the Bulls on forward Sean Lampley. Chicago had held Dueñas’s rights since selecting him in the second round of an earlier draft, but he was playing professionally in Spain rather than in the NBA. Charlotte wanted the opportunity to bring a seven-footer across the Atlantic while preserving other draft assets. Chicago preferred a current selection over keeping an international prospect’s rights indefinitely. No veteran NBA contract was part of the agreement, and neither team obtained a first-round pick. The entire return involved draft and signing rights rather than guaranteed appearances for either side.

sections.heading: Dueñas Did Not Become a Charlotte NBA Center
sections.body: Dueñas had built an established career in European basketball, but that did not translate into regular-season NBA games for the Hornets. Charlotte acquired his contractual rights and the possibility of signing him, not an active center who joined the roster the next week. His European club achievements and Spain appearances were meaningful in their own context but cannot be assigned as Charlotte points, rebounds or playoff starts. The Hornets C grade recognizes a low-cost chance at acquiring a different style of big man while acknowledging there was no realized NBA rotation return. That makes the transaction relatively modest despite the player’s stature and international reputation. The distinction between draft rights and actual playing time is essential: this entry is not a trade in which Charlotte received an established NBA starter.

sections.heading: Chicago Used No. 44 on Sean Lampley
sections.body: The Bulls exercised the incoming No. 45 overall (sometimes numbered No. 44 when the forfeited pick is excluded) pick on California forward Sean Lampley. Being selected gave Chicago a prospect to evaluate, but draft position alone does not guarantee an NBA career, and the transaction did not create an immediate Chicago rotation scorer comparable to the veterans the club needed. The Chicago C inherited grade balances the real second-round opportunity with limited subsequent first-team impact. The original Even Trade wording is consistent with the equal modest grades. Charlotte tried to secure a developed overseas big man without spending a first-rounder; Chicago turned an international right it was not using into another chance at a rookie. Neither franchise emerged with a clearly established long-term NBA player from the swap. The selection’s later rights or professional career should be tracked separately from the cash-free 2001 agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte and Chicago each receive C. Charlotte obtained the NBA rights to Roberto Dueñas, who never became a Hornets regular-season player. Chicago acquired the No. 45 overall (sometimes numbered No. 44 when the forfeited pick is excluded) second-round selection in 2001 and used it on Sean Lampley. Both sides traded speculative signing opportunities rather than established NBA contributors.

sections.heading: Cleveland Acquired Two Players and Draft Rights for Wesley Person
sections.body: On June 26, 2002, Cleveland sent veteran shooting guard Wesley Person to Memphis and acquired Nick Anderson plus the draft rights to Matt Barnes. Memphis had taken Barnes late in the second round that night and was willing to transfer his rights as part of the package. Cleveland was changing its personnel in the period before the franchise selected LeBron James the next summer; Memphis sought outside shooting from a veteran who had spent multiple seasons as a Cavaliers starter. Anderson had been a productive Orlando scorer earlier in his career, but he was near the end of his NBA tenure. The incoming draft rights were a future player option, not an established guard who immediately delivered points for Cleveland. No first-round selection was attached.

sections.heading: Person Gave Memphis an Experienced Perimeter Option
sections.body: Person had averaged double-digit points in most of his Cleveland seasons, and Memphis could use his three-point shooting to complement younger players. His time with the Grizzlies was shorter than his earlier Cleveland stay, but he supplied a veteran NBA scorer in a direct exchange without surrendering a premium draft asset. The inherited Memphis B- grade captures practical short-term playing value, rather than treating the move as a star acquisition. His future performance with other franchises does not belong in Memphis’s return, just as his extensive Cavaliers totals predated the trade. Memphis was still a rebuilding team, so the presence of another veteran shooter did not itself guarantee a playoff berth. The deal gave the club a defined perimeter scoring role at a time when its younger backcourt was developing.

sections.heading: Anderson and Barnes Rights Followed Different Paths
sections.body: Anderson brought experience but did not become a major Cavaliers scoring contributor after the agreement. Barnes’s NBA rights were a speculative investment with more long-term potential, yet his later productive seasons around the league cannot be counted as Cleveland playing time without establishing where and when those rights moved. Cleveland’s inherited B- grade equals the Memphis B-, with a Slight Cavaliers Edge label reflecting a preference for receiving two different possibilities rather than the one veteran. The direct on-court result from Anderson was limited, while the drafted Barnes would ultimately have a long NBA career away from Cleveland. That distinction prevents a common hindsight error: using Barnes’s later championship or playoff achievements as if they had occurred in Cavaliers uniform. Both franchises obtained different kinds of assets without a clearly decisive immediate transformation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Cavaliers Edge in the inherited headline, with B- grades for both Cleveland and Memphis. Cleveland received Nick Anderson and the draft rights to Matt Barnes for Wesley Person. Memphis gained an established veteran perimeter scorer; Cleveland received an aging guard and a young player whose later NBA career developed away from the Cavaliers.

sections.heading: Sacramento Acquired a Future First-Rounder for Dan Dickau
sections.body: On June 26, 2002, Sacramento sent the newly drafted rights to Gonzaga point guard Dan Dickau to Atlanta. The Kings received a future first-round selection that eventually materialized at No. 25 in 2003, associated with Carlos Delfino. The agreement was reached on draft night, before Dickau had played a single NBA regular-season game. Sacramento had an established backcourt with Mike Bibby, making future draft capital more flexible than a rookie whose immediate playing time was uncertain. Atlanta wanted another guard prospect capable of developing as a ball handler and outside shooter. The future first was a substantial asset relative to the second-round rights Sacramento was giving up. Neither party transferred a veteran NBA contract or cash in the recorded deal.

sections.heading: Dickau Was a Limited Rookie Contributor in Atlanta
sections.body: Dickau arrived in Atlanta as a young second-round guard with a strong college shooting reputation. His initial NBA role was smaller than the workload he had carried at Gonzaga, and he never became the franchise’s long-term starting point guard. He later played for other NBA clubs, including an improved scoring season in New Orleans, but those later games should not be credited as Atlanta’s direct trade return. The Hawks D+ inherited grade reflects an unsuccessful attempt to find lasting guard production at the cost of an incoming first-round choice. Dickau was a legitimate NBA prospect and earned professional playing opportunities; the issue was the comparative return from the specific first-round asset surrendered. Atlanta had been rebuilding and could have used that selection in several ways, raising the opportunity cost of the draft-night agreement.

sections.heading: The 2003 First-Round Selection Provided Greater Flexibility
sections.body: The first-round choice linked to the trade became No. 25 in 2003, used on Argentine wing Carlos Delfino. The selected player’s subsequent NBA club history must be traced through the rights holder, because the Kings may have used or moved the pick through a different transaction chain before Delfino signed an NBA contract. What Sacramento secured in 2002 was the actual first-round selection rather than an unexercised conditional second. That gave the franchise a potentially valuable additional rookie or exchange asset while maintaining its strong immediate roster. The Kings A- inherited grade versus Atlanta D+ reflects the asymmetry between a first-round choice and a short-term second-round guard return. Dickau’s later seasons elsewhere did not compensate Atlanta for the long-term draft resource that it relinquished.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento earns A- for a future first-round asset that became the 2003 No. 25 choice associated with Carlos Delfino. Atlanta receives D+ after getting Dan Dickau’s rookie rights, which did not produce a long Hawks starting career. The pick offered Sacramento substantially more future options than Atlanta realized from the second-round guard.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Veteran David Wesley for Three Assets
sections.body: On October 29, 2007, New Jersey acquired veteran guard David Wesley from the New Orleans Hornets franchise. The Hornets received Bernard Robinson, center Mile Ilić and cash considerations. Wesley had enjoyed some of his best NBA seasons earlier with Charlotte and New Orleans, but by 2007 he was close to the end of his career. The Nets were seeking an inexpensive option behind an experienced backcourt led by Jason Kidd and Vince Carter. New Orleans accepted two younger roster opportunities and financial compensation instead of retaining the veteran. The deal was not a one-for-one veteran swap; the cash and two separate players are necessary to reconstruct the true agreement. The inherited date places the transaction before the 2007-08 regular season and both clubs’ transaction ledgers identify the same general exchange.

sections.heading: Wesley Did Not Become a Nets Rotation Regular
sections.body: Wesley did not recreate his earlier Hornets scoring years in New Jersey. His career ended without a meaningful new Nets regular-season campaign, so the return is best viewed as a veteran rights and payroll transaction rather than the acquisition of a reliable reserve scoring season. New Jersey’s C- inherited grade reflects this small realized basketball impact. The Nets had experienced starters in place but needed available younger depth as those players aged; acquiring Wesley did not solve that larger structural problem. Using his former Charlotte Hornets or New Orleans totals as if they had been scored in New Jersey would give readers a misleading sense of trade success. The fact that the Nets were still competitive in the preceding years does not change the limited outcome of this specific October 2007 agreement.

sections.heading: The Hornets Received Cash and Two Player Options
sections.body: Bernard Robinson had appeared as a Charlotte wing and a New Jersey reserve, while Mile Ilić was a young center who had not established an important NBA playing role. New Orleans obtained the ability to evaluate or redirect both players as well as the documented cash consideration. Those assets were not guaranteed long-term starters, and the inherited Pelicans B+ grade might look generous if measured only by later box scores. The economic value and roster flexibility explain some of the grade advantage over New Jersey C-. At this stage the Hornets were preparing to build around Chris Paul and David West, so even modest contract adjustments could be useful. The Pelicans Win wording is supported most clearly by receiving actual assets for Wesley, who did not go on to give the Nets sustained on-court production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. The New Orleans franchise receives B+ for Bernard Robinson, Mile Ilić and cash. New Jersey gets C- after acquiring David Wesley, who did not establish a substantive Nets regular-season role. The Hornets obtained additional roster options instead of holding a guard whose most productive NBA seasons were already over.

sections.heading: The Pistons Obtained Two Picks and Pete Chilcutt for Polynice
sections.body: On February 20, 1994, Detroit traded center Olden Polynice to Sacramento. The Kings sent forward Pete Chilcutt, a 1994 second-round pick and a conditional future first-round selection. The second became No. 48 in 1994, associated with Jevon Crudup. The protected first required a later qualifying draft position and ultimately became No. 17 in 1999, associated with Cal Bowdler. This was a meaningful package of immediate reserve depth and two draft opportunities for a veteran center. The Pistons were rebuilding after their earlier championship era, while Sacramento wanted a more established rebounding center in its rotation. The lottery and protection conditions are crucial, because Detroit did not receive two immediate first-round selections or an unconditional high pick.

sections.heading: Polynice Supplied Sacramento with Real Frontcourt Work
sections.body: Polynice was an experienced NBA center and rebounder, rather than an untested draft prospect. He became a regular Sacramento frontcourt player after the trade and was capable of providing rebounding and physical defense on a club seeking stability. That immediate playing contribution supports the inherited A- Kings grade despite the significant future assets Sacramento gave up. His earlier Los Angeles Clippers and Seattle production cannot be added to his Sacramento contribution, but he did become more than an emergency one-month rental. The Kings wanted a player who could start or cover substantial center minutes, and Polynice supplied that type of role during the years that followed. Whether his playing tenure justified surrendering a protected first is a separate question from whether Sacramento received an NBA-caliber player at all.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Multiple Paths to Replace a Veteran
sections.body: Chilcutt supplied a different frontcourt profile from Polynice, with shooting and reserve size rather than the same rebounding strengths. The 1994 second-rounder became associated with Jevon Crudup, while the conditional first eventually resolved in 1999 as a No. 17 selection linked to Cal Bowdler. Those draft outcomes must be tracked through subsequent rights holders, not mechanically counted as Pistons seasons if Detroit traded or redirected the selections. Detroit A in the inherited grades slightly exceeds Sacramento A-, matching the Pistons Win label. Its advantage rested on receiving a veteran reserve and two future draft assets for a center the club was willing to move. Sacramento obtained a capable interior player, but Detroit preserved more opportunities to rebuild its roster over several years.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit earns A after receiving Pete Chilcutt, a 1994 No. 48 second-round pick connected to Jevon Crudup and a protected future first ultimately tied to 1999 No. 17 Cal Bowdler. Sacramento receives A- for Olden Polynice, who supplied sustained center and rebounding work. The first-round protections are central to the value.

sections.heading: Portland Obtained the Rights to Jason Sasser on Draft Night
sections.body: On June 27, 1996, the Trail Blazers acquired the NBA draft rights to forward Jason Sasser from Sacramento for future considerations. The Kings had taken Sasser in the second round during the previous evening’s draft sequence, giving Portland an opportunity to evaluate another young wing. The exact future considerations are not named in the inherited transaction record, so it would be irresponsible to invent a draft selection, cash amount or player who joined Sacramento. This was an exchange of speculative rights rather than a trade of NBA rotation veterans. Portland wanted to add developmental depth as the franchise continued adjusting after its early-1990s Finals teams, and Sacramento chose flexibility instead of keeping the specific draft selection. The lack of defined consideration limits how firmly the outcome can be graded.

sections.heading: Sasser Never Became a Long-Term Blazers Rotation Player
sections.body: Sasser spent portions of his professional career in and around the NBA, but did not become a reliable long-term starting forward for Portland. He had impressed as a college player at Texas Tech and brought scoring talent to the draft, which explains why the Blazers were willing to acquire his rights. Professional development, however, was uncertain at the end of the second round. His later NBA or overseas accomplishments should be counted only where they actually occurred, not projected backward as guaranteed Portland production. Portland’s inherited C grade recognizes the chance to sign and develop a player at modest cost while acknowledging limited realized NBA playing time for the acquiring franchise. This is a case in which the right to negotiate was more certain than any subsequent box-score return.

sections.heading: Sacramento’s Consideration Is Not Sufficiently Specified
sections.body: The Kings received future considerations, but the source record does not establish a later selection or player that can be securely identified as the result of this trade. The proper editorial treatment is to report the incomplete asset description, not to fill it with assumptions about other Sacramento drafts. The Kings C grade is therefore a modest holding assessment based on a future obligation or transaction flexibility rather than demonstrated player production. Equal C marks and an Even Trade label are defensible because neither side can be shown to have secured an enduring NBA starter from the documented agreement. A future source-led reconciliation should determine what, if anything, the considerations ultimately became before any stronger retrospective winner is adopted. The certainty ends at Sasser’s rights reaching Portland and Sacramento’s promise of later value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Portland and Sacramento each receive C. The Blazers acquired the draft rights to Jason Sasser, who did not become a long-term Portland starter. Sacramento obtained future considerations whose final settlement is not identified in the inherited transaction record. Without a verified downstream asset, neither return justifies a stronger claim.

sections.heading: Denver Collected Eric Washington and a Future Second
sections.body: On June 25, 1997, Denver acquired the rights to guard Eric Washington from Orlando, plus a 1999 second-round draft pick. Orlando received the rights to center Jason Lawson. The later second-round selection became No. 55 in 1999, associated with forward Kris Clack. The agreement was a modest swap of draft rights and a future selection rather than a move that sent an established veteran scorer across the country. Both franchises were looking for inexpensive development options after difficult seasons. Denver chose a guard prospect and another chance to draft, while Orlando favored a young interior player. The 1999 pick requires its own downstream history; acquiring a draft right does not automatically mean the selected player spent an NBA season with the original club.

sections.heading: Washington Offered a Prospect, Not an Immediate Lead Guard
sections.body: Washington came from Alabama after a productive college career, but the transition to the NBA was difficult. He did not become a franchise-defining Denver starting guard, and the Nuggets still faced a difficult rebuilding period. His rights were a real asset, however, and the club could evaluate whether he offered depth behind its established guards. Denver’s inherited C+ grade credits the combination of two developmental opportunities rather than proven scoring from Washington alone. The 1999 second-rounder gave the front office flexibility in a later draft when the roster might have different needs. That additional selection made Denver’s asset position somewhat stronger than the one prospect moved to Orlando. It should not be inflated into a guaranteed 1999 star because the pick was in the late second round.

sections.heading: Lawson Did Not Establish a Lasting Magic Center Role
sections.body: Lawson was a center prospect coming out of Villanova, and Orlando gained his NBA rights instead of giving up an active starting big man. He did not become a lasting Magic first-team contributor. The club’s C- grade reflects an understandable search for inexpensive interior size that did not yield the substantial playing return a young rebuilding organization would hope for. The inherited Even Trade label, despite Denver C+ against Orlando C-, represents a generous neutral conclusion and should not be presented as equal numerical grading. Denver acquired both Washington and another second-round option; Orlando received one center right. Neither side obtained a proven high-level NBA regular, limiting the transaction’s historical impact. The late-pick uncertainty is more important here than either prospect’s college scoring statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade in the inherited verdict, though Denver grades C+ against Orlando C-. Denver received Eric Washington rights and the 1999 No. 55 second-round pick tied to Kris Clack. Orlando acquired the rights to Jason Lawson. None of the prospects became a long-term starting NBA contributor for the acquiring club.

sections.heading: Denver Received Keon Clark’s Rights While Orlando Got a Future First
sections.body: On January 21, 1999, Denver acquired forward Johnny Taylor and the draft rights to center Keon Clark from Orlando. The Magic received a conditional future first-round pick, which eventually became the 2000 No. 10 selection used on Keyon Dooling. The complicated conditions allowed Orlando to choose between specified Denver or Milwaukee draft placements in 1999 or a 2000 Denver selection. That protection structure is an important part of the trade and distinguishes it from a simple center-for-guard swap. Denver was rebuilding and looking to acquire a young defensive big man, while Orlando wanted the chance at a more valuable lottery prospect in a later draft. The trade occurred during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season, so the normal early-season development calendar did not apply.

sections.heading: Clark Developed into a Valuable Denver Shot Blocker
sections.body: Clark eventually gave Denver a real NBA frontcourt player with rebounding and rim protection, rather than an unsigned right that expired. He emerged as one of the more promising defensive centers on the Nuggets roster and went on to play meaningful minutes before a subsequent trade to Toronto in 2001. Johnny Taylor supplied additional wing or forward depth but was not the same kind of core piece. Denver’s inherited A- grade is supported by the development of Clark into a regular NBA player and the franchise’s opportunity to manage that young asset through later transactions. His productive years with Toronto and Sacramento after leaving Denver should not be counted as Nuggets games; they demonstrate his broader potential, not an extra direct Denver return. The original agreement nevertheless secured a center prospect who actually contributed to the Nuggets.

sections.heading: Orlando’s Pick Became the Tenth Selection in 2000
sections.body: The Magic ultimately received an actual first-round choice at No. 10 in 2000, which was associated with Keyon Dooling. Subsequent draft-night rights transfers must be traced before counting Dooling’s later seasons as Orlando playing production. In asset terms, a top-ten first was an impressive return for a player whose Denver value was not yet established. Orlando’s B inherited grade reflects the opportunity to turn prospect rights into higher draft capital. The canonical Even Trade decision, with Denver A- and Orlando B, can be read as a recognition that both obtained substantial assets. Clark offered Denver tangible defense and developmental growth; Orlando converted its part into a premium future selection. Neither franchise could know the later draft placement on the 1999 trade date.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade in the inherited classification, although Denver earns A- and Orlando B. Denver acquired Johnny Taylor and Keon Clark’s rights, gaining a productive young frontcourt player. Orlando secured a conditional first that ultimately became the 2000 No. 10 pick associated with Keyon Dooling. Both returns had genuine future value.

sections.heading: Dallas Swapped Sean Rooks for Eric Murdock and a Draft Pick
sections.body: On June 28, 2000, Dallas sent backup center Sean Rooks to the Los Angeles Clippers. The Mavericks received veteran guard Eric Murdock and a protected 2000 first-round selection that instead became a second-round choice, No. 31, used on Vanderbilt forward Dan Langhi. The protection terms gave Dallas a later pick if the first-round condition failed, and the inherited ledger identifies the No. 31 outcome rather than an additional first. Dallas was reorganizing its rotation around Dirk Nowitzki, Steve Nash and Michael Finley, while the Clippers sought dependable interior size. Neither incoming Dallas asset was an immediate All-Star, and no further player-for-player compensation is listed. The difference between a protected first and the actual conveyed second is crucial to grading this draft-night trade.

sections.heading: Rooks Became a Veteran Clippers Frontcourt Option
sections.body: Rooks was an experienced center who could cover reserve minutes behind younger frontcourt players. His role in Los Angeles was different from a high-volume offensive star, and his Clippers time should be evaluated through team-specific appearances instead of extending the account to his earlier Atlanta and Dallas career. The Clippers were not competing for a championship in 2000-01, but they needed experienced interior bodies while developing young talent. Rooks provided a practical roster option without acquiring a large contract or lottery selection through this agreement. The inherited B- Clippers grade reflects frontcourt usefulness even as the club later made other center acquisitions and adjusted the rotation. His NBA career ended after several more seasons; those later appearances for other teams do not all belong to this trade.

sections.heading: Murdock and No. 31 Offered Dallas Flexibility Rather Than a Star
sections.body: Murdock was a veteran point guard whose best NBA playmaking years came earlier in Milwaukee. Dallas had its primary point guard in Nash, so the incoming veteran offered a different kind of bench insurance. The No. 31 choice became Dan Langhi, a late draft opportunity who did not establish a major Mavericks starting role. The Mavericks’ B- grade equals Los Angeles B-, and the inherited Mavericks Win headline reflects a preference for two assets over one backup center. Dallas was about to become a far more competitive franchise, but that ascent was driven principally by its established stars and other roster decisions, not by treating Murdock or Langhi as a hidden championship centerpiece. This modest swap was about positional options and converting an older center into guard depth and an inexpensive draft chance.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win according to the inherited headline, with B- grades for both Dallas and the Clippers. Dallas received Eric Murdock and the actual 2000 No. 31 second-round selection used on Dan Langhi after the first-round protection condition. Los Angeles received reserve center Sean Rooks. Neither side added an elite long-term scorer.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Lonzo Ball Into a Younger Two-Way Wing
sections.body: On July 6, 2025, Chicago acquired Isaac Okoro from Cleveland in a direct exchange for veteran point guard Lonzo Ball. The Cavaliers announced both sides and explained that they wanted another experienced passer and defender while maintaining their winning core. Ball had returned from a prolonged knee absence in 2024-25, appearing in 35 Bulls games after missing two complete seasons. Chicago instead took on a 24-year-old wing who had been the fifth overall selection in 2020 and already had considerable defensive experience. The agreement did not carry future first-round picks, cash, or an additional third-team player. The teams were exchanging distinct skill sets: Cleveland valued Ball as a secondary creator, while the Bulls wanted greater day-to-day wing availability.

sections.heading: Okoro Actually Started Sixty-Two Bulls Games in 2025-26
sections.body: The immediate Chicago playing return was substantial. Okoro appeared in 63 Bulls games during 2025-26 and started 62, averaging 9.3 points, 2.7 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 26.9 minutes per night. He shot 46.0 percent from the floor, though his 33.0 percent three-point accuracy limited the value of his floor spacing. The club finished 31-51, so his starting job cannot be presented as the main reason for a winning season. His defensive assignments and dependable minutes did give Chicago a real rotation player, however, unlike a trade asset held only as draft rights. The inherited Bulls A- grade reflects that immediate starting role plus Okoro being younger than the outgoing Ball. It is not an argument that he became an offensive star after switching teams.

sections.heading: Cleveland Chose Guard Depth After Ball’s Injury History
sections.body: Ball brought size, advanced passing and the ability to defend guards, but his long history of knee issues made the acquisition a health-dependent gamble. Cleveland had a more established competitive roster than Chicago and was trying to reinforce secondary ball handling rather than develop another young starter. The Cavaliers C inherited grade acknowledges what a healthy Ball could supply without overstating his Cleveland playing output or importing his New Orleans years. The comparison with Okoro must consider Chicago getting 62 starts in the very next season. The Cavaliers accepted more availability uncertainty for a veteran whose playmaking fit their backcourt. This was an exchange of roles with an observable first-year Chicago workload rather than a cash-only salary maneuver.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A- because Isaac Okoro started 62 of 63 games in 2025-26, averaging 9.3 points and 2.7 rebounds. Cleveland receives C for Lonzo Ball, whose value as a veteran passer came with the injury concerns that limited his prior Chicago availability.

sections.heading: Detroit Targeted Duncan Robinson in a One-for-One Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: On July 7, 2025, Detroit announced that it had acquired veteran shooter Duncan Robinson from Miami through a sign-and-trade, sending forward Simone Fontecchio to the Heat. The Pistons were strengthening outside shooting for a young group around Cade Cunningham, while Miami needed to reset its wing contracts and lineup. The official Detroit release confirms that the agreed trade was a direct exchange of those two players with no first-round choice involved. Robinson was an established long-range threat who had played more than four hundred games for Miami, including two NBA Finals runs. Fontecchio was a capable floor spacer but had not occupied the same sustained specialist role for Detroit. The difference in offensive usage was a concrete reason for the trade.

sections.heading: Robinson Delivered an Efficient Full Pistons Season
sections.body: Robinson appeared in 77 Pistons games during 2025-26, averaging 12.2 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.1 assists. His 41.0 percent three-point shooting gave Detroit an efficient source of perimeter offense across a nearly complete season. The career-best years Robinson had in Miami cannot be counted again as Pistons production, but these 77 appearances establish his direct value from the 2025 agreement. He was not acquired to become the main on-ball scorer alongside Cunningham. Instead, his movement and shooting required opposing defenses to track him off the ball, creating spacing within an offense with multiple creators. The inherited Pistons B grade reflects acquiring that distinct, repeatable function rather than a projected All-Star transformation. Detroit received the more heavily used long-range specialist from the two-player swap.

sections.heading: Fontecchio Supplied Miami With a Different Contract and Role
sections.body: Fontecchio had appeared in 91 Detroit games across his previous two seasons, with nine starts and averages of 7.6 points and 3.1 rebounds according to the trade release. Those statistics are his Pistons record, not the production Miami received after the move. The Heat acquired a forward who could defend across positions and shoot at a moderate volume while changing their payroll structure. Their B- inherited grade recognizes a usable NBA player and contract flexibility, but not an established replacement for Robinson as a proven high-volume shooter. Detroit benefited from the clearer offensive fit, while Miami pursued a different salary and supporting-frontcourt arrangement. Because no pick was involved, there is no future prospect to inflate either side’s return. The first posttrade season provides evidence of Robinson’s practical value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit earns B for Duncan Robinson, who played 77 games at 12.2 points while hitting 41.0 percent of his threes in 2025-26. Miami receives B- for Simone Fontecchio, a versatile forward whose role and contract offered a different type of roster benefit.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Acquired Porter and a 2032 Unprotected First
sections.body: Denver finalized a July 2025 exchange sending Michael Porter Jr. and its unprotected 2032 first-round selection to Brooklyn for Cameron Johnson. Official announcements from both franchises establish the exact assets and explain their separate objectives. The Nuggets wanted a more flexible lineup around Nikola Jokić, with Johnson offering dependable shooting and a different contract trajectory. Brooklyn acquired a championship-experienced forward still in his twenties alongside a premium distant draft option. Porter had been a starting scorer during Denver’s 2023 title season, so parting with him was more than a minor salary adjustment. The first-round pick is unprotected, making the long-term cost materially different from a heavily conditional second-round prospect or cash compensation.

sections.heading: Porter Expanded Into a Brooklyn Lead-Scoring Role
sections.body: In 2025-26 Porter started all 52 Brooklyn games he played, averaging 24.2 points, 7.1 rebounds and 3.0 assists. His scoring role grew markedly from his 18.2 points in 77 Denver starts during the previous season. He became a main half-court offensive option rather than one of several finishers beside Jokić and Jamal Murray. His 36.3 percent three-point shooting was lower than in some Denver seasons, but his larger shot volume demonstrated what Brooklyn could ask him to do. The Nets also retained the unprotected 2032 first-round choice, whose eventual value remains unknown. The inherited Nets A+ grade credits both a productive immediate scorer and the flexibility of a future premium pick without claiming to know the player the selection will eventually become.

sections.heading: Johnson Shot Efficiently but Had a Smaller Denver Workload
sections.body: Cameron Johnson appeared in 54 Denver games during 2025-26, averaging 12.2 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists while shooting 43.0 percent from beyond the arc. That is legitimate starting-caliber spacing, not a failed acquisition. Denver went 54-28 in the regular season, although that record reflects contributions from Jokić and the entire roster rather than the trade alone. The Nuggets A- grade recognizes Johnson’s offensive efficiency and roster fit. The higher Brooklyn A+ reflects Porter’s 24.2-point season and the added unprotected draft asset. Future medical availability and the 2032 draft result could change a longer-term verdict, but the first season already gives both clubs measurable, distinct returns. Denver did not receive the outgoing first back as part of this deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A+ after Michael Porter Jr. scored 24.2 points in 52 starts during 2025-26 and the club acquired an unprotected 2032 first-round pick. Denver receives A- for Cameron Johnson, who averaged 12.2 points and shot 43.0 percent from three in 54 games.

sections.heading: Charlotte Accepted Connaughton and Two Future Seconds for Micić
sections.body: On July 6, 2025, the Charlotte Hornets obtained Pat Connaughton and second-round selections in 2031 and 2032 from Milwaukee. The Bucks received guard Vasilije Micić. The NBA official offseason trade tracker confirms all three Charlotte assets, so the agreement should not be portrayed as a straight guard-for-guard swap. Charlotte was taking a veteran role player on a declining usage trajectory while recovering two opportunities to draft or trade younger players several years away. Milwaukee valued the possibility of using Micić as another experienced ball handler or reorganizing the contract. Connaughton had played important minutes on the Bucks 2021 title team, but those earlier championship appearances are not Charlotte games. The future second-round picks have real option value even though their eventual selections cannot yet be identified.

sections.heading: Connaughton Played Forty-Two Charlotte Games in 2025-26
sections.body: Connaughton appeared in 42 Hornets regular-season games in 2025-26, with no starts and an average of 2.6 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.4 assists. He shot 40.4 percent from three, providing a bench spacing option in limited minutes. His role was clearly smaller than the one he held in Milwaukee earlier in his career, which makes the two draft choices particularly important in evaluating what Charlotte received. The club could use him as a veteran in practices and occasional small rotation assignments without expecting him to be a high-volume scorer. The inherited Charlotte C+ grade credits usable depth plus future picks, not a 2021-level production claim. The Hornets also had multiple younger guards competing for minutes, so the reserve role fit their roster development needs.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Immediate Return Was an Experienced Point Guard Option
sections.body: Micić had previously played in Oklahoma City, Charlotte and Phoenix, with European championship experience before joining the NBA. Milwaukee acquired that ball-handling résumé but did not receive Charlotte’s 2031 or 2032 draft choices. The Bucks C grade is based on the option to use or redirect a guard contract, rather than a guaranteed future lottery pick. There is no basis to credit Milwaukee with Connaughton’s former Bucks title-season games once it traded him away. The two distant seconds offer Charlotte multiple possibilities that cannot yet be evaluated through a realized player outcome. A narrow Charlotte preference is justified from the asset quantity and 42 direct appearances, while uncertainty about the distant picks prevents claiming that the agreement has already produced two new NBA rotation players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte earns C+ for Pat Connaughton, who logged 42 games with 2.6 points per game in 2025-26, plus 2031 and 2032 second-round selections. Milwaukee gets C for Vasilije Micić and the opportunity to change its backcourt contracts. Neither future pick has a known NBA player outcome.

sections.heading: Charlotte Swapped Nurkić for Sexton and a Second
sections.body: The Hornets acquired Collin Sexton and a 2030 second-round pick from Utah in late June 2025, while the Jazz received center Jusuf Nurkić. The NBA offseason transaction tracker and both team announcements confirm the exchange. Charlotte was adding a quicker scoring guard for a roster built around LaMelo Ball and young wings; Utah wanted a more experienced big man to support its frontcourt. Nurkić had arrived in Charlotte in another February 2025 trade with Phoenix, so moving him a few months later was part of a broader sequence rather than his first change of team that year. The second-round draft asset belonged to Charlotte after this swap and is not yet associated with a selected NBA player. There was no incoming first-round pick.

sections.heading: Sexton Supplied Real Guard Offense Before Another Move
sections.body: Sexton played 42 Charlotte games during 2025-26, including 12 starts, and averaged 14.2 points with 3.7 assists in 22.3 minutes. Those were meaningful offensive contributions as another ball handler and perimeter scorer, even though he was not the franchise’s lead creator. The team finished the regular season 44-38, an improvement in which many young players also participated. Sexton later appeared for Chicago in the same season, so that separate stint must not be added to his Hornets production. Charlotte’s B+ inherited grade credits scoring production while also recognizing the extra 2030 pick. The direct return was not merely the nominal value of a future selection, because Sexton played a sizable role before Charlotte reconfigured its roster again. His efficiency and bench scoring were the immediate benefits.

sections.heading: Utah Received a Veteran Center Instead of a Second Guard
sections.body: Nurkić offered rebounding, size and passing from the center position, making him a different asset from Sexton’s quick guard scoring. Utah could use him alongside younger forwards while reshuffling its frontcourt rotation. The Jazz B- inherited grade reflects a genuine veteran NBA center rather than an empty salary slot. But Utah also surrendered the future second-round pick that Charlotte retained, creating a cost beyond the player-for-player comparison. The 2030 selection remains unresolved and should not be credited with a future prospect’s statistics. The inherited Charlotte Win decision accounts for receiving both a usable scorer and draft optionality, while Utah acquired a traditional center better suited to its immediate needs. The evaluation should compare the club-specific 2025-26 play rather than attributing Nurkić’s past Portland and Phoenix numbers to Utah.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B+ after receiving Collin Sexton, who scored 14.2 points with 3.7 assists across 42 Charlotte games in 2025-26, plus a 2030 second-round selection. Utah receives B- for Jusuf Nurkić, a veteran center with a different role, while giving up the pick.

sections.heading: The Grimes-Martin Exchange Was Amended After a Physical Review
sections.body: On February 4, 2025, Dallas and Philadelphia agreed to trade Caleb Martin to the Mavericks for Quentin Grimes and a 2025 second-round pick. The agreement changed after medical review: Philadelphia also sent its own 2030 second-round selection to Dallas as an additional piece, according to a February 6 report from NBC Sports Philadelphia. The 2025 second eventually became No. 35, used on Johni Broome. This detail matters because the initial NBA transaction tracker does not mention the subsequent 2030 amendment, while the final canonical trade does. Dallas wanted playoff-tested forward defense shortly after its Luka Dončić blockbuster, and Philadelphia sought a younger shooting guard who could have a bigger role. The exchange involved two real NBA players and selections going in both directions.

sections.heading: Grimes Became a High-Usage Sixers Scorer Immediately
sections.body: The 76ers official October 2025 announcement confirms that Grimes averaged 21.9 points, 5.2 rebounds and 4.5 assists over 28 Philadelphia games after the move, starting 25. He made at least 20 points in sixteen of those contests, a dramatic change from his lower-usage Dallas role. The club also obtained the 2025 No. 35 selection used on Johni Broome, a separate future asset that should not be credited with points before the rookie played. The Sixers B+ inherited grade reflects a young perimeter scorer producing large numbers quickly and an additional draft opportunity. Philadelphia did not receive a finished All-Star franchise career from Grimes in February, but the direct posttrade box scores were strong evidence that the deal benefited its rotation.

sections.heading: Martin Was an Injury-Affected Dallas Reserve
sections.body: Martin was recovering from a right hip sprain when the teams revisited the trade terms. In the rest of 2024-25 he played 14 Dallas games with no starts, averaging 9.8 points and 5.4 rebounds per 36 minutes, not per game. His actual team-specific per-game scoring was more limited because his minutes were restricted. During 2025-26 he appeared in 58 Dallas regular-season games, including twelve starts, providing some defensive-forward depth without matching Grimes’s initial 21.9-point Philadelphia burst. Dallas also received the 2030 second-round choice through the amendment, so its return was not solely Martin’s court time. The inherited Dallas D+ grade reflects the difference in immediate production and the health-related uncertainty, weighed against the possibility that Martin could help in tougher matchups. The 2030 pick remains a future opportunity rather than a known NBA player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B+ after Quentin Grimes averaged 21.9 points in 28 games and the club obtained the 2025 No. 35 second-round choice. Dallas receives D+ for Caleb Martin and a 2030 second-rounder added after a medical review; Martin played 14 Dallas games during the remainder of 2024-25.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired a Traditional Backup Center for Dario Šarić
sections.body: On July 13, 2025, Denver completed a one-for-one trade sending forward-center Dario Šarić to Sacramento for Jonas Valančiūnas. Both franchises announced the terms publicly, with no draft picks or cash listed in the final agreement. Denver had just completed other moves around Nikola Jokić, including the Cam Johnson trade, and wanted an experienced center who could handle interior work while the star rested. Valančiūnas had played 81 games split between Washington and Sacramento in 2024-25, averaging 10.4 points and 7.7 rebounds across both clubs. Šarić had appeared in only sixteen Nuggets games, making him a smaller rotation loss. The clubs were choosing between different big-man specialties rather than exchanging an emerging lottery prospect for an established All-Star.

sections.heading: Valančiūnas Actually Supplied Sixty-Five Nuggets Games
sections.body: The Lithuanian center played 65 Denver games during 2025-26 with six starts, averaging 8.7 points, 5.1 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 13.4 minutes. His 58.2 percent field-goal shooting reflected the value of efficient interior finishing. Denver’s official preview of the acquisition positioned him as the likely backup to Jokić, with occasional double-big combinations possible. His actual minutes support that contingency-center use rather than a claim that he displaced the league’s premier offensive center. The Nuggets reached 54 regular-season wins that year, but a team result involving Jokić, Jamal Murray and the rest of the roster cannot all be assigned to a backup acquisition. Denver’s C+ inherited grade recognizes meaningful reserve size and rebounding with limited long-term impact.

sections.heading: Sacramento Chose the Different Contract and Offensive Profile
sections.body: Šarić had played for Philadelphia, Phoenix, Golden State and several other clubs, and his appeal to Sacramento was frontcourt shooting and passing rather than the low-post scoring associated with Valančiūnas. The Kings announced that he had 493 career NBA appearances and averages of 10.4 points and 5.3 rebounds prior to arrival, but those are career numbers and should not be counted as new Sacramento output. Their inherited A- grade and Kings Win verdict favor the roster or salary flexibility gained, although the confirmed 65 Denver games make that historical assessment worth further source-led review. Neither club obtained another first-round asset in this exchange. The basketball comparison is limited to an experienced backup center in Denver against a floor-spacing forward sent to Sacramento, with any later rights or roster moves evaluated independently.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win in the inherited A- for Sacramento versus C+ for Denver grading. The Kings obtained Dario Šarić in exchange for Jonas Valančiūnas, who provided 65 Nuggets games with 8.7 points and 5.1 rebounds in 2025-26. The confirmed Denver center contribution warrants consideration in future grade reviews.
